10 dead, 64 injured in Mexico fireworks explosion at church festival
The cause of the blast next to the Nuestra Senora de la Luz church in Temascalcingo has not been determined. An investigation is under way
Pyrotechnic material exploded during the festival for a patron saint in a town in Mexico State, collapsing a wall, killing at least 10 people and injuring another 64, Mexican authorities said.
The explosion happened on Saturday night next to the Nuestra Senora de la Luz church in Temascalcingo, a municipality in central Mexico with 66,000 residents. Hundreds of them were preparing to watch a fireworks display that is part of a religious festival when the blast happened.
The municipality is about 160km (100 miles) northwest of Mexico City.
The cause of the explosion has not been determined and the Mexico State Attorney General’s Office has opened an investigation.
A local bishop said two priests are among the injured.
A video on social media shows the aftermath of the blast, with dozens of people walking through smoke and debris in search of survivors.

Amazon cargo plane crashes, bursts into flames at Miami airport after overshooting runway
All runways were closed after the incident at Miami International Airport, one of the nation’s busiest. It was not known if anyone was hurt
An Amazon cargo plane barrelled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, striking multiple vehicles and bursting into flames in a crash that sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky and forced the closure of all runways at one of the nation’s busiest airports.
More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the crash, arriving to find the aircraft on fire as crews worked to extinguish the flames and assess patients. Officials had not yet released information on injuries or deaths.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said the aircraft overran the runway at around 2pm local time after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue officials said the plane struck multiple vehicles after leaving the runway.
Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said the FAA was sending investigators and issued a full ground stop at Miami International as emergency crews responded.
The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two articulated lorries, according to images from the scene. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.
All runways and taxiways were closed, an airport spokesperson said. About 250 flights were delayed at the airport as of late afternoon on Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.

Isro will never be privatised, its role won't be diminished: Space Agency &amp; INSPACe chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
20:23:39 UTC
05:23:39 KST

Isro dismisses privatisation speculation, says role will only strengthen
NEW DELHI: Allaying fears of some of its staff that the organisation will be privatised and its role reduced to an R&D lab, Isro on Sunday dismissed “speculations and misinformation” about any diminution of its role, calling such reports “baseless and incorrect”. “We wish to categorically state that Isro will neither be privatised nor will its importance be diminished,” the space agency said.Isro further said it “will continue to remain India’s principal institution for advanced space research and technology development, national and strategic missions, space science and exploration, and critical and frontier space capabilities”.Space promoter and regulator Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (INSPACe) chairman Pawan Goenka also said on Sunday that Isro “will remain the bedrock of Indian space sector” and it will remain at the core of India’s space programme leading frontier research and the next generation of national space programmes like space station and crewed lunar mission.In a long statement, the space agency said, “Participation of the private sector in space is not about reducing its role. It is about enabling Isro to focus even more strongly on the next generation of India’s space programme, while industry scales mature technologies and capabilities. What is changing is not the importance of Isro, but the scale and structure of India’s space ecosystem.”“The transition is therefore towards an Isro-led national space ecosystem,” the agency said.
The agency also said that its “role will progressively strengthen in areas where its scientific expertise matters most: frontier R&D, advanced technologies, human spaceflight, next-generation launch systems, deep-space and planetary missions and strategic national capabilities. It will continue developing cutting-edge technologies, including advanced payloads for communication, navigation and Earth observation, sensors, propulsion systems and other critical technologies.”After nine Isro employee associations have sought a “written clarity” from the agency chairman on the private sector shift, Goenka in a post on X late on Sunday evening said, “Let me say it unequivocally: Isro' s role is by no means diminishing. It will remain the bedrock of the Indian space sector.On scaling up the production of rockets and satellites in India, the INSPACe director declared that the country has set an “ambitious target of 50 launches a year by 2030”. “A goal of this scale cannot be achieved by one organisation alone. Govt and private industry have to build this future together,” he said.Explaining the reasons for opening up the sector, the INSPACe chairman said, Goenka said, “The reforms since 2020 are about expanding India’s overall space ecosystem. IN-SPACe will facilitate and authorise greater non-govt participation, while NSIL will help commercialise mature capabilities.”He said the idea of space reforms is to “let industry increasingly manufacture and scale mature launch vehicles, satellites and other systems, while Isro focuses on what it is uniquely placed to do: advanced R&D, scientific missions, strategic missions, new technologies, and infrastructure that is too complex for the private sector to develop on its own”.Assuring Isro staff that they are going to handle big projects and responsibilities, Goenka said, “Isro will remain at the core of India’s space programme leading frontier research and the next generation of national missions, including the Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035, an Indian crewed mission to the Moon by 2040, next-generation launch systems, and sustained lunar and planetary exploration.” Goenka said, “The direction is not a smaller Isro. It is a larger Indian space ecosystem, with Isro pushing the technological frontier.Congratulating Isro for the recent GSLV MK II successful launch, Goenka, in a post on X on Sunday said, “EOS-05 is a major achievement by Isro, and this is just the beginning.”
On the growing space sector in the country, the INSPACe regulator said, “From barely a handful of space startups five years ago, India today has over 450. Indian private industry has already flown a rocket to orbit (while referring to Skyroot’s Vikram-1 rocket’s successful launch on July 18). Isro’s research will continue to push the frontiers of what is possible. Private industry must translate that momentum into manufacturing at scale: more rockets, more satellites, more launch capacity and new technologies. That is how we will build a complete space ecosystem and create the capacity to match our ambition.”He said the “opportunity before us is immense: build in India, launch from India and serve the world from India. We are well on our way to taking India’s space sector to a new orbit, figuratively and literally.”

Details

Conversations are simply conversations, just as a photo of a safe with money is merely a photo of a safe with money and has nothing to do either with me or with the prosecutor’s office; according to the lawyers, it is simply a photograph from another criminal proceeding
He also commented on information regarding his travels and his family’s household matters.
Any expenses were incurred exclusively within the framework of the current legislation and my declared income, without any violations. As for obtaining a U.S. visa and purchasing a laptop: my wife prepared the documents and obtained the visa independently, and she does not have a new laptop! Regarding the 280-square-meter house in which our family lives under a lease: we chose it back in winter, but it required finishing work and equipment setup. It was in this context that the work of the contractors, the alarm system, and household appliances were discussed. We moved into the house on May 1, 2026. My permanent place of residence will be declared in accordance with the law
He added that his position does not exempt him from scrutiny, but neither does it cancel the requirement to prove accusations with facts.
Recall

Fireworks blast in Mexico kills at least 10
MEXICO CITY - Fireworks stored inside a church in Mexico detonated during a village festival, killing at least 10 people, official said Sept 6.
More than 60 were injured in the accident on the night of Sept 5 in the town of Santa Maria Canchesda in central Mexico, the local government said.
Video broadcast by news outlets showed the huge blast came as people stood outside the church celebrating and enacting a ritual in which a bull made of straw and fitted with fireworks is burned and carried around town.
The explosion knocked down walls of buildings and ignited a fire in the town square, prompting people to flee in panic, the video showed.
Some people were trapped under the debris of fallen buildings, news reports said. AFP

Ukraine cannot be settled like a business deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
20:11:19 UTC
05:11:19 KST

Ukraine cannot be settled like a business deal
Diplomatic efforts to end an acute and bloody armed conflict should always be welcomed and the persistence of Donald Trump’s administration, which has pursued this goal for more than a year and a half, also deserves recognition, even if the results so far can hardly be called outstanding.
At the very least, the White House remains the only actor in the West both attempting to change the situation and possessing significant leverage over it. Trump and his closest associates probably do genuinely want the war to end as its continuation distracts Washington from foreign policy priorities they regard as more important. But why, then, does Trump’s diplomatic initiative keep going round in circles, with each new attempt ending in another disappointment?
Trump and his principal envoys tend to approach the conflict as an extraordinarily difficult but essentially technical problem, as a puzzle to be solved in isolation from the wider international system. This reflects the worldview of the current White House, where international affairs are a collection of practical problems to be resolved in ways that strengthen America’s position, preferably with some commercial benefit attached. Given the professional backgrounds of the president and his two principal intermediaries, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, this is hardly surprising.
Such an approach can be useful as an instrument, but it becomes less useful when it substitutes for an understanding of the processes that produced the conflict in the first place and, to use the Russian formulation, its root causes. Any durable settlement requires some understanding of what must change in relations between the major powers if similar confrontations are to be avoided.
Trump repeatedly insists that the war would never have begun had he been president in 2022 with the implication that Joe Biden and the Democrats were simply too incompetent to prevent it. Trump has occasionally acknowledged that NATO’s long expansion eastward contributed to the crisis, but he generally shows little interest in the broader military and political processes behind it.
Yet American and NATO policy towards Ukraine wasn’t created by one administration or a handful of officials in Washington and Brussels, rather it developed over decades from a particular conception of Western strategic interests. The crisis that entered its most acute phase in 2022 was, from Moscow’s perspective, the culmination of processes underway since the end of the Cold War.
This helps explain why Washington continues to underestimate how much the outcome matters to the principal participants. For both Russia and Ukraine, too much is at stake for the conflict to be settled through the kind of transaction Trump instinctively favors, given their interests are obviously opposed, but both regard the outcome as fateful. Western Europe, having invested heavily in Ukraine’s cause, also has a direct political stake in the result, so every new attempt by Washington’s two brokers therefore encounters the same obstacle in that none of the parties sees this as simply another deal.
There’s another contradiction in the American position because Washington wishes to become the principal mediator in a conflict whose continuation it has materially supported.The US position has certainly changed under Trump as Washington’s previous fixation on Ukraine has diminished considerably. Trump would prefer America to step back while retaining decisive influence over what happens next, but that is precisely where the difficulty begins.
Transferring the financial burden, political responsibility and risks to the Western Europeans while continuing to dictate the terms requires a degree of obedience from junior partners that Washington can no longer guarantee. EU governments and Kiev have also learnt how to deal with this unconventional president and when they can’t persuade him, they have become increasingly adept at circumventing his pressure.
The one American instrument against which there would be little defence is a complete cessation of military support, but Trump is unlikely to take that step, even if he were personally inclined to do so because facilitating an outright Russian victory isn’t his objective. He may care less than his predecessor about the precise shape of the eventual settlement, but a complete Ukrainian defeat would be another matter. Nor would abandoning Ukraine enjoy much support across the American political establishment, where there is virtually no constituency for a fundamental rapprochement with Russia.
The White House therefore doesn’t envisage the radical change in American policy that would be necessary to transform the conflict, but without one, events tend to return to their previous course as a prolonged and extremely fierce confrontation whose duration nobody can confidently predict.
In such a confrontation, those fighting the war and bearing its risks ultimately matter more than mediators or outside sponsors. None of this means Witkoff and Kushner’s shuttle diplomacy is pointless, given communication between adversaries is indispensable, and the present infrastructure for official dialogue remains inadequate. Also, informal channels can help restore understanding where formal diplomacy has broken down, but informal diplomacy has limits.
Friends and business associates may establish contacts and discover areas in which compromise is conceivable, but they don’t themselves make peace. The shuttle diplomacy of a presidential son-in-law and a trusted business partner may eventually serve as a catalyst for serious negotiations, however, if that moment comes, the settlement will have to be negotiated by officials and institutions possessing state legitimacy and the power to implement what they sign. Personal connections can open the door, but they can’t, by themselves, end a war.
This article was first published by Russia in Global Affairs, translated and edited by RT.

Swans show what 'Bloods' culture is supposed to look like in Brisbane boilover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
20:07:07 UTC
05:07:07 KST

analysis
Swans show exactly what 'Bloods' culture is supposed to look like in Brisbane boilover
When Sydney chairman Andrew Pridham declared his side's premiership hopes "torpedoed" after suspending five players, he was right.
Preparing for a finals campaign is a delicate exercise. A little shift here or there can have major impacts. The less things change, the better.
At least, that is what conventional wisdom says.
Last year, Adelaide's excellent home-and-away season was detonated by Izak Rankine's suspension for a homophobic slur on the eve of the finals.
Rankine's actions drew a dark cloud over the entire football club, and without him on the field in the finals, the Crows unsurprisingly limped out in straight sets.
Winning a final with five of your first-choice players sidelined? That seemed like mission impossible for the Swans.
A lot has been made of Sydney's famed "Bloods" culture in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal. What is it? What is it supposed to look like? Is it real or just a PR myth?
While the club rightly admitted the culture was not what it once was off the field, on the field there appears to be little sign of slippage.
With Sydney decimated by the suspensions, the Swans appeared to be their rivals' easy ticket to a deep September run, the helpless carcass hungry animals in an African savanna would feast upon.
Brisbane, by virtue of a slight percentage edge over Hawthorn, had the apparent gift of facing the Swans in one qualifying final while the Hawks looked doomed as they headed to Perth to take on Fremantle in the other. How quickly things can change over one weekend.
Sydney has been one of the AFL's model clubs over the past two decades as a picture of professionalism from the top down, and performances like the one against Brisbane remind you exactly why the Swans have been revered for so long.
Turn on a Swans game, and you know what you're getting. Regardless of who is in the line-up or who is in the coaches' box, Sydney shows up with a baseline of effort and intensity, backed by a relentless never-say-die attitude.
All of these traits make up Sydney's true "Bloods" culture on the field.
If you wanted an example of what it looks like, the culture was on full display as Sydney eviscerated the two-time reigning premiers in front of an SCG crowd that was as raucous as it has ever been.
The louder the crowd got, the better the Swans played. The better the Swans played, the louder they got. The crowd and the players worked hand in hand like a beautiful symphony, and the tidal wave they created swallowed Brisbane up entirely.
It is hard to imagine an 18-5 team flying under the radar, but that is exactly what Sydney has done so far this season, right up until the Pullman Hotel scandal.
While the AFL world was consumed by Fremantle's leap from a cute team to a bona fide premiership threat and Brisbane's bid to threepeat, Sydney quietly ticked along in the background to the best home-and-away season in its history.
What Sydney couldn't recoup in terms of talent in the absence of Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — arguably three of its top six players by any metric — it made up for with sheer, unadulterated hard work against Brisbane.
That is not to say the Swans are a team bereft of star power in the absence of the suspended five.
In Charlie Curnow, Sydney still has the AFL's most terrifying key forward, in the metronomic Brodie Grundy, it still has arguably the best big man on his day in the non-Max Gawn division, in Errol Gulden, it has a Rolls-Royce of a midfielder capable of being the lead actor in any team's engine room, and in the incandescent Tom Papley, it has a small forward that can bend the energy of a match like no other.
It is no surprise that all of these guys, as well as many others, were excellent in the win over Brisbane.
"The two weeks of training up to that point, we trained the house down," Papley told Nine's Sunday Footy Show about the lead-up to the Lions game.
"That's the best we've trained all season. The drills we did were all about pressure, closing space, chasing, tackling, and surging the ball forward, and we trained so well and came together on game day.
"I'm so proud of the boys. It was amazing.
"There were board members in the rooms after the game saying it was the best win in the club's history apart from the premierships.
"The job's not done yet, but the desire and passion we played with … inside the four walls we believed and that's what we kept doing."
Sydney has played in, and won, bigger games in its history. It will continue to do so going forward as well.
But with the context of everything that has happened in the lead-up to this one, and then the Callum Mills injury sprinkled over the top as an additional bit of nightmare fuel, Sydney will have to go a long way to find a performance it is prouder of.
The Swans still face an uphill task to win this year's flag, even with a home preliminary final to come in a fortnight.
As the Swans have experienced in their past four Grand Final appearances since their last premiership in 2012, even the best-laid plans with a perfect lead-up can go up in smoke on the final day of the season.
But for one day at least, the Swans showed everyone just exactly what "Bloods" culture is supposed to look like.

Amazon cargo plane overshoots runway at Miami airport, striking vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Amazon cargo plane overshoots runway at Miami airport, striking vehicles
An Amazon cargo plane overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Sept 6, shutting down the airport’s runways and taxiways and prompting an emergency response.
The Boeing 767-300, operated by 21 Air as Prime Air Flight 7598, overshot the runway around 2pm after arriving from Luis Munoz Marin International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
The plane struck multiple vehicles near the airport and emergency units were assessing patients, according to a post on X from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, which reported heavy flames and smoke when it responded to the incident.
“Prime Air Flight 7598 overran Miami International Airport’s diagonal runway and is disabled at the north-west end of the airport,” Indira Almeida-Pardillo, a spokesperson for Miami International Airport, said in a statement. She said all runways and taxiways were closed as of 3pm and a ground stop was in effect.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue responded to the scene, Almeida-Pardillo said.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned of significant delays and possible cancellations in a post on X.
21 Air, a Miami-based cargo airline, began operating Boeing 767-300 freighters on behalf of Amazon in 2024.
Amazon’s in-house cargo airline has tilted its focus to larger aircraft that can handle longer distances and bulk shipping, with the 767 model that crashed in Miami now accounting for the biggest portion of its fleet. Amazon Prime also has 10 Airbus A330-300 freighters, as well as smaller narrow-body 737s for regional routes.
Representatives for 21 Air and Amazon didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
The FAA said it will investigate the incident.
While the circumstances of the accident remain unknown, the crash stands to be the worst cargo-related incident since UPS Airlines Flight 2976 was destroyed on Nov 4, 2025, after it impacted the ground shortly after takeoff at Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport in Kentucky, killing the 3 crew members aboard the airplane and 11 people on the ground.
The aircraft involved in the crash was more than 32 years old, having first flown June 1994. Over the decades, it changed hands, including operations for Air Europa, Kenya Airways and Atlas Air, a cargo specialist, after being converted into a cargo aircraft in 2016, according to data compiled by the Planespotters website.
The Boeing 767 is no longer in production as a commercial aircraft but still widely flown. The manufacturer still makes the plane in low numbers as military refuelling planes. BLOOMBERG

Ukrainian intelligence warns of Russian missile buildup and potential provocations against NATO
The Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine (FISU) reported this on Facebook, according to Ukrinform.
The parties discussed Russia’s strategic plans and coordination of international efforts to pressure the aggressor state to end the war.
Particular attention was paid to the Kremlin’s plans for the fall and winter, primarily regarding an increase in ballistic strikes against Ukraine’s critical infrastructure and provocations against European NATO members.
The FISU said the Russians had accumulated around 400 hypersonic missiles of various types for the purpose and had deployed additional launchers in the border regions of Bryansk, Kursk, and Voronezh.
The meeting also addressed the potential capacity of Russia’s military-industrial complex to produce around 300 ballistic missiles by the end of the year.
The participants noted that one of the problems hampering the Kremlin’s ability to maintain its production capacity is that around 60% of the enterprises involved in the manufacturing process are under international sanctions.
The foreign intelligence team raised the issue of measures needed to disrupt Russia’s plans to produce ballistic missiles. Particular emphasis was placed on urgently imposing sanctions on at least 55 enterprises and companies involved in supplying electronic components and machine tools, as well as conducting financial transactions for the benefit of Russia’s military-industrial complex.
As Ukrinform reported, Prime Minister of Ukraine Sergii Koretskyi discussed Ukraine’s financial needs for this and next year with advisers to the leaders of Germany, the United Kingdom, and France.

Kushner refrains from saying is US will toughen pressure on Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
20:03:28 UTC
05:03:28 KST

WASHINGTON, September 6. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner has refrained from saying whether the United States is going to increase pressure on Russia if no visible progress is made toward settling the Ukrainian conflict in the foreseeable future.
"There's no such thing, you know, in the world as forever enemies or forever allies," he told a news conference after talks with Vladimir Zelensky in Kiev, answering a relevant question.
According to Kushner, Trump is looking at the Ukrainian conflict through the prism of the "idea of what the best outcome could be and what benefits all people." "You know, President Trump comes from the business world. In the business world you think about things in the context of win-win," he said. "War is negative sum, you know. Everyone loses from war, whereas you know business and peace is positive sum, and hopefully you can find big benefits from that in a big way."
"Our role is to try to be the ones who are pursuing the peace," he stressed, adding that attempts to settle the conflict in Ukraine are "a very important and noble pursuit."
"And we're going to keep doing it with everything we have," Kushner noted. "And President Trump obviously has a lot of different ways to play it, but he's always focused on what are the best interests of America and the United States.".

The psychological effects of padel and pickleball, according to science
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
20:00:38 UTC
05:00:38 KST

Pickleball participation was associated with greater happiness, life satisfaction, social integration and lower depression, while padel was more closely studied in relation to confidence, anxiety and mental fatigue, according to a systematic review published in Frontiers in Psychology.
Physical activity is widely linked to better mental health, yet many people do not meet recommended activity levels. Padel and pickleball have attracted attention because they are social, relatively accessible and can be played across a range of ages and skill levels. Padel is played on an enclosed court where the ball can rebound from the walls, while pickleball uses a smaller court, a perforated plastic ball and slower-paced play that emphasizes strategy and interaction.
The researchers conducted the review because most previous studies had concentrated on physical fitness, injuries and sporting performance. Less was known about whether these sports were related to mental health and wellbeing. The review ultimately revealed a stark divide in the existing literature: padel has mostly been studied in competitive settings, while pickleball research has frequently focused on recreational play among older adults.
Led by Lena Lauxtermann at the University of Vienna, the researchers searched for studies published through October 8, 2024. Of 71 records screened, 14 studies were included, representing 1,403 participants. Eight padel studies included 538 people and six pickleball studies included 865. Women represented 42% of the overall sample, or approximately 589 participants.
The pickleball findings were mainly linked to wellbeing. Participation was associated with greater happiness, stronger social connections and higher life satisfaction. One study found that happiness was positively related to participation, while another linked more serious involvement in pickleball with lower depression. Social integration appeared particularly important for female players. During the COVID-19 pandemic, reduced opportunities to play were associated with increased loneliness and poorer mental health, suggesting that the social contact provided by the sport may be part of its benefit.
The padel studies focused more on athletes’ performance-related emotions. Higher-level players generally reported greater self-confidence and lower physical symptoms of anxiety. Anxiety also changed according to ranking, gender, match stage and whether players won or lost. Mental fatigue increased across consecutive matches and was linked to slower reactions and poorer accuracy. Motivation sometimes rose during mentally demanding matches, which may help explain why players continued performing despite feeling mentally tired.
The findings suggest the two rapidly growing racket sports may offer different mental-health benefits, but stronger research is needed to determine whether playing them directly causes improvements.
The authors summarized: “Padel studies primarily target performance aspects like self-confidence, anxiety, and mental fatigue, while pickleball research highlights wellbeing gains in life satisfaction, happiness, and social integration.”
Some limitations are to be noted. The results should not be interpreted as proof that either sport prevents depression or anxiety. For example, many studies relied on self-reported experiences, and all of the included studies were observational rather than randomized controlled trials. Padel research also overrepresented elite and competitive players, while pickleball research focused mainly on older adults. Additionally, the available research was geographically narrow, with all included studies originating from just three countries: the United States, Spain and Finland.
The study, “Padel, pickleball and wellbeing: a systematic review,” was authored by Lena Lauxtermann and Brendon Stubbs.

Fact check: Election fraud claims spread in Saxony-Anhalt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
19:59:00 UTC
04:59:00 KST

Fact check: Election fraud claims spread in Saxony-Anhalt
September 6, 2026
On Sunday, Saxony-Anhalt held one of Germany's most consequential elections in years. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a decisive lead, putting the party in a position to potentially form the first far-right state government in Germany since World War II.
In the days before the vote, false and misleading claims seized on the election's importance, with social media users alleging fraud, vote-rigging and irregularities in the handling and counting of ballots.
DW Fact Check previously documented some of these tactics as part of Matryoshka, also known as Operation Overload, a Russian-linked influence operation targeting German elections.
Below, we take a closer look at some more recent claims.
Fake video shows election workers destroying AfD ballots
Claim: "German election workers recorded themselves outright destroying ballots that were cast for the populist party 'Alternative For Germany' (AfD), during Germany's recent elections," reads a post viewed 10,000 times on X, posted by a QAnon-associated account, a far-right American political conspiracy theory and political movement.
A one-minute video shows a white-gloved man unpacking ballots from red envelopes, laying them on a table, and drawing a black X through ones that select the AfD. A ballot marked for the CDU is set aside, as a voice says in German, "these are OK."
The same video was shared by numerous other accounts, in German and English across social media platforms X and YouTube.
Verdict: False
There are several telltale signs that this video is staged. Most obviously, all three crossed-out ballots contain the same name.
They're also missing a hole punch in the top right corner, a regulation that ensures ballots can be used with a template for blind or visually impaired voters. The envelopes are also already unsealed.
The Gnida Project, a Russian disinformation watchdog group, said the video was part of the Storm-1516 campaign.
Storm-1516, a unit controlled by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, was also active ahead of Germany's 2025 federal election.
Read more on disinformation around Germany's postal voting system
Russian disinfo campaign alleges CDU fraud
Claim: The CDU is engaging in fraud in the Saxony-Anhalt election. "The social media pages of deceased residents of Saxony-Anhalt have become a platform for the #CDU's election campaign," reads one post on X, sharing a spoofed DW video.
"According to T-Online, non-existent citizens are set to vote by post for the #CDU in the Saxony-Anhalt election," reads another.
Verdict: False
DW Fact check reviewed five videos following a near-identical template: each was about a minute long and was posted by an account with zero followers and nearly no other posts. The videos feature a reputable news outlet's logo in the corner — including DW, ARD, WIRED, and BBC — and make claims about the CDU committing election fraud.
The claims range from the CDU using a database of Nazi soldier names to register fake ballots, to residents receiving campaign messages from deceased relatives.
Each video ends with a message urging viewers to "share this video with your family and friends in any way you see fit".
One of the videos claims T-Online disinformation reporter Lars Wienand had "obtained evidence that the CDU will attempt to rig the election." Wienand confirmed he had reported no such thing, writing to DW that "it's not the first time that suspected Russian disinformation had misused my name and image."
Julia Smirnova, disinformation expert and senior researcher at the Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy, told DW the posts were part of the Matryoshka Russian disinformation campaign, also known as Operation Overload.
"As with other Matryoshka videos, the reach is mostly inauthentic," she wrote in an email to DW.
DW Fact Check has previously documented the same operation targeting candidates in Germany's state elections. We identified more than 180 fake posts on X, Bluesky and TikTok, many of them using the logos and formats of established media outlets to spread fabricated allegations about politicians.
Read more on Russian disinformation targeting German elections
Did Halle start counting ballots too early?
Claim: "Unbelievable scandal! In Halle, absentee voting ballots are already being counted before 6 p.m. That's blatantly illegal!" reads a post on X with over 160,000 views, posted by a right-wing journalist.
Below is a screenshot of German newspaper ZEIT's online news blog, with an entry, originally written in German, titled: "Counting of absentee ballots from 60 polling districts begins in Halle-Neustadt".
Verdict: Misleading
The screenshot accurately shows a screengrabbed ZEIT liveblog entry, published at 3:15 pm.
Only ZEIT made an error, with the reporter clarifying to DW over email that their reporting was just describing "preparatory tasks" and not the actual counting of ballots.
The ZEIT blog entry has since been corrected with a "transparency note" that reads, "An earlier version of this blog post stated that the count had already begun. In fact, preparations were only underway. We have corrected the error."
The Saxony-Anhalt's state election regulations specify that ballots are not supposed to be officially counted until the voting period ends at 6 p.m. They can, however, be opened in advance to facilitate later ballot-counting.
Edited by: Sarah Steffen

Iran’s quota system prices petrol in three tiers – 1,500 tomans per litre for a consumer’s first 60 litres in a given month, 3,000 tomans per litre for their next 50, and 5,000 tomans per litre after that. The toman is an informal unit equivalent to 10 Iranian rials.
On Sunday, government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani said the price for the third tier would double to 10,000 tomans (about 4.5 US cents).
“The rate will increase to 10,000 toman rials from the morning of September 8,” Mohajerani said in remarks carried by state media.
“Different numbers were mentioned in expert meetings but because the president had promised the people, the rate of 10,000 tomans was set,” she added.

Iran raises price of petrol as US applies economic pressure

Iran raises price of petrol as US applies economic pressure
TEHRAN - The Iranian authorities on Sept 6 announced they were raising the price of petrol for heavier consumers, as the United States steps up sanctions seeking to isolate the country’s economy.
Iran’s quota system prices petrol in three tiers – 1,500 tomans per litre for a consumer’s first 60 litres in a given month, 3,000 tomans per litre for their next 50, and 5,000 tomans per litre after that. The toman is an informal unit equivalent to 10 Iranian rials.
On Sept 6, government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani said the price for the third tier would double to 10,000 tomans (about 5.7 Singapore cents).
“The rate will increase to 10,000 toman rials from the morning of September 8,” Mohajerani said in remarks carried by state media.
“Different numbers were mentioned in expert meetings, but because the president had promised the people, the rate of 10,000 tomans was set,” she added.
She later clarified that the price of the first and second tiers would not be changed.
Iran, a major oil producer with some of the world’s cheapest fuel, has for years heavily subsidised petrol, making any changes to pricing politically sensitive.
The development comes as the Iranian currency was trading on the black market on Sept 6 at more than 2.2 million rials to the US dollar, according to websites that track the rate.
Before the start of the Middle East war on Feb 28, the rial traded at around 1.7 million to the dollar, and in late April it hit what was then a record low of 1.8 million.
Late in August, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent laid out plans for the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran, hoping to use financial pressure to hasten the end of the war.
The new measures build on a sanctions regime by the US and allies that has been in place since 2018, when President Donald Trump withdrew from an international deal struck with Tehran on its nuclear programme.
The United States has also put Iran’s ports under a naval blockade, attempting to reduce its oil exports to zero. AFP

What's in a name? Population Authority shares most popular baby names ahead of Rosh Hashanah
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06

04:38:08 KST

Mohammed, Ariel, and Avigail topped Israel’s lists of the most popular names given to babies during the Hebrew year 5786, according to Population and Immigration Authority data released on Sunday ahead of Rosh Hashanah.
A total of 179,398 babies had been registered in Israel’s Population Registry as of Sunday morning, September 6, the authority said.
Mohammed was the most common name among boys across Israel’s general population, followed by Ariel, Yosef, Adam, David, Omer, Rafael, Lavi, Michael, and Eitan.
Among Jewish boys, Ariel took first place. David ranked second, followed by Rafael, Lavi, Uri, Michael, Eliya, Eitan, Yehuda, and Ari.
Ariel’s position at the top continues its strong showing in recent years. In 2024, it was also the most popular name among Jewish boys according to Population and Immigration Authority figures, while David ranked second and Lavi third. Earlier baby-name data showed Ariel leading Jewish boys in 2024.
Most popular names among girls
Avigail was the most popular girls’ name both across the general population and among Jewish Israelis in 5786.
In the overall ranking for girls, Avigail was followed by Miriam, Lia, Libi, Tamar, Yael, Ayala, Sarah, Ella, and Naya.
Among Jewish girls, Libi came in second after Avigail, followed by Tamar, Yael, Lia, Ella, Ayala, Sarah, Noa, and Naya.
Avigail has maintained an unusually strong run at the top of the rankings. Population and Immigration Authority figures for 2024 also placed the name first among Jewish girls, marking its second consecutive year in the top spot at the time. Avigail also topped Israel’s 2024 rankings
More recent Central Bureau of Statistics data covering children born in 2024 similarly found Avigail to be the most popular name among Jewish girls, while traditional and biblical names continued to dominate many of the rankings. That analysis placed David first among Jewish boys in its separate dataset, followed by Levi and Ariel. Israeli parents continued to favor traditional names in CBS data
Mohammed’s place at the top of the overall boys’ ranking also continues a long-running pattern. The name topped the nationwide boys’ list in data released ahead of Rosh Hashanah in 2022 as well, when Adam and Yosef followed it. Mohammed has led nationwide baby-name rankings in previous years
Jerusalem leads Israel in births
Jerusalem recorded by far the largest number of registered births during 5786, with 23,336 babies.
Bnei Brak ranked second with 8,225 births, while Tel Aviv-Jaffa was third with 7,405.
Beit Shemesh followed with 6,974 births, ahead of Ashdod with 4,031 and Haifa with 3,421.
Rishon LeZion registered 3,413 births, Netanya 3,343, Petah Tikva 3,338, and Modi’in Illit 3,113.
The figures were released as Israel prepared to enter the Hebrew year 5787, with Rosh Hashanah beginning on Friday evening.

'Now measured in the millions': The common process being used to scam Australians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
19:35:54 UTC
04:35:54 KST

in brief
- Scammers are exploiting the growing use of CAPTCHAs to trick people into running malicious code outside their browser.
- An expert has practical tips on how to minimise your risk.
CAPTCHAs are meant to protect our online infrastructure from bots. Scammers, however, are turning them against us.
Cybersecurity experts have seen a rise in fake CAPTCHA scams, with the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) releasing a warning this week about the ruse.
The fake CAPTCHAs direct internet users to input code outside of their browser, which grants hackers access to the device and, in some cases, browser session information.
The scams often ask them to paste a script into a computer's terminal, allowing the attacks to bypass anti-malware security systems.
Hammond Pearce, senior lecturer at UNSW School of Computer Science and managing director of the Digital Lies & Cyber Literacy Foundation, said the ability to bypass anti-malware protections made fake CAPTCHA scams particularly dangerous.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"You haven't got very many of the protections of the operating system working for you," he told SBS News.
Previously, CAPTCHAs were commonly required for creating online account. However, they're now common when making the first connection with a website, greatly increasing the number that internet users are asked to complete.
Pearce attributes this to "the explosion of AI agents online" as websites attempt to prevent artificial intelligence from going through them.
The increased prevalence of CAPTCHAs means it's easier for dodgy ones to slip through.
Pearce said he'd "expect it more on slightly dodgier websites" but hackers "can try and hijack your connection so that you get that when you're trying to get to a normal website".
Pearce also said the number of fake CAPTCHA attacks "are now measured in the millions".
How to avoid fake CAPTCHAs
According to Pearce, it's now much harder than it used to be for criminals to leverage a person's internet connection against them.
Major browsers such as Chrome, Firefox and Edge have used significant resources to make themselves "about the safest piece of technology there is on your computer", Pearce said.
He said users should be suspicious if a CAPTCHA asks them to type something or leave the window.
"If it's actually asking you to type some random thing on your keyboard, you should immediately start getting suspicious," Pearce said.
"Be very wary of anything that might take you out of the safety of the web browser."
He says that, if something feels off, internet users should ask themselves: "Why? Why do I need to do this?"

Veena feared she would be a resentful grandmother. One rule stopped this
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
19:31:43 UTC
04:31:43 KST

What does grandparenting look like today? Insight explores whether the demands on modern-day grandparents are keeping them physically fit and mentally well, or if the younger generations’ wants and needs are being prioritised to the detriment of grandparents. Watch Insight episode Grandparenting Tuesday 8 September at 8.30pm on SBS or SBS On Demand.
Veena Gopinath recently became a grandmother to twins. When she found out her daughter was pregnant, Veena was excited for her, but not for herself.
"It wasn't a joyful instant emotion in any way, shape, or form," the 56-year-old told Insight.
"I was like, 'Oh my God, how am I going to do this?'"
The Sydney-based small business owner says her feelings about becoming a grandmother were strange.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"In my mind, I was still young and our son had just finished school.
"So, life was just becoming more fun for me — I had time and money and resources to look after myself."
When Veena became a mother 32 years ago, her parents put their lives on hold to help her adjust to motherhood.
"Both my parents came from India, and they stayed for 12 months ... I was totally pampered."
"That was the message I was given — to be a grandparent like that — and it was a really tough act to follow ..."
Deciding she didn't want to put herself through the same thing, Veena set clear boundaries with her daughter four months after she gave birth.
"She doesn't expect anything more than what I offer," Veena said.
"I have said that I will never commit to regular babysitting for her."
But there are a few exceptions to this boundary.
"If they want to go on a date night, I'll help them out because that's important for their marriage; and then if there are urgent or emergency things, of course I'll help."
"My view is that they need to find resources and create their own babysitting and money to handle those things. It's not my thing to help them out."
The tipping point
Myra Hamilton is a sociologist at the University of Sydney whose research focuses on gender, work and care.
She says that grandparents who set clear boundaries around what they're willing to do regarding childcare are less likely to experience negative impacts on their health and financial security. She says grandparents providing occasional or regular childcare has its benefits.
"[It] actually can be positive for grandparents' mental health, their mood; it can be positive for their physical health, their fitness or their balance or mobility; and some studies even find that it can be positive for cognitive health ..."
But the sociologist said there is a "tipping point" when it's no longer beneficial.
"Our own research has found what we call a tipping point of about 13 hours of childcare per week ..." she said.
"That's when you started to see things like they were less likely to say they felt they had a choice, they were more likely to feel obligated, they were less likely to enjoy providing the childcare."
Prioritising family
Unlike Veena, Fiona Ninnes has a standing agreement with her daughter, who is a single mother working full-time, for regular childcare.
But prioritising grandparenting responsibilities has meant personal sacrifice for the retired teacher and her husband — including her no longer having time to participate in community theatre and having to relocate.
The couple used to live in the Southern Highlands, 90 minutes' drive from Sydney, but had to downsize to a Sydney apartment when the commute to babysit became too taxing.
"It's affecting our hip pocket, but we don't have the petrol costs ... because we can now jump on a train.
"I don't know if it's exactly balanced, but we're happy with it."
The 67-year-old minds her five-year-old and two-year-old grandchildren every Tuesday afternoon and all day Wednesday.
"Both of them have had a lot of health issues ... They were both going to daycare but had to be withdrawn because of the health issues.
"[My granddaughter] was constantly in hospital. If a child [got] a cold, she would get pneumonia."
When she's not babysitting, the retired teacher likes to spend time with other family members — including her four other grandchildren.
"But if one of our other [grandchildren] is in hospital, then yeah, I can often feel like I'm a piece of string stretched in too many different directions."
When that happens, Fiona knows it's time to take a step back to stave off burnout.
"If I've done 10 days straight and I'm absolutely exhausted because it's 24/7, I have to say, 'Okay, well, you've got a nanny coming in'."
"Even though I absolutely adore spending time with them ... it is exhausting."
'I didn't want to take money from my own daughter'
Like Fiona, Kaaran Moody also provides regular childcare for her daughter Christine, who transfers Kaaran some money each week as a token of appreciation.
"I told her I didn't want money for looking after him because I just love him, and I love her, and I wanted them to get ahead financially.
"But she insisted on paying me whether I wanted it or not."
While Kaaran says she felt very guilty for accepting the money, she says it is helpful.
"I didn't want to take money from my own daughter, especially because we never had a hand when we were young parents, and we wanted to give her what we'd never had.
"But at the same time, I wouldn't have been able to afford petrol. And I was able to take him to activities ... buy him toys, games and books."
The 56-year-old and her daughter worked together as early childhood educators at an Adelaide childcare centre before Kaaran offered to mind her grandson at home and stopped working.
When Christine returned from maternity leave, she would drop her son off in another class at the daycare and work in the other, which proved difficult.
"He wasn't eating; he wouldn't sleep; and she would come into the room, and he would just be really distressed, wanting her to cuddle him," Kaaran said.
"And she couldn't because she's literally at work."
Grandparenting in Australia
For grandparents who provide regular childcare in Australia, 70 per cent change their working hours, 50 per cent reduce their working hours, and one in five reports changing jobs to accommodate their childcare responsibilities, a 2020 survey by the University of Sydney found.
The survey also reported that one in three grandparents believed providing childcare to their grandkids negatively impacted their finances — by working less and earning less super, and through the direct costs of childcare, such as buying nappies and baby food.
Hamilton notes that childcare can be expensive, hard to find a placement, sometimes not culturally appropriate, and often "not flexible enough".
"When you ask grandparents why they're providing regular childcare, the most common reason they provide is to support their adult children in paid work," she told Insight.
"Especially their adult daughters and daughters-in-laws — supporting them to invest in their careers."
Hamilton said that grandparenting is often gendered — with grandmothers being more likely to take on childcare duties. And these duties are often taken on during a time when some older women are also trying to work and save for their financial future.
The sociologist says that men and women often take on different roles in providing care for grandchildren.
"Grandmothers are more likely to provide routine childcare tasks (like bathing, feeding, and putting the child down for a nap) ... Whereas grandfathers are more likely to be involved in things like transporting the grandchild to and from daycare or play-based tasks."
"And we also find that more of the hours that grandfathers spend providing childcare are spent with the grandmother also present, whereas grandmothers are more likely to be providing that care on their own."
'It's probably not a natural role'
Before becoming grandparents, family lawyer Franco Pomare expected that he and his wife would take on traditional grandmother and grandfather roles.
"I would've thought my wife would've taken on the greater role," he said.
"I would eventually slow down at work and I would pick up the slack."
However, Franco's wife, Lydia, had a stroke five years ago, which left her with limited mobility, cognitive impairment and memory loss.
"The heavy lifting I think, is normally done by a grandmother," the 66-year-old said.
"But that hasn't occurred."
Franco has reduced his hours at his family practice, where he works with his daughter Gabriella, to be a more involved grandfather.
He does school pick-ups for his six-year-old grandson and spends more time at home with his wife and her carer, who look after Gabriella's two-year-old daughter.
"It's probably not a natural role," Franco said.
"But I'm adapting to it."

Hawaii declares state of emergency as Hurricane Lowell approaches islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
19:12:36 UTC
04:12:36 KST

Hawaii has declared a state of emergency as powerful Hurricane Lowell makes its way toward the islands, with the first impacts expected as soon as Monday.
The storm is the third system in just over three weeks to threaten Hawaii during an active hurricane season in the central Pacific. Lowell remained a category 3 hurricane early on Sunday morning, packing winds of 125 miles per hour while moving north-west at six miles per hour.
According to the forecast, Lowell will reach Hawaii as a category 2 hurricane. Its center could pass roughly 130 miles west of Ni’ihau or 170 miles west of Kauai between Monday evening and Tuesday morning.
The threat comes amid unusually intense hurricane activity across the Pacific.
As of Saturday, Hurricanes Karina, Lowell and Marie were all churning in the Pacific at the same time, marking the region’s first triple-hurricane stretch in a decade. The National Hurricane Center (NHC) was also monitoring a fourth potential system off the coast of Mexico.
The Pacific averages only eight hurricanes per year, according to the NHC, making three simultaneous hurricanes highly unusual.
Lowell’s projected offshore path is expected to keep the storm’s most dangerous winds away from Hawaii’s islands. But heavy rain, high surf and dangerous coastal conditions are still expected.
A tropical storm warning is in effect for Kauai and Ni’ihau, where wind gusts above 39 miles per hour are possible over the next 48 hours.
Lowell is the third storm in a matter of weeks to hit Hawaii as the climate crisis continues to increase the intensity and frequency of storms and other weather events.
Tropical Storm Moke struck the southern part of Hawaii’s islands two weeks ago, bringing heavy rainfall and strong winds. That came just days after Hurricane Lala hit the region.
The Hawaii governor Josh Green said Lala alone had caused at least $43m in infrastructure damage on the Big Island, along with another $4.6m in damage to homes.
The escalating storm activity comes as the UN warns that this year’s El Niño is forecast to become the strongest on record in four decades.
A statement released on Thursday described El Niño as being “supersized before our eyes”, adding that the world is in “the danger zone of extreme weather”.
The latest data on the natural climate phenomenon shows a near 100% likelihood that the latest El Niño will continue through February 2027, the statement said. The stronger an El Niño becomes, the greater the chance it will significantly alter rainfall and temperature patterns around the world and help fuel extreme weather.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has previously warned there is a 69% chance that this El Niño will be the strongest in 70 years.

Woman laid to rest in coffin made from mushrooms in Australian first
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
19:00:12 UTC
04:00:12 KST

A woman has been buried in a coffin made from mushrooms in New South Wales in an eco-friendly first for Australia.
Carolyn, aged in her 70s, was laid to rest on Friday by friends and family at Springwood Cemetery in the Blue Mountains.
The mushroom coffin, created by the Dutch firm Loop Biotech, was grown from mycelium – the root network of fungi – and hemp fibres.
The coffin is grown in mould in a climate-controlled room, taking just a week to fully form. Once buried, it takes about 45 days to become part of the soil.
The process is akin to composting, as the body and coffin gently biodegrade and transform into nutrient-rich soil in far less time than a traditional wooden casket, which can take up to 50 years to break down.
Carolyn’s husband, David, said picking the mushroom coffin aligned with his wife’s values of giving back.
“She was always there to help others. It feels very true to who she was that even after her death, she can still do something for others while giving something back to nature,” he said.
While Carolyn is the first to be buried in the coffin in Australia, Loop Biotech’s founder Bob Hendrikx said there had been thousands of others across Europe and the US.
“Five years ago when I started, there was lots of interest from Australia,” Hendrikx said. “It was a little bit harder to ship overseas [at the time].”
Hendrikx hopes the mushroom coffins, which weigh about 30kg each, could improve the sustainability of the Australian funeral sector by shortening the decomposition process.
“It’s about giving back to nature: we have the mushroom, which is grown and dissolves into nature, but the actual benefit is that … it’s enriching the soil,” he said.
“The body needs to just return to nature and let nature do what it’s done best forever.
“If a kangaroo dies in the forest, it’s just going to be part of the cycle of life.”
Dr Hannah Gould, a cultural anthropologist at the University of Melbourne, believes people are becoming increasingly interested in environmentally friendly farewells.
“As people perhaps become less religious, other kinds of values or community groupings become more important, and one of those that we’ve seen is eco-death.
“This idea that perhaps that you don’t go up to heaven after you die, you return to the earth, has been an increasingly popular narrative around death and dying.”
While about 70% of Australians choose to be cremated, it has a substantial environmental impact: the emissions from a typical cremation are estimated to be equivalent to 125kg of carbon dioxide.
In recent years options such as alkaline hydrolysis (a cremation-like process that uses water instead of fire), natural burials without embalming, and even shallow burials have become available. A natural burial uses a cardboard coffin with rope handles and will emit less than 10kg of carbon dioxide equivalent, according to PlanetMark analysis.
Gould believes that as Australians are living longer and more people are dying from prolonged illnesses, more time is being spent thinking about how to depart and farewell loved ones.
“They’ve maybe seen or organised a funeral for their parents and it hasn’t gone so well,” she said. “And they’re now deciding that they want to do things differently. So we’re seeing a huge rise in funeral planning.”

Trump administration appeals again to US Supreme Court over mail-in voting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
18:47:03 UTC
03:47:03 KST

Trump administration appeals again to US Supreme Court over mail-in voting
How the nation’s highest could rules could have major implications in this year’s midterm elections.
The administration of United States President Donald Trump has made another appeal to the Supreme Court to allow new restrictions on mail-in voting ahead of the midterms in November.
Two days after a federal judge blocked the US Postal Service (USPS) from enforcing Trump’s executive order, the administration on Sunday escalated the matter to the country’s highest court, asking justices to temporarily allow the agency to track mail-in ballots and decide whether they could be rejected. The ongoing legal battle comes even as some states have already begun sending out postal ballots.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US judge repeats block on Trump’s bid to limit voting by mail
- list 2 of 3Top US general says no plans to deploy troops for 2026 midterm elections
- list 3 of 3What’s behind the vote-by-mail controversy in the US?
US District Judge Indira Talwani issued an order on Friday that said Trump’s directives, which would grant the federal government power over the handling of mail-in ballots, are likely unconstitutional. In the US, elections – including ones for federal office – are carried out by states.
The judge also criticised the timing of the executive order’s implementation, writing that, with just two months until election day, it “threatens disenfranchisement of millions of United States citizens who seek to vote by mail”.
But in its emergency filing on Sunday, the Trump administration countered Talwani’s ruling: “Contrary to the claims of the district court and respondents that the Postal Service is trying to federalise the rules for mail-in voting, the Postal Service’s final rule imposes only modest envelope-design and addressee-information requirements for federal-election ballots sent via U.S. Mail”.
US Solicitor General John Sauer, who argues cases before the Supreme Court on behalf of the federal government, said Trump’s order would not seize control of states’ right to administer elections, but would only impose “reasonable preparation requirements” for mail-in ballots.
“[The rule] requires States to upload the name, address and barcode information of intended recipients of ballot mail in an online portal — information that election officials would necessarily already possess to send ballot mail under the Rule to those recipients,” Sauer wrote in the filing. “The Rule ensures that States remain responsible for determining voter eligibility and eligibility to vote by mail, and it does not dictate ballot content, mailing or receipt deadlines, or ballot-counting procedures.”
Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson set a deadline of Wednesday for responses to the Trump administration’s request.
Sunday’s filing marks the third time the Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to intervene. The court recently allowed the plan to move forward but did not rule on whether it was legal.
With control of the US Congress up for grabs in November, how the Supreme Court rules on the appeal could have major implications.
Despite voting by mail himself, Trump has long sought to limit it during his time in office, falsely claiming that it is ripe with fraud. Opponents say the president’s motivation is simpler, arguing that Democrats vote by mail more than Republicans.
An analysis conducted by the States United Democracy Center found that many voters, no matter their political affiliation, cast their ballots by mail. The research found that one in four registered Democrats and one in five registered Republicans voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election.

"It was a very good dialog. We (US negotiators - TASS) asked a lot of questions. He (Putin - TASS) asked a lot of questions, and I think it's very, very important to be discussing this now," he added.

Why some legal experts believe Neo-Nazis may win in the High Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
18:42:04 UTC
03:42:04 KST

In short:
Several legal experts believe there is a significant prospect that the federal government's ban on Neo-Nazi group White Australia may be overturned by the High Court.
The group, also known as the National Socialist Network, had been planning to launch a political party when it was outlawed in May by the government under new hate speech laws
What's next?
The matter is set to be heard in the High Court on September 8 and 9, with judgment not expected for several weeks or months.
Some of Australia's leading legal minds believe there is a significant prospect of the High Court overturning the federal government's recent ban on the nation's most high-profile Neo-Nazi group.
A victory in the nation's highest court for White Australia, also known as the National Socialist Network, could embarrass Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who in May said he was confident the new laws the government used to ban the group would withstand legal challenge.
It would also pave the way for the white supremacist group, with its sordid history of violence, criminality and racist demonstrations, to form its planned political party in a blaze of publicity.
In May, White Australia became the second group to be listed as a prohibited hate group under laws introduced in the wake of last year's Bondi Beach terror attack.
The organisation was trying to form a political party when it was outlawed by Minister for Home Affairs Tony Burke.
It is now attempting to have the laws overturned on the grounds that they are unconstitutional.
Constitutional law expert Anne Twomey said the federal laws appeared to have been rushed through in January without sufficient scrutiny.
"There would be political issues if it was seen that the government had lost to the White Australia Party," she told ABC NEWS Verify.
"But on the whole, the bigger issue is does this legislation survive and how might it be used in the future?
"And how consistent is it with our democratic system as imposed and required to operate by our constitution?" she said.
NSW Labor MP and former barrister Stephen Lawrence is worried White Australia leader and convicted criminal Thomas Sewell may be about to get more undeserved publicity.
"Imagine the optics. Thomas Sewell launching the White Australia Party on the steps of the High Court after having a big win there. We would be handing these people a political gift."
Complicated legal arguments
The constitutional legal arguments Sewell and his White Australia Party are presenting to the High Court are complex.
Put simply, the first argument is that the federal government does not have the power to make this law.
The second is that this law breaches the implied freedom of political communication.
The third is that this law breaches the separation of powers between the government and the judiciary.
Constitutional law expert Anthony Gray said the federal government's position was also multi-layered.
"They're arguing that the harm that may be caused by a proscribed group justifies the intrusion on what otherwise would be protected political communication," he said.
Professor Twomey said there was relevant historical legal precedent from when the federal government attempted to ban the Communist Party in the 50s.
"People were profoundly shocked when the High Court held that that legislation providing for the dissolution of the Communist Party was invalid," she said.
"So, it is possible and it has happened before to the extent that the Menzies government did find its legislation was found to be constitutionally invalid by the High Court."
ABC NEWS Verify sent questions to Mr Burke. A spokesman said the minister would not comment while the case was still ongoing.
Principle over ideology
Professor Twomey said that while the views of the White Australia Party might be distasteful to many Australians, it is not something the High Court can take into consideration.
She said the court would examine how these laws could hypothetically be used by a less democratic or authoritarian government.
"Do we really want on our statute books legislation that could be used in an abusive manner in a way that really undermines the democratic system? And so that's the bigger picture that the High Court needs to address," she said.
Professor Gray agreed that it was about legal principle rather than ideology.
"This is one of the things with freedom of speech that it's easy to defend freedom of speech for people whose views are what we call reasonable or views with which we agree," he said.
"It becomes challenging when we're dealing with an organisation that — or with people who — express views with which we may disagree."
The Director of Public Affairs at the Australia/Israel and Jewish Affairs Council, Jamie Hyams, said he believed the legislation struck the right balance.
"So on the one hand, you want to preserve our democracy, and by not giving governments too much power, but on the other hand, you need to give governments the power to deal with threats to our democracy.
"There are safeguards in there. The government is meant to act on advice from ASIO and also has to brief the leader of the opposition on it before they bring anything in."
What happens if the government loses?
If White Australia is successful in this High Court case, it could still end up outlawed by other legal means.
Professor Gray said the federal government would likely attempt to redraft the legislation.
"That's happened in the past where the Commonwealth has been knocked back by the High Court, they've then redrafted their law, and then that was deemed to be valid," he said.
Mr Hyams said if the White Australia Party was victorious, it should not be interpreted as any kind of endorsement by the High Court.
"It will be decided very narrowly on constitutional grounds," he said.
"If the legislation is overturned, hopefully there'll be some guidance in there about how similar legislation can be brought forward that doesn't, in the opinion of the court, breach their concerns about the constitution."
The matter is set down to be heard in the High Court on September 8 and 9, with a judgment not expected for several weeks or months.

A $3.4b collapse exposes the mess of our housing industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

analysis
Bathla's collapse exposes many issues in Australia's housing industry
Maybe housing developers should be required to live in what they build.
In the lead-up to the $3.4 billion collapse of developer Bathla Group a fortnight ago, the NSW Building Commission conducted more than 40 inspections of its sites over concerns about building quality.
And then a few days later, The Financial Review carried a story headed: "The Bathla family mansion has to be seen to be believed. French cobblestones and a wrought iron gate. Multiple pools alongside a basketball court and a tennis court."
So, no housing quality problems for the Mohan family behind Bathla, it seems.
The collapse of Bathla is a disaster for the national housing supply and affordability project: its now-stalled pipeline of 14,000 apartments represents about 18.5 per cent of new housing stock to be built in the state this year, and NSW is already running well behind its target.
But it also highlights three other issues:
- A three-way collision between the rise in construction costs, tighter controls on construction quality and the need for more, not less, affordable (that is, cheap) housing.
- The mess that is Australian construction regulation, with each state doing its own thing.
- The fact that banks prefer to lend against existing houses and have largely abandoned the building of new ones, leaving it to more expensive private credit, further raising the cost of new housing.
Bathla's collapse hurts affordable housing targets
Bathla was one of Australia's biggest providers of affordable housing and was caught by all three of those things.
NSW launched a crackdown on apartment construction quality after structural failures at Opal Tower in 2018 and Mascot Towers in 2019, creating the Building Commission NSW in 2023 and the Building (Approvals and Practitioners) Act 2026.
Which raises an obvious question: how come the 2000+ page National Construction Code (NCC) didn't already prevent the quality issues that Bathla is now being pinged for?
The answer most likely lies in the system of private inspections and approvals that allow developers to shop around for lenient certifiers.
For example, the Environmental Protection Authority has alleged that a private certifier falsified approval documents on four Bathla development sites.
NSW now has a hybrid system where day-to-day, mandatory construction checks are still done by private building certifiers, either contracted by the developer or the local council, and the Building Commission then acts as the auditor, investigator, and disciplinary force, randomly inspecting the work of both builders and certifiers to make sure no one is cheating.
Also, despite its many pages, and apart from not being properly policed, the NCC doesn't cover many of the issues Bathla buyers have been complaining about, such as missing doors and poor finishes.
New insurance requirements ramp up pressure
Bhart Bhushan, Bathla's managing director and co-founder, and his brother Rajinder Mohan, blame the company's collapse largely on the federal budget in May, when changes to capital gains tax and negative gearing led to a drop in investor demand for apartments.
That wouldn't have helped, but a more important factor would have been the introduction in NSW of mandatory Decennial (10-year) Liability Insurance (DLI) on August 14, 11 days before Bathla went under.
Ten-year insurance is expensive and hard to get, especially for a developer with a reputation for poor quality.
To qualify for a 10-year DLI policy in NSW, a developer must undergo rigorous, data-based risk assessments, often tied to independent ratings like the iCIRT (Independent Construction Industry Rating Tool).
Bathla is not one of the 219 companies on the iCIRT registry, so insurance was likely either expensive or impossible
Without access to DLI, Bathla was forced back to the statutory alternative — a 2 per cent bond, locked up for 10 years.
Because DLI requires insurers to conduct rigorous, multi-stage construction audits while the building is going up, Bathla's lenders knew the Building Commission NSW might refuse to issue completion approvals.
If that happened, the apartments couldn't be sold, and the lenders would be stuck with a stranded asset and default.
Financiers could see that either expensive insurance or a 2 per cent bond would drain the company's liquidity, so they started refusing to roll over Bathla's debts, which triggered the voluntary administration.
Loading
What could possibly go wrong?
And who are the lenders? Not banks, and they don't actually lend to Bathla.
The outfits that are in a $3 billion Bathla-shaped hole are private credit firms, which are really asset managers that raise money from investors by offering interest rates of 7 per cent and more and lend it for a margin on top of that to businesses that can't get a loan from a bank.
Bathla operates through hundreds of special purpose vehicles (SPVs) that do the projects, and private credit firms have their exposure to these, not Bathla, which means there is a complex maze of different projects at different stages of life, each with its own lender.
Some lenders are trying to finish projects themselves, while others have a vacant block of land with a set of plans, and none wants to fund Bathla's head office, with 165 staff.
Why aren't the banks involved in this industry? Because after the GFC, the banking regulator, APRA, changed the capital rules to favour real estate security over the future cash flows of businesses like property developers.
This is also part of why pre-fab housing manufactured in factories and assembled on-site has never gained a foothold in Australia despite the obvious cost benefits — it's hard to get finance.
Meanwhile, NSW has become an outlier in a messy tapestry of national construction regulation and policing.
While NSW has empowered a new well-funded government agency in response to the Opal and Mascot Towers scandals, Victoria, Queensland, WA and SA are sticking with private certifiers to sign off on residential construction work.
No state government wants to ban private certifiers and return fully to local council inspections because it would result in housing construction grinding to a halt — councils across the country have wound down their building departments and don't have the capacity to do it anymore.
But since they're all working off a National Construction Code, you'd think it would make sense for the policing of it to be national as well.
Private construction of affordable housing, with private credit, subject to private inspections of quality and safety.
What could possibly go wrong?
Alan Kohler is a finance presenter and columnist on ABC News. He hosts the podcast That’s Business with Alan Kohler in the ABC Business Daily feed on Friday. He also writes for Intelligent Investor.
