Literature awards under threat from AI, writer says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:42:11 UTC
01:42:11 KST

Artificial intelligence (AI) is dealing a heavy blow to literature and literary judging, Taiwanese writer Chu Yu-hsun (朱宥勳) said on Saturday, adding that nearly 40 percent of the novel submissions he reviewed this year appeared to be AI-generated.
Chu wrote on Facebook that this year has been his most painful as a judge, as the literary community attempts to fend off an infinitely replicable industrial production line with limited human labor.
In many cases, he said he only realized he was dealing with a new AI writing model after reading a batch of entries and noticing the same stylistic patterns appearing repeatedly.
Photo: Reuters
He said he observed a noticeable difference between AI-generated submissions received in the first and second halves of this year.
Preliminary judging previously involved selecting outstanding works, but judges now have to rank submissions while also trying to determine whether they were written by humans, Chu said.
“It is like a baseball pitcher throwing three balls at once, two of which are illusions,” he wrote. “The batter has to figure out which one is real before deciding whether to swing.”
Reading 200 submissions containing 20 AI-generated entries required as much effort as reading 400 or 500 works, he said, adding that the current system is destined to undermine judging quality and cannot effectively defend against AI-generated content.
He added that mistakes were inevitable, adding that he could misidentify human-written works as AI-generated and fail to detect some AI-generated submissions.
Even if his accuracy rate was as high as 95 percent, reviewing 1,000 entries would still result in 50 incorrect judgements, Chu said.
AI-generated submissions would eventually destroy the literary award system, he said.
Working conditions for judges have deteriorated so severely that compensation would need to be raised substantially to maintain quality or every literary award would be riddled with problems, he said.
Chu said that starting next year, he would refuse to serve as a judge for any literary award that does not explicitly prohibit AI-generated works, while prioritizing events that adopt stronger preventive measures, such as requiring contestants to sign declarations affirming the originality of their work or preserve records of their creative process.
He also issued a stern warning to contestants who use AI to create their entries.
“I know there is no point in trying to persuade you, because you simply do not have the talent or soul of a creator. As a result, you lack the pride and self-discipline that creators hold themselves to,” Chu said.
“Make the most of the last few chances you have to game the system and pocket the prize money,” he added.
“Once the literary award system collapses, you would not even know where to submit your work or where you can get your writing seen and noticed,” he said.

Trump envoy ‘feels good’ about Russia-Ukraine peace talks
US special envoy Steve Witkoff has expressed optimism about Washington’s renewed efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict following talks in both Moscow and Kiev, saying the Trump administration hopes to find a diplomatic solution.
Witkoff and US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner met Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky in Kiev on Sunday, a day after holding more than three hours of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin. Sunday’s trip marked the US envoys’ first official visit to the Ukrainian capital as part of Washington’s peace efforts.
Witkoff said on Sunday that he “felt good” about the discussions in both capitals and that Washington hopes diplomacy can bring an end to the conflict. He also suggested that direct talks involving all three sides could take place soon, pointing to “a trilateral that we’re hopeful will be announced in short order.”
The latest diplomatic push began in Moscow on Saturday, where Putin received Witkoff and Kushner for talks lasting just over three hours. Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov later described the meeting as “substantive, constructive, extremely candid, and trusting.”
According to Ushakov, the American envoys presented several ideas on possible paths toward a settlement, while Putin reiterated Moscow’s readiness to continue working with Washington to seek a political and diplomatic solution. The Russian leader also stressed that any lasting agreement would have to address what Moscow describes as the root causes of the conflict.
According to an Axios source familiar with the meetings, during the talks in Kiev on Sunday Zelensky discussed Ukrainian preparations for continuing the war through the winter, while Kushner and Witkoff stressed they want a breakthrough before then.
A White House official also told Axios the Moscow discussions were substantive, saying the two sides had discussed plans for the next steps that are expected to be announced in the coming weeks.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has earlier thanked Trump for his efforts to help resolve the conflict, saying the US president continued seeking a settlement despite the difficulty of the situation. Putin also reiterated Moscow’s commitment to refrain from strikes on Kiev during a three-day period beginning at midnight on September 5, intended to allow the US envoys to travel safely to the Ukrainian capital.

Joyful spending is the US’ guilty pleasure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:42:08 UTC
01:42:08 KST

Americans like to spend money, and they are good at it, but they also feel kind of bad about it.
Three-quarters of Americans say they feel guilty when they spend money on something that brings them joy rather than putting it toward a long-term financial goal, an Ally Bank survey showed. I can confirm this feeling, especially after seeing my credit card statement following my most recent vacation.
At the same time, the survey also states that almost 70 percent of respondents say they spend “the right amount on joy.” Clearly guilt is part of the joy, which says something about the religious nature of US society that is beyond the scope of economics.
Illustration: Yusha
Still, as an economist who specializes in retirement saving, I try never to lose sight of what the purpose of saving is — and it is not necessarily delayed gratification. The goal is to spread joy evenly across your life. Since earnings increase over time, in theory you should spend wildly and go into debt when you are young, save lots when you are in middle age and earnings peak, and then spend down your savings when you retire.
Through it all, you should spend about the same amount on what brings you joy. Sure, maybe you skip a few nights out in anticipation of future joy — a trip to Tahiti, say, or a kitchen renovation.
However, the rub here is risk. What if you stop working for a few years in middle age, or the stock market crashes just before you retire? That is where economics comes in. It says that you should spread the joy around, and it assumes that experiencing a big drop in your living standards is worse than never having any joy at all.
So economists like me tend to advise people to have precautionary savings — enough to smooth out the uncertainties in life — or to spend less when you are young and more as you get older, so you never have to experience a drop in living standards.
Whether your spending is truly excessive and worthy of guilt depends on your financial circumstances, and your preferences for joy today versus joy tomorrow. Ally Bank, based on its survey and what it is calling the “Joy Index,” argues that Americans can afford to spend more on joyful things.
However, the data suggest they already are.
The Bank of America Institute tracks spending on the bank’s credit cards. It estimates a 6 percent increase in spending in June. Some of it was on necessary things such as gas, but more than 4 percent was driven by more discretionary purchases, such as leisure travel, clothes and electronics.
Some of the largest increases came from spending on leisure travel and restaurants. The institute also estimates that discretionary spending has increased in the past year across all income groups — but especially for the top 5 percent of high earners.
The good news is that the number of people who pay off their credit card balances each month has increased across all income groups. (Although there was also a slight increase in the number that pay only their minimum balance, especially among lower-income groups.)
The New York Federal Reserve also finds an increase in delinquencies and rising credit card debt. The bottom line is that there are some people at all income levels risking financial trouble.
As the US becomes more prosperous, it is natural to expect more discretionary spending, especially among the growing upper-middle class. Eating in a restaurant was once a rare luxury; now it is a standard component of household consumption.
The next time you feel tempted to shame someone for spending US$20 on a restaurant burrito, remember that it is better than spreading a can of beans on a tortilla at home.
I am not one to judge (so says that credit card statement), but to me the question raised by the so-called Joy Index is this: Are Americans spending too much on joy today at the expense of joy tomorrow?
In my expert opinion, the amount of guilt you should feel about any given purchase is correlated to your financial capacity to manage risk if circumstances change. To some extent, Americans are better protected than they used to be; a lot of wealth might be in the stock market or real estate, but net worth has increased in the past five years, especially for the middle class. This might be driving more joyful, guilt-tinged spending.
Personal finance is not just about spending versus saving. It is about risk management. This is where there is some cause for concern: Much of the increase in wealth comes from increased retirement savings, which is a good long-term goal and much of those savings are invested in the stock market. Some evidence suggests that this investment comes at the expense of more liquid assets. All of which means that, if the stock market falls and people need cash, they might experience that dreaded drop in living standards — and a lot more guilt, and a lot less joy.
Allison Schrager is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering economics. A senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute, she is author of An Economist Walks Into a Brothel: And Other Unexpected Places to Understand Risk. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

====================================================================================================

Notes from Central Taiwan: Taiwan’s  demographic  time bomb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:42:06 UTC
01:42:06 KST

Another doleful set of demographic announcements this month from the National Development Council (NDC), with the number of young people shriveling as the proportion of old people grows.
“Taiwan’s 18-year-olds, the typical age for entering college, will fall below 200,000 for the first time in the 2027 academic year to 195,309, down from 200,406 in 2026,” this paper reported citing NDC sources.
Meanwhile, the administration of President William Lai (賴清德) announced a goal of training at least 500,000 AI professionals by 2040. Although this could include foreign recruits and retraining those already in the workforce, the math is stark: Ministry of the Interior figures show that 181,601 people were born in 2018 to graduate at 22 from university in 2040. For the period from 2010 to 2018, representing people who will be in their 20s and 30s and trainable as AI talents around 2040, the total number of births was just under 1.8 million. Good luck getting under a third of them to train as “AI talents,” whatever that means. How many of them will become farmers?
Photo: Lu Hui-chou, Taipei Times
WHERE ARE THE WORKERS?
Lai’s 500,000 AI talents may be rhetoric, given plummeting birth rates. Yet it is also clear from a glance at the numbers why the government has been so slow in waking up: through 2018, the birth numbers appear to be relatively stable, falling between 160,000 and 200,000 each year, and peaking at over 200,000 in 2012, 2014, 2015 and 2016. There is nothing in those numbers to suggest that a decade after hitting 213,598 births in 2015 the nation would be at half that number. Indeed, 2018 saw more births than 2010 (181,000 vs 166,000). But the government has not explained how much of its 500,000-person target would come from new graduates, retrained workers or overseas recruitment.
The NDC projects that Taiwan will be short 480,000 workers by 2030, a number widely quoted and likely an underestimate given that the demographic figures released this month were downward revisions of earlier estimates (the labor shortage number was 276,000 job vacancies in September last year). Professionals and technical workers — who may have greater opportunities to work abroad — make up a substantial share of these vacancies, as current labor market shortages show.
Photo: Reuters
It’s not just the people who will leave. Firms that cannot find warm bodies may set up elsewhere, in advanced nations still producing children or still entertaining demographic bumps. At home wages and benefits will have to rise as well if firms are to retain personnel, cutting into Taiwan’s major competitive advantage of underpaid, overworked labor. A key consequence of aging is slowing economic growth. Are we living in the golden twilight of Taiwan?
The Political Consequences of Ageing Societies, a 2022 paper on the political consequences of aging, warns: “If age-based resource competition persists and remains unaddressed, it may put policies that rely on intergenerational solidarity, from pension and health care over fiscal policy to combating climate change, potentially at risk.” Or, translated: as the gruel gets thin, the knives get sharp.
Taiwan’s elites, who refuse to permit robust immigration or make urgent changes to the work culture and political economy, appear to have decided upon a policy of national suicide. What kind of politics can we expect from a land of labor shortages, a rising proportion of elderly and a restive population of young professionals, all of whom can see that within a decade or two the nation they know will shrivel and vanish?
Photo: Chen Chih-chu, Taipei Times
The 2024 national election results do not give us many hints of future politics. Comparing the 2016 and 2024 election maps at the township level also shows that the two national elections were broadly similar, with townships flipping where one would expect them to flip. Local elections are local and dependent on unpredictable factors like politicians angry at their own party running independent candidacies or sudden discoveries of corruption. It is hard to look at the numbers and see an impending political re-alignment.
‘GREEDY GEEZERS’
As James Schulz and Robert H. Binstock observed on the US in Aging Nation: The Economics and Politics of Growing Older in America, in the 1970s the discourse on the aged shifted from viewing the elderly as people to be revered and cared for to “greedy geezers.”
By the 1980s and 1990s, the aged were being portrayed as powerful, influential and wealthy. David Broder, the influential Washington Post columnist, in 1973 wrote that “The significant, semi-hidden story in the ... federal budget is that America’s public resources are increasingly being mortgaged for the use of a single group within our country: the elderly.”
Something similar may happen in Taiwan. The gains of the last two decades have largely gone to the over-60 crowd. In a nation with a proper population pyramid there would be a push to claw that back, but the old have far more political clout than the relatively poorer under-40 population. The 2022 paper cited above notes that elderly voters “display more interest in politics, have more political resources, turn out more in elections and have greater access to political power.”
Moreover, they “behave like a ‘single-minded voting block’ that displays strong and uniform preferences for old-age pension spending and health care.”
Because they vote as a block, they are easier and less costly to mobilize.
The current election cycle is at least dropping some hints of this. The Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) candidate for Taitung, Chen Ying (陳瑩), promised that if elected, she would provide fully subsidized dentures, hearing aids and smart bracelets for the elderly. The Lai administration is going to launch its “health tokens” program next month, a month before the November local elections. The program, open to adults above age 18, was announced in the context of Taiwan’s super-aged society, whose “chronic diseases have become a major challenge to public health,” Lai said. Conspicuously absent is pension reform, a major issue during previous administrations.
Does this portend a shift in spending? Traditionally the government has spent more on public infrastructure than on defense, but with both labor pools and user pools shrinking, it will be interesting to see whether massive investments in road construction and water engineering continue throughout the 2030s, given the likely demand for spending on health services and defense. Politicians, habituated to buying private votes with public dollars, will be tailoring their messages to the old and their health concerns. This augurs further convergence between the domestic policies of the two major parties, as both will be appealing to the same pool of aging voters.
Another factor is going to be anthropogenic warming, which will slam rural, coastal and mountain communities filled with the aged. A study in the journal Climate Change last year of coast aquaculture communities in Dongshi Township (東石) in Chiayi County observed that “half of the emigrant households cited perceived climate-related issues as a factor in the decision of household members to migrate.” Climate events will drive more of the aged out of farming as their farms encounter extreme events whose costs are too great for them to bear. Heating will also make things like air conditioning and in-home health warning systems for the old a matter of public policy.
One has to wonder: If you were Beijing, would you want to annex all the problems Taiwan is going to experience in the next two decades?
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.

The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT)-controlled legislature in February 2006 established the National Communications Commission (NCC). One of the purposes of the NCC was to circumvent the control of the Government Information Office (GIO), long the KMT’s tool for overseeing the local media, by the administration of Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) president Chen Shui-bian (陳水扁). The NCC’s commissioners were originally apportioned according to the ratio of party control of the legislature. Single-person households rise to 40.5% nationwide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:42:06 UTC
01:42:06 KST

The number of single-person households nationwide reached about 3,993,100 last year, accounting for 40.5 percent of all registered households, Ministry of the Interior data showed.
Single-person households have become the dominant structure in Taiwan, exceeding the combined share of two-person and three-person households for the first time, the data showed.
There were 8.933 million households nationwide in 2020, of which single-person households accounted for about 34 percent, two-person households about 20.5 percent and three-person households about 18.1 percent, ministry statistics showed.
Photo: Taipei Times
The combined share of two-person and three-person households had accounted for about 38.6 percent, about 4.6 percentage points higher than single-person households.
However, the total number of households nationwide increased to about 9.85 million last year, marking a substantial growth of about 917,000 households in five years.
During the same period, the number of single-person households surged by 951,100, significantly exceeding the growth in total households over the same time span.
The proportion of single-person households rose sharply to 40.5 percent last year, exceeding the combined share of two-person and three-person households at 38.19 percent, the data showed.
Asked why single-person households are becoming the dominant structure in Taiwan, a real estate agent said that on top of the main factors — non-marriage and childlessness — there are also other connected factors, such as the nation’s super-aged society.
Sinyi Realty Inc (信義房屋) research and development department project manager Tseng Ching-te (曾敬德) said that over the past few years, there have been fewer marriages — about 100,000 to 120,000 — compared with the 120,000 to 170,000 new housing units completed each year.
The growth rate of single-person households is significantly outpacing the number of marriages and new housing unit handovers each year, he said.
Aside from home purchases by single people, a new house tax policy that took effect in 2024 might have been another factor, Tseng said.
The policy raises tax for hoarding multiple houses, he said, adding that tax collection for it started last year.
To qualify for preferential taxes for self-occupied homes, owners must complete household registration for the property, Tseng said.
Given that taxes on newer properties are higher, the policy has prompted a wave of household registrations, so the number of single-person households between 2023 and last year might be inflated, he added.

Japan’s luxury ice revered by bars around the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:42:02 UTC
01:42:02 KST

In the historic Japanese city of Kanazawa, craftsmen painstakingly shape and slice blocks of ice destined to chill negronis in some of the world’s trendiest bars.
The men work for Kuramoto Ice, a century-old company in Ishikawa on the Sea of Japan coast and one of dozens of Japanese firms producing ultra-clear, premium ice.
This luxury product, believed by those in the industry to melt more slowly than regular blocks, is a staple of Japan’s cocktail culture, but its popularity is also spilling over to bars abroad, from the US to Australia, who pay as much as ￥200 (US$1.28) per cube.
Photo: AFP
Kuramoto Ice is of the country’s few international exporters, and has seen total sales more than double since exports began in 2019.
“We take our time and freeze water slowly, keeping it in motion... That’s how we end up with good ice,” said Kazuhiko Kuramoto, the firm’s fifth-generation head.
“My heart leaps with joy when I see ice that looks like a jewel,” he said as he poured cold hojicha tea into a glass filled with a large, clear sphere.
Using a technique that originally came from the US, specialist Japanese ice makers freeze water over a period of 48 to 72 hours, far longer than the few hours typically required for homemade ice or the 30 minutes it takes industrial ice machines.
As freezing begins and the ice forms from outside in, various impurities in the water get pushed towards the center, but the Japanese method involves removing that tainted water and replacing it with a fresh batch. Constant stirring helps remove air bubbles, resulting in completely transparent ice, known as junpyo in Japanese.
Although there is little scientific evidence, it is said that the technique also results in a colder, denser product that would cool rather than dilute a cocktail.
Native — a bar in Singapore that made this year’s Asia’s 50 Best Bars list — imports about 900kg of ice from Kuramoto each year.
“Local ice is more economical, but Kuramoto Ice is clearer, denser and melts more slowly,” co-owner Yong Wei said.
In Kanazawa, workers haul large blocks of ice across the factory floor, before starting on the delicate work of carving perfect spheres, cubes and rectangular blocks with cut corners.
Once packaged, the finished products — which could be made to precisely fit any glass — are stored in a room at minus-10°C before shipment.
Kuramoto is not blind to the environmental cost of transporting cubes of ice thousands of kilometers across the world, but insisted that small goods such as his have a relatively low environmental impact.
He said he had dreamed of reaching American bars since visiting Las Vegas more than a decade ago and realizing low-quality ice that melts easily and waters down the flavor was being used in expensive cocktails. The time-consuming ice-making technique often used in Japan, which tends to produce a higher quality product, had largely been phased out in the US.
At a Hilton Hotel bar near Tokyo, bartender Shingo Miyachi prepares a negroni with one of Kuramoto Ice’s big, clear cubes.
The ice fits perfectly in the glass, and its clarity makes it nearly invisible.
“Ice really has a huge impact on the taste of a cocktail,” Miyachi said. “[If it melts,] it especially affects the lingering aftertaste once you’ve taken a sip.”
Ice handling is considered an essential skill for Japanese bartenders, who often begin their training by learning to break it with precision.
“When you look at the ice and see the level of attention to detail, you can pretty much tell how seriously the bartender takes the flavor of the cocktail and how much care they’ve put into it,” he said. “A cocktail only really comes into being when the glass, the ice, and the liquid become one as a single unified whole.”

Unknown Publisher

01:42:01 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) is preparing a large business delegation to accompany him on his visit to Washington, two sources said, an unusual move given US skepticism toward Chinese investment and Beijing’s strained ties with private enterprise.
Xi rarely travels abroad with corporate executives, many of whom fell from of favor after Beijing’s regulatory crackdowns on the technology, education and property sectors that began in 2020.
“The White House is not tracking a Chinese CEO delegation,” an US official said. They did not explain what they meant by tracking.
Photo: Reuters
The business delegation for the Sept. 24 summit has not been reported before. Reuters could not determine which executives would join the delegation.
The move is aimed in part at signaling China’s willingness to support investment and commercial ties with the US, while offering the White House some possible economic wins ahead of midterm elections, one of the sources familiar with discussions said.
Xi last brought a sizeable business contingent to the US in 2015, including Alibaba Group Holding Ltd (阿里巴巴) founder Jack Ma (馬雲), Tencent Holdings Ltd (騰訊) founder Pony Ma (馬化騰), and executives from Chinese banks and state-owned firms.
During that visit, China signed a US$38 billion agreement for 300 Boeing Co aircraft and Xi met US technology executives including Apple Inc’s Tim Cook, Meta Platforms Inc’s Mark Zuckerberg and Amazon.com Inc founder Jeff Bezos.
By contrast, US President Donald Trump has travelled to China with large delegations of US executives, including on visits in 2017 and May this year, seeking greater access to Chinese markets. Trump took 18 executives, including Nvidia Corp CEO Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) and Tesla Inc CEO Elon Musk, to China in May.
The two nations announced formal mechanisms to manage trade and investment ties in May. However, three separate sources briefed on the matter said the US-China Board of Investment is unlikely to produce significant deliverables at the summit because of the challenging US environment for Chinese investment.
Expectations for the summit remain modest, with limited prospects for major breakthroughs, the sources said.
Beijing and Washington remain divided over which products should qualify as “non-sensitive” under the US-China Board of Trade, the three sources said.
About 10 categories of “non-sensitive” goods are being discussed for inclusion, but this could change closer to the summit, one of the sources said.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Thursday that both countries would make “some announcements on agriculture and non-tariff barriers” during the summit, without providing specifics.
US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent, Greer and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng (何立峰) meet early this month to discuss summit deliverables, four sources said. Reuters could not determine the exact date or location of the talks.

Photo: EPA

Of the envoys’ trip to Kyiv, he said: “No matter what happens next, contacts of this kind are undoubtedly always beneficial.”

Overwork, stress can damage vision, doctor warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:55 UTC
01:41:55 KST

Overwork and prolonged stress could damage vision, a doctor warned, after a 45-year-old woman who worked overtime late into the night for several nights experienced a sudden deterioration of the vision in her left eye.
The office worker, surnamed Yang (楊), experienced the sudden drop of visual acuity in her left eye to 0.3 after working overnight for several days amid heavy job-related stress, Madou Sin-Lau Hospital Department of Traditional Chinese Medicine doctor Ho Po-yi (何柏逸) said.
The woman also noticed that objects appeared darker and distorted, Ho said.
Photo: Liu Wan-chun, Taipei Times
She was diagnosed with central serous chorioretinopathy, a condition in which fluid leaks under the retina, forming a small blister that affects the central part of a person’s vision.
Her visual acuity gradually improved to about 0.8 after undergoing an integrated treatment regimen combining traditional Chinese and Western medicine, Ho said.
Excessive eye use can impair blood and lymphatic circulation around the eyes, causing fluid to accumulate and resulting in localized swelling and increased intraocular pressure, he said, adding that in severe cases, it can damage vision.
Central serous chorioretinopathy is a common disorder affecting the macula or nearby areas of the retina. It most frequently occurs among those aged 20 to 50.
People who are under prolonged psychological stress, overworked, experiencing heightened sympathetic nervous activity or exhibiting an impatient, “Type A” personality are at higher risk, Ho said.
People with cardiovascular disease have 2.25 to 2.3 times the risk of developing disorder than the general population, he added.
Typical symptoms include a dark spot in the center of the field of vision, distorted or shrunken images and a sudden decline in visual acuity, he said.
In most cases, the swelling is naturally reabsorbed within three to six months, but recurrent episodes should not be taken lightly and the condition should never be left untreated, Ho said.
People with milder symptoms can be treated with “ophthalmic acupuncture,” in which fine needles are inserted into specific acupuncture points along meridians around the eyes and within the eye socket, he said.
The treatment can stimulate microcirculation, help the accumulated fluid be naturally reabsorbed, and regulate the nerves around the eyes and intraocular pressure, he said.
Combined with acupuncture at points farther from the eyes and traditional Chinese herbal medicine to strengthen the spleen, promote fluid metabolism and soothe the liver, the approach aims to address an underlying tendency toward inflammation and fluid retention, he said.
An ophthalmic acupuncture session costs about NT$200 out of pocket, he said.
People should avoid staying up late and overexerting themselves, and find ways to relieve work-related stress, manage chronic illnesses and protect their eyes, Ho said, adding that people can also gently massage acupuncture points around their eyes.
Anyone who notices that objects viewed with one eye appear distorted, smaller or obscured by shadows should seek medical attention promptly, particularly when it is accompanied by severe headaches, nausea, vomiting or loss of part of the visual field, he said.

BOOKMAN BILINGUAL 雙語書林： Chinglish or Natural English? 中式英語或道地英語？
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:51 UTC
01:41:51 KST

1. 我忽然想起了一首以前聽過的歌。
ˇ Suddenly I recalled a song I once heard.
ˇ Suddenly I was reminded of a song I once heard.
Photo: AdobeStock 圖片:AdobeStock
χ Suddenly I reminded a song I once heard.
註：remind 是「提醒」、「使想起」；recall 含有「回想起」、「想起」的意思。前者指「某人／某事提醒某人某件事情」，後者為「某人主動地想起了某事或某人」，試比較下列句子：
I reminded him that there would be a lecture in the evening.（我提醒他晚上有演講。）
Photo: Adobe Stock 圖片:Adobe Stock
He recalled that there would be a lecture in the evening.（他想起晚上有演講。）
2. 他們創造了許多經濟奇蹟。
ˇ They have worked (/performed/done) economic wonders.
χ They have created economic wonders.
註：中文「創造」用法較廣泛，但英語裡的 create 不可濫用。例如：「創造了奇蹟」，不能說 to create miracles (wonders)；應說 to work (perform, do) miracles 或 to do mighty work。下列幾句中 create 的用法是正確的：
Dickens created many characters.
MLA Style—This style was created by the Modern Language Association of America in 1985.
3. 僅僅一年他發明了不少有用的機器。
ˇ In one year alone he invented quite a number of useful machines.
χ In one year alone he discovered quite a number of useful machines.
註：discover 是「發現」，發現的事物是客觀存在，而前所未知的。例如：
Columbus discovered America in 1492.
I discovered that it was too late to catch the last train.
invent 是「發明」，發明的事物以前並不存在，經人們創造出來的。例如：
The art of printing was invented in the Han dynasty.
He has invented numerous tools that help researchers better study anatomy.
invent 有時指「捏造」。例如：
The pupil invented an excuse for his being absent.
4. 這位技師教他們怎樣操作機器。
ˇ The technician taught them how to operate the machine.
χ The technician taught them how to master the machine.
註：to master 一般指「精通」，是對知識而言，沒有「操作機器」的意義。可以說 to master a language，不可說 *to master a tractor (an airplane) 等等。
5. 你願意和我去公園散步嗎？
ˇ Do you care for a walk in the park with me?
ˇ Do you care to take a stroll in the park with me?
χ Do you mind to take a walk in the park with me?
註：徵詢某人是否樂於做某事，或對某物是否感到興趣，應用 to care to do something 或 to care for (/about) something。例如：
Do you care to go to the concert (/movies) with me?
Would you care for an orange (/another cup of tea)?
徵詢某人對做某項事是否介意或反對時，才用 mind，例如：
Do you mind if I smoke?
Would you mind passing me the salt and pepper?
I hope you don’t mind if I smoke.
Do you mind if I turn off the air conditioner?
Exercises
A. 他提醒我下午跟客戶有約。
He __________ me that I had an appointment with my client in the afternoon.
1. reminded 2. recalled 3. was reminded of 4. remembered
B. 我可以開電視機嗎？
Do you __________ if I turn on the television?
1. mind for 2. mind
3. care about 4. cares
Answers:
A. 1 B. 2

www.bookman.com.tw

Army’s second nationwide brigade-level exercise to run for 10 days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:50 UTC
01:41:50 KST

The second edition of the Army’s nationwide brigade-level force-on-force exercise next month will take place over 10 days instead of seven, a military source said yesterday.
According to the source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, this year’s Lu Sheng (陸勝) Exercise will involve the Taoyuan-based Army 269th Mechanized Infantry Brigade and the Kaohsiung-based 564th Combined Arms Brigade and take place from Oct. 14 to 23.
As with the inaugural edition in 2025, this year’s drill will focus on testing 24-hour combat readiness, dispersed command-and-control operations, unscripted and realistic war scenarios, and rules of engagement (ROE) to assess the two key combat units’ defensive capabilities in the event of a Chinese invasion, the source said.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of National Defense
Last year’s Lu Sheng exercise lasted seven days and six nights, while this year’s drill has been extended to nine nights and 10 days, the source added.
Another key feature of Lu Sheng is the deployment of the US-developed Team Awareness Kit (TAK), which allows Army commanders to track friendly forces, mark enemy units and receive real-time updates.
The Army also uses a new “firepower value” system during the exercise to assess the combat effectiveness of different military units or weapons systems, according to the source.
Su Tzu-yun (蘇紫雲), director of the Institute for National Defense and Security Research’s Defense Strategy and Resources Division, said that “firepower value” is a fundamental metric used during military exercises or tabletop war games, similar to a batter’s batting average or a pitcher’s earned run average in baseball.
Using the system, the Army can calculate which brigade has the upper hand in a force-on-force confrontation based on factors including distance, troop strength, and military equipment, he said.
Another institute scholar, Shu Hsiao-huang (舒孝煌), said the force-on-force Lu Sheng exercise would make it easier for the Army to identify potential vulnerabilities within each brigade, including in fire support integration, target acquisition and logistics, and make adjustments accordingly.
Lu Sheng was first held in 2025, when the Army integrated regional brigade-level drills into a single exercise.
Previously, brigade-level exercises were held under the names Chang Ching (長青) in central Taiwan, Chang Tai (長泰) in northern Taiwan, and Chang Sheng (長勝) in southern Taiwan.

Nepalese rescuers buoyed by miracle finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:44 UTC
01:41:44 KST

Nepalese rescuers faced challenging conditions yesterday as search operations after catastrophic floods entered their 12th day, buoyed by the extraordinary rescues of four survivors.
The glacial and mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border has killed at least 1,372 people and left more than 5,500 missing across the two countries.
Rescuers found two more people alive on Saturday, joining two saved the day before in what have been described as miraculous tales of survival.
Photo: AFP
Three of those have been found in hydropower tunnels where the government initially said it believed more than 100 workers could be alive.
“Search and rescue is going on at the tunnels despite geography, adverse weather and lack of connectivity,” Nepalese Minister of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation Biraj Bhakta Shrestha said.
Rescue workers were experiencing “multiple challenges,” he added.
The wall of icy water and debris tore through mountain districts on Aug. 26, destroying roads, bridges and other infrastructure.
On Saturday, rescuers pulled a Chinese man alive from deep inside a hydropower tunnel, and a 64-year-old Nepalese woman, Chandrika Shrestha, from her mud-covered home.
Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the latter rescue had “given hope to the entire nation.”
A day earlier, two Nepali hydropower workers were rescued at the Trishuli 3A tunnel, where searches continue alongside multiple other sites, with at least 12 hydropower projects affected.
Biraj Bhakta Shrestha said work was continuing to restore electricity in several areas.
“Places that have unreachable, we’ve tried to restore power with solar,” he said.
Nepalese Minister of Foreign Affairs Shisir Khanal called the disaster a “Himalayan tsunami” and warned reconstruction costs could run into the billions of dollars.
The UN has said the magnitude of the destruction makes delivering aid an immense challenge, and has launched a US$50 million appeal to help more than 84,000 people.
With mortuaries overflowing, Nepal has buried hundreds of bodies in mass graves, after taking DNA samples for identification, police said.
Only about 100 bodies have been identified and handed over to families.
Nepal would hold a national day of mourning today, the 13th day since the disaster, in line with a traditional period of mourning in Hindu rituals.
While the exact cause of the glacial collapse is unclear, climate change is accelerating glacial melting worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.
In Nepal, rescuers have retrieved 1,341 bodies, while around 4,996 people remain missing, according to the disaster agency.
Chinese state media report that 31 people have been killed and 531 are missing in Tibet.

KMT and TPP halt election cooperation amid Jhubei spat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:44 UTC
01:41:44 KST

The Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) yesterday said it would halt all electoral cooperation with the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) in Hsinchu County, after the allied opposition parties refused to defer to each other’s preferred candidate in the Jhubei City mayoral race.
On Thursday, the second-to-last day to formally enter the race, the KMT’s Wu Hsu-chih (吳旭智) and TPP’s Chiu Chen-yuan (邱臣遠) registered as candidates for Jhubei mayor in the local elections on Nov. 28.
They would face off against Democratic Progressive Party candidate Tseng Sheng-kai (曾聖凱).
Photo: Liao Chen-huei, Taipei Times
While Wu initially tried to downplay the KMT-TPP standoff, saying that cooperation in the race was still possible, comments by another local KMT candidate appeared to fan the flames.
Hsu Hsin-ying (徐欣瑩), the KMT’s nominee for Hsinchu county commissioner, of which Jhubei City is a part, said on Friday during an interview that the parties had not made any agreement on who should defer to whom in the Jhubei race, and that the TPP had never formally pledged to support a primary.
On Saturday, TPP Chairman Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌) accused the KMT and Hsu of “going back on their word,” and then making matters worse by “continuing to lie about it in public.”
At a meeting of the TPP’s Central Committee yesterday morning, the party passed a resolution suspending electoral cooperation with the KMT on all races in Hsinchu County.
TPP Secretary-General Chou Yu-hsiu (周榆修) said after the meeting that the KMT and Hsu’s “inability to keep promises” had “seriously damaged the foundation of mutual trust that the TPP and KMT have gradually built over the last two years.”
Chou also called on TPP members to unite behind its nominee in the Jhubei race, warning that any party members who publicly support or stand on stage with an opponent would face disciplinary measures, including possible expulsion.
The larger opposition KMT and smaller TPP reached an agreement in March to coordinate candidates and cooperate on policy positions in the elections.
Under the agreement, the TPP has agreed to support the KMT’s mayoral or magistrate nominees in New Taipei City, Taichung, Tainan, Kaohsiung and Yilan County.
Meanwhile, the KMT is supporting the TPP’s candidate in Chiayi City, while the parties have agreed to jointly support an independent in Chiayi County and an independent former TPP member in Hsinchu City.
Hsu was the founder in 2015 of the Minkuotang, a KMT splinter party. Wu is also a former Minkuotang chairman.
Jhubei, and Hsinchu County in general, have grown rapidly and gained prominence in the past few years because of their proximity to Hsinchu Science Park.

How a principal saved 900 students from the flood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:43 UTC
01:41:43 KST

School principal Rajendra Dawadi was inside his school near Nepal’s Trishuli River with about 900 students last week when a colleague delivered an urgent warning.
“My accountant came to the school and said, ‘The flood is coming, the flood is coming,’” Dawadi said.
He quickly ordered an evacuation, and teachers hurried hundreds of students from classrooms to higher ground. Minutes later, he watched the Trishuli Bazaar Secondary School he had run for years collapse into a raging torrent.
Photo: AFP
“If the information was wrong, we would lose a day of schooling,” Dawadi said. “But if it was true, we were going to lose our lives.”
Students were panicked and one girl fainted, he said. Bus drivers bringing in other students were asked to turn back, including one driver who had just entered school grounds.
The timely evacuation saved about 900 lives. Now, standing above the scarred banks of the river in Nuwakot District more than a week after the disaster, Dawadi described himself simply as “a principal without a school.”
The tsunami-like wall of water, ice and debris unleashed by a massive glacial and rock collapse along the Nepal-China border killed at least 1,362 people and has left more than 5,500 missing across the two countries.
Five students died in the flooding outside the school, as well as a teacher and a security staff member, Dawadi said.
The staff member, who left the school after him, “had probably wanted to close the gate,” he said.
Authorities in Trishuli Bazaar had not provided an evacuation plan, Dawadi said.
Some residents tried to cross the bridge, but were swept away. Others took refuge on higher ground.
“When I looked back, the school was standing there like the finest of buildings, and in five minutes, everything collapsed,” Dawadi said. “It’s also the school where I studied. There was nothing left.”
Santoshi Dotel was in accounting class when the evacuation order came. At first, she struggled to comprehend the danger.
“We never would have thought the flood could reach such a scale,” she said.
She initially went down to the river with her friend to try to cross and reach her family home.
Then the water surged.
“The bridge was swept away,” she said. “I started to cry because I thought I would never get home and that there was nothing we could do.”
Her friend pulled her up a hillside as the flood roared below.
Santoshi broke down into tears as she recalled the anguish of not knowing for hours whether her parents had survived.
It was only four days later that a helicopter finally reunited her with her family.
“I found my mother as I stepped out of the helicopter,” she said. “She hugged me and started to cry. My mind just stopped working.”
Her mother, Durga Dotel, had feared the worst.
“Seeing the river in flood, I had lost all hope that my daughter had survived,” she said.
According to figures cited by Save the Children, at least 69 schools were destroyed or damaged, disrupting the education of nearly 19,000 children.
Dawadi said the disaster was “far worse” than the earthquake that hit Nepal in 2015.
“The school had been completely destroyed [after the earthquake], but we rebuilt it,” he said. “This time, we’ve lost the land and the building. We need a school again. But first, we need somewhere safe to build it.”

Military budgets more arms production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:37 UTC
01:41:37 KST

The military is significantly expanding domestic production capacity to improve self-sufficiency in equipment and ammunition during wartime, the Ministry of National Defense’s proposed budget for next year showed.
The Armaments Bureau’s Production and Manufacturing Center plans to invest more than NT$14.15 billion (US$447.4 million) from this year to 2032 to establish or expand production capacity at four of its factories, it showed.
The project covers production capacity for armored vehicles, artillery, ammunition, explosives, optical equipment, specialized batteries, and chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear defense gear.
Photo: Lee Hui-chou, Taipei Times
Demand for various types of ammunition is expected to increase as new tanks are fielded, troop numbers grow and reserve combat capabilities are reinforced, the bureau said.
It plans to expand production lines for warhead bodies, cartridge cases, primers, propellants, explosives, gun barrels, optical equipment and gas masks, while introducing semiautomated and automated equipment.
Budget documents show that the bureau allocated more than NT$328.8 million for the project this year, and funding would rise to more than NT$1.52 billion next year. Budget payments are expected to peak from 2028 to 2030, reaching as much as NT$4.13 billion in 2029. The project is scheduled to be completed in 2032.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
The project was intended to be financed through the Executive Yuan’s proposed NT$1.25 trillion special defense budget and was not included in this year’s national defense budget. After the Legislative Yuan’s final version excluded certain commercial procurement, contracted manufacturing and production-capacity projects, the ministry began securing funding through supplementary budgets and annual government budgets, and the project was subsequently included in next year’s budget.
With the military’s procurement of 108 M1A2T tanks, the project plans to establish domestic production lines for 120mm tank rounds.
When the military began pursuing the M1A2T procurement in 2019, it said the bureau already had production capacity for 105mm tank rounds and would establish 120mm tank round production capacity through industrial cooperation, technology transfer and local development.
The bureau sought bids last year for a 120mm tank ammunition assembly system.
Separately, as the army continues taking delivery of US-made High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems (HIMARS), locally developed Thunderbolt-2000 rocket artillery systems are set to receive additional war reserve ammunition.
The army would allocate more than NT$691.7 million to commission the National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology to produce Thunderbolt-2000 high explosive rockets, the budget proposal showed.
The procurement would cover MK-30 and MK-45 war reserve rockets and is scheduled to be completed next year, bolstering the military’s multiple-launch rocket firepower to stop an amphibious landing.
The Thunderbolt-2000 can be equipped with different rocket pods depending on operational requirements.
The MK-30 has a range of about 15km to 30km. Each launcher can carry up to three rocket pods, with a total capacity of 27 rockets.
The Thunderbolt-2000 is an important component of the army’s counter-landing planning, as MK-30 rockets are suitable for hitting landing aircraft and troops advancing toward the shore or assembling for an assault.
The MK-45 extends the range farther offshore to amphibious transfer areas, as it can engage targets about 25km to 45km away. Each launcher carries two pods containing a total of 12 rockets that could be fired in rapid salvos, providing dense fire coverage over large areas.
MK-30 and MK-45 rockets can be fitted with different warheads depending on the mission.
The budget documents identify the rockets being procured as “high-explosive rockets,” which are primarily intended to use blast and fragmentation effects against area targets such as troops, vehicles and defensive positions.
By comparison, the HIMARS offers longer-range precision-strike capabilities. It can attack high-value targets such as enemy command posts, air defense positions and assembly areas. Its precision-guided rockets have a range of about 70km, while Army Tactical Missile System missiles can reach targets up to 300km away, providing a deep-strike capability.
The HIMARS and Thunderbolt-2000 have complementary capabilities, with the former serving as a longer-range precision system and the latter providing shorter-range area fire.

Drone operators fined NT$16 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:36 UTC
01:41:36 KST

Authorities fined drone operators a total of NT$16 million (US$505,849) in 72 cases last year and the first half of this year, with more than 80 percent of the contraventions occurring at airports, reservoirs and science parks, the Civil Aviation Administration (CAA) said.
YouTuber Chung Ming-hsuan (鍾明軒) was fined NT$330,000 for illegally operating a drone near the Ma-anshan Nuclear Power Plant in June and for failure to display a registration number on the aircraft.
Last month, the triggering of a drone-detection sensor in the controlled area surrounding Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport forced the north and south runways to suspend takeoffs and landings for 10 minutes, affecting nine flights.
Photo courtesy of Taoyuan City Councilor Hsu Yu-shu
The CAA fined drone operators in 47 cases last year and 25 in the first half of this year, the agency said.
Twenty-four of the fined infractions took place in airport restricted airspace, 19 at reservoirs and 15 in science parks, it said.
The remaining 14 cases occurred in other restricted areas, such as Taipei Main Station and power plants, it added.
Commercial aircraft travel at high speeds and low altitudes during takeoff and landing, and a drone being sucked into an engine or colliding with an aircraft could cause a major disaster, Chaoyang University of Technology Department of Aviation Technology director Lu Yen-liang (盧衍良) said yesterday.
Reservoirs and power plants are subject to air restrictions to prevent drones from crashing into and damaging equipment, contaminating water sources or causing secondary disasters, he said.
As centers of high-tech industry, science parks must guard against aerial photography to prevent trade secrets from being leaked, Lu said.
A drone crash at a science park could also damage sensitive equipment and injure workers, he added.
While enforcing no-fly zones at airports is a top priority because drone incursions can threaten flight safety, local government no-fly zones have fewer resources and depend more on public reports, meaning some contraventions might go undetected, former National Cheng Kung University Department of Transportation and Communication Management Science associate professor Melody Dai (戴佐敏) said.
Drones are prohibited in reservoirs and science parks, and flying them without approval can result in fines of NT$30,000 to NT$1.5 million under the Civil Aviation Act (民用航空法), and the drone would be confiscated in serious cases, CAA drone office executive secretary Keng Hua (耿驊) said.
People can download the Ministry of Transportation and Communications’ Drone Map app or go to the CAA’s drone management system to see maps of restricted airspace, Keng said.
As of the end of June, there were 36,066 valid drone licenses and 42,016 registered drones, CAA data showed.
One drone operator surnamed Chen (陳) said he checks the CAA’s official Web site before every flight to see whether drones are permitted in the area, but some operators might be unaware of the rules or take their chances and enter restricted airspace.
Notifications from government apps about restricted airspace might not be enough for beginners, who might accidently contravene regulations, drone operator Wu Ming-yang (吳明陽) said.
Retailers should put warning labels on drones and promote the regulations, he said.
Wu called for the legalization of drone flights during the 30 minutes before sunrise and after sunset so photographers can capture better footage.

Doctor warns against lancing boils at home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:36 UTC
01:41:36 KST

A doctor last week warned against treating boils at home, after an octogenarian woman attempted to lance a boil on her buttocks with a sewing needle, but ended up developing a bacterial infection, causing the boil to grow to the size of a baseball.
Tseng Yu-kang (曾禹康), an attending colorectal surgeon from Taichung Veterans General Hospital who sees patients at the Dajia Branch of Lee General Hospital, said that the woman, who lived alone, believed the boil was not particularly serious.
In a scene that could have been depicted in a historical drama, the woman attempted to lance it using a sewing needle that she had heated over a flame to disinfect it, Tseng said.
Photo: Chang Hsuan-tse, Taipei Times
By the time she sought treatment, the affected area had swollen to the size of a baseball, and it took nearly an hour to thoroughly clean out the pus-filled wound, he said.
Jabbing the needle at what might have been inflammation of the hair follicle likely forced the pus into the deeper fascial layer, triggering a more severe infection that eventually swelled into a large and painful boil, he said.
Puncturing a puss-filled boil on the buttocks with the needle is like using a syringe to inject poison into the body, Tseng said.
Fascia is like a highway for bacteria, he said.
If bacteria spread through the loose tissue beneath the skin, they can cause blockages in small blood vessels and tissue death, and without prompt medical attention, the infection could lead to fatal sepsis, he said.
Tseng urged people not to treat boils themselves, as it could worsen the condition.
About 90 percent of infections around the anus originate from infected glands inside the anus, while some start in the skin, Tseng said.
Prolonged pressure on the buttocks, combined with poorly ventilated clothing and dampness from sweat, can help bacteria thrive, he said.
Bacteria can enter through hair follicles or tiny breaks in the skin, causing deeper infections and boils, he added.
Squeezing a boil with the hands or tools before it has come to a head can inadvertently spread bacteria and even cause cellulitis, Tseng said.

Fuel prices to remain stable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:35 UTC
01:41:35 KST

CPC Corp, Taiwan (CPC, 台灣中油) on Saturday announced that it would keep its domestic gasoline and diesel prices steady this week, and Formosa Petrochemical Corp (台塑石化) followed suit yesterday, despite a spike in international crude oil prices.
This week would be the sixth consecutive week that CPC and Formosa have maintained domestic crude oil prices, despite crude oil prices moving higher in the wake of renewed hostilities between the US and Iran.
Front-month Brent crude oil futures — the international oil benchmark — last week gained 9.28 percent to settle at US$96.28 per barrel on the Intercontinental Exchange in London, while West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures — the US oil benchmark — increased 9.69 percent to US$91.48 per barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
CPC said its floating price mechanism, based on a weighted average of 70 percent Dubai and 30 percent Brent crude, showed that the average international crude oil price rose to US$99.82 last week from US$91.56 per barrel the previous week.
A stronger New Taiwan dollar, which averaged NT$31.682 last week against the US dollar, compared with NT$31.775 a week earlier, helped CPC slightly ease crude oil purchasing cost pressure, it said.
Retail gasoline prices this week would remain at NT$30.5, NT$32 and NT$34 per liter for 92, 95 and 98-octane unleaded gasoline respectively at CPC and Formosa stations, while prices of premium diesel would remain at NT$29.3 per liter at CPC stations and NT$29.1 per liter at Formosa pumps, the companies said.

At the Met, snakes have to audition for the opera
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:34 UTC
01:41:34 KST

Pretty much everyone on stage at the Metropolitan Opera in New York must audition — even the snake who would briefly take center stage in an upcoming adaptation of a Mozart classic.
In charge of deciding who gets the s-s-s-s-starring reptilian role is Zoe Ziegfeld, a carnival performer-turned-opera actor cast as the snake handler in the Met’s version of Cosi fan tutte, inspired by Coney Island in the 1950s.
Ziegfeld takes each snake, lets it slither and wrap around, then hoists the animal over their head, rehearsing what they would do under the bright lights at center stage for each performance. Ziegfeld looks each one in the eye, almost face-to-face as they evaluate the snake’s demeanor.
Photo: AP
“I need to know that the animal is comfortable with people and with what we are doing,” Ziegfeld said.
In the cold-blooded competition, a boa constrictor named Princess won. She is a larger snake with a better visual presence on stage.
“We will be moving forward with Princess [the big sun-glow boa constrictor who is yellow-peach] in rehearsals on a trial basis! She is a wonderful snake, and the trial is not about her, but rather about me and my strength,” Ziegfeld wrote in an e-mail after the auditions were over.
This is the third time Ziegfeld has played the role of the snake charmer in the Met’s adaptation of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s 1790 opera.
In Mozart’s original, two Italian soldiers decide to test their lovers’ fidelity by pretending to head off to war. They then disguise themselves and try to seduce each other’s girlfriends. In this version, the plot remains mostly the same, but the setting is a 1950s Coney Island carnival complete with vibrant scenery and sideshow performers.
When Ziegfeld tried out several years ago, live snakes were not allowed in the audition space. Instead, Ziegfeld brought a video of their snake-charming act, then hammered home their carnival sideshow bona fides by knocking a nail into their own nasal cavity in what was called the Human Blockhead act.
The snakes came to their audition thanks to Nancy Novograd and her company All Tame Animals.
The first two snakes to audition were a bit small. One might have clashed with Ziegfeld’s top.
The key is personality, Novograd said.
“Animals have to perform as do human talent. Sometimes they have a set type of behaviors that they have to demonstrate. And sometimes they just have to get along with the talent,” Novograd said. “So in this case, they have to be the right color, size, and Zoe has to like them.”

Exchange reserves climb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:34 UTC
01:41:34 KST

Taiwan’s foreign exchange reserves rose to again exceed US$600 billion last month, ending two months of declines, the central bank said on Friday.
Foreign exchange reserves are overseas assets held by a central bank that can be readily deployed, including foreign currency deposits and government securities.
Last month, reserves rose US$7.633 billion from a month earlier to US$601.904 billion, the biggest monthly increase in more than a year, Department of Foreign Exchange Director-General Eugene Tsai (蔡炯民) said during a news conference at the central bank in Taipei.
Photo: Reuters
The increase was driven mainly by investment returns on the central bank’s foreign currency assets, appreciation of major non-US currencies against the US dollar and the bank’s intervention in the foreign-exchange market to maintain orderly trading, Tsai said.
Last month, the US Dollar Index fell 0.49 percent, while most major currencies strengthened against the greenback. The euro and British pound each gained 0.68 percent, the Canadian dollar rose 0.91 percent, the yen advanced 0.49 percent and the yuan appreciated 0.35 percent, central bank data showed.
The New Taiwan dollar was the strongest performer, rising 2.51 percent against the greenback during the month, as foreign investors posted net inflows of about US$1.2 billion to hunt for bargains in the local equity market, Tsai said.
To help maintain the local foreign exchange market stable, the central bank intervened by buying US dollars and selling NT dollars to moderate the greenback’s losses, he said.
Tsai did not disclose how much the central bank spent in last month’s market intervention. The bank announced in a joint statement with the US Department of the Treasury last year that it would release the figure on a quarterly basis.
Tsai said it remained unclear whether the yen’s appreciation was driven by official intervention or short-covering. The yen has unique characteristics as a major international currency, including its role as a safe-haven asset and its use in carry trades, he said.
Movements in the yen could influence other Asian currencies, but the direction of individual currencies would ultimately depend on their own supply-and-demand dynamics, Tsai said.
Meanwhile, the central bank data showed that as of the end of last month, foreign investors held US$1.861 trillion in Taiwan-listed stocks, bonds and NT dollar-denominated deposits, up from US$1.663 trillion at the end of July.
These holdings were worth 309 percent of Taiwan’s total foreign exchange reserves last month, compared with 280 percent a month earlier, the central bank said. A strong rebound in the TAIEX, which rose 6.98 percent in the month, reflected the increase in these foreign holdings, it said.

Building Canada’s post-US economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:33 UTC
01:41:33 KST

US President Donald Trump first hit Canada with substantial tariffs in 2018, targeting aluminum and steel. He did so again after returning to office last year, targeting dozens of goods, although he later exempted those compliant with the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement.
Last week, after trade talks broke down, he repeated his favorite trick, imposing 50 percent tariffs on a vast array of Canadian imports, including wine and mittens. Canada responded with “dollar-for-dollar” retaliatory tariffs.
Trump’s tariffs have come nowhere close to delivering a US manufacturing revival. Instead, they have inflicted losses on businesses and slowed growth in both countries. His actions have also shown that any protectionist US president could exploit trade integration with an ally for practical or ideological ends.
Canada is deeply vulnerable. Its merchandise exports to the US account for one-fifth of its GDP, and nowhere is this dependence more acute than in the auto industry. Given that automobile manufacturing depends on tightly integrated regional supply chains across North America, Europe and Asia, it is difficult to imagine a viable Canadian auto industry without ready access to the Great Lakes-centered manufacturing ecosystem.
To reduce its strategic vulnerability to Trump’s extortion, Canada must develop industries that can operate freely across continents. We analyze these opportunities — and explain how Canada can seize them — in our forthcoming book Canada After America: A Strategy for Prosperity in a Changed World.
Canada’s natural resources are obviously an enormous asset. The planned West Coast oil pipeline is essential to bringing Alberta’s petroleum to Asian markets. Investments in new and expanded mines, and in the infrastructure needed to export their output, are also laudable. Global demand for Canada’s resources is robust, and, crucially, the country does not need access to American supply chains to extract them.
The same goes for several other value-added industries. Pharmaceuticals, manufactured from widely available basic chemicals, derive most of their value from the knowledge embedded in each medicine. Medical devices are expensive, high-value goods often purchased by hospitals rather than individual consumers, and can incorporate specialized inputs from around the world.
Consider aerospace. Like automobiles, it involves intensive manufacturing, but planes are produced at relatively low volumes and according to extremely stringent quality standards. The necessarily slow pace of building an airplane enables genuinely global supply chains, with components sourced from numerous advanced economies.
Canada already has an established aerospace industry, led by Bombardier. It also has a number of notable biotech companies. Yet several of its European peers, including much smaller countries, generate tens of billions of dollars more in exports from these sectors.
All these distance-resilient industries depend heavily on new knowledge and invest in research and development (R&D) accordingly. Although Canada is home to world-leading research universities and a highly educated population, it is a notorious laggard in private-sector innovation. Canadian business R&D spending has hovered at about 1 percent of GDP for decades.
According to the latest Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development data, the US, Germany, Japan, South Korea, Sweden and Israel all spend between two and six times as much relative to GDP.
Canadian private-sector R&D is also unusually concentrated among small companies. In the world’s leading tech economies, by contrast, large firms account for the lion’s share of business R&D expenditures.
Contrary to popular belief, research is chiefly conducted not by start-ups, but by the likes of Space Exploration Technologies Corp and AstraZeneca: firms that have scaled and have the financial wherewithal to invest heavily in developing new technologies.
Canada has relatively few champions of that scale, which helps explain why small and medium-size enterprises (SMEs) account for such a large share of its R&D.
Information and communications technology is a striking exception. Canada’s per-capita R&D spending in the sector is among the world’s highest, and the country has produced several large, business-facing firms like Shopify and OpenText. The core constraint is therefore not a systemic inadequacy. Rather, Canada struggles to build large firms in industries that are more capital and regulation-intensive than software.
The problem is compounded by the structure of government support for private R&D. Canada provides substantial R&D funding through tax credits, but the program, though recently reformed, remains biased toward small firms. Tax credits also leave companies reliant on uncertain refunds after investments have been made. Other countries, like Israel and Germany, have traditionally funded private R&D through upfront grants.
Canada’s growth is further impeded by sluggish regulatory approvals and government procurement practices. The country’s healthcare system relies on multistage reviews of new medicines involving sequential federal and provincial approvals. Other countries expedite approvals by conducting these reviews concurrently. For a Canadian pharmaceutical company developing a new drug, such delays can make the difference between profitability and bankruptcy.
A more ambitious approach to procurement could foster innovation. Government R&D budgets are often below 1 percent of GDP, while purchases of equipment and supplies typically exceed 10 percent.
For example, in Israel, companies compete to solve public problems like emergency-room overcrowding. South Korea requires government agencies at every level to devote 20 percent of their procurement budgets to promising new technologies and companies approved by an independent agency. Governments act as anchor customers, helping innovative firms grow.
Sweden, Switzerland, Denmark, Israel and others show that small countries can cultivate thriving tech industries. Canada can do the same, but first it must confront difficult political questions about healthcare regulation and SME funding. Whatever tensions these debates provoke would pale in comparison to the consequences of remaining subject to the whims and malignant whimsy of its unreliable southern neighbor.
Ricardo Hausmann, a former minister of planning of Venezuela and former chief economist at the Inter-American Development Bank, is a professor at Harvard Kennedy School and director of the Harvard Growth Lab. Eric Protzer is a senior research fellow at the Harvard Growth Lab. Hausmann and Protzer are coauthors of the forthcoming Canada After America: A Strategy for Prosperity in a Changed World.
Copyright: Project Syndicate

EU chief due in Greenland to boost ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:32 UTC
01:41:32 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen headed to Greenland yesterday for a two-day visit aimed at reaffirming the bloc’s support for the Danish autonomous territory coveted by US President Donald Trump.
Today, she is due to sign a joint declaration between the EU and Greenland.
“Greenland is becoming increasingly important to the EU as a gateway to the Arctic and because of its geopolitical location, critical raw materials and role in Arctic security,” Royal Danish Defence College researcher Marc Jacobsen said.
Photo:AFP
Trump was adamant earlier this year about Washington’s need to control the vast Arctic island for reasons of national security, although he ultimately ruled out annexing it by force.
A Danish-Greenlandic-US working group has since met regularly to find an agreement on cooperation going forward.
Following Trump’s threats, European countries broadly backed Denmark and Greenland, and in January, Von der Leyen vowed “massive” EU investment in Greenland to step up security in the Arctic.
Greenland is not a member of the bloc although Denmark is.
Brussels has also proposed doubling direct EU aid to Greenland to 530 million euros (US$615.49 million) under the bloc’s next budget for the 2028-to-2034 period.
The Financial Times said Von der Leyen is expected to propose an additional 200 million euros in support during her visit.
Her visit coincides with the start of NATO’s Arctic Shield military exercise, bringing together soldiers from 10 countries.
University of Quebec geopolitics researcher Mikaa Blugeon-Mered said the timing is “not insignificant coincidence.”
The Trump administration has repeatedly accused Denmark of neglecting Greenland and Arctic security. Copenhagen has since reinvested in the region, as has NATO, which launched its Arctic Sentry mission at the start of the year.
“The EU cannot provide Greenland with a military security guarantee in the way NATO can, but it can provide something politically important: a clear signal that Greenland is not standing alone,” Jacobsen said.
The message is all the more important as the US has kept up pressure on Greenland.
“We’ve been getting ‘postcards’ from Trump or those close to him about Greenland every month, showing that they haven’t forgotten,” Blugeon-Mered said.
One such image Trump posted on Truth Social in May showed him peering over the island, with the headline “Hello, Greenland!”
Greenland is also struggling to develop its mining industry, which could help it fund its independence from Denmark.
In this area, Greenlandic and European interests are “highly complementary,” Jacobsen said.
“Greenland needs investment, infrastructure and markets if it is to realize its mining ambitions, while the EU is looking for more secure and diversified access to critical raw materials,” he said.
However, turning Greenland’s geological potential into reality is proving more difficult than expected.
About 135 mining permits are held by more than 60 companies, but only two mines are in operation.
“The question is whether the current geopolitical momentum will ultimately be a game-changer,” Jacobsen said.
Blugeon-Mered said von der Leyen’s visit to Greenland — her second in two years — was a strong signal that European investment is long-term.
