Far-right AfD wins key German state election but may fail to secure majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:17:39 UTC
01:17:39 KST

The populist, far-right, anti-immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has emerged as the winner in a crucial state election in Germany, exit polls have projected, securing a historic result and more than doubling its support. The AfD now appear on the brink of becoming the first far-right party to gain power in Germany at state level since the second world war.
Initial exit polls showed the party to have secured 44.4% of the vote, a larger share than predicted, and decisively larger than that of the Christian Democrats (CDU) of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, in a contest that was being followed across the world. However, it still remains unclear as to how and whether the AfD will be able to form a government, having ruled out entering a coalition and being refused any form of cooperation by the mainstream parties.
The CDU was trailing massively on around 18.4% and the far-left Die Linke was third with 9.3%, with the Social Democrats on 8.4% and the Greens on 8.7% by around early evening. The smaller BSW reached the 5% hurdle needed to re-enter parliament, against expectations. The party, an offshoot of Die Linke, has agreed to cooperate with the AfD on issues such as energy price reform.
Participation was at a record high of 76.5%.
Votes are still being counted, but it appeared initially that the AfD might have failed to secure an absolute majority – the condition it has said is central to it taking power, given its refusal to govern with another party.
The CDU and all other mainstream parties have also refused to collude with the AfD in a government, in what is referred to as a Brandmauer, or firewall. The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classed as “rightwing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency.
Addressing jubilant supporters, Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, said: “We have made history in this country”. Speaking to public broadcaster ARD, he said his party was ready to reach out to all powers that strove for political change.
“We extend a hand to all democratic forces that wish to pursue better policies,” a beaming Siegmund said after exit polls had been published. He said themes such as migration and domestic security were not up for debate.
The CDU described its result as “bitter” but said it would not back down from its refusal to rule together with the AfD, which the far-right party has also ruled out.
Franziska Hoppermann, general secretary of the CDU, called it a “defeat overall” for the Christian Democrats. “And it is also a defeat for all those who have borne responsibility in the democracy in Saxony-Anhalt over the past 35 years,” she added, in reference to the difficult post-communist era.
She ruled out any discussion over Merz’s future, which analysts have suggested will increasingly become a topic of debate after his party’s defeat. In one recent poll, only 9% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt said they were satisfied with Merz’s politics. Siegmund on Sunday evening called Merz “a very good campaigner for the AfD”.
Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader, said the result gave her party a “clear government mandate” and that it would “talk to all the parties” to work out a strategy as to how the AfD could rule.
About 1.7 million people were eligible to vote in the east-central state of 2.1 million residents.
Final polls had shown the AfD to have around 40-41% of support, and the party appears to have almost doubled its 2021 result of 23.7%.
The number of undecided voters in advance of the vote was much lower than at previous elections, polling showed.
The small state has been governed since 2002 by Merz’s conservative CDU, together with two smaller parties.
The Saxony-Anhalt election had been seen as the biggest test yet for Merz, who is very unpopular, along with his government, a coalition with the SPD. Merz has thus far failed in his promises to reset Germany’s struggling economy or stop the rise of the AfD, which has been making regular and steady gains since it entered parliament in 2017 and is now the Bundestag’s leading opposition party. Irregular immigration has reduced since Merz has been in office, but not to an extent that has appeased the average voter.
In national polls, the CDU has also been overtaken by the AfD, which has its eyes on victory at the next federal elections in 2029 or 2033.
If the AfD manages to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt, Siegmund has promised to immediately start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools and halt the building of new windfarms.
He wants to change the slogan of the state from “Think Modern” to “Think German”, and to reintroduce the singing of the German national anthem in schools.
Siegmund also sought in the campaign to capitalise on a mood of “ostalgie”, or nostalgia for communist East Germany, and to tap into discontent among east Germans. He has made repeated references to a rise in foreigner-related crime, even as the crime rate has fallen dramatically. AfD is pro-Kremlin, urging a stop to support for Ukraine and pushing for Ukrainians to no longer receive refugee status.
Siegmund turned up to vote on Sunday morning with his wife, riding an East German-era moped in the party colours, which was also a prominent prop during the election campaign in rallies across the state. In a statement in front of the polling station, he voiced his optimism that the party would achieve “45%, and some”, and saying he wanted to “build bridges”.
Tensions before the election were high, with a considerable police presence and a number of demonstrations taking place across the state. Thousands of opponents of the AfD gathered in the state capital, Magdeburg, on Saturday, for a “festival of democracy”.
On Saturday evening, a message beamed on to the facade of Magdeburg Cathedral read: “We do not abandon what we love. True love of the homeland is not the AfD.”
The bishop of Magdeburg, Gerhard Feige, in an address to a gathering of churchgoers, warned against forces “that want to sow discord, stoke mistrust and fear”. He drew parallels with history, warning that a democracy has the potential to abolish itself. “Not everyone who votes or is elected democratically is a democrat,” he said.
The German Economic Institute has warned of the far-reaching consequences for the German economy, in Saxony-Anhalt and beyond. It said the AfD’s immigration policy would be “calamitous” for the state, which has an ageing, dwindling population and is heavily dependent on foreign workers.
Critics have also warned that an AfD-run state, due to the Kremlin-friendly stance of the party, could leak sensitive information to Russia. The AfD has dismissed such claims. It has said it would seek to reform the domestic intelligence service, calling it biased.

Iran touts military response as US maintains blockade, hits tankers

Iran touts military response as US maintains blockade, hits tankers
Tehran says the time for proportionate retaliation is over after a US strike on Iranian tankers inside the blockade line.
Tehran, Iran – The United States continues to rely on a mix of military force and economic sanctions against Iran, which has so far only prompted authorities in Tehran to consider more forceful responses.
The US Central Command (CENTCOM) released video on Saturday showing three Iranian crude oil tankers being hit – one off Kharg Island, Iran’s main oil export hub, another near Jask and a third in the Gulf of Oman. Two were “permanently disabled”, while a third sank after extensive bombing, CENTCOM said.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iran President Pezeshkian calls for unity as US ramps up economic pressure
- list 2 of 3US says it hit Iran oil tankers accused of helping ‘regional proxies’
- list 3 of 3US, Iran engaged in tanker war: Where is the months-long conflict headed?
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) later aired video of its own, showing explosives-laden projectiles crashing into multiple ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
“Aggressor US must know that it has no way but to leave the region and stop its malignance,” the IRGC said in a statement on Sunday. It added that a US-built sea drone was hit while trying to enter Iranian waters in the vital waterway, through which one fifth of the world’s oil and gas passes in peacetime.
The IRGC also said on Sunday it had fired several ballistic missiles towards a US aircraft carrier and another warship that are part of the network of vessels imposing the months-long naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports. Both vessels sustained some damage and fled, said the IRGC, although there was no immediate evidence of a successful hit and CENTCOM said the attacks were “evaded”.
The IRGC said it considered the acknowledgement by the US that missiles were launched towards its warships as “live evidence of the enemy’s strategic defeat and proof” of the force’s “offensive capabilities”.
Speaking during a private meeting of parliament members on Sunday, Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Tehran has inflicted “significant blows” to US bases across the region to the “frustration” of leaders in Washington.
“The Americans have surely understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end and our recent strikes against aggressor bases was only a start,” said Ghalibaf, who is also Iran’s chief negotiator with the US.
Any further attacks against Iranian interests will be met with “faster, heavier and more painful” strikes from Iran, he warned.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the US attacks on Iranian ships illegal and a “war crime” that runs counter to the United Nations Charter.
Who is the blockade hurting?
US and Iranian officials provide different readings of what is transpiring after months of disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the naval blockade imposed since mid-July.
The administration of President Donald Trump says more vessels have transited the strategically important waterway over recent weeks under US guidance, despite threats and attacks from Iran, with traffic allegedly nearing pre-war levels on some days. That account is countered by Iranian authorities, which say the strait remains closed.
The US military said about 90 commercial vessels have been redirected as part of the blockade, with several more disabled or boarded.
Crude oil exports from the Middle East during August were down 39 percent since the January and February baseline of 18.5 million barrels per day (mbpd), according to TankerTrackers. It said the current deficit is now 7.2mbpd, down from 12.4mbpd in May.
“Although most may recover in the coming months, Iran’s exports of 1.68mbpd (baseline number) may likely remain at zero for the foreseeable future; depending on any agreement,” the maritime intelligence company posted online on Sunday.
Iranian authorities have confirmed that they have been unable to get crude oil past the US warships imposing the blockade.
But they pointed out it does not equal a total halt to exports, with President Masoud Pezeshkian saying late last month that up to 90 million barrels of oil were exported during the brief period that the memorandum of understanding signed with the US in June was in effect.
Some of the oil is kept in floating storage outside the blockade, allowing Iran to gradually sell it at a discount to its main oil customer, China, despite US sanctions.
Washington is counting on those supplies running out in the foreseeable future.
“There’s probably only about 30 million barrels of Iranian crude oil left that China hasn’t bought,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Sunday. “So that will run out soon and there will be no problem with China buying because they have no product.”
Bessent again hailed the “one-two punch” of the blockade and sanctions as part of what the Trump administration has branded Operation Economic Outcast, aimed at reducing Iran’s trade with neighbours and further isolating 90 million Iranians.
Iranian authorities have not said how much longer they expect to be able to sell oil amid the US onslaught, nor have they elaborated on whether they are exploring potential alternative routes.
But experts have said that while overland and rail routes can move limited refined products, fuel oil and liquefied petroleum gas towards Afghanistan, Iraq, Central Asia and beyond, they cannot offer a viable and scalable replacement for the volume transported by very large crude carriers through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s Economy Ministry on Sunday established an “economic war headquarters” to counter the pressure, as the country deals with one of the world’s highest inflation rates, unemployment, energy imbalance and a host of other deep-seated issues.
But IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi suggested that the US was taking several times more economic damage from the war and blockade than Iran.
“If the US wants to deal one dollar in economic damage to Iran, it may deal several dollars’ worth of costs and damages to itself,” he said, pointing to lowered US strategic energy reserves and decreased aluminium exports from the region as examples.

The spectre of a far-right state government drew thousands of the AfD’s opponents to a rally on Saturday in Magdeburg, the regional capital, with banners saying “life is better without Nazis”.
“I’m very worried,” demonstrator Laura Saalfeld told AFP.
“Whatever the results, the atmosphere will change. Far-right sympathisers will show themselves more openly on the streets.”
Smiling face, radical agenda
Siegmund, the AfD’s telegenic top candidate, has ambitions to lead a political revolution from Saxony-Anhalt that would propel the party to national victory in 2029.
On the campaign trail, Siegmund—a former entrepreneur with a sharp undercut hairstyle and a huge social media following—has been mobbed by adoring fans, many wearing T-shirts bearing his likeness.
The party has tapped into a sense of nostalgia for communist East Germany as well as lingering resentment about an enduring wealth gap with the west decades after the 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall.
In line with the sometimes defiant sense of local “Ossie pride”, Siegmund has often ridden the iconic local Simson bike, including to the polling booth Sunday in his hometown of Tangermuende.
While Siegmund has been dubbed the friendly face of the AfD, his campaign promises have been radical, including targeting irregular migrants with a “remigration and deportation offensive” from day one.
The party’s anti-“woke” agenda also includes vows to replace LGBTQ pride rainbow flags at public schools with the German standard, and to change history teaching to lessen the emphasis on the Third Reich.
In order to replace migrant workers, the AfD wants to lure back German expatriates, while offering “baby bonuses” for families to reverse the shrinking of the population in the small state of 2.1 million people.
The German Economic Institute has warned the AfD’s immigration policy would be “ruinous” for Saxony-Anhalt, which is highly reliant on foreign-born workers, especially in the health sector.
Others have voiced fears an AfD-run state security apparatus could leak sensitive information to Russia, which Moscow could use to destabilise Germany.
The Kremlin “makes no secret of the fact that the AfD is the most important instrument for destabilising Germany for (Russian President Vladimir) Putin,” Thuringia state interior minister Georg Maier told the Handelsblatt daily.
The strong AfD win also heaps pressure on Merz, who has vowed to reboot a stagnant economy and restrict irregular immigration, but has seen his party beaten by the AfD in national surveys too.
Political scientist Wolfgang Schroeder of Kassel University said that after an AfD win in Saxony-Anhalt, “Merz’s critics will become even more vocal, and calls for better leadership will become impossible to ignore”.

Wages in manufacturing grew faster than the average in Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:14:30 UTC
01:14:30 KST

By Orsolya Soosaar, Economist at Eesti Pank.
Data from Statistics Estonia show the average gross monthly wage rose in the second quarter by 5.5% to 2243 euros. Wage growth slowed in the private sector, while the collective agreements signed last year meant it was faster in the public sector in education, healthcare and public administration. The rise of 6.8% in the minimum wage from the start of April boosted the growth in wages that are below the average, while the growth in wages above the average slowed.
Recovering growth in the economy has supported growth in exports, and the improved performance of industry stands out in the wage data because of wages rising faster than the average in manufacturing and construction. Employers are again looking for additional staff, and that is supporting growth in wages and is reflected in a rise in the number of vacancies, especially in construction. The average wage in those sectors fell relative to the average in the economy during the recession, and it is now climbing back.
The labour force survey run by Statistics Estonia shows that unemployment was at 6.6% in the second quarter of 2026, and there were an estimated 10,000 fewer people out of work than a year earlier. The number of people in employment was also lower at the same time though, meaning that unemployment fell because labour force participation declined. Participants in the labour force are those who are in employment and those who are unemployed but are actively looking for work and are ready to start work within a short time.
Labour force participation may have fallen partly because the number of jobs on offer has been low for a long time and competition for vacancies has been tight. Equally, the change this year in the conditions for receiving unemployment benefits may have reduced the motivation for those who were previously not in the labour market to register as unemployed, and so may have affected their search for work. People who had not recently been in employment, such as those who had been studying full-time, at home with children, or caring for relatives, earlier had the right to receive unemployment benefits, but the basic level of unemployment insurance that has replaced those benefits requires them to have been in work previously.
Source: eestipank.ee

Exit polls: Germany’s far-right AfD holds clear lead in Saxony-Anhalt election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:12:36 UTC
01:12:36 KST

BERLIN — Germany’s far right claimed its biggest electoral success since World War II in Sunday’s regional vote in Saxony-Anhalt, with the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party advancing to the cusp of genuine power for the first time.
The state election is seen as a key test of whether the anti-immigrant, Russia-friendly AfD — now comfortably the most popular party in the EU’s biggest economy — can turn its electoral strength into a position in government.
The party itself is candid that it sees the eastern region of Saxony-Anhalt as a blueprint for its national ambitions, using the slogan: “It begins here.”
Advertisement
“We’ve made history. We’re taking back our country. It starts here in Saxony-Anhalt,” Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s candidate for regional premier, said at a victory event in the city of Magdeburg where a crowd chanted his name — “Uli, Uli” — in unison.
With almost all of the ballots counted, the AfD was set to win some 44 percent, a landslide on high turnout which would give it 39 seats in the regional parliament — just shy of the 42 seats needed to rule outright.
The political haggling over whether the AfD can wield power is now likely to center on whether it can come to an arrangement with the BSW, a populist-left party founded by a former member of East Germany’s communist party. The alternative is to persuade lawmakers from other parties to defect.
Sunday’s election is a catastrophe for the Christian Democratic Union of Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Its support crashed to less than 18 percent — a devastating implosion from the 37. 1 percent it scored in 2021.
The success of the AfD in this small state of just 2.1 million inhabitants has even sparked speculation about a potential Kanzlertausch, or chancellor swap.
Siegmund argued the result was a direct signal to Merz.
Advertisement
“Of course, it’s also a message directed at Berlin … Each day of having this man in the chancellery is one too many. That’s how people in Saxony-Anhalt see it, too.”
By 10 p.m., Merz was conspicuous by his absence, not having appeared to address the result, which is widely seen in Berlin as a turning point in the country’s post-war history.
Electoral math
The electoral arithmetic of whether the AfD can govern is still coming down to the wire.
The AfD’s national co-leader Alice Weidel immediately hailed a “historic result” and said the party had “a very clear mandate for governing.”
But Siegmund will now need to determine whether he can drum up support from members of other parties — even on an individual basis — to take him to the 42-seat majority.
Weidel said her party “always has an outstretched hand” for coalition partners. Siegmund also said he was willing to cooperate with other members of the legislature either as “a caucus or an individual representative.”
Advertisement
The most likely partner is the populist BSW party of Sahra Wagenknecht, which has denounced the “firewall” of mainstream parties against the far right as antidemocratic, and looks set to have four lawmakers. But the AfD has also made overtures to CDU members to peel off and join forces.
The BSW has proposed installing a “nonpartisan” premier to lead the state government with “shifting alliances” in parliament. But the AfD is unlikely to agree to such an arrangement; it appears more probable that the BSW could ultimately help the AfD’s lead candidate take power on a more informal basis.
Tino Chrupalla, the AfD’s other national co-leader, predicted the AfD would only get stronger if the other parties united against it to keep it out of power.
“Our position is clear. If the others think they know better and that this election result isn’t a sign of things to come, then they should go ahead [without the AfD], but the next election result will then be 50 plus,” he said.
Body blow to Merz
The outcome is a bruising blow for the CDU, which has governed the region over the past 24 years. CDU General Secretary Franziska Hoppermann called it a “very difficult result” and an “overall defeat” for the Christian Democrats.
Sven Schulze, the current prime minister of Saxony-Anhalt, also conceded the severity of the defeat, particularly since turnout appeared to be very high.
Advertisement
“The winner of the election, the AfD, is now the strongest force in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt, and we in the CDU will have to deal with this result,” he said.
That four in 10 voters in Saxony-Anhalt supported the AfD — even though the state’s intelligence agency has designated its local branch a right-wing extremist organization, and members of lead candidate Siegmund’s inner circle have reportedly belonged to an organization modeled on the Hitler Youth — underscores the widespread distrust in mainstream parties, the media and public institutions in eastern Germany, a region under communist rule during the Cold War.
The party achieved its best result since its founding in 2013 by vowing to deport migrants with a “remigration offensive,” to push for closer relations with Moscow — including by bringing back school exchange programs with Russia — to remove rainbow flags from schools, and to introduce a “baby welcome grant” of €2,000 for the first two children and €4,000 for each additional child. The party also pledged to reform school curricula to reduce material on Germany’s Nazi past in an effort to end what some of its politicians call a “guilt cult.”
However, the party’s success was apparently due less to its own pledges than to voters’ rejection of mainstream parties, particularly Merz and his conservative bloc. Only 9 percent of voters in Saxony-Anhalt approve of Merz’s performance, according to an ARD exit poll.
Saxony-Anhalt is the German state with the lowest average net income, and economic anxiety — over declining industry and rising energy costs — was a major factor motivating voters. Some 70 percent said they were “greatly worried” that rising prices would prevent them from paying their bills, according to an ARD survey, while 58 percent feared they would be unable to maintain their standard of living.
Surveys show that the AfD also leads in the eastern state of Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania, where voters go to the polls on Sept. 20. In Berlin, a traditionally left-wing capital where voters cast ballots the same day, the AfD is also performing strongly with around 18 percent support.
The Saxony-Anhalt result surpasses the AfD’s previous breakthrough in the eastern region of Thuringia, where it won 32.8 percent of the vote in 2024. After that election, the CDU was reduced to forming a minority coalition with left-wing parties.

Germany’s far-right AfD wins key Saxony-Anhalt election by landslide
BERLIN - Germany’s far-right AfD won a landslide victory in a key regional election on Sept 6 in the ex-communist east, according to exit polls, but it remains unclear whether it can win an absolute majority to govern.
“We have made history today,” said a jubilant Ulrich Siegmund, the 35-year-old lead candidate of the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany party in Saxony-Anhalt state, as the vote count continued.
The AfD won at least 44 per cent, more than doubling its support, and far ahead of the 18.5 per cent for the centre-right CDU of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, according to projections by public broadcasters ARD and ZDF.
The CDU’s state premier Sven Schulze called the outcome “a severe blow” but – depending on the final count and the fate of smaller parties – may still try to cobble together a multi-party coalition to cling to power.
All major parties have agreed on a “firewall” of non-cooperation with the AfD, whose state branch is categorised as “right-wing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency.
The AfD’s national co-leader Alice Weidel – who has long condemned the “firewall” concept as undemocratic – praised her party’s result as “sensational” and said that “we have received a very clear mandate to govern here”.

‘Appalled’
In a white-knuckle evening, the CDU’s only hope would be to potentially forge an unwieldy coalition with a razor-thin margin together with the centre-left SPD and the Greens, and with the support of the far-left Die Linke party.
A wild card is whether the small BSW party – economically leftist, but veers hard right on immigration – will cross the five-per cent hurdle for re-entry into parliament, and whether it would then lend its support to the AfD.
A first-ever AfD state government would be a shock for many in Germany, which has been at pains to atone for its dark history of World War II and the Holocaust and so far kept extremist parties at bay.

Siegmund has ambitions to become state premier and lead a political revolution from Saxony-Anhalt that would propel the party to national victory in 2029.
On the campaign trail, Siegmund – a former entrepreneur with a sharp undercut hairstyle and a huge social media following – has been mobbed by adoring fans, many wearing T-shirts bearing his likeness.
The party has tapped into a sense of nostalgia for communist East Germany as well as lingering resentment about an enduring wealth gap with the west decades after the 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall.
In line with the sometimes defiant sense of local “Ossie pride”, Siegmund has often ridden the iconic local Simson bike, including to the polling booth Sept 6 in his hometown of Tangermuende.
While Siegmund has been dubbed the friendly face of the AfD, his campaign promises have been radical, including targeting irregular migrants with a “remigration and deportation offensive” from day one.
The party’s anti-“woke” agenda also includes vows to replace LGBTQ pride rainbow flags at public schools with the German standard, and to lessen the emphasis on the Third Reich in history teaching.
The German Economic Institute has warned the AfD’s immigration policy would be “ruinous” for Saxony-Anhalt, which is highly reliant on foreign-born workers, especially in the health sector.

German far-right set for big win in eastern state - projections
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:10:46 BST
01:10:46 KST

German far-right set for big win in eastern state, projections show
- Published
Germany's AfD is heading for a big victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of its mainstream rivals, according to initial projections. It is not yet clear if that would be enough to take power in the state but the AfD says it has won a mandate to govern.
The far-right Alternative for Germany is set to win a record 44% of the vote, well ahead of the conservative CDU on 17.8%.
The AfD's charismatic leader in the state, Ulrich Siegmund, said it was "sensational" and they wanted to start governing as soon as possible.
No far-right party has won control of a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing, local education and culture.
Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund.
The AfD's projected result is higher than earlier opinion polls suggested, and Siegmund along with joint national leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla were overjoyed as the news emerged.
Commentators and political opponents spoke of the outcome as a watershed and break with the past. Main TV channel Das Erste cancelled its legendary crime drama Tatort to focus on what the result meant.
"This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," Siegmund told supporters. "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal."
US President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the German TV projection on his Truth Social platform, and then Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev took a screengrab of Trump's post and praised a "historic win for the pragmatic AfD".
Dmitriev had earlier praised the Russia-friendly AfD as "the party of hope and reason, co-operation truth and hope for Germany". Ahead of Germany's federal election last year, US Vice-President JD Vance endorsed the party, in a move criticised in Germany as political interference.
The AfD's leaders will not know if they have enough seats to govern until they see which of the smaller parties get into the state parliament. Siegmund has so far refused to lead a minority government, but the party's national leaders see it as a possibility.
A big questionmark hangs over whether one populist left-wing party, BSW, gets over the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament.
If BSW fails, then the AfD's chances of a majority increase. If they get in, the AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament.
A crowd of supporters at the AfD election night party HQ erupted in cheers as the projections came up on the screen.
A short while later, people burst into singing Germany's national anthem.
"We have made history in this state," Siegmund said. His opposite number in the CDU, Sven Schulze, conceded victory and said his party would have to deal with the result: "This was an extremely tough and intensive election campaign."
Germany's centre-left SPD described the outcome as "truly dramatic" and national leader Lars Klingbeil, whose party is in government nationally with the CDU, described the outcome as a "signal to Berlin" and he was adamant that they would hear it.
AfD stands for Alternative für Deutschland and it openly pro-Russia and anti-migration. It has not only dominated the election campaign, it is emerging as the dominant force in the result as well. Although the outcome was initially unclear, the party's supporters believe they are on the march.
Turnout in Saxony-Anhalt was particularly high at an estimated 78%, and AfD supporters in Magdeburg praised Siegmund's success in winning over voters.
One man called Ollie said: "This man gives us what no-one else can give."
"No matter what government, they all just promise things to get better. This is a party for the working people. It is the alternative for Germany," he told the BBC.
Another AfD voter called Bert said people in the east could sense things were not going well: "Things need to improve for us, for my family - I have three children. I'm in fear, I'm really in fear that safety erodes more and more."
Other parties refuse to go into coalition with the AfD, operating a Brandmauer or firewall aimed at keeping the far right out of government. In Saxony-Anhalt, the BSW has offered to co-operate with the AfD on some issues if it gets into the state parliament.
The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states.
They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power.
Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally. It would not be able to achieve either if it ran the government of one of 16 states.
But it would have significant local powers. The party has been particularly critical of the Bauhaus school of design which the Nazis shut down in the city of Dessau after they came to power in 1933. The AfD has called it "the dead-end of modernism", prompting some to accuse the party of using similar language to the Nazis.
Responding to the news from Saxony-Anhalt, the veteran head of the Jewish community in Munich and Bavaria, Charlotte Knobloch, said it frightened her. "On days like this I find it hard to recognise my homeland any more," the 93-year-old Holocaust survivor said, appealing for mainstream parties not to stand by and allow "this decline".
One of the AfD's top figures in Saxony-Anhalt, Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, has also been criticised for his approach to Russia. When asked why he had a Russian army mug in his office, he said it was just a souvenir, and "it's not our war".

Far-right AfD wins vote in Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state: Exit polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06

Far-right AfD wins vote in Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state: Exit polls
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has won the election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, according to exit polls.
The AfD won 44.5 percent of the vote, exit polls for the ARD broadcaster suggested on Sunday. That is more than twice the 18.5 percent for the incumbent centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU), led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
“We have achieved exactly what we wanted to achieve,” said AfD’s lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund. “We have made history in this state.”
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel also hailed a “historic” result, which has given the far-right party a clear mandate to govern, though it was not immediately clear whether it would be able to form a government.
“The reality is the AfD has got the lion’s share of the votes in this election, according to the exit polls. But the question is: is it enough to get them control of the state? Right now, we cannot say for sure,” reported Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane from Magdeburg in eastern Germany.
Exit polls suggest the party has narrowly missed securing an absolute majority in the state parliament in Magdeburg.
Siegmund said he wanted to extend a hand to all parties willing to bring about a fundamental political transformation in the state. However, the AfD will not bend to other parties’ will, he stressed.
The AfD has never participated in a ruling coalition in Germany’s 16 states nor its federal government, as all other mainstream parties refuse to work with it, a policy infamously known as the “firewall”.
Blow to Merz’s authority
Sunday’s result is another blow to the authority of Merz, whose popularity has declined as his coalition government struggles to revive growth in Europe’s largest economy.
His centre-right CDU came a distant second. Depending on the eventual count, the CDU’s state leader, Sven Schulze, would hope to still be able to form a new multi-party coalition to block the AfD from power.
AfD has tapped into a sense of nostalgia for communist East Germany, as well as lingering resentment about the enduring wealth gap with the west decades after the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989.
In line with the sometimes defiant sense of local “Ossie pride”, Siegmund has often ridden the iconic local Simson bike, including to the polling booth on Sunday in his hometown of Tangermuende.
While Siegmund has been dubbed the friendly face of the AfD, his campaign promises have been radical, including targeting undocumented migrants with a “remigration and deportation offensive” from day one.
AfD’s agenda
The party’s anti-“woke” agenda also includes promises to replace LGBTQ pride rainbow flags at public schools with the German standard and to change history teaching to lessen the emphasis on Hitler’s Third Reich.
In order to replace migrant workers, the AfD wants to lure back German expatriates, while offering “baby bonuses” for families to reverse the shrinking population in the small state of 2.1 million.
The German Economic Institute has warned that the AfD’s immigration policy would be “ruinous” for Saxony-Anhalt, which is highly reliant on foreign-born workers, especially in the health sector.
Others have voiced fears that an AfD-run state security apparatus could leak sensitive information to Russia, which Moscow could use to destabilise Germany.
The Kremlin “makes no secret of the fact that the AfD is the most important instrument for destabilising Germany for [Russian President Vladimir] Putin,” Thuringia state interior minister Georg Maier told the Handelsblatt daily newspaper.

Israel should consider changing Hatikvah as its national anthem - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:04:57 UTC
01:04:57 KST

Several countries have changed their national anthems. In Australia, where I was born and raised, we used to sing the British national anthem of “God Save the Queen,” which underwent a slight change in previous years, depending on the gender of the monarch.
In April 1984, the anthem was officially changed to “Advance Australia Fair.”
In New Zealand, they have two national anthems, one of which is “God Save the King” and the other being “God Defend New Zealand,” which is in tribute to the indigenous Maori population.
Prior to the end of apartheid, South Africa also had two national anthems, but in 1997, abandoned both, and adopted a new anthem.
Other countries wishing to correct historic grievances or bowing to a change of regime have also altered existing anthems or brought in new ones.
In Russia, for instance, the anthem has been changed at least three times. The present anthem is sung to the same tune as that of Soviet times, but the lyrics were changed in December 2000.
Prior to the fall of the Berlin Wall and the reunification of Germany in November 1989, the East Germans had a different anthem to those of the West Germans. The East German anthem was “Risen from the Ashes,” whereas in West Germany they sang “Germany Above All,” omitting some of the Nazi-era lyrics.
For Jews, the world over, Israel’s national anthem “Hatikvah” – the Hope – which was originally a poem written in 1878 by Naftali Herz Imber, is the universal national anthem. The melody was adapted from a Moldavian folk song by Romanian immigrant Samuel Cohen. The lyrics speak of the Jewish people’s longing to return to Zion.
Most national anthems are in tribute to the country or the nation as a whole. But “Hatikvah” is clearly the anthem of the Jewish people and does not take into account the minorities who are also part of the nation of Israel.
Making Israel's national anthem more inclusive
A major step toward making Israel more acceptable to the Arab world would be to change the anthem to something in which the lyrics would be more neutral and could apply to any sector of the population. “Jerusalem of Gold” comes close, but includes the Temple Mount in the text. Though unofficially Israel’s second national anthem, it would have to be altered slightly so that another expression could be found for Temple Mount which has both political and religious connotations.
Whether “Jerusalem of Gold” replaces “Hatikvah” or whether a new song is composed, what remains important is change in order to make the national anthem inclusive.
Debates on this subject go back to long before the establishment of the state.
Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, who was Ashkenazi chief rabbi under the British Mandate, wrote a possible alternative to “Hatikvah” under the title of “HaEmunah” (“The Faith”). This was fine for religious Jews, but not for the rest of the population.
The debate on the anthem has been going on for more than a century, with agreement yet to be reached. Non-Jews respectfully stand to attention when “Hatikvah” is played, but cannot bring themselves to sing about the Jewish soul and Zion.
Jews in other countries often face a similar problem in hospitals run by Catholic orders. Almost every room in such hospitals features a crucifix on the wall and a portrait of the Virgin Mary.
Even secular Jews feel uncomfortable in such an environment, but most of the Catholic hospitals are really good, and the nursing staff amazingly kind and considerate.
It’s not quite the same, because hospital stays are relatively brief and seldom repeated. But many events attended by non-Jews begin or end with “Hatikvah,” which was inspiring on the road to statehood, but is no longer suitable when we have a state
If we want everyone to sing the anthem with pride and a sense of belonging, we must agree to change.

US withdrawal from Iraq will be watched closely by Iran-backed militias, Kurds - analysis
Unknown

2026-09-06

The US is to meet a September 30 deadline for withdrawing from Iraq, Kurdish media outlet Rudaw reported on Sunday.
It was one of several reports that indicate the US is committed to taking away air defense systems from the Kurdistan Region. The full details of this are unclear and hard to confirm. What matters is not necessarily if it is accurate, but that people will think it is happening.
Rudaw wrote, “The United States will withdraw its defense systems from the Kurdistan Region along with its remaining troops by the end of September under an agreement with the Iraqi government, a senior Iraqi security official said on Sunday.”
The report noted that “Qasim al-Araji, security advisor to Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, told Rudaw that the withdrawal includes all defense systems, including remaining ones in Erbil, adding that the phased removal of troops and military equipment has already begun.”
Araji said, “On September 30, coalition forces will completely withdraw from Iraq, and this is the implementation of the agreement made between the previous government and the global coalition…The American side has expressed its full readiness to implement the agreement and withdraw by the specified deadline.”
US pressuring Iraq to control militias
This comes as the US is also pressuring Iraq to rein in Iranian-backed militias and disarm them. So far, none of the militias have disarmed. It doesn’t seem possible that any weapons will be collected in September. If no militias were disarmed in the last months, why would they hand over their guns now?
Instead, what they will do is put more conditions on disarmament. Some may also claim they already put their guns under “state control.” Most of the militias are part of the Baghdad-backed Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF). As such, they will claim the PMF controls their weapons already. This is a kind of bait and switch.
Rudaw said there is progress with the militias. “Araji said discussions with the armed groups were moving in a positive direction.”
Araji said, “After the withdrawal of the coalition, an agreement will be reached on a comprehensive mechanism to place all weapons under the control of the state and the commander-in-chief of the armed forces.” He added that “discussions are proceeding very well and there is positive understanding.”
It’s worth noting that the militias were supposed to hand over their weapons by September 30. Now the handover is overdue. This is how the can gets kicked down the road.
For the Kurdistan Region, this is a problem because the militias and Iran have already targeted the region with more than 1,000 drone and missile attacks since February 2026.
Iran has even targeted the offices of the Kurdish Regional Government’s prime minister and president. Iran is indicating that it wants to strike at dissident groups in the Kurdistan Region and also that it can do as it wants.
Not clear if air defenses will remain
In the past, reports said that US and coalition air defenses had downed some of the drone attacks. It is not clear if some of the defenses will actually remain. The US has a large consulate in Erbil. It is logical that the US will want to defend it. The consulate, as well as a UAE consulate, has been targeted in the past.
Yet, Rudaw said, “the US has already relocated eight Patriot surface-to-air missile batteries to Jordan, while Britain has transferred its Rapid Sentry system to Cyprus.”
The report added context, noting the “US and British forces have defended Erbil airport and surrounding areas using anti-missile and counter-drone systems stationed at the base. Despite those defenses, at least five American soldiers and contractors have been killed in attacks in recent months, Rudaw understands.”
The report also names five Iranian-backed militias as refusing to disarm. These include Kataib Hezbollah, Sayyid al-Shuhada and Harakat al-Nujaba. Kataib Hezbollah is believed to be the most dangerous in terms of its threat and close ties to the IRGC.
In 2020, when the US killed IRGC Quds Force head Qasem Soleimani, he was riding with Kataib Hezbollah leader Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis. Muhandis was also killed.
Kataib Hezbollah killed three Americans in Jordan in a drone attack in 2024. It has also attacked Saudi Arabia. The militias, such as the three mentioned above, often play a role in the “Islamic Resistance” in Iraq, which has carried out attacks on Israel, the US, and others in recent years.

Gaza's Zeitoun neighbourhood mourns 100 victims, including 70 children, found under rubble
Large crowds gathered in Gaza City’s Zeitoun neighbourhood on Sunday to attend a solemn mass funeral for 100 people whose remains were only recently retrieved after they were killed in the Gaza War.
Their bodies were recovered from under the rubble of destroyed homes in the neighbourhood and were taken to the Baptist Cemetery, in a scene which highlighted the scale of the tragedy endured by Gaza’s residents during the genocidal war.
The funeral was organised by the Zeitoun Neighborhood Families Association in coordination with the General Directorate of Civil Defence and the Missing Persons Committee.
Relatives of those found were in attendance while mourners carried photographs of the deceased and banners bearing tribute to them.
Civil Defence teams that had carried out the recovery and transportation of the bodies also took part in the funeral.

Before the funeral began, an atmosphere of grief filled the area. Family members gathered to take a final look at the remains of their loved ones after waiting so long to learn of their fate.

Bassal said that the operation to recover the bodies had been about returning victims to their families and giving them the right to say goodbye and bury their loved ones.
“How long will Gaza remain in this pain? How long will a father raise his children for years, only for them all to die in a single moment? Why are innocent people being killed? And how long will Gaza continue to bleed?” he asked in anguish.
Bassal said that the Civil Defence still need to search for approximately 8,000 people under the rubble, despite limited resources and a total absence of support from the world.
Omar Nofal, representing the Missing Persons Committee said, “Behind every body found is a name, a family, and a story that has waited a long time.”
Nofal emphasize that the bodies of those killed had been under the rubble for three years but said that this was “not a failure on the part of Civil Defence, but a failure of humanity, and of a world that constantly boasts about human rights, children's rights, and women's rights.
“But the only truth is that, in this world, rights belong to the powerful, and the law that prevails is the law of the jungle.”
“Civil Defence did not recover a single weapon from beneath the rubble, but it recovered nearly 70 boys and girls,” Nofal added. “It recovered colourful dolls and little teddy bears, while more than 8,000 people remain beneath the rubble to this day.”
After the farewell speeches, mourners carried the coffins and the funeral procession moved through the streets of Gaza City toward the Baptist Cemetery.
At the Baptist Cemetery, families and mourners gathered around the bodies for the final time before the burial ceremonies began. The coffins were lowered one after another into the graves, while family members stood at their edges, taking their final looks before the victims were laid to rest.
For the Zeitoun neighborhood, the funeral was not so much the end of the story as a collective recovery of a part of its memory, while other families continue to wait to learn the fate of their missing loved ones.

Israel election panel allows parties to track who has voted in real time ahead of High Court review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:04:39 UTC
01:04:39 KST

The Central Elections Committee voted on Sunday to allow party representatives inside polling stations to report in real time which voters have cast ballots, restoring - for now - a central part of parties’ Election Day turnout operations ahead of the October 27 election.
The information at issue does not reveal how anyone voted, which remains secret. What it does do is tell parties whether a particular person has voted or not. Campaigns can compare that information with their databases and concentrate calls, messages, home visits, and transportation efforts on likely supporters who have not yet reached the polls.
Sunday’s decision is not the final legal word. The High Court of Justice will resume hearing Likud’s petition at 8 a.m. on Wednesday, after the parties update the court on the committee’s decision.
The full committee approved the proposal by 19 votes to 11, with three abstentions, departing from the position of committee chairman and Supreme Court Deputy President Noam Sohlberg, who ruled in August that transferring identified voter information to political parties was prohibited.
Under the committee’s decision, the reporting will be allowed only under restrictions: Information may not be transferred from special polling stations, parties may not record when an individual voted, and the data may be used only to encourage voter turnout.
Special polling stations are those where voting is conducted using double envelopes, including polling stations in prisons and hospitals, military polling stations, and specially accessible polling stations intended for people with limited mobility.
Information must be destroyed after the election
The information may not be transferred to another party or outside body and must be destroyed after the election by the parties themselves, a CEC spokesperson confirmed.
It remains unclear whether the ban on transferring the information to an outside body also applies to companies operating parties’ voter-tracking applications.
The proposal was presented by attorney Ilan Bombach, who represents Likud in the proceedings. The committee is composed primarily of political-party representatives, with seats allocated according to the factions in the outgoing Knesset; the coalition holds a majority.
The court has not ruled that Sohlberg lacked the authority to impose the original ban. Instead, an arrangement approved last Thursday transferred the underlying question to the full committee for a fresh decision, with Sohlberg’s rulings placed before it as his legal opinion.
The State Attorney’s Office will represent Sohlberg at Wednesday’s hearing, while the committee’s legal adviser will represent the full committee, according to the spokesperson.
That allowed the court to bypass the authority dispute for the time being. Now that the committee has permitted the practice, the central question is expected to become whether its decision complies with privacy and election law.
Wednesday’s hearing will proceed as though the court has already issued a conditional order requiring the respondents to justify their position. In practical terms, that allows the case to move directly into substantive review without another preliminary stage.
Likud has argued that this system has operated openly for several election cycles and is essential to its ability to bring supporters to the polls. It said Sohlberg’s original prohibition was imposed after parties had already planned their campaigns around the practice and that aggregate turnout figures could not replace identified reporting.
The privacy concern extends beyond the secrecy of the ballot
Sohlberg, the attorney-general, and the Privacy Protection Authority took the opposite position. They argued that information entrusted to polling-station officials for administering and supervising the election cannot be repurposed for political-party operations without legal authorization.
Sohlberg found that whether a person voted, when they voted, and the circumstances of their vote constitute personal information. He ruled that the fact that parties had used the information in previous elections did not make its transfer lawful.
The privacy concern extends beyond the secrecy of the ballot. Information showing that someone voted at a hospital, prison, women’s shelter, or another special polling station could reveal sensitive details about that person even without disclosing their vote. Sunday’s decision seeks to address that concern by excluding special polling stations and prohibiting the transfer of voting times.
Critics maintain that identified information from ordinary polling stations can also become sensitive when combined with party databases. In communities with predictable voting patterns, even the fact that a person voted may support inferences about their political views. Real-time access can also expose voters to targeted pressure or repeated approaches before polls close.
Sohlberg had proposed an alternative under which the committee would publish aggregate turnout figures for every ordinary polling station at least four times on Election Day, without identifying individual voters. Sunday’s decision instead preserves identified reporting under the new restrictions.
The parties must now explain to the High Court how the committee’s decision affects their positions. The justices may then determine whether the safeguards are sufficient or whether identified voter reporting remains incompatible with privacy and election law.

New report flags widespread failures in Canadian universities’ antisemitism response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:04:32 UTC
01:04:32 KST

B’nai Brith Canada has launched its Canadian Campus Climate Report Card, an institutional accountability initiative designed to evaluate the state of Jewish life and the climate for Jewish students on university campuses as the new academic year gets underway.
The initiative is part of B’nai Brith’s broader Project Accountability, which operates on the principle that academic institutions must be held accountable for the environments they foster and for how effectively they respond when students face antisemitism, harassment, or discrimination.
The initial launch features a pilot assessment covering four universities where students have reported particularly hostile social climates: York University, the University of Toronto, Queen’s University, and McGill University.
Unlike traditional incident trackers that catalog instances of antisemitism, the report cards evaluate 28 criteria across three core categories: administrative policies and actions, campus conduct and climate, and Jewish life on campus.
The methodology combines student surveys with a qualitative review of university policies, anti-hate measures, course offerings, and the availability of kosher dining and Jewish services. Each criterion is weighted equally across the categories.
Initial findings from the pilot program highlight that while all four institutions demonstrated strong traditional Jewish life indicators, such as active student groups, chaplaincy support, and religious services, the campus climate and administrative response metrics yielded widespread red scores.
Administrators received poor marks for their handling of antisemitic incidents
At McGill University, York University, and the University of Toronto, administrators received failing or critical marks regarding their handling of harassment, event disruptions, and transparency in reporting antisemitic incidents.
“The goal isn’t simply to hand out grades,” said B’nai Brith Canada’s CEO Simon Wolle in a press release on Wednesday. “It is to give students, parents and the community a clearer picture of what is happening on campus. We want to recognize where universities are getting it right, identify where they’re falling short, and help universities do better.”
Wolle added, “Our Report Cards must serve as an impetus for Canadian institutions to revise their policies, where they fall short, and improve programming if it is insufficient to meet the needs of Jewish students.”
B’nai Brith intends for the report cards to serve as an ongoing benchmark to push Canadian tertiary institutions to tighten their policies and enforce anti-hate codes.

Israel’s next leader must be ambitious for Israel, not themselves - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:04:14 UTC
01:04:14 KST

On October 27, Israelis will once again choose a government.
We will spend the coming weeks arguing about Gaza, Iran, the haredi draft, the economy, judicial reform, the Palestinians, and the consequences of the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks. We will scrutinize party platforms, coalition possibilities, and opinion polls.
But perhaps we should be asking: What sort of person wants to be prime minister in the first place?
It is a peculiar ambition. The hours are appalling. Privacy mostly disappears. Every mistake becomes public property. Your appearance, your family, your finances, and sometimes even your choice of lunch become legitimate subjects for discussion. Roughly half the country may regard you as the person qualified to save the nation, while much of the other half regards you as the person most likely to destroy it.
Why would anybody want the job?
Many politicians still motivated by public service
Political psychologists have been asking versions of this question for years, and their findings are fascinating. Research into “political ambition” suggests that politicians are not simply power-hungry egomaniacs, as the popular stereotype would have it. Many are strongly motivated by public service. Studies of political candidates have found genuine evidence of what psychologists call “self-transcendence,” the desire to improve society and help others.
That is worth remembering in an age when cynicism about politicians comes so easily.
But alongside the desire to serve sits something else: the desire to influence. Political leaders tend to have a greater “need for power” than the rest of us. Again, that is not necessarily bad. If you are convinced that your country is heading in the wrong direction, it is perfectly reasonable to want the authority to change course.
Then there is a third characteristic: unusually strong self-belief. Research has associated political ambition with traits including extraversion and grandiose narcissism. That does not mean that every politician is a narcissist, still less that we should diagnose politicians we dislike with psychiatric disorders.
It means something simpler. To seek the premiership requires an extraordinary degree of confidence in yourself.
Israel has almost 10 million inhabitants. To seriously aspire to become prime minister requires believing that, among all those people, you possess some combination of judgment, ability, and vision that makes you particularly suited to lead them. Most of us never have that thought.
Those who do are, almost by definition, psychologically unusual.
Pirkei Avot (Ethics of the Fathers) understood the danger long before anyone invented political psychology. Shmaya teaches: “Love work, hate authority, and do not become overly familiar with the government.”
“Hate positions of power.” It is a striking instruction. Judaism clearly does not oppose leadership. The Torah is filled with leaders. Jewish communities cannot function without people willing to take responsibility.
The warning is not against exercising authority. It is against falling in love with it. And that distinction ought to matter to us as voters. Does a candidate want power because there is something that they believe desperately needs doing, or has acquiring and retaining power become the objective itself?
How can we possibly know? Not from campaign advertisements. Every candidate will assure us that they seek office only out of devotion to the people of Israel.
We have to watch their behavior. How does this person react when contradicted? Can they admit a mistake? Can they tolerate talented people around them, or does everyone eventually have to demonstrate personal loyalty? Do they distinguish between criticism and betrayal? Do they listen to advice that they do not want to hear?
When something goes badly wrong, is the first instinct to ask, “What did I get wrong?” or “Whom can I blame?”
Perhaps above all: can this person distinguish between what is good for the country and what is good for his or her political survival?
This is not an argument for timid leadership. In fact, Pirkei Avot gives us the opposite warning as well. Hillel says: “In a place where there are no people, strive to be a person.”
The traditional commentators understand this, among other things, as an instruction to step forward when nobody else is capable of taking responsibility.
Leadership sometimes requires enormous confidence. Moses’ humility did not prevent him from confronting Pharaoh. David’s greatness did not consist of avoiding difficult decisions. There are moments when standing back is not modesty but cowardice.
So Judaism presents us with a beautiful tension. Do not crave leadership. But when leadership is needed, do not run away from it.
Perhaps that is exactly the personality we should be looking for in October. Someone who wants the job enough to do it, but not so much that possessing the job becomes an end in itself.
Someone confident enough to make terrible decisions under pressure, but humble enough to wonder whether somebody else might know better. Someone strong enough to withstand public hostility, but not so insulated from criticism that they stop hearing it. Someone ambitious for Israel, rather than merely ambitious for themselves.
Our electoral system encourages us to think primarily about parties. Formally, we vote for lists rather than directly for a prime minister. In reality, personalities dominate Israeli elections. Faces stare at us from billboards. Campaigns revolve around leaders. Pollsters constantly ask which individual is “most suitable” to be prime minister.
If personality is already part of the election, we should examine it more seriously. Not whether we like the candidate, or if they gave a good speech, or if they performed brilliantly in a television interview.
Character is revealed most clearly when things go wrong. How did this person behave after failure? How did they treat an opponent once the cameras were switched off? Did they keep people around who disagreed with them? Have they ever publicly accepted responsibility for anything?
These questions matter in every election. In Israel in 2026, they matter enormously.
The next prime minister will inherit a country still carrying the wounds of the October 7 massacres and the Israel-Hamas War that ensued. Israeli society remains divided, bereaved, and exhausted. Enormous decisions lie ahead concerning security, the economy, the haredi draft, our relationship with the Palestinians, our relationship with the wider world and, perhaps most difficult of all, our relationship with one another.
Policies matter enormously. But policies do not make decisions. People do. Sometimes, the intelligence is incomplete, advisers disagree, and every option carries terrible risks.
What remains is the person; their judgment, temperament, humility, courage, and ego. Their capacity to listen; their ability to say, “I was wrong.” So by all means, before October 27, let us ask our politicians what they intend to do. But perhaps we should spend more time asking who they are.
Shmaya warned us to distrust the love of power. Hillel reminded us that good people must sometimes step forward and exercise it. Somewhere between those two teachings lies the leader that Israel needs.
The writer is a rabbi and physician. He writes and teaches on Jewish ethics, leadership, and resilience. His work appears on rabbidrjonathanlieberman.substack.com and youtube.com. @rabbidrjonathanlieberman
