Saxony-Anhalt: Far-right AfD secures huge lead in key vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:02:00 UTC
01:02:00 KST

Saxony-Anhalt: Far-right AfD secures huge lead in key vote
Published September 6, 2026last updated September 6, 2026
What you need to know
- Far-right AfD hails 'sensational' results in the Saxony-Anhalt vote
- AfD expected to struggle with coalition building as many parties reject cooperation
- Left-wing populist BSW open to working with AfD on some issues
- Merz's CDU suffers worst Saxony-Anhalt result since German reunification
It is election day in Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state. Follow all the developments here.
WATCH: AfD's Siegmund vows to 'take our country back'
"We have made history," said Ulrich Siegmund, the lead candidate for the far-right AfD, after the party won around 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt.
Projected results put BSW in Saxony-Anhalt state parliament
The latest projected results show the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) will get seats in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament.
The left-wing populist party will have five seats and has said it would work with the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which picked up 39 seats according to the projected results. The AfD had earlier seemingly ruled out working with the BSW.
The Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which headed previous coalition-led state governments, only managed to get 15 seats, while the socialist Left Party ,the center-left Social Democrats and Greens look set to get 8 seats each.
'Only idiots and traitors' celebrate AfD's success in Poland: PM Tusk
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk reacted to the election results in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt by criticizing those in his country that celebrate the far-right AfD party's success.
"In Poland, only idiots or traitors can celebrate the AfD's success," Tusk wrote in Polish on his X account.
According to Tusk, some of those he means are from Poland's opposition parties, including the right-wing populist PiS party.
WATCH: AfD celebrates, CDU reels from election setback
The far-right AfD party has achieved a huge victory in the election in the state of Saxony-Anhalt. But it appears it has not got enough votes to take control of the government there.
AfD's Siegmund says victory in Saxony-Anhalt will 'shake all of Germany'
The AfD has "written history" with the Saxony-Anhalt result, the party's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund told supporters on Sunday evening.
"Our vision for 2026 has come true," Siegmund said in his victory speech in Magdeburg. "We are going to get our country back, and we are starting with Saxony-Anhalt."
He said the result would "shake all of Germany" and send a "self-confident signal" across the country.
"The people in this country are giving us their trust. We will not disappoint them," Siegmund said. "We will not become like these other parties. We are the Alternative for Germany."
Siegmund also attacked media coverage of his party, saying the AfD had shown that "no matter how much fake news there was about us, we cannot be divided."
"In other parties you hide the chancellor. In the AfD, we stand together," he added,
The remark appeared to target the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which kept Chancellor Friedrich Merz largely out of its campaign in Saxony-Anhalt.
FACT CHECK: Russian disinformation campaign fabricates election fraud media reports
Claim: The CDU is engaging in fraud in the Saxony-Anhalt election. "The social media pages of deceased residents of Saxony-Anhalt have become a platform for the "CDU's election campaign," reads one post on X, sharing a spoofed DW video.
"According to T-Online, non-existent citizens are set to vote by post for the #CDU in the Saxony-Anhalt election," reads another.
Verdict: False
DW Fact check reviewed five videos following a near-identical template: each was about a minute long and was posted by an account with zero followers and nearly no other posts. Each of the videos feature a reputable news outlet's logo in the corner — including DW, German public broadcaster ARD, Wired magazine, and the BBC — and make claims about the CDU committing election fraud.
The claims range from the CDU using a database of Nazi soldier names to register fake ballots, to residents receiving campaign messages from deceased relatives.
Each video ends with a message urging viewers to "share this video with your family and friends in any way you see fit."
Julia Smirnova, disinformation expert and senior researcher at the Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy, told DW the posts were part of the Matryoshka Russian disinformation campaign, also known as Operation Overload.
"As with other Matryoshka videos, the reach is mostly inauthentic," she wrote in an email to DW.
One of the videos claims T-Online reporter Lars Wienand had "obtained evidence that the CDU will attempt to rig the election." Wienand confirmed he had reported no such thing, writing to DW that "it's not the first time that suspected Russian disinformation had misused my name and image."
DW Fact Check has debunked other Russian disinformation targeting German elections: Fact check: Russian disinformation targets German elections
Saxony Anhalt result 'inspiring,' AfD Bundestag member tells DW
AfD Bundestag member Markus Frohmaier called the far-right party's results in the Saxony Anhalt election "inspiring" and praised Ulrich Sigmund's campaign performance as "amazing."
When asked by DW about the party's priorities going ahead, Frohmaier mentioned "illegal mass migration" and internal security.
"I think the AfD is the only party that's able to solve these issues," he said, adding that he believes the result sends out a message to the world that "Germany is back."
"Germany is able to protect national interests," Frohmaier said, adding that this has not been the case for "many decades."
Frohmaier said he still hopes the party will manage to secure a majority of seats without having to join a coalition with other parties.
AfD's lead candidate Siegmund rejects leftist BSW as coalition partner
The lead AfDcandidate in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, Ulrich Siegmund, has poured cold water on the prospect of cooperation with the leftist populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).
Siegmund said the BSW was "not part of the solution but part of the problem."
The remark comes after BSW's Claudia Wittig signaled openness to working with the AfD on individual policy issues.
Wittig argued that excluding the AfD entirely from government would be "completely undemocratic" given its strong election result. At the same time, she rejected both Siegmund and Christian Democratic Union (CDU) candidate Sven Schulze as premier, instead calling for a nonpartisan head of government.
Most of the other parties have rejected the possibility of working with the AfD.
Preliminary results confirm AfD far ahead of rivals
The latest preliminary results, published on Sunday evening, put the AfD at 44.2%, slightly less than the 44.5% projected by the exit polls.
At the same time, the AfD's closest rival, the CDU, seems set to win 18% — half a percentage point less than predicted earlier.
FACT CHECK: Fake video claims to show AfD ballots crossed out
Claim: "German election workers recorded themselves outright destroying ballots that were cast for the populist party 'Alternative For Germany' (AfD), during Germany's recent elections," reads a post viewed 10,000 times on X, posted by a QAnon-associated account, a far-right American political conspiracy theory and political movement.
A one-minute video shows a white-gloved man unpacking ballots from red envelopes, laying them on a table, and drawing a black X through ones that select the AfD. A ballot marked for the CDU is set aside, as a voice says in German, "these are OK."
The same video was shared by numerous other accounts, in German and English across X as well as on YouTube.
Verdict: False
There are several telltale signs that this video is staged. Most obviously, all three crossed-out ballots contain the same name.
The ballots are also missing a hole punch in the top right corner, a regulation that ensures they can be used with a template for blind or visually impaired voters. The envelopes are also already unsealed.
The Gnida Project, a Russian disinformation watchdog group, said the video was part of the Storm-1516 campaign.
DW Fact Check has also debunked other false claims around Germany's postal voting system: Fact check: Germany's postal voting system isn't rigged
Jewish council leader 'personally appalled' by AfD result
Josef Schuster, president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, reacted with alarm to the Alternative for Germany’s strong showing in Saxony-Anhalt.
"The outcome of the election is still open, but one thing is already clear: A party officially classified as confirmed far-right extremist is only just short of governing a German state on its own," Schuster told the Welt newspaper.
Schuster's comments were in reference to the 2023 decision made by Germany's domestic intelligence agency BfV, which declared the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch a confirmed far-right and extremist over antisemitic, anti-Muslim and racist statements made by its functionaries.
"I am personally appalled by this election result," Schuster said, adding that the AfD’s goals had been clear for months.
The AfD’s program in Saxony-Anhalt includes a tougher deportation policy, major changes to school curricula and integration policies, a stronger emphasis on nationalism and traditional German identity, and restrictions on some cultural and public institutions.
"Those who voted for it today — despite or because of these goals — bear responsibility for this result," Schuster said.
"The damage that the so-called Alternative for Germany could now cause if it assumes responsibility is immense," he said, arguing that education is crucial to preserving an open society and fighting antisemitism.
AfD's Chrupalla claims mandate to govern after Saxony-Anhalt victory
Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leader Tino Chrupalla says his party secured a mandate to govern with its strong election result in Saxony-Anhalt.
"We have halved the CDU, so from that point of view it’s a great evening," Chrupalla told journalists in Magdeburg, referring to an earlier remark by Christian Democratic Union (CDU) leader and chancellor Friedrich Merz that AfD's result could be cut in half.
Chrupalla called the outcome "sensational."
"Ulrich Siegmund will be the new premier of Saxony-Anhalt," he said. "From here, we will change Germany."
If the party falls short of an absolute majority, Chrupalla said it would be open to talks and even suggested an AfD minority government could be tolerated by other parties.
Lead candidate Siegmund, however, later rejected that option, saying there would be "no arrangements involving a minority government or anything like that." He said the AfD would, in principle. be open to a coalition partner willing to change migration and energy policy, but that he currently saw no such party.
No left-wing cooperation with the AfD, Left co-chair says
Co-leader of Germany's Left Party Heidi Reichinnek said her party will not cooperate with the AfD in the wake of the Saxony-Anhalt elections under any circumstances.
She called the AfD a "right-wing extremist" party.
"We will do our best to prevent the AfD from reaching a position of power, but we cannot do this on our own," Reichinnek told German public broadcaster ARD, while also calling all other parties to keep up the so-called "firewall," the policy of excluding any political cooperation with the AfD.
"Many people here are scared, people with migrant backgrounds, queer people. I'd like to tell them: You are not alone," Reichinnek said.
BSW open to working with AfD on policy issues
The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) has signaled that it could cooperate with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) on individual policy issues in Saxony-Anhalt.
"We will always decide on the substance," BSW lead candidate Claudia Wittig told Germany's public broadcaster ARD.
She used the example of energy prices, saying that such issues "can be done together with the AfD," while there may be less common ground in other areas.
Wittig also argued that, given the AfD’s strong result, it would be "completely undemocratic not to involve them in government in some way."
At the same time, she rejected both AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund and incumbent Christian Democratic Union (CDU) Premier Sven Schulze as potential heads of the next state government.
"We want a nonpartisan premier," Wittig said.
She also argued that her leftist populist party could help bridge an increasingly polarized political landscape.
The BSW, founded in 2024 around former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht, advocates for greater social and economic equality but also calls for more restrictive positions on migration and criticizes Germany’s foreign policy.
Current projections put the party at exactly 5.0%, right on the threshold needed to win seats, but a minor shift in numbers could see it miss out on the state parliament.
Greens hail gains, warn of AfD surge in Saxony-Anhalt
There was massive jubilation at the Greens' election event in Magdeburg when the party's own result appeared on screen, DW correspondent Giulia Saudelli reported. Some staff members were in tears of joy and relief.
The Greens reached 8.9% in the first projection, significantly outperforming pre-election surveys that had generally put them at around 5%. If the result holds, it would be a historic result for the party in Saxony-Anhalt.
Lead candidate Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz said civil society had placed its hopes in the Greens.
"We will not disappoint that hope," she said, adding that the party would "always be the antagonist of the right" in the state parliament.
Greens co-leader Felix Banaszak also welcomed his own party's result.
"Many had already written off the Greens," Banaszak said, adding that the party was now on course for its best-ever state election result in Saxony-Anhalt. "That fills me with joy and pride."
At the same time, he said he was deeply concerned by the AfD’s strong gains.
"These are dramatic conditions that are emerging here," Banaszak said.
DW reporter Saudelli also reported shocked faces as party members saw the AfD and CDU results and considered the difficult task of forming a government without the far-right Alternative for Germany.

Escitalopram reduces impulsivity and anger in women with severe premenstrual irritability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:00:34 UTC
01:00:34 KST

A study of women suffering from severe premenstrual irritability and anger found that escitalopram reduced their irritability and anger in the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. Participants on escitalopram also demonstrated a lower frequency of anticipatory responses and greater consistency in response speeds in a sustained attention test. The paper was published in Psychological Medicine.
The menstrual cycle is a recurring biological process in which hormonal changes prepare the body of a woman for a possible pregnancy. It is commonly divided into the menstrual, follicular, ovulatory, and luteal phases. The cycle begins with menstruation, when the uterine lining is shed and menstrual bleeding occurs. Ovulation occurs around the middle of the cycle, when a mature egg is released from the ovary. The last is the luteal phase, during which progesterone becomes dominant and the uterine lining is maintained in preparation for a possible pregnancy. If pregnancy does not occur, estrogen and progesterone levels fall toward the end of the luteal phase, leading to the beginning of a new menstrual cycle.
For some women, these hormonal changes are accompanied by recurring emotional, behavioral, and physical symptoms that become particularly pronounced before menstruation. These changes, called premenstrual symptoms, are thought to be linked to normal fluctuations in sex hormones across the menstrual cycle. In more severe cases, the symptoms may form part of premenstrual dysphoric disorder, or PMDD. In this disorder, several symptoms repeatedly emerge during the luteal phase and largely disappear after menstruation begins.
Studies have shown that selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs, a type of medication used to treat depression, can be effective in reducing the symptoms of PMDD within only a few days. This suggests that serotonin, a neurotransmitter affected by SSRIs, might play an important role in premenstrual symptoms. It seems to be particularly effective in reducing irritability, anger, and rapid mood shifts.
Study author Maria Gröndal and her colleagues conducted a study in which they examined possible cognitive components of impulsivity in premenstrual irritability. They also examined the women’s sustained attention and the effects of intermittent treatment with escitalopram, a widely used SSRI.
Study participants were 27 women suffering from severe premenstrual irritability and anger, selected from an initial pool of 203 prospective participants. Participants were included in the study if they showed at least a 50% increase in irritability/anger symptoms from the follicular phase to the luteal phase of a menstrual cycle, and had a mean rating of irritability/anger over a threshold study authors defined over the last 5 days of the menstrual cycle. Participants’ average age was 33 years. 85% of them had a university degree. Participants received 1000 SEK (around $100) for each of their three lab visits, plus reimbursement for travel or loss of income.
The study extended over three of the study participants’ menstrual cycles. The first cycle did not involve any intervention. In cycles 2 and 3, participants were randomly assigned to either receive 20mg of escitalopram per day during the luteal phase of cycle 2 and placebo (an identically looking pill with no effects) during the luteal phase of cycle 3, in a single-blind design, or to receive these same treatments in the reverse order (placebo in cycle 2, escitalopram in cycle 3).
Participants completed a sustained attention test (the Conners Continuous Performance Test 3 – CPT 3) twice, once in the luteal phase of cycle 2 and once in the luteal phase of cycle 3. They also completed an assessment of impulsivity twice – once in the follicular phase and once in the luteal phase of the cycle when they were receiving placebo. Participants also rated their symptoms on a daily basis using an online survey. The symptoms they rated were irritability/anger, depressed mood, mood swings, and tension/anxiety.
Results showed that participants reported significantly higher levels of negative urgency (the tendency to act impulsively when experiencing negative emotions) during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle compared to the follicular phase. They also showed lower levels of sensation seeking. There were no differences between phases of the menstrual cycle in the other two aspects of impulsivity (lack of premeditation and lack of perseverance).
On the sustained attention test, perseverations (anticipatory, repetitive, or random responses) were significantly higher during the placebo cycle than during the escitalopram cycle. During the menstrual cycle when participants were receiving placebo, they also showed greater variability in their response speeds. In other words, escitalopram reduced participants’ anticipatory responses and made their reaction speeds more consistent. Escitalopram treatment also caused a significant reduction in self-rated irritability, anger, and mood swings in the luteal phase.
“The current study showed that intermittent treatment with escitalopram during the symptomatic luteal phase of the menstrual cycle may have a beneficial impact on specific aspects of impulsivity and inattentiveness in women with severe premenstrual irritability and anger. Moreover, our findings showed that self-reported urgency increased, whereas self-reported sensation seeking decreased in the luteal versus the follicular phase, suggesting that different facets of impulsivity may be of different significance to premenstrual complaints,” study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific knowledge about premenstrual disorders and ways to treat their symptoms. However, it should be noted that the study was conducted on a very small group of women, selected for severe premenstrual irritability and anger. Results of studies involving larger groups of women may not be identical.
The paper, “The effects of intermittent escitalopram treatment on impulsivity and inattention in women with premenstrual irritability and anger,” was authored by Maria Gröndal, Christin Englund, Jakob Näslund, Karl Ask, Elias Eriksson, and Stefan Winblad.

====================================================================================================

Pupils with Send plans in England likely to double to one in 10 in rush for support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:00:09 UTC
01:00:09 KST

Schools and councils across England are expecting the proportion of children with special needs plans to double to one in 10, with families rushing to secure support before ministers bring in changes.
Headteachers have reported an “unreal” surge in applications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs) mandating support for needs or disabilities such as speech and learning difficulties, autism or ADHD. In 2025, just one in 20 school-age children had EHCPs.
The number of pupils with EHCPs has risen by more than 11% in each of the past two years, and projections by local authorities seen by the Guardian are anticipating similar double-digit annual increases over the next three years. Similar levels nationally would mean just under 10% of all school-age children with an EHCP in 2029.
Such a rapid increase would outstrip the government’s own forecasts and eat into funding for improving specialist support in mainstream schools, undermining its plans for immediate reform while straining school and council budgets.
School leaders said their special educational needs (Send) coordinators had worked through the summer to deal with the influx of requests for assessments, as secondary schools say that many more year 7 pupils are arriving with EHCPs or applications.
One described the volume of requests as “unreal”, while other schools said they expected to have double the number of incoming pupils with EHCPs when the new academic year begins this month.
Bill Revans, the County Councils Network’s spokesperson on special educational needs and disabilities (Send), and the Liberal Democrat leader of Somerset council, said: “It is clear there has been a particularly sharp surge in assessment requests to our member councils this year since the government announced its planned reforms in February.
“Our previous analysis had predicted the number of EHCPs will rise to 840,000 by 2028-29, however, it is now likely these numbers will be exceeded.
“This translates to very real financial pressures on local authorities, and despite the government commitment to wipe 90% of existing Send deficits built up by councils over the past decade, we expect the debt to be re-accrued by as soon as this time next year.”
EHCPs are legal documents agreed between local authorities and families in England detailing the support required for children and young people up to the age of 25, allowing access to extra funding or places in special schools. While more than 530,000 school-age children have EHCPs, an additional 1.3 million have identified special needs, according to official data.
The costs are met out of local authority high needs budgets but the massive growth in EHCPs has led to councils amassing sustained deficits, and require a statutory override granted by central government to avoid many local authorities becoming technically bankrupt.
Georgia Gould, the schools minister overseeing the changes, said the government was carefully considering the responses to its white paper, which aims to give children earlier diagnosis and intervention and moderate the need for EHCPs. The white paper’s timeline would mean more children get individual support plans alongside increased support in mainstream schools; while EHCPs would be designed for those with more profound needs and disabilities from 2030.
During a visit to Thomas Lord Audley secondary school in Colchester, Gould said parts of the planned changes would begin operating this year, including the government’s new “experts in hand” scheme that puts specialists directly into mainstream schools and nurseries.
“I’ve spoken to parents around the country, and lots of families and children have been really let down by the system,” Gould said. “So they are really concerned, and any change can feel worrying for those families.
“That’s why we want to put in place tangible change they can see and feel in classrooms and in their communities. And we’ve been clear that we will build a new and inclusive system before we bring in wider changes.
“We’re really determined to put that support in place so parents don’t need to fight, the support will be readily available at their school, and so no child falls through the cracks.”
Gould acknowledged that it was “going to take time to build that trust, to work with families for them to see that day to day. All the work we are doing, the investment, the teacher training, the sharing of best practice, is so important.”
Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said the reports of increases in EHCPs chimed with “what we hear from school leaders”.
Whiteman said: “While it is hard to give a definitive reason for why this is happening, it appears likely that the government’s plans to restrict future EHCPs to children with the most complex needs may have led to more families and schools applying before these changes kick-in.”
Ipsea, a charity that helps families navigate the special needs system, said its helplines had received most calls about EHCP provision since March, after the changes were announced.
Madeleine Cassidy, Ipsea’s chief executive, said: “The government’s proposed Send reforms risk making an already fragile system worse by removing the statutory protections and vital safeguards available to children and families when support is delayed, denied or inadequate.”
The surge in applications has led some local authorities to dramatically raise their own forecasts. A report by Hampshire council in July showed applications so far this year were at record levels and forecasted a 58% increase in EHCPs between 2026 and 2030. Manchester council is also anticipating a 40% increase in school-age children with EHCPs by 2029.
William Burns, a social care policy adviser for the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy, said a forthcoming survey of local authority treasurers was likely to reveal that the renewed push for EHCPs was creating financial pressures.
Burns said: “The government’s own modelling suggests demand for EHCPs could return to today’s levels by 2035, yet current levels of demand are already placing severe strain on the system. It is therefore difficult to see how recreating today’s volume of need, even within a reformed framework, can be considered a sustainable end state.”

‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:00:09 UTC
01:00:09 KST

Georgia Gould is in a race against time. And the minister responsible for overhauling England’s special educational needs provision is hoping that a state school in Colchester will help her beat the clock.
Gould visited Thomas Lord Audley secondary school last week to see the secrets of its success in persuading local parents that it can help children with special needs thrive in a mainstream setting.
Under the government’s proprosals announced in February, more funding and universal support are to be given to mainstream schools to accommodate children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send).
The schools minister told the Guardian that institutions such as Thomas Lord Audley are doing many things that will become national policy under the new system.
“What they are doing here is a really powerful example of best practice,” Gould said, explaining how the school engages with families and pupils a year or more in advance of entry, and draws up bespoke plans for pupils’ needs similar to the government’s proposed digital records to track and share day-to-day support for children with special needs, called individual support plans.
Gould said: “Part of the work we are trying to do, to transform the system towards inclusion, is to take the best practices from schools like this, and make sure that people can see the evidence and the impact they have on things like attendance … And then we want to spread that practice.
“Of course, schools want to do everything in their power to support children and it’s important that they get a blueprint to be able to do that.”
The hope is that the new tiers of support and national standards will be in place by 2030, when the government wants education, health and care plans (EHCPs) – which many families now use to access support – to be narrowed down to those with the most profound educational needs and disabilities.
But the government’s white paper will allow existing EHCPs to remain in place after 2030. In doing so it may have created a surge of applications from families who fear missing out if they don’t get in before that deadline. That surge means the legacy of EHCPs will absorb funding desperately needed by the new system of support that does not require parents to jump through legal hoops.
“We’re really determined to put that support in place so parents don’t need to fight and battle and go through a bureaucratic process,” Gould said, highlighting evidence she has seen from Rochdale schools that offer early intervention for speech and language difficulties.
“They’ve seen an 85% reduction in referrals for speech and language support because they were able to meet much more of that need at a universal level earlier on, and then those children who did go for an assessment were ones who really needed that specialist extra support. There are models that show this is possible, so we want that early support to be available to everyone.”
Simon Essex, the executive head of Thomas Lord Audley, said the school had earned the trust of parents in Colchester so that it is now oversubscribed.
“We want to serve our community,” he said. “We don’t want any young people who live nearby who can’t come here because we can’t meet their needs.
“That’s our goal, and if that attracts others then we will work hard with the local authority to make it work. That’s why I’m hoping that the funding the government will bring will enable all schools to have the same mindset that we have for these young people.”

Radically rewriting world and Chinese history without solid proof could threaten China’s international image and national identity, a leading Communist Party journal has warned.
There has been a growing trend to promote a less Western-centric view of history in recent years, while Beijing has also been keen to promote the idea that Chinese civilisation has a long and continuous history.

Some of the most eye-catching theories have cast doubt on key aspects of ancient Greek history, which risk damaging Beijing’s relationship with Athens and other governments.

Long-term proteges and verifiable reality must be jettisoned for Saving Private Nige | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
15:42:10 UTC
00:42:10 KST

We’ve all been there. It’s a lovely summer’s day and you just want a bit of me time. A quiet lunch of champagne and oysters. As you do. Anything to get away from having to pretend you are interested in the people of Clacton. Hell, it’s bad enough being expected to actually visit Clacton – who in their right mind would want to do that? – let alone having to talk to the little people who live there.
So, you’re just minding your own business when who should turn up but two of your closest mates in politics – or contractors who you’ve barely heard of, as you prefer to call them – saying they have been having meetings with an American donor and his son who have already given you more than £30,000 for an opinion poll you have commissioned and now want to bung you another £500,000. And these guys would like to meet you.
The cheek of it. Two strangers, one of them even a foreigner, who want to take up an hour of your time. And all you’re going to get for it is half a million quid. Who do they think you are? Don’t they know the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne stumped up a £5m gift? Admittedly, several hundred Cameo users have bought you for £80 a pop, but that was at least a few months ago. Things have changed. Besides, that wasn’t really being bought. More a short-term rental.
These wasters are basically insulting you. But you’re a tolerant kind of guy. You choose to indulge them. If you have a fault it’s that you’re never chippy and are unfailingly polite. Everyone tells you that. So you go along with them even though they have nothing of value to offer you. Yes, Yes. That’s fascinating. Thank you so much. But all along, you’re not really listening at all. You’re just zoning out. Trying to chill out in the sun. All you’re really thinking is of getting the first train out of Clacton.
Over the past few days, Reform have been in a tailspin over the Channel 4 News sting that appeared to show the party was intensely relaxed about breaking the law by taking money from overseas. First, they tried to style it out. It was a hoax. Nothing to see here. It was an establishment plot carried out by anti-establishment climate protesters. Go figure. Then, as the net closed in, they started to panic. No one had a clear line on anything. Dan Jukes, Nigel Farage’s long-term protege, and James Orr, the lawyer turned Cambridge academic turned Reform head of policy, left the party. Anything to buy some breathing space. All that mattered now was Saving Private Nige. Everyone else was expendable.
So for his interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg that was recorded on Saturday but broadcast on Sunday morning, Nige was keen to distance himself from any allegation of wrongdoing. That person in the film that people said was him? It was actually an avatar. Who knows how many versions of Nige might be in play at any one time? He’s a very busy man.
But whichever Nige it had been, he was certain that he hadn’t been listening as the people around him were discussing in some detail not only how they exactly planned to break the law but how they had done so in the past. I mean, that was just pub talk. Who doesn’t like to boast about apparently criminal behaviour over a couple of drinks?
Laura K seemed rather taken aback by this. She wasn’t the only one. Because it turns out Nige is capable of holding down his part in a conversation when he isn’t even listening. What a gift that must be. Most of us distinctly remember him saying, when the talk turned to the polling, that Nige insists he had no idea he had been funded by foreign money, that the polling had been “amazing”, had provided “bang for buck” and “it had worked – boom”. Perhaps he was just talking in his sleep. Or had had his brain hacked by the establishment. He even made a point of thanking the donors.
Not that they were donors, of course. Maybe that was the bit that hurt the most. The realisation that the offer had never been genuine. Then came the distancing. Jukes and Orr had been “injudicious at best”. That would suggest that at worst they might have been … maybe that’s one for the lawyers.
What you had to remember was that Nige had never been close to Dan. Had never really liked him. Come to think of it, he had no idea why he had allowed him to be his right-hand gofer for the last 10 years. As for James, he was just an ingenu. A dreamer. It was totally unreasonable to expect someone who had trained as a finance lawyer to know anything about … er, the law concerning party funding. And it was just daft to think that a Cambridge ethics professor should behave ethically. Orr’s thesis had been on “divine lawmaking”. Perhaps breaking the law had been God’s will.
Dan and James had just been freelancing. They didn’t really work for Reform. So any alleged law breaking was one step further removed from Nige. Besides, as Reform leader, it wasn’t his job to be the compliance officer. Even though no one apparently knew the rules governing party donations better than him. He was the world’s leading expert. That was by the by. His job was just to be the frontman. To smile and shake a few hands. He had just been doing what he had been told.
Yes, said Laura, by now totally confused. But you did appear to be up to speed as the potential donor outlined how a scheme like that would be breaking the law and told him, “it’s all above board”, she said. Worried that she might be losing the plot. No, said Nige. What he had said was: “Is it all above board?” Except he hadn’t. He had definitely said it as a statement. Still, that cleared up one thing. The reason he hadn’t been listening was because he had hearing difficulties. One that made him turn every sentence on its head. Hopefully the police will take that into consideration if they get round to starting an investigation. Nige could do with a break.

Niger military accuses France of orchestrating failed mutiny: What to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
15:42:00 UTC
00:42:00 KST

Niger military accuses France of orchestrating failed mutiny: What to know
French officials deny involvement but tensions between two countries remain high.
Niger’s military government has accused France of orchestrating a failed mutiny that rocked the capital, Niamey, last week.
France denied any involvement in the events in its former colony, but the accusation indicates that tensions between them remain high.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Niger displays arsenal seized after failed military mutiny
- list 2 of 3Niger accuses France of orchestrating failed military mutiny
- list 3 of 3France denies Niger’s accusation it orchestrated failed military mutiny
Here’s what you should know:
What happened last week?
Shortly after midnight on August 29, renegade soldiers targeted Base 101, a major military facility inside Niamey’s international airport complex.
Authorities said the mutineers detained some of their comrades and opened fire at “certain sensitive sites” in the capital.
Fighting spread to the presidential palace and temporarily knocked the state broadcaster off air, with explosions and gunfire echoing around Niamey for hours until Niger’s army, helped by Russian paramilitary fighters known as the Africa Corps, contained the mutiny.
State media said hundreds of soldiers took part, with dozens killed or arrested.
The mutiny happened three years after Abdourahamane Tchiani seized power in a coup that overthrew President Mohamed Bazoum, saying the elected government had failed to contain armed groups. However, violent unrest has persisted, while governance grievances and economic challenges remain.
What has Niger’s military government said?
As with previous rounds of unrest, Niger’s military authorities blamed France and other West African countries.
“This operation, with its international ramifications, was instigated and sustained by a vast network of collusion headed by the French regime of Mr [Emmanuel] Macron,” said Soumana Boubacar, Niger’s government spokesperson, in a statement read out on TV on Friday.
“Traitorous and renegade elements, to whom promises of great things were made, were tasked with carrying out unfulfilled ambitions of Macron and his cronies in our country,” he said, adding that such “undermining manoeuvres will always fail”.
The Niger Council of Ministers, which functions as the cabinet since the 2023 coup, said a “substantial body of evidence has been compiled regarding this attack and Niger reserves the right to bring the matter before international courts”. Details were not provided.
Niger also accused a number of regional countries of being involved, including the regional economic bloc ECOWAS. Benin’s government, one of the countries accused, rejected the accusations.
In contrast, Niger thanked Russia, Algeria and allies in the Sahel region – Burkina Faso and Mali – for their support.
What has been the French response?
France dismissed the allegations as “pure fantasy”.
“There never was any intention, nor means that France would have mobilised,” French Foreign Minister, Jean-Noel Barrot, told the French radio station, RFI.
“All of this is, as usual, a way of wrongly blaming France for something it is simply not responsible for.”
Tensions between the two countries have increased following the 2023 coup.
Niger has since ordered the withdrawal of about 1,500 French troops, expelled the French ambassador, revoked a number of bilateral military agreements and suspended French state-funded stations, such as France 24 and RFI, from broadcasting there.
Is Niger’s security situation worsening?
Henri Nsaibia, West Africa senior analyst at Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), said the Nigerien armed forces’ fight against armed groups linked to ISIL and al-Qaeda could be weakened following the mutiny.
“The regime will likely divert resources from fighting jihadist groups to monitor internal threats,” he said.
Niger’s security situation is facing several challenges.
Since the 2023 coup, nearly 6,000 people have been killed in more than 1,400 violent incidents, according to ACLED. The casualties represent a sharp increase compared to the three years before Tchiani was in power, when nearly 3,200 people were killed in more than 1,300 violent incidents.
“Niger still experiences less intense violence than neighbouring Mali and Burkina Faso, but faces a wider range of armed threats,” said Nsaibia.
What’s the history of French colonialism in Niger?
France’s influence has dropped dramatically throughout its former colonies in West Africa in recent years in the wake of failed military interventions and allegations of interference.
The rise in anti-French sentiment has helped coup leaders in a number of countries claim legitimacy, including in Niger, where France has a long history of brutality.
France’s 1899 military campaign in Niger is still remembered for its intense violence, mass executions and destruction of towns and villages.
Niger became part of France’s colonial empire the following year and gained independence in 1960, but Paris still meddled in its internal politics and economic policies.
In recent years, discussions about potential reparations as compensation for the looting and extraction of the country’s resources during and after French rule have intensified.

Israeli attack drone maker hits a big production milestone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
15:41:51 UTC
00:41:51 KST

- SpearUAV says it has nearly 1,000 Viper 300 loitering munition drones ready for delivery worldwide, without naming specific customers or countries.
- The Israeli company disclosed a $20 million contract for the system in December 2024, with options to expand to about $60 million.
Israeli drone maker SpearUAV says it has nearly 1,000 Viper 300 loitering munition systems ready for delivery to customers around the world, a production milestone the Tel Aviv-based company announced without naming which countries or units are receiving the systems.
The Viper 300 is a small, capsule-launched drone that soldiers can fire either on foot or from an armored vehicle, then use to loiter over an area, identify a target using onboard artificial intelligence, and strike it directly.
SpearUAV designed the system for infantry squads and armored units, positioning it as an alternative to larger, fixed-wing attack drones for close-in engagements. The company said its production has reached “hundreds of systems a month,” though it did not specify an exact current output rate or break down the nearly 1,000-unit figure by customer or region.
The drone weighs 2.8 kilograms (6.2 pounds) including its launch capsule and payload, reaches speeds of about 27 meters per second (60 mph), and has a range of 5 kilometers (3.1 miles) with up to 20 minutes of flight time. Unlike fixed-wing drones, the Viper 300 uses a quadcopter design that lets it hover in place, which SpearUAV has said gives it an advantage in dense urban terrain or when tracking a moving target closely rather than flying past it.
SpearUAV disclosed its first major publicly confirmed contract for the system in December 2024, when it announced a $20 million deal with an undisclosed customer that included options to expand the agreement to roughly $60 million. The company said at the time it expected to begin deliveries under that contract in 2025 and described it as part of a record year for new orders. SpearUAV has also built a version of the launcher, called the Multi Canister Launcher, that lets militaries mount several Viper drones directly onto armored vehicles, and the Viper 300 has separately been included in Rafael’s pitch to the United Kingdom’s Ministry of Defence for an autonomous resupply program known as Project Theseus.
The Viper 300 sits within a broader family of SpearUAV systems that includes the smaller Viper 40, the larger Viper 750 built for naval use, and the Viper I, an interceptor version designed to shoot down drones and other aerial threats rather than strike ground targets. SpearUAV has not disclosed the total value of contracts tied to the nearly 1,000 Viper 300 systems it now says are ready for delivery, nor identified any of the international customers driving that order volume.

The death toll from devastating flash floods in Nepal has reached at least 1,342, with thousands still missing, officials and local media reports have said.
The combined death toll from flash floods and mudslides along the Nepal-China border rose to at least 1,385, while 5,519 people remained missing 11 days after the disaster struck, according to official data from the two countries on Sunday.
Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said around 5,000 people, including 589 foreigners, remained missing.
More than 13,000 people have so far been rescued from the flood-hit areas.
Chinese authorities said at least 43 people have been confirmed dead, while 519 others remained missing in Tibet.
Of those missing, 850 are foreigners, according to official figures from Nepal and China.
‘We are not getting enough to eat’
With roads and bridges damaged due to massive floods and landslides, thousands of expectant and new mothers are struggling hardest to find a female-friendly space to breastfeed, get proper food and reach emergency care if labour turns dangerous, the local English daily Kathmandu Post reported.
The mothers also complain about cigarette smoke, the smell of alcohol and, on top of all that, unhygienic food and water, which upset their and their babies' stomachs.
Also, there are no vaccination facilities for children in the shelter camps.
"We are not getting food on time either. We are not getting enough to eat,” a new mother who wished to be identified only as Pariyar said.
Pariyar fled her home when floods struck her hometown, Trishuli, on the morning of August 26 and is now staying with dozens of strangers under one roof in a shelter camp.
“They aren’t giving any special food for babies. We are forced to feed that same heavy adult food to the small child. What would help most is simple: If only we had a decent, proper place to stay. That would bring some peace of mind," Sharmila Shrestha, another mother, complained.
She and her two kids sleep in a crowded classroom of a school-turned-shelter camp.
Hardest-hit districts
According to UN Population Fund estimates, around 4,430 pregnant women are living in areas across the 15 municipalities in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, the districts hardest hit by last week’s devastating floods.
Based on the estimates, around 500 births could be expected in the following month, with roughly 74 women potentially requiring emergency obstetric care.
At Trishuli Hospital, the maternity ward has become an improvised outpost of crisis medicine.
Basanti Pancha, the head of the department, said the hospital has performed nine deliveries since the floods but was struggling to keep pace with everything else.
Women have kept arriving for fever, reduced fetal movement and urinary tract infections in pregnancy, she added.
Electricity is also unreliable, and a generator is the only source of power for surgeries.
“Previously, Kathmandu was just a two-hour road trip away. But now, by road, nobody knows how many hours it will take because of the landslides," Pancha added.

U.S. peace envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Kyiv on Sunday as the Trump administration renewed its push to end Russia's four-and-a-half-year war in Ukraine.
Kushner and Witkoff travelled from Moscow, where they held three hours of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Saturday but did not appear to secure a breakthrough in the conflict.
Previous rounds of U.S.-mediated peace talks encouraged by President Donald Trump, who campaigned on a promise to quickly end the war, have yielded few results. He suggested on Friday that the U.S. had a fresh proposal, though he did not elaborate.
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov described Saturday's meeting as "highly useful," while a White House official told Reuters that next steps would be announced in the coming weeks.
The two envoys met Zelenskiy and other top Ukrainian officials in central Kyiv.
Zelenskiy, who believes Washington will be key to any peace deal, has said a window of opportunity to make peace exists before the U.S. begins focusing on its next presidential election.
After the first round of talks between Ukrainian and U.S. negotiators that lasted about three hours, the U.S. envoys said that they were looking forward to making more progress.
"Substantive, important, and we are very encouraged,” Witkoff told reporters after the talks, which also included a working lunch.
Zelenskiy said that more talks, which would also include European representatives, were planned later on Sunday. British, French and German national security advisers were in Kyiv on Sunday.
"Security guarantees are needed. A dignified post-war peace is needed. Our proposals have been drawn up," Zelenskiy said as his negotiating team was preparing to meet U.S. envoys.
Cautious optimism on the streets of Kyiv
Witkoff and Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, have visited Moscow several times in their roles as peace envoys. But Sunday is their first visit to Kyiv in their capacity as U.S. negotiators.
Their visit has long been sought by Ukraine's leadership, and on the streets of Kyiv, which has been bombarded heavily in recent weeks, some residents were hopeful.
"The issue can be solved in the blink of an eye. We want peace. I've fought myself, so I know what war is like. We need peace, because there's no other way," said military veteran Stepan Yermak.
In previous talks, the sides have remained far apart on key issues, including the future of the eastern Ukrainian region of Donbas. Russia has demanded Ukraine's withdrawal from an entrenched belt of towns that it still controls there, but Kyiv has refused, reasoning that it can still hold on.
For Ukraine, hard security guarantees from its European allies and the U.S. are crucial to deterring Russia from invading again.
"We need an agreement that will never be broken," said Svitlana Kurylenko, a 19-year-old cafe worker.
"Just leave Ukraine alone and let people live in peace."
Temporary halt in strikes
Though the front lines of the ground war remain largely static, both Russian and Ukrainian forces have intensified long-range air strikes in recent weeks.
Russia has pounded the Ukrainian capital day and night with missiles and drones for the past two weeks, including an attack on Friday on the headquarters of the SBU security service.
The Kremlin has said it would pause strikes on Kyiv until Monday, while Zelenskiy has said Ukraine would also halt strikes on Moscow.
There was no let-up in fighting along the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile) front, however, and Russia bombarded other Ukrainian cities on Saturday.
Ukraine has inflicted damaging hits throughout the summer on Russian refineries, oil terminals and the warehouses of online retailer Wildberries, in an attempt to raise the cost to Moscow of continuing the war.
Ukraine said on Sunday it had struck the Ryazan oil refinery, around 480 kilometers (300 miles) inside Russia, overnight, causing a fire.

IFA 2026: Xiaomi wants its smart-home cars on European roads by 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
15:37:05 UTC
00:37:05 KST

Xiaomi is done being just a phone brand. At IFA 2026, it laid out plans to launch electric cars in Europe by 2027, all wired into a smart-home ecosystem it calls Human x Car x Home.
Xiaomi may still be best known for its smartphones. But at IFA 2026, the Chinese technology company presented plans for a future that no longer fits inside people's pockets.
Home appliances and connected devices have become an increasingly important part of its business. Now, Xiaomi is putting greater emphasis on four wheels — and the shift is hard to miss at IFA.
Inside the company's exhibition space in Berlin, one of the first things visitors encounter is a futuristic-looking car carrying the familiar Xiaomi logo, but on a very different scale.
Xiaomi cars are already a familiar sight for consumers in China. Now the company wants to bring them to European roads too.
In that spirit, Xiaomi announced at IFA 2026 that it plans to launch its electric vehicles in Europe in 2027, marking the next stage of its expansion beyond smartphones and consumer electronics.
But simply selling cars is not the company's ultimate goal. Like many of the technology companies exhibiting in Berlin, Xiaomi is increasingly focused on connecting different parts of everyday life.
It calls its approach "Human x Car x Home", an ecosystem designed to link personal devices, the car and technology around the home. In practice, the idea is to let you steer your home from behind the wheel of your car.
Euronews took a closer look at Xiaomi's vision at IFA 2026 to see how that ecosystem is supposed to work.
'Human x Car x Home': The vision
Rather than treating the car as a separate product, Xiaomi wants to integrate it into the same connected system that already links devices around the home. The aim is for users to move between different environments while staying connected to the devices they rely on every day.
At IFA, Xiaomi demonstrated what that could look like in practice. From inside the car, users could control devices back at home, including opening and closing connected curtains and switching the air conditioning on or off.
This means the car could effectively become another control point for the smart home. Someone leaving work, for example, could adjust the air conditioning before arriving home, while other connected devices could be controlled directly from the vehicle.
Xiaomi says AI and its HyperOS operating system are intended to provide the technological link between these devices. Its longer-term vision goes beyond users manually controlling individual appliances, with AI eventually using contextual information to coordinate devices across the car, smartphone and home.
For Xiaomi, the car is therefore not only a new product category, but another part of a wider connected ecosystem — extending its technology beyond smartphones and the home and onto the road.
Alongside its more concrete plans, Xiaomi has also left room for imagination, exploring what could become possible further down the road.
Among the concepts presented at IFA is the Xiaomi Vision Gran Turismo. The electric hypercar concept was developed for the Gran Turismo racing game series and explores ideas around design, aerodynamics and digital interaction.
For now, however, this vehicle remains firmly a concept rather than a preview of a production model expected to hit the road any time soon.
Local partners
But despite leaving room for experimentation, Xiaomi also made clear that its European ambitions go beyond concepts. At its IFA press conference on 3 September, the company took concrete steps towards its planned market entry.
During a signing ceremony, the company signed letters of intent with eight German automotive retail groups: Emil Frey Germany, the Ernst Dello Group, Autohaus Dinnebier, Hahn Automobile, the LUEG Mobility Group, Fett & Wirtz, SPT Avior and Penske-Jacobs.
Germany, however, is only intended to be the starting point, with Xiaomi planning similar partnerships in other European markets.
"Europe is a key market for our global strategy," Xiaomi Chief Marketing Officer Xu Fei said during the press conference.
The company is also planning significant investment to support this broader strategy. Between 2026 and 2030, Xiaomi says it intends to invest more than €24 billion globally in research and development, with a focus on areas including AI, operating systems, semiconductors, intelligent vehicles, robotics and smart manufacturing.

Azerbaijan starts local production of naval drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
15:35:01 UTC
00:35:01 KST

- Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev toured a joint Azerbaijani-Turkish production facility building SALVO and KAYRA unmanned surface vessels on September 6.
- The facility, run by Azerbaijan's MIRAS and Turkey's DEARSAN Shipyard, marks a shift from importing Turkish naval drones to producing them domestically.
Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev visited the country’s navy on September 6, where officials showed him two unmanned surface vessels now being built inside Azerbaijan through a joint production line with a Turkish shipbuilder.
Aliyev and First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva were briefed on the SALVO armed unmanned surface vessel and the KAYRA kamikaze unmanned surface vessel at a facility jointly operated by MIRAS Military-Industrial Company, a state defense manufacturer under Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Defense, and Turkey’s DEARSAN Shipyard.
Defense Minister Col. Gen. Zakir Hasanov briefed the president on the visit, according to a statement from the presidential press service. The two leaders toured the production line and watched the vessels undergo practical testing, and the statement did not disclose how many units of either vessel have been built or when full-rate production is expected to begin.
The SALVO is a Turkish-designed unmanned boat that first completed live-fire testing in 2022, when it struck a moving target in the Sea of Marmara using a Roketsan Cirit 70mm laser-guided missile fired from a remote turret, alongside a stabilized 12.7mm machine gun made by Aselsan. Built with a composite hull roughly 15 meters (49 feet) long, the vessel can reach speeds up to 60 knots and operate out to about 300 nautical miles (555 kilometers) from its controllers, who can run it from shore-based command posts or from other ships.
Dearsan has marketed the SALVO for reconnaissance, surface warfare, facility patrol and armed escort missions. Azerbaijan’s navy first publicly displayed a Turkish-built SALVO during a live-fire exercise in the Caspian Sea in August 2025, though it was not clear at the time when Baku had acquired the vessel.
The KAYRA is smaller and built for a different purpose. At about 7 meters (23 feet) long with a composite hull, it can reach a top speed of 50 knots and operate out to roughly 200 nautical miles (370 kilometers), according to Dearsan’s own specifications. Rather than carrying a separate weapons system, the KAYRA is designed as a one-way attack vessel, packed with its own warhead and intended to ram and destroy enemy ships, patrol boats, port infrastructure or naval bases directly.
Wednesday’s visit marks a shift from Azerbaijan simply operating Turkish-built naval drones to producing them jointly on Azerbaijani soil. The Ministry of Defense-linked MIRAS has increasingly partnered with Turkish defense firms in recent years, part of a broader defense-industrial relationship between Baku and Ankara that expanded significantly following Turkey’s military support to Azerbaijan during the 2020 war over Nagorno-Karabakh. Azerbaijan has separately developed its own smaller kamikaze drone boats, including the Kalan and Sugovushan models shown at a defense exhibition in 2024, though those remain considerably smaller than the Turkish-designed SALVO and KAYRA.

Isro says its 'next chapter' is leading national space ecosystem

ISRO “would neither be privatised nor will its importance be diminished”.
BENGALURU: Two days after nine employee bodies at Isro centres sought written clarity on the future role of the organisation amid space-sector reforms, Isro on Sunday hinted at its “next chapter” while categorically stating that it “would neither be privatised nor will its importance be diminished”.“Isro will continue to remain India’s principal institution for advanced space R&D, national and strategic missions, space science and exploration, and critical and frontier space capabilities. Participation of the private sector is not about reducing Isro’s role. It is about enabling Isro to focus even more strongly on the next generation of India’s space programme, while industry scales mature technologies and capabilities,” Isro said.Also read:Isro will remain ‘bedrock of Indian space sector’, says GoenkaWhat is changing is not the importance of Isro, but the scale and structure of India’s space ecosystem, it said, adding that the space-sector reforms institutionalised through the Indian Space Policy 2023, along with progressive liberalisation of FDI policy, aim to create a larger, stronger and globally competitive Indian space ecosystem.“Industry, start-ups and academia are being enabled to participate across the space value chain, complementing and multiplying Isro’s capabilities.
The reforms should therefore be seen as ecosystem expansion and capability multiplication, not privatisation,” Isro said.As India’s industrial and technological capabilities have grown, mature and scalable activities can increasingly be undertaken by Indian industry, it said, adding Isro has already transferred multiple technologies to industry.“Transferring a mature technology doesn’t mean Isro is withdrawing from that domain. It enables large-scale production, commercialisation, innovation and access to global markets while allowing Isro’s scientific and technical manpower to concentrate on advanced research, next-generation technologies and complex national missions,” It said.The transition is therefore towards an “Isro-led national space ecosystem.” “...Isro’s role will progressively strengthen in areas where its scientific expertise matters most: frontier R&D, advanced technologies, human spaceflight, next-generation launch systems, deep-space and planetary missions and strategic national capabilities,” it said.The agency added that it’ll continue developing cutting-edge technologies, including advanced payloads for communication, navigation and Earth observation, sensors, propulsion systems and other critical technologies.“Meanwhile, mature and routinely manufactured systems can increasingly be scaled through industry. Production of mature launch vehicles, routine satellites and other established systems can increasingly be undertaken by industry or PSUs through appropriate competitive processes,” Isro said.This, it says, allows Isro to devote more resources and scientific manpower to the next generation of technologies and missions, while the wider ecosystem provides the investment, manufacturing capacity and scale required by an expanding national space programme.Pointing out that the transition was important in the context of Space Vision 2047, it said technologies needed for establishing the Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035, crewed mission to Moon by 2040, developing next-generation and reusable launch systems, pursuing sustained lunar and planetary exploration, and establishing India as a major global space power, require Isro to remain focused on advanced research and capabilities that cannot simply be substituted by commercial activity.The objective is “therefore to enable industry to scale mature capabilities while Isro pushes India towards the next technological frontier”.“The Department of Space provides overall policy direction, Isro remains the core organisation for advanced R&D, technology development and national missions. IN-SPACe facilitates and authorises the participation of non-government entities, while NSIL undertakes commercialisation and industry-led utilisation of mature capabilities,” Isro said.
It added that industry and start-ups contribute investment, innovation, manufacturing capacity and market access. “At the same time, ownership and control of critical national space infrastructure and strategic capabilities will continue to remain with the Govt. Private participation in operations and services will be enabled where appropriate and will remain subject to national-security, safety and other regulatory requirements. Strategic and nationally critical capabilities will continue to be governed by security, safety, quality and national-interest considerations,” it said.

Roundup: Chinese motorcycle brands gain traction on racetrack, among French fans
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06

MAGNY-COURS, France, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Chinese motorcycle brands are gaining visibility both on the racetrack and among French enthusiasts, as strong results in international competition coincide with growing consumer interest in one of Europe's major motorcycle markets.
At the FIM Supersport World Championship's French Round, which concluded Sunday at the Nevers Magny-Cours Circuit, riders Valentin Debise and Federico Caricasulo delivered a strong weekend for Chinese manufacturer ZXMOTO and the Evan Bros Racing team.
The pair secured a historic one-two in Friday's Superpole, with home rider Debise taking his first career WorldSSP pole ahead of Caricasulo. They finished third and fifth respectively in Race 1, while Debise claimed another third-place finish and Caricasulo finished eighth in Sunday's Race 2.
Speaking to Xinhua ahead of the race, Debise said ZXMOTO's approach to motorcycle development was one of the reasons he decided to join the fledgling racing project.
"At the beginning, that's what convinced me to join ZXMOTO, because that's what they told me: 'We want to make the best motorcycle. That's what matters,'" Debise said.
The French rider, who made his first trip to China during the recent summer break, said the drive for constant improvement he observed there had strengthened his confidence in the potential of China's motorcycle industry in France and across Europe.
For ZXMOTO, its debut WorldSSP campaign is also part of a broader push into Europe. Huang Qin, head of the company's foreign trade department, said the largely European championship provides a platform to raise its profile in a key overseas market.
In France, ZXMOTO is working with motorcycle importer and distributor DIP. Anthony Barneaud, who oversees the brand at the company, said it had already received "a significant number of pre-orders" ahead of the first deliveries to French dealers.
Barneaud said ZXMOTO's WorldSSP performances had created a "real surprise effect," generating greater interest from riders and dealers. More broadly, he said Chinese brands were gradually changing perceptions by showing French motorcyclists they could offer reliable, well-equipped motorcycles at competitive prices.
Away from the track, Chinese manufacturers were also drawing attention from spectators browsing motorcycle displays around the circuit.
"Chinese motorcycles offer very good value for money," said Ludovic, a French motorcycle enthusiast. A long-time fan of Italian brands, he said Chinese manufacturers had increasingly caught his attention.
Interest is also visible online. The 2026 ZXMOTO 820RR attracted more than 10,000 unique visitors to its model page over the latest quarter on French motorcycle website Motoplanete, making it the site's most-viewed motorcycle model page during the period. The CFMOTO 1000 MT-X 2026, from another Chinese brand, ranked second.
Other Chinese manufacturers were also visible at Magny-Cours. A QJMotor display drew a steady stream of spectators during the weekend.
A staff member from SIMA, QJMotor's importer in France, told Xinhua that Chinese manufacturers' progress in international racing had helped increase their visibility among French riders. "It's important for us," he said.
The interest comes as Chinese motorcycle brands continue to expand their presence in France. In May, they accounted for 15.7 percent of new motorcycle registrations, according to French publication L'Automobile Magazine. Registrations rose 58 percent year-on-year that month, meaning roughly one in six newly registered motorcycles was from a Chinese brand.
Huang said attracting attention through racing and new products was only a first step. Building lasting consumer trust in mature overseas markets would also require competitive products, sustained participation in top-level racing, a strong dealer network and reliable after-sales service.
"Only then can we achieve sales in mature markets and build a strong reputation for the brand," Huang said. ■

====================================================================================================

Xinhua Headlines: RMB use expands in Africa amid growing financial connectivity and trade
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
23:34:14 CST
00:34:14 KST

* As China-Africa trade continues to expand, the RMB is being used not only for trade settlement, but increasingly for payment and clearing and, more recently, for financing.
* Deepening economic ties between China and Africa are providing stronger support for the wider use of the RMB in cross-border transactions.
* The continued development of payment infrastructure is an important factor in expanding the cross-border use of the RMB in Africa.
* The expansion from trade settlement to bond financing shows that the RMB is taking on a broader role in international economic activities.
by Xinhua writers Xu Jiatong, Wang Yue
NAIROBI, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- China's currency, the renminbi (RMB), is playing a bigger role in Africa as trade with the continent flourishes. From the launch of direct RMB settlement services in Tanzania to expanded connectivity with the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) in Kenya and Namibia, as well as the establishment of RMB clearing arrangements for Africa, such recent developments highlight the growing role of the Chinese currency in cross-border transactions.
As China-Africa trade continues to expand, the RMB is being used not only for trade settlement, but increasingly for payment and clearing and, more recently, for financing. This expansion is driven by growing demand from China-Africa trade and investment, while an improved financial infrastructure is making cross-border RMB transactions more accessible.
CROSS-BORDER RMB
The international use of a currency is closely linked to demand generated by trade and investment. Deepening economic ties between China and Africa are providing stronger support for the wider use of the RMB in cross-border transactions.
In August, Stanbic Bank Tanzania launched a direct RMB settlement service, allowing Tanzanian businesses trading with China to make and receive payments directly in RMB.
Direct RMB settlement can reduce unnecessary currency conversions and provide businesses with an additional payment option, Tanzanian Deputy Minister for Industry and Trade Dennis Londo said.
In Zambia, the RMB has also been used for mining tax payments. The country's central bank began accepting RMB payments for mining taxes in October 2025.
For Zambia, where copper exports are a major economic pillar and China is a key trading partner, the RMB payment channel provides businesses and the government with another option for managing foreign exchange needs.
According to the People's Bank of China's RMB Internationalization Report 2025, cross-border RMB receipts and payments between China and Africa totaled 155.33 billion yuan (23.14 billion dollars) in 2024, up 28.1 percent year on year. RMB receipts and payments related to trade in goods reached 56.37 billion yuan (8.4 billion dollars), up 35.9 percent.
From 2020 to 2024, cross-border RMB settlement between China and Africa nearly doubled, rising from 80.02 billion yuan (11.92 billion dollars) to 155.33 billion yuan (23.14 billion dollars), representing an average annual growth rate of 18.1 percent.
For businesses, the appeal of using the RMB is straightforward. When trading partners have regular RMB payment and receipt needs, settling transactions directly in RMB can reduce conversion costs and help mitigate exchange-rate risks.
With China granting zero-tariff treatment to 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations, trade facilitation between China and Africa is expected to improve further, potentially generating additional demand for cross-border RMB services.
IMPROVING RMB ACCESSIBILITY
While trade explains why businesses choose a currency, financial infrastructure determines how easily they can use it.
Africa provides a clear example of this process. In late July, Stanbic Bank Kenya launched CIPS services, followed in August by Standard Bank Namibia, which became the first bank in the country to provide such services. Standard Bank of South Africa was previously the first African commercial bank to join CIPS.
In June, the People's Bank of China authorized Standard Bank of South Africa and the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China to serve as joint RMB clearing banks for Africa, further strengthening the region's cross-border RMB payment and clearing network.
Bank of China said its RMB business currently covers more than 20 African countries, with the bank serving as an RMB clearing bank in South Africa, Zambia and Mauritius.
Huang Meibo, dean of the Institute for International Development Cooperation at Shanghai University of International Business and Economics, told Xinhua that improved payment infrastructure is making cross-border RMB transactions more convenient in African markets.
As more local banks connect with RMB cross-border payment systems, businesses are gaining broader access to RMB services, while links between the RMB and local financial markets are becoming closer, Huang said.
These developments mark a transition from individual banks providing RMB services to a broader ecosystem involving payment systems, clearing banks and commercial banks.
For market participants, payment convenience, transfer efficiency and access to RMB liquidity can all influence their willingness to use the currency.
The continued development of payment infrastructure is therefore an important factor in expanding the cross-border use of the RMB in Africa.
GROWING FINANCING
If trade settlement provides the foundation for international RMB use, financing and asset allocation represent a deeper stage of currency internationalization.
This trend is emerging in African financial markets. According to Kenya's 2026/2027 Annual Borrowing Plan, the Kenyan government plans to explore issuing RMB-denominated panda bonds as part of efforts to diversify external financing sources and ease fiscal pressures.
Egypt issued 3.5 billion yuan (521.5 million dollars) in panda bonds in 2023, becoming the first African country to issue panda bonds in China's domestic bond market. In 2025, the African Export-Import Bank issued a 2.2 billion yuan (327.8 million dollars) panda bond, the first such issuance by an African multilateral development bank.
The expansion from trade settlement to bond financing shows that the RMB is taking on a broader role in international economic activities.
For African countries, access to China's RMB-denominated capital markets can diversify financing sources and provide new options for entities with trade and investment links with China. For RMB internationalization, participation by overseas governments and financial institutions in China's bond market expands the currency's role in financing and investment.
At the same time, RMB internationalization remains a long-term process. Wider global use of a currency depends not only on trade volumes, but also on financial market depth, availability of RMB-denominated assets, payment network efficiency and overseas investors' willingness to hold RMB assets over time.■

US envoys hold ‘substantive’ talks with Zelenskyy in first visit to Kyiv

US envoys hold ‘substantive’ talks with Zelenskyy in first visit to Kyiv
The meeting comes a day after the US’s Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
United States special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have held talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on ending Russia’s war against his country, marking their first visit to Kyiv since the full-scale Russian invasion in February 2022.
The meeting on Sunday came a day after the two met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
