- list 2 of 3What the US militarisation of Latin America could look like
- list 3 of 3China, Nepal race to find thousands still missing 12 days after floods
“It is very important that the delegation has arrived to see us. We have been waiting a long time for Steve and Jared, Witkoff and Kushner,” Zelenskyy said, thanking US President Donald Trump for “allowing them to come” despite the war. “To us, it is very important to do everything so that this war ends,” he added.
“We’ve had a very meaningful discussion, substantive, important, and we are very encouraged and we look forward to continuing this as long as it takes,” Witkoff said after the talks.
On his part, Kushner said that Trump wanted “not just to figure out how we end the current war, but how do we create the right conditions and arrangements for a long-term, durable peace,” adding that the US team had “learned a lot from the trip.”
Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said little new information came out of the talks.
“The thing that stood out is really that we haven’t learned very much new from it, sort of kicking the can down the road,” she said.
“President Zelenskyy saying that when it comes to the most important issues, like the issues of territory, that it would have to take place at the leader’s level, that is something that he has said time and time again,” MacAlpine added.
“But the real takeaway here was this visit in itself by the US envoys here to Ukraine, and the promise that they may return.”
Earlier, Zelenskyy published a video of himself meeting Trump’s envoys in central Kyiv, saying, “Talks have begun.”
Ukraine’s top security officials and negotiators were also present.
British, French and German national security advisers joined the Ukrainian president, Kushner and Witkoff for the second round of talks in the Ukrainian capital.
“We are grateful that the Europeans are with us today… Here we are all on the same side,” Zelenskyy said.
He added that the war with Russia “at the moment” looked likely to continue into winter.
“We very much hope that we will be able to reach agreements with our American partners, and we are counting on the support of our European partners if the war continues in winter – and this is how it appears at the moment,” he said.
Zelenskyy also said that Ukraine would hold further talks with the US, France and Germany, but did not elaborate.
The US envoys arrived in the Ukrainian capital by train from Poland, hoping to revive negotiations to end Europe’s worst conflict since World War II after a summer of heightened tensions. While Witkoff and Kushner have visited Moscow eight times, they have never held talks in Kyiv until now.
Zelenskyy took the US envoys to see Kyiv’s historic Saint Sophia’s Cathedral, which sits opposite the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) security building that was hit by a Russian drone on Friday.
Moscow’s four-and-a-half-year invasion of Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
Previous rounds of US-mediated peace talks encouraged by Trump, who campaigned on a promise to quickly end the war, have yielded few results. He suggested on Friday that the US had a fresh proposal, though he did not elaborate.
‘Highly useful’ meeting
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov described Saturday’s meeting in Moscow, which ran more than three hours, as “highly useful”, while a White House official told the Reuters news agency that the next steps would be announced in the coming weeks.
Ushakov called the talks “extremely frank”, saying the US team “put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement”, though he gave no details.
In televised comments before those talks, Putin said Russia would ensure the safety of the envoys while in Kyiv. “We will do everything that depends on us to ensure the safety of the negotiation process and mediators such as yourselves,” Putin told Witkoff and Kushner.
Earlier on Saturday, Putin had thanked Trump for persisting in his efforts to end the war despite it being “not simple”.
Trump said again on Friday that his envoys were bringing a “proposal” to end the fighting. “We have an idea for peace,” he said, without elaborating.
US efforts have so far failed to bring about a breakthrough in the war, in part because of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Meanwhile, Russia has occupied large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine, and Putin has insisted Moscow is intent on seizing the rest of the east.
In previous talks, the two sides have remained far apart on a range of key issues, including the future of Ukraine’s eastern regions of Luhansk and Donetsk. Russia has demanded Ukraine’s withdrawal from an entrenched belt of towns that it still controls there, but Kyiv has refused, reckoning it can still hold out for years.
For Ukraine, hard security guarantees from its European allies and the US are crucial to deter Russia from invading again.
No strikes on capitals
Both Russia and Ukraine have pledged not to strike each other’s capital for three days around the US team’s visit. Yet despite the ceasefire agreement for the two cities, fighting continued elsewhere.
The Russian Defence Ministry said on Sunday that its forces had struck a Ukrainian cargo vessel in the Black Sea, which it said was carrying military equipment supplied to the Ukrainian army by Western countries, Russian state news agency Tass reported.
The ministry said earlier it had shot down 400 drones in the past 24 hours, according to the Interfax news agency.
It added that strikes were carried out during the day on Ukrainian infrastructure facilities used by the country’s armed forces, as well as drone storage sites.
The Ukraine Air Force, meanwhile, said Russia had attacked overnight with 108 drones and missiles. It also said on Sunday that it had struck the Ryazan oil refinery, about 480km (298 miles) inside Russia, overnight, causing a fire.

Israeli strikes on Lebanon kill several despite truce
September 6, 2026
At least four people were killed in Israeli strikes on Lebanon on Sunday, which comes despite a ceasefire between the two countries, according to the Lebanese Health Ministry.
The Lebanese officials also said around 20 other people, including children, were wounded in the strikes.
The office of Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun called the strikes a "dangerous escalation" that targeted "purely civilian administrations and health centers."
"President Aoun held the Israeli side fully responsible for this ongoing escalation, calling on the United States and the international community to take immediate action to stop these violations and hold the perpetrators accountable," his aides said in a statement.
In turn, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the strikes were a response to "a blatant violation" by Hezbollah militants.
"Terrorists from the Hezbollah terrorist organization launched two drones towards IDF soldiers operating in the Security Zone in southern Lebanon," the military said in a statement, adding that there were no reports of Israeli soldiers wounded.
What do we know about the strikes?
Early on Sunday morning, the Israeli military issued an online evacuation alert for Arab Salim, saying it identified a "Hezbollah facility" there.
Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) said the Israeli military subsequently carried out a strike on the building mentioned in the original evacuation warning.
NNA also reported that "enemy warplanes launched a strike on another house, destroying it." Two women were killed in the strike.
Another two people were killed in Israeli strikes near the town of Nabatieh al-Fawqa, which lies on the edge of Israel's "security zone" that it occupies in southern Lebanon.
Lebanon's Health Ministry said an Israeli strike "totally destroyed" a disused hospital. The Health Ministry called the incident "another grave violation of international humanitarian law."
The Israeli military said its targets included what it described as a Hezbollah command center inside a building that was previously used as a hospital, as well as a weapons depot.
"The strikes were carried out in response to Hezbollah’s attempted attack yesterday in the Ali Taher Ridge area and to remove threats posed by Hezbollah," it said.

'I am going to an Arab party, they aren't coming to me': Segalovitz explains Ra'am move - interview

Former Yesh Atid lawmaker Yoav Segalovitz will occupy the second position on Ra’am’s ticket in Israel’s October 27 election, putting a Jewish Zionist immediately behind the leader of a party built primarily around an Arab Muslim constituency. Segalovitz told The Media Line that he will join Ra’am’s parliamentary faction but will not become a formal member of the party, a distinction that allows him to retain his political identity while running on its slate.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
At a joint press conference in Nazareth, Segalovitz introduced the partnership by listing the differences between himself and Ra’am chairman Mansour Abbas. Segalovitz described himself as a Jewish, secular Zionist who served as an army officer and rose to one of the highest ranks in the Israel Police. Abbas, he said, is an Arab, a religious Muslim, and a social conservative. “What connects us is that we are all Israelis,” Segalovitz said. “That is our shared identity.”
The arrangement gives Segalovitz a prominent position in a party that could again become important to the formation of a government. Ra’am participated in the coalition that governed Israel from 2021 to 2022, but several opposition leaders now say they will not form another government dependent on an Arab party. Segalovitz argues that his candidacy can begin changing that calculation, even if it does not produce an immediate electoral shift.
“I do not see Ra’am or Mansour Abbas as a threat,” he said. “They want to be part of the country, and I think we need to be strong enough to extend a hand in return.”
Former Israel Police, Lahav 433 official joins Ra'am
Segalovitz, 67, previously headed the Israel Police Investigations and Intelligence Division and the Lahav 433 national crime unit. During the previous government, he became the official responsible for coordinating the state’s campaign against organized crime and violence in Arab communities. That work gave him relationships with Arab mayors and local leaders well before he began discussing a political partnership with Abbas.
His decision to leave Yesh Atid and enter Ra’am’s slate has met resistance across much of the political system. Opposition Leader Yair Lapid said he believed Segalovitz was making a mistake, although he respected his former colleague for acting on his convictions. Yisrael Beiteinu chairman Avigdor Liberman has said Ra’am cannot be a coalition partner, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has made the opposition’s potential dependence on Abbas a campaign issue, presenting voters with a choice between his government and a rival bloc supported by Ra’am.
Segalovitz said those positions leave Arab citizens fully integrated into much of Israeli life but excluded when political power is discussed. Arab citizens account for approximately 21% of Israel’s population and work throughout its medical system, universities, industries and public services. The distinction becomes visible, he said, when people move from daily life into party politics. “At a hospital, nobody asks questions,” Segalovitz said. “You enter political life, and everyone puts on some kind of narrative; some kind of suit tailored to his measurements. That is where you see the lack of connection.”
He rejected the argument that political cooperation with Arab parties became unacceptable after the Hamas-led massacre of October 7, 2023. In his announcement, Segalovitz said that more than 34 members of Israel’s Arab community were killed in the attack and that six Bedouin citizens were abducted to Gaza. Arab communities also suffered casualties and property damage from missiles fired during the conflicts with Hezbollah and Iran.
Segalovitz acknowledged that October 7 increased fear among Jewish Israelis when Arab political participation is discussed. He said, however, that the responsibility of political leaders is not to reinforce that fear. “There is no future for the State of Israel as I see it without partnership with Arabs,” he said. “The differences are there. I emphasized that in my statement. I am not hiding them.”
He described himself as a “bridgehead” between parts of Jewish and Arab society that rarely meet inside the same electoral framework. By accepting the second position rather than asking Abbas to join a Zionist party, Segalovitz said he intended to send a stronger message. “I am going to an Arab party. They are not coming to me,” he said. “A Jewish Zionist, a former police officer, number two in Ra’am. There is a powerful message in that.”
Segalovitz said the initial response within Arab communities had gone beyond support from Ra’am voters. The day after the announcement, he visited Baqa al-Gharbiyye, where residents approached him in the street to wish him success, including people who told him they did not intend to vote for the party. In Nazareth, he said, Arab journalists privately described an unusual level of excitement surrounding the move.
He also said he had received supportive messages from former commanders and senior figures in Israel’s security establishment, although he did not identify them. Segalovitz argued that excluding more than one-fifth of the population from meaningful political influence is damaging not only to democratic representation but also to Israel’s security and economy.
Violent crime will be immediate policy test
The immediate policy test, he said, will be violent crime. Segalovitz wants the next government to restore the interagency programs he oversaw as deputy public security minister and consider expanding them. Data compiled by the Abraham Initiatives showed that the number of Arab citizens killed in criminal violence fell from 126 to 116 during his only full year in government. It rose to 244 the following year, after the government changed. “Personal security comes first, and that means crime,” he said. “The situation is so serious that this must be at the top of the next government’s priorities. Root treatment will take longer, but significant action has to begin immediately.”
Segalovitz also supports expanding civilian service among young Arab citizens, presenting it as both a contribution to the state and a means of providing structure and opportunities for those aged 18 to 24. He said the program should not be imposed by the government. “It has to come from Arab society to the state, not from the state to Arab society,” he said, adding that Ra’am is already pursuing initiatives in that area.
Beyond crime, Segalovitz identified education, healthcare, welfare, employment, and infrastructure as priorities. He said the state has also avoided dealing seriously with the accumulated problems facing Bedouin communities in the Negev, including planning, housing, public services, and their relationship with state institutions. He did not place responsibility solely on the current government, saying the issue had been neglected for many years and could not be reduced to disputes over home demolitions.
The longer-term challenge, he said, is moving more Arab graduates into fields such as technology and other higher-paying sectors rather than allowing educational advancement to remain concentrated in a limited number of professions. “Arab society, as I see it, is first of all a major economic, cultural and social opportunity for the State of Israel,” he said. “It is not a threat.”
Asked what would constitute success four years from now, Segalovitz did not cite a seat target or government position. He said he wanted the partnership to become sufficiently established that Israelis would stop asking why he had joined Ra’am and begin asking what the alliance had accomplished, where it had failed, and what should be done differently. The work, he said, requires planning for the next 20 years rather than one parliamentary term. “If I have to put it in one phrase,” Segalovitz said, “I want the act I have taken not to be an episode.”

Israel cuts gasoline prices by 50 agorot after Smotrich approves temporary excise relief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
15:28:41 UTC
00:28:41 KST

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich signed an order on Sunday cutting the price of gasoline by 50 agorot per liter beginning at midnight, bringing the self-service price of 95-octane gasoline down from NIS 8.25 to NIS 7.75 per liter, Walla reported on Sunday.
The state will absorb the difference by temporarily relinquishing part of the excise tax it collects from drivers.
The decision came less than a week after gasoline prices jumped last week to a level matching the record set in Israel in September 2012. The sharp increase resulted from higher global gasoline prices and refining margins, the dollar-shekel exchange rate, the linkage of the excise tax to the Consumer Price Index, and an update to the marketing margin and full-service surcharge.
Immediately after the new price was announced, Smotrich instructed Finance Ministry officials to find a way to reduce by 50 agorot the amount drivers pay at gas stations. The chosen solution was a temporary reduction in the excise tax, one of the main components of gasoline prices in Israel. Rather than having drivers bear the full increase, the state will forgo some tax revenue in the coming period.
The timing, however, complicated the decision. Elections are scheduled for October 27, and cutting the price by 50 agorot per liter less than two months before voters go to the polls raised concerns that the measure could amount to election economics.
Smotrich signs order cutting gasoline price by 50 agorot until after elections
The Finance Ministry's legal adviser determined that the price reduction could be implemented during this period, citing, among other things, the precedent set when Avigdor Liberman served as finance minister, and the excise tax was reduced close to an election. Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara also approved the move.
The order will remain in effect until October 31, four days after the election. This means drivers will receive the discount beginning Sunday night and will continue to benefit from it throughout the election campaign, while Smotrich will be able to present the public with an immediate and noticeable reduction in one of the more significant expenses faced by households.
Finance Ministry officials say the goal is not only to ease the burden on drivers. Expensive fuel also raises transportation, distribution, and shipping costs, which can quickly translate into higher prices for food, deliveries, and services. Lowering the price is intended to reduce at least some of that pressure and prevent the increase at gas stations from spilling over into the prices of other products.
Ultimately, the move contains a certain irony. The state imposes a heavy tax on every liter of gasoline, and to shield the public from what had become a record-high price, it is now temporarily giving up 50 agorot of the tax it imposed in the first place.

Ukrainians push to legalize pornography, raise millions for war effort - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
15:28:32 UTC
00:28:32 KST

Ukraine is reportedly considering legalizing sex work to help its battered economy and fund the war against Russia, the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.
In Ukraine, the production, possession, or distribution of pornography is illegal and is punishable by up to seven years in prison.
Despite this, the adult entertainment industry in the country has grown considerably but operates with the cooperation of a corrupt police force, the WSJ reported.
Ukrainian authorities have begun demanding taxes from adult content creators. However, anyone who complies effectively admits their involvement in criminal activity.
One Ukrainian lawmaker, Yaroslav Zhelezniak, is pushing for a bill that says legalizing pornography in the country would help boost the economy and could leave up to $25 million in tax revenues available to Ukraine’s war chest.
He predicts that the revenues could help pay for up to 30,000 drones.
Ukrainian MP pushes to legalize pornography to help fund war against Russia
"These women either don’t pay taxes and face criminal charges for that, or they pay taxes and get charged with violating pornography laws,” Zhelezniak, who chairs the finance committee in Ukraine’s Parliament, told the WSJ. “It’s a tragicomic situation.”
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, authorities turned a blind eye to the adult entertainment industry in the country. Recently, three regions of Ukraine received as much as $20,000 in bribes, according to the office of the Ukrainian General Prosecutor.
Two years into the invasion, OnlyFans’s parent company, Fenix International, found that 7,900 Ukrainians made more than $131 million on OnlyFans in 2023 alone, the WSJ reported.
Kyiv began sending letters to content creators who filed tax declarations that, unbeknownst to them, would be charged with tax evasion and illicitly producing adult content.
One of them, Svitlana Dvornikova, told the WSJ that while she was getting her daughter ready for school one morning, police seized $20.000 in cash, her laptop, and hard drives.
“They had a list of webcam models, and knew all their addresses,” Dvornikova told the WSJ. She said the officers offered her the option to bribe them to keep the matter quiet, but she declined.
Another woman told the WSJ that officers searched her apartment in a similar manner. She was later summoned to a court hearing, but did not go because she was scared that she would be forced to pay a bribe.
Many Ukrainian OnlyFans models, including Dvornikova, have since left the country or temporarily left to live elsewhere in Europe.
“This is a victimless crime,” Lesia Mykhalenko, a tax lawyer who has represented more than 100 OnlyFans models, told the WSJ. “It unnecessarily burdens the legal system at a time when we should be focused on defending the country.”
After a case was filed against her, Dvornikova filed a petition that was later featured on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s website. In it, she described herself as a “conscientious taxpayer,” and said that instead of marking her as a criminal, the government should be thankful for the near $900,000 she had paid in taxes, which she claimed was worth “hundreds of Russians killed on the front line.”
Her petition got over 25,000 signatures within a week, the WSJ reported. In turn, Zelensky said he would make parliament consider Zhelezniak’s legislation to legalize porn.
The bill Zhelezniak co-authored to legalize porn passed its first reading in Ukraine’s parliament in July and is due for a second reading.

Chinese nationals accused of posing as descendants of Nazi victims to obtain German citizenship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
15:28:03 UTC
00:28:03 KST

The Dusseldorf public prosecutor’s office is investigating 32 people, many of them Chinese, said to have posed as descendants of Jewish victims of the Nazis in order to fraudulently obtain German citizenship, the news magazine Der Spiegel has reported.
The fraud involves people claiming to be descendants of Jews persecuted by the Nazis, with falsified documents and biographical information being submitted to the Federal Office of Administration in Cologne.
The legal mechanism that makes this possible is Article 116(2) of Germany’s Basic Law, which provides for the restoration of German citizenship to former German citizens whose citizenship was stripped between January 30, 1933, and May 8, 1945, for political, racial or religious reasons, and to their descendants.
Der Spiegel details one specific example involving Chinese national Liu H., reportedly the subject of an international manhunt on suspicion of kidnapping and murder.
According to the magazine, Liu H. orchestrated various schemes to evade Chinese justice, including adopting new biographies, inventing names, and traveling under false identities. In 2024, Liu H. obtained German nationality under the name Derrick Wong, and subsequently obtained a passport.
How did Liu H. successfully obtain a passport?
According to Der Spiegel, he stated in his application that he was a grandson of Karl Siegfried and Gertraud Suesskind, who fled Germany to what was then British Mandatory Palestine. Liu H. is not one of their descendants.
Another Chinese national, Tian C., living in London, is also said to have unlawfully obtained a German passport by claiming descent from the same Siegfried-Suesskind couple.
The Dusseldorf public prosecutor’s office and the BKA (Germany’s FBI) are said to have been working on the case for about a year now.
According to the report, around 30 Chinese nationals are being investigated. Many of them are well-known, and some face allegations of serious crimes and have been the subject of international manhunts.
Der Spiegel noted that German citizenship cannot be revoked easily, and that an unlawful naturalization can only be withdrawn within 10 years.
All the suspects are said to live abroad, meaning that German investigators cannot easily bring them in for questioning. The accused are said to now live in Cyprus, Israel, the United Kingdom and the United States. In about half of the cases, German citizenship is said to have already been granted.
The Jerusalem Post reached out to the Dusseldorf public prosecutor’s office for confirmation of the report.

Report of suspected attack on baby dolphin in Ceuta area where migrants are staying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
15:23:40 UTC
00:23:40 KST

The DAUBMA association has filed a complaint with the Civil Guard after a dolphin calf died on Trampolín beach in Ceuta, providing images to help clarify what happened and identify the alleged culprits.
A bottlenose dolphin calf was found dead at around midday on Wednesday on Trampolín beach in Ceuta, according to 'El Faro de Ceuta', and in circumstances that the Association for the Defence of Urban Trees, Biodiversity and the Environment (DAUBMA) considers an attack. The organisation has filed a formal complaint with the Guardia Civil and requested that proceedings be opened to clarify what happened.
According to the association's account, the animal reached the shore alive, disoriented, possibly because of the fog in the area that morning. Once on land, DAUBMA says, several people dragged it out of the water and hit it on the head with a stick.
The organisation says it has photographs, videos and social media screenshots that also show blood beneath one of the animal’s eyes, as well as some of the people present trying to wipe it away. In its view, this points to a direct attack and to manipulation of the carcass that is incompatible with any attempt to help the animal. All of this material has been made available to the Guardia Civil.
A verified video that circulated widely, with no perpetrators identified
The footage, first shared on social media, was recorded on the part of the beach where people who entered Ceuta during the mass crossing on 30 and 31 July remain camped.
A worker from the cleaning company Ecoservicios, who was in the area, witnessed the scene and warned those present that they should stop what they were doing and call an environmental collection service.
After that warning, according to witnesses, they tried to return the animal to the sea, although it was no longer showing any signs of life. So far there has been no formal identification of those responsible: that is precisely what DAUBMA is seeking with its complaint to the Guardia Civil.
The case has sparked outrage online, and a local resident, Nadia García Gómez, has launched a petition on change.org calling for those responsible to be identified.
García Gómez stresses that she does not belong to any association and argues for a firm response to animal abuse: "This cruel act must be tried and punished", she wrote online, in which she asks the authorities "to do something about it". The petition points out that the bottlenose dolphin is a strictly protected species in the EU and that injuring or killing an individual can constitute a criminal offence.
DAUBMA and CECAM respond to criticism
Responding to those who ask where animal rights associations are when dead wildlife is found in Ceuta, DAUBMA and CECAM say their work focuses on documenting cases and passing them on to institutions, while lamenting the lack of any response.
They explain that more than three months ago they submitted to the Government Delegation a dossier on other cases of dead or affected animals, including dolphins and turtles showing, they say, signs of having fallen victim to drift nets, which are banned in the EU, but have received no reply.
They add that an attempt to file a complaint with Seprona was initially not processed, so they went to the duty court with technical and graphic material; the court, according to their account, ordered the case to be provisionally closed pending a Seprona report that has still not arrived.
Both organisations say they coordinate with emergency services, the Guardia Civil, Semar and collection companies, and call on the authorities to ensure that wildlife protection does not remain mere rhetoric.

China prepares £40bn stimulus for financial sector amid fears over sluggish growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
15:16:43 UTC
00:16:43 KST

China will inject $54bn (£40bn) into its financial sector as Beijing attempts to shore up banks and insurers in the face of faltering economic growth.
A host of financial institutions said they were due to receive billions of yuan in capital from state institutions including the ministry of finance and even the company that runs the country’s tobacco monopoly.
The stimulus is designed to help China bolster the ability of its financial sector to invest in the stock market and lend to businesses, amid signs that the world’s second largest economy is struggling to escape weak growth.
The country’s largest life insurer, China Life Insurance, will get 35bn yuan, while the China Taiping Insurance Group said it would receive 7bn.
The People’s Insurance Company of China said it planned to raise up to 15bn yuan through a private placement of A-shares – stock that specifically allows investors to trade in China-based companies – to the ministry of finance, with the proceeds used to replenish its capital.
The initiative could help bolster state insurers that have been directed by Beijing to support the stock market with medium- and long-term funds, while positioning them to help regulators manage smaller, higher-risk insurance companies.
The insurance sector has been struggling with eroding profitability owing to persistently low interest rates, with numerous small and mid-sized insurers reporting deteriorating solvency ratios, a measure of financial health.
“The injection is an important step by the country to enhance the financial sector’s ability to serve the real economy and promote the high-quality development of the financial and insurance industries,” China Life said, adding that it would strengthen the group’s ability to withstand risk.
Separately, three state lenders on Sunday also announced they will receive a combined 290bn yuan in capital injections.
The plan was first announced at an annual parliamentary meeting in March this year, extending a financing tool that had helped bolster some other big state banks last year.
The Agricultural Bank of China and the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, two of the country’s largest state banks, said they planned to raise up to 160bn yuan and 100bn yuan respectively through private A-share placements to the finance ministry, China National Tobacco Corp and its subsidiaries.
The two lenders said the proceeds would be used entirely to replenish cash reserves, helping them sustain credit expansion, as Beijing leans on state banks to support growth despite weak demand for loans.

Along with the rest of the country, Assam is gearing up to observe the “Seva Sankalp Abhiyan” from September 17 to October 17, commemorating the completion of 25 years of dedicated public service and political commitment by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in parliamentary politics.According to the release, Prime Minister Narendra Modi first took oath as the Chief Minister of Gujarat on October 7, 2001. Subsequently, the widely acclaimed and dynamic leader assumed office as the Prime Minister of India for the first time on May 26, 2014.Having secured the mandate of the people for three consecutive terms, he continues to serve as the Prime Minister, backed by the unwavering support and confidence of the people of the country.To mark the completion of 25 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s journey in public and parliamentary life, a vibrant calendar of 13 programmes has been prepared for nationwide observance from his birthday on September 17 to October 17.According to BJP Assam Pradesh spokesperson Pranjal Kalita, extensive preparations are already underway for the implementation of programmes centred around initiatives such as “Namo Seva Gatha,” “Anganwadi Utsav,” “Rangoli,” “Parivartan Ki Kahani,” “Seva Setu Abhiyan,” “Seva Ke Nimitta Bhagidari,” “Jan Sevak Mahakumbh,” “Painting, Elocution and Quiz Competitions,” “Viksit Bharat Sankalp Yatra,” “Seva Jyoti Yatra,” and the “National Innovation Competition,” among others.

After a devastating flood in Nepal, rescuers found an elderly woman alive after ten days, although her family had already believed her dead. Seventy-three-year-old Chandika Kumari Shrestha survived beneath the rubble of her own four-story house. Reuters reports, UNN writes.

Ten days later, rescuers found her alive inside the ruins of a house in the devastated village of Betrawati. The woman survived in a narrow air pocket surrounded by water and mud.
The four-story house was swept away by the flood and ended up amid unstable ground. When we were passing by, we heard a voice: "Save me"
During a rescue operation on Saturday that lasted 45 minutes, Darnal and his team found Shrestha in an enclosed space and took her to a military hospital.
Shrestha was one of hundreds of people reported missing in Betrawati—one of the areas of Nepal hardest hit by the flood. The area was covered with white sediment that had compacted almost to the consistency of concrete. Rescuers continue to find dozens of bodies.
The town's market and most of the residential buildings, some of them up to four stories high, were almost completely buried under the rubble left by the flow of water that swept through the valley. The disaster claimed the lives of more than 1,300 people across Nepal. Thousands of people are still considered missing.
Five days earlier, 24 decomposing bodies were found in the Betrawati market area. They were in a building that had previously housed a small shop, Darnal said.
Eleven days have passed since the glacial collapse that caused the devastating floods, yet around 5,000 people are still considered missing.
Hundreds of bodies were carried by the water onto riverbanks far from the devastated Rasuwa district. In Chitwan, hundreds of kilometers from the site of the disaster, several mass burials have already been held for unidentified bodies that were in an advanced state of decomposition.
Although hope is gradually fading, Nepalese authorities continue searching for people who may remain in tunnels or beneath thick layers of mud that hardened over the destroyed buildings.
Since Friday, rescuers have pulled three people from tunnels, including a Chinese citizen who was found near the Trishuli River. More than 900 people are believed to be trapped beneath the rubble in the area.
Other people, like Shrestha, also managed to survive in extremely difficult conditions. Among them was an 8-year-old boy, whom rescuers also reunited with his mother.

HMS Queen Elizabeth sailed this weekend for three months of training and operations around the United Kingdom and northern Europe, in her new role as NATO’s command ship for the Allied Response Force, the Royal Navy stated.
The 65,000-tonne carrier and her crew of more than 800 will work through an intensive programme alongside allies, having assumed the NATO role in July, which is the first time either Queen Elizabeth-class ship has performed it.
Captain Claire Thompson, the commanding officer, said: “We’ve returned from summer leave rested and ready for the next phase of our training. Sailing this autumn is a key milestone for both our NATO commitment, as the Afloat Command Platform, and also on our journey back to the Royal Navy’s very high readiness aircraft carrier, a duty we will resume from our sister ship HMS Prince of Wales in 2027.”
She said: “Sailing with an embarked battle staff, integration and training is essential whilst relearning the skills required to conduct safe and effective aviation as we ensure that we are prepared to deliver operational activity at the heart of NATO should it be required.”
The ship will undertake advanced training under Flag Officer Sea Training, exercising across the full spectrum of modern naval warfare, and will rehearse how an allied naval force would operate together in a crisis. The programme continues into next year with participation in major NATO exercises, preparing her to take over from HMS Prince of Wales as the flagship and high readiness strike carrier in late 2027.
Queen Elizabeth completed her second planned docking period at Rosyth and returned to Portsmouth in May, and the Royal Navy took charge of the Allied Reaction Force maritime component in July for a twelve-month period.

Israel’s PM Netanyahu orders West Bank settler outposts to be removed
TEL AVIV - Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered unauthorised settler outposts in the West Bank to be dismantled, two people familiar with the matter said on Sept 6, amid pressure from the US to crack down on settler attacks on Palestinians.
The order applies to outposts established by settlers without official authorisation from the Israeli state, the sources said. Outposts typically consist of prefabricated caravans and house a small number of settlers.
The state has from time to time demolished such structures and also formally recognised others, allowing them to access government funding.
It was not immediately clear when the operation would begin.
UN bodies and most governments deem all Israeli settlements illegal under international law and consider the West Bank to be occupied territory under military control. Israel argues the territory is disputed, not occupied.
US urges Israel to act against settler violence
Netanyahu had ordered the eviction of the unauthorised outposts in response to pressure from the United States, the country’s closest ally, the sources said.
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee on Sept 5 denounced violent settlers as terrorists and called for them to face severe consequences following a meeting with several Palestinian Americans in a West Bank Palestinian town.
Israeli website Ynet earlier reported the orders targeted around 100 outposts across the occupied territory.
The Israeli prime minister’s office and the military, who would normally take part in clearing any outposts in the West Bank, did not immediately respond to a request to comment.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, asked at a conference in Jerusalem about the Ynet report, said Netanyahu has given “an instruction to evict places built in Areas A and B”, referring to parts of the West Bank in which most Palestinians live.
Under the Oslo Accords, interim peace agreements reached in the 1990s between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), the West Bank was split into three zones: A, B and C.
Smotrich, a settler himself who has overseen settlement housing projects and formally recognised homes built illegally, said while he disagreed with Netanyahu’s decision, the government had made huge strides in advancing settlements in Area C.
Hundreds of outposts across the West Bank
There are 340 outposts in the West Bank along with 146 settlements formally recognised by the Israeli government, according to Peace Now, an Israeli organisation that is critical of settlement expansion and advocates for a two-state solution.
In August, Israeli settlers besieged the homes of Palestinians in a nearby village, including one owned by a Palestinian American, before the military forced them from the area. The village’s Palestinian residents have said they have continued to face harassment and intimidation by Israeli settlers.
The Israeli government has condemned settler violence, though perpetrators are rarely arrested and even less frequently prosecuted.
On Sept 5, US ambassador Huckabee said it was in Israel’s own interest to take action against settlers carrying out what he described as “criminal behaviour and terrorism”. REUTERS

Report urges Britain to offer EU nuclear protection
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:05:19 BST
00:05:19 KST

Britain should explore what it calls a Deterrence Union with the European Union, formally extending its nuclear and conventional deterrent over the bloc in exchange for bespoke access to European defence funds, according to a report published by the Council on Geostrategy.
The paper, titled Towards a Hercules Hold: Maintaining a transatlantic defence industrial base, is written by Paul Mason and William Freer and carries a foreword by Tan Dhesi, the Labour MP for Slough and chair of the House of Commons Defence Committee.
Its central argument is that the transatlantic defence industrial base has begun to split, with Washington reprioritising resources towards hemispheric defence and countering China while the European Union deploys instruments such as the €150 billion SAFE facility in pursuit of strategic autonomy, and that those European mechanisms increasingly mandate the exclusion of third countries. Britain, sitting outside the European Union while maintaining deep security ties with Washington, is described as squeezed between two diverging defence giants and facing what the authors call a dangerous Hobson’s choice in capability standardisation.
The bridge has stopped working
The authors argue that the role Britain has traditionally assigned itself, acting as a transatlantic bridge, no longer serves the purpose it was designed for.
They write: “The historic approach of acting as a more passive transatlantic ‘bridge’ will prove insufficient to securing British interests. Instead, Britain should see itself as central to establishing a ‘Hercules hold’ to grip and sustain two diverging pillars. By focusing defence investment on select capabilities and championing interchangeability, HM Government can wield the influence necessary to maintain access to US technology while accelerating European rearmament.”
According to the report, further bifurcation risks cutting European allies off from cutting-edge American research and development along with North American surge capacity, leaving European nations with widening gaps in the high-end capabilities where the United States leads, among them ballistic missile defence, hypersonic strike and space systems, while integrated transatlantic defence firms face severe supply chain disruption.
What is being proposed
The Deterrence Union is the recommendation likely to attract most attention, since it would involve Britain formally offering nuclear protections to the European Union in return for deeper access to its defence market.
Alongside it the authors recommend championing hardware and munitions interchangeability across NATO, so that equipment can be physically swapped between allied platforms, and investing in a select portfolio of high-value technological chokepoints where British engineering becomes indispensable to both Washington and Brussels. They also call on the government formally to back the Canadian-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank as a source of non-exclusionary funding for transatlantic projects.
Interchangeability is the same concept the First Sea Lord set out in an interview published last month, describing it as going beyond interoperability so that it becomes agnostic which nation is conducting a given task, with allied navies acting for each other’s collective requirements and able to exchange capabilities.
Why the timing matters
The report lands as the American review of force posture in Europe gets under way. Elbridge Colby, the Under Secretary of War for Policy, told a meeting in Brussels last week that the review would examine the strategic posture of American forces on the continent even as Washington prioritises the Western Hemisphere and the First Island Chain, and confirmed that allies had been sent a written questionnaire seeking their views.
British access to European defence funding instruments has been under negotiation since 2024, and the SAFE facility in particular has been the subject of argument over the terms on which non-member states can participate.
Dhesi, who wrote the foreword, pressed the Prime Minister at Prime Minister’s Questions on Wednesday to commit to a pathway to three per cent of gross domestic product on defence by 2030, telling the Commons that Britain faces a significantly increased threat level and a United States leadership for which European security is no longer a priority.
The Council on Geostrategy is a London-based think tank founded in 2021 which focuses on British foreign and defence policy, the Indo-Pacific, and the maritime and technological dimensions of national strategy. Paul Mason is a journalist and author who co-presents the organisation’s Defence Talks podcast.

US envoys meet Putin: What’s behind latest diplomacy on Russia-Ukraine war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
15:00:16 UTC
00:00:16 KST

US envoys meet Putin: What’s behind latest diplomacy on Russia-Ukraine war?
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner meet Putin in Moscow and head to Kyiv as part of Trump’s new efforts to broker an agreement.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have held talks with President Vladmir Putin in Moscow, in what appears to be new efforts by the Trump administration to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that the envoys were bringing “a proposal to end the war” – Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II – and a senior Russian official said it was an “important peacemaking visit”.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Witkoff and Kushner will travel to ‘end’ Russia’s war in Ukraine: Trump
- list 2 of 4Trump sends envoys to Russia, Ukraine with new peace plan
- list 3 of 4At least 5 killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine as US envoys visit Moscow
- list 4 of 4US envoys arrive in Kyiv for Ukraine war talks after meeting Putin
Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and Witkoff, the US special envoy, are expected to arrive in Kyiv on Sunday, reviving diplomacy when both countries have escalated attacks. Both Moscow and Kyiv announced a three-day ceasefire to coincide with the latest trip.
So what’s behind the latest initiative by the US envoys and will it help end the war?
What was the outcome of the meeting?
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said the high-level talks were “highly useful” and lasted for more than three hours, according to Reuters.
Witkoff and Kushner “outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement,” said Ushakov, without providing any further detail, but added that the talks had been “substantive, very frank and constructive”.
Videos show Putin meeting the US envoys in the famous Red Drawing Room at the Kremlin on Saturday and telling his guests that the situation they are exploring “is, of course, not an easy one”.
The question remains whether Russia is willing to compromise, said Al Jazeera correspondent Yulia Shapovalova from Moscow. “Moscow demands that Ukraine not join NATO and hand over four Ukrainian regions to Russia, including territories not controlled by Russian forces.”
In September 2022, Putin proclaimed the annexation of four partially occupied Ukrainian regions – Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia. The move was not recognised by the international community, including the UN. Ukraine has refused to cede territory to Russia.
The Trump administration has ruled out a seat for Ukraine at NATO – which Russia has opposed. Trump had initially been critical of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, but has since mended ties after berating the Ukrainian leader in the Oval Office in February last year.
In August, Trump met Putin in Alaska, but the summit failed to reach a deal to end the war.
Why are the US envoys in Moscow?
Witkoff and Kushner have been involved in a number of diplomatic talks, including the Iran war, the so-called ceasefire agreement between Hamas and Israel and the Ukraine-Russia war.
Witkoff was appointed as the special envoy to the Middle East and later assigned the task of helping end the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Kushner also played a major role in the 2020 Abraham Accords that saw a number of Muslim countries recognise Israel. The initiative has been criticised for prioritising Arab-Israeli normalisation without addressing the question of a Palestinian state.
The details of the latest Ukraine peace plan are unclear, but Trump reportedly said last week, “we have an idea for peace”, without providing any additional details.
US officials from the National Security Council, State Department and the Treasury were also part of the delegation. The presence of Treasury official Gene Lang, who oversees US sanctions policy, including on Russia, indicates that the ongoing financial, economic and trade sanctions on Russia might have been part of the discussions in Moscow.
The Trump administration has ramped up sanctions on Russia aimed at forcing it to end the war. The Iran war has, however, diverted Trump’s and global attention away from the Ukraine-Russia conflict.
The Iran war has also strained transatlantic ties as Trump has accused his European and NATO allies of not helping him in efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran has used as leverage in talks. He has also been critical of NATO allies for not sharing the burden of collective defence, particularly against Russian threats.
NATO members from Europe have since stepped up their spending and offered to provide security guarantees to Ukraine after a deal is signed with Russia.
The latest push comes amid deadly Russian missile and drone attacks on Ukraine, while Kyiv has stepped up drone attacks on Russian energy sites.
What is Witkoff and Kushner’s next stop?
They have arrived in Kyiv for their first visit to meet President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
It was their second visit to the Kremlin this year and the eighth since the start of the war.
Experts say Ukrainians are sceptical of the US envoys.
“The view in Ukraine [is] that Witkoff, and to some extent Kushner, are most susceptible to accepting Russia’s narrative,” said Alexey Muraviev, a senior research fellow of defence and strategic studies at Edith Cowan University in Australia.
Witkoff told Putin that the US president had sent his best wishes and thanked him for the limited ceasefire during the delegation’s visit. The special US envoy was also recorded telling Putin that “we will have all these incredible stories and memories, and yours will be right at the top of it all”. The Russian president conveyed his gratitude to Trump and said Moscow would do its utmost to ensure the safety of the mediators.
The choice of words and tone won’t sit well with Ukrainians, explained Al Jazeera correspondent Audrey McAlpine from Ukraine’s capital, Kyiv.
While the visit there is seen as significant, the interaction between the envoys and Putin is an indication of “that familiarity between Witkoff and Putin”, she said.
Where the war stands now?
Russia and Ukraine announced a halt in attacks on each other’s capitals until Monday. The no-shoot policy is to ensure the envoys travel to the talks.
However, attacks have been reported in other cities in both the warring countries. At least seven people were killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine, while a Ukrainian drone attack killed one person in Russia’s Belgorod region.
In recent months, the two sides have intensified drone strikes, killing dozens. Ukraine’s production of low-cost, long-range drones has increased the number of attacks on industrial and logistical sites deep within Russia.
“There are growing concerns about the level of Ukraine’s resilience given the collateral damage that the Russian attacks have caused to Ukraine’s infrastructure ahead of the incoming winter,” Muraviev said, while pointing out that Putin is looking for a more long-term strategic deal.
Recent drone incidents reported in a number of European countries have raised suspicions that Russia is responsible, although no proof has been published. They included a failed drone explosion at Germany’s Leipzig airport and a fire at a drone factory in Poland.
Why is Trump pushing for a new deal now?
The US president has said that tens of thousands of people are dying on both sides every month due to the Ukraine-Russia war. During his re-election campaign in 2024, Trump said he would end the war within 24 hours, but that deadline has been revised several times.
He has hosted Putin in Alaska and held talks with Zelenskyy several times but has failed to find an agreement to end the war.
Recent steps by the Trump administration are interpreted as an attempt to revive relations between the US and Russia after months of stalled diplomacy.
CIA director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow last month to meet with Russian intelligence officials and the US invited Russia’s Finance Minister, Anton Siluanov, to a recent G20 meeting. His attendance was criticised by several European countries who refused a group photo with the Russian diplomat in protest.
Trump is expected to meet Putin next in November during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China, according to media reports. Russia’s Deputy Foreign Minister, Sergei Ryabkov, said on Sunday that Moscow has not ruled out a trilateral meeting between the Russian, Chinese and US presidents, the TASS state news agency reported.
Trump’s latest diplomatic push comes as the Iran war remains deadlocked and the Ukraine-Russia conflict has turned into a war of attrition. The war with Iran has become hugely unpopular domestically ahead of the crucial midterm elections in November. If Trump’s Republican party loses its majority in Congress, it would become extremely hard for the president to push his agenda.
A peace agreement in the longstanding war in the coming weeks could be a major boost for him ahead of election day.

Shutting down the office bore is one thing – but can you use the same tactics in everyday life? | Polly Hudson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
15:00:08 UTC
00:00:08 KST

The last thing you need in a meeting that could have been an email is attachments. Sadly, it’s sod’s law that there’s one oblivious person in every work gathering who raises extra, unnecessary queries using as many words as possible, and holds everybody up. Now, Forbes magazine has helpfully supplied three phrases business leaders can use to stop rambling questions from hijacking or lengthening proceedings, without embarrassing the hijacking lengthener.
But obviously it’s not only the office where we encounter those seemingly hellbent on derailing interactions, so can we steal Forbes’ gameplan for boring chat in real life?
Many conversations are DOA, too dull to rescue, but others – at a party, the school gates, a random bump-into – can be going fine until a third party ruins it by asking for or providing superfluous details that stymie the story. Sometimes you’re not married to that party, so you can’t give them a Paddington hard stare or pinch them. What does Forbes advise?
“Phrase one: route the tangent somewhere else. Say, ‘Let me pause you there. That’s worth discussing, but it’s more than we can cover here … Send me the rest, and I’ll follow up after the meeting.’” Clearly too formal for a casual natter, but there’s still gold in them thar hills. “I’d love to hear all about this when there’s time – text me later,” may be the most artful get-out-of-chat-free card ever played. Next?
“Phrase two: close a question you’ve already answered. Say, ‘We covered that earlier, so I’m going to keep us moving.’” Bit brutal, so IRL maybe reply, “But, anyway …” and then steer the convo in the direction you want to go (presumably towards the exit).
And finally: “Phrase three: give the floor to someone else. Say, ‘I want to make sure we hear from people who haven’t spoken yet. Let’s take the next question from someone new.’” It was good while it lasted, but unfortunately every technique has its limits. There’s no way of saying this, whether in the pub or at the conference room table, that won’t be loudly and clearly received as STFU.
Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

Breadcrumb
More than 140 killed amid Houthi offensive in Yemen
Fighting between Yemeni government forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in southwest Yemen killed more than 140 combatants between midday Saturday and early Sunday morning, military sources said.
Two military officials with the Saudi-backed government forces told AFP that 84 of their troops were killed, mostly in missile attacks, while four Houthi military sources said 57 rebel fighters were killed in the same period.
Days-long clashes have erupted in Yemen over control of a gateway to the Red Sea in the deadliest fighting in the Arabian Peninsula country since a 2022 ceasefire between the two sides collapsed in July.
Beginning on Thursday, the Houthis launched an offensive aiming to cut off the government-held port city of Mokha, under fire for weeks, and advance towards areas bordering the Bab al-Mandab chokepoint at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
According to an AFP tally compiled using various military and medical sources from both sides of the conflict, more than 300 combatants and some civilians have been killed since the start of the Houthi assault on Thursday.
One military official with the internationally recognised government based in Aden said fighting had subsided in the early hours of Sunday morning.
The military official said government "forces were able to establish positions for themselves north of Hays after advancing in the area", referring to a frontline district less than 30 kilometres inland from the Red Sea coast.
But the official added the Houthis had advanced west of Taiz, south of Hays, in their push towards the Bab al-Mandab.
With Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz to commercial ships, the Bab al-Mandab chokepoint has gained importance as a transit route for oil from Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest exporter of crude.
In July, a fragile truce between the Houthis and Yemen's government fell apart after the rebels welcomed an Iranian plane to the capital Sanaa, setting off a spate of attacks.
The fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and government troops supported by US ally Saudi Arabia signals the emergence of a new front in the wider Middle East war, which broke out in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
The Houthis have also announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and have begun targeting its ships and territory.

'Only got worse since Oct. 7': Over 1,300 doctors have left Israel since 2023, study shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
14:54:18 UTC
23:54:18 KST

At least 1,370 physicians left Israel between 2023 and 2025, following Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's judicial overhaul, nearly double the number who left during the same period a decade earlier, according to a new Tel Aviv University study published Sunday.
The study was conducted by Prof. Itai Ater of the Coller School of Management, who heads the Economists for Democracy forum; Prof. Nittai K. Bergman, head of the Berglas School of Economics; and Doron Zamir, a doctoral student at the Coller School of Management.
The group has already published several reports documenting increased emigration since 2023, particularly among academics, engineers and other highly skilled professionals.
"Economists have been warning since 2023 about the departure of highly skilled workers as a result of the government's policies," Ater told Haaretz.
"It began in the context of the judicial overhaul and has only worsened since Hamas' October 7 attack, the war and the disparities between those serving and those not serving [in the military]. We economists warned that citizens who can leave would do so. The documents we published seek to determine whether these warnings were justified."
The study uses the Central Bureau of Statistics' definition of an emigrant who has left Israel. Under this definition, physicians are considered to have emigrated if, during the first year after their departure, they spent more than 270 days outside Israel and, since their departure, have not spent more than three consecutive months in the country.
The researchers also limited the analysis to people who had lived in Israel for at least three years before their departure. This was intended to exclude immigrants who arrived in Israel following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Some have argued that many of these immigrants have since left the country, potentially distorting the emigration figures.
Because many physicians eventually return to Israel, for example, after completing their residency, the researchers also accounted for returnees. After adjusting for these groups, the study found that Israel lost an average of 255 physicians per year during the period examined, five times the annual average of the previous decade.
To provide a clearer picture of the trend, the researchers examined emigration rates among physicians aged 45 and older, those who have generally completed their residency and are expected to train the next generation of doctors in Israel.
The study found a worrying trend in this group as well: between 2023 and 2025, one in five physicians who emigrated was at least 45 years old, compared with one in seven during the previous decade.
An analysis by medical specialty shows that among ear, nose and throat, dermatology, and ophthalmology physicians, specialists who are already in high demand in Israel, 6.2 percent of those working in these fields left the country during the period examined (116 physicians). Among physicians in these specialties under the age of 60, the figure rises to 9.4 percent.
Another concerning figure involves surgeons: 188 surgeons left Israel during this period, representing 6 percent of all physicians working in the field, and 8.8 percent of those under the age of 60.
A breakdown by district shows that most of the physicians who left had lived in the Tel Aviv District, where 5.4 percent of physicians emigrated, compared with just 1.5 percent of physicians who lived in West Bank settlements.
The data on physicians under the age of 60 comes alongside a report published by the Finance Ministry last week, which found that in the coming years, approximately 24 percent of specialist physicians working in Israel's public hospitals will be approaching retirement age.
It also found that about 25 percent of physicians currently working in Israel have already passed retirement age and continue to work because of the shortage of doctors.
Atar concludes that what is particularly troubling is not the current situation, but the trend revealed by the study.
"The big question is what will happen after [the election in] October. If the trend doesn't change, the numbers we are seeing now will become much more painful," he said.

Ukrainian Drones Hammer Major Russian Oil Refinery, Knocking Out Key Gasoline Unit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
14:49:04 UTC
23:49:04 KST

- Category

Ukrainian Drones Hammer Major Russian Oil Refinery, Knocking Out Key Gasoline Unit
Ukrainian drones struck the Ryazan Oil Refinery in Russia overnight on September 6, hitting a key processing unit used in the production of high-octane gasoline components and triggering a fire at the facility.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Analysis of footage from the attack indicates that the drones targeted the refinery’s Izomalk-2-LIN-800 low-temperature isomerization unit. Videos published by the open-source monitoring channel Exilenova+ showed a fire burning inside the refinery complex following the strike.
The Izomalk-2 unit processes low-octane pentane-hexane fractions into high-octane components used to produce automotive gasoline, including fuel meeting Euro 5 environmental standards.
Ryazan regional governor Pavel Malkov confirmed that a fire had broken out at an industrial facility following the drone attack, without identifying the site.
“Debris caused a fire at one of the enterprises; according to preliminary information, there were no casualties. Emergency services are working at the scene,” Malkov said.
Other sections of the Ryazan refinery have also been hit repeatedly. Previous strikes targeted its ELOU-AVT-3, ELOU-AVT-6, and AVT-1 crude-processing units. Satellite imagery from August 3 indicated that two of the refinery’s four primary crude-processing units had been disabled.
The Ryazan Oil Refinery, owned by Russia’s Rosneft, is one of the country’s largest refining facilities, with an annual processing capacity of approximately 17 million tonnes of crude oil.
The facility produces gasoline, diesel, aviation fuel, and other petroleum products. Its infrastructure also includes hydrocracking, catalytic reforming, vacuum gas oil hydrotreatment, and other processing systems.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces struck Russian military infrastructure in the Bryansk region, hitting a radar station, an electronic warfare system, and a relay supporting a MESH communications network, according to Ukraine’s General Staff.

Delhi building collapse: 3 dead, 6 rescued; 'will spare no one', CM Rekha vows action - top developments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
14:46:10 UTC
23:46:10 KST

The eyewitness said the collapsed building was called ‘Hostel Daze’
NEW DELHI: Five people were killed and five were rescued after a five-storey boys' paying guest (PG) accommodation collapsed in southwest Delhi's Satya Niketan area on Sunday, officials said. Rescue operations were under way to search for any remaining people trapped under the rubble.The collapse involved a building known as 'Hostel Daze', which was being used as a boys' PG. An adjacent building also collapsed, according to eyewitnesses.JPN Apex Trauma Centre (AIIMS), on late Sunday, informed that it received 10 patients from the Satya Niketan building collapse. Four were brought dead, while one critically injured patient later succumbed. Three are admitted and undergoing treatment, one underwent limb surgery, and one with minor injuries was discharged after observation.
3 killed among 9 rescued as rescue operation continues
The AIIMS Trauma Centre said eight injured people were brought to hospitals following the incident. Seven were taken to the AIIMS Trauma Centre, while one was admitted to Safdarjung Hospital. Two of those brought to AIIMS were declared brought dead.The death toll later rose to three, with authorities confirming that six people had been rescued from the rubble.
Two National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) teams were deployed at the site, while two additional teams were kept on standby, NDRF Inspector General NS Bundela said. Rescue teams were working in coordination with the State Disaster Response Force, Delhi Fire Service and other agencies.
Eight fire tenders on spot
The Delhi Fire Service received information about the collapse at around 1.30 pm, following which eight fire tenders and multiple rescue teams were rushed to the spot. Police also cordoned off the area as rescuers searched through the debris.Eyewitnesses said several students were believed to be inside the building when it collapsed. A local resident claimed the PG had around 15 rooms, with two to three students staying in each room, and that around 35 to 40 students were residing on its upper floors.Residents said many students were inside their rooms because it was Sunday. Several locals joined the rescue operation, removing debris with their hands and whatever tools were available.
Basement construction work under scanner
Residents alleged that construction or repair work was under way in the basement and that water had accumulated there. A local resident who has lived in the area for around two decades claimed the building's foundation was weak.
Another resident said he had been inside the building shortly before the collapse and managed to get out minutes before the structure came down.The adjacent building was also reportedly leaning after the collapse, raising concerns about the safety of nearby structures.
Students from several states among residents
Residents said most students staying at the PG were from Kerala, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh and attended colleges including Motilal Nehru College, Atma Ram Sanatan Dharma College and Sri Venkateswara College.One resident said students were paying around Rs 12,000 per bed at the accommodation. Residents also raised concerns about the condition of buildings in the congested locality, where several residential properties have reportedly been converted into student PG accommodations.
CM Rekha Gupta visits collapse site
Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta visited the site and reviewed the ongoing search and rescue operation. Emergency teams continued clearing the rubble and searching for anyone who may still be trapped."No one will be spared," she says.
The Rekha Gupta-led Delhi government has ordered a magisterial inquiry into the incident and directed that an FIR be registered against the building owner, the chief minister’s office (CMO) said.The decision was taken following an on-site review and a preliminary assessment of the incident, the CMO said.“Following an on-site review and based on the preliminary assessment, the chief minister has ordered a Magisterial Inquiry of the incident and an FIR against the building owner,” the CMO said.
It added that those found responsible for the incident would be held fully accountable and face the strictest provisions of the law.
PM Modi expresses condolences
Prime Minister Narendra Modi expressed condolences over the deaths in the Satya Niketan building collapse and prayed for the speedy recovery of those injured. He said authorities were working at the site and assisting people affected by the incident.

Mediterranean Sea now at spa temperature, daily average 28.54°C on 13 August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
14:41:44 UTC
23:41:44 KST

On 13 August the Mediterranean averaged 28.54°C, its highest level since comparable records began in 1940, Aemet reports, capping a summer with the warmest July on record at sea and in mainland Spain.
Surface waters across the Mediterranean Sea reached an average temperature of 28.54ºC on 13 August, the highest recorded since at least 1940, Spain's State Meteorological Agency reported on Sunday.
Aemet itself noted on social media that throughout almost the whole of August the sea was breaking daily temperature records, one after another, with barely any respite.
The warning comes just weeks after Mercator Ocean International, which implements the Copernicus marine service, confirmed that July had already been the hottest month ever measured in the Mediterranean. The average that month was 27.07ºC, with a margin of uncertainty of ±0.27ºC, beating the previous maximum, set in July 2025 (26.68ºC), by four tenths of a degree.
Mercator Ocean's comparison series begins in 1993, meaning that both bodies, despite using different methods and reference periods, concur in describing a sea that has entered a thermal regime not seen before.
This pattern has been in place for months
Data from late June were already pointing that way. Aemet (source in Spanish) warned at the time that Mediterranean temperatures had reached levels more typical of the second half of August, when the sea is usually at its warmest.
At the start of the summer, temperatures rose to 2.6ºC above normal, to the point that the sea exceeded the average usually seen in mid-August while it was still June, an anomaly the agency itself described as exceptional.
On a planetary scale, the phenomenon is not confined to the Mediterranean. July 2026 was the month with the highest global ocean surface temperature in the entire record, with an average of 21ºC between 60º north and 60º south.
Across the Mediterranean basin, 27% of the sea experienced its warmest July since 1993 and around 70% of the surface ranked among the four hottest Julys ever measured, ruling out the idea that the record can be explained by just a few exceptional locations.
It is important to stress that the sea-temperature record cannot be singled out as the direct cause of the high temperatures recorded on land, as many different factors come into play in the atmosphere. It can, however, alter conditions along the coast: water releases heat more slowly than the land surface, so a Mediterranean this warm makes it harder for temperatures to fall at night, increases humidity and leads to hotter nights near the shore.
The build-up of energy in the sea also affects ecosystems. Prolonged marine heatwaves subject organisms adapted to specific thermal ranges to considerable stress and can alter species distribution, increase mortality and change the functioning of entire coastal communities.
With the figure recorded on 13 August, the Mediterranean has once again surpassed the record it had set only a few weeks earlier, in a summer which, on land and at sea, keeps breaking its own records.

US President Donald Trump has criticised the alleged exchange-rate gap between the Canadian and US dollars, calling the "imbalance" unacceptable.
"Canada's (currency) Dollar imbalance with the US is unacceptable," Trump wrote on his social media platform Truth Social on Sunday. "It has been that way for years - but no longer!"
Trump did not elaborate on what he meant by the remark.
The Canadian dollar has historically been weaker than its US counterpart for most of the past 15 years. The long-term average stands at about $1 to 1.24 Canadian dollars.
Since 2015, the currency has mostly traded between 1.20 Canadian dollars and 1.45 Canadian dollars against the greenback. It only reached or exceeded parity during part of the 2007-2012 commodity boom, when the Canadian dollar was stronger than the US dollar.
Dollar-for-dollar retaliation
The US dollar currently trades at around 1.38 Canadian dollars, meaning one Canadian dollar is worth roughly 72 US cents.
A weaker Canadian dollar makes Canadian goods cheaper for US buyers and US goods more expensive for Canadian consumers. Trump has repeatedly criticised the trade gap with Canada amid an ongoing trade war between the two neighbours.
Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered negotiators to return home from Washington.
The US subsequently moved to impose 50 percent tariffs on key Canadian goods. Carney has vowed dollar-for-dollar retaliation starting September 8.
It remains unclear whether Trump plans to take any action regarding the currency gap. The White House has not issued further details on the president's remarks.
