The petition will be lodged with Charles, Jamaica’s head of state, on Monday.
“We’re a resilient people. We were able to bounce back from [Hurricane] Melissa, for example,” said Olivia Grange, who arrived in London at the weekend with members of Jamaica’s National Council on Reparations.
“But we still have a lot of work to do, and you can imagine if we did not have those inherited problems, the legacy that came out of slavery, how much better we would have been able to do so,” she told the Guardian.
First announced in June last year, the petition asks the monarch to use his authority to request legal advice from the judicial committee of the London-based privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.
It wants Charles to ask whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful, if it constituted a crime against humanity, and whether Britain is under an obligation to provide restitution to Jamaica for slavery and its enduring consequences.
Grange said that these questions and a privy council response were critical to progressing the country’s reparations claims.
Between the 15th and 19th centuries, more than 12.5 million Africans were kidnapped, forcibly transported to the Americas and sold into slavery.
Grange said that Jamaica had been the first Caribbean nation to create a national reparations mechanism, establishing it in 2009. She said the aim was to address the enduring impacts of slavery that put countries such as Jamaica at a grave economic disadvantage and affected its ability to respond to modern-day challenges in the Caribbean, such as the climate crisis.
“We have inherited systems that continue to deprive our country and our people. The legacy in education, even in health, the way we eat, our diet because of what we were fed, our ancestors were fed,” she said.
Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines who was instrumental in setting up the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, echoed Grange’s sentiments.
“The present is very much the past, because what we are dealing with is the legacies of underdevelopment which you can source, and we do source, to native genocide and enslavement of African bodies,” he said on Sunday.
“People must remember this: that European nations were enriched because of the enslavement of African bodies.” Gonsalves is an elder and adviser for the Repair Campaign, a social movement for reparatory justice.
He said Jamaica’s visit was a critical milestone among a number of upcoming events, including a Caribbean reparations conference in Barbados later this month, and planned advocacy at the upcoming UN general assembly in late September and the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua in November, which King Charles is scheduled to attend.
There are growing global calls for Britain and other former colonial powers to recognise hundreds of years of transatlantic slavery that treated African people as chattel as a crime, and to engage in a process of reparatory justice.
In March this year, 123 nations voted for a landmark UN resolution that described chattel slavery as the gravest crime against humanity. In June, the Caribbean launched a manifesto outlining the “moral, ethical and legal case for reparations”. And last month, a UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination said countries were legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other measures to address the enduring legacy of racial discrimination.
The UK was one of several European countries that abstained from voting in the March UN resolution, and in October 2024, the former British prime minister Keir Starmer resisted pressure from member states to include reparations in the Commonwealth heads of government meeting agenda.
Grange said she hoped the visit would facilitate a unifying response to the complicated history.
A palace spokesperson said Charles “has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today.”
Later on Sunday, the delegation hosted a remembrance church service in Brixton, and later in the week they are due to meet UK members of parliament. Grange said there would also be a visit to the British Museum to discuss repatriation of Jamaican artefacts.
She said: “We may have different history, different heritage, different skin colour, but it’s about humanity. It’s about, as a people, being able to live together, to work together, and to respect each other.
“And in our efforts to seek reparatory justice, we will use the opportunity to also promote and encourage what Jamaica is known for, One Love, because we have the song of the century through Bob Marley.”

Some Americans call us ‘Europoor’ - but there are seven ways we’re exceedingly rich | Emma Beddington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
13:00:07 UTC
22:00:07 KST

I’m sorry to break this to you, but you may be “Europoor”. This is, apparently, what proud American patriots (the kind who describe themselves in those terms on their flag-forward X profiles anyway) are calling us Europeans, mocking us for our low salaries, high taxes and dependence on public transport.
GB news presenter Tom Harwood declared this dig “entirely accurate”, but is it? Well, sort of. US post-pandemic GDP growth is more than double that of the eurozone (15.6% compared with 7.2%; the UK is even worse on 6.3%). As for wages, once you adjust for national differences in the cost of essentials such as housing, food and services, the US average is $86,977 compared with the UK’s $66,299, Germany’s $76,286 and France’s $60,483, according to the OECD. A Sunday Telegraph investigation of the “Europoor” question highlighted astronomically powerful growth of the US tech sector supercharged by AI, making it easy to raise and make big money unencumbered by “old world” regulation and taxation. “We don’t want to be like what Europe has become,” said the Republican pollster Brent Buchanan.
There are massive, obvious caveats. GDP is a wholly inadequate proxy for quality of life or even prosperity: the UN’s proposed alternative dashboard of 31 indicators includes the likes of “respect for the planet” and wealth inequalities, against which the US would surely take a beating. US mortality rates are higher than European ones and life expectancy is lower, so, when a medical diagnosis or accident could bankrupt you, how rich do you really feel?
But, actually, this Europoor stuff is hitting me where it hurts: my New York-based grad student son out-earns me, and his junior nurse girlfriend is paid six figures – that’s more than I made in a city law firm. Quite right – nurses should earn more than corporate lawyers – but it’s hard to imagine them ever choosing to live here in the UK (an NHS nurse’s starting salary is £32,073).
To console myself as I contemplate years of getting even Europoorer, flying long-haul to hug my son, I’ve been counting the ways we’re Eurorich. Sure, healthcare, social protections, holidays, blah blah – but what about the really important stuff?
Cheese
“The United States offers over 1,000+ cheese varieties and styles,” the Cheese from the USA website claims, to which I would counter: “But do any of them taste of anything?” I doubt a single Freedom Cheese can clear a train carriage like a ripe époisses.
Bikes
Apparently, Americans buy 130m bicycles a year, but I suspect that’s thanks to a handful of legmaxxing California billionaires. Anyway, 130m also feels like the number of bikes parked outside Amsterdam Centraal station on any given day (in 2019, 41% of Netherlanders said the bike was their main mode of transport).
Saints
The US has 11 saints – pathetic. I’ve seen the remains of more than 11 saints in a single European mini-break; Ireland alone has an estimated 1,000.
Wholesome food
Let’s take stock of this summer’s US food safety scares. Lettuce, blueberries, jalapenos, fruit bars, granola, eggs, alfalfa sprouts, mangoes, sourdough, tofu … basically anything healthier than Flamin’ Hot Cheetos is a gamble; Gwyneth Paltrow is probably claiming asylum in Puglia as I write.
Weird rulers
Sure, they have their stable genius, but nothing can match absolute monarchy and centuries of inbreeding for floridly unhinged leadership. Charles VI of France thought he was made of glass; the future Peter III of Russia court-martialled a rat for eating one of his toy soldiers.
Characterful teeth
The US has, I read, “entered the age of veneer regret”, with people rueing their decision to drop big money on massive, gleaming, Hollywood teeth. Not over here! We’ve still got teeth Breugel the Elder would recognise (in the UK it’s partly because we can’t access affordable dentistry, but sssh).
Disturbing folklore
Scratch the surface of any European country and some weird, sinister custom emerges. At Belgium’s Matî l’Ohê festival they mourn a bone by waving celery; Austria’s demon-chasing Perchten festival involves dressing like a horned haystack; in Wales’s Mari Lwyd, people take a horse skull on a pole from door to door singing for midwinter. In the name of carnival, we throw herring in northern France, execute a pretend mare in Czechia and hunt people dressed as bears all over the place. And really, what’s better – purchasing power or an annual opportunity to wave celery at a bone? I know my answer.

Sahin Demir
06 September 2026•Update: 06 September 2026
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun on Sunday condemned renewed Israeli attacks on the southern city of Nabatieh and surrounding towns, saying the targeting of state institutions and health facilities marked a “dangerous escalation.”
In a statement posted by the Lebanese presidency on US social media company X, Aoun said the attacks caused civilian casualties, severely damaged a Finance Ministry building and destroyed Ghandour Hospital.
He said the attacks went beyond repeated violations of the cessation-of-hostilities arrangement and the framework agreement by attacking Lebanese state institutions, public service facilities, a hospital and health centers.
Aoun said the attack on the Finance Ministry building, following an earlier strike on a State Security center that caused fatalities, demonstrated “a continuing pattern” of attacks extending beyond alleged military targets to civilian government and health facilities.
He accused Israel of seeking to disrupt the functioning of Lebanese institutions and services provided to the public.
The Lebanese president held Israel fully responsible for the continuing escalation and called on the US and the international community to act urgently to halt the attacks and hold those responsible accountable.
He said Lebanon remained committed to measures aimed at preserving its sovereignty, stability in the south and the safety of its citizens.
The remarks came after a series of Israeli airstrikes on Nabatieh and surrounding areas on Sunday killed four people and injured 20 others, according to a preliminary toll from the Lebanese Health Ministry.
The ministry said the strikes completely destroyed Ghandour Hospital in Nabatieh al-Fawqa. It said 17 hospitals across Lebanon have been damaged by Israeli strikes since March 2, while three hospitals in southern Lebanon have been put out of service.
The attacks came despite a US-sponsored framework agreement signed on June 26, which provides for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army.
Since March 2, Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed 4,358 people and injured 12,359 others, while displacing more than 1 million people, according to Lebanese authorities.

He said the government was committed to tackling narcotics with the same approach it used against Naxalism and terrorism.“Before 2014, the fight against narcotics was largely conducted in small units and isolation,” Shah said, adding that agencies had often focused on catching small-time accused. The government, he said, had now made the anti-narcotics fight a national security priority.Detailing the approach Shah stated that the government has strengthened its anti-narcotics drive through NCORD, state anti-narcotics task forces and joint coordination between agencies, along with the MANAS helpline and a revamped NCB. It also created the NIDAN database of narcotics offenders and a nationwide data-driven map of drug hotspots and trafficking patterns.
The government now uses a “bottom-to-top” and “top-to-bottom” reverse investigation model, tracing small drug seizures back to their source and large consignments forward to their intended users to uncover the wider network.Shah also highlighted the government’s claims on internal security, saying terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir was declining and the sentiment of separatism had weakened since the abrogation of Article 370.
He said those who had envisioned a Maoist “red corridor” from Tirupati to Pashupati had laid down arms and joined the mainstream, while more than 10,000 youths in the northeast had also surrendered their arms.Shah said Naxalism, which had persisted for five decades, had become a thing of the past. “We have eradicated Naxalism and will deal with menace of narcotics in the same manner,” he asserted.

Ayoub fell into the dry well on Wednesday while walking home in the village of Errokn, in the municipality of Ghassoul. He stepped on a wooden board covering the well opening, which gave way beneath him, and he plunged into the shaft, which was about 80 metres (262 feet) deep and 40cm (15.75 inches) in diameter.
Rescuers were unable to descend into the well, so they dug a parallel shaft to reach the boy through a horizontal passage, using machinery alongside technical experts, work that continued over several days. Loose soil and hard rock layers complicated the effort, officials said.
Authorities in el-Bayadh formed a crisis response unit under the provincial governor, Noureddine Belarbi, involving civil protection, security and military personnel.
Large crowds of residents gathered near the site over the following days to follow the operation and offer support to the family, while additional civil protection units were deployed as the rescue entered what officials described as a “decisive” phase on its fourth day.
Ayoub’s death has revived public debate in Algeria over the safety of unsecured wells in rural areas, with commentators questioning the lack of regulation covering such structures, particularly in isolated regions.
The case recalled the 2018 death of a young man who fell into a 100-metre (328-foot) well in Msila province, where a rescue operation lasted nine days before his body was recovered, and the widely followed 2022 case of Moroccan toddler Rayan, who died after falling into a 32-metre (105-foot) well and being trapped for more than 100 hours in an operation that drew global attention before he was pulled out and later confirmed dead.

The government counts on the judges in Jerusalem to strike down their laws - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:47:35 UTC
21:47:35 KST

“There are judges in Jerusalem,” and the government knew it.
The phrase, popularly associated with former prime minister Menachem Begin and the principle that governments must respect judicial rulings, is usually invoked as an expression of faith: However great the political pressure, the law will ultimately be upheld. In this case, however, it describes something considerably more cynical.
The coalition passed a temporary amendment on July 14 that would have halted arrests, investigations, and other enforcement proceedings against qualifying haredi (ultra-Orthodox) yeshiva students who failed to report for military service. It did not exempt them from the draft; their legal obligation to serve remained; the state would simply have been prevented from enforcing it.
The amendment was passed even though the coalition was warned repeatedly, and in the clearest possible terms, that it could not survive legal scrutiny. It then left the law effectively undefended in court. When nine justices unanimously struck it down, the politicians responsible attacked the court for producing the expected result.
The law never took effect. Justice Ofer Grosskopf froze it the day after it passed, pending the petitions that produced Thursday’s judgment.
Grosskopf’s order was enacted against an already settled legal backdrop. After the statutory framework allowing yeshiva-student deferments expired in 2023, the High Court unanimously ruled in June 2024 that the government no longer had the authority to refrain from drafting eligible students.
Subsequent rulings ordered the state to enforce that obligation meaningfully. Its problems were not discovered after the vote by an overreaching court hunting for an excuse to intervene. The Knesset’s own legal advisers warned lawmakers “once, twice, and three times,” as Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg put it, that the legislation had departed entirely from the bill that passed its first reading.
That original bill was intended to increase haredi enlistment and national service, encourage employment, and reduce inequality.
By the time the coalition had finished with it, it contained no enlistment targets, effective sanctions, or alternative enforcement system. Its principal achievement was to remove the consequences of refusing to report.
Knesset legal team warns High Court that legislative process fundamentally defective
The Knesset’s legal team eventually told the High Court that the legislative process was fundamentally defective.
Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara opposed the law on both procedural and constitutional grounds.
IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir warned that it would encourage noncompliance and was “clearly and unequivocally inconsistent” with the military’s needs.
The government was permitted to obtain separate legal representation – and it still offered no substantive legal defense. Instead, it submitted a short position saying the result of the case was “known in advance.”
That sentence should follow every attack now being directed at the court. This was not a law that unexpectedly encountered a newly invented judicial obstacle; the coalition was told, at every stage, that it was crossing the basic procedural boundaries that turn a proposal into law.
It crossed them anyway.
Nine justices, along with the petitioners and state and Knesset attorneys, were then required to spend their time litigating what lawmakers had already been told before the legislation passed.
If the law somehow survived, the coalition would obtain temporary immunity from enforcement for haredi draft evaders. If it was struck down – as almost everyone involved understood it would be – haredi politicians would obtain something else: another judgment around which to rally their voters and another opportunity to portray the court as the enemy of Torah.
The law failed, and Shas immediately called the justices “the greatest generators of chaos in the country,” accused them of trampling democracy and claiming that they were intervening in the election on behalf of the Left.
The government passed an indefensible law, forced the court to intervene, and then presented that intervention as proof that the court is persecuting the community the law purported to protect.
The fear within haredi society is real. The messaging to families, explicit and implicit, is that military enlistment threatens their children’s religious identity and standing within their community and that enforcement of an obligation imposed by Israeli law amounts to persecution of Torah students.
But that fear was not created by the High Court. It is the product of decades in which political and religious leaders, with the state’s cooperation and frequent capitulation, allowed a separate understanding of citizenship to take hold: that the laws governing military service were ultimately negotiable for one community, even when they remained compulsory for everyone else.
The state bears deep responsibility for that failure. It failed to ensure that every Israeli child receives an education in the rights and obligations of citizenship, and it allowed temporary arrangements to become an assumed way of life and repeatedly postponed the moment at which it would have to tell haredi citizens the truth.
Haredi leadership must take responsibility
But haredi leadership bears responsibility as well.
Citizenship cannot mean access to representation, budgets, benefits, and political power while its obligations are framed as oppression whenever they become inconvenient.
This is why Sohlberg’s despair, which carries through very clearly in the decision, is so poignant.
Sohlberg is not a judge hostile to Torah study looking at haredi society from the outside. He is an observant Jew, a graduate of a hesder yeshiva, and a jurist whose opinions are steeped in Jewish law and religious texts.
At the July hearing, an attorney representing a haredi organization claimed that the Torah prohibited enlistment under the current conditions. Justice David Mintz, also observant, responded: “I simply cannot believe what I am hearing.”
In Thursday’s judgment, Sohlberg answered the claim at greater length.
“With the signing of another chapter – as bleak as those before it – in the saga of haredi enlistment and precisely ‘out of recognition of the value of Torah study’ and the Torah’s values, I cannot refrain from what has nearly become a fixed ritual,” he wrote.
He would try once again, he said, to make clear “to anyone willing to listen, that this is not the way of Torah. Far from it.”
Sohlberg cited Moses’s question to the tribes that sought to remain outside the coming battle: “Shall your brothers go to war while you sit here?”
The court did not order the arrest of Torah students because they study Torah. As Sohlberg stressed, enforcement applies because they have not complied with a legal obligation to report for service.
Nor did the court create the haredi draft crisis; the Knesset preserved the duty to enlist and then attempted to switch off its enforcement for one group.
What took place was a twisting of the institutions of justice into political stage props. The coalition knowingly passed a defective law, relied on the court to dispose of it, and then condemned the court for doing so.
There are judges in Jerusalem – the government counted on it. Now, it is counting on the public not to notice.

Lebanese Sunni MP Fouad Makhzoumi: Lebanon can sign Abraham Accords once Hezbollah is disarmed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:47:33 UTC
21:47:33 KST

Lebanon can join the Abraham Accords once Hezbollah is disarmed and can no longer use the country as a “launching pad” for attacks against Israel, Lebanese Sunni MP Fouad Makhzoumi told Middle East 24 last week.
Makhzoumi, who has previously urged the Lebanese military to demonstrate its willingness to confront Hezbollah’s arms trafficking by establishing a checkpoint in Beirut’s Dahieh neighborhood, said diplomatic relations and trade with Israel would be possible once “our side, as Lebanese, disarms the militias.”
As it stands, he said, Lebanon has a border that is outside the state’s control, allowing arms to be smuggled into and out of the country.
“I don’t see any reason why we cannot sign peace with Israel,” Makhzoumi said, adding that it was possible for Lebanon to “achieve” membership in the Abraham Accords.
The CEO and executive chairman of Future Pipe Industries, a major international conglomerate, and the founder and leader of Lebanon’s National Dialogue Party, he framed Lebanon’s economic recovery and future growth as depending on the state’s ability to tackle corruption within the judicial system and dismantle Hezbollah’s “parallel state.”
Lebanon's central bank to conduct audit of transactions
Lebanon scored 23 out of 100 on Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, ranking 153 out of 182 countries.
Makhzoumi’s comments also came the same week that Lebanon’s central bank announced that France-based consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal would conduct an audit of transactions dating from October 1, 2019, through December 31, 2023.
For Makhzoumi, restoring investor confidence requires more than financial reforms. He argued that capital will not flow into Lebanon until there is a regulatory framework that is fairly applied to every investor, one military force representing the country and one law applied equally to all.
Achieving those conditions, he said, requires Lebanon to disarm Hezbollah, “make sure that there is no opportunity for somebody to take me to a war under ideological reasons,” establish a strong banking system that complies with international regulations, and “have peace with Israel.”
Such a shift could also open the door to greater investment from Lebanon’s regional partners. Notably, the United Arab Emirates, a signatory to the Abraham Accords, has become a major investor in Lebanon. UAE Foreign Trade Minister Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi led a delegation of more than 80 prominent figures to Lebanon last month, where the two countries signed an intergovernmental memorandum of understanding aimed at strengthening bilateral relations.
Regional analysts who spoke with The Jerusalem Post suggested that increased UAE investment could help Beirut distance itself from Iran and Hezbollah.
Makhzoumi said he is already in discussions with individuals interested in investing in southern Lebanon, where Hezbollah has created economic and social dependency by filling gaps in employment, healthcare and education.
Makhzoumi attempts to bring Lebanon's wealthy diaspora home
New investment, he argued, could encourage members of Lebanon’s wealthy diaspora to return.
“I myself operate in 50 countries, and wherever you go in the world, you find a Lebanese that has been successful, whether in a big corporation, or in a state, or in an advisory role,” he said. “So I am confident that the Lebanese will be willing to come and to build their country, but give me a state, give me a place that I can afford to bring my children back, and to make sure that they can live happily under the law, and not to be threatened by Hezbollah or by any other militia.”
The lack of economic and political stability has driven many young Lebanese to seek opportunities abroad, Makhzoumi said. Many leave the country after graduating because they cannot envision a future in a country where assassinations occur, the threat of war remains, and Hezbollah can threaten their security.
That emigration has accelerated amid Lebanon’s prolonged economic crisis, which began in 2019. According to figures published by the American University of Beirut, emigration increased by 450% in 2021 and 2022, with around 79,134 Lebanese citizens leaving the country in 2021 alone. The trend left a giant gap in numerous industries, especially in the healthcare sector.

Kozuk was frustrated by the late concession but remained confident in his squad.
“Hapoel Beersheba are Hapoel Beersheba because of their philosophy, and if, in the final minutes, we sit back like cowards, that’s not who we are,” Kozuk said. “The first half was tremendous. We have to do what the coach asks. I attribute this to everyone who was on the pitch, including the coach.
“Against Maccabi Tel Aviv, we’ll need to do what we did for 94 minutes. We’ll have a squad that is good enough in terms of quality for the season in Europe, and we’ll try to keep this squad healthy.”

Ironi Tiberias also earned three points, defeating Maccabi Petah Tikva 2-1 despite playing with 10 men for more than an hour.

However, Ironi Tiberias refused to fold, and Chris Kouakou set up Ari Cohen, who fired home the winner to complete an impressive victory.
“It’s a weight lifted off our shoulders now that we’ve erased the point deficit that we began the season with,” Tiberias coach Alon Ziv said. “The players put in an incredible display of fighting spirit with 10 men. We played really good football, and there were stages when there was only one team on the pitch.”

Oscar hopes and Eurovision: Cultural challenges Israel faces next year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:47:16 UTC
21:47:16 KST

In the latest episode of The Jerusalem Playlist, hosts Ezra Taylor and Hannah Brown discuss the biggest stories shaping Israeli culture, from Eurovision’s evolving rules to the films expected to make an impact during Israel’s awards season and at the Venice Film Festival.
The episode opens with Eurovision and the question of whether Bulgaria will be able to host the 2027 competition. Taylor and Brown discuss Netta Barzilai’s role in Israel’s Eurovision history, noting that she was the last Israeli artist to win the competition in 2018.
The hosts examine new Eurovision rules that state a country may become ineligible to host if it is involved in armed conflict, facing a sensitive geopolitical situation, or dealing with circumstances that could affect regional security and stability. While the rule was widely viewed as potentially affecting Israel, Taylor and Brown discuss whether Bulgaria could also face questions after Iran threatened the country over its decision to allow US aircraft to refuel there.
Shifting towards Israeli cinema
The conversation then shifts to Tell Me Everything, an Israeli film by director Moshe Rosenthal that follows a family during the 1980s and 1990s. Hannah Brown explains that the film centers on a young boy who discovers that his father is gay while preparing for his bar mitzvah, during the height of the AIDS epidemic, and explores the fear, confusion, and trauma that follow within the family.
The film has received 16 Ophir Award nominations, with Brown explaining the importance of the awards within Israel’s film industry. The Ophir Awards are considered Israel’s equivalent of the Oscars, and the Best Picture winner becomes Israel’s official submission for consideration in the Academy Awards’ Best International Feature category.
The episode concludes with a look at the Venice Film Festival and Israeli films making their mark on the international stage. Taylor and Brown discuss Nasa, a new film by two of the creators of No Other Land, as well as the broader history of Israeli cinema at Venice, where films have often explored questions of identity, politics and conflict.

A differentiated &quot;color-coded&quot; threat alert system has begun operating in Kyiv
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
15:46:23 EEST
21:46:23 KST

A differentiated "color-coded" threat alert system has begun operating in Kyiv
Kyiv • UNN
The capital authorities have introduced yellow and red alert levels for drone and missile threats. However, the Pecherskyi district has not yet been connected.
As of September 6, a differentiated alert system for aerial threats has been introduced in Kyiv. People will now receive separate notifications depending on the type and level of danger. The Kyiv City State Administration reports this, according to UNN.
Details
Starting at 6:00 a.m. on September 6, 2026, by decision of the Government, Kyiv residents and city residents will be able to receive the following air-raid alert notifications:
-  Yellow level - "Drone threat"; 
-  Red level - "Massive drone threat"; "Missile threat"; "Missile-and-drone threat"; 
-  "All clear" - no threats or dangers are present. 
According to the available information, each new notification displays the type and level of threat current at that moment. If the type of threat changes, the new notification automatically replaces the previous one.
A separate "All clear" notification is not issued between different types of threats. For example, if a "Drone threat" notification is followed by a "Missile threat" notification, this means that the missile threat is now current. An "All clear" notification means that, at that moment, none of the listed aerial threats has been recorded in the city
However, the differentiated alert system has currently been introduced in all districts of Kyiv except Pecherskyi District.
In Holosiivskyi and Sviatoshynskyi districts, it operates partially. This is because, in certain areas, differentiation by type of threat is currently technically impossible. Therefore, the procedure for audio alerts there remains unchanged: if any aerial danger or threat arises, the standard siren signal is sounded without separate differentiation by type of threat and without an audio "All clear" signal
We remind you
In Ukraine, alert systems for existing threats will be updated, and two levels indicating a specific threat will be introduced - yellow and red. In addition, clearer geographical differentiation of alerts will be developed.

US envoys visit Kyiv to revive Ukraine-Russia talks to end war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:42:00 UTC
21:42:00 KST

U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff held talks Sunday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to end the war with Russia, a day after they met with Russia's Vladimir Putin.
The Americans arrived in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv by train, hoping to revive negotiations to end Europe's worst conflict since World War II following a summer of escalation.
Zelenskyy published a video of his meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Kushner and business partner Witkoff in central Kyiv, saying: "Talks have begun."
Witkoff and Kushner had visited Moscow eight times but had not held talks in Kyiv until now, despite the city enduring deadly strikes since Russia's February 2022 invasion.
Ukraine's top security officials and negotiators were also present and several European national security advisors.
Zelenskyy showed the U.S. envoys Kyiv's historic Saint Sophia's Cathedral, which stands opposite the SBU security building that a Russian drone hit Friday.
Moscow's invasion of Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
Witkoff and Kushner met with Putin on Saturday to "advance President Trump's agenda of peace in the war in Ukraine," a White House official said.
"The two sides discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks, and look forward to equally productive meetings tomorrow in Ukraine."
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov called the talks "extremely frank," saying the Americans "put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement," but did not elaborate.
The Russian side told the Americans that Moscow was "confident" it could achieve its military goals of seizing the rest of eastern Ukraine, Ushakov added.
Both Russia and Ukraine had vowed not to strike each other's capitals for three days during the Americans' visit.
Zelenskyy Sunday said Ukraine was "ready for the conversation."
"Ukraine has always been and will remain constructive," the wartime leader said on social media ahead of their visit.
The country's airspace has been closed since Moscow launched the war, and visiting leaders have been arriving by train.
In televised comments before the talks, Putin said Russia would ensure the safety of the envoys in Kyiv.
"We will do everything that depends on us to ensure the safety of the negotiation process and mediators such as yourselves," Putin told Witkoff and Kushner.
Earlier Saturday, Putin had thanked Trump for persisting in his efforts to end the war despite the task being "not simple."
Of the envoys' trip to Kyiv, he said: "No matter what happens next, contacts of this kind are undoubtedly always beneficial."
Trump said Friday that his envoys were bringing a "proposal" to end the fighting.
"We have an idea for peace," he said, without elaborating.
U.S. efforts have so far not led to a breakthrough in the war and peace efforts have stalled.
Russia has occupied large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine, and Putin has insisted Moscow is intent on seizing the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Despite the cease-fire pledges for the capital cities, fighting continued elsewhere.
Ukraine's air force said Russia attacked overnight with 108 drones and missiles, while Moscow said it shot down 258 drones.
On Saturday, Putin said he "noted that the Ukrainian side significantly reduced" its strikes on Russia and Moscow.
However, Kyiv said Russian strikes killed 10 people across the country Saturday, including a child and family members in the Kharkiv region and two people outside Kyiv.

Iraqi Shia factions seek to 'lobby Trump' in bid to keep arms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:39:48 UTC
21:39:48 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraqi Shia factions seek to 'lobby Trump' in bid to keep arms
Iraqi Shia political forces are reportedly considering a lobbying campaign in Washington aimed at persuading the Trump administration to accept Iran-aligned armed factions retaining their weapons, as Baghdad's push for militia disarmament increasingly shifts towards regulating their arsenals.
The initiative would seek to convince US officials that the factions could retain their weapons while operating within restrictions agreed with the Iraqi government, according to a report published by Iraqi newspaper Al-Mada on Sunday.
Citing an Iraqi political source, the newspaper said Shia political actors were seeking the assistance of former US officials and political figures with connections in Washington to communicate the proposal to the Trump administration and US military establishment.
The source suggested the initiative was being pursued with Iranian backing, though this has not been independently confirmed.
The reported lobbying effort comes as factions and their political allies appear increasingly confident that they will not be required to fully disarm.
A source within Iraq's ruling Shia Coordination Framework told Al-Mada that armed factions could retain their weapons throughout the current government's four-year term.
The source said pressure on the factions had diminished compared with a month earlier, with Iran-aligned groups increasingly confident that they would be able to resist demands for complete disarmament.
The reports mark the latest indication that Baghdad's efforts to establish a state monopoly over weapons are shifting away from the prospect of dismantling factional arsenals towards regulating what weapons the groups can possess.
Former Iraqi prime minister Nouri al-Maliki said last week that negotiations were no longer using the term "disarmament", describing the issue instead as one of regulating or containing weapons.
Maliki, one of the most influential figures in the Coordination Framework, said a joint committee negotiating with armed groups was discussing distinctions between heavy, medium and light weapons.
The talks could result in weapons capable of striking targets inside or outside Iraq being brought under state control while factions retain other categories of arms.
Maliki also indicated that the armed factions themselves would continue to exist.
Supporters of Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) and allied armed factions have also long pointed to their role in the fight against the Islamic State group as justification for preserving their military structures. That legacy could provide part of the political case for allowing some factions to remain armed under tighter state regulation.
The apparent shift follows months of pressure on Baghdad to bring weapons outside the formal security establishment under government control.
The government had previously set 30 September as a deadline for resolving the issue.
Government spokesman Haider al-Aboudi said in June that armed groups had been informed that the date represented "the end of this issue", warning that weapons remaining outside the state framework afterwards would be dealt with under Iraqi law.
However, the government subsequently softened its position, with al-Aboudi later saying that 30 September referred to the withdrawal of the US-led coalition rather than a final deadline for factions to surrender their weapons.
Negotiations have since focused on reaching an accommodation with powerful armed groups, many of which operate formally within or alongside Iraq's PMF while retaining independent command structures and close relationships with Iran.
Al-Mada reported that discussions include the possibility of using amendments to legislation governing the PMF as part of an agreement with the factions.
The proposed compromise would seek to strengthen government oversight while avoiding a confrontation with groups that have rejected demands to surrender their arsenals.
Some factions remain firmly opposed to disarmament.
Harakat al-Nujaba political bureau chief Ali al-Asadi said last week that the group's "resistance weapons" were sacrosanct and would not be surrendered.
Al-Nujaba has also rejected integration into conventional parliamentary politics, distinguishing it from factions that combine armed wings with political representation inside the Iraqi state.

Germany strengthens protection against Russian drones and cyberattacks amid acts of sabotage
Kyiv • UNN
Following a drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, Germany will strengthen the protection of critical infrastructure. The plan includes countering drones, AI and "CyberDome".
Germany will create a comprehensive system to protect against drones, cyberattacks and acts of sabotage following an attempted attack on Leipzig Airport by a Russian drone. Bild reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
Following the failed drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, Germany is stepping up its efforts to combat Russian acts of sabotage. Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (56, CSU) plans to create a comprehensive protective shield against further attacks
According to the publication, Alexander Dobrindt said that Russian hybrid attacks had already become a daily reality for the country.
Russia’s hybrid attacks using bomb-laden drones against airports, agents in our cities, cyberattacks on our networks and sabotage of our infrastructure are a daily reality. These attacks will intensify, but we can protect ourselves
According to available information, under the Federal Ministry of the Interior’s new security plan, drone protection will also be extended to companies operating in critical infrastructure sectors, including water supply, energy and the defense sector. They are to be granted legal powers not only to detect drones but also to actively counter them.
Expansion of the Federal Police’s mobile drone protection unit: New rapid-deployment units (helicopters, vehicles), stationed in strategically important cities—Frankfurt am Main, Munich, Hamburg, Berlin, Stuttgart, Düsseldorf, Leipzig, Hanover and Cologne—are intended to provide comprehensive protection against drones in the airspace over critical transport hubs, airports, railway stations and Berlin’s government district. This includes not only interception, but also the neutralization of bombs carried by drones and explosive devices
In addition, according to available information, in the future, drone protection is to be the responsibility not only of the Federal Police and other authorities, but also of companies operating in critical infrastructure sectors.
Germany also plans to make greater use of artificial intelligence, biometric facial recognition and video systems to search for spies and people who may be preparing attacks. In addition, AI is to help automatically detect weapons and suspicious behavior.
Separately, plans also call for the creation of a national protective shield called "CyberDome"—a dense network of digital sensors for detecting and intercepting hacker attacks on government institutions and businesses.
We remind you
Germany directly accused Russia of organizing the drone attack on Leipzig Airport on the night of August 5. Berlin will tighten border controls when Russian citizens enter the country.

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir told Israel Police Commissioner Danny Levy on Sunday that he will not approve a sweeping round of senior police appointments until after the election, citing concerns over how the move could be perceived so close to the vote.
The decision affects 141 senior officers: 11 assistant commissioners and 130 commanders and chief superintendents who had been due to receive new assignments in the coming round.
The appointments had been expected to move forward a day later, despite an existing shortage of senior officers in the force.
Ben-Gvir said making such appointments about a month and a half before the election could create the appearance of an improper last-minute move.
“It is not appropriate to make senior appointments about a month and a half before the election, since this could be perceived by part of the public as a grab,” he said in a statement.
“Accordingly, all appointments will be frozen until after the election, except for urgent cases that will be examined individually.”
The decision effectively postpones a broad reshuffle of the police command structure until after voters go to the polls, while leaving room for exceptions in cases deemed urgent.

New Israeli parties face unusual problem: not enough letters in the alphabet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:24:35 UTC
21:24:35 KST

Israel’s election campaign is already a battle over ideology, voters, candidates, alliances and leadership. But as the deadline for submitting party lists approaches, another contest is unfolding almost entirely out of public view: the race for the letters that will appear on ballot slips.
In Israel, those letters are more than a technical detail. They are one of the most recognizable parts of a party’s identity on Election Day. Likud has long been associated with “Mahal” (מחל), Shas with “Shas” (שס), United Torah Judaism with gimel (ג') and Yisrael Beytenu with lamed (ל'). This time, several new parties and alliances are entering the race, all of them looking for a ballot designation in an already crowded political alphabet.
Under election law and Central Elections Committee rules, parties represented in the outgoing Knesset receive priority over the letters or combinations they used in the previous election. A new list that wants to use a designation already claimed by an existing faction needs written consent from the party that holds the right to it. This year, the rules were expanded to allow parties to use combinations of up to three letters rather than only one or two, partly in anticipation of a larger number of competing lists.
The letters already taken
A Central Elections Committee document shows that many of the most familiar ballot designations are effectively reserved. Among them are “Emet” (אמת), expected to be used by the Democrats; gimel (ג') for United Torah Judaism; “Peh” (פה) for Yesh Atid; “Mahal” (מחל) for Likud; “Shas” (שס) for Shas; “Vam” (ום) for Hadash-Ta’al; “Ken” (כן) for Blue and White; tet (ט') for Religious Zionism; and lamed (ל') for Yisrael Beytenu.
Yesh Atid is running this time as part of the new Beyachad alliance led by Naftali Bennett and is expected to register under new letters rather than retain “Peh” (פה). The combination historically associated with Meretz also no longer enjoys the same priority it once had because Meretz failed to enter the Knesset in the previous election. “Emet” (אמת), previously associated with Labor, remains protected through the rights now held by the Democrats.
That leaves only a relatively narrow group of letters currently available: bet (ב'), dalet (ד'), zayin (ז'), yud (י'), nun (נ'), tzadi (צ'), kuf (ק'), final kaf (ך), final peh (ף) and final tzadi (ץ).
On paper, that may sound like a reasonable selection. In practice, some are far more attractive than others. Political parties want a ballot symbol that is short, memorable and easy to repeat in campaign advertising. Within weeks, the chosen letters will appear on posters, television spots, social media and the familiar election-day message: “At the ballot box, vote…”
Bennett, Eisenkot and others need new symbols
The pressure is greatest on the new parties and alliances. Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar, Ofer Winter’s Amcha Yisrael, Bennett’s Beyachad and other new lists must all choose letters or combinations of their own. Otzma Yehudit and Noam also need to settle on ballot designations after running in the previous election as part of the Religious Zionism slate under tet (ט').
Several new parties declined to tell Ynet which letters they are seeking because revealing a preferred letter in advance could allow a rival to register first or try to block its use. In a campaign where several new lists are searching at the same time for something short, recognizable and marketable, even a single letter can become a political asset.
Why getting in line matters
That is where the filing deadline becomes more interesting. Representatives arriving at the Knesset for early registration will receive a number determining their place in line for formally submitting their lists, and that order can matter when two parties want the same letter and neither has an existing legal claim to it.
The principle is straightforward: after the rights of incumbent parties are protected, the list that files first gets priority over an available ballot designation. In other words, arriving earlier can mean getting the better letter.
Early registration opens Sunday at 5 p.m. On Monday, formal submission of party lists will begin at 1 p.m. and continue until 5 p.m. Tuesday is the final day, when parties can begin arriving at 4 p.m. and submit their lists until 10 p.m. Central Elections Committee Chairman Noam Sohlberg may extend the deadline until midnight, the absolute cutoff.
By then, the big political questions will not be limited to who merged with whom or which candidates made the slate. Some parties may also discover that one of their first campaign battles was over something much smaller: a few remaining letters of the Hebrew alphabet.

Explainer: Russia’s Influence Tendrils in Western Academia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:24:00 UTC
21:24:00 KST

For centuries, Western understanding of Ukraine has been shaped by the perspective of the Russian Empire and its successors. Russia’s initial invasion of Ukraine in 2014 led some Western academics and policymakers to reassess long-held assumptions about Ukraine. It also brought greater scrutiny to Western academics who promoted viewpoints preferred by the Kremlin.
Still, Russian influence operations have persisted, attempting to promote narratives that reinforce Russia’s view of the world while diminishing Ukraine’s own. “Things are changing but the focus on Russia, Russian language, literature and culture have been structurally part of Western academia for decades if not centuries and that does not change overnight,” said Serhii Plokhy, a history professor at Harvard University.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ties between Russia and Western academics run deep. Many professors at leading Western universities studied or worked in Russia as part of their academic careers. Some Ukrainian analysts argue that these relationships also created opportunities for recruitment or financial influence. “Some of whom have maintained ties with Russia since the days of the USSR, may have been recruited by Russian intelligence services, or simply receive financial or other incentives from Moscow,” said Serhii Kuzan, chair of the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center.
Russia’s long history of influencing the West
Influencing Western audiences has been a state strategy of Russia’s for decades. In 1984, Soviet defector Yuri Bezmenov, who had worked for the KGB-linked Novosti Press Agency before defecting to the West, publicly claimed that Moscow devoted far more attention to ideological subversion than traditional espionage. Bezmenov described a long-term process of “demoralization,” followed by destabilization and crisis.
Germany Unveils Anti-Sabotage Plan After Leipzig Airport Attack
“At its core is reflexive control, which means feeding an adversary curated information so that he arrives, seemingly of his own free will, at a decision Moscow has already scripted for him,” said Douglas Davis, a physician and geopolitical analyst who works extensively with Ukrainian civil society and defense circles. “The Western academic who independently ‘concludes’ that NATO provoked the war is the intended output of that mechanism.”
These Soviet “active measures” included propaganda and information operations targeting Western academics as potential agents of influence. “The Russian propaganda system began developing during the Soviet era and today uses the entire arsenal of methods honed since then to coerce cooperation, ranging from bribery to blackmail and intimidation,” said retired Ukrainian defense intelligence colonel Vitalii Ostapchuk.
Soviet efforts to shape Western perceptions went back much further. During the Holodomor, meaning “death by hunger” in Ukrainian, millions of Ukrainians starved under Soviet policies of forced collectivization and grain confiscation in 1932-33. Walter Duranty, The New York Times’ Moscow correspondent, downplayed and denied the famine, even as journalists such as Gareth Jones reported mass starvation across Ukraine.
Academic journals and publishers can also play a role. A recent VoxUkraine report found nearly 400 cases between 2022 and 2025 where Russian academic publications distributed by Springer Nature identified occupied Ukrainian territories, including Sevastopol, Simferopol and Donetsk, as part of Russia.
“The Kremlin uses all possible tools, including culture and academia, to promote its narratives,” said Ilona Sologub, editor of the Ukrainian analytical outlet VoxUkraine. She added that there is little pressure from the Western academic community to stop cooperating with Russian academics. “Russian scientists are heavily involved in development of technologies for Russian military production, and on the other level, their presence at conferences and other events legitimizes the aggressor,” she said.
Russian academics who continue to publish in Western journals often try to avoid political debate, even when writing about topics related to the war. “Most often they hide behind the ‘science unrelated to politics’ argument,” said Sologub.
Russia’s influence operations are largely directed from the top, although individual agencies have room to operate independently. “In Russia, the system for conducting influence operations is centralized and managed by members of the Russian president’s inner circle,” Ostapchuk said. “At the same time, the FSB and GRU have opportunities for local initiative within the broader system.”
How Russia builds influence in Western academia
Branislav Slantchev, a political science professor at the University of California, San Diego, said it is important not to view everything as part of a single conspiracy.
“There are several distinct mechanisms at work here, and it is important not to collapse them into a single conspiracy narrative,” said Slantchev. “Some are more direct, including RT, Sputnik, state-funded conferences and covert financing. Others rely on prestige, access, ideological alignment, and institutional incentives.”
Russia has actively attempted to build institutional ties with Western universities. The Kremlin-backed Russkiy Mir Foundation has established Russian centers at universities and educational institutions around the world. This includes providing grants and support for Russian-language and cultural programs. Participation in these programs does not necessarily mean that academics promote Kremlin narratives, but they provide another way for Moscow to build relationships within foreign academic institutions.
For Western academics studying Russia, access can be important. “Scholars who depend on visas, archives, interviews, and fieldwork access in Russia can become vulnerable to subtle forms of pressure and self-censorship,” said Slantchev.
“Notably, Russia in Global Affairs was co-founded with support from RIA Novosti and has Western academics on its editorial board alongside Sergey Lavrov,” Slantchev added. Western academics have participated in Russian conferences, joined advisory boards, received honorary professorships and maintained access to Russian political elites. These relationships, Slantchev said, can create incentives for academics to reproduce narratives that broadly align with Moscow’s view of the world.
One prominent example is the Valdai Discussion Club, which regularly brings together Russian officials and foreign academics and analysts. Slantchev noted that Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly used the forum to present his worldview to an international audience. Over the years, numerous Western academics have participated.
Among them is John Mearsheimer, a famous international relations professor at the University of Chicago, who has argued that the West bears primary responsibility for Russia’s war in Ukraine. For the past four years, Mearsheimer was on record saying that Ukraine’s defeat was imminent. His 2018 book, “The Great Delusion,” received Valdai’s Best Book of the Year Award in 2019. Slantchev added that Mearsheimer later acknowledged in the preface of his 2023 book, “How States Think,” that his research had been supported by “a small grant from the Valdai Discussion Club” that he received in connection with the award.
“Mearsheimer is quoted frequently as an academic in the mass media even though this is not at all the opinion of those who actually study the region,” said Sarah Ann Oates, a political communications professor at the University of Maryland. “The Kremlin can cherry-pick poorly informed, but influential theorists such as Mearsheimer to push their propaganda narratives,” Ann Oates added. Mearsheimer did not respond to my request for comment.
However, Mearsheimer’s views on Ukraine have not always aligned with those promoted by Moscow. In 1993, he argued that Ukraine should retain a nuclear deterrent, warning that Russia could someday attempt to reconquer the country.
Take the case of Stephen Cohen, the late professor of Russian studies at Princeton and New York University. Cohen argued for years that NATO expansion had provoked Russia and placed much of the responsibility for deteriorating relations with Moscow on the West. Following Russia’s first invasion in 2014, Russian state media frequently featured Cohen on channels such as RT, in addition to Jeffrey Sachs, an economist at Columbia University.
For Moscow, the value isn’t necessarily in converting academics or high-profile media figures into supporters of Russia, but in using respected Western voices to validate arguments the Kremlin wants circulating abroad.
Such arguments include NATO and the West causing the Russia-Ukraine war, Russia is too powerful for Ukraine to prevail and must therefore give in to Russian demands, among other arguments presented by the Kremlin. Both Cohen and Sachs were active promoters of such arguments.
How Russian narratives gain credibility
The strategy can be especially effective because a Russian narrative carries more credibility in the West when it comes from a professor at a respected university, such as Columbia or Princeton University. Slantchev described this as “credibility transfer.” Russian narratives can move through conferences, academic journals, think tanks and media appearances before reaching Western audiences through people they are more likely to trust.
However, not everyone who promotes arguments favorable to Moscow has a vested interest in Russia or stands to benefit financially. Some simply share parts of the Kremlin’s worldview. “Some Western intellectuals are deeply disillusioned with the West and therefore sympathetic to actors perceived as challenging American or liberal international dominance,” said Slantchev.
But policing this debate is not an option. “There’s no central body policing this in academia, and there shouldn’t be,” said Seva Gunitsky, a professor of political science at the University of Toronto. “The problem is academic institutions are poorly equipped to distinguish heterodox-but-legitimate scholarship, versus the laundering of narratives that exploit the conventions of academic freedom,” Gunitsky said.
“Those are very different things, but they look similar from the outside, which is what makes the laundering effective.”

Ukraine's Prosecutor General denies involvement in scam call center protection racket

Ukraine's Prosecutor General denies involvement in scam call center protection racket
Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko on Sept. 6 denied any connection to a criminal organization running protection for scam call centers to launder millions of hryvnias, allegedly involving a senior official in Kravchenko's office.
The alleged criminal scheme was uncovered by Ukraine's two chief anti-corruption bodies — Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) — on Sept. 5.
The Prosecutor General's Office later confirmed that searches were conducted in Kravchenko's office as part of the probe.
"I have no involvement whatsoever in covering up illegal call centers, I have not issued any instructions to facilitate such activities, and I have not used the powers of the Prosecutor General for this purpose," Kravchenko wrote on Telegram on Sept. 6.
"Regarding the Prosecutor General's Office employee who is implicated in the investigation, decisions have already been taken. He has been suspended from his duties," Kravchenko wrote.
That employee is understood to be Serhii Kropyva, who NABU detained on Sept. 4, law enforcement sources told the Kyiv Independent. A court is considering restricting his movements as the investigation is ongoing.
According to investigators, the official created the group in mid-2025, recruiting serving prosecutors and associates outside the Prosecutor General's Office.
The group allegedly received systematic bribes in exchange for allowing scam call centers to operate without interference. The call centers targeted both Ukrainian citizens and foreigners, investigators said.
Kravchenko also announced that all staff working on cases involving illegal call centers would now have to undergo polygraph testing.
"No position will protect anyone," he said.
However, Kravchenko himself has been implicated in the plot.
Recordings released by NABU refer to someone identified as the "boss" who protected the group Kropyva is thought to have led, who had the patronymic "Andriiovych," and who previously led the State Tax Service.
Ruslan Andriiovych Kravchenko served as head of Ukraine's State Tax Service from December 2024 to June 2025.
An earlier Telegram post by the Prosecutor General's Office confirms that the investigation understands the term "boss" as referring to Kravchenko.
"During the investigative proceedings, full access was granted to my office and to everything that needed to be inspected. No obstacles were put in the way. I have nothing to hide," Kravchenko said.
The case comes amid a series of high-profile NABU investigations, including probes involving Zelensky's former Deputy Chief of Staff Iryna Mudra and former Chief of Staff Andriy Yermak, as well as the major Energoatom corruption case.
The Prosecutor General heads the overall system of court prosecutions in Ukraine and is appointed directly by the president.
The EU has made it a condition of Ukraine's eventual membership of the bloc that Kyiv "depoliticize the position of the Prosecutor General, including by making the selection and dismissal procedures more objective, transparent, and merit-based, taking into account European standards."
A proposed reform to address that concern was introduced in the parliament, but was shot down by the law enforcement committee on Aug. 19.

Israeli strikes kill four, destroy hospital in southern Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Breadcrumb
Israeli strikes kill four, destroy hospital in southern Lebanon
Israeli strikes across southern Lebanon killed four people and wounded 20 on Sunday, Lebanon’s health ministry said, after the Israeli army issued its first evacuation order in several weeks and claimed it was responding to alleged Hezbollah drone attacks.
Two women were killed in the town of Arab Salim, in Nabatieh district, while two other people were killed in Nabatieh al-Fawqa, the ministry said. The provisional toll included several women and three children among the injured, with casualties also reported in Nabatieh and Kfar Rumman.
At around 6am local time, the Israeli military ordered residents within 300 metres of a building in Arab Salim to leave, describing the site as a Hezbollah "facility" but providing no evidence for the claim.
The warning marked the first such evacuation order issued by Israel in Lebanon in several weeks. Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency (NNA) said Israeli warplanes struck a different house after the warning, destroying it and killing the two women, before subsequently attacking the building named in the Israeli notice.
The health ministry said six people, including two girls, were wounded in Arab Salim. In Nabatieh al-Fawqa, two people were killed and two injured, while further casualties were reported in Nabatieh’s al-Rahibat neighbourhood and in Kfar Rumman.
Israel said it had launched the strikes after Hezbollah fired two drones towards Israeli troops operating in southern Lebanon. It accused the group of a "blatant violation" of the ceasefire framework, although no Israeli casualties were reported.
Civilian infrastructure hit
In Nabatieh al-Fawqa, an Israeli strike destroyed part of the Ghandour hospital, according to NNA. The hospital had been out of service for years, but its destruction added to the devastation of civilian infrastructure in a district repeatedly subjected to Israeli attacks.
NNA also reported that a heavy strike in Nabatieh targeted a historic building and damaged offices used by the Lebanese finance and agriculture authorities, as well as nearby shops and cafes.
Israeli artillery later hit the outskirts of Aitaroun, the forested Jounine area and the Doha area of Kfar Rumman, all in or near Nabatieh district, where Israel has intensified attacks in recent days.
Sunday’s attacks came a day after Israeli strikes killed five people in southern Lebanon including an 18-year-old woman in Mayfadoun.
'Security zone' plans
The escalation coincided with reports that Israel’s military is considering a partial withdrawal from southern Lebanon, reducing the depth of its self-declared security zone from roughly 10km to between three and four kilometres from the border.
Israeli state broadcaster Kan reported that security officials had held internal discussions over creating a narrower zone, reportedly called the "Gray Line", following Israeli operations at the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge. Any redeployment would require political approval, the report said.
Israel claimed this week to have taken "operational control" of the ridge, which overlooks a large area of southeastern Lebanon and lies about 15km from the Israeli border. The military said it had cleared underground Hezbollah routes there, while Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said troops would remain in the security zone until Hezbollah was disarmed.
Lebanese authorities and rights groups have repeatedly condemned Israel’s continued air strikes and ground presence as violations of the ceasefire arrangement.
Israeli strikes have killed more than 4,300 people since Hezbollah entered the regional conflict in response to US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February 2026.

‘This is my home’: Turkish tourists confront Israeli man at Jerusalem’s Jaffa Gate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:13:14 UTC
21:13:14 KST

A brief encounter at Jerusalem’s Jaffa Gate turned confrontational Sunday when two Turkish tourists responded to an Israeli man who had come to greet visitors to the Old City by shouting, “This is my home. You are welcome.”
The exchange was captured on video and quickly drew attention because it came against a broader backdrop of concern in Israel over Turkey’s efforts to deepen its influence in Jerusalem, Gaza and the Palestinian arena.
In July, ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth reported on an official 769-page book published by the Turkish Presidency’s Directorate of Communications titled Our Palestinian Cause. The book portrays Israel as committing “genocide and war crimes,” presents Zionism as the root of the conflict and includes a chapter quoting senior Hamas officials under the heading “The struggle against Israeli oppression.”
A recent report by the Jerusalem Center for Applied Policy, or JCAP, which examined the publication, argued that Turkey’s strategy does not center on direct military confrontation with Israel. Instead, it focuses on diplomatic, legal and public influence.
According to the report, those efforts include promoting legal proceedings against Israel in international courts, applying political pressure and expanding Ankara’s role in Palestinian affairs.
The struggle over Turkish influence is also playing out around the future of Gaza. Turkey is seeking a significant role in shaping the postwar arrangement in the Strip, while Israel opposes the inclusion of Turkish troops in any international force that could eventually operate there.
Against that backdrop, the exchange at Jaffa Gate offered a much more direct expression of the tensions surrounding influence, sovereignty and identity in Jerusalem.
Former Israeli ambassador Ran Yishai, head of research at JCAP, said the incident was not the first in which Turkish tourists had displayed what he described as a false sense of ownership in Jerusalem.
“The incident at Jaffa Gate in Jerusalem, which is not the first of its kind in which Turkish tourists walk around Jerusalem with a false sense of ownership inspired by Erdoğan’s conduct, further illustrates the need to implement the recommendation to deny visas to Turkish tourists entering Israel until relations between the two countries are based on an updated framework,” Yishai said.
He said that framework should begin with Turkey canceling arrest warrants issued against senior Israeli officials and ending its support for legal action against Israel at international courts.
JCAP chairman Haim Silverstein went further, saying Turkish Islamist tourists posed a danger.
“The Islamist tourists from Turkey are dangerous and incited against Israelis,” he said. “This group should be removed immediately from Israeli territory, and the sooner the better.”

New Medium-Term program sees single-digit inflation by 2029
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:11:46 UTC
21:11:46 KST

AA Photo
Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz unveiled Türkiye’s Medium-Term Program (OVP) for 2027-2029 on Sept. 6, outlining updated economic forecasts and policy priorities while projecting that inflation will fall to single digits by 2029.
Speaking at the Presidential Complex in Ankara, Yılmaz said Türkiye had made significant progress in fighting inflation.
“We have made significant progress in combating inflation. Inflation, which rose to 75.5 percent in May 2024, has entered a clear downward trend thanks to the policies we have implemented,” he said.
Yılmaz stated that inflation was expected to resume its decline in the final quarter of 2026 and reach 28.4 percent by year-end.
He also noted that the Central Bank estimated the direct and indirect impact of the war on inflation at around seven percentage points.
“We aim to reduce inflation, which we expect to reach 28.4 percent in 2026, to 21 percent in 2027, 13.5 percent in 2028 and 9 percent in 2029,” Yılmaz said.
Yılmaz also said that Türkiye’s 2026 economic growth forecast was revised down to 3.3 percent from 3.8 percent.
Under the new program, the government forecasts economic growth to accelerate to 4.2 percent in 2027, 4.6 percent in 2028 and 5 percent in 2029.
“By the end of 2028, we expect our national income to exceed $1.8 trillion for the first time and per capita income to surpass $20,000. We expect Türkiye to become the world’s 16th-largest economy and the 11th-largest in terms of purchasing power,” Yılmaz said.
He added that the government aims to raise national income above $2.2 trillion and increase goods and services exports to $450 billion by the end of the program period. According to Yılmaz, per capita income is expected to reach $25,000 by the end of the program.
Expected energy imports for 2026 were revised upward to $71 billion from $63 billion, while tourism revenue projections were lowered to $65 billion from $68 billion, Yılmaz said.
The forecast for the current account deficit-to-GDP ratio at the end of 2026 was revised upward to 2.6 percent from 1.3 percent.
The current account deficit-to-GDP ratio is projected at 1.9 percent for 2027, 1.8 percent for 2028 and 1.6 percent for 2029.
Yılmaz said the government aims to gradually reduce the budget deficit and expects the 2026 deficit to come in at 3.1 percent of GDP, below the previously forecast 3.5 percent.
He added that the government targets reducing the budget deficit-to-GDP ratio to 2.8 percent by the end of the program period.
Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek and Central Bank Governor Fatih Karahan also commented on the newly announced Medium-Term Program.
Şimşek said Türkiye faced serious shocks in 2023 and stressed the importance of reducing vulnerabilities stemming from the current account deficit.
“The improvement has been very substantial when gold is excluded,” he said.
Şimşek also rejected the notion that public-sector savings were being achieved through cuts to investments.
“The perception that public savings are being achieved by cutting investments is not correct,” he said.
He added that public expenditures would increase alongside planned appropriations and that there had been a significant rise in public-sector savings.
Karahan said they did not see any revision in the outlook that would justify pessimism regarding inflation.
“We are seeing positive inflation data in areas that affect monetary policy,” Karahan said.
The Medium-Term Program entered into force after being approved by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and published in the Official Gazette.

Ukraine Confirms First Combat Missions of Swedish ASC 890 Early-Warning Aircraft
Ukraine has begun operational combat use of the Swedish-supplied ASC 890 airborne early warning and control aircraft, adding a long-range surveillance capability designed to detect aerial threats and coordinate fighter operations.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense on September 4, the transfer of the ASC 890 was announced in May 2024 and confirmed in August 2025, with the aircraft’s first combat missions over Ukraine recorded in March 2026.
The ASC 890, also known as the Saab 340 AEW&C, is designed to provide long-range detection and tracking of aircraft, missiles, and other aerial targets while supporting the coordination of combat aviation.
“In combination with the F-16, Mirage 2000 and Gripen, it forms the basis of a modern network-centric air combat system according to NATO standards,” Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said.
Sweden announced the transfer of ASC 890 aircraft to Ukraine in May 2024 as part of what was then its largest military aid package for Kyiv. The aircraft were intended to strengthen Ukraine’s ability to identify targets at extended ranges and improve coordination between its air assets.
The ASC 890 is equipped with the Erieye airborne radar system, which provides significantly greater detection ranges against low-flying targets than ground-based radar stations because of the aircraft’s elevated operating position.
Ukraine’s F-16 fighters have also undergone modifications enabling them to interact with the Swedish airborne early-warning aircraft, allowing information gathered by the ASC 890 to be integrated with Ukraine’s fighter operations.
Earlier, Ukraine and Sweden signed a declaration of intent covering the potential acquisition of 100–150 JAS 39 Gripen E/F fighter jets, with localized production in Ukraine considered as part of the long-term procurement plan.

Poland scrambles aircraft over suspected airspace breach
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
13:09:40 BST
21:09:40 KST

Polish Operational Command has dispatched a military helicopter to verify a suspected violation of Polish airspace by an unidentified object approaching from the direction of Belarus, the command stated on Friday.
Announcing the activity, the Operational Command of the Armed Forces Branches said the work is being conducted through the Air Operations Centre and Air Component Command, and involves checking radar system records covering the area.
It said: “Due to suspicion of a violation of the airspace of the Republic of Poland by an unidentified object approaching from the direction of Belarus, the Operational Command of the Armed Forces Branches, through the Air Operations Centre and Air Component Command, is conducting verification activities. As part of the verification of radar system records in the area, a military helicopter has been dispatched.”
The command was careful to set out what it does not yet know. It said: “The ongoing actions aim to confirm the nature of the registered object and rule out, among other possibilities, that the registered signal was the result of meteorological phenomena or anomalies.”
It added that no activity by Russian long-range aviation connected to strikes on targets in Ukraine had been observed in recent hours, that the situation is being continuously monitored, and that further information will follow once verification is complete and the details of the incident confirmed.
The reference to weather is not a throwaway line, though, as Radar returns can be generated by temperature inversions, precipitation, flocks of birds and a range of atmospheric conditions, and a command that scrambles aircraft every time a return appears will exhaust its crews and its credibility in short order.
A great many of the airspace incidents Poland has dealt with over the past three years have occurred during Russian strike packages against western Ukraine, when Polish and allied aircraft are launched as a precaution and objects periodically stray across the border. The absence of that activity means whatever was registered is unlikely to be a strayed cruise missile or a drone drifting off course from an ongoing attack.
Poland has repeatedly scrambled aircraft in response to Russian strikes on Ukraine, and objects have crossed into Polish territory on several occasions, including a missile that killed two people at Przewodów in November 2022, which was subsequently assessed as a Ukrainian air defence round.
The direction of approach carries its own significance of couyrse as Belarus hosts Russian forces and has been the origin of a range of hybrid activity directed at Poland, including the sustained pressure on the border through organised migration since 2021, and Polish forces maintain a substantial presence along that frontier.
