Labor urges Greens, Coalition to pass social media reforms after 'dawdling and delay'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:09:31 UTC
21:09:31 KST

IN BRIEF
- Labor is urging the Senate to back reforms aimed at strengthening enforcement of the under-16 social media ban.
- The government is also set to unveil draft reforms mandating the ability to opt out of social media algorithms.
Labor is urging the Greens and Coalition to pass laws that would strengthen the eSafety Commissioner's powers to gather information from social media companies and increase fines tech giants face for breaches of the teen social media ban.
When Labor introduced the bill in late June, Communications Minister Anika Wells said an eSafety investigation had suggested several major social media companies were exploiting loopholes in the law.
"The commissioner has found these companies adopting a number of dirty tricks to undermine Australia's law that are straight out of the big-tech playbook," Wells said at the time.
"It is clear ... that social media companies are deliberately failing to comply with our laws."
The bill would give the eSafety Commissioner enhanced information-gathering powers that Labor argues are necessary to ensure social media companies take 'reasonable steps' to prevent under-16s from creating or retaining social media accounts, as required under the ban.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
In March-April, the eSafety Commissioner found 81.5 per cent of 10-15-year-olds were still using at least one age-restricted platform, a small decline from the 85.9 per cent it found before the ban came into effect on 10 December 2025.
However, the government has reported that more than five million social media accounts belonging to under-16s have been deleted, deactivated or restricted since the ban came into effect.
Meta — the parent company of Facebook and Instagram — said in mid-August that it had taken down more than 750,000 accounts and said those numbers would "continue to grow".
"We share the Australian government's goal of ensuring young people have safe, age-appropriate experiences online, and we are meeting our obligations under the law," the company added in a statement released at the time.
'Put politics to the side'
In early July, Greens and Coalition senators voted to send Labor's bill to a Senate inquiry, which eight weeks later recommended the reforms be adopted.
Wells said on Sunday that the decision to send the bill to an inquiry was "the kind of dawdling and delay that has enabled social media companies to get away with harming our kids for so long".
"We have to put politics to the side and pass this bill this week, so the eSafety Commissioner can hold social media companies accountable," she said.
When voting to refer the bill to the inquiry, Liberal Senator Sarah Henderson accused Labor of trying to "ram through" the new powers without proper scrutiny.
"Rather than Anika Wells' mad scramble to fix her broken ban, much more needs to be done to protect children online," she said.
The Greens also said Labor needed to go further.
"We need to urgently regulate algorithms, and make it clear that social media companies are responsible for the extreme harm their platforms perpetrate," the left-wing party said in its additional comments to the inquiry report.
'Digital duty of care' reforms
The regulation of social media algorithms is an issue that will soon come to the fore in Canberra, with Labor set to release details of proposed laws that would force tech giants to give users the ability to opt out of algorithms.
An exposure draft of the so-called 'digital duty of care' reforms is expected to be released in the coming sitting fortnight.
It would put the onus on social media companies to mitigate risk on their platforms, including actively removing illegal or harmful content.
The option to opt out of algorithms would be mandatory, giving users the choice to take their social media feeds back to the friends-only content they once were.
Several areas are expected to be identified as off-limits to minors due to the potential for psychological harm, including content that promoted harmful body image.
The changes would prevent boys from being bombarded with violent and misogynistic material, Labor's Matt Thistlethwaite told News24's Sunday Agenda program.
"Many Australian parents have said that they're concerned about their children being exposed to this material," he said.
"We think that the platforms have a responsibility to try and keep young Australian kids safe.
Greens call for larger fines
However, the measures could struggle to pass the Senate in their current form, with Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young saying proposed fines of up to $100 million for breaching the laws were insufficient.
Hanson-Young told reporters that tech companies would see such fines as part of the cost of doing business, and called for penalties to be calculated based on each firm's global profits.
"The power of big tech is so immense and you can't take them on and hit them at their business model with half-baked measures," she said.
"The government's really going to have to toughen up.
"Either take on big tech properly, or you'll end up putting in place a scheme that really does bugger all."
The Greens are awaiting details of the exposure draft before deciding how to vote, while Senator Hanson-Young has proposed her own bill, calling for an algorithm opt-out to be the default setting.
That measure has been the focus of a campaign by Teach Us Consent's Fix Our Feeds, which has been pushing for linear social media feeds to be the default option.
In a linear social media feed, content would appear in chronological order, with users only seeing posts from people or accounts they have chosen to follow.
The organisation's founder, Chanel Contos, recently said an algorithm opt-out was a good first step, but the measure did not go far enough to stop boys and young men being exposed to harmful content.
"It would fundamentally make the transition onto social media for 16-year-olds and other children safer, and it would bring the principle of affirmative consent to our screens," she told the National Press Club in early September.
Coalition says govt should focus on fixing ban
The Opposition is also yet to establish its position on the proposal, but leader Angus Taylor on Sunday expressed doubts about Labor's plan.
He said parents should have more control over what their children could see on social media, but he was "deeply sceptical" that the proposal wasn't an attempt to censor people's feeds.
Taylor accused Labor of butchering the already implemented under-16s social media ban, which the Coalition supported, adding the government should focus on fixing that policy.
"The government should be focused on that because it's not working," he said.
"So then going off and starting on some other thing ... there's good reason to be sceptical about that."

What does the law say about inheritance? Know your rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:08:42 UTC
21:08:42 KST

What does the law say about inheritance? Know your rights
Natasha Singh / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Sep 06, 2026, 17:38 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
What can a daughter, wife, widow or mother legally claim?
For generations, inheritance in India has been shaped by family relationships, religious personal laws and the nature of the property being inherited.A daughter may have an equal right with her brother in one situation, but not necessarily in another. A widow may be entitled to a share in her husband's estate, while a woman may also own property in her own right through inheritance, gifts or other means.The biggest question often arises when a person dies without leaving a will. In such cases, known as intestate succession, the applicable law determines who inherits and in what proportion. The rules differ across religious communities.The Hindu Succession Act, 1956, governs succession among Hindus and also applies to Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs, subject to its provisions. Muslims are generally governed by Muslim personal law on intestate succession, while Christians and Parsis are principally covered by the Indian Succession Act, 1925.So what can a woman legally claim?
Inheritance rights
Hindu women: Daughter has equal coparcenary rights
One of the biggest changes in women's inheritance rights came with the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, which made a daughter a coparcener by birth in a Hindu joint family governed by Mitakshara law, with the same rights and liabilities as a son.
The Supreme Court's 2020 judgment in Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma clarified that this right is by birth and does not depend on the father being alive when the 2005 amendment came into force.Marriage also does not take away a daughter's coparcenary rights.But an important distinction must be made between coparcenary property and a parent's self-acquired property.If a Hindu father dies intestate leaving behind his wife, son and daughter and the property is his self-acquired property, all children and the widow are Class I heirs. In a simple example involving Rs 1 crore, the wife, son and daughter would each receive about Rs 33.33 lakh.Advocate Rupali Jain explains why the calculation can be very different for coparcenary property. If the Rs 1 crore is Mitakshara coparcenary property, the father's notional share is first calculated. His share is then distributed among the relevant Class I heirs.On that calculation, Jain says, "wife receives about Rs 11.11 lakh and each child Rs 44.44 lakh."The example highlights an important point: a daughter is not automatically entitled to "half" the property simply because she is a daughter. The nature of the property must first be established.Another common misconception is that every property owned by a parent is ancestral property in which children have a birthright. That is not necessarily so.
Muslim women: Share depends on the family structure
Muslim inheritance in India operates under Muslim personal law, which does not follow the same joint-family property model.Islamic inheritance rules identify different categories of heirs and prescribe shares depending on which relatives survive the deceased. The applicable school of Muslim law can also matter.The daughter will generally receive half the son's share but the actual calculation depends on all the surviving heirs.A widow's share also depends on whether the deceased leaves descendants. Broadly, under commonly applied Sunni rules, a widow receives one-eighth where there are children or certain descendants and one-fourth where there are none."The share of a Muslim woman therefore has to be calculated based on the complete family structure," said advocate Pritish Sunil Teckchandani.Muslim testamentary succession is also different. Generally, a Muslim's power to make a will is restricted to one-third of the estate without the consent of the heirs, subject to applicable personal-law rules.
Christian women: Sons and daughters inherit equally
For Christians, intestate succession is primarily governed by the Indian Succession Act, 1925.Where a Christian man dies without a will leaving a widow and children, the widow receives one-third of the estate, while the remaining two-thirds goes equally to the children.For example, if a Christian man dies leaving a wife, one son and one daughter and an estate worth Rs 90 lakh, each would ordinarily receive Rs 30 lakh. "The widow and each child would ordinarily receive one-third each," said Teckchandani.The position changes depending on which relatives survive the deceased, but there is no distinction between sons and daughters in the straightforward situation described above.Unlike Hindu law, Christian succession has no equivalent concept of coparcenary rights by birth. A Christian daughter does not become a co-owner of her father's property merely because she is his daughter; her inheritance generally arises upon succession.
Parsi women: Daughter does not lose out to son
Parsi intestate succession is governed by special provisions in Part V of the Indian Succession Act. The exact entitlement depends on the relatives who survive the deceased.Thus, where a Parsi man dies intestate leaving a widow, son and daughter, the son and daughter inherit on an equal footing under the applicable rules.The calculation can change where there are more children, a predeceased child, grandchildren or other specified relatives.
What happens when there is no will
When a person dies without a valid will, the property does not automatically go to the eldest son or the closest male relative. The applicable succession law determines who inherits.For Hindus, the Hindu Succession Act lays down a hierarchy of heirs. A widow, son, daughter and mother are among the Class I heirs of a Hindu man who dies intestate.For Muslims, inheritance is calculated under applicable Muslim personal-law rules rather than a Class I heir system.For Christians and Parsis, the relevant provisions of the Indian Succession Act apply.This is why there is no single formula for a woman's inheritance in India. Her share can depend on her religion, relationship to the deceased, the relatives who survive, the nature of the property and whether there is a valid will.
Inheritance rights of women in India.
What if there is a will — but the daughter gets nothing
“For self-acquired property, a Hindu father can generally leave the entire property to his son and exclude his daughter through a valid Will. A daughter has no compulsory share in such property merely by virtue of being his daughter,” said Tekchandani.This is where the nature of the property becomes particularly important.A person can generally make a will determining how property that they legally own and can dispose of should be distributed. Therefore, a Hindu father can ordinarily leave his entire self-acquired property to his son and exclude his daughter."The daughter has no compulsory share in such property merely by virtue of being his daughter," said Teckchandani.But a will cannot simply wipe out another person's existing coparcenary interest. A daughter who already has a coparceny share cannot be deprived of that existing interest merely through her father's will."An unfair will is not necessarily an invalid will," explained Teckchandani. However, a woman can challenge a will if there are grounds to question its validity. These can include forgery, lack of testamentary capacity, coercion, undue influence, improper execution or other suspicious circumstances.Jain said courts may examine factors such as whether the testator was elderly, ill or dependent on the beneficiary, whether the beneficiary isolated the testator from other family members, whether there was a sudden departure from an earlier will, or whether the beneficiary was involved in preparing or executing the document."The person alleging coercion must produce credible evidence; mere suspicion or the fact that one child received substantially more property is generally insufficient," said Jain.Medical records, previous wills, messages, bank documents and testimony from doctors, neighbours, lawyers and attesting witnesses may become important evidence.
Legal steps to challenge a will
How can one challenge an unfair will
The first step is to establish what the will says and what property it covers.A woman challenging a will should obtain the will, death certificate and relevant property documents. If probate or letters of administration proceedings are pending, she can enter the proceedings and raise objections."If probate proceedings are filed, enter appearance/file objections or a caveat, after which the proceeding becomes contentious," explained Jain.If no such proceedings are pending, the appropriate civil remedy will depend on the circumstances.The court can examine whether the will was properly executed and attested, whether the deceased had testamentary capacity and whether there was fraud, coercion, undue influence or another circumstance affecting its validity.
What if a woman is denied her share in property
The first step is to establish the property's ownership and character. Sale deeds, title documents, mutation records, partition deeds, gift or settlement deeds, wills and other records can help determine what a woman is actually entitled to.Depending on the dispute, a woman may approach a civil court seeking remedies such as partition and separate possession, declaration of rights, cancellation of an invalid document or an injunction.One of the biggest risks comes when family members ask a daughter to sign a release deed, relinquishment deed, family settlement, partition document or NOC without fully understanding its consequences."The biggest mistake is giving up legal rights informally in the name of maintaining family relations, without understanding the property's character or documenting the settlement," said Jain.A woman should determine whether the property is self-acquired, inherited or coparcenary, establish her legal share and obtain independent advice before signing away any interest.
What if the family says she has already given up her share
A daughter may be told that she has no claim because she is married, that her brother "needs the property", or that her share was already given to her through wedding expenses or stridhan.Whether a woman has actually relinquished a property right depends on the applicable law and whether there is a legally valid document or transaction establishing that relinquishment."Family pressure can make people sign documents simply to avoid conflict, but such documents can have significant and sometimes irreversible consequences," said Teckchandani. A verbal family understanding and a legally valid relinquishment or settlement document are not necessarily the same thing.
So, what is a woman’s share in family property
Well, there is no single answer to this question.For a Hindu woman, a daughter can have equal coparcenary rights with a son, while inheritance of self-acquired property after an intestate death follows a different calculation.For a Muslim woman, the share depends on the applicable personal law and the complete family structure. For Christian and Parsi women, succession is principally governed by the Indian Succession Act, with sons and daughters generally treated equally in the relevant intestate situations.A will can also change the outcome, particularly when it concerns property that the testator was free to dispose of. But a will that is unequal is not automatically invalid, nor can it simply extinguish an existing legal interest such as a coparcenary share.
For women facing an inheritance dispute, the key questions are therefore: What personal law applies? Who survived the deceased? What kind of property is involved? Was there a valid will? Was the property already transferred or partitioned? And has the woman actually and legally relinquished her share?Knowing the answers to those questions is often the difference between walking away from property and successfully asserting a legal claim.

Israeli forces dismantle Hamas cell during raid in West Bank’s Akraba area
Israeli authorities say the group was planning attacks against civilians, while troops also uncovered an M16 rifle and explosives
Israeli security forces arrested 10 members of a Hamas cell and located a rocket and a cache of weapons during an operation in the Akraba area of the West Bank, Israeli authorities said Sunday.
The operation was conducted jointly by the Israel Defense Forces, the Israel Security Agency, known as the Shin Bet, and Yamam, the Israeli police’s national counterterrorism unit, according to a joint statement issued by the IDF and the security agency.
Israeli authorities described the detainees as members of a Hamas cell that had been working to prepare attacks against Israeli civilians.
During searches in the area, security forces found a rocket without a launcher, the statement said. The rocket was dismantled at the scene.
Israeli authorities said that questioning of one of the detainees subsequently led forces to a concealed weapons cache. The cache contained an M16 rifle and a large quantity of explosives that were allegedly intended for the production of explosive devices.
The rifle and explosive materials were also dismantled at the site, according to the statement. Authorities did not say whether the rocket was operational or provide information about where it was manufactured.
The Israeli military and security agency said operations against suspected armed groups would continue across the West Bank as part of efforts to prevent attacks and protect Israeli civilians and residents of the area.

View from Russia: Experts on why Kushner and Witkoff came to Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:04:02 UTC
21:04:02 KST

View from Russia: Experts on why Kushner and Witkoff came to Moscow
The latest visit to Moscow by Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff has triggered a fresh wave of speculation in Russia about what Washington is really trying to achieve.
With US President Donald Trump under pressure at home and much of his administration’s foreign-policy bandwidth consumed by Iran, the trip has been interpreted less as a breakthrough mission than as a signal – one that may be aimed as much at domestic American politics and alliance management as at Russia itself.
Russian analysts see the visit in different ways. Some believe the Americans are simply sounding out Moscow before returning to Kiev, trying to gauge whether any space remains for movement on Ukraine. Others argue the mission is part of a broader performance of diplomatic activity by the Trump White House, intended to project momentum where little real progress is possible. Still others view it as an exercise in ‘shuttle diplomacy’, useful mainly for information-gathering and atmospherics rather than for producing concrete results.
Roman Romanov, American studies specialist, lecturer at the Faculty of International Relations, Political Science, and Foreign Regional Studies at RSUH
I have two explanations regarding the visit and the format of this visit. First, the American side has already shown several times that it is interested in maintaining dialogue with both Moscow and Kiev. And this visit – or rather, this tour – is aimed at “synchronizing watches.” What does that mean? The Americans are trying to understand what conditions might be acceptable to the parties for resuming an active negotiating process. In other words, what can be offered to both sides so that they are prepared to move the dialogue in the direction of progress.
The second explanation is purely domestic-political for the United States. Against the backdrop of the failure of the Iran campaign, it is necessary to demonstrate some other kind of political activity that at least theoretically resembles progress with a concrete result. Trump has done this kind of thing more than once.
Do they have any ready-made proposals? I do not think so, because, first, at the moment a significant part of US foreign-policy resources is concentrated on Iran, and second, because despite the constructive role of both Witkoff and Kushner, they still act more as envoys of the American president on a specific issue than as direct participants formulating the American president’s position on this issue.
It is difficult to explain why they first went to Moscow and then to Kiev. One can assume they first want to hear Moscow’s stance, because it is in a more advantageous position – Russia is advancing, winning on the battlefield – so the US believes it would be more expedient first to hear out Moscow’s demands and gauge how much they’ve changed since August 2025, since the meeting in Anchorage.
At the same time, although we do not observe public participation by the EU, through closed channels the European Union surely communicates its interests. Their representatives are not there, but the position the Americans are shaping includes the EU’s position as well.
Dmitry Dtobnitsky – Russian political scientist specializing in American studies, expert in US foreign and domestic policy
These negotiations will continue – that’s the only perspective they have. What are we negotiating with the US about? About how to stop the conflict in Ukraine? Let’s be serious. First, this conflict is much broader than Russia’s military operation. It is a geopolitical conflict with very high stakes, the kind that happens with Europe once every several decades or even centuries. The Cold War period with the US was still an exception in that there were at least attempts to play at détente from time to time.
The world has entered an era of major transformation. In that sense, the narrow focus is – will they reach an agreement on Ukraine? No. Every time you think about that, you have to recall how it all started, why it is like this, how wrongly the world is structured, how important it is for Russia to insist on its interests, why the European bureaucracy itself cannot accept that, because otherwise that would mean the end of both it and the political class of many countries. Why can’t this conflict stop? Because it can’t be settled. Someone has to win. Just as with the US and Iran (which, incidentally, is a much more local conflict) – it is impossible to agree, there can be no deal. There can only be some movement in which one of the sides explicitly or implicitly recognizes its defeat. It may not be total defeat, but at least at some stage one side wins and the other side does not recognize it. Such a process will last a long time, but in the end there will still be some de facto consolidation of the results of this conflict. Not a negotiated one, unfortunately, but a factual one. Diplomats may formalize such a conclusion, or they may not. Frankly, that is no longer important.
When we talk about Russia-US negotiations on Ukraine, there are two extremes, and both miss the essence. Yes, we are negotiating, and we constantly demonstrate that Russia and the US have nothing to fight over. We are ready to coexist with the US on the same globe. That is exactly why Putin says: “Of course, Kushner and Witkoff are welcome guests, come. What else should we show you from Moscow’s kitchen?” You see, the US cannot conduct negotiations on Ukraine because it cannot force either Kiev, London, or Brussels to accept Russia’s reasonable demands. And how are they going to pressure Russia? I think the Trump administration more or less understands that it is pointless. So what kind of negotiations on Ukraine can there be?
Some say [Russian Finance Minister] Siluanov and [US Treasury Secretary] Bessent will come to some understanding, and perhaps there will be incredible financial, economic, or investment cooperation between the US and Russia. I have said many times that there can be no serious cooperation between Russia and the US. There are neither material nor geopolitical grounds for it. Are we now supposed to throw away all the achievements of localizing our civilian aviation industry and start buying Boeing again? Are we going to hand over half of the most convenient Arctic territory on the planet to the US? Is that it? Or are we going to sell all Russian oil through Mr. Kushner? How do you imagine that? Some say: “Investments will come here.” But that would mean that instead of creating a sovereign financial system, we would say: “No, let’s reintegrate ourselves back into the collapsing dollar system. Let’s support it with our achievements of the past five years.” It’s obvious that there can be no real cooperation.
One can have symbolic cooperation. It is a wonderful look when two great countries can do something together. The most we will get is a hockey match and an ‘Apollo-Soyuz’. It must be understood that these are purely token steps, which only demonstrate that nothing particularly substantial can happen. It does not mean it will be forbidden. It simply will never play a substantial role. Even in 2019, before Covid and the military operation, trade turnover between Russia and the US was negligibly small. And that is understandable: it is geopolitics, geoeconomics – you cannot jump over that. And now, after so much effort has been spent to become independent and to work with Eurasia on a new basis, to say, “No, now let’s start doing something again with the Americans” is just laughable. That will not happen.
Andrey Manoylo, doctor of Political Sciences, professor at Moscow State University, head of the Department of Information and Hybrid Wars at APN Alter
Why did Kushner and Witkoff fly to Moscow for the sixth time? It’s both simple and complicated at the same time. Kirill Dmitriev, being one of the corners of the ‘Anchorage triangle’ (a configuration of three equidistant centers of power – [Foreign Minister] Sergey Lavrov, [Kremlin aide] Yury Ushakov, Dmitriev), is a red rag both for Ushakov, the “social architect” of Anchorage, and for the more skeptically minded Sergey Lavrov. Especially given his ability to remain in the media spotlight.
That is precisely why the visit of Witkoff and Kushner – direct competitors of the ‘triangle’s’ hardline diplomacy – may have been planned as a simple diversion: to annoy those with whom [CIA chief] John Ratcliffe had contacts in Moscow. To show that the ball is now in Dmitriev’s court.
In all seriousness, though, Witkoff and Kushner did not bring anything strategic to Moscow. Their direct and, most likely, only task is to gather feedback from Ratcliffe’s visit.
Dmitriev is a gifted figure, but he is not an intelligence officer with an innate poker face, nor is he a career diplomat. Dmitriev is a living person, he is talkative, and “a chatterbox is a godsend for a spy.” I am convinced these two are flying in with an intelligence questionnaire. They will extract all the information from Dmitriev – what people are talking about in the president’s circle, rumors, gossip, among which there will also be leaks of genuinely secret information.
Ratcliffe made a lot of noise. His visit is still agitating minds; some see in him almost a messenger of the Apocalypse. It is no coincidence that people immediately started talking about mobilization – which in reality is “utter nonsense” (as our president said), about some secret Security Council meetings right in the middle of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit, and even about war with Norway. It is obvious that Ratcliffe stirred something up, and the American duo came to find out how ready that brew is. They have no other tasks.
And one more important point. What Witkoff and Kushner are doing now with Dmitriev is the well-known practice of ‘shuttle diplomacy’. We know it from the events preceding the collapse of the Soviet Union. The author of the term was Henry Kissinger, who once bought Mikhail Gorbachev’s trust by saying: “Gorby, while you and I are trying to break the ice of hatred, our foreign ministries with their slowness are ruining everything – they are slowing down the reset of our relations. Let’s push them aside and solve things directly. We are not stupider than our subordinates, are we?” Gorbachev happily agreed, realizing that by removing the Foreign Ministry from the talks, he was ridding himself of criticism – no one would contradict him. But practice showed that the Foreign Ministry was the very mechanism that protected against hasty decisions, even if they seemed correct and the only possible ones. Gorbachev lost, and together with him the entire Soviet Union lost.
And this is not the only case that confirms the rule: however attractive ‘shuttle diplomacy’ may look, it always leads to defeat, and defeat leads to catastrophe. Having such rich historical experience and so many examples, we still continue enthusiastically to play at ‘shuttle diplomacy’ with Kushner and Witkoff. Why? That’s a good question.
Gevorg Mirzayan, specialist in American studies
The US began sending signals about its readiness for dialogue after Russia sharply intensified its retaliatory strikes on Ukraine and put the Kiev regime before the inevitable catastrophe of the coming winter. It is possible the Americans will ask us to stop, and then Trump could show voters, before the congressional elections, a nice picture of his successful peacekeeping mission.
The meeting between Bessent and Siluanov at the G20 summit also fits into this scheme – no serious issues were raised there; the important thing was to demonstrate the positive attitude of the US administration toward bilateral interaction.
Well, we are ready for peace in Ukraine, but only on our own terms – and those terms are unchanged and well known to Washington.
Yegor Tropov, political scientist specializing in American studies
The latest visit by the American negotiating delegation is primarily a symbolic step toward restoring dialogue and laying the groundwork for the future development of relations between Russia and the United States. In the four-sided diplomatic process, it is the American side that is most interested in the quickest possible signing of a peace document – though one that is more formal and declarative than a genuine and lasting peace.
For the sake of media image and his political role as the chief mediator, Donald Trump is ready to conduct numerous negotiations that verbally move towards peace, whereas in reality what leads to peace is only the lack of political will, finances, and weapons on the part of Europe and Ukraine to continue resisting – resources they still have enough of for years to come.
At the same time, one should not underestimate the importance of symbolism in the art of diplomacy: interstate communication, the establishment and strengthening of professional and personal relationships can play a much more significant role in the future – under conditions of a full-scale warming of interstate relations and the resumption of full-fledged economic and political cooperation.

Rising loneliness among US veterans is closely tied to psychiatric burden and suicide risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:00:21 UTC
21:00:21 KST

New research indicates that loneliness is a widespread and worsening issue among United States military veterans, with more than one in five reporting frequent feelings of isolation. The study, published in J Clin Psychiatry, provides evidence that higher levels of loneliness are strongly linked to increased risks of psychiatric disorders and suicidal thoughts. These findings suggest that addressing social disconnection could be an important target for improving veteran mental health and preventing suicide.
The research was led by Robert H. Pietrzak, a professor of psychiatry at the Yale School of Medicine and professor of public health at the Yale School of Public Health. He and his team aimed to update our understanding of how social disconnection affects former military personnel. Loneliness is generally defined as the subjective feeling of being left out, isolated, or lacking in companionship. It is not just about being physically alone, but rather experiencing a painful gap between the social connections a person wants and the ones they actually have.
“Loneliness was already highly prevalent among U.S. veterans in 2019–2020, but the demographic composition of the veteran population and broader social environment have changed since then, particularly following the COVID-19 pandemic,” Pietrzak told PsyPost. “We wanted to provide updated national estimates of the prevalence of loneliness and determine whether it is independently associated with psychiatric disorders and suicide-related outcomes after accounting for a broad range of sociodemographic, military, trauma, health, and social factors.”
Data from 2019 and 2020 showed that more than half of U.S. veterans experienced at least moderate loneliness, with nearly one in five feeling lonely on a frequent basis. Since then, the social landscape has shifted considerably. The researchers noted that the veteran population has been changing, with an increasing proportion of younger, female, and racially diverse individuals transitioning out of the military. This demographic shift is an important detail, as a study covered by PsyPost in 2015 found that younger generations of military personnel tend to experience lower levels of social integration, making them more vulnerable to mental health struggles and suicide.
In addition to these demographic changes, the lingering social effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and broader societal stressors may have worsened feelings of isolation. Because loneliness often co-occurs with serious mental health conditions, the researchers wanted to explore exactly how current levels of loneliness correspond to specific psychiatric burdens. For instance, research covered by PsyPost in 2018 highlighted that veterans battling both post-traumatic stress disorder, or PTSD, and depression face an exceptionally high risk of suicidal thoughts. Pietrzak and his team sought to determine if loneliness was acting as a similar, widespread risk factor that spans multiple psychiatric conditions.
To investigate these trends, the researchers analyzed data from the National Health and Resilience in Veterans Study. This nationally representative survey gathered responses from 2,612 U.S. veterans between December 2025 and January 2026. The participants were drawn from a large, probability-based panel designed to reflect the broader U.S. household population. By weighting the data, the researchers ensured their findings could be generalized to the entire population of living U.S. veterans.
The survey measured loneliness using a standard three-item questionnaire. Participants were asked how often they felt left out, how often they felt isolated from others, and how often they felt they lacked companionship. Based on their responses, the veterans were placed into one of three categories: hardly ever lonely, moderate loneliness, or frequent loneliness. The researchers also collected data on a variety of mental health indicators, including symptoms of major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, PTSD, alcohol and drug use disorders, and various measures of suicidal thoughts and behaviors.
The results indicated that loneliness is highly prevalent among veterans. Overall, 58.7% of the respondents reported experiencing at least moderate loneliness. When broken down further, 36.3% fell into the moderate loneliness category, while 22.4% reported frequent loneliness. When compared to the estimates from 2019 and 2020, the prevalence of moderate loneliness remained relatively stable. However, the rate of frequent loneliness increased from 19.7% to 22.4%. The researchers estimate that this percentage increase translates to roughly 460,000 additional veterans experiencing frequent loneliness across the country.
“Loneliness is not simply an unpleasant feeling—it is a major public health concern,” Pietrzak explained. “Prior work has found that chronic loneliness is associated with an increased risk of premature mortality comparable to the risk associated with smoking as many as 15 cigarettes per day.”
The study also provides evidence of a strong relationship between the severity of loneliness and mental health struggles. Veterans in the moderate loneliness group had notably higher odds of meeting the screening criteria for depression, anxiety, PTSD, hazardous alcohol use, and suicidal thoughts over the past year, compared to those who were hardly ever lonely.
For veterans experiencing frequent loneliness, the psychiatric burden was even heavier. Compared to the hardly ever lonely group, frequently lonely veterans were much more likely to screen positive for six of the eight mental health measures assessed, excluding only drug use disorders and lifetime suicide attempts. The differences were stark when looking at suicidal ideation. Only 3.8% of veterans who were hardly ever lonely reported having suicidal thoughts in the past year. That figure jumped to 14.8% for moderately lonely veterans, and soared to 32.3% for those experiencing frequent loneliness.
When the researchers compared the frequently lonely group directly to the moderately lonely group, the risks were still elevated. Frequently lonely veterans showed much higher odds of facing almost all the measured mental health challenges, with particularly high associations for depression and future suicidal intent. These associations held up even after the researchers accounted for other potential influencing factors, such as age, sex, income, combat experience, physical health conditions, and history of childhood trauma.
“The magnitude of the associations among frequently lonely veterans was particularly striking,” Pietrzak noted. “Even after extensive adjustment for sociodemographic, military, trauma, health, and social factors, frequently lonely veterans had 32 times the odds of screening positive for depression compared with veterans who were hardly ever lonely; they also had substantially greater odds of having attempted suicide relative to less lonely veterans.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study relied on self-reported survey data, which means the results depend on the participants’ willingness and ability to accurately describe their feelings and symptoms. Additionally, the researchers used a cross-sectional design, capturing a snapshot of the veterans’ experiences at a single point in time. Because of this, the study cannot determine the direction of the relationship between loneliness and mental health.
“Because the study was cross-sectional, it cannot establish that loneliness causes psychiatric disorders or suicidality; these associations are likely bidirectional and mutually reinforcing,” Pietrzak explained. “The findings also should not be interpreted to mean that every lonely veteran has a mental disorder or is suicidal, but rather that loneliness may be an important marker of elevated vulnerability that warrants further assessment and support.”
There is also a possibility that by statistically adjusting for certain psychiatric conditions, the researchers might have understated the direct relationship between loneliness and suicide-related outcomes. Despite these limitations, the findings indicate that loneliness is a growing issue that requires ongoing attention from mental health professionals.
“An important next step is to use longitudinal data to clarify how loneliness and mental health measures influence one another over time and to identify veterans at greatest risk for persistent or worsening loneliness,” Pietrzak told PsyPost.
The researchers suggest that loneliness represents a key target for future prevention and treatment efforts. Because social isolation is something that can be modified, initiatives like peer support programs, community engagement activities, and social prescribing, where healthcare providers connect patients with community groups and social activities, could play a major role in improving veteran well-being. By focusing on helping veterans build stronger social connections, health systems might be able to reduce the broader psychiatric burden and lower the risk of suicide.
“Loneliness is modifiable, which makes these findings concerning but also actionable,” Pietrzak said. “Routine assessment of loneliness, followed by efforts to connect veterans with appropriate clinical, peer, and community resources, may provide an additional avenue for improving mental health and strengthening suicide-prevention efforts.”
The study, “A Growing Epidemic of Loneliness Among US Military Veterans: National Trends, Psychiatric Burden, and Suicide Risk,” was authored by Robert H. Pietrzak, Ian C. Fischer, and Peter J. Na.

How to make the perfect Sri Lankan chicken curry – recipe | Felicity Cloake's How to make the perfect …
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

“Every family in our sunny little island craves this creamy chicken,” says Sri Lankan journalist Zinara Rathnayake, “devouring each morsel with carbs of choice: string hoppers, thin rice noodle mats; hoppers, bowl-shaped pancakes; and kiribath, slender rice cooked with coconut milk. All our family recipes may slightly vary, but this glorious dish pins down the labour and love that goes into every Sri Lankan curry.”
After all, Sri Lanka is a country that’s “rich in spices”, chef Peter Kuruvita explains. “Most Sri Lankan cooking,” he writes in Lands of the Curry Leaf, “features unapologetically punch-you-in-the-face, get-the-adrenaline-pumping flavours. But [in part thanks to tropical crops such as coconut, lemongrass and pandan leaf] the heat is more an intensity of spice than actual physical ‘chilli heat’.” Boldly aromatic rather than delicately fragrant, rich and light at the same time, kukul mas, which SH Fernando Jr’s book Rice & Curry calls “a mainstay of Sri Lankan cuisine”, is surprisingly quick to make once you’ve prepared, or bought, the spice blend, yet it tastes as if it’s been simmering for hours.
The meat
“Choosing a chicken is a fine art,” Kuruvita writes in his book Serendip, “and there are two types: a curry chicken and a broiler … The chickens were always sold skinless, as it was a lot quicker for the men to rip the feathers off with the skin rather than to pluck them. The meat was cut up for us and placed in a large ‘elephant ears’ leaf. When we got home, all we had to do was add the spices and cook the curry.” Most recipes indeed call for whole chickens, cut up on the bone – a good cleaver should make this easy, or, if you’re buying from a butcher, they’ll do this for you even quicker. That said, I’m with Fernando, who writes: “I use thighs with the bone in when I make this dish as breast meat tends to dry out.” If, like Karan Gokani of Hoppers, you use thigh fillets, you may wish, as he does, to replace the water with chicken stock; I also favour removing the skin, but that’s up to you.
The marinade
Many recipes, as Kuruvita notes, simply add the chicken to the pot as it is, but Gokani, Kuruvita and Jeffrey Alford and Naomi Duguid in their book Mangoes & Curry Leaves all marinate the meat first: Gokani in ginger, garlic, turmeric, curry powder and salt; Kuruvita in vinegar and curry powder; and Alford and Duguid in curry powder and garlic. Though all the curries taste great, the marinated chicken comes out a clear winner with my testers and I, “because it seems to marry better with the sauce”. If you’ve bought, or already made your curry powder, there’s no need to delay cooking for too long, but it’s well worth blending it while you prepare the rest of the dish, or indeed if you want to get ahead.
The base
All the curries I try are based on onions in some form. Alford and Duguid go for shallots and Rathnayake red onion, both of which mirror the smaller, sweeter and fierier pink onions used in Sri Lanka. Everyone also adds garlic, and ginger is fairly common, too, a combination that echoes the sweet heat of the onions. Kuruvita’s is the only curry not to include tomatoes – fresh in most cases, though Fernando stirs in tomato paste in the end – which feels a shame, because they add a pleasantly fruity note to the sauce.
Curry leaves are almost mandatory – only Alford and Duguid leave them out – and I can’t resist the transporting perfume of lemongrass and pandan leaves. The latter, long green leaves sometimes referred to as screwpine, though they has nothing to do with the pine family, can usually be found in the freezer section at south-east Asian food specialists. If you can’t track any down, leave them out, but I adore their haunting flavour that, to me, combines toasty notes of dulce de leche with a grassy freshness; they also make incredible desserts.
This sweet, zesty freshness can be underlined with a cinnamon stick and some cardamom pods (some recipes also add cloves), with chilli powder and fresh green chillies bringing the heat (though Fernando adds cayenne pepper and Kuruvita black mustard seeds). Many of these spices are also present in the roasted curry powder that’s the backbone of the dish, so adding a little extra during cooking simply nudges them a little higher in the overall flavour profile.
The roasted curry powder
In Sri Lanka, Fernando explains, “spices are usually bought whole, raw and in bulk. They are dried out in the sun in hand-woven palm frond baskets before roasting and grinding.” Using ready-made blends, he suggests, is like swapping freshly ground beans for instant coffee – though Rathnayake, whose mother’s recipe is featured on the website of Kolamba, a Sri Lankan restaurant in London’s Soho, suggests that the stuff sold in Sri Lankan supermarkets (it may be labelled “meat curry powder”) is perfectly acceptable. If you don’t already have an arsenal of individual spices at your disposal, you may well find this the most convenient option.
If you have a wealth of spices to hand, however, it’s really not hard to make the roasted powder that’s usually paired with meat dishes, which, in this survey at least, always contains coriander, cumin, fenugreek, cloves, cardamom, cinnamon, pandan and curry leaves, and often turmeric, fennel, black pepper and mustard seeds as well.
There’s usually some toasted rice in there, too; not only, Gokani explains, for its nutty flavour, but to act as a thickener, though Kuruvita also includes a thickening powder made from extra rice, desiccated coconut and more spices, which gives his sauce considerably more body than many of the others. Alford and Duguid add cashew nuts on top, which supply a sweet nuttiness, while Kuruvita calls for a startling number of dried chillies, which may be something to consider if you find you’d like a little more fire. I’ve based my curry on the Hoppers version, because I like its sweet, peppery warmth, but, as with all such blends, I suspect there’s a lot of room for tinkering around the edges, particularly heat-wise.
Liquid and cooking
The gravy is usually diluted with a mixture of coconut milk and water, though Kuruvita, who includes solid coconut in his thickening powder and tips in an unusual amount of oil, doesn’t bother with the milk. If, as mentioned earlier, you’re using boneless chicken, I’d recommend replacing the water with good, jellied chicken stock.
Cooking the onions until they’re soft and sweet is vital, but there’s no real need to fry most of the spices here, because they’ve already been toasted. Chicken on the bone takes some time to cook through, so most recipes cover the pan and leave it to simmer gently for 30-40 minutes; bear in mind that the coconut milk will split and separate during this time, but it will still taste just as good as it did when it was emulsified. If you’d prefer a thicker gravy, by all means reduce it further after removing the meat, or thicken by stirring in some extra ground rice mixed with a little water to make a paste.
Serving
Gokani recommends serving this curry with rice or bread, plus a fresh sambol, or turning it into a kottu, a Sri Lankan favourite involving curry, chopped roti, eggs, onions and chillies (which is also a very good vehicle for leftovers, should you have any!)
Perfect Sri Lankan chicken curry
Prep 35 min
 Marinate 30 min+
Cook 50 min
 Serves 4-6
For the roasted curry powder (or use 3 tbsp shop-bought Sri Lankan roasted curry/meat curry powder) 
4g green cardamom pods
  4 tbsp coriander seeds
  2 tsp cumin seeds
  1 tsp fennel seeds
  ½ tsp fenugreek seeds
  ¼ tsp black peppercorns
  2 cloves
  5g cinnamon stick
  8g rice
  3g fresh curry leaves (use a little less if you have only dried ones)
5cm piece pandan leaf
For the curry
1 tbsp grated root ginger
  2 garlic cloves, peeled and grated
1 tsp fine salt
  1 whole chicken, or 6 chicken legs or thighs, skinned, if you prefer, chopped into on-the-bone pieces
  2 tbsp coconut oil, or neutral oil
1 red onion, peeled and thinly sliced
2 garlic cloves, peeled and thinly sliced
1 tbsp grated root ginger
  1 lemongrass stalk, trimmed and lightly bruised
4 cardamom pods, squashed
1 cinnamon stick
  1 tsp chilli powder
  ½-1½ tsp roasted curry powder (see above and method), to taste
1 sprig fresh curry leaves
  2 ripe plum tomatoes, roughly chopped
2 green finger chillies
  10cm piece pandan leaf
  100ml coconut milk
  Rice and a lime wedge, to serve
Rub the ginger, garlic and salt all over the chicken, then leave to marinate while you prepare the other ingredients (and for up to four hours).
For the curry powder, stir the dried spices in a large, heavy-based frying pan on a medium heat until browned and aromatic, then tip out and leave to cool.
Toast the rice until lightly browned, add to the cooling spices, then toast the curry leaves and 5cm piece of pandan until they’ve dried out and add those to the mix, too.
Once everything is cool, put all the spices and rice in a blender or mortar, then whiz or pound to a powder.
Now for the curry. Put the oil in a wide, heavy-based pan on a medium-low heat, then fry the onion for five or six minutes, until soft. Stir in the garlic, ginger, lemongrass, cardamom, cinnamon and chilli powder, fry for a minute or so, then stir in the curry leaves and tomatoes and fry until the tomatoes soften.
At this point, unless your pan is very large, you might find it easiest to scoop out the contents before you cook the chicken.
Toss three tablespoons of curry powder with the marinated chicken, then add to the pan with a little more oil, if necessary. Turn to coat, then, if necessary, return the tomato mix to the pan and add the chillies and 10cm piece of pandan leaf.
Measure out 200ml water, stir in a splash to help dislodge anything that’s stuck to the base of the pan, then pour in the rest of the water and bring to a simmer. Cover, turn down the heat and leave to cook for 15 minutes.
Turn over the chicken pieces, stir in the coconut milk, cover the pan again and leave to cook for another 15 or so minutes, until cooked through. Leave to cool slightly, then adjust the seasoning if required, just before serving with rice and perhaps a wedge of lime.
- 
  How do you make your kukul mas? Is this homely dish an emblem of Sri Lankan cuisine, as Zinara Rathnayake suggests, or would you make the case for something else entirely? And please, do share your recommendations for Sri Lankan restaurants around the world – I’d love to hear them.

Man arrested over flag-day scam targeting animal charity donations
Man, 22, arrested after 14 people allegedly hired to act as volunteers to collect donations for Hong Kong Saving Cat and Dog Association
The rare street scam came to light during the group’s flag day on Saturday, a Social Welfare Department-approved fundraising initiative under which about 800 registered volunteers from the Hong Kong Saving Cat and Dog Association deployed across Kowloon from 7am to noon, the South China Morning Post learned.
Flag days are a traditional fundraising practice in Hong Kong under which approved charities recruit volunteers to collect donations on the streets. Volunteers carry a designated donation bag and a sheet of small stickers, which replaced the traditional small paper flags that donors once pinned to their clothing many years ago.
When passers-by drop coins into the bag or make a digital donation, the volunteer places a sticker on their clothing as a token of appreciation and recognition. The events are typically held on Saturdays, or occasionally on Wednesdays during school holidays. In Cantonese, flag days are called mai kei yat – or “flag-selling day”.
Genuine volunteers reported on social media that a group of strangers had mixed into the crowd, openly displaying fake flag sheets and bags that were a different shade of blue.
A police source said the complainant noticed individuals impersonating association staff near Langham Place in Mong Kok.

Iran shakes with 80 earthquakes in a week
TEHRAN – A total of 80 earthquakes have been recorded across the country in a week from August 29 to September 4, according to the seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran.
Statistically, 74 earthquakes with magnitudes smaller than 3, five earthquakes with a magnitude between 3 and 4, and one earthquake with a magnitude between 4 and 5 have occurred in the country, irsc reported.
Of the total quakes, one had a magnitude of 3.8 on the Richter scale, which occurred on September 1st in Kohgiluyeh-Boyerahmad province.
Among the provinces of the country, Khorasan Razavi experienced the highest number of earthquakes with 10, followed by Yazd, Kohgiluyeh-Boyerahmad, and Mazandaran each with 7 earthquakes.
During the same period, four earthquakes hit Tehran. No earthquakes were recorded in Isfahan, Alborz, Zanjan, Sistan-Baluchestan, Qom, Qazvin, Kordestan, Gilan, and Markazi, provinces.
A total of 2,380 earthquakes with a magnitude of more than 2.5 on the Richter scale were recorded across the country over the past calendar year (March 2025–March 2026), according to the Seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran, Mehr news agency reported.
Out of recorded earthquakes, 910 had a magnitude greater than 3, 130 had a magnitude greater than 4, and 15 had a magnitude greater than 5 on the Richter scale.
The Iranian plateau is located in a very seismically active region of the world and is known not only for its major catastrophic earthquakes but also for the disasters relating to natural hazards, especially earthquakes.
About 2 percent of the earthquakes in the world occur in Iran, but more than 6 percent of the victims of the world’s earthquakes during the 20th century are reported from Iranian earthquakes.

Iran hosts over 40% of world’s rare plant species: study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:54:02 UTC
20:54:02 KST

Iran hosts over 40% of world’s rare plant species: study
TEHRAN — A comprehensive international study has found that Iran is home to 75 of the world’s 180 known species of Melanocrommyum, underscoring the country’s status as a major global hotspot for plant biodiversity.
The study was conducted by Iranian researcher Alireza Dolatyari of the National Center for Genetic and Biological Resources, in collaboration with researchers from Uzbekistan, China, and Turkey, ISNA reported.
Focusing on Allium subgenus Melanocrommyum, the study analyzed 4642 georeferenced occurrence records representing 170 taxa together with plastome- and ITS-based phylogenetic datasets to assess species richness, weighted endemism, phylogenetic diversity, phylogenetic endemism, relative phylogenetic endemism, categorical neo- and paleo-endemism, turnover, and environmental correlates of phylogenetic diversity.
The results confirm the Irano–Turanian region as the main evolutionary center of Allium subgenus Melanocrommyum, with the strongest concentration of species richness, phylogenetic diversity, and phylogenetic endemism in the Central Asian mountains, especially the Tian Shan and Pamir–Alay systems. These areas contain both high species numbers and geographically restricted evolutionary history, indicating their role as centers of diversification and long-term lineage persistence.
The researchers identified two prominent centers of endemism, one in northwestern Iran (Ardabil and East Azarbajian provinces) and the other in Uzbekistan (Kyzylkum, Navio Region), highlighting that intermediate climate and solar radiation played a key role in shaping these patterns.
The National Center for Genetic and Biological Resources is tasked with collecting, identifying, standardizing, preserving, propagating, distributing, and promoting the sustainable use of genetic and biological resources, helping safeguard Iran’s biodiversity from various threats.
To improve Iran’s scientific standing in biotechnology, the center has established a platform to consolidate scientific and research activities, ensuring the sustainable preservation of the country’s biological treasures for future utilization.
In November 2025, the head of the Iranian parliament’s environment fraction, Somayeh Rafiei, underlined paying special attention to endemic and native plant species and implement plant diversity conservation projects in the country.
Zagros [forests in the western part of the country] is one of the top 20 global biodiversity hotspots, and nine out of 11 ecosystems in the world have been identified in the country, which is why Iran has a rich diversity of flora and fauna, ISNA quoted Rafiei as saying.
The country is home to over 8,500 plant species, most of which are found in Zagros, while there are only 5000 plant species known in Europe, she added.
Emphasizing the significance of developing a gene bank and genome map for plant genetic resources in the country, especially those that are disappearing, the official called for supporting research projects on plants.
She also underlined prioritizing endemic and native species, focusing on those that have medicinal values and those that are drought-resistant and play a key role in ensuring food security.
Working together to preserve Iran’s precious biodiversity
Iran ranks among the top 20 countries in the world for biodiversity and is home to a variety of plant and animal species. However, in recent years, certain actions have destroyed habitats and pushed many species to the brink of extinction.
More than two million plant and animal species have been identified worldwide to date, including some 43,000 species found in Iran. The world is home to 11 major types of ecosystems, encompassing aquatic, terrestrial, natural, and artificial ecosystems, nine of which are found in Iran. In addition, 41 of the world’s 42 recognized types of wetlands have been identified in the country.
According to the Department of Environment, some 2,000 animal species, including mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and inland fish, and about 1,200 fish species have been identified in the country’s ecosystems. Of these species, 210 mammal species, 640 bird species, 300 reptile species, 23 amphibian species, and 350 inland fish species can be mentioned.
According to statistics, Iran can be considered the cradle of genetic diversity in the world. Even in international classifications, it is considered among the countries with high biodiversity. However, Iran’s biodiversity, like the rest of the world, faces many challenges such as habitat destruction, overhunting, drought, and climate change.
Given the current circumstances, let’s all join hands to protect biodiversity, because the future of the Earth, the future of life, and the future of the next generations depend on our decisions and actions today.

British forces deploy to Arctic island for NATO deterrence
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:53:21 BST
20:53:21 KST

British forces have deployed to the remote Norwegian island of Jan Mayen alongside Norwegian and American personnel as part of a NATO operation intended to strengthen deterrence and readiness in the High North, the Ministry of Defence has said.
Royal Marines and RAF personnel took part in Operation Atlantic City between 26 August and 4 September, working alongside the Royal Norwegian Navy, Norwegian Home Guard and United States Marine Corps. The deployment formed part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry activity. Jan Mayen lies around 620 miles from mainland Norway in the Norwegian Sea, north of the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap. The MOD described the island as occupying a strategically important position for the defence of northern Europe and the wider Euro-Atlantic area.
Personnel from LXX Squadron RAF deployed alongside elements of UK Commando Force, with the trilateral force integrating sensor and communications systems during the exercise.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: “The High North is vital to the security of the UK and our NATO Allies. This operation demonstrates the strength of our partnership with Norway and the United States, and the ability of our Armed Forces to operate together in even the most demanding Arctic conditions. It is a clear signal of our enduring commitment to NATO security and to defending our shared interests in the High North.”
The MOD said the operation tested the ability of allied forces to work together in an environment where distance, extreme weather, limited infrastructure and rapidly changing conditions place additional demands on logistics and planning. Training in the region included maritime operations, surveillance, movement, survival and joint activity between the participating forces. The deployment was also used to integrate different sensing and communications systems in support of NATO’s wider situational awareness in the Arctic.
Operation Atlantic City ran at the same time as naval manoeuvres under Operation Northern Viking 26, allowing participating forces to use overlapping maritime and sensing resources across the European theatre while supporting Arctic Sentry.
The MOD said: “The operation has seen UK forces work alongside the Royal Norwegian Navy, the Norwegian Home Guard, and US Marine Corps units integrate various sensor and communications systems, allowing NATO to be better prepared for potential threats.”
The deployment follows similar allied training around Jan Mayen last year and comes as NATO increases its focus on the High North, where the Alliance is seeking to improve its ability to monitor activity and operate in difficult Arctic conditions.
British participation in Arctic Sentry forms part of a wider NATO effort to increase vigilance across northern waters and improve the ability of allied forces to operate jointly at short notice.
The MOD said Arctic training gives UK personnel practical experience of operating in some of the most demanding weather and terrain faced by NATO forces, including environments where infrastructure is limited and reinforcement or resupply can be difficult. Operation Atlantic City was intended to build that experience while also strengthening interoperability between British, Norwegian and American forces deployed in the High North.

Turkish Navy vessels continue operations after 2 maritime accidents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:52:42 UTC
20:52:42 KST

AA Photo
Three Turkish Navy deep-sea search vessels continued recovery efforts on Sept. 6 for people missing following two maritime accidents in the Marmara and Mediterranean seas.
The TCG Akın reached the wreck of a vessel that sank off Istanbul’s Silivri district on Sept. 2 after colliding with another ship. A remotely operated underwater vehicle (ROV) was deployed to the site to definitively identify the wreck.
The ROV, which conducted deep-sea imaging and sonar scans, initially captured the name Tuğberk İmamoğlu on the hull.
The wreck was located at a depth of 720 meters, about 50 meters from the reported collision site.
The cargo ship Tuğberk İmamoğlu and the tanker Alsu collided at around 3:15 a.m. on Sept. 2, approximately 18 nautical miles (35 kilometers) south of Silivri, in one of the busiest shipping corridors in the Sea of Marmara.
Efforts were also continuing to locate the vessel’s 10 missing crew members after the ship sank within 11 minutes due to its heavy cargo.
The search operation followed a preliminary expert report into the collision, which pointed to malfunctions in the vessel’s electronic navigation systems as well as shortcomings in the allocation of duties among the crew.
According to the report, released on Sept. 3, the sinking vessel was operating in “ghost ship” mode shortly before the accident, meaning it was not transmitting Automatic Identification System (AIS) data.
AIS enables ships to broadcast information including their position, course and speed to nearby vessels.
Following the accident, the vessel’s first captain, Ahmet Erarslan, and third captain, Murat Evciman, were arrested on charges of causing death and injury through negligence.
Both captains said in their statements that the Tuğberk İmamoğlu had collided with their vessel.
Evciman said he had joined the ship only one day before the accident and had seven months of seafaring experience.
In another maritime accident, search and recovery efforts entered their second week on Sept. 6. The TCG Işın and TCG Alemdar continued searching for the remains of 15 people after a passenger ferry capsized off Turkish Cyprus’ Kyrenia.
The high-speed passenger vessel Filo Jet, which operates between Kyrenia Port in Turkish Cyprus and Taşucu Port in Türkiye’s southern Mersin province, began taking on water from its bow shortly after departing around noon on Aug. 30.
The vessel carrying 267 people capsized while attempting to return to the port.
As the wreck lies at a depth of 514 meters, conventional divers and other vessels were unable to reach it.
The death toll from the accident has so far been confirmed at 13.
Turkish Cypriot Prime Minister Ünal Üstel said DNA testing would be used to identify the remains recovered from the wreckage as accurately and conclusively as possible, leaving no room for doubt.

Health projects in food and pharmaceutical sectors near completion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:50:27 UTC
20:50:27 KST

Health projects in food and pharmaceutical sectors near completion
TEHRAN - Thirteen health development projects in the food and pharmaceutical sectors at medical sciences universities are nearing completion, with priority given to projects that have reached more than 70 percent physical progress.
Abbas Mahdizadeh, an official at the Food and Drug Administration, said eight projects have been completed and brought into operation this year, with plans to complete around 30 additional buildings and warehouses in the food and pharmaceutical sectors by the end of 2027.
He added that expanding and upgrading pharmaceutical warehouses and laboratories remain among the key priorities in funding allocations. Given the vital role of pharmaceutical reserves and infrastructure in times of crisis, he stressed that the projects must be carried out in compliance with the required technical and safety standards.
In June 2024, Abdolazim Behfar, an FDA official, outlined the agency’s legal measures to ensure food safety, emphasizing that food production facilities, as well as imported shipments containing raw materials and finished products, are subject to strict monitoring. He made the remarks on the occasion of World Food Safety Day, which is annually celebrated on June 7.
The Day aims to draw attention and inspire action to help prevent, detect, and manage foodborne risks, contributing to food security, human health, economic prosperity, agriculture, market access, tourism, and sustainable development.
The official added that during the Iranian calendar year 1402 (March 2023–March 2024), a total of 4,884 complaints concerning food products were investigated. During the same period, approximately 5,100 non-compliant food production and distribution units were identified and referred to judicial authorities.
Based on Iran FDA supervision, 266 unauthorized production units were identified, and more than 170,000 items of contraband were discovered, Behfar stated.
“Additionally, 148,000 illegal and counterfeit products were discovered, and about 3.8 million kilograms of food and beverage shipments that did not comply with regulations were destroyed over the past year,” he further noted.
The universities of medical sciences across the country are the executive arms of Iran FDA, which inspects major distribution centers of health-oriented products, Behfar said.
Food safety is a collective responsibility – everyone from producers to consumers needs to play their part.
However, there are exceptional situations where even if we have all played our part, the unexpected intervenes and food safety is compromised.
 
 Even then, there is always something we can do to avoid illness.
Food safety incidents can range from minor events to major international crises, whether it is a power outage at home, a food poisoning at a local restaurant, a voluntary recall of contaminated products by a manufacturer, an outbreak from imported products, or a natural disaster.
Food safety hazards do not recognize borders, so in an increasingly interconnected global food supply, risks posed by unsafe food can rapidly evolve from a local problem to an international emergency.
 
 This year’s theme, ‘Food safety: prepare for the unexpected’, underlines the importance of being prepared for food safety incidents, no matter how mild or severe they can be.
Food safety incidents are situations where there is a potential or confirmed health risk associated with food consumption. A food incident can happen, for example, due to accidents, inadequate controls, food fraud, or natural events.
While being ready to manage food safety incidents requires dedicated efforts from policymakers, food safety authorities, farmers, and food business operators, consumers can also play an active role.
Food safety has a critical role in assuring that food stays safe at every stage of the food chain - from production to harvest, processing, storage, distribution, all the way to preparation and consumption.
With an estimated 600 million cases of foodborne illnesses annually, unsafe food is a threat to human health and economies, disproportionally affecting vulnerable and marginalized people, especially women and children, populations affected by conflict, and migrants.
An estimated 420,000 people around the world die every year after eating contaminated food, and children under 5 years of age carry 40 percent of the foodborne disease burden, with 125,000 deaths every year.

U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff were in Kiev on Sept. 6 for their first visit to the Ukrainian capital, a day after discussed “substantive plans” with Russia’s Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin on ending more than four years of war between the neighbors.

“We will do everything that depends on us to ensure the safety of the negotiation process and mediators such as yourselves,” Putin told Witkoff and Kushner.
Earlier on Sept. 5, Putin had thanked Trump for persisting in his efforts to end the war despite it being “not simple.”
Of the envoys’ trip to Kiev, he said: “No matter what happens next, contacts of this kind are undoubtedly always beneficial.”
Trump said on Sept. 4 his envoys were bringing a “proposal” to end fighting.
“We have an idea for peace,” he said, without elaborating.
U.S. efforts have so far not led to a breakthrough in the war, and peace efforts have stalled in part because of Washington’s war with Iran.
Russia occupied large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine, and Putin has insisted Moscow is intent on seizing the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Both Moscow and Kiev committed to suspending strikes as the negotiations took place.
“The Russian president, the commander-in-chief, has given the order from midnight not to strike Kyiv for three days,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
Zelensky said he had spoken to the U.S. envoys and also promised Kiev would not strike Moscow.
However, Kiev said that Russian strikes had killed 10 people across the country on Sept. 5, including a child and his family members in the Kharkiv region and two people outside Kiev.
Zelensky accused Moscow of trying to disrupt the visit of the U.S. envoys with overnight attacks on Kiev’s two airports, as well as on civilian targets.
