German warship fires ballistic missile in message to Russia
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:40:40 BST
20:40:40 KST

A German warship has fired an Israeli-made LORA ballistic missile during a live test in the North Atlantic, with the German Navy saying the launch demonstrated a strike capability with a potential range beyond anything it had previously operated.
German media reports, citing a German Navy spokesman, said two German frigates had deployed to waters between Ireland and Iceland for the test on Tuesday night. Images from the exercise show a containerised launcher positioned on the deck of a German vessel. The messaging here could hardly be clearer.
By disclosing a test that had deliberately been kept secret, NATO was sending a direct signal to Moscow: European forces are developing longer-range strike options, and not every capability will be visible before it is ready. NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum said the test had been kept secret until after it was completed and involved a German frigate firing the missile in the North Atlantic.
The command stated: “Kept secret. Now revealed. The German Navy just tested the Israeli LORA ballistic missile from a German frigate in the North Atlantic — quietly, deliberately and with a range of 500+ km.”
Kept secret. Now revealed. 🚀🇩🇪
The German Navy just tested the Israeli 🇮🇱 LORA ballistic missile from a German frigate in the North Atlantic — quietly, deliberately and with a range of 500+ km.
NATO 3.0 looks like this:
Europe is taking more responsibility, building serious… pic.twitter.com/K8x2JE61Gs
— NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum – JFCBS (@NATOJFCBS) September 2, 2026
It added: “NATO 3.0 looks like this: Europe is taking more responsibility, building serious capabilities and keeping a few cards close to the chest. Deterrence just got a little more interesting.”
Vice Admiral Jan Christian Kaack, Inspector of the German Navy, said: “With the successful launch of a ballistic missile last night in the North Atlantic, we made naval history. I am extremely satisfied with this achievement.”
Kaack added that the system “can be successfully deployed from our units, and the potential range exceeds anything we have known before.”
In his original statement, the German Navy chief said the trial opened a new chapter for maritime deterrence and readiness, stating that the system could be operated successfully from German units and that its possible reach exceeded previous German naval capabilities.
The test was conducted with Israel Aerospace Industries’ LORA, or Long-Range Artillery Weapon System. According to IAI, the missile has a range of around 400 kilometres and an accuracy of within 10 metres, while NATO’s public account of the German test referred to a range of more than 500 kilometres. Israel Aerospace Industries said the missile was launched from an operational German vessel equipped with a command trailer and launcher. According to the company, the missile followed its planned trajectory, navigated to the target and successfully struck it, with both the weapon system and missile meeting the objectives of the trial.
Boaz Levy, Chairman of IAI, said: “This is an unprecedented achievement for IAI and the Israeli Ministry of Defense. The successful trial of the LORA missile, launched from a naval vessel and striking its target with exceptional precision, took place overnight in Germany – the country where the world’s first ballistic missile was developed.”
He added: “This trial demonstrates Israel’s technological strength and the unique cooperation between Israel and Germany. It marks another significant achievement alongside the deployment of the Arrow 3 system on German soil, further strengthening Germany’s defense and deterrence capabilities and deepening the strategic partnership between our two countries.”
IAI chief executive Guy Bar Lev said: “Israel Aerospace Industries is proud to take part in strengthening the strategic cooperation between the State of Israel and the Government of Germany. This significant milestone is underscored by the operational live-fire exercise (OPEX) of the LORA system, one of the world’s most advanced and combat-proven ballistic missile systems.”
The German Navy is using its OPEX initiative to trial technologies and operational concepts as part of its Marine 2035 and Beyond programme. The process is intended to allow new systems to be tested rapidly under conditions intended to resemble operational use as closely as possible.
The North Atlantic launch comes as Germany expands its investment in long-range strike and air and missile defence. The country has also begun fielding the Israeli-developed Arrow 3 ballistic missile defence system as part of its wider effort to strengthen national and NATO defensive capabilities.

China’s practical push for Middle East peace and better global governance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:38:27 UTC
20:38:27 KST

China’s practical push for Middle East peace and better global governance
As the protective umbrellas of distant powers grow increasingly tattered, and as regional wars and broken global institutions feed on each other, China is emerging as a constructive force for regional security and improved global governance.
From the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek to talks between Chinese and Egyptian leaders in Cairo, Beijing has floated a series of concrete proposals that inject a measure of certainty into a turbulent world.
 
  
 
 A loud and clear voice in Bishkek
At the 26th SCO heads-of-state summit on September 1, 2026, held amid accelerating global upheaval and the rise of unilateralism and bloc confrontation, China’s president, Xi Jinping, posed an important question: what kind of multipolarity does the world need, and how should countries help shape it? He urged leaders to shoulder historical responsibility and steer events rather than drift with them.
Marking the organization’s 25th anniversary, the Bishkek Declaration reaffirmed support for Iran’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, condemned military strikes on Iranian territory as violations of the UN Charter and international law, and insisted that conflicts be settled by political and diplomatic means.
It also called for reforming global governance so that all countries can participate, decide, and benefit equally, and rejected bloc politics and confrontation as solutions to international problems. In a climate of sustained American pressure on Iran, the SCO’s stance carries unusual weight.
 
 
 A new security architecture for the Middle East
The Middle East has long been a geopolitical tinderbox. American intervention, beginning with the first Arab-Israeli war, helped plant the seeds of lasting disorder; more recent Israeli and American actions against Iran have only deepened the instability.
In talks with Egypt’s president, Abdel-Fattah al-Sisi, Mr Xi outlined a four-point proposal for a new regional security framework.
First, the region’s peoples must take charge of their own destiny and resist outside interference, an implicit rebuke to decades of American meddling.
Second, security requires comprehensive approaches, with the Palestinian question remaining central rather than being sidelined, as in the Abraham Accords that isolated Iran while bypassing the core issue.
Third, lasting peace rests on development; shared economic interests can dry up the soil in which conflict grows.
Fourth, outside powers should abandon double standards and let the United Nations play a genuine role.
Taken together, the four points sketch a security order based on common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security—distinct from arrangements designed primarily to preserve American primacy, and closer to what most regional states say they want.
 
   
  
 From idea to results: The Global Governance Initiative’s first year
A year after Mr. Xi launched the Global Governance Initiative on the 80th anniversary of the United Nations, nearly 160 countries and international organizations have endorsed it. More than 60, including Iran, have joined the “Friends of Global Governance” group.
An International Organization for Mediation, proposed by China, is now operating. A World Data Organization and a World Artificial Intelligence Co-operation Organization have been established in China, and the city of Xiamen is bidding to host the secretariat of the agreement on marine biodiversity.
These steps suggest that Beijing is trying, in practice, to move global governance away from zero-sum thinking toward arrangements that are fairer and more inclusive.
Looking east rather than west reveals a different worldview. China speaks of harmony and mutual benefit, not of winners and losers.
While some powers weave exclusive security nets and brandish the threat of maximum pressure, China uses bilateral and multilateral channels to manage differences through dialogue, to replace coercive hegemony with shared security, and to pursue stability through development.
That approach is making China an increasingly important source of steadiness in an unsettled world.

Iranian forces reportedly attacked a U.S. naval drone attempting to enter the Strait of Hormuz Sunday, just hours after striking ships in retaliation for U.S. attacks on three oil tankers.
The latest round of clashes, which began with U.S. raids last week, comes amid a deadlock in their six-month war.
Iran has maintained its stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz while Washington continues a counterblockade of Iranian ports.
Washington is also seeking to choke Iran's economy, rolling out sanctions on entities with financial links to the Islamic Republic in a bid to force it into submission.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), the ideological arm of Iran's military, said Sunday it "attacked an American military unmanned surface vessel" attempting to enter the strait, according to a statement carried by state television.
Hours earlier, the IRGC said its naval forces "targeted three oil tankers on the unauthorized route of the Strait of Hormuz and three vessels affiliated with the child-killing America in other areas."
It warned ships not to attempt to transit by unapproved routes.
On Saturday, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees American military operations in the region, said it struck tankers linked to the IRGC, accusing the most powerful arm of the Iranian military of unsuccessfully firing at American warships.
"Following Iran's failed attacks, CENTCOM permanently disabled the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask," it said.
"American forces also completely destroyed the unladen crude oil carrier M/T Kylo ... in the Gulf of Oman, striking the vessel in multiple critical locations to render it inoperable after the crew was directed to abandon ship."
Video posted by CENTCOM showed large fireballs and billowing flames after projectiles slammed into the ships.
The three vessels were "part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies," it claimed.
The Guards, meanwhile, claimed the two American warships they targeted had been "forced to retreat" after "suffering damage," but CENTCOM said those ships successfully evaded Iranian attacks.
CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said after the operation: "If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost – taking out three of yours."
The Iranian Foreign Ministry hit out at Washington over the strikes on oil tankers, calling them "illegal and aggressive actions."
A correspondent for Iranian state TV in Jask in the southern province of Hormozgan said one of the tankers was empty and the second was carrying oil. The crews were transported to shore on lifeboats, they said.
Another state TV correspondent on Kharg Island said the attack there caused no casualties.
Iran's Khatam-al Anbiya central military command warned that if the U.S. continued its attacks, then Tehran's retaliation against U.S. warships would be "more severe than before, and there is a possibility of their expansion."
The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump has tried to downplay the significance of the six-month conflict, which has proven increasingly unpopular at home as midterm elections near.
U.S. Vice President JD Vance went so far as to say that he "wouldn't call it a war."
Trump reiterated that view Friday, calling the war "small potatoes" for Washington.
Iran's Security Chief Mohsen Rezaei warned this week that the Islamic republic had adopted a "new strategy" against Washington that "will shatter your foundations."
The U.S. has been trying to step up pressure on Tehran in a bid to wrestle control of the Hormuz Strait, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed.
A fragile cease-fire between the two sides collapsed in July after attacks on commercial ships in the strategic waterway.
Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly threatened to claim sovereignty over the strait, even posting a map showing it as "new U.S. territory."
Vance has insisted the U.S. will not reopen talks with Iran until it ends attacks on commercial shipping in Hormuz.

Flights canceled, airports shut over Indonesia volcanic eruption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:36:00 UTC
20:36:00 KST

Indonesia was forced to cancel flights at Jakarta International Airport and service at other domestic airports were also disrupted Sunday when Anak Krakatau volcano erupted, spreading ash across western parts of the country.
Indonesia’s Geological Agency said the volcanic island located in Indonesia’s Sunda Strait between the main Java and Sumatra islands had showed signs of activity since Friday before erupting for 30 seconds at 3:53 a.m. Sunday. Closed-circuit camera footage showed lava flares from the volcano.
No casualties were reported and no evacuation order was issued. The nearest settlement is more than 16 kilometers (10 miles) away, but authorities warned residents and visitors to stay at least 3 kilometers from the active crater.
Volcanic ash spread across parts of Jakarta and Lampung province on Sumatra’s southern tip, Indonesia’s Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said.
AirNav Indonesia closed airspace around Soekarno-Hatta and Halim Perdanakusuma airports in Jakarta, as well as four other airports, including Radin Inten II Airport in Lampung, because of volcanic ash.
By mid-afternoon, the closure had affected 516 flight movements, with 202 in Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta airport alone that affected about 22,800 passengers, on Sunday. The airport was ordered closed until at least 5:30 p.m.
Indonesia’s Directorate General of Civil Aviation said it was closely monitoring the eruption's impact on air travel and coordinating with airlines, airport operators, air navigation services and the meteorology agency.
"Safety remains our top priority in every operational decision,” Lukman F. Laisa, Ministry of Transportation director general of civil aviation, said in a statement.
He warned flight schedules could face cascading disruptions affecting aircraft rotations, fleet availability and terminal capacity as airlines work to restore operations.
The eruption also disrupted services at Bali’s I Gusti Ngurah Rai International Airport and at Medan.
Indonesia’s volcanology agency and the Darwin Volcanic Ash Advisory Centre identified two ash clouds using satellite imagery. One plume rose to 6,100 meters (20,000 feet) and drifted northeast over Jakarta, Banten, West Java and nearby waters.
A second cloud reached 15,200 meters and spread over parts of Banten, Lampung and Bengkulu provinces, the southern Sunda Strait and sections of the Indian Ocean west of Sumatra.
Lana Saria, head of Indonesia’s Geological Agency, said activity at Anak Krakatau has intensified since July, with Sunday’s eruption the strongest during the current period of unrest.
The repeated eruptions indicate a continued supply of magma and volcanic gases beneath the volcano, she said, though officials cannot predict whether a larger eruption will occur.
"We continue to evaluate the volcano’s development based on all monitoring data, not solely on the number of eruptions or the height of the ash column,” Saria said in a video briefing.
She said the main hazards include volcanic ash, high concentrations of gas and the ejection of hot rocks and other material around the crater area.
Anak Krakatau, which means "child of Krakatau," is the offspring of the famous Krakatau, whose monumental 1883 eruption triggered a period of global cooling.
The eruption caused a tsunami in 2018 that killed at least 430 people in Sumatra and Java. Researchers believe volcanic activity triggered an underwater landslide and caused a large chunk of Anak Krakatau’s southwest slope to collapse and displace a large volume of water.
Scientists said Anak Krakatau island was only about a quarter of its original size after that eruption.

Unknown

2026-09-06
11:35:44 UTC
20:35:44 KST

The Jerusalem District Court on Sunday sentenced Rabbi Moshe Yazdi, 63, to 18 years in prison after convicting him of sex offenses and financial crimes involving two of his female students.
The court also imposed a one-year suspended sentence and ordered Yazdi to pay each of the two victims 150,000 shekels in compensation.
Yazdi, a Jerusalem resident, was convicted in March. In their ruling, the judges said they were convinced he had engaged in sexual relationships with women who were his students or members of the Amudei Shalom community he led.
“The defendant exploited his religious and social status, the age gap between himself and the women, and the great respect and admiration they had for him,” the judges wrote. “In many cases, he also exploited the difficult family, financial or emotional backgrounds of the women.”
Yazdi founded and led the Amudei Shalom association in Jerusalem’s Bukharan Quarter, where he served as a rabbi and community leader.
An indictment filed against him in 2022 accused him of numerous sex offenses involving women from the community who attended his lessons. According to the indictment, Yazdi preached that followers should suppress their own views and feelings in deference to “the opinion of Torah” and religious scholars.
He was ultimately convicted of sex offenses and money laundering offenses involving two of the eight complainants in the case.
According to the verdict, Yazdi used his position and the relationships of trust and dependence he had built with the women to commit the offenses.
During sentencing arguments, prosecutors Avihai Dweck and Eyal Lidani described the conduct as exceptionally grave and said it reflected a systematic and prolonged pattern of abuse.
The prosecution said Yazdi exploited the women’s personal and religious distress over a period of years, using the trust and dependence he had cultivated with them.
Prosecutors also said he used manipulation and religious concepts to present some of the acts as “spiritual corrections.”
They described multiple acts of rape and indecent assault carried out over years, saying the offenses caused significant harm that continues to affect the victims.
On the financial charges, prosecutors said Yazdi, who was in the midst of bankruptcy proceedings, used the bank accounts of students to conceal money from creditors.
They also urged the court to consider that Yazdi had not accepted responsibility for his actions and had forced the complainants to endure the full legal process.

Ukrainian Armor Unveils Novator 2S Medical Evacuation Vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:35:06 UTC
20:35:06 KST

Ukrainian Armor LLC has unveiled the Novator 2S armored medical evacuation vehicle, developed on the basis of the Novator 2 armored vehicle.
The company told Militarnyi about the vehicle’s features.
The Novator 2S is equipped with a specially designed armored capsule adapted specifically for the evacuation of wounded personnel. Compared with the baseline Novator 2, the medical variant features a different interior layout, wider rear doors, and equipment intended for use by medical personnel. The vehicle can transport up to four wounded personnel in a lying position or up to six in a seated position.
According to a company representative, it is not possible to use the standard Novator 2 armored capsule for a fully-fledged medical vehicle without structural modifications.
“The Novator 2 can be used for evacuation, but it cannot perform the role of a dedicated medical evacuation vehicle. The capsule is specifically designed for the medical variant,” explained a representative of Ukrainian Armor.
The armored capsule of the Novator 2S meets the PZSA-4 protection level (Ed.: a Ukrainian ballistic protection class for specialized and armored vehicles). According to the company representative, it provides protection against 7.62 mm armor-piercing bullets.
The mine protection system is designed to withstand a blast from an explosive device containing up to 6 kg of explosive charge in TNT equivalent beneath the vehicle’s floor.
The developers paid particular attention to the vehicle’s running gear, as the evacuation vehicle is required to operate on damaged roads and off-road terrain.
The vehicle continues to use the Ford F-550 chassis as its base, which is further reinforced. The company strengthens the frame and axles, while some running-gear components – including control arms, links, bump stops, and bushings – are developed and manufactured in-house. The vehicle is also fitted with heavy-duty shock absorbers and stabilizer bars.
“All of this is our own development, including reinforced vehicle mounting components, so that it can withstand all the loads encountered during evacuation,” a company representative said.
These modifications are intended to improve the vehicle’s survivability when operating over difficult terrain and reduce the risk of running-gear failure under load.
Like the Novator 2, the Novator 2S is equipped with foreign-made RunFlat inserts. These allow the vehicle to continue moving after a tire is damaged, enabling the evacuation to be completed without stopping.
A separate mechanism with a winch has been developed for the spare wheel, making it easier to lower and raise it. According to the company representative, this solution was implemented specifically on the medical version.
The driver’s compartment is separated from the medical compartment by a partition, while a window has been retained between the two areas for access. The lower section of the partition is completely enclosed. This is intended to prevent blood, medical fluids, or other objects from entering the driver’s workspace while the vehicle is in motion.
The vehicle provides sufficient power for operating a basic set of medical equipment, while military personnel can connect additional autonomous power sources if required. Access to electrical power makes it possible to operate additional medical equipment, including refrigerators for storing blood, patient monitors, and other systems.
The medical compartment is also equipped with task lighting and blackout lighting. In particular, there is a mode using red LED lamps for nighttime operations, reducing the vehicle’s visual signature.
Such vehicles have an armored capsule, but their interiors do not provide dedicated berths for casualties requiring evacuation in a lying position, nor sufficient space for a medic to work while the vehicle is moving.
“This configuration is specifically designed for casualty evacuation. There are berths for patients to lie down, as well as organizers within easy reach that can be positioned in whatever arrangement is most convenient for the medic while working,” the servicemember noted.
He identified the large interior volume and wide rear doors as among the main advantages of the new version, as they simplify the loading of wounded personnel.
“In older armored vehicles, such as APCs or IFVs, the doors are very small – you can barely get in or out. Here, there is enough room for the medic, dedicated space for the wounded, and the ability to treat them inside the vehicle,” he explained.
Under the planned configuration, the crew can consist of a driver, a medic, and a medical assistant, with the remaining space used to accommodate casualties.
The berths intended for patients in a lying position can also be used, when necessary, to transport lightly wounded personnel in a seated position.
At the same time, the servicemember noted that it is difficult for a single medic to simultaneously treat several seriously wounded casualties. Therefore, the actual number of casualties carried will depend on their condition and the specific mission.
Thanks to its armor protection and off-road mobility, the Novator 2S is primarily intended for evacuating wounded personnel from the most dangerous areas, closer to the line of contact.
At this stage, the vehicle must provide protection for both the crew and casualties while retaining sufficient mobility over difficult terrain.
“The kill zone is quite wide at the moment, while the speed of evacuation by unmanned ground vehicles is low. The main problem is that an UGV cannot provide medical care to a wounded person. It is not a medical professional, and we all know about the ‘golden hour,’” said Vladyslav Belbas, CEO of Ukrainian Armor.
The servicemember also pointed out that during the CASEVAC stage, the vehicle will often have to operate on poor roads or off-road.
“If this is CASEVAC, there most likely won’t be a good road to the position. There may be fallen trees, dirt, sand, snow, or rain. The vehicle’s protection matters the most,” the servicemember said.
In the servicemember’s unit, standard Novator vehicles as well as Roshel armored vehicles are already used for such missions. However, their interior layouts are not specifically optimized for medical evacuation. In the Novator 2S, the interior space was designed from the outset to accommodate casualties and allow the medic to work.
The evacuation vehicle can then transport the casualty to a stabilization point or hand them over for the next stage of evacuation.
According to the servicemember, the requirements for the vehicle can vary at each stage depending on the operational direction, road conditions, evacuation distance, and the level of enemy UAV activity.
For operations during the initial evacuation stage, the servicemember considers equipment for immediate life-saving care and control of major hemorrhage to be the most essential.
First and foremost, this includes additional tourniquets, wound dressings, splints, and equipment for infusion therapy.
According to the servicemember, during transportation the medic can monitor the tourniquets that have already been applied and, when conditions permit, convert or reposition them.
“Essentially, everything included in a combat medic’s backpack should also be readily available in this vehicle,” the servicemember explained.
He also cited the air-conditioning system as an additional advantage of the Novator 2S, as it allows the required temperature to be maintained inside the armored capsule.
If the vehicle is additionally equipped with oxygen equipment and patient-monitoring systems, its capabilities could be expanded to support operations during subsequent stages of medical evacuation.
The final equipment package will depend on the specific unit, operational direction, length of the evacuation route, and the level of threat posed by Russian UAVs.

Prosecutor General denies involvement in covering up illegal call centers
This is said in a statement posted by the Prosecutor General on Telegram, Ukrinform reports.
“In connection with the investigation into possible facilitation of the activities of illegal call centers, I consider it necessary to clearly state my position: I have nothing whatsoever to do with covering up illegal call centers, I did not give instructions to facilitate such activities, and I did not use the powers of the Prosecutor General for this purpose,” the statement says.
Kravchenko also said he had suspended from official duties an employee of the Office of the Prosecutor General (OPG) who is involved in an investigation by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), and had ordered preparations for a personnel decision on the employee’s dismissal in accordance with the procedure prescribed by law.
At the same time, he stressed that the employee’s guilt would ultimately be established by a court.
Kravchenko also said he would not limit the response to a single personnel decision. He ordered an investigation into the work of the Department of International Cooperation, where the NABU investigation suspect worked, as well as the unit responsible for combating cybercrime. The review will include an audit of decisions that were made and the results of the units’ work.
“I separately ordered that all employees of structural units involved in procedural supervision and investigations into illegal call center cases undergo polygraph tests. This applies to everyone without exception,” the Prosecutor General said.
He assured that personnel and administrative decisions would be made based on the results of the reviews, and, where there are grounds, criminal-procedural decisions would also be taken.
Kravchenko emphasized that over the past year, law enforcement officers had detained prosecutors and served them with notices of suspicion, while the OPG had not concealed such cases and had itself publicly reported them.
The Prosecutor General said that after taking office, he had instructed law enforcement agencies to step up efforts against fraudulent call centers.
According to statistics he cited, over the past 12 months law enforcement officers have conducted more than 1,050 searches, shut down about 340 call centers and halted the operation of more than 5,000 operator workstations. Currently, 147 criminal proceedings are under investigation, while more than 183 people have been served with notices of suspicion. Indictments against 93 people have already been sent to court.
At the same time, he stressed that no results can serve as an excuse for abuses within the Prosecutor’s Office.
Kravchenko also said that during NABU investigative actions, investigators were given full access to his office and everything they needed to inspect, and that no obstacles were created.
The Prosecutor General said that the safe shown in a photo circulating in the media and on social networks is not located at the Prosecutor General’s Office.
“It has nothing to do either with my office or with any other OPG employees. Claims to the contrary are false,” Kravchenko said.
He also added that media reports about his disappearance were untrue.
“I understand that many people would like me to ‘hide,’ end up in hospital, or something else. I will disappoint my ‘fans’: yesterday I was at work, today I am working as usual, with a little sport as well. We continue working,” the statement says.
As reported earlier, on September 4, the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office and the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine announced that, as part of Operation Carthage, they had uncovered a criminal organization headed by the head of one of the Prosecutor General’s Office’s units that systematically received bribes from fraudulent call centers and laundered the proceeds.
According to investigators, the OPG official created the group in mid-2025, involving serving prosecutors and close unofficial associates. According to Ukrainska Pravda, the Deputy Head of the Prosecutor General’s Office Department of International Cooperation, Serhii Kropyva, was detained.

Kyiv protests new UN map separating Crimea from Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:34:26 UTC
20:34:26 KST

Ukraine could not support a U.N. resolution on a new world map, because it depicted the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula as separate from Ukraine, lawmaker Kira Rudik said on Sept. 5.
"In 2026, the U.N. should not need a reminder: Crimea is Ukraine. Shame," the liberal lawmaker said on X.
Ukraine was one of only seven countries not to vote in support of a new U.N. world map — designed to better reflect the size of Africa relative to Europe and North America — in a vote on Sept. 4, because of how the new map treats Crimea.
The "Correct the Map" resolution was proposed by Togo, supported by the African Union, and adopted by 164 countries.
With the resolution adopted, the U.N. will stop using the traditional Mercator projection world map, which makes countries farther north appear larger than they actually are, and start using a projection that preserves countries' actual size.
Ukraine abstained from the vote, along with five other countries. The U.S. was the only country to vote against the resolution.
The map shows Ukraine's Crimea in gray, distinct from the shade of green used for the rest of the country.
Russia illegally occupied and annexed Crimea in 2014, but it remains a Ukrainian territory in international law.
Though the map does not color Crimea to match Russia, it does suggest, through its coloration, that the territory is in some way separate from Ukraine
Ukraine's official objection registered with the U.N. described the Equal Earth projection's depiction of the country as "wholly unacceptable."
The five other countries abstaining from the vote were Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, and Serbia.
The EU's U.N. delegation supported the resolution, but in its explanatory statement said: "We underscore that the resolution neither addresses nor affects questions relating to sovereignty, territorial status, delimitation, or the internationally recognized borders of States."
"The resolution does not imply recognition of, support for, or acquiescence in any claim concerning disputed territories, changes to existing borders, or alterations to the legal status of any territory," the statement reads.
The U.S was the lone country to vote against, but not because of border concerns. The U.S representative accused the map of being part of a "radical ideological project" that seeks to promote reparations.

These smart bricks know what object they make up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:31:42 UTC
20:31:42 KST

Cells do not have brains. Yet somehow, as an organism grows, cells know where to go and what to be without top-down direction. And acting together, cells are collectively intelligent, ultimately building complex final forms—whether that be a flower, a whale, or even you. Mimicking this ability in machines could one day lead to self-healing circuits and computers that can assess and repair damage as it happens, and new research published in Nature Communications shows how smart “bricks” could move us closer to that goal.
A future in which machines build themselves is “all about local self-organization where you don’t have one failure point,” says Sebastian Risi, the paper’s senior author and a computer scientist at IT University of Copenhagen and Sakana AI.
First, the researchers created simulations of cubes, each with an independently operated neural network, assembled into nearly 500 3D shapes across seven object categories—boats, cars, chairs, guitars, houses, planes and tables—and tested whether the cubes could identify their category. Each virtual cube contained a list of numbers called a vector with its memory and a guess about object category, both of which can evolve over time. Each cube’s neural network told it how to update its vector based on its neighbors’. Together, the cubes formed what’s called a neural cellular automaton. (The classic example of cellular automata is John Conway’s Game of Life, devised in 1970, in which pixels flash on and off based on how many neighbors they have.)
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The simulated cubes passed messages and altered their vectors based on, first, their own immediate environment, such as whether they were on an edge, then their neighbors’, and so on. After the neural network was trained, cubes named their object class with 85 to 100 percent accuracy—houses proved trickiest. “It’s remarkable that the bricks can infer the global shape of the collective using only local information,” says Sabine Hauert, who studies swarm robotics at the University of Bristol and was not involved in the work.
The virtual cubes could often identify their shape even if 15 percent of them had been removed, as well as decide which cubes were missing and regenerate neighbors. And the team found that systems of more than 18,000 cubes could still guess the objects they were in.
Finally, the researchers tested their system using real blocks, each a few centimeters across, with circuitry inside that ran computations locally. When up to 197 were connected into a shape, they accurately identified what object they were 100 percent of the time.
Risi says a near-term application is in edutainment: build a dinosaur that then roars, or use construction bricks that tell you where to place the next one. Over the long term, the researchers envision modular robots that assemble themselves, no instruction manual required.

The Best Laptop Backpacks for Work, Travel, and Everything Between (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Though I’ve been working from home for the past 15 years, both freelance and full-time, this often means needing to be available 24/7, so I typically carry my laptop everywhere I go—including sports practices, day trips, and vacations.
I have used many laptop backpacks in this time, and the dividing line between a work backpack that’s comfortable and fits seamlessly into your daily routine and one that’s aggravating at every turn is a fine one. If you’ve got limited closet space, it also helps if the backpack can pull double duty and be used for travel and/or hiking. The backpacks below are ones either I or another WIRED reviewer have used extensively in real life, taking on planes, hiking trails, vacations, and work trips.
For more bag and backpack recommendations, Bag Check features WIRED staffers’ favorite totes, sleeves, and packs. For more portable gear, check out our guides to the Best Wireless Chargers, Best Bluetooth Trackers, and Best Travel Adapters.
Updated September 2026: I've added the Paramount Daypack Lite 20L and the Navigator Backpack to my main picks. I've also included the Eagle Creek Tour Lite Travel Pack, North Face Base Camp Voyager Pro, Bagsmart Moss Backpack, Brown Buffalo Conceal Pack, and GoRuck G1 to our honorable mentions list.
Featured Products
Best Laptop Bag
I took this backpack on a weeklong work trip, where I bitched about it endlessly to everyone who would listen. However, I must fairly and objectively conclude that this bag offers tremendous value for the money. It's a light, attractive, rucksack-style backpack that's sleek and understated enough for work, and it's under $120. The 27-liter capacity accommodated enough gear for a full day's worth of travel, from a scarf for the plane to a water bottle, snacks, and other in-flight accouterments. It has a slim profile and lies close to your back, so it's not hard to carry and won't swing into people on the subway. The pockets are very minimal—just an exterior laptop pocket, an interior tablet sleeve, an interior zip pocket, and two large catch-all pockets—but they work if you already put your belongings in pouches anyway.
Certain design elements just felt cheap. I didn't like the curved zipper that gives you access to the main compartment—zippers that don't run straight are doomed to get stuck. One of the catch-all pockets is annoyingly located on the cover flap, where anything inside will flap and bang around. The luggage pass-through is a bare piece of webbing. However, it all works: it's light, affordable, and looks nice. The fabric is also water-resistant, so you can wear it in the rain! For most people, that's all that really matters. —Adrienne So
Best Laptop Bag for Commuting
Thule's newest addition to its already solid backpack lineup was made specifically for schlepping gear to and from work on a daily basis, and it shows. The silhouette is sleek and aerodynamic, making it suitable for bike commuting (there's even a loop on the front to attach a bike light), and it's just big enough for a laptop, several notebooks, and maybe a jacket without feeling too big or bulky. The water bottle holder on the side is stretchy for a variety of sizes.
I also love the amount of organization inside for smaller things like pens and notebooks (the flap folds down for access to the interior, too, so you can access these things next to your desk), as well as the hidden yet easily accessible small pocket under the flap for wallet, keys, and phone. It's not the roomiest pack, so you're not carrying gym gear in this or taking it on an overnight trip, but if you're just going to and from the office with basics and a laptop, this is the most well-engineered option I've tried.
Best Laptop Bag for Travel
Aer has a lock on the tech-minimalist aesthetic with its no-frills, black Cordura bags; this is the larger version of the popular City Pack. Though there is a newer version of the Travel Pack—the Travel Pack 4 is supposedly more streamlined—my husband and I have both been using this bag constantly for two years and have zero complaints, which is rare. It's also still in pristine condition, despite going on at least 10 work trips between the two of us.
Any backpack need you might have, the Travel Pack can probably cover it, from hiking to one-bag travel. The front zip pocket has built-in organization for all your pens, cords, and notebooks, and the main compartment opens clamshell-style for packing cubes or gym gear. It covers all the bases without feeling too fiddly. However, note it's not the lightest pack and would likely be frustratingly bulky for commuters.
Best Minimalist Laptop Bag
I have never received as many approving comments on a backpack as I have when I tested this one on a three-day work trip (I was told by three people in a day that I sold them on it). It's a good-looking, structured bag with vegan leather accents and gigantic padded back panels and padded shoulder straps. There are little details like vegan leather pull tabs on the interior pockets, so you're not fumbling around for the pocket opening (I have never had this problem, but you do you). The fabric is also waterproof, and you can buy optional accessories like a rain cover.
I really liked the interior organization—for example, the padded, suspended tech pocket has two pockets, one for your laptop and one for your iPad or Kindle. However, all those padded panels and good-looking accents come at a price—this bag is disproportionately heavy. I couldn't go on a 20-minute bike ride without stopping to give my shoulders a break. Other details seem like they were designed by aliens who had never seen backpacks before. My tiny 18-ounce Owala tips right out of the water bottle pocket because its lip slants forward. The capacity is surprisingly small for how bulky it is, and a 100-percent plastic backpack just should not cost $249. However, everyone else loves this backpack, so here it is. —Adrienne So
Best Trendy Laptop Bag
Given that Comfrt is primarily known for its viral “airplane mode” hoodies, I was impressed with this au courant puffy backpack’s finish and construction for the price. (Though note there's no warranty, just a 30-day return policy.) My teen son has been testing it now for about three weeks, packing it to the gills and throwing it into his locker and on the ground for after-school sports. Though it looks like it might be fragile, the water-resistant polyester exterior still has nary a scratch or tear.
The straps are well-padded, the laptop compartment in the back is lined with a minky fabric, and there's a hidden pocket for valuables. It's also got a luggage pass-through and two generously sized pockets on either side for water bottles or whatever else (my son keeps a Shark ChillPill in one). Best yet, this pack fits far more than it seems like it will at 25 liters—more than some of the similar-sized backpacks on this list. It's perfect for high school or college students who need to pack in textbooks as well as incidentals and gym clothes. Color options include black (shown), navy, espresso, and pink.
Best Camera Bag
Gear editor Julian Chokkattu tests dozens of camera bags, and this roll-top model is his all-time favorite. It's a 2025 update to Wandrd's popular Prvke (pronouned "provoke") line, adding zippered access to the rolltop, a larger side-access opening, and more internal organization. Julian likes that it never feels cramped like other camera bags.
He also recommends pairing it with Wandrd's Essential Camera Cube (Photo Bundle) to get the most out of it. The straps and back are well padded, and he's been comfortable carrying it for hours.
Best Laptop Bag for Organization
The pockets on the front of this burly, workhorse are so versatile and accessible—five exterior organizational pockets, where most backpacks have one or two. You can access the laptop pocket from either the interior of the backpack or the side. There are internal compression straps, so you can tie things down or organize them inside the bag. It's made from PFC-free, Bluesign-certified, recycled, high-denier ballistic nylon. There are lots of thoughtful design details; for example, the water bottle pocket is in the center of the bag, and not the side, so carrying a full water bottle doesn't give you scoliosis after a long day. The zippers are YKK coil zippers, instead of toothed ones, so they don't get stuck or tear at your knuckles if you drag them against the zipper while rummaging around.
I have two complaints, which is that the backpack itself is slightly too tall for the luggage pass-through to work with my carry-on. The handle doesn't extend all the way through the pass-through. Also, all this hardware and sewing comes at a price. It is heavy, and it's expensive. But it will last you forever. I have this pink one, and my spouse has a 10-year-old black Synik 22 that still looks brand-new. —Adrienne So
Retrofit an Existing Backpack
WIRED's laptop expert, Luke Larsen, swears by this padded laptop sleeve if you don't need a full backpack or just want to add a bit more padding to your laptop (or multiple laptops). It's got plenty of room for accessories like a keyboard or laptop stand, and he was able to fit a power adapter and cable. He was able to barely fit the 16-inch size inside his Herschel laptop bag, but if you have a smaller laptop, the 14-inch size may be a better universal fit for most bags.
More Laptop Bags We Like
Eagle Creek Tour Lite Travel Pack for $159: This rugged yet lightweight pack features a lifetime warranty, a generously sized water bottle holder, a strap for carrying it horizontally, and one roomy clamshell-style compartment with compression straps. The laptop compartment is divided and well padded, and the beefy straps make the whole thing feel comfortable and well balanced. There just isn't enough organization to make it practical for work.
The North Face Base Camp Voyager Pro Travel Pack for $203: As an unrepentant overpacker, I love the modular system this bag is a part of—you can attach the either the smaller 15-liter Voyager Pro Lightweight Pack ($80) or Voyager Pro Crossbody ($75) to the front via clips and MOLL-E webbing, and the Base Camp Voyager Travel Pouch ($30) to one of the front straps for easy access to phone, keys, and passport. I carried both configurations around a weekend-long soccer tournament and felt like a decorator crab. (In the best way.) I did, however, find the larger and smaller backpacks a bit too big and small, respectively, for work, and the fabric to be a bit stiff and unyielding for daily use—it's likely best kept to outdoor pursuits.
Bagsmart Moss Backpack for $90: Another thoughtfully designed pack from Bagsmart, with the softest, minkiest laptop compartment of any pack I tested. It's on the smaller side, but I carried it for 4 miles full of groceries and felt nary a pinch or strain. The only issue I had was with the appearance—I thought it looked like something a college-aged girl would carry, but partway into my test period someone asked me if it was a little kids’ backpack, and now I can't unsee it.
The Brown Buffalo Conceal Pack for $239: Streamlined and sleek with a Cordura exterior, this bag features two pockets lined with a Velcro-type material to which you can affix organizers (not included), or you can slip a laptop into either one. I used this pack to commute to and from the hospital where my husband was having surgery, and because there's no smaller zip pouch, I wished I had one of the “Mods" to hold my phone and keys. I also had mixed feelings about the water bottle holder being inside the backpack, though it does make for a less lopsided carry.
GoRuck G1 for $395: This is WIRED operations manager Scott Gilbertson's do-anything, go-anywhere bag. He says it's the best backpack he's ever used and has been a trusty and versatile companion for the past three years. While it's made specifically for rucking, it's also got a laptop compartment, so you can tote your computer while you're marching up hills with other heavy things.
Janji Revy Pack for $198: I was going to include this as my best running backpack, since one way you can sneak exercise into your day is if you run to and fro from your home to your workplace, kids' school, or coffee shop. However, this backpack sold out before I could write about it, so the hunt continues. —Adrienne So
Away Commuter Backpack for $182: We very much like everything Away makes, from carry-on luggage to toiletry bags. This bag is attractive, water-resistant, and full of organized pockets; the hardware also feels premium. But $225 is steep, and we have other options with similar functionality for cheaper. —Adrienne So
Cotopaxi Allpa Travel Pack Del Dìa for $230: WIRED senior innovation writer Jeremy White loves Cotopaxi's Allpa Travel Pack so much he wrote an entire paean to it, praising the ethical manufacturing practices and ability to fill it with packing cubes. (It's also got a padded laptop slot.)
Able Carry Daily Backpack for $139: This pack is thin, so you can stuff it to the brim before it starts to get bulky. And stuff it full you can, because it has a pocket for everything. The Thirteen Daybag for $158 is similar but slightly smaller. —Adrienne So

Mission Workshop Rhake for $435: This roll-top bag has a ton of pockets, and its two-layer weatherproof construction and Velcro closures keep the contents dry. But those pockets aren't easy or fast to access, it's heavy, and it's even pricier than when we first tried it (and rising). —Adrienne So
Adventurist Classic Backpack for $65: This affordable, attractive backpack rings in at well under $100, and for every backpack purchased, 25 meals are donated to families across the United States. It's pretty much just a leather pouch that you wear on your back; however, the showy leather straps were annoying and useless. —Adrienne So

Where Civilians Are Hunted, Theater Endures: Kherson to Host International Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

The 28th Melpomena Tavrii International Theatre Festival will take place Sept. 12–19 under its longstanding motto, #TheaterWhereWeAre. Despite Russia’s war, the festival will return to Kherson, with performances also staged in Mykolaiv and at participating theaters across Ukraine.
Founded in 1999, Melpomena Tavrii has presented 610 productions by around 230 theaters from more than 100 cities and more than 20 countries.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Kyiv Post spoke with festival president and artistic director of the Mykola Kulish Kherson Theatre Oleksandr Knyha about why the festival continues in one of Ukraine’s most dangerous cities, what theater means to Kherson residents today and why keeping the stage alive has become an act of resistance.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Kyiv Post: Melpomena Tavrii continues despite the war, and in extremely difficult conditions. Why is it so important to keep the festival in Kherson?
Oleksandr Knyha: In 2022, after we escaped occupied Kherson, I wrote on social media: “Melpomena will definitely take place in Ukrainian Kherson. Despite everything!”
As soon as the city was liberated, we returned and began restoring the theater. Our team was scattered across Ukraine and Europe, while some people remained in occupied Kherson. We created a format that allowed our friends to participate and, most importantly, helped us tell the world what was happening in our city.
Zelensky Meets Negotiators Ahead of Talks With US Envoys
For us, Melpomena Tavrii has become a symbol of resistance. The festival was a symbol of Ukrainian identity even before the full-scale war.
The theater itself has been badly damaged. How do you work under these conditions?
We no longer work in our theater building because it is in a red zone. It has been heavily damaged and shelled, and we are trying to save it. Practically no windows remain. The roof is badly damaged.
On March 8, 2026, a rocket from a multiple-launch rocket system hit the theater roof. Had it landed about 10 centimeters higher, it would have hit the auditorium.
The team told me, “Let’s cancel the program. Nobody will come.”
I said, “No. We won’t cancel it. Even if one person comes, it will be therapy for that person.”
And the auditorium was full.
It turned out that even being destroyed, even having bombs falling around us, is not enough to stop us. We are needed.
People come to us like to a source – to drink healing water and keep going.
                                                                                                                                                                         
So theater has become a form of psychological support?
Yes. I don’t want to use overly grand words, but it really is a mission. It is our duty and our responsibility to people.
For years, we worked to make Kherson a theatrical city. We had six performance venues and could stage three productions simultaneously, all selling out. Audiences would line up at the box office.
Today, people write to me saying that simply knowing the theater is still working in Kherson gives them hope that they will return one day.
When people ask whether we ever considered moving the theater elsewhere, I say that we never even considered it.
We are together with our city and together with our people.
                                                                                                                                                                         
You have also taken the story of Kherson abroad. How do international audiences respond?
This summer we toured internationally and presented the monodrama “One-Day Hero” at the Mostra Internacional de Teatro in Portugal.
“One-Day Hero” is a performance based on Volodymyr Tuka’s play “Play22,” or “The Hero’s Journey.” At its center is the story of a Kherson veteran who witnessed the occupation, left the city and then joined the Armed Forces of Ukraine to defend his country. He was wounded while serving at a position. The actor is the playwright himself.
                                                                                                                                                                         
I was deeply moved by the Portuguese audience. After the performance, people stood in line to thank the actor and hug him.
One of the spectators was Turkish director Kubilay Eldelikara, chairman of the festival jury. He understood neither Ukrainian nor Portuguese and watched the performance through a translator on his phone. At the end, he was sitting with tears in his eyes, while his wife was crying.
The jury created a special award for Ukraine, and we also received an award for best direction.
It was a performance about our war and our experience – yet it touched people who had never lived through it themselves.
Kherson is facing another difficult winter. How does the humanitarian situation affect your work?
Winter is approaching, and the city’s thermal power plant has been destroyed. Last winter, we learned to save energy locally. We have two shelters where we work and only start heating them shortly before an event.
After the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam in 2023, German benefactors gave us several large stoves. We installed one in the staff café and prepared firewood from damaged trees.
We created a ritual. Spectators would first come into our café, where there was warmth, a fire, coffee and pastries we baked despite everything. Then we invited them into the auditorium.
We wanted to preserve not simply the possibility of watching a performance somewhere in a basement, but the atmosphere of hospitality that belongs to a theater.
This year we deliberately linked two cities: Sept. 12 is Mykolaiv City Day, and Sept. 19 is Kherson City Day.
Mykolaiv has become a refuge for us. When things become extremely difficult in Kherson, we can rest there or perform on a large stage.
For actors, that matters. They spend the year working in small spaces, basements or adapted venues. In Mykolaiv, they can step onto a large stage again.
Melpomena has retained its international character. Who will join the festival this year?
Georgia will definitely be represented, as will Portugal and Turkey. A Polish theater also wanted to join us.
For us, maintaining the festival’s international status is very important.
What personally keeps you going?
My family, my children, my wife, my Kherson.
I am an honorary citizen of Kherson. I was not born there – I was born on the Kinburn Spit, in the small village of Pokrovka, which is now occupied. But Kherson became my home.
I have led this theater for 36 years and have lived in Kherson all this time.
When people see me in the city, they say, “You’re in Kherson! That’s wonderful.”
I think that simply seeing me there is a symbol for them: “He didn’t betray us.”
Kherson has always been a city of many nationalities and cultures. That atmosphere is part of what I love about the city.
What are you working on now?
Together with director Serhii Pavliuk and our creative team, we have built what we call a Living Theater – a theater that brings people together, attracts them and supports them.
We are developing new projects, including a small, naive opera about Polina Raiko,one of the leading figures in the Ukrainian naïve art, and what we call the paradise destroyed by the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam.
We are also working with children. Together with Wings Foundation, we produced “Margarita and the Teddy Bears.” We held auditions in Kherson, right in bomb shelters, selected 14 children and worked with them for two months.
                                                                                                                                                                         
The play is about refugees in Poland. A mother tries to comfort her daughter by telling her how beautiful their new surroundings are. But the girl says she does not want to be there. She wants to go home to Kakhovka because her teddy bear is there.
Her teddy bear, like her home and street, was left underwater after the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam.
The production has toured across Ukraine, Poland and Slovakia. We are now negotiating a performance in Romania.
I understand our people very well because I am displaced myself. Everything we owned was left on the left bank of the Dnipro, in Oleshky. My own children are scattered around the world.
As a family, we dream of the time when we can all be together again.
What is your biggest dream now?
Of course, to return to Kherson and bring our entire team back together. To start working, working and working. To rebuild everything.
To bring my whole family together.
Over these years of war, we have accumulated so much anger – an enormous amount of anger. We have to channel it not into destruction, but into rebuilding and restoring all of Ukraine, and Kherson in particular.

Germany Finds Explosive Devices at Power Substations Amid Growing Sabotage Wave
German police discovered suspected explosive and incendiary devices near two electricity substations in Saxony as authorities investigate a series of recent attempts to disrupt the country’s energy infrastructure.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to German outlet Bild on September 5, the devices were found near substations in the Görlitz and Bautzen districts, close to the Brandenburg state border and facilities operated by energy company LEAG. Four devices were reportedly discovered near the Graustein substation and seven near the Berwalde substation.
Saxony Interior Minister Armin Schuster confirmed on September 4 that authorities were dealing with “unknown explosive devices” near two substations. Police in Görlitz said officers worked through the night to secure evidence, while searches of nearby high-voltage infrastructure continued.
The discoveries follow several similar incidents at German energy facilities in recent days. On September 2, suspected devices were found near a substation in Brandenburg, while another apparent act of sabotage occurred near Cologne.
Investigators are examining whether the incidents are connected. According to Bild, police received a letter on September 3 in which the author claimed responsibility for the latest incident and other attempted attacks on energy infrastructure over the previous week.
German media identified the suspected author as a 49-year-old man from North Rhine-Westphalia.
During a search of his apartment in Gevelsberg, investigators reportedly found potassium nitrate and potassium perchlorate, substances that can be used in explosive mixtures. The suspect was not at the property, and police later located his vehicle in a forest. A search for him remains underway.
The author of previous letters had reportedly described the attacks as opposition to fossil-fuel energy. Several of the targeted substations are located in regions associated with lignite mining and electricity generation.
The cases come amid broader security concerns surrounding German critical infrastructure. German authorities have recorded more than 165 suspected sabotage incidents since the beginning of 2026, alongside nearly 750 cases involving suspicious drones over military sites and critical infrastructure, according to German media reports.

Greek PM rules out snap elections after unveiling tax cuts, wage hikes

Greek PM rules out snap elections after unveiling tax cuts, wage hikes
ATHENS, Sept 6 - Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis ruled out snap elections on Sunday a day after announcing a string of tax cuts and wage hikes, as he seeks to recover lost ground in opinion polls ahead of a general election due next year.
His centre-right government, which was re-elected with 40.5% of the vote in 2023 promising to increase incomes, remains ahead in opinion polls but support has slipped to below 30% amid a protracted cost-of-living crisis and allegations of corruption.
"Elections will be held in spring 2027," he said during a press briefing on Sunday, dismissing media speculation about snap elections this year. He added that he believed his party could still secure an outright majority and win a third consecutive four-year term.
On Saturday, Mitsotakis announced income tax breaks and wage hikes worth €3.5 billion ($4.06 billion), equivalent to 1.5% of GDP, to be rolled out over the next four years. He also pledged to cut unemployment to 6% and reduce public debt to below 110% of GDP by 2030.
The measures include an annual bonus of €400 for pensioners and €500 for public servants, a zero tax rate on annual incomes of up to €20,000 for farmers and families with three children, and a gradual reduction in advance tax payments for the self-employed and businesses to 50%.
After a financial crisis in 2009 that triggered fears Greece would crash out of the euro zone, the country is now one of the best-performing in Europe.
Greece's economy is expanding at an annual rate of 2%, outpacing the euro zone average. It expects a primary surplus of about 4% this year, double what was initially expected, giving fiscal space to fund the new measures. REUTERS

Can you guess the real size of each country on the new world map?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:15:09 UTC
20:15:09 KST

Can you guess the real size of each country on the new world map?
Pick which country is bigger, then watch it morph from Mercator to Equal Earth projection to see how close you were.
The map of Africa is much larger than most people think. However, most classroom maps and atlases still understate it – a distortion embedded in the Mercator projection that has shaped world maps for more than four centuries.
The distortion in question is not subtle. On a Mercator map, which was designed for European colonial exploration and maritime trade in the 16th century, Greenland appears roughly the size of Africa, which is actually about 14 times larger.
The exaggeration increases the farther you travel from the equator, so it falls almost entirely on one half of the world, inflating Europe, including Russia, and North America while shrinking Africa, Latin America and South Asia.
To address this, the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) voted 164 to 1 on Friday to adopt a resolution promoting the Equal Earth projection, which shows continents in their true proportions, as an alternative to Mercator.
Led by Togo on behalf of the African Group and backed by the African Union, it encourages schools, institutions and tech companies to switch, correcting the shrinking of Africa and other equatorial regions. The African Group is the largest regional voting and dialogue bloc at the UN, consisting of 54 African Union member states.
Map quiz: Pick the bigger country
See it for yourself: pick which country is bigger, then watch it morph from Mercator to Equal Earth to see how close you were.
How did countries vote?
The United States was the only country to vote against the resolution calling the measure a “radical ideological project”. Serbia, Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova and Ukraine abstained.
US representative Yaryna Ferencevych said before the vote that the resolution is “the reason this institution is losing its credibility”. “Instead of focusing on genuine problems … this body is debating map projects from the 16th century,” she said.
Friday’s resolution is nonbinding, intended only to encourage the world’s default maps to change. The UN said it does not ban Mercator or impose a replacement, but simply encourages wider use of the Equal Earth projection.
Togo’s Foreign Minister Robert Dussey told the UNGA that maps shape education, imagination and collective perception, and that the resolution affirms African reality.
The African Union adopted Equal Earth in March. Togo is planning a meeting in Lome early next year, with UNESCO, the African Union and technology companies including Google, to work out what implementation looks like in practice.
Why flat maps lie
Every flat map lies because the Earth is a sphere and no projection can flatten it without distorting something: shape, area, distance or direction.
Gerardus Mercator, a cartographer and geographer who published the world map in 1569, chose to preserve angles and straight bearings, a trade-off that made sense for 16th-century ships but has kept shaping perceptions of the world for nearly 500 years since. Equal Earth makes the opposite trade-off, preserving true area so continents can be compared honestly, at the cost of slightly bending their outlines.

23 dead, over 310 cholera cases reported in Sudan’s West Kordofan: Local group
Unknown

Adel Abdelrahim and Sahin Demir
06 September 2026•Update: 06 September 2026
At least 23 people have died and more than 310 cholera cases and suspected infections have been reported in two areas of West Kordofan in southern Sudan, a local relief group said Sunday.
The Dar Hamar Emergency Room, a community-based relief organization, warned in two separate statements of deteriorating health and humanitarian conditions in Humeir village and Hilla Hussein in Al-Udayyah locality.
The group said Humeir was facing a “serious health situation,” with 120 suspected cholera cases admitted to an isolation center and 11 deaths recorded.
It said the isolation center lacked intravenous fluids and life-saving medicines as the number of suspected cases continued to rise.
The group appealed to health authorities and humanitarian organizations to urgently provide medical supplies, warning that conditions could deteriorate further.
In a separate statement, the group said the health and humanitarian crisis had worsened in Hilla Hussein, where more than 190 cholera cases and 12 deaths from the disease had been recorded.
Transportation disruptions have isolated the area and made it difficult to evacuate critically ill patients for treatment, it added.
The group also warned of a worsening food crisis, saying conditions had forced some residents to use animal feed to provide for their children.
It called on humanitarian organizations to immediately provide medicines and food assistance to residents.
The group did not specify the period during which the deaths, confirmed cases and suspected infections were recorded in the two areas.
On July 14, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned that continued fighting and disease outbreaks were taking a heavy toll on civilians across Sudan.
The World Health Organization said on July 7 that 1,330 confirmed cholera cases and 114 deaths had been recorded amid the outbreak in Sudan.
Sudan has been engulfed in a conflict between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since April 2023, killing tens of thousands of people and displacing around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

“At its current pace, it would take the Russian occupiers over two years to capture that remaining land.,” he said.

20:13:23 KST

The Tel Aviv District Court convicted former UTrade chief analyst Roy Cuzin on Sunday of helping the algorithmic-trading company obtain approximately NIS 77 million from some 600 clients through fraud.
Cuzin pleaded guilty to multiple counts of aiding aggravated fraud. Judge Dana Amir convicted him after prosecutors filed an amended indictment setting out a narrower account of his role in the scheme.
The prosecution and defense will jointly ask the court to sentence Cuzin to 22 months in prison and impose a NIS 25,000 fine.
Cuzin served as UTrade’s chief analyst from 2012 to 2015. The company offered automated trading services using an algorithm that selected investments for its clients.
Under its agreements with customers, UTrade was required to return their investments within seven to 10 days of a withdrawal request.
UTrade owed customers NIS 42 million by end of 2015
The amended indictment states that the company’s recruitment process relied on false claims and the concealment of important information about its operations. Among other things, prospective clients were given misleading information about the separation of customer and company funds, potential conflicts of interest, and regulatory oversight.
Cuzin admitted specifically to helping present customers with false figures about UTrade’s previous investment returns. Because he supervised the company’s trading program and had access to its trading accounts, he knew the figures did not reflect the company’s actual performance, according to the amended indictment.
UTrade encountered financial difficulties in 2015 after much of its customers’ money was used for company expenses and other investments – rather than trading.
As the company struggled to meet withdrawal requests, Cuzin helped owner and manager Aviv Talmor persuade dozens of customers to accept repayment plans lasting several months. Customers were told the delays resulted from temporary technical difficulties, without being informed of the company’s financial condition.
Cuzin also helped sign customers to agreements promising accounts “protected against losses” if they left their money with UTrade for 12 months. He admitted he knew that leaving the funds with the company put them at risk.
By the end of 2015, UTrade owed its customers approximately NIS 42m, while its customer account held only about NIS 173,000 and $50,000, according to the amended indictment.
The indictment draws an important distinction between Cuzin’s conduct and that of Talmor. It states that Talmor directed the unauthorized transfer of customer funds without Cuzin’s knowledge. Cuzin’s conviction concerns his assistance in presenting false returns and persuading customers to leave their money with the company or accept delayed repayment.
Talmor was previously convicted in the affair. The Supreme Court increased his sentence from four to five years in prison in 2024 and left a NIS 250,000 fine in place.
Cuzin was questioned under caution in 2016 and left Israel shortly afterward. He and several others were indicted in 2018, but the proceedings against him could not advance while he remained abroad.
After moving among several countries, Cuzin was arrested in Mexico in July 2025. Mexican authorities approved his extradition in December, and Israel returned him in January to stand trial.
James Genn contributed to this report.

AfD nears first far-right victory in Germany since World War II as Saxony-Anhalt votes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:13:07 UTC
20:13:07 KST

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) surged into first place in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, exit polls showed, putting a far-right party on the cusp of power at state level for the first time since World War Two.
The AfD won 44.4% of the vote, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservatives trailing well behind on 18.3%, and the center-left Social Democrats and environmental Greens both clearing the minimum threshold to enter parliament, according to an exit poll from the ARD broadcaster.
As counting continued, it remained unclear whether the AfD had secured enough votes to win an absolute majority in parliament. But the wider political significance of the election, which saw turnout over 80%, according to the ZDF broadcaster, was clear.
"We have made history in this country," said Ulrich Siegmund, the 35-year-old AfD lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, who drew thousands to his campaign rallies and who repeatedly cast victory in the state as a first step towards securing national power in federal elections due in 2029.
The vote is seen as a barometer for the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has attempted to chip away at the AfD's popularity by taking a tougher line on migration and security.
Recent surveys place the AfD at just over 40%, followed by Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) at 23%.
An absolute majority would allow AfD to bypass efforts to keep party blocked
An absolute majority would allow the AfD to bypass mainstream parties' efforts to keep the party blocked out of power by refusing to work with it under a longstanding "firewall" policy.
Achieving an absolute majority is a high bar to clear in Germany's proportional electoral system, which was designed in part to encourage coalition governments and make it difficult for one party to rule alone.
If the AfD falls short of an outright majority, a CDU-led administration under incumbent state premier Sven Schulze is the most likely outcome, though the exact shape of any coalition would depend on which parties enter.
Weeks of coalition talks could follow Sunday's vote.
AfD 'can no longer be stopped'
For the AfD, the Saxony-Anhalt election is a stepping stone towards its larger ambitions of securing national power in the next federal election scheduled for 2029.
"No matter the outcome of tomorrow's election, we have already made history," said Siegmund at a final rally on Saturday evening.
"Because what we have started here in Saxony-Anhalt – that is currently sweeping across all of Germany – can no longer be stopped," he told the crowd in the state capital, Magdeburg.
Should it win, the AfD plans to shift schools and cultural institutions towards more traditional values, marginalize immigrants and deeply reform the public broadcasting system.
However, without an absolute majority, the AfD, which has been classified as "far-right extremist" by the state security service, would struggle to enter government due to the firewall.
Siegmund, who arrived to cast his vote in his hometown of Tangermuende on a blue Simson moped, greeted by throngs of excited fans, has ruled out entering a coalition with other parties.
He argues that it is impossible for the AfD to govern with the mainstream politicians who have been driving Germany into the ground over the past three decades and instead is aiming to win 45% or more of the vote.
Falling short of that opens the prospect of complex coalition negotiations, dependent on which parties can hit the 5% hurdle.
Polls show one of the CDU's current coalition partners, the Free Democratic Party, falling short, while the other, the Social Democratic Party (SPD), is under 10%.
The small far-left Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), the only party that has not ruled out a coalition with the AfD, is also likely to miss out.
For Schulze, who is favored in polls as voters' top choice for leader, combining with the SPD and Greens might not be enough for a majority, but the CDU has ruled out a coalition with the far-left Left Party that could help it reach that threshold.
One option could be a minority government led by Schulze that would depend on passive tolerance from the Left – a model used in the neighboring eastern German state of Thuringia.
