My Brief Summer Fling With Siri AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

When I first tested the developer beta of Apple's Siri AI by taking it as my tour guide around San Francisco, I was convinced the overhauled smartphone assistant would be an “everything tool” on the iPhone. The answers felt reliable enough and more helpful than previous versions of Siri. Also, the chatbot-style app for Siri felt very sleek, very Apple-y.
Over the next month, I kept experimenting with the Siri AI in the iOS 27 beta. The tool was quite powerful, especially with the personal context brought in by indexing the contents of my phone. Finding an ancient text message or photo has never been easier. Even so, my usage of the smartphone assistant slowly started tapering off.
It’s not that Siri AI isn’t better now. It is! This new version is quite the step change, which makes my reaction even more devastating. Siri AI isn’t revolutionizing how I interact with my phone the way I'd initially hoped, especially as an AI assistant built directly into the device and factoring in that Apple gives more thought to preserving my privacy than many other AI companies.
Even though I wasn't going out of my way to interact with Siri AI, I didn’t mind how it was now, essentially, the search bar for the smartphone. As the summer months faded, I wasn’t souring on Siri AI. Instead, I just grew more neutral.
Old habits die hard. Soon I was back to my regularly scheduled doomscrolling on Instagram and aimless Yelp expeditions. I was manually typing and swiping for myself rather than relying on a smartphone assistant for help. And I was already low-key locked in with another chatbot, Anthropic’s Claude, and already used that app fairly often on my phone.
Even though some AI power users may not go all in on this new Siri, analysts say this won’t matter, since everyday users are often fine with Apple’s default software. “Will Siri bear the weight of criticism for not being as good as some of its peers? Sure,” says Dipanjan Chatterjee, vice president and principal analyst at Forrester, a research and consultancy company. “Will it make a difference to the vast installed base of iPhone users and cause them to look elsewhere? Not a chance.” Some iPhone users trust Apple with their data in ways they don't with any other company. Siri AI may reap those same benefits.
Tech analysts see Apple’s long-cultivated consumer trust in data privacy as potentially a compelling distinction. Ramon Llamas, a research director analyzing the mobile device market at the International Data Corporation, believes users deep in the Apple ecosystem, who previously had qualms about the safety of other AI tools, may be open to trying the new Siri.
My experience with Siri AI—loving it and then leaving it for dust—may be an outlier. Many other beta testers are still rocking with the smartphone assistant.
“In the past, I was unwilling to trust that Siri could do anything useful,” says Avi Greengart, founder and lead analyst at Techsponential. “But with the latest beta software, I'm finding myself not only using it more, but for more things: Siri is now able to find information buried on my phone faster and more efficiently than any other method, its world knowledge is vastly better than before, and even dictation works better.”
That said, the cultural backlash to generative AI has been brewing. Another solid segment of iPhone owners may choose to avoid the new Siri altogether because of the AI attached to its name. Whether it’s a moral objection or broader distrust of AI tools, these holdouts are unlikely to be won over by Siri’s feature improvements.
Ultimately, my own summer fling with Siri AI was short-lived. But I promise, it’s not you. It’s me.

These Cyborg Cockroaches Could Save Your Life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Small robots and drones have increasingly been used to help respond to disasters, reaching locations that are too hard or too dangerous to send humans, such as collapsed buildings. Many of these efforts have been focused on search and rescue. But new research shows how bugs—with their ability to crawl through even narrower gaps in rubbled—outfitted with electrodes could be used as the next generation of first responders.
A research team from the University of Queensland (UQ) and the University of New South Wales (UNSW) have developed the “Paraborg” to not only help with searching for victims, but also administer first aid. While the idea of receiving medical care from a cockroach might be a little skin-crawling, the new cyborg bug could one day help buy human rescuers valuable time in a disaster zone.
“Cyborg insects have been designed for ‘search and explore’ missions for the past couple of decades,” Tan Vo Doan, a bio-robotics researcher at UQ, says in a press release. “We wanted to take the next step.”
The team relied on a giant burrowing cockroach that inhabits northern Queensland to develop the Paraborg, which they documented in a recent paper published the journal Advanced Science. The armored cockroach is up to 87 millimeters (3.5 inches) in length and weighs up to 40 grams (1.4 ounces).
Taking advantage of this large size, the research team developed two types of Paraborgs with different functions: one equipped with a camera to film the condition of disaster victims, and another with an automatic injection mechanism to administer medication. Cockroaches can carry up to 1.5 times its body weight. In practice, a cockroach equipped with the injection mechanism saw its total height increase by about 15 millimeters and its weight by about 17 grams, which the study found did not significantly impair its normal movements. To create the cyborg cockroaches, the team anesthetized them when the electrodes and microchips were attached, and they lived as normal cockroaches once the equipment was removed.
By applying electrical stimuli to electrodes embedded in the cockroach’s antennae and cerci—a pair of protruding sensory organs at the rear of the abdomen—researchers were able to remotely control the bug’s direction of travel and walking speed.
They were able to steer the roach by stimulating each antenna independently, while stimulating both cerci controlled the pace. The scientists administered different frequencies between 10 and 40 hertz after finding that anything over 50 hertz became ineffective over time.
The injection mechanism is a small device that deploys a syringe using a spring system. That triggers a process that breaks the seal between a chamber containing citric acid and another containing baking soda. The resulting chemical reaction—basically the same one you might’ve done as a kid to make a volcano with baking soda and vinegar—creates enough carbon dioxide to push the plunger on the syringe and administer medication.
For the study, the research team remotely controlled a cockroach to travel from its starting point through three checkpoints and administer an injection to a simulated target.
The results showed that the success rate for injections made at close range—within 150 millimeters of the target—topped out at approximately 95 percent. The success rate for the entire sequence of tasks—from departure to completion of the injection—was 72 percent.
The researchers also successfully demonstrated teamwork, where one cockroach uses a camera to locate a simulated target while another serves as the injector.
Although the research team has previously developed cyborg beetles capable of climbing vertical walls, they note that larger cockroaches are better-suited for carrying specialized rescue and medical equipment.
While the results of the new research are promising, the experiment didn’t replicate the complex environmental conditions found at actual disaster sites, such as debris, uneven terrain, and shifting landscapes.
Vo Doan expressed hope that, if resources can be secured to speed up research and field testing, a rescue team of cyborg insects could be deployed at actual disaster sites within five to 10 years.
“Rather than building one robot to do everything, we can harness the natural strengths of different insects and equip them for different missions,” Vo-Doan says.
This story was originally published in WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

19 lakh lives impacted as Ganga breaches flood mark in Patna
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:29:53 UTC
19:29:53 KST

The Ganga was flowing at 50.57 metres at Gandhi Ghat at 6am on Sunday, 0.05 metres above its previous highest flood level (HFL) of 50.52 metres recorded on August 21, 2016.
NEW DELHI: More than 19.57 lakh people have been affected by floods across 11 districts of Bihar as of Sunday, with authorities putting downstream areas on high alert. This comes after the Ganga, following heavy rain, crossed its previous highest flood level at Gandhi Ghat in Patna.The Ganga was flowing at 50.57 metres at Gandhi Ghat at 6am on Sunday, 0.05 metres above its previous highest flood level (HFL) of 50.52 metres recorded on August 21, 2016. While the trend was stable at Gandhi Ghat, authorities warned that Hathidah and subsequent gauge stations could be affected over the next one to three days.
The rising water levels have prompted heightened vigilance across several downstream districts, with officials monitoring river levels, embankments, vulnerable locations and low-lying areas and keeping rescue machinery ready.
19.57 lakh people affected across 11 districts
According to officials, flooding has affected around 19.57 lakh people in 330 gram panchayats across Patna, Bhojpur, Saran, Vaishali, Bhagalpur, Begusarai, Buxar, Samastipur, Munger, Katihar and Araria.The latest figures indicate a worsening impact compared with earlier assessments, when around 16.85 lakh people across 61 blocks and 300 gram panchayats had been reported affected.With several rivers continuing to flow above danger levels, authorities have intensified relief and rescue operations in the affected districts.
The Water Resources Department has warned that the Ganga at Hathidah may also cross its previous HFL, increasing the risk for Begusarai, Lakhisarai, Munger, Bhagalpur and Katihar.“Officials and field-level authorities have been directed to remain alert and continuously monitor water levels, embankments, vulnerable locations and low-lying areas, while taking precautionary measures as required.“Engineers have been asked to keep flood-control resources and machinery ready. People in affected areas have been advised to avoid going near the river and remain cautious,” the advisory stated.Local administrations have also been asked to keep a close watch on boat operations, prevent overloading and ensure residents receive regular updates about the flood situation.
Ganga breaches danger levels at several locations
The Ganga is above the danger mark at several locations in Bihar.At Buxar, the river was 0.08 metres above the danger mark, although its level was declining. At Dighaghat in Patna, it was 1.54 metres above the danger mark, while at Gandhi Ghat it stood 1.96 metres above it.At Hathidah, the Ganga was 1.74 metres above the danger mark and continued to rise. Munger recorded a level 0.51 metres above the danger mark, with the river showing a rising trend.The river was also 2.01 metres above the danger mark at Sultanganj and 0.65 metres above it at Bhagalpur. The Ganga remained above the danger mark at Kahalgaon as well.At Pandarak in Patna, the river was flowing at 43.92 metres at 6 am, 0.19 metres above its previous HFL of 43.73 metres recorded on August 16, 2021.In contrast, the Ganga remained below the warning level in Prayagraj and Varanasi. Its level was rising in Prayagraj but declining in Varanasi.
Several rivers remain above danger levels
The flood threat is not confined to the Ganga. Several other rivers in Bihar are also flowing above their respective danger levels.The Gandak is above the danger mark at Dumariaghat and Hajipur, while the Kosi has crossed the mark at Baltara and Kursela. The Budhi Gandak is above the danger level at Khagaria.The Punpun is above the danger mark at Sripalpur, while the Bagmati has crossed it at Benibad. The Ghaghra is also flowing above the danger level at Darauli.The combination of rising river levels and further rainfall has kept authorities on alert, particularly in downstream and low-lying areas.
Relief operations expanded across flood-hit districts
The administration has deployed significant resources to assist people affected by the floods.A total of 110 community kitchens are currently operating in various districts to provide food to affected residents. Earlier official figures had put the number of operational community kitchens at 80, with around 1.21 lakh people receiving meals through them.One relief camp is also operational, providing accommodation, food, medical assistance and other essential facilities to 326 flood-affected people.Authorities have distributed around 45,900 polythene sheets and 11,700 dry ration packets as part of relief efforts.Boats are being used extensively to evacuate residents and maintain movement in areas affected by rising waters. The latest deployment stands at 1,345 boats across the state, compared with 1,158 reported earlier.
SDRF, NDRF teams deployed
With the possibility of further flooding, 27 State Disaster Response Force teams and 10 National Disaster Response Force teams have been deployed across different districts.The teams have been tasked with undertaking rapid relief and rescue operations, while district administrations continue to monitor vulnerable areas and river embankments.Officials have also been instructed to ensure that flood-control equipment and machinery remain ready for deployment as required.
Rain forecast raises concern over further rise
The flood situation could remain challenging over the coming days as the Bihar Meteorological Service Centre has forecast light to moderate rainfall at several places across the state over the next two days.Heavy rainfall is also possible at some locations.Authorities are therefore preparing for the possibility of further increases in river levels, particularly in areas already affected by flooding. The state government and district administrations are continuing to monitor the situation and deploy relief materials, boats and rescue teams according to local requirements.
Rail services affected on Patna-Gaya section
The flooding has also disrupted railway operations in parts of the state.The East Central Railway said on Sunday that some trains had been cancelled or diverted because of the “alarmingly high water level at bridge number 21" connecting Punpun and Parsa Bazar stations on the Patna-Gaya section.The development adds to the disruption caused by rising waters as authorities continue to focus on evacuation, relief and the safety of residents in flood-affected areas.
Barrage discharge data recorded at 9 am on Sunday showed that the Sone Barrage at Indrapuri was releasing 2,27,739 cusecs of water, although the flow was declining.The Kosi Barrage at Birpur was releasing 1,68,400 cusecs, with the discharge remaining stable. The Gandak Barrage at Valmikinagar was releasing 1,29,000 cusecs, also with a stable trend.With multiple rivers remaining above danger levels, further rainfall forecast over the next two days and the Ganga already having crossed its previous HFL at Gandhi Ghat, authorities have urged residents in vulnerable areas to remain cautious and avoid approaching swollen rivers.

2026-09-06
10:28:43 UTC
19:28:43 KST

The decision to make Aliyah can take years. Sometimes it develops over months, and sometimes it follows a single moment that changes everything. But once the ticket is booked and the suitcases begin to close, the big questions about Zionism, identity and belonging quickly give way to much more practical ones.
What do you do on your first day? Where do you register? How do you receive your documents? Which health fund should you choose? When do you open a bank account? What happens to money left overseas? How do you find a job without starting your career from scratch? And if something happens in the middle of the night, who do you call?
On September 8, ynet Global will hold the Global Aliyah Live Summit, a special international day of broadcasts devoted to Aliyah and the life that comes after it.
The summit will be broadcast in Hebrew, English, Russian and French, bringing together senior public officials, Aliyah and absorption organizations, and experts in healthcare, banking, employment and housing with the people currently experiencing the process themselves: new immigrants.
The first 24 hours: you landed. What now?
One of the summit’s central panels will focus on the moment when months or years of preparation suddenly become reality: the first 24 hours in Israel.
After the flight, the welcome and the first photo in the country comes Israeli bureaucracy, which can feel like an entirely new system that newcomers have to learn from scratch.
Which documents do you receive when you arrive? What has to be done immediately and what can wait? How do you begin dealing with government offices? When should you register with a health fund? How do you open a bank account? What benefits are available to new immigrants, and how do you access them?
The panel will bring those different steps together and help make sense of the stage when everything is unfamiliar, from the country and language to the systems and unwritten rules of daily life.
What to do before you board the plane
Some of the mistakes new immigrants make begin before they ever land in Israel.
The summit will therefore also focus on the days and weeks before Aliyah: which documents to bring, what to arrange with banks in the country of origin, what to do with savings and assets abroad, when to start looking for work in Israel and which arrangements can be completed before departure.
But those final days are not only about lists and documents. New immigrants participating in the summit will also talk about the moment Aliyah stops being an idea and becomes real: saying goodbye to family and friends, leaving a job, packing up a home, dealing with uncertainty and realizing that within days they will need to build a new routine in another country.
The money stays the same. The rules change
Opening a bank account in Israel may sound like a technical step, but for new immigrants it can raise an entire set of questions.
A special financial panel, featuring experts and representatives including Bank Leumi and mortgage advisers, will explain how financial life in Israel works for newcomers.
How do you transfer money from abroad? What happens when some income or assets remain overseas? How does Israel’s credit system work? What should you know about foreign currency, fees and international transfers?
The discussion will also move to a question many olim face later: whether and when to buy a home in Israel.
Mortgage advisers will explain what purchasing property looks like from a new immigrant’s perspective and what should be checked before making one of the biggest financial decisions of a lifetime.
You made Aliyah. Your career does not have to stay behind
A doctor, engineer, tech professional, teacher, executive or entrepreneur can arrive in Israel with 10 or 20 years of experience and discover that the first challenge is explaining to the local job market who they are.
That is why one of the summit’s major topics will be how to bring your career with you.
Employment specialists, including representatives of centers that work with new immigrants, will address questions facing almost every working-age oleh: When should you begin searching? How should a résumé be adapted for the Israeli market? How do you build a professional network from scratch? Which professions require Israeli licensing? And what happens when substantial overseas experience does not automatically translate into an equivalent position in Israel?
The discussions will also cover entrepreneurship, retraining and the options available to those who want to start a business.
The goal is not simply to help newcomers find work, but to help them bring to Israel the knowledge, experience and skills they have already spent years building.
Health funds, family doctors and one number to remember
Israel’s healthcare system can also take time to understand, particularly for people arriving from countries where medical care works very differently.
Representatives from Clalit Health Services will explain how to register with a health fund, choose a doctor, make appointments and access services available to new immigrants from the beginning of their lives in Israel.
The summit will also address a question nobody wants to face but everyone needs to know how to answer: what happens in a medical emergency?
A dedicated segment will explain how to contact Magen David Adom, what happens after dialing 101, what information dispatchers need and what new immigrants should know about Israel’s emergency medical system.
Among all the new phone numbers, passwords and apps that come with moving countries, 101 is one number worth knowing from day one.
Not just talking about olim, but talking with them
Alongside officials, experts and organizations, the summit will also feature new immigrants at different stages of their lives in Israel, and they will not be there only to tell success stories.
They will talk about what surprised them, what was harder than expected, where bureaucracy caught them unprepared, what their first weeks looked like, how they found a job or apartment and what they know now that they wish they had known before boarding the plane.
That combination of official information and firsthand experience will be one of the summit’s central themes.
Sometimes the best answer to a question from someone planning Aliyah comes from someone who made it a month ago.
From the Ministry of Aliyah to the Jewish Agency
The Global Aliyah Live Summit will feature senior officials and representatives from many of the central organizations involved in Aliyah and integration in Israel, including the Ministry of Aliyah and Integration, the Jewish Agency for Israel, the World Zionist Organization, Keren Hayesod, Ofek Israeli, Nefesh B’Nefesh, Clalit Health Services, Bank Leumi, the Jerusalem Municipality, Masa Israel Journey and Magen David Adom, along with employment organizations, advisers and other professionals.
Participants will also include the Minister of Aliyah and Integration and the chairman of the Jewish Agency, who will address the broader picture: Who is making Aliyah today? What has changed in recent waves of immigration? What barriers still confront newcomers? And what does Israel need to do not only to bring Jews to the country, but to help them stay and succeed?
Broadcast schedule, Israel time
13:00-14:00 — Live broadcast in Russian, in cooperation with Vesti
14:00-17:00 — Live broadcast in English on ynet Global and ynet
17:00-18:00 — Live broadcast in French on ynet Global
Four languages, one country
The September 8 broadcast will be held in Hebrew, English, Russian and French and is intended both for people already in Israel and for Jews around the world at different stages of planning Aliyah.
Throughout the day, the discussions will cover nearly every part of starting a new life in Israel: healthcare, money, work, housing, mortgages, rights, bureaucracy, community and everyday life.
Behind all of those practical questions is one larger one: How do you turn the dream of Aliyah into a life that actually works?
ynet Global’s Global Aliyah project has been following olim and prospective immigrants throughout the year with guides, articles, personal stories and practical information about life in Israel. On September 8, that conversation moves live.
For those who have already booked a ticket, those planning to arrive within the next year and those still sitting in Paris, London, New York, Toronto or Moscow wondering whether the time has come, the summit is designed to offer answers to the large and small questions that come with the decision.
Because Aliyah does not end when you land at Ben Gurion Airport.
That is where it really begins.

The entrance of the Higher Education Board headquarters in Ankara. (AA Photo)
The Higher Education Board (YÖK) has launched an investigation into 23 foundation universities for exceeding the 25 percent tuition hike cap set for the 2026–2027 academic year.
The move follows a July 8 directive capping tuition increases for returning students at 25 percent, an upper limit that excludes preparatory and first-year classes.
According to a YÖK statement issued on Sept. 4, the investigation was launched following complaints that certain universities exceeded the tuition increase cap, reinforcing regulatory oversight and preventing unauthorized fee hikes.
As part of the investigation launched following the claims from students and parents received by YÖK, the tuition fees set by these universities will be compared with the actual rate of increase charged to students.
Within the scope of the investigation, the authorities are going to examine whether the tuition increases implemented by the private universities in question exceed 25 percent.
However, details regarding which universities are included in the investigation were not disclosed in the statement.
In an earlier statement, YÖK had announced that applications, reports and complaints deemed to have resulted in adverse consequences for students would be reviewed daily and with utmost urgency.

Germany, Kosovo unite against ticks carrying deadly virus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:25:00 UTC
19:25:00 KST

Germany, Kosovo unite against ticks carrying deadly virus
September 6, 2026
It can spot its prey from up to 200 meters (about 650 feet) away — but unlike many of its fellow species, it doesn't lurk in the grass waiting for its victim to come closer. Instead it runs after it, chasing animals and humans alike.
The Hyalomma tick, often called "the great hunting tick," was previously found mostly in Africa, Asia, and southern Europe. But climate change means it can now survive further north and it has already been spotted in Germany and various Eastern European countries. Kosovo, in southeastern Europe, has been a hot spot for the tick for some time now.
The Hyalomma tick is also a vector of the highly pathogenic virus for Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a potentially deadly disease with a high fatality rate. Symptoms of the disease are comparable to those of Ebola fever or the Marburg virus. These are capable of destroying blood and lymphatic vessels, which can lead to internal bleeding and death.
Kurtesh Sherifi first read about Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever in the newspaper in 2005, when he was completing his studies as a veterinarian in Berlin. The article said that 11 people in his homeland, Kosovo, had contracted the disease and five had died. He was already interested in pathogens that can be transmitted between animals and humans, known as zoonoses, and Crimean-Congo fever intrigued him.
Back home, Sherifi started work with the faculty of agriculture and veterinary medicine at the University of Pristina. But the budget for research was tight. Kosovo, a small country with only about 1.6 million citizens, didn't have a high-security laboratory or the equipment necessary for investigating the Crimean-Congo fever virus.
Seeking German cooperation
Sherifi got in touch with Germany's largest institution for study in this area, the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg.
One of the researchers was Petra Emmerich, a virologist and expert on what are known as Risk Group 4 viruses — viruses that cause severe, often fatal, diseases and usually have no widely available treatment. The Crimean-Congo virus is in that risk group.
Emmerich also acts as a reservist in the German military, which is especially interested in viruses that could be used as biological weapons. She was sent to Kosovo in 2009, which is when she met Sherifi.
A lively exchange began between the researchers. In Kosovo, a structure was established to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma tick and the virus. In 2013, the researchers' joint work began to receive funding through the German Biosecurity Program, run by the country's Foreign Ministry and "intended to help partner countries tackle biological threats."
"It's give and take," said Emmerich of the scientific partnership. "We have the diagnostic expertise and the necessary resources but we don't have the patients." Doctors from Germany regularly come to Kosovo with Emmerich where they can exchange information with their counterparts there.
Raising public awareness is another important pillar of the Germany-Kosovo cooperation.
Farmers in Kosovo are particularly susceptible to infection — and not solely due to ticks biting them, but because they often use their bare hands to remove ticks from animals. If infected blood from the animals gets into a small wound on the human hand, the virus can be transmitted to the human.
"This is quite likely how a large proportion of the [infected] population in Kosovo got infected," Sherifi explained.
Patients require intensive care, isolation
He and Emmerich have visited schools to educate students about the dangers of the virus and how to protect against it. For example, certain tick repellents help, as do long pants and sturdy shoes.
Not all Hyalomma ticks carry the virus, and most people who are bitten by a Hyalomma tick do not become ill. However, the larger problem is that there is neither a vaccine nor any specific course of treatment for those who do end up suffering from Crimean-Congo fever.
"If you do get sick, it's particularly severe," Emmerich explained. The disease begins with nonspecific, flu-like symptoms including fever, chills, aches and headaches. In severe cases, a patient will begin bleeding from the skin, nose and gums and may also experience gastrointestinal bleeding. The worst causes can result in organ failure.
Patients require intensive care and isolation because they are highly contagious.
Much of the treatment in intensive care focuses on maintaining a patient's vital functions, but they are also given the antiviral drug, ribavirin. But, as Emmerich said, "ribavirin is not all that effective in acutely ill patients." That is something the scientists have seen firsthand with cases in Kosovo.
The best answer is prevention, which is why it's also very important for the researchers to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma ticks and for them to recommend avoiding certain areas where the ticks are prevalent, if possible.
Successful tick tactics
Over the years, the researchers have not only collected thousands of the ticks but they have also conducted so-called seroprevalence studies. These use blood tests to find antibodies from past infections. This allows the scientists to determine whether humans or animals have come in contact with the virus.
Farm animals are particularly suitable for this type of study, Sherifi said, as the virus doesn't affect them. And unlike wild animals and humans, they usually remain in a clearly defined area. That means that if antibodies are detected in the blood of these animals, it's clear the virus is circulating in that area.
In Kosovo, the number of serious infections has dropped drastically in the past decade, amounting to just five cases in total. In the previous decade, there were about 100 cases. Sherifi and Emmerich believe this indicates how successful their work has been.
Of course, that doesn't mean the ticks and the virus won't spread further in Europe, and the researchers both expect this to happen.
Hyalomma ticks with the Crimean-Congo virus have just been detected in France although, so far, no humans have been infected there.
"Over the past 13 years, Hyalomma ticks have spread geographically," said Emmerich. "As a virologist, that's something to think about, and it needs to be closely monitored."
This is why it's important for the German and Kosovar scientists to pass on what they've learned to countries that haven't yet had as much experience monitoring the Hyalomma ticks, such as Macedonia and Albania.
This article was originally written in German.

Cholera outbreak in West Kordofan killed 23 and infected 310, Sudanese group says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:24:28 UTC
19:24:28 KST

At least 23 people have died and more than 310 cholera cases and suspected infections have been reported in two areas of West Kordofan in southern Sudan, a local relief group said on Sunday.
The Dar Hamar Emergency Room, a community-based relief organisation, warned in two separate statements of deteriorating health and humanitarian conditions in Humeir village and Hilla Hussein in Al-Udayyah locality.
The group said Humeir was facing a “serious health situation,” with 120 suspected cholera cases admitted to an isolation centre and 11 deaths recorded.
It said the isolation centre lacked intravenous fluids and life-saving medicines as the number of suspected cases continued to rise.
The group appealed to health authorities and humanitarian organisations to urgently provide medical supplies, warning that conditions could deteriorate further.
In a separate statement, the group said the health and humanitarian crisis had worsened in Hilla Hussein, where more than 190 cholera cases and 12 deaths from the disease had been recorded.
Transportation disruptions have isolated the area and made it difficult to evacuate critically ill patients for treatment, it added.
Heavy toll
The group also warned of a worsening food crisis, saying conditions had forced some residents to use animal feed to provide for their children.
It called on humanitarian organisations to immediately provide medicines and food assistance to residents.
The group did not specify the period during which the deaths, confirmed cases and suspected infections were recorded in the two areas.
On July 14, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned that continued fighting and disease outbreaks were taking a heavy toll on civilians across Sudan.
The World Health Organization said on July 7 that 1,330 confirmed cholera cases and 114 deaths had been recorded amid the outbreak in Sudan.
Sudan has been engulfed in a conflict between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since April 2023, killing tens of thousands of people and displacing around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

“Magic Land” is Yonka Dragomanska's love song to Bulgaria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:22:48 UTC
19:22:48 KST

Sunday 6 September 2026 12:25
Sunday, 6 September 2026, 12:25
PHOTO You Tube
Font size
Yonka Dragomanska has lived in Vienna for years, but she makes a point of calling herself a Bulgarian singer. She is also a composer, singing teacher and children’s choir director, and the founder and conductor of the Yagoda Choir in Vienna.
Dragomanska was born and raised in Pazardzhik in a musical family and has been singing since she was a small child. Her grandmother Yagoda, after whom the choir is named, was a folk singer of the calibre of Nadka Karadzhova, one of Bulgaria’s best-known traditional folk singers. She was invited to join the Bulgarian National Radio ensemble, but family circumstances prevented her from accepting. 
Yonka’s mother, Violeta, played the accordion and sang in two-part harmony with Yonka from her early childhood. One childhood memory has stayed particularly vivid: sitting for hours in an old pear tree in the family garden in the village of Gelemenovo, singing and making up her own songs.
PHOTO YouTube
Like many creative people, Yonka has more than one talent. Alongside music, drawing had a place in her heart from an early age. After moving to Vienna, she was accepted to study architecture in the class of world-renowned architect Zaha Hadid. But even as she was living that dream, Yonka did not give up music. In Vienna, her talent was noticed by the Vladigerov brothers, who helped her take her first steps as a professional singer.
Later, she met her first vocal teacher, Svetla Ivanova, who awakened her love of opera and prepared her for admission to a private conservatory in Vienna. Yonka graduated with honours and went on to perform oratorio and operatic repertoire.
Her love of Bulgarian music and homesickness eventually prompted her to set up the Yagoda Choir. Its members are Austrians and people of various other nationalities who learn and perform Bulgarian folk songs. Many had never sung before joining.
Dragomanska has developed her own exercises in breathing, voice production and vocal technique, which she uses at the beginning of every rehearsal. The singers first translate the lyrics and then practise speaking them in rhythm to get the Bulgarian pronunciation and diction right.
Over the years, the Yagoda Choir has performed in some of Vienna’s most beautiful concert halls and on some of its most prestigious stages, bringing Bulgarian folk music to large international audiences.
PHOTO YouTube
In 2026, Yonka Dragomanska wrote her first original song, “Magic Land”. It is a song about Bulgaria, love for one’s roots, the strength of a happy childhood and the resilience of the human spirit. The lyrics grew out of memories that still give her strength today, while the melody seemed to find its own way to the words.
The arrangement is by Petar Aleksiev, who also plays piano on the recording, and Alex Nushev. The violin part is performed by Slava Atanasova, concertmaster of the Sofia National Opera orchestra.
The video was filmed in both Austria and Bulgaria. The Austrian footage includes locations around Semmering and the Rax mountain and was shot by Martin Zayranov – a musician and first violinist with the Wiener Symphoniker who is also an aerial photographer and drone cameraman – with the involvement of another Bulgarian, pianist Martin Pulz.
Austrian cinematographer and director Klaus Hundsbichler, who has worked with Dragomanska on her opera projects, also took part. His previous work includes filming ZZ Top and Frank Zappa, as well as productions and films featuring opera stars Anna Netrebko and Rolando Villazón.
The Bulgarian footage was put together by Viktor Dimchev and Aleksandar Duhtev using aerial images from Travel TV’s drone archive. Among the locations are Leshten, Veliki Preslav, the Rhodope Mountains, Ruse, Dzhebel, Kaliakra and Sinemorets. Slava Atanasova’s scenes were filmed in Sofia’s Borisova Garden.
“For me, ‘Magic Land’ is not simply a song, but a meeting between two cultures and two worlds that are part of my life. That is why I wanted the video to show this connection – the beauty of Bulgaria through the eyes of someone who lives and creates in Austria, but deep inside carries Bulgaria and the love of her roots,” Yonka Dragomanska says.

Column: China's role in driving higher-quality development of the SCO
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
18:16:55 CST
19:16:55 KST

by Xin Ping
The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit drew to a successful conclusion on Sept. 1 in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan. The SCO countries held a substantive and productive discussion on the organization's next phase of development, which produced more than 30 cooperation documents, spanning everything from transport, logistics, and biotechnology to artificial intelligence, energy, and drug control. These deliverables mark tangible progress by SCO members in implementing the 10-year development strategy laid out at the Tianjin Summit.
FROM TIANJIN TO BISHKEK
China has been central to the SCO story: not merely as a founding member, but as a key contributor to the SCO's evolution.
Last year at the Tianjin Summit, a milestone in the growth of the SCO, China and other member states jointly crafted a strategic blueprint for the organization's next decade, ushering in a new stage of high-quality development.
This year's SCO summit comes at a time when the world enters a new period of turbulence and transformation, and global governance stands at yet another critical crossroads. Rising to the occasion, and with a view to promoting higher-quality development of the organization, China called on the SCO countries to step forward to shoulder the historical responsibility and steer human development to a promising future -- by staying committed to putting development first and opening up the prospects for shared prosperity; taking security as a key goal, and fostering an environment of common security; putting people first, and cementing the foundation for everlasting friendship; promoting dialogue and consultation, and striving for more equitable and orderly governance.
FROM VISION TO ACTION
Being an architect is only half the job. China has also shown itself to be a real doer.
Over the year since the Tianjin Summit, China's initiatives have moved from papers to projects. Seven cooperation platforms covering green industry, the digital economy, scientific and technological innovation, energy, higher education, vocational and technical education, and artificial intelligence have been launched, generating more than 160 projects. Nearly three-quarters of the planned 10-million-kilowatt additions in solar and wind power have been implemented, while more than two-thirds of the 100 "small and beautiful" livelihood projects have been approved. Also, the action plan for high-quality economic and trade cooperation has continued to support growing trade between China and other SCO countries.
On Sept. 1, China released the List of Achievements of China's Actions to Promote the Development of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Action (2025-2026), cataloguing more than 150 Chinese-initiated documents, events, and projects since the Tianjin Summit. China's contributions to the advancement of the SCO are there for all to see.
This year, China brought to Bishkek not only a vision for the way forward, but also more initiatives and projects in support of the SCO development. These include the establishment of a China-SCO port economic cooperation center in Tianjin and a basic education cooperation center in Beijing, the launch of an international AI application cooperation center and 100 technological cooperation projects with fellow SCO countries, and the training of more green industry professionals through China-SCO cooperation, among other things. These initiatives will inject fresh momentum into the organization's development.
This is where China's role in the SCO becomes particularly visible. While summits set the direction, regional cooperation is ultimately judged by what happens after the cameras leave.
Looking back, the SCO has been an impressive success: what began in 2001 as a group of six countries working together to build military trust along their borders and combat terrorism, separatism and extremism, has grown into a family of 27 countries spanning Asia, Europe and beyond -- representing nearly half of the world's population and an economic aggregate approaching 30 trillion U.S. dollars, and covering fields of cooperation from politics and security to economic and people-to-people exchanges.
The productive Bishkek Summit has once again proven that the SCO is a steadfast pillar for peace, a responsible force for openness, and an anchor of stability in a turbulent world. As the SCO embarks on its next quarter-century journey, China will continue to contribute its wisdom and strength to the higher-quality development of the SCO, injecting fresh and sustained momentum to regional peace, development and shared prosperity.

New Study: The worrying trend of doctors leaving Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:14:42 UTC
19:14:42 KST

New Study: The worrying trend of doctors leaving Israel
About 1,370 doctors left Israel in three years, almost double compared to the same period in the previous decade
A study by Tel Aviv University researchers found that approximately 1,370 doctors left Israel for at least 12 months between 2023 and 2025, a 94% increase compared with the 705 doctors who left during the corresponding period a decade earlier, between 2013 and 2015.
The departure was evident across all medical specialties, with 6.2% of pediatricians and 6.2% of ophthalmologists, dermatologists, and electrophysiologists leaving, along with 6% of surgeons, 4.7% of intensive care physicians, and 3.9% of internists. The study found the share of experienced doctors among those leaving rose sharply, accounting for over 20% of all departures in the past three years, compared with about 14% in the previous decade.
Among physicians under 60, the highest departure rates were recorded among ophthalmologists, dermatologists, and ENT doctors, at 9.4%, followed by surgeons at 8.8% and pediatricians at 6.4%.
Geographically, the Tel Aviv District recorded the highest number of departures, with 429 physicians leaving between 2023 and 2025, representing 5.4% of doctors in the district and 7.4% of those under 60. The Central District followed with 290 departures, then Haifa with 190, Jerusalem with 132, and the South with 125.
Even after accounting for Israeli doctors who returned, the study found Israel lost a net 509 doctors in 2023-2024, an average of about 255 per year, nearly five times the annual average net loss of 54 doctors recorded between 2010 and 2019.
The researchers cautioned that a doctor being abroad for a year does not necessarily indicate a permanent departure, since many leave temporarily for internships, advanced training, or research. However, they said the surge in long-term departures, particularly among veteran and experienced doctors less likely to be leaving for training purposes, is a worrying sign that some temporary departures are turning into permanent decisions to stay abroad.
"Since 2023, the State of Israel has been losing its best people," Prof. Ater said. "We all have family members waiting for surgery or other medical treatment. The departure of nearly 1,400 doctors directly translates into longer waits, less effective medical treatment, and ultimately a serious impact on our quality of life."

Another Israeli force entered the grounds of Burqa Boys Secondary School northwest of Nablus, with no injuries or arrests reported, according to the sources.
The raids came on the first day of the 2026-2027 academic year, as 846,289 students returned to schools across the occupied West Bank. The students are enrolled in 2,537 government, private and U.N.-run schools, with around 54,000 teachers.
According to the Palestinian Education Ministry, 634,294 students are enrolled in 1,967 government schools, while 163,787 attend 480 private schools. Another 48,208 students attend 90 schools run by the U.N. agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA).
The new school year comes amid escalating attacks by the Israeli army and Jewish settlers across the occupied West Bank, particularly in rural areas and Bedouin communities, including attacks affecting schools and other educational facilities.
In occupied East Jerusalem, the ministry said the academic year began despite Israeli measures targeting Palestinian schools, teachers, students and curricula.
The ministry said it had opened four additional schools in remote and Bedouin areas for primary-level students amid Israeli threats of demolition and forced displacement in communities in Area C of the occupied West Bank.
It also allocated $1.5 million to provide buses for students in affected areas to help ensure access to schools.
In the Gaza Strip, administrative and teaching staff are scheduled to return on Sept. 16, while students are expected to resume classes on Sept. 19, according to the ministry.
Authorities are preparing around 700 in-person learning sites across the enclave for more than half a million students, as well as 25 temporary schools. Online education will continue for students unable to reach the in-person facilities.
The ministry said the arrangements would allow around 541,000 students in Gaza to continue their education with the resources currently available.
Hundreds of thousands of students in Gaza have been deprived of regular schooling since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, while many schools have been turned into shelters for displaced Palestinians.
The Israeli army has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000 in a brutal war that has destroyed or damaged much of Gaza’s civilian infrastructure.

Daughter of ex-Trump envoy Kellogg pushes back on father's call to conscript Ukrainian women
Ukrainian women should be encouraged to join the military, but not be forced to, said Meaghan Mobbs, a president of an aid-providing NGO and daughter of the former U.S. special envoy for Ukraine, Keith Kellogg.
In a Sept. 6 interview with public news outlet Suspilne, Mobbs came out against comments her father made in August, where he said he supports mobilizing Ukrainian women into the military.
"People sometimes think that my dad and I are always exactly in the same mind. Not in this case," Mobbs said.
"His frame of reference is from my experience in Afghanistan. My mom was born in Afghanistan. So, if women can fight, why not?"
Mobbs previously served military tours in Afghanistan. She is now the president of the R.T. Weatherman Foundation, which provides direct assistance to soldiers serving in Ukraine and their families.
"Where I disagree... They should volunteer to fight," Mobbs said.
She pointed out that serving does not just mean fighting from a trench, and that there are a broad range of roles, some of which she thinks women are especially well-placed to serve in, suc as intelligence or medical support.
Mobbs nevertheless said that women are also often good shooters and excellent at handling weapons.
"Men and women are different. And this is normal. We have to accept this reality," Mobbs said.
"(But) we have to involve women volunteers in the roles for which they are best suited, and encourage other women to join."
"I don't think that right now, in the interests of Ukraine, we have to forcefully mobilize women," Mobbs said.
In her work advocating for foreign soldiers serving in Ukraine, Mobbs also advocates for making it easier to acquire Ukrainian citizenship.
"I know a lot of foreigners who would love to get Ukrainian citizenship. But the path to this is quite difficult now," Mobbs said.
"A lot of them are dating Ukrainian women, getting married to Ukrainian women," which Mobbs calls "a fantastic thing because you create more Ukrainian babies."
"If you have a mixed family where a foreign volunteer marries a Ukrainian woman, and they have a baby, it's only a plus for Ukraine because it develops the economy, it improves the demography," Mobbs said.
Hopeful about Witkoff-Kushner visit
Mobbs' interview was released hours ahead of an expected visit of U.S peace negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Kyiv – their first trip to the Ukrainian capital in that capacity.

Mobbs hopes that the U.S. will end up doing more to help Ukraine in "the first truly good-to-evil war that we've seen," from boosting sanctions to allowing Kyiv to use Starlink on Russian territory.

Germany plans anti-drone shield after Leipzig attack: report

Germany plans anti-drone shield over Leipzig attack — report
September 6, 2026
Germany is planning a comprehensive protective shield to prevent attacks like the failed assault on Leipzig airport, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Sunday.
On August 4, several small drones targeted Leipzig-Halle Airport in eastern Germany, with one hitting a parked plane, while another is thought to have struck an inbound cargo jet.
German intelligence agencies blamed Russia for the incident, which Moscow has denied.
What did Dobrindt say about the shield?
Dobrindt told Bild am Sonntag newspaper that Russia's hybrid attacks are now a "daily" reality, adding: "These attacks will increase, but we can defend ourselves and protect ourselves."
The newspaper cited information from the Interior Ministry showing the government plans to expand the federal police's mobile drone-defense units.
The measures include vehicles and helicopters that can be quickly deployed to protect airspace over key cities like Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin to counter drone attacks.
Bild said the shield would not only intercept drones, but could also defuse drone bombs and other explosive devices.
The newspaper described how a change in the law would allow critical infrastructure operators — including water, power and defense companies — to detect and defend against drone sabotage.
Russia's Lavrov accuses Merz of wanting war
On Sunday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov claimed the German accusations levelled against Russia were "by and large, the start of a real war."
He reiterated Russia's denial of any involvement with the Leipzig drone attack and criticized German Chancellor Friedrich Merz for wanting to boost the country's military capability in response to hybrid threats.
"All these statements by Merz about making Germany the leading military power in Europe once again — they are being put into practice. He is, in effect, declaring war on us," Lavrov told Russian state-run TV channel Vesti.
He also criticized Germany's closure of Russian House cultural center in berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn.
New tech planned to boost cyber security
Bild also described how a national protective cyber shield would be set up to detect and intercept hacking attacks.
The measure comes amid hundreds of cyberattacks on government departments, infrastructure and companies each day, many of them blamed on Russia, other states and criminal gangs.
The newspaper said the government also wants to increase the use of AI, biometric facial recognition and video surveillance, especially at transport hubs, to identify suspected attackers before they carry out attacks.
Over 1,000 drone sightings in 2025
The head of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), Holger Münch, told Bild in December that more than a thousand suspicious drone flights were recorded over Germany last year.
These incidents mostly targeted military sites, airports, ports and defense firms and were treated as surveillance or harassment, rather than attacks.
Leipzig airport has been targeted by sabotage before. In July 2024, a suspected Russian incendiary parcel caught fire at the airport's DHL hub.
The cargo hub is also utilized by the Ukrainian military and NATO to airlift arms for use in the Ukrainian defense against Russia's invasion.

U.S. Marines demonstrate a new way to fight from the coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:09:44 UTC
19:09:44 KST

- The 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit ran two separate forward bases at once near Camp Pendleton, one for tracking ships and one combining command operations with aircraft refueling.
- The exercise builds on the Marine Corps' Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations concept, introduced in 2019 to support distributed operations in contested waters.
U.S. Marines with the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit ran two separate forward operating sites at once during a training exercise near Camp Pendleton, California, testing whether the unit can track ships at sea, direct combat operations, and keep aircraft armed and fueled from multiple locations simultaneously rather than a single base.
One site, called a sensing expeditionary advanced base, paired coastal surveillance radars and electronic sensors with small drones flown by Marines from Battalion Landing Team 2/4. When the radar picked up a surface vessel in nearby sea lanes, drone operators launched their aircraft to visually confirm and track it, then sent the imagery and coordinates back to the MEU commander in real time.
“We pull those grids, capture the imagery, and send that critical data directly back to the MEU commander,” said Sgt. Javier Guzman Granados, a drone operator with the battalion. Because ships move constantly, operators said the tracking data has to move fast before contacts drift out of range or the picture goes stale.
Miles away, Marines set up a second site combining a forward command element with a fuel and rearming point for aircraft. That command post linked the two forward bases, an operations center aboard Navy ships offshore, and aircraft flying overhead, while the adjacent fueling site let helicopters and other aircraft rearm and refuel without flying back to a ship or a main base.
“Forward arming and refueling points minimize the time aircraft spend out of the fight and maximize their time in the air,” said Sgt. Cody Quittner, a bulk fuel specialist with Marine Medium Tiltrotor Squadron 364. “Instead of flying all the way back to the ship or a main base for fuel and ordnance, aircraft come directly to us, rearm, refuel, and immediately return to supporting the infantrymen on the forward line.”
Running both sites at the same time meant splitting logistics, transportation and security personnel across two separate locations rather than concentrating them in one place, which Quittner said exposed how many people and moving parts it takes to stand up even a single site.
“One of the major takeaways from this training evolution is the sheer number of moving parts required to establish a site and deliver that capability,” Quittner said.
The exercise reflects a broader shift in how the Marine Corps trains its expeditionary units. The service introduced its Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations concept in 2019 as part of a larger overhaul called Force Design, built around the idea that small, mobile Marine units operating from austere, temporary locations ashore can extend the Navy’s sensor and strike coverage in contested waters, rather than relying solely on large amphibious landings. The concept was developed with a potential Indo-Pacific conflict in mind, and the Marine Corps has spent the years since testing it through unit exercises like this one. The 13th MEU ran an earlier version of this training in 2022 at San Clemente Island, California, using aircraft including the RQ-20B Puma and Shield AI’s V-BAT drone to build a picture of maritime activity for the MEU and its Navy counterparts.
“Connecting the land and sea is where the Marine Corps makes our money,” said 1st Lt. Joseph Nameth, a platoon commander with Battalion Landing Team 2/4.

Hong Kong to propel belt and road market expansion, finance chief says
Paul Chan’s pledge comes ahead of 11th Belt and Road Summit in Hong Kong this week
Hong Kong will step up support for belt and road enterprises seeking to expand into new markets and tap regional growth, reinforcing its role as a pivotal business hub and platform for deeper exchanges, the city’s finance chief has said.
“The gradual relocation of mainland China’s industrial chains towards belt and road regions is a response to this reality,” he wrote.
This year’s summit is being held under the theme “Advancing high-quality development, embarking on a new journey”. For the first time, there will be a dedicated “Go Global Chapter” to support mainland firms expanding overseas.
Mainland firms have established around 58,000 overseas entities, creating more than 2 million local jobs annually, with an investment stock of US$3.4 trillion, nearly 90 per cent of which is in developing economies, according to Chan.

Drones attacked the sanctioned vessel Lady Maria in the Mediterranean Sea, which is reportedly used to transport Russian weapons.
The NEVZOROV Telegram channel published footage of the attack.
The vessel was targeted by drones equipped with a system for dropping munitions. The strikes caused a small fire to break out on board.
According to data from the MarineTraffic vessel-tracking service, the ship departed the Algerian port of Oran and was headed for an undisclosed destination.
The latest route updates indicate that the vessel was sailing through the Mediterranean Sea, passing near the island of Crete on its way toward Syria.
The vessel Lady Maria (IMO 9220641) is currently under U.S. OFAC sanctions under the name STELLA-MARIA. The vessel has been linked to the Russian company MG-FLOT LLC (formerly TransMorFlot LLC) under the sanctions regime established by Executive Order 14024.
In addition to the United States, Ukraine also imposed sanctions on the vessel on May 23, 2026. The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) stated that Lady Maria is involved in transporting military cargo and weapons for Russia.
According to intelligence reports, the vessel has been used on the Novorossiysk–Tartus route. It has also been linked to the transportation of weapons from Syria to Russia.
Other vessels operated by MG-FLOT LLC are also subject to sanctions. The company’s vessels have likewise been used to transport ammunition from North Korea.
There is currently no confirmed information on whether the drones were Ukrainian. However, the activity of Ukrainian intelligence and security services in these waters is not new.
In May 2026, Greek fishermen found a Ukrainian Magura naval drone near the southern part of Lefkada, an island in the Ionian Sea in western Greece.
In December 2025, the Security Service of Ukraine struck a tanker belonging to Russia’s shadow fleet in the neutral waters of the Mediterranean Sea for the first time.
Moreover, given that the vessel has been used to transport weapons to Syria, an Israeli strike cannot be ruled out. Israel has previously carried out attacks on Iranian ports, including Bandar-e Anzali on the Caspian Sea.

U.S. Army Rangers evaluate drone-launching mothership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:00:09 UTC
19:00:09 KST

- Petrel Technologies says the 75th Ranger Regiment tested its AERO Sky drone in a live-fire mothership role, carrying strike drones, while also using it as an airborne communications relay.
- The aircraft previously demonstrated an armed FPV-launching role with the 101st Airborne Division in April, and Petrel has not disclosed further Army testing plans.
Petrel Technologies says the U.S. Army’s 75th Ranger Regiment is evaluating its AERO Sky drone in a live-fire mothership role, with the aircraft shown carrying externally mounted strike drones during the exercise.
The company described the work in a post captioned “Golden hour. Live fire. Mothership operations with 75th Ranger Regiment, U.S. Army.” Petrel said the AERO Sky also functioned as an airborne relay node during the exercise, keeping command-and-control links active for units operating beyond direct line of sight.
According to the company, the system requires a single operator, can launch within minutes, integrates with the Android Team Awareness Kit mapping software used across the military, and can route communications across mesh networks, satellite links and LTE cellular connections depending on what’s available in the field. Petrel’s post did not specify how many strike drones the aircraft carried during this exercise or confirm whether any were released against a target.
This is the second publicly disclosed Army evaluation of the AERO Sky this year. The Defence Blog reported in April that Petrel had validated the aircraft alongside the 101st Airborne Division during a live-fire exercise at the Joint Readiness Training Center at Fort Polk, Louisiana, where the drone deployed armed first-person-view attack drones directly from the air. The newly disclosed work with the 75th Ranger Regiment appears to combine that same strike-mothership configuration, carrying FPV drones as payload, with the aircraft’s communications relay function, two of three mission sets, alongside logistics, that Petrel has said the aircraft is designed to handle.
The AERO Sky is a Group 3 unmanned aircraft, a category covering drones larger than small quadcopters but still light enough to be moved and operated without heavy support equipment. The aircraft has an 11-foot wingspan, a maximum takeoff weight of roughly 100 pounds, and a payload capacity between 30 and 50 pounds, depending on configuration, with six to eight hours of endurance. It combines vertical takeoff and landing with fixed-wing flight, letting it launch without a runway while still flying efficiently enough for extended missions. Petrel builds the airframe from a blend of carbon fiber and balsa wood, materials the company has said keep the unit cost around $90,000 and allow the aircraft to be assembled in about four minutes.
Petrel Technologies was founded by CEO Jacob Stonecipher and Chief Operating Officer Chris Rothe, a former Green Beret. The company originally operated under the name Sustainable Skylines, building drones to tow advertising banners over Miami Beach, before the founders pivoted the business toward military applications and emerged from stealth in February.

America’s 911 System Is Dangerously Out of Date
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

“911, what is your emergency?”
For the millions of Americans who have dialed 911, these are the familiar and comforting words we hear upon placing the call. It is the question that guides us through a moment of chaos or crisis, the linchpin to saving lives and protecting health.
But in recent years, an increasing number of 911 callers have heard something a little different:
“911, where is your emergency?”
It is very nearly the same question, but the slight change underscores vast differences in people’s experiences seeking help in an emergency. In an era when parents can monitor their children’s movements in real time, and ride-share drivers know the precise corner to stop, many Americans may be surprised to learn a sobering truth: the 911 professionals who answer the phone are often unable to automatically pinpoint a caller’s precise location, and cannot always rely on callers themselves to provide it.
The extra time it takes to figure out exactly where to send help, even if it’s a few extra seconds, costs lives. But the United States has let our 911 emergency response system languish for decades, failing to make the necessary investments to bring it into the digital age. That inaction should be unacceptable to every American. Upgrading 911 technology should be a national priority, and Congress must provide sufficient funding to ensure it works in every community.
When America’s 911 system launched in 1968, it was built to serve people calling from landlines at fixed locations. Callers were tracked using address directories that listed the location of the phone they were calling from. As a result, emergency personnel could be dispatched almost immediately. It made sense, and it worked fast.
Nearly 60 years later, we are living in a completely different era. In 2024, more than three-quarters of 911 calls came via either cellphones or Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) and other wireless voice services. Since some states do not break down calls by service type, that number is likely even higher. By contrast, only about 7% came from landlines. In many states, landlines now account for less than 5% of 911 calls. That number is likely to decline further in the years ahead.
Our current 911 system isn’t built for this. Often, a 911 professional can trace a call only to the cell tower that received it, which can be a fair distance from a caller’s exact location. As many as 20% or more of calls are traced to the wrong tower. Unlike apps like Google Maps or Life360 that can continuously track a phone’s precise location, 911 call takers must rely on carrier data when the call was first made. Updates come in 20- to 30-second intervals. If the call needs to be transferred, this process must start from scratch. This wastes precious time. It is especially hard in rural areas, where towers can be few and far between, or dense locations like high-rise apartments.
Asking “where is your emergency” may sound like an easy fix, but that incorrectly assumes a caller can always answer the question. Callers may be in an unfamiliar location. They may be navigating imminent danger, such as an intruder or attacker, that prevents them from sharing. They may give the wrong address, or they may move locations from the moment a call is placed to the time help arrives. Even the emergency data that may be stored in a person’s cell phone for precisely such a circumstance can’t be accessed by call takers or dispatchers.
Simply put, our nation’s 911 system is rapidly becoming obsolete.
Past attempts to fix these errors have failed. The ENHANCE 911 Act, enacted in 2004, authorized up to $250 million in annual federal grants to help states upgrade their 911 systems. But those appropriations were never made. Other funding opportunities for states wound up being far smaller. Ultimately, the legislation was not reauthorized by Congress, and national funding efforts dried up. In recent years, federal funding for 911 upgrades has ground to a halt.
Congress should right this wrong by fully funding NextGen 911 services, which would provide 911 professionals and Emergency Communications Centers with the life-saving information they need—such as accurate location information—to do their jobs. Thirty-eight states have pledged to upgrade to NextGen 911. If fully implemented, 911 would shift from an analog relic to an Internet Protocol-based system. That would allow for more advanced communication technologies, including receiving 911 “calls” via text or video, that would be especially useful for 911 callers who are either unaware of or unable to share their location. It would also help callers with disabilities, such as people who are deaf or hard of hearing, access the system as well.
Full NextGen 911 rollout nationwide is estimated to cost approximately $15 billion. The cost of inaction is far higher. Fixing access to location data would free up 911 professionals to rapidly triage calls. It would also mean a quicker and more accurate on-scene response, helping callers and emergency personnel alike.
When 911 launched, cell phones did not yet exist, and America’s emergency response system is still largely stuck in that bygone era. This is an emergency of our own making, and it is fixable. Our leaders must answer the call for help.

Iran war likely to drag on for another six months, ex-US defense secretary warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

Donald Trump’s war with Iran is likely to drag on for another six months, Leon Panetta, the former US defense secretary, has warned, as the US president struggles to find his way out of the controversial conflict.
Panetta declared in an interview that the war with Iran – launched by Trump over six months ago – risks becoming another “forever war in the Middle East”, with no clear end in sight.
“It’s no mystery that the United States and Iran are caught in a terrible stalemate, in which there really are very few options available to bring this war to an end,” said Panetta, who also served as CIA director under Barack Obama, suggesting the conflict is on course to become “another failed war” in the Middle East “like Iraq and Afghanistan”.
“I think the likelihood is this war is going to continue for another six months without being resolved,” he added.
Panetta spoke to the Guardian days after the US army secretary, Dan Driscoll, abruptly resigned, departing amid the conflict, following reports of tensions with the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, over a series of firings.
US service members “are going to war at a time when there’s tremendous turmoil at the Pentagon, in the command structure, which really creates a sense that there’s nobody in charge”, Panetta, who served as defense secretary from 2011 to 2013, added. “And I just think that, whether it’s Iran, or whether it’s our adversaries, they’re now looking at the United States, and see weakness in terms of our ability to be able to really implement our military capability of defending our country.”
He said: “My biggest concern right now is we live in a very dangerous world, with the primary threats coming from China, from Russia, from North Korea, and from terrorism, and yes, from Iran as well. But what I’m concerned about is that we’re sending a message of weakness to our primary adversaries.
“And while they continue to meet and support each other in this axis that’s been created, I think they look at the United States as being particularly weak right now, and that’s a horrible message to send at a time when we’re facing those kinds of threats.”
In a statement, the Pentagon insisted it was “firing on all cylinders” under Hegseth’s leadership.
“The premise that the Department is in disarray is completely baseless and an insult to every dedicated professional and warfighter in this building who comes to work every day to defend this nation,” the chief Pentagon spokesperson, Sean Parnell, said. “This is what reform looks like.”
The White House was also contacted for comment.
In March, just three weeks after the US and Israel launched their military operation in Iran, Panetta told the Guardian he believed Trump was stuck between a “rock and a hard place” as he weighed whether to expand the war in a bid to eliminate Iran’s leverage over the strait of Hormuz, or “just simply walk away and declare victory”, despite the risk of perceived failure.
Earlier this week Panetta said he “absolutely” believed Trump remains in that position. “He’s boxed himself in,” he said.
Trump now has three options, according to Panetta. The first would be to walk away and “admit that it’s a failed war”, something Panetta finds it difficult to see Trump doing.
The second would be to draw out the current “stalemate, with periodic attacks going back and forth, tit for tat”, and both sides attempting to “avoid the startup of a more dangerous war” while refusing to either negotiate or surrender.
That approach, Panetta believes, would produce “what all parties feared”: another protracted war in the Middle East.
The third option, he said, would be for the US to take control of the strait of Hormuz, and remove Iran’s “most dangerous leverage point” over the US, “which is the ability … to close and disrupt” the global trade chokepoint.
“So the president either steps up and does what’s necessary to open up the strait of Hormuz, or, as I said, he just continues to play … this game of pretending that somehow he’s winning a stalemate when the fact is he’s not,” Panetta said.
Asked if he believed the war is “winnable” for the US, Panetta replied: “It’s only winnable if there is a dramatic change in the attitude of the United States that makes clear that the objective, the primary objective by the United States at this point in time, is to reopen the strait of Hormuz.”
He also argued that Trump has damaged his credibility by repeatedly erroneously claiming that a deal to end the war is imminent, and that the strait of Hormuz is open.
“So the real question is, is he going to make a decision to actually deliver?” Panetta asked. “For a lot of reasons, right now, he’s caught in the worst of every world because not only does he not have credibility, but any threats he makes are totally ignored.”
Earlier this week, JD Vance told reporters that he would not describe the current military conflict with Iran as a “war”. And asked whether he expected the conflict to be over by November’s US midterm elections, the vice-president replied: “I think the reality is I don’t know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians.”
Panetta told the Guardian he believes many Americans have “lost faith” in Trump’s “ability to handle this war”, pointing to recent polling that he said found that a majority of Americans believe that conflict with Iran was a mistake and are against it.
He also said he hopes the Pentagon and Trump’s broader administration learn from what happened with the extremely long deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln, which arrived in Thailand this week after a record-breaking deployment supporting US operations against Iran that lasted more than 260 days without a port visit, amid reports of deteriorating living conditions and mental health aboard.
“Bottom line is, you do not deploy people endlessly into a war zone without making some kind of plans for rotation,” Panetta said.
“So it’s not just that the war is going badly – I think there’s also kind of a lack of trust in our military as to whether or not they are properly supporting our men and women who are putting their lives on the line.”
