Israeli strikes kill four in Lebanon after alleged Hezbollah drone launch
Israeli air strikes on southern Lebanon Sunday killed four people, two of them women, the country's health ministry said. Israel's military said that the strikes were a response to an alleged Hezbollah drone launch targeting troops in the Israeli-occupied "security zone" in the country's south.
Lebanon said Israeli air strikes in southern Lebanon killed four people on Sunday in the latest escalation despite a months-long ceasefire.
Israel alleged that the strikes were in response to Hezbollah launching drones against its troops in the country's Israeli-occupied south.
Lebanon's health ministry reported two people killed in south Lebanon's Nabatieh al-Fawqa and two women killed in nearby Arab Salim.
It said 20 other people, including several women and three children, were wounded in those locations as well as in the city of Nabatieh and the town of Kfar Rumman, adding that the toll was provisional.
Watch moreUNIFIL peacekeepers patrol south Lebanon, caught between Israel and Hezbollah
Israel's army said it was striking south Lebanon after Hezbollah fighters launched two drones towards Israeli soldiers operating in Israel's self-declared "security zone" in the south. It did not report any troop casualties.
Shortly before the statement, Israel's military had issued its first "evacuation" notice in Lebanon in several weeks, warning residents near a building it identified as a Hezbollah "facility" in Arab Salim to leave their homes of an attack on the site.
It did not issue warnings for other areas where strikes were reported.
Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) said that after the Israeli warning for the building, "enemy warplanes launched a strike on another house, destroying it" and killing the two women.
It said the Israeli military subsequently "carried out a strike on the home" threatened in the evacuation warning.
'Security zone'
The NNA said a strike in Nabatieh al-Fawqa destroyed part of the Ghandour hospital, adding that it had been out of service for years.
It also said a heavy air strike on Nabatieh city targeted a historical building and damaged offices belonging to state finance and agriculture authorities, while shops and cafes in the vicinity were also damaged.
It also reported a strike on a motorcycle in the area.
Lebanon was drawn into the Middle East war in March after Hezbollah attacked Israel in response to the US-Israeli war against the Shiite group's ally Iran.
Israel responded with airstrikes and a ground invasion that Lebanon says have killed more than 4,300 people and driven more than a million more from their homes.
Israeli troops are still operating inside a self-declared "security zone" around 10 kilometres deep inside Lebanon along the border. Israel in June released an updated map expanding this occupied zone.
Violence has lessened since a US-Iran memorandum of understanding on the broader conflict in June, while Israel and Lebanon signed a framework agreement later that month.
But Lebanon still reports Israeli strikes, artillery shelling and broad demolitions of civilian buildings in southern villages and towns.
On Friday, Israeli strikes in the country's south and east killed four people, including an 18-year-old woman, authorities said, as Israel said it struck Hezbollah targets in response to a drone launch towards its soldiers.
Earlier this week, Israel said it had taken "operational control" of the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge near Nabatieh.
Hezbollah has not commented on the announcement or confirmed that Israel has captured the site.
Also this week, the International Committee of the Red Cross facilitated the transfer to Lebanon of five people detained by Israel.
Israel and Lebanon began direct negotiations after the latest hostilities erupted, with fresh talks expected this month, though no date has been announced.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

UIPM integrates Obstacle World Championships into Beijing's city vibe
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:44 CST
17:41:44 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- As the UIPM 2026 Obstacle World Championships concluded at Beijing's Universal CityWalk on Sunday, UIPM President Rob Stull and Secretary General Shiny Fang described the event as a successful example of integrating competitions into urban settings.
It marks the second consecutive year the obstacle worlds is held in Beijing. Last year, the National Olympic Sports Center hosted the first edition after obstacle was incorporated into modern pentathlon.
"I was very happy with the previous venues. They were beautiful and well-organized. But this venue [Universal Studios] is really about entertainment, and that is the difference," Stull said. "Universal is such a worldwide known brand. Out of a sports venue, and get into a themed park. For everybody, it's a great opportunity."
At the 2024 Paris Olympics, many events were held at the iconic urban sites, including the Palace of Versailles and the Eiffel Tower.
"We saw what could be done in terms of these iconic sites. It was really cool and highly successful for everyone. We took some inspiration from the Paris Games, absolutely," said Stull.
As a new discipline within modern pentathlon, obstacle will replace equestrian and make its Olympic debut at the 2028 Los Angeles Games.
"The next Games in Los Angeles is a very different setup. Los Angeles doesn't have locations like Paris, but we have Hollywood," Stull said. "Modern pentathlon is in the urban cluster. It's about 3x3 basketball, skateboarding, BMX freestyle, to name a few. These are whole youth things with urban vibes."
This year's five-day Obstacle World Championships features the 100m individual, 400m individual, 4x100m relay, 3km individual and 3km team competitions, while U11 and U13 groups are introduced to the 100m and 3km events.
"For the young kids in Asia, they have their typical sports such as table tennis and badminton. Normally, we think these types of things like the obstacle run is more for western people. But the truth is that every kid has a nature. When they see the obstacles, they just want to overcome all these," said Fang. "That is why we try to encourage more children and teenagers to participate in this challenging event."
According to the UIPM calendar, the Obstacle World Championships will also take place in Beijing in the next two years.
"We will be happy to come back here at the Universal Studios, but we don't have an answer yet. Not only the Universal Studios but also other famous places could be considered as well. I believe we have more opportunities next year," said Fang. ■

Chinese literature finds growing readership in Russia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:38 CST
17:41:38 KST

by Xinhua writers Vladislava Chugueva, Zhang Chaoqun
MOSCOW, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Literature from China is finding an increasingly receptive audience in Russia, with works by Chinese authors gaining popularity and attracting growing interest from local publishers.
At the ongoing 39th Moscow International Book Fair, where China is the Guest of Honour, more than 2,000 titles and nearly 5,000 copies of China-themed books are on display as part of the Guest of Honour program themed "Reading China."
For Russian publishers, the growing appeal of Chinese literature has created new opportunities to introduce a wider range of Chinese works to the market.
Eksmo, one of Russia's largest general-interest publishing houses, has become a key publisher of translated Chinese-language works.
Eksmo editor Daria Shpakovskaya told Xinhua that books set in ancient China are particularly popular among young Russian readers.
"It doesn't matter whether it's fantasy or not. The men in robes, the women in beautiful costumes, the intrigue, the complicated relationships -- that's what makes it great. It's something new, and that's what really draws people in," she said.
The rising appeal of Chinese literature has also been fueled by the rising presence of Asian animation, television series and games in Russia.
"Interest in China is now fashionable, and even though I'm no longer young, I see that the children of my friends are immersed not in European culture, but in Asian culture," said Andrey Chernikov, an international copyright specialist at Eksmo.
Shpakovskaya said that through literature, television and visual arts, Russian readers are gaining a better understanding of Chinese culture, which helps foster closer cultural exchanges between the two countries. She noted that many young Chinese people are also choosing to study in Russia.
"We are very pleased that the Chinese side has also become interested in the Russian market. There is a real cultural exchange. We are interested in their literature, and they are interested in ours," she said.
Eksmo also publishes Russian-language editions of novels by Chinese writer Mo Yan. The editions have gained popularity in the Russian market, with stylish cover designs to attract younger readers.
Shpakovskaya added that young readers are drawn to Mo Yan not only because of his reputation as a renowned Chinese writer, but also because his works feature diverse narrative styles and explore a wide range of themes.
Staff at the publishing house said that while Mo Yan is regarded as a major literary figure, the modern presentation of his works has helped bring his writing to a younger generation.
"Mo Yan's readership consists not of teenagers, but rather of new-adult audiences," Shpakovskaya said. "Still, many dedicated fans of Asian literature and members of fandom communities are willing to take on his dense and complex works." ■

China Focus: Overseas visitors look beyond landmarks to experience everyday China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:22 CST
17:41:22 KST

TIANJIN, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Wearing a pair of mixed reality glasses, Ugandan content creator Kaziro Grace Mukisa found himself standing among Beijing's old streets, where virtual figures from the ancient Chinese myth "Classic of Mountains and Seas" appeared to emerge from the pages of the book and blend into the real world around him.
He reached out repeatedly, adjusting his view and interacting with the digital images floating in front of him.
"You could see animated characters appearing alongside real-life scenes. It was very vivid and immersive," Mukisa said at the 2026 China Culture & Tourism Industries Expo in north China's Tianjin Municipality, which concluded on Sunday.
Around the expo, technology is giving visitors new ways to engage with Chinese culture.
At the four-day event, visitors encountered a wide range of emerging tourism experiences. Humanoid robots performed on stage, a robotic horse walked steadily along a simulated mountain trail, and a robot chef prepared food. Visitors could also immerse themselves in traditional Chinese crafts, including New Year paintings, porcelain making and the inside painting of snuff bottles.
Sri Lankan tour guide Amila was drawn to a camping vehicle displayed at the expo. After stepping inside and carefully examining its space and facilities, he said the vehicle was a fresh experience for him and offers many more possibilities when traveling.
Amila, who has visited China many times over the past two decades, said he had witnessed improvements in tourism services and infrastructure.
"China has rich historical and cultural heritage as well as diverse natural landscapes. I love visiting museums in different places and exploring World Heritage sites," he said, adding that services such as online ticket booking, facial recognition entry and smart audio guides have made travel more convenient.
In Tianjin, some overseas visitors are looking beyond the city's best-known attractions, choosing mountain homestays or wandering through local neighborhoods instead.
Tuane van der Merwe from South Africa recently traveled to the city's Jizhou District with her parents, choosing a mountain homestay instead of popular urban attractions. Surrounded by nature, they could view the Great Wall from their accommodation.
"Here, you can see the city and nature together as one," Tuane van der Merwe said. "It's just amazing."
Another travel blogger, Billy, explored Tianjin's neighborhoods, focusing on ordinary scenes rather than famous landmarks: breakfast shops filled with morning aromas, people walking along the Haihe River and conversations echoing near bridges at dusk.
For him, these everyday moments revealed another side of the city.
Such experiences are emerging as China's inbound tourism continues to grow. A recent economic impact study by the World Travel & Tourism Council showed that international visitor spending in China reached 135 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, up 10.5 percent year on year, exceeding the global average growth rate of 3.2 percent.
Meanwhile, easier entry policies have given international travelers more options. Since China optimized its transit visa-free policies in December 2024, inbound travel facilitation measures have continued to take effect. Data from the National Immigration Administration showed that China recorded 22.91 million inbound foreign visits in the first half of this year, up 20.4 percent year on year. Of those, 77.7 percent were made under visa-free entry facilitation policies.
Olesia Razumnaia, general manager of Sunmar Travel Agency in Russia, said overseas tourists were increasingly shifting from simply visiting attractions to experiencing local culture and daily life, with more interest in immersive and experiential travel.
China is responding by developing more diversified tourism products. The country's tourism development plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) calls for creating themed tourism products featuring food, traditional crafts, history and culture, technology experiences, wellness, study tours, festivals and shopping.
"Tourism is not only a bridge for cultural exchanges and closer connections between peoples, but also an important window for presenting a real, multidimensional China," said Wang Wei, vice president of the China Association of Travel Services and senior vice president of Trip.com Group.
Richard Matuzevich, senior manager of the External Liaison Department of the World Tourism Cities Federation, said China's diverse tourism experiences allow visitors to discover a more complete and modern picture of the country.
"A first visit is about getting to know China. A return visit is about experiencing China," he said. ■

Australian housing affordability hits record low in 2026: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:12 CST
17:41:12 KST

CANBERRA, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Housing affordability in Australia deteriorated to a record low in the 2026 financial year, with elevated home prices and higher mortgage rates substantially reducing households' borrowing capacity, a report finds.
A typical-income household earning about 125,000 Australian dollars (about 90,000 U.S. dollars) a year could afford to buy just 12 percent of homes sold nationwide, the lowest level on record and below the previous low of 14 percent in the 2008 financial year, according to the report released Saturday by realestate.com.au.
Affordability is particularly challenging for low-income households. Those earning 76,000 Australian dollars annually could afford to buy just 2 percent of homes sold in the past year, essentially locking them out of the housing market, the Housing Affordability Report said.
The decline came following the Reserve Bank of Australia's three consecutive interest rate hikes in February, March and May to dampen inflation, the report noted.
Higher borrowing costs more than offset income growth and softening home prices toward the end of the financial year. As a result, housing affordability has declined nationwide, it said.
Affordability declined in all states in the 2026 financial year, with South Australia becoming the country's least affordable state, overtaking the state of New South Wales, the report showed.
A median-income household in South Australia could afford just 7 percent of homes, with the state capital Adelaide's median home value reaching 940,000 Australian dollars, it said. ■

Major Chinese banks plan A-share placements to boost core capital
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:40:49 CST
17:40:49 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Agricultural Bank of China (ABC) and Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) on Sunday announced plans to raise up to a combined 260 billion yuan (about 38.4 billion U.S. dollars) through A-share issuances to designated investors to replenish their core Tier-1 capital.
ABC said in a filing with the Shanghai Stock Exchange that it plans to issue A-shares to China's Ministry of Finance, China National Tobacco Corporation and its relevant subsidiaries, with total proceeds of up to 160 billion yuan.
After deducting issuance expenses, all proceeds will be used to replenish the bank's core Tier-1 capital. The final fundraising amount will be subject to the issuance plan approved by regulatory authorities, according to ABC.
ICBC said separately that it plans to raise up to 100 billion yuan via an A-share issuance to the Ministry of Finance, China National Tobacco Corporation and related subsidiaries.
The bank said the net proceeds will also be used entirely to replenish its core Tier-1 capital. The capital increase will be implemented after completing the required internal and external approval procedures. ■

Kremlin Says Ukraine Talks With U.S. Envoys Were 'Useful.' No Sign of Breakthrough.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:40:35 UTC
17:40:35 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin held more than three hours of "highly useful" talks on Saturday with two U.S. envoys seeking a deal to end the Ukraine war, a Kremlin aide said, but he gave no indication of any breakthrough.
The aide, Yuri Ushakov, said Americans Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner "outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement." Ushakov did not say what these ideas were.
He said Putin had told the pair that Russia was making "real progress" on the battlefield and was confident of achieving its goals, while stressing the necessity of addressing "all the root causes of the conflict."
These are statements that Moscow has made repeatedly since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Russia's smaller neighbor in February 2022. Both sides have intensified long-range air strikes in recent weeks while the front lines remain largely static.
Putin praises Trump's efforts
A White House official told Reuters the talks had been "substantive" and that next steps would be announced in the coming weeks.
There was no comment from Witkoff and Kushner, who were visiting Moscow for the first time since January on behalf of President Donald Trump. They flew out of Moscow soon after the talks and are due to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Kyiv on Sunday.
"The talks went beyond a mere exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis. Economic issues and potential major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in some detail," Ushakov said. "Overall, one can say that the negotiations were timely and highly useful for both sides."
Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev posted on X that the meeting had been an "important peacemaking visit." He and Ushakov were both present at the meeting.
The Russian president praised Trump's efforts to end the war.
"Understanding that he is entering a difficult situation, he nevertheless does not stop his efforts to help bring about a settlement and to make his contribution to resolving the Russian-Ukrainian conflict," Putin said in televised remarks at the start of the talks.
Trump suggested on Friday that the U.S. had a fresh proposal aimed at ending the war but did not elaborate.
Putin promised to ensure the safety of the U.S. negotiators. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said earlier that Putin had ordered the Russian military not to strike Kyiv for three days because of their trip.
A vast gulf in positions
Over the previous 10 days, Russia pounded the Ukrainian capital day and night with missiles and drones, including an attack on Friday on the headquarters of the SBU security service.
Ukraine has inflicted damaging hits throughout the summer on Russian refineries, oil terminals and warehouses of online retailer Wildberries, in an attempt to raise the cost to Moscow of continuing the war. Zelenskiy said Kyiv was prepared to refrain from strikes on Moscow through Monday.
Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on how to end the war, the deadliest in Europe since World War Two.
A person close to the Kremlin, speaking before reports emerged of the trip by Trump's envoys, said Putin was still intent on capturing more territory.
"There is no chance of reaching an agreement regarding the front line until Putin finishes securing the remaining part of the Donetsk region," this person told Reuters, adding that the Kremlin leader was confident — based on reports from his commanders — that this would happen by the end of the year.
Western military analysts see such a possibility as remote, given Moscow's slow rate of progress. Ukraine has refused to surrender land it has successfully defended at huge cost, and rejects such terms as tantamount to surrender.
The Kremlin said on Friday the position that Putin set out in a speech two years ago — that Ukraine should cede the entire territory of four regions claimed by Russia and abandon its plan to join NATO — was "unshakeable."

Giant mechanical elephants open Taipei Arts Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:40:10 UTC
17:40:10 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Three giant mechanical elephants took over the streets of Taipei’s Shilin District on Saturday, with crowds peaking at about 100,000 for the opening of the 2026 Taipei Arts Festival.
The free outdoor performance, titled “Trois Elephants Passent…” (“Three Elephants Pass…”), was staged by French street theater company Compagnie Oposito in collaboration with Taiwanese performers.
The three mechanical elephants, each nearly 5 meters tall, were accompanied by performers, musicians, and large mechanical birds as they traveled along Jihe Road toward the Taipei Performing Arts Center.
The procession began at 7:14 p.m., a time chosen to reference 1914, when Taipei’s first zoo was established. The approximately one-hour parade was followed by a stage performance outside the performing arts center, per a press release.
Horns and heavy drumbeats accompanied the elephants as costumed performers moved through the streets alongside the giant machines. The production combined street theater, music, and visual spectacle, temporarily turning the area into an open-air theater.
The Taipei Department of Cultural Affairs said crowds along the parade route reached about 100,000 at the event’s peak. The department described the performance as an opportunity to transform Taipei into a “city theater without a roof.”
The turnout also created difficulties for spectators. Some people complained online about crowded viewing areas, long waits, and problems moving through the area, per China Times.
Organizers recommended that people attending Sunday’s performance use alternative viewing locations if they could not find a suitable position along the route. The performance was also scheduled to be livestreamed on the Taipei Performing Arts Center’s YouTube channel from 7:14 p.m. to 8:45 p.m.
Sunday’s parade was scheduled to begin at 7:14 p.m. at the Shin Kong Life Insurance Shilin Education Center and proceed to the Taipei Performing Arts Center plaza.
Traffic restrictions were planned around the route. Jihe Road between Zhongzheng and Wenlin roads was to be closed during the performance, with drivers advised to use Chengde Road, Zhongshan North Road, or Wenlin Road as alternative north-south routes, per Liberty Times.
Compagnie Oposito, founded in 1982, is known for large-scale street performances and urban festivals. The production was inspired in part by images of animals traveling through Taipei’s streets when the city zoo moved from Yuanshan to Muzha in 1986.
The 2026 Taipei Arts Festival will continue through Oct. 25 with performances and cultural events across the city.

Russia is failing to export its new grain harvest in time and is losing export revenues - intelligence
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:38:20 EEST
17:38:20 KST

Russia is failing to export its new grain harvest in time and is losing export revenues - intelligence
Kyiv • UNN
In August, Russia’s grain exports fell 2.5-fold. In September, wheat shipments could decline by another 52.1–62.5%.
russia has faced problems exporting grain from the new harvest. In August, its shipments fell 2.5-fold, while in September wheat exports may drop by more than half again. This is reported by the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, according to UNN.
Details
russia is failing to ship out grain from the new harvest in time. From August 1–20, exports fell 2.5-fold, to 1.4 million tonnes, while wheat exports fell 2.6-fold. In September, wheat exports may decline by a further 52.1–62.5%, to 1.8–2.3 million tonnes—the lowest level since 2010. Excess grain is driving down the domestic market. Over the week, prices for wheat, barley, sunflower and soybeans fell by 3.3–8.5%, and over the year by more than 40%
In addition, according to available information, on August 28 Rostov Region, which accounts for nearly 10% of russia’s harvest, introduced a state of emergency due to problems with grain exports.
the kremlin is responding by preparing state purchases, concessional loans, subsidies and loans secured by unsold crops. The cancellation of the export duty and compensation for expensive shipments to alternative ports are also being considered. This will not solve the problem. Up to 70% of russia’s grain exports passed through southern ports, while alternative routes lack sufficient capacity. Transporting grain to the Baltic Sea adds $30–50 per tonne, making exports even less profitable
According to the intelligence service, the problems have already affected major agricultural companies. Net profit at the russian agricultural holding Rusagro collapsed by 99% in the first half of the year—from 4.8 billion to 55.88 million rubles.
The state is effectively paying for grain to remain in storage. Concessional loans will not create demand, subsidies will not increase port capacity, and cheap money will not replace broken logistics. If exports do not recover, stocks will grow, prices will fall, and the losses will be shifted onto the budget and banks of the russian federation
Previously
Due to the shutdown of ports in Rostov Region, grain that cannot be exported has piled up. Wheat exports have fallen to their lowest level in 16 years.

Vast new archaeological site opens in Geneva
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:34:21 UTC
17:34:21 KST

Vast new archaeological site opens in Geneva
The grand opening ceremony for the new Saint-Antoine archaeological site (SaSA) delighted the public on Saturday in Geneva. Located beneath the Théodelinde Esplanade, this space, covering nearly 1,000m², showcases exceptional remains spanning two millennia of history.
“There was already a large crowd at the opening,” said Cindy Dulac, the manager of SaSA. Many local residents, curious visitors and families came to explore this new site, which has taken years of work to complete.
Its story began in 2010 during the redevelopment of the esplanade, when some exceptional archaeological remains were discovered. The site was then subjected to meticulous excavations between 2012 and 2015. Given the significance of the heritage finds, the authorities decided to protect them and make them accessible to the public.
More
Why Switzerland is an archaeological treasure trove
A project with a budget of CHF14.5 million ($18 million) was subsequently approved. The extensive construction project began in September 2023 and was completed recently.
Two thousand years of history
Three skylights provide natural light to highlight the historical periods on display. Even without descending into the site, it is possible to see part of the excavations from the new esplanade. Entry is via one of the skylights. Visitors descend a few steps to immerse themselves in two millennia of Geneva’s history.
The temperature is pleasant (22.5C) and the light soft. Visitors can wander around a 1st-century Gallo-Roman settlement, a necropolis containing over 300 graves used between the 3rd and 13th centuries, and part of the 5th-century funeral church of Saint-Laurent. There are also remains of 16th-century fortifications.
Further research
One skeleton is of particular interest to visitors. “It is that of a woman who was between 25 and 50 years old at the time of her death,” explained the guide. She shows no signs of having suffered any violence, he added. This is the only skeleton on display to the public. The others are being kept for further research.
More
A sensational Swiss discovery thanks to volunteers: archaeology for all
The SaSA is also designed as a scientific platform. There is still much research to be carried out on the remains that have been discovered, said Dulac. Scientists will be invited to take up residencies. A cultural space is open for contemporary artists to hold temporary exhibitions.
The opening celebrations continued until late Saturday afternoon. Younger visitors were able to try their hand at archaeological excavations, using spades and trowels in large containers. The official part of the event took place on Friday evening in the presence of officials from the canton and the City of Geneva.

Accepting donations from a foreign company, including donations in kind such as polling, could constitute a criminal offence and the party has been reported to the police.
Senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform’s head of policy James Orr have both stood down pending the outcome of an internal party investigation.
As my colleagues note in the story, Farage himself remains under pressure over a separate clip in which he was heard saying “it’s all above board” after one of the reporters who was posing as the UK-based son of a wealthy US backer told the Reform leader he had been in discussions with Jukes and Orr for some time.
“I’ll be the registered donor,” the son says. “But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that’s done and all those conversations are had the money is available.”
On Saturday, during the party’s conference in Birmingham, Farage continued to bat away suggestions of impropriety. “I’m not a compliance officer,” he told the BBC. “I frankly wasn’t even listening,” he said in reference to the meeting with the undercover reporters in Clacton.
Farage has framed the investigation, carried out by Verbatim Investigations, which was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting, as another example of an establishment stitch up, and has denied any wrongdoing, as have Orr and Jukes.

Why China’s shrinking population may be a blessing, not a curse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:30:07 UTC
17:30:07 KST

Alex Lo has been an SCMP columnist since 2012, commenting on China and international affairs.
There is little in common between Daron Acemoglu and Xi Jinping. As a strong advocate of the Western model of liberal democracy, Acemoglu, co-recipient of the 2024 Nobel Prize in economics, may be considered the ideological opposite of the Chinese president.
But on a crucial point about China’s future, the two may, strangely, be on the same page: an across-the-board introduction of cutting-edge technology may enhance productivity and maintain economic growth. It may counteract the negative impact of drastic population decline in the decades ahead.
While that may be an emerging consensus among economists and other social scientists, it still runs counter to the popular narrative that a rapidly greying China is doomed. The official figures released in January, for example, set off alarmism. China’s population fell by 3.39 million last year to just over 1.4 billion – a fourth consecutive decline and the steepest so far. Births dropped by 17 per cent to 7.92 million, the lowest since records began in 1949. Roughly 323 million Chinese, close to a quarter of the population, are now over 60.
The reaction was swift and familiar: China will grow old before it grows rich, its workforce will hollow out, its pension system will buckle, its ascent will end.
Some concerns are warranted. If 2.1 children per woman is the population replacement rate, then those countries with the lowest birth rates – China at 0.63, Japan at 0.6, and South Korea at 0.46 – are projected by 2050 to experience population declines of 20-30 per cent relative to 2023; their share of the population aged 65 and over to reach 30-40 per cent; and older workers (aged 45 and over) to comprise 60 per cent of the labour force.
02:58
What might China do to address its record low birth rate and declining population?
But that’s not the whole story. In fact, much of it is missing, and the alarm has outrun the analysis. “What if the historical evidence tells us that collapsing birth rates, paradoxically, are good for the economy,” economist Joeri Schasfoort asks in his YouTube channel, “because they force companies to innovate?”

“In recent weeks, we established Zionist Home-The Reservists together, with a clear goal: establishing a Zionist government, and making an effort for it to be as broad as possible,” the two said.
They added that the party had succeeded in establishing “an important and significant place” for itself and attracting many supporters.

Hendel in contact with parties to form bloc, spox. tells 'Post'

Hendel confirms agreegment with economist Yaron Zelekha

Earlier in the day, Hendel had been in contact with all the parties in the third bloc regarding an alliance for him to join, his spokesperson told The Jerusalem Post after the announcement of the split.

Russian attacks killed at least nine people and injured at least 68 across Ukraine over the past day, Ukrainian authorities reported on Sept. 6.
Firefighters were deployed in both Kyiv Oblast and Dnipropetrovsk Oblast to extinguish large fires following Russian attacks.
Two people in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast were injured, said the Governor Oleksandr Hanzha. No casualties were reported in Kyiv Oblast at the time of publication.
The attacks come amid an agreement between Russia and Ukraine that neither country's capital would be attacked while U.S envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are visiting to discuss peace talks.
At the time of publication, officials have not reported any hits in the city of Kyiv overnight, despite a drone air raid alert and attacks in the surrounding region.
The arrival of Witkoff and Kushner to Kyiv, expected around late morning on Sept. 6, is the first such visit by the two envoys to the Ukrainian capital.
Russia launched 108 drones against Ukraine overnight, according to the Ukrainian Air Force. Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 82 drones and six S8000 Banderol missiles. Russian missiles and drones struck 11 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at seven locations.
In Kharkiv Oblast, four people were killed and eight injured as a result of Russian attacks, Governor Oleh Syniebuhov said.
Among those killed were an 11-year-old boy and a 19-year-old woman in the town of Chuhuiv.
In Kherson Oblast, three people were killed, and a further 19 were injured, including two children, said Governor Oleksandr Prokudin.
Russia killed one person and injured a further 25 in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, said the local military administration. Attacks later in the morning injured two women.
In Mykolaiv Oblast, Russian Shahed drone attacks on transport infrastructure killed one driver in the Halytsynove community, said Governor Heorhii Reshetilov.
Russia injured two people in Donetsk Oblast and forced a further 915 people, including 136 children, to be evacuated from front-line areas, said the region's governor, Vadym Filashkin.
Seven people, among whom was one child, were injured by falling debris from a Russian drone in Khmenytskyi Oblast, said Governor Serhii Tyurin.
Three people were injured in Odesa Oblast on the morning of Sept. 6, said Governor Serhii Lysak.
Cherkasy Oblast, Poltava Oblast, and Sumy Oblast were also attacked, but no significant damage was reported.

Türkiye plans 30-year privatization of Bosphorus bridges, highways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:17:00 UTC
17:17:00 KST

AA Photo
Türkiye has adopted a new decision regarding the privatization of two state-operated Bosphorus bridges in Istanbul, along with highways, ring roads and connecting roads.
Under the new framework, the bridges, highways and ring roads will not be privatized as a single package but may be offered either together or separately.
A presidential decree published in the Official Gazette on Sept. 5 expanded the privatization program covering the Bosphorus (15 July Martyrs) Bridge and the Fatih Sultan Mehmet Bridge, as well as four highways, to include the Nigde-Pozanti Motorway, the Gaziantep Ring Motorway and the Caglayan Junction-Yenisehir Junction section of the Bursa Ring Road.
Under a 2010 decision, the bridges and highways were planned to be privatized as a single package through the transfer of operating rights for a period of 25 years from the date of physical handover.
The latest presidential decision introduced three key changes. The bridges and highways may now be privatized either as a whole or in separate groups, while the operating period has been extended to 30 years.
In a written statement on the decision, the Privatization Administration (OİB) emphasized that efforts concerning the highways and bridges operated by the General Directorate of Highways and included in the privatization portfolio do not involve the sale of public assets.
The administration said the model is based on transferring operating rights for a specified period while ownership remains with the state.

India supplied about 60 per cent of the diesel transiting through the Bab-el-Mandeb towards Europe in August, strengthening its role as a key source of refined fuel as Russian exports remain depressed and US shipments begin to decline, according to a report.Around 2,00,000 barrels per day of diesel, or gasoil, crossed the strategic shipping route for Europe last month, close to year-earlier levels after flows nearly stalled in March and April. Indian refiners accounted for roughly 60 per cent of that volume, energy analytics firm Vortexa said in a report.
India, the world’s fourth-largest refiner, has 258.1 million tonnes per annum of installed capacity, above domestic fuel demand. It exported 61.5 million tonnes of petroleum products in 2025-26, making it a major global supplier, PTI reported.However, sustaining these flows could become difficult. India’s crude and condensate imports fell to about 3.8 million barrels per day in August from 4.8 million barrels per day a year earlier, data showed.Russian diesel exports averaged only around 1,50,000 barrels per day during the first 25 days of August, down about 6,10,000 barrels per day year-on-year and 81 per cent below the five-year seasonal average.
The scheduled easing of Russia’s diesel export ban from September 1 may not quickly restore supplies, with Ukrainian drone strikes continuing to disrupt refineries and export infrastructure. Vortexa recorded 32 refinery attacks across July and August.
The Perm refinery, with capacity of 2,60,000 barrels per day, was left operating at only about 28 per cent of its crude distillation capacity after an attack, while no diesel cargoes have left Tuapse since a May strike.The US supplied about half of Europe’s seaborne diesel imports from outside the region in August, at around 5,20,000 barrels per day. But shipments fell from nearly 5,40,000 barrels per day in the first half of August to about 3,50,000 barrels per day in the second half.

A large AfD victory would pile more pressure onto Merz and his increasingly unpopular coalition. The party has been polling at more than 40%.

A large AfD victory would pile more pressure onto Merz and his increasingly unpopular coalition.

The CDU has ruled out forming a coalition with the AfD. However, Merz's party could work with other parties. At the same time, the CDU has also ruled out cooperation with the Left party by adopting an incompatibility clause at a party conference.
Polling stations in Saxony-Anhalt are open from 8 am to 6 pm.

In China, 531 people are still considered missing after the massive flood
Kyiv • UNN
The flood destroyed China's border port with Nepal. Thirty-one people were killed and 531 are missing, including more than 250 foreigners.
In China's border zone, which was devastated by a catastrophic flood, rescuers continue searching for 531 people reported missing. CNN reports, according to UNN.
Details
All that remains of the former Gyirong port is a rocky fissure. The high-altitude hub was completely washed off the face of the earth, leaving behind a lunar landscape of rocks, gravel and mud, which rescuers are still searching
Before the deadly disaster, this port was a bustling border crossing between China and Nepal. Hundreds of tourists and traders passed through it every day. On August 26, the port was hit by a powerful surge of water, which triggered a landslide and a massive flood.
Not a single survivor has been found at the port, which became an information-gathering center for families both in China and around the world. The answers are not immediately apparent here. The public five-story border control facility, which towered over the surrounding area in the imposing style of Chinese government institutions, was destroyed. All that can now be seen of the building is the remains of its foundation
According to Chinese authorities, 31 people have died, while another 531 are considered missing. More than 250 of those being sought are foreigners.
According to the publication, Chinese authorities have still not released a list of the people who were at the port during the disaster or are considered missing. This has raised questions about transparency, particularly among families desperately seeking news about missing loved ones.
In addition, search-and-rescue efforts are being hampered by the mountainous terrain, heavy rains and the risk of further landslides. Barrier lakes have also formed as debris and mud blocked parts of the river, creating an additional risk.
According to the authorities of China and Nepal, the deaths of more than 1,000 people have been confirmed in total following the disaster on August 26, while thousands still remain missing.

Zionist Home-The Reservists chairperson, Chili Tropper, has begun holding a series of consultations, assessments, and talks as he weighs four possible political paths ahead of the deadline to submit Knesset candidate lists, in what could be the most consequential days of his political career.
The first option is to continue alongside Yoaz Hendel in an independent run through the election. Some within the party are pressing for precisely that course, arguing against rushing to withdraw from the race or join an existing party.
The hope is that there is still a chance to build momentum in the final days and fight to cross the electoral threshold.
Joining up with Eisenkot, Bennett, or Liberman
The second option, considered one of the most serious, is to join Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar. With this scenario, Tropper would make the move together with his associates, Shira Shapira and Elisaf Peretz, creating a political alliance as a group rather than making the move on his own.
That possibility is being examined and is considered one of the two most likely alternatives from Tropper's perspective.
A third possibility is a similar move involving Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad, with Tropper joining together with Shapira and Peretz. That option, however, is more complicated.
Bennett currently has little room to offer them, while his alliance with Yair Lapid has already added pressure to the candidate list, further reducing the number of available slots and limiting his room to maneuver.
Another possibility under consideration is joining Avigdor Liberman. Here, too, the difficulty is similar: The demand is not for a place for Tropper alone, but for a package that would include all three members of his group, and Liberman is struggling to offer an arrangement of that scope.
Of the four possibilities currently on the table, two appear more realistic: joining Eisenkot or deciding to go all in on an independent run.
Pressure is expected to intensify in the coming days as the deadline for submitting the Knesset lists approaches.
Tropper will have to decide whether to gamble on the strength of his independent political bid and remain in the race, or choose a new political home that can secure places for both him and his associates in the next Knesset.
Tropper declared he would not help Netanyahu build a coalition
Last month, Tropper declared that he would not serve in a Netanyahu-led government. In an interview with 103FM in July, Tropper said his party would not help establish a government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. He said he would not be part of a coalition dependent on parties that are not Zionist.
"I have not hidden my opinion about Netanyahu. I am not among those who hate or despise him, but everyone who was there on October 7 needs to finish their term," the MK said.
Tropper added that he would not provide Netanyahu with the votes needed to reach a 61-seat majority because, in his view, such a government would rely on non-Zionist political forces.
"I, as part of such a coalition, cannot be there," Tropper said.
The remarks sparked an uproar in an internal WhatsApp group belonging to Tropper and Hendel's party. Hendel sought to calm tensions, saying: "We will go with whoever brings the largest number of Zionist recommendations. Netanyahu repeatedly says that he is continuing with his coalition, a coalition that depends on non-Zionist votes, and therefore it is not relevant for us to be part of it."
Unlike his party colleague, Hendel did not categorically rule out serving in a government led by Netanyahu.
"If a broad unity government is formed with Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman, Netanyahu and others, we will be part of it," Hendel said.

After fighting ISIS, Kurdish women fighters search for a place in Syria's new order - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:13:54 UTC
17:13:54 KST

More than 1,500 fighters from the Kurdish Women’s Protection Units (YPJ) are seeking a place in Syria’s new security institutions after the force was excluded from the army integration arrangements that followed the dissolution of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) as an independent military organization.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
YPJ commander Nowruz Ahmed said Syrian officials rejected the group’s proposal to enter the army as an independent women’s brigade or battalion. Speaking to Reuters from a military base in Qamishli in an interview published September 2, Ahmed said the proposal grew from the force’s years of combat experience against the Islamic State group (ISIS).
“We were aiming to join the army, because our forces have experience and expertise that would enable them to protect themselves in an organized way in the form of an independent brigade or battalion,” Ahmed told Reuters.
The YPJ is now discussing a possible role within the Interior Ministry’s special operations forces. Ahmed told Reuters that the YPJ has more than 1,500 fighters and has asked whether they could be incorporated as a single force. She said a response was expected in the coming days.
The dispute concerns more than employment within the new state. YPJ leaders want their members to remain together as an organized women’s formation rather than be split among different units or assigned individually across the country.
“When we hear that the men will be integrated into the army while we are told there is no place for us, it is natural for us to feel excluded,” a Kurdish fighter who asked to be identified as Hevrin Jwan to protect her identity told The Media Line. “We did not carry weapons for a short period. We spent years fighting and training, and we have military experience that we do not believe can simply be ignored,” she said.
YPJ fought ISIS alongside US-backed SDF
The YPJ was formed during Syria’s civil war and fought alongside the US-backed SDF in campaigns that drove ISIS from large parts of northern and eastern Syria. Its all-women ranks became internationally recognized during the fight against the terrorist group.
That wartime role now collides with Damascus’ effort to bring armed formations under unified state command. On August 25, SDF commander Mazloum Abdi announced that the SDF had ended its mission as an independent military force after integration into Syrian army brigades.
The January integration agreement called for SDF military and security personnel to enter the Defense and Interior ministries individually following security vetting.
Another Kurdish fighter, who asked not to be named, told The Media Line that the reported rejection raised concerns about the role envisioned for women in Syria’s armed institutions.
“If the disagreement is about the structure of the unit or who it reports to, that is something that can be negotiated,” she said. “But when the message is that there is no place for us in the army at all, the problem becomes much bigger. We want to be part of state institutions, but without being asked to give up everything we have built over the past years,” she said.
The Syrian Defense and Interior ministries did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment about the discussions. Interior Ministry spokesman Noureddine al-Baba told Kurdish broadcaster Rudaw that YPJ fighters would be welcome in the ministry, without specifying their duties or whether they could serve as a unified formation. He said Interior Ministry personnel could be deployed across Syria.
Sources familiar with the discussions have also spoken of an earlier proposal for the fighters to join the tourist police. A YPJ spokeswoman denied that such an offer had been made.
For many YPJ members, the negotiations concern their collective identity as much as their future assignments.
“They always look at women as weak,” YPJ fighter Goksu Afrin told The Media Line. “We do not derive our strength from men or from the current state, and we insist on maintaining our own distinct identity. This is our choice, and this is our cause. We are open to everyone.”
Kurdish commander says women fighters have constitutional right to role
Another Kurdish commander said Syria’s constitution should guarantee a defined role for women fighters.
“We did not wait until today for someone to defend us,” she told The Media Line. “We women defended ourselves.”
Service in the Interior Ministry’s special operations forces could offer a compromise: formal entry into the state while preserving some collective structure and leveraging the fighters’ training. Whether Damascus will accept that arrangement remains unclear.
“We do not want a confrontation with the state, and we do not want to remain outside its institutions,” one fighter told The Media Line. “But we also do not want the price of integration to be the end of our existence as an organized women’s force.”

When a DNA test reveals unexpected Swiss ancestry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:10:00 UTC
17:10:00 KST

When a DNA test reveals unexpected Swiss ancestry
At the age of 53, Robert Thayer discovered his genes didn’t match his presumed family tree. Finding himself suddenly connected to the Liechti family, he travelled to Switzerland to visit the hamlets his ancestors had lived in before emigrating to the United States.
On a cloudy day in May, a small white car takes a right into Erlenbach im Simmental, a little village in the valley behind Spiez, canton Bern. Finding its way on the narrow streets through the houses, the car turns onto the single-lane country road that heads up the hill, closely followed by a second car. The scenery is picturesque: idyllic steep green meadows on both sides of the road, a stunning view over the valley, and little traffic that would otherwise require precise manoeuvring.
In the white car, Albert Liechti checks with his wife whether this is the way they’d taken the previous time. She confirms it is. Liechti, 82, is a passionate genealogist, and today, for the second time, he’s bringing some of his distant American relatives on an ancestry tour in canton Bern. In the second car, Robert Thayer, his wife, his sister Gloria and her son are slightly overwhelmed by all the twists and turns up the hill. This is a road only used by locals who know where they’re going.
The mystery of history
A twist of fate is what brought the American tourists here in the first place. In 2018, Robert found out he wasn’t a Thayer. When his sister gifted two of her brothers a DNA test, their results surprisingly linked them to the Leichty family (an Americanised spelling of the Swiss surname Liechti).
“It would seem that there had been an encounter between my grandmother and the farmer across the street. We grew up not knowing our father was the illegitimate child of this relationship. We don’t even think he knew,” Robert explains.
“The Leichty and the Thayers lived in adjacent farms. They lived very close to each other,” he adds – so close that Robert and his siblings didn’t know they were going to school with their cousins. “Good thing we didn’t date them,” Robert and Gloria laugh.
The unexpected revelation and the matches provided by his DNA test got Robert into genealogy research. “Both Elizabeth and Jacob Leichty Sr. were the common ancestors to myself and my closest DNA matches, and also my paternal great-grandparents,” says Robert. “What isn’t certain and may never be is which one of their sons living at the time of dad’s conception in 1926 was our biological grandfather: Jacob Robert Jr. or his brother Frederick Ernest”.
Today Robert is a member of the Collin County Genealogical Society, of which he leads the special interest group “All things technology”, where he discusses how AI is helping to decode handwritten documents and the ethical concerns around this technology being used for genealogical research.
The research into his biological grandfather’s lineage in Switzerland is how Robert got to know Albert Liechti, his guide for the day. “About five years ago, I came across an article by AlbertExternal link published in the December 2018 newsletter of the Genealogical-Heraldic Society of Bern,” Robert says. “In that piece, he documented several generations of my ancestors, including my previously unknown fourth great-grandparents, Christen Liechti and Katharina (née Augsburger)”.
Through the article, he found Albert’s email address and got in touch with him, starting a fervent exchange of genealogical information. A couple of years later, the two decided to take a Y-DNA test, and discovered they have a common ancestor who lived in Landiswil, canton Bern, around 1530.
A Y-DNA test analyses the Y chromosome, which is passed down almost unchanged from father to son through the direct paternal line. Because only biological males carry a Y chromosome, females can’t take this test.
To trace the maternal line, both men and women can take a mtDNA test, which analyses mitochondrial DNA passed down virtually unchanged by the egg cell.
Nearly all mainstream commercial at-home kits use Autosomal DNA tests. This analyses genetical material inherited from both parents, grandparents etc, making it the best and most affordable way for finding relatives, from immediate family to 5th or 6th cousins.
A trip down history lane
For his 40th wedding anniversary, Robert and his wife decided to travel to Switzerland for the first time, to see the country where Jakob and Elizabeth Liechti lived before boarding a ship headed for New York in 1883. Albert naturally offered to take them on a small tour of the Bernese Ober- and Mittelland, to show them the houses where their ancestors lived, and the churches where they were christened and married.
Albert had already taken Robert’s cousin Siena on the same tour the year before. He meticulously researched the places of residence of some of their ancestors, chatted with the current owners about the possibility to stop by for a quick visit, and prepared a precise itinerary that would take the group up and down the Bernese hills, starting in Spiez – where Robert’s second great-grandparents got married in 1849 – and ending in Ätzlischwand, where four Liechti families lived between 1612 and 1715.
The group diligently follows Albert’s lead, who keeps a close eye on his watch to get back to the car in time to drive to the next location. Robert’s sister Gloria is fascinated by the old buildings, while her son documents their trip with his camera and they all marvel at the postcard scenery surrounding the small quiet hamlets.
“I feel like this is such a blessing,” says Robert emotionally. “I owe [Albert] so much for what he’s done, and I don’t know how to repay him. He’s like, ‘I don’t want repayment’ but I just feel like I owe him thousands of US dollars for this. Most people pay good money to have somebody take you on a tour of their homeland. I guess that’s the beauty of this passion for genealogy”.
It’s just the beginning
At their last stop in Ätzlischwand, Elisabeth and Alfred Jegerlehner, the current owners of the house and farm Albert has brought the group to see, treat everyone to a small Zvieri, a traditional Swiss-German afternoon snack. Cured meat, Swiss cheese, and biscuits are passed around, while guests and hosts exchange a few anecdotes thanks to Albert’s translation from English to Swiss German and vice-versa.
Upon departure, they all embrace each other tightly, as if they’d known each other for years, and extend mutual invites for future visits. Robert is looking forward to translating all the voice memos he’s recorded throughout the day of Albert speaking Swiss German with people they met along the way. The two distant relatives say their goodbyes, knowing they’ll be keeping in touch to advance in their genealogical research.

Iran to tackle economic issues, threatens ‘more painful’ response to US attacks
- Iran vows a stronger, faster response to any US attacks amid ongoing military clashes and economic sanctions.
- Iran faces severe economic challenges from US sanctions, focusing on reforms to stabilise currency, inflation, and unemployment.
- US and Iran continue tit-for-tat strikes, with US hitting Iranian tankers linked to the IRGC, escalating tensions in the Gulf region.
AI generated
TEHRAN – Tehran said on Sept 6 it will step up efforts to tackle problems created by the US sanctions that are crippling its economy, even as a senior Iranian official warned of a “more painful response” if Iran comes under further attack.
Six months after the United States and Israel struck Iran, the war appears to be at a stalemate. A preliminary ceasefire accord reached in June has unravelled, and little progress has been made in diplomatic efforts to get the peace process back on track.
After a pause in military action for much of August, tit-for-tat strikes have resumed, with the US Central Command (CENTCOM) saying it hit three Iranian tankers on Sept 5 in response to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launching ballistic missiles at two US Navy ships.
Following the attacks, Iran’s Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said on Sept 6 the US should understand the rules of the game in the war against Iran have changed “before it is too late”.
“From now on, any attack against Iran’s interests and security will receive a faster, heavier and more painful response,” he said in a speech published on his Telegram channel.
Tehran has shown it still retains the capability to attack US interests in neighbouring countries and to shut down oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil supplies flowed prior to the conflict.
However, the US campaign to throttle Iran’s economy by blockading its oil exports and stopping sanctions evasion is growing increasingly difficult to withstand, three senior Iranian sources have said.
In his speech, Ghalibaf added that, alongside the military front, Iran’s main battle is now over production and people’s livelihoods.
He cited sharp currency fluctuations, inflation, unemployment and market management as major challenges, adding that Iranians can tolerate hardship but not mismanagement or inaction, and expected the government to act quickly.
Iran’s Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said Tehran plans to respond to US economic pressure with reforms, and rejected the idea that sanctions would cause it to change course.
“They speak of economic pressure and isolation, of breaking off financial ties, and they think that by pressuring the economy of a country they can change the decisions of its people,” he said.
“I have to clarify one point: The responsibility of reforming Iran’s economy is with its government and people, not with the US Treasury,” he added.
Separately, Deputy Economy Minister Morteza Zamanian said the ministry’s “Economic War Headquarters” was doubling down on its work to resolve problems caused by the war.
Iran is the third-largest producer in the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries. It exported 90 per cent of its crude via its Kharg Island export hub before the war. Flows have been disrupted since a US blockade of Iranian oil exports began in mid-April.
On Aug 31, US President Donald Trump issued a one-line social media post accompanied by an AI-generated video depicting Kharg Island being “blown to smithereens”. The Iranian authorities have vowed a strong response if Kharg is attacked.
In an interview aired on state TV on Sept 6, Iran’s Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad said the island has been hit around 550 times in previous months but continues to operate.
Iran has also imposed a blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, creating an issue for Trump by pushing up fuel prices globally ahead of midterm elections for his Republican Party in November.
On Sept 5, CENTCOM said it struck tankers linked to the Iranian Guards, after the IRGC launched ballistic missiles at two US Navy ships.
“Following Iran’s failed attacks, CENTCOM permanently disabled the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask,” it said.
It added that it also “completely destroyed the unladen crude oil carrier M/T Kylo in the Gulf of Oman, striking the vessel in multiple critical locations to render it inoperable after the crew was directed to abandon ship”.
Video posted by CENTCOM showed large fireballs and billowing flames after projectiles slammed into the ships.
The three vessels were “part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies”, it said.
‘Higher economic cost’
The Guards, meanwhile, claimed the two American warships they targeted had been “forced to retreat” after “suffering damage”, but CENTCOM said those ships successfully evaded Iranian attacks.
CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper said after the operation: “If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost, taking out three of yours.”
The Iranian foreign ministry hit out at Washington over the strikes on oil tankers, calling them “illegal and aggressive actions”.
A correspondent for Iranian state TV in Jask, in the southern province of Hormozgan, said one of the tankers was empty and the second was carrying oil. The crews were transported to shore on lifeboats, they said.
Another state TV correspondent on Kharg Island said the attack there caused no casualties.
Iran’s Khatam-al Anbiya central military command warned that if the US continues its attacks, then Tehran’s retaliation against US warships will be “more severe than before, and there is a possibility of their expansion”.
The Trump administration has tried to downplay the significance of the six-month conflict, which has proven increasingly unpopular at home as midterm elections near.
US Vice-President J.D. Vance went so far as to say that he “wouldn’t call it a war”.
Trump reiterated that view on Sept 4, calling the war “small potatoes” for Washington.
Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei warned this week that the Islamic republic had adopted a “new strategy” against Washington that “will shatter your foundations”.
Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly threatened to claim sovereignty over the strait, even posting a map showing it as “new US territory”.
Vance has insisted the US will not reopen talks with Iran until it ends attacks on commercial shipping in Hormuz. REUTERS

WHO "deeply concerned" as Russia destroys three of its warehouses in Ukraine in three months
Over the past three months, Russian forces have destroyed three humanitarian aid warehouses used by the World Health Organisation (WHO) in Ukraine, including one of its main warehouses, destroying medical supplies intended for frontline and hard-to-reach areas.
Source: WHO Regional Office for Europe (WHO/Europe)
Details: The WHO/Europe attributed the destruction of the warehouses to airstrikes, but failed to mention that Russia was responsible.
The organisation said one of the incidents occurred on 3 September. That was when Russian forces struck one of Ukraine's largest pharmaceutical warehouses – the Biocon logistics complex in the Boryspil district of Kyiv Oblast.
The WHO also mentioned the destruction of a humanitarian warehouse in Dnipro in early August. Half of the medical supplies and equipment stored there, which were intended to help around 225,000 people in frontline and hard-to-reach areas, were lost in the attack.
Another warehouse in Kyiv Oblast used by the WHO was damaged during a large-scale wave of Russian attacks on the capital and the oblast in July.
Silviu Domente, WHO Representative to Ukraine, said: "When humanitarian warehouses storing critical supplies are attacked, the impact goes far beyond the loss of buildings or equipment. It can delay or disrupt the delivery of essential health support to people who need it most. Right now, our teams are spending valuable time and resources moving supplies from site to site to keep them safe; time and resources that should go into delivering health care, not protecting it from attack. We are deeply concerned by the growing pattern of attacks on health in Ukraine, including on humanitarian storage facilities." Dr Domente did not name the aggressor.
According to the UN's Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, at least 20 warehouses storing humanitarian supplies have come under attack in 2026. In addition, the WHO has confirmed 15 attacks on warehouses storing medical supplies.
The organisation said it continues to work with Ukraine's Ministry of Health and other partners across the country despite the attacks. In particular, alternative arrangements for storing medical supplies have already been found following the latest strikes.
Quote from Domente: "We will continue to do everything we can to keep humanitarian health support moving across Ukraine. I also want to express my deepest gratitude to Ukraine's health-care workers, who continue to provide care to their communities with extraordinary courage and resilience, despite the enormous challenges they face every day."
Details: The WHO said that this year it has provided equipment and medical supplies to more than 300 facilities across the country, reaching an estimated 3 million people.
Background:
- In a single attack on the night of 1-2 June, Russian forces damaged five medical facilities in Kyiv.
- As of May, Russian forces had carried out more than 3,000 attacks on Ukraine's healthcare system.

How are NATO DIANA innovators improving wound care on the front lines?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:07:44 UTC
17:07:44 KST

Combat wound care and management have come a long way over the last few decades. And while advances in trauma care have helped save countless lives on the battlefield, preventing infection and supporting recovery after the initial injury can be just as important.
In operational environments where evacuation may not be possible and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an increasing concern, there is a growing need for technologies that improve the way we treat wounds in the battlefield.
Innovators in NATO DIANA’s 2026 cohort are helping to meet that need by developing new approaches to wound care. From light-activated antimicrobial therapies to phage-based precision therapeutics and treatments, innovative solutions could revolutionise wound care for both civilian trauma patients and military personnel.
GutSee – Decoding the microbiome to treat infections
GutSee Health is a UK biotechnology company pioneering precision therapies for bacterial diseases. Its proprietary AI platform uses microbiome data to create precision treatments based on bacteriophage therapy. Phages are naturally occurring viruses that seek out and destroy specific bacteria without harming beneficial ones. This makes them useful for treating a variety of problems, from infected battlefield injuries to ongoing gut conditions like irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).
Although the science behind phage therapy is well established, developing these treatments remains fragmented, manual and focused on individual patients.
GutSee’s platform brings four key stages into one integrated process. First, it matches bacterial strains with the phages most likely to destroy them. Second, it predicts how bacteria may evolve and mutate, helping treatments stay ahead of emerging resistance. Third, it designs mixtures of several phages combined with beneficial bacteria to improve the overall bacterial balance rather than simply remove a harmful pathogen. Finally, it connects treatment design with manufacturing and clinical use. Together, these stages form a continuous learning cycle that improves treatment recommendations, accelerating therapy development by up to 98% compared with traditional laboratory-heavy processes.
GutSee is initially focusing on combat and civilian wound infections, working with NATO, governments and foundations, with support from the Ukrainian government. Longer term, GutSee plans to license its platform for further areas, including gut disorders and oncology.
LightOx – Using light to help control wound infections
LightOx is developing light-activated treatments that help kill harmful bacteria that colonise wounds. They produce a simple gel that can be applied directly to a wound. The gel is activated by a light, and the treatment helps kill harmful bacteria in a targeted way, right where the infection is developing.
In battlefield injuries, bacteria can quickly enter damaged tissue and cause infections that slow healing and increase the risk of complications, including sepsis, amputation, or even death. This is especially challenging when common antibiotics stop working against drug-resistant bacteria. LightOx’s approach offers a tool to help control infection in wounds while injured personnel await further treatment, while also fighting AMR.
Earlier this year, LightOx was recognised for its light-activated treatment for infected wounds, with an Outstanding Achievement Award at the Medilink Healthcare Business Awards 2026.
Deep Breathe – Helping medics detect hidden chest injuries faster
In battlefield trauma, injuries to the lungs or chest can be difficult to spot without hospital equipment, but failing to detect them can delay critical care. Deep Breathe, based in Canada, have developed a solution involving a portable ultrasound that frontline medical teams can use to detect serious chest and torso injuries faster, as well internal abdominal bleeding.
Deep Breathe combine ultrasound with AI that recognise signs of injuries such as a collapsed lung, bleeding in the chest, or bruising of lung tissue. Designed to work on phones or tablets and in places with limited or no connectivity, the technology could help medics make faster, more informed decisions closer to the point of injury, improving triage in remote areas and difficult environments.
By bringing this kind of support closer to the battlefield – at the point-of-injury – Deep Breathe’s solution could help improve diagnosis and treatment, avoiding unnecessary invasive procedures, and speeding up life-saving decisions when every second matters.
Biocellis – Instant detection of biological and chemical agents
After a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) attack, effective treatment requires a quick response and knowledge of the intoxicating agent. Biocellis is a company from France that has developed an ultra-sensitive diagnostic testing system that can rapidly detect and identify biological and chemical agents.
Traditionally, rapid testing methods sacrifice sensitivity and most sensitive tests do not provide results fast enough. Biocellis has patented a bioluminescence immunoassays platform that delivers laboratory grade sensitivity in less than 60 seconds. The technology uses a compact, portable format that is ideal for point-of-care and high-throughput screening.
Rapid and reliable detection helps clinicians treat patients with the most effective remedies available. Biocellis helps medical professionals understand what they are up against so that they can quickly provide the treatment and care that patients need.
These technologies are already filling some of the most urgent gaps in battlefield medicine. By giving frontline medical teams better tools to save lives and improve care when conditions are at their most challenging.
Through NATO DIANA, these innovators gain access to the tools and resources they need to take their promising, cutting-edge technologies from concept to real-world use. Through expertise from technical and defence mentors, opportunities to test their technologies, and access to operational exercises like Vigorous Warrior, innovators are supported by DIANA to ensure their solutions are not only technically strong, but deployable and relevant in the demanding environments where they are needed most.
Source: diana.nato.int

Russia Strikes Kyiv Airports Ahead of Scheduled US Delegation Arrival
Russia deliberately targeted airports in Kyiv and Boryspil overnight on September 5, in what Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said may have been a response to preparations for a possible US delegation to arrive in Ukraine by air.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Zelenskyy said the strikes marked the first deliberate Russian attacks on the two airports in a long time and linked them to discussions about allowing US representatives to fly directly into Ukraine.
“Obviously, such Russian strikes on airports are a reaction to discussions and preparations for the possibility of the American side using an aircraft to arrive in Ukraine and land at either Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian president said Russia used Shahed-type attack drones in the strikes, describing the attack as a response to US diplomatic efforts.
Zelenskyy also said Ukraine would adjust its operation concerning Russian airspace next week, citing the risks created by drones and missiles operating over Russia. He did not provide further details on what the changes would involve.

“Of course, there are no threats to diplomacy from our side and there will not be any. Ukraine is interested in bringing peace closer. Russia will be held accountable for what it does,” Zelenskyy said.
The overnight Russian attack also struck other locations across Ukraine. Zelenskyy said four people were killed and five wounded after a civilian enterprise was hit in Kamianske, Dnipropetrovsk region. Residential buildings were damaged in Kherson, Boryspil, and the Kharkiv region, while Russian drones targeted shopping centers in Sumy and Mykolaiv.
The airport strikes came as preparations continue for potential visits by representatives of US President Donald Trump. Zelenskyy said on September 4 that Ukraine would suspend aerial strikes against Russia for the period necessary to ensure the safe travel of Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and his son-in-law Jared Kushner.

France can’t finance Ukraine forever – Le Pen party head
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:06:37 UTC
17:06:37 KST

France can’t finance Ukraine forever – Le Pen party head
France lacks money for itself and simply cannot keep funding Ukraine indefinitely, Jordan Bardella, the president of Marine Le Pen’s right-wing National Rally (NR) party, has said.
The main French opposition party faced harsh criticism from its rivals earlier this week after its vice president, Louis Aliot, said that NR “would turn off the tap” for Kiev if it comes to power after the 2027 presidential vote. Le Pen is seen as having strong chances to succeed in the election next year, no matter who her rival will be in the second round.
Bardella weighed in on the issue during his speech at the Ambrosetti Forum in Italy on Saturday, saying that Ukraine needs support from France and other Western nations during the conflict with Russia, but “our objective should not be to finance the war ad vitam æternam,” which means ‘forever’ in Latin.
France has a national debt of €3.5 trillion ($4.6 billion) and cannot be “giving money that we no longer have” to Vladimir Zelensky’s government, he argued.
“The extremely serious and worrying state of French public finances means we can’t give money without any guarantees or assurances that this money will be repaid one day,” the National Rally president said.
Paris has been one of the strongest backers of Kiev in the EU after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022, providing it with billions in military aid and supplying various sophisticated weapons, including CAESAR self-propelled howitzers and Mirage fighter jets.
According to Bardella, the Americans were “much smarter” than the Europeans when it came to assistance for Kiev “because the money they gave to Ukraine is secured against rare earth mining.” He was referring to the deal agreed upon between Washington and Kiev last year, which grants the US preferential access to Ukrainian mineral resources.
During US President Donald Trump’s second term, Washington also significantly reduced aid to Ukraine, making European NATO members pay for American-made arms supplied to the country.
Earlier this week, Trump warned that he intends to present Europe with a belated bill for billions of dollars that Washington spent arming Ukraine under his predecessor, Joe Biden. He previously estimated that Biden gave Zelensky more than $300 billion worth of weapons for “free.”
Le Pen said on Thursday that the National Rally is skeptical about further assistance to Ukraine because it believes that the conflict with Russia needs a diplomatic solution.
A poll by Harris Interactive in late August suggested that Le Pen has the support of 34% of the French public, which should guarantee her a place in the second round of the presidential election, where she would likely win comfortably against either her left-wing rival Jean-Luc Mélenchon or the centrist candidate, former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe.
Russian officials said repeatedly that foreign weapons being sent to Kiev will not prevent Moscow from achieving its military goals, but will merely prolong the fighting, while increasing the risk of a direct confrontation between Russia and NATO.
