2 years after Israeli forces killed Aysenur Ezgi Eygi, family still waits for justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:05:00 UTC
17:05:00 KST

Two years after Israeli forces killed Aysenur Ezgi Eygi in the occupied West Bank, her family says there has been virtually no progress toward accountability for her death.
"It's exactly where it was on day one," Hamid Ali, Eygi's husband, told Anadolu from his home in Seattle. "We're still asking for the same thing, which is an investigation as a first step into getting justice for her."
Eygi, 26, a dual Turkish-US citizen, was killed Sept. 6, 2024, while participating in a protest against Israeli settlement expansion in the West Bank town of Beita, near Nablus.
The Israeli military said she was hit "indirectly and unintentionally" by Israeli military fire that "was not aimed at her" as its forces fired at protesters allegedly throwing rocks.
Witnesses and her family disputed the Israeli account, saying she was targeted deliberately during a peaceful protest.
A Washington Post investigation found she was shot around 20 minutes after clashes had ended, when protesters had already retreated more than 200 yards (182 meters) from Israeli forces.
Then-Secretary of State Antony Blinken called Eygi's killing "unprovoked and unjustified" days after the shooting.
But two years later, the US has not opened an independent investigation into her death despite repeated calls from her family and members of Congress.
Washington instead deferred to an Israeli inquiry that has never produced a public finding.
For Eygi's father, Mehmet Suat Eygi, the absence of an investigation has left little hope that the US will deliver the accountability his family has sought.
"I don't have much hope for justice because America is the financier of Aysenur's killing. America therefore cannot investigate itself," he told Anadolu.
The lack of movement in Eygi's case comes as the number of Americans killed by Israeli forces or settlers has continued to grow.
Eygi is among 14 US citizens killed by Israeli forces or settlers since 2003, according to the rights group DAWN, which tracks the cases. None has resulted in a criminal prosecution.
The list includes Sayfollah Musallet, a 20-year-old beaten to death by settlers in the West Bank in July 2025, and Nasrallah Abu Siyam, a 19-year-old shot near Jerusalem in February.
Brad Parker, associate director of policy at the Center for Constitutional Rights and part of the legal team supporting Eygi's family, said two years have brought no US criminal investigation or other accountability measures.
“There's no new developments on the investigation front, criminal investigation from the US, or really anything focused on accountability for Aysenur's killing,” he said. "There's absolutely no follow-up, no update.”
He added that the family has little confidence that an Israeli-led investigation would produce meaningful accountability, pointing to previous cases, including that of Shireen Abu Akleh, a Palestinian-American journalist for Al Jazeera who was fatally shot on May 11, 2022.
"There's no indication that the Trump administration is interested in holding perpetrators accountable for killing American citizens in the West Bank, in Gaza, sort of anywhere," he said.
"The impunity that exists is perpetuated over the years by lack of action by the US government," Parker added.
With no independent federal investigation, the family's push for accountability has increasingly extended to Washington state, where Eygi grew up.
A joint memorial calling for a US investigation into her death advanced through the state Legislature this year but failed to win final passage before the end of the legislative session.
"The support we got from the members of the Washington State Legislature in that memorial was so heartening," Ali said.
He attributed its failure primarily to timing and legislative maneuvering, saying Republicans in the Washington State House used the limited time remaining in the session as leverage over other issues.
“I don't think it was because of lack of support. I think it was just more of a strategical kind of failure,” Ali said.
While pursuing accountability, Eygi's family and friends have also sought to preserve her memory in the community where she grew up.
Around her birthday on July 27, friends and supporters gathered in Seattle to paint a community mural of her portrait, designed by artist James Hesketh.
"It's not all negative. We've been building community," Ali said.
He said the family hopes Eygi's legacy will encourage ordinary people to believe their actions can matter.
“She’s become a symbol, and we can't really help that,” he said. “But it doesn't mean that what she did was exceptional.
“I don't think she thought by going to the West Bank and being a part of the protests, she was going to change the tide of the war or free Palestine,” he added. “But she understood that you can do something, and it does make a difference. It does have an effect.”
For Eygi's father, the two-year anniversary is also a measure of a loss that time has done little to diminish.
“It is impossible to get used to a life without Aysenur. She is always on our minds, every second,” he said.
Despite the lack of accountability, he said Eygi's emergence as a symbol of solidarity with Palestinians and protests against Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza was a source of pride.
"Ultimately, justice has not been served. What remains for us is a life without Aysenur."
Anadolu asked the US State Department whether it supports an independent investigation into Eygi’s killing, given the lack of accountability from Israel's inquiry.
“The Department of State has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans. Embassy Jerusalem remained in touch with the family of Aysenur Eygi and the Government of Israel as it investigated this case,” it said.
The Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment. The Israeli military also did not respond.
The Turkish Foreign Ministry called Eygi's killing a "murder committed by the Netanyahu government," and Turkish prosecutors opened their own investigation into her death.
As Eygi's family enters a third year without the independent US investigation it first demanded after her killing, Ali said it is preparing for a longer fight.
"We've been developing a long-term strategy and what we want to do for Aysenur, for her legacy, but also to help others, unfortunately, who might be in a similar situation," he said.

17:02:35 KST

The Hague’s historic jenever distillery is fighting for its life
Brandon Hartley
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The iconic Van Kleef Distillery dates back to 1776. It’s faced countless challenges since then, but the latest round could force it to close or substantially change.
For over two centuries, the Van Kleef Distillery in The Hague has been mixing up unique liqueurs and genever made with time-tested recipes. Vincent van Gogh is one of the customers known to have sampled its spirits.
Despite its rich history and status as the last remaining distillery in the city, owner Fleur Kruyt says Van Kleef is currently facing a series of setbacks that could shut down its long-time location on the Lange Beestenmarkt.
“Right now I have the same colour hair as my grandmother at the age of 96,” she told DutchNews during an interview in the distillery’ tasting room.
Kruyt has spent the past several years trying to come up with solutions to appease her landlord and city officials as she strives to expand Van Kleef’s operations, modernise its museum, and, more than anything else, prevent its doors from closing altogether.
It’s all enough to turn the hair of even the most steadfast and indomitable of small business owners completely white.
But these challenges are only the latest in Van Kleef’s tumultuous history. Over the years, it’s contended with the sudden death of an owner, a crime wave, overzealous safety inspectors, and the Covid pandemic.
The first few centuries
 The distillery dates all the way back to the late 18th century. It originally opened in 1776 as Distilleerderij “Anker” before being taken over by the Van Kleef family in 1842.
Kruyt is convinced Van Gogh stopped by at least once. The famous artist may have even been a regular given his proclivities. He lived down the street from 1869 to 1873 and spent those years working at Goupil & Cie, an art business in The Hague owned by his uncle.
Along with the rest of the Netherlands, the distillery managed to endure the impacts of the Spanish flu pandemic and two World Wars, but it was a safety inspection in 1986 that came much closer to shutting it down.
Explosive concerns
 The officials declared the 40,000 litres of alcohol sitting in the distillery’s vats were a huge safety risk that made it an almost literal ticking time bomb. They decided it was no longer safe to distill alcohol on the property.
At the time, Van Kleef was teetering on the edge of bankruptcy. The surrounding neighbourhood was considered a “no-go zone” for many of the city’s residents and the distillery wasn’t getting much foot traffic.
“If you walked these streets as a woman at night back then, you were either a prostitute or tired of your life,” Kruyt said. “There was lots of criminality. No one came here anymore.”
After much discussion and planning, production was moved off site. The building itself was purchased by a local development company called Stadsherstel Den Haag and Van Kleef officially became a tenant in its long-time home.
The books were eventually balanced after it attained historical status and Van Kleef finally reopened as a multipurpose operation in 1995. Along with the museum and a tasting room, Van Kleef’s liqueurs are bottled and labelled there to this day.
Even more setbacks
 The construction of a tram tunnel and the redesign of the street out front dragged on for over a decade and further drove customers away.
The distillery’s revenue dropped by 80% when the city began installing barriers around the neighbourhood to discourage auto traffic in 2009. Its suppliers and customers had to navigate a maze every time they tried to go there.
Kruyt, who was operating Van Kleef with her husband Louis Centazzo at the time, was forced to use their house as collateral on a loan to keep it open. Then he suddenly died in 2015, leaving her to manage the distillery on her own.
Foreclosure followed and Kruyt moved into an apartment on the property. The hits kept coming as gentrification quickly transformed the neighbourhood and raised the distillery’s monthly rent along with it.
Then the Covid crisis began, which forced Van Kleef to shut down its tasting room. Undaunted, Kruyt and her crew came up with clever ways to ensure revenue would keep coming in.
She joked that “booze was declared a necessity” during the pandemic. Kruyt developed a “vaccine” after inspiration struck while she was giving her dog injections for arthritis. “The Van Kleef Vaccine” is a mix of Limoncello, Vitamin C, and ginger-infused liqueur.
At first, Kruyt fretted that it wouldn’t go over well with customers who had spent weeks social distancing and worrying they’d be the next ones to catch Covid. Those fears proved unfounded.
“And the first people who bought it? Doctors and pharmacists,” she recalled. “They found it really cool. I thought, ‘If these people find it funny, I don’t care about the rest!’”
A “ginitiser” sold in spray bottles soon followed. It, too, was a hit.
The current dilemmas
 “We’ve always managed and, whenever I feel bad, I turn on the television and see how it could be a lot worse,” Kruyt said before discussing the latest round of threats to the distillery.
The city’s decision to impose a flat €50-a-day parking fee has taken another bite out of Van Kleef’s revenue. The policy was so controversial it was even covered by The Guardian in 2023. If all this wasn’t enough, Kruyt broke her ankle while on a summer holiday and the recovery process required several surgeries.
Determined to keep the distillery where it’s been for over 200 years, Kruyt has been combating another wave of financial woes coupled with bureaucratic headaches, soaring energy bills, and other increased costs. Even the price of the glass that goes into Van Kleef’s bottles has gone up recently.
A crowdfunding campaign has been underway since 2025. Plans were also made to expand operations to attract more visitors, but negotiations with Stadsherstel Den Haag have proven challenging.
After over two years of discussions about everything from the future of the museum to renovations for the apartments on the property, Kruyt said the situation has been handed over to a new director named Jan-Willem de Bruijn.
“Stadsherstel Den Haag is currently taking a comprehensive look at the complex,” De Bruijn told DutchNews. “This means that, in addition to the shop and the tasting room, we are also focusing on the redevelopment of the museum and garden as well as upgrades in the apartments. In doing so, we aim to invest sustainably in the preservation of this unique and characteristic part of The Hague.”
Delays with permitting haven’t helped. DutchNews contacted the office of Alderwoman Saskia Bruines for comment about this and other matters concerning the distillery, but had not received a response as of press time.
Fighting onward
 Regardless of what happens next, Kruyt says Van Kleef will continue in one form or another, even if that means turning it into a distillery-and-wholesaler-only operation at a facility closed to the public and likely located on the outskirts of The Hague.
“But all of this history would go away,” she said as she gestured towards the centuries-old equipment in Van Kleef’s museum.
Takeaway liqueurs and tastings have covered the costs of maintaining the distillery’s historical inventory, but the current circumstances have made that impossible to continue. As Kruyt faces another round of discussions with Stadsherstel Den Haag, she’s determined to stay optimistic.
“We met with Jan-Willem a few weeks ago,” she said. “We’re really happy that he is taking everything seriously and trying to preserve the heritage that we have here.”
Still open for business
 Visitors to Van Kleef can currently visit the small museum, enjoy drinks and snacks in its tasting room, host gatherings in a former storage cellar turned conference room, and purchase bottles of liqueurs made with recipes that date back to the 17th century.
Among them is Bridal Tears, which contains flakes of 24-carat gold. It was once a popular wedding gift. The bawdy tales and traditions surrounding it and two accompanying liqueurs could fill an entire book.
In an age of alcoholic beverages with preservatives and other ingredients that are difficult to describe, let alone pronounce the names of, Van Kleef is still doing things the old-fashioned way.
“All of our recipes have been preserved,” Kruyt said. “We have an archive full of them that began in the 1840s. Everything you’re tasting is real in the sense that there’s no artificial flavouring or colourings.”
The distillery continues to attract international visitors and aficionados of liqueurs. Kruyt said a few of them are household names, but she demurred when asked for the details.
“What happens at Van Kleef, stays at Van Kleef,” she said. “So any celebrities out there, you can come here and we won’t talk about you.”

On September 6, Ukrainian forces used long-range FP-1 UAVs to strike one of Russia’s largest oil-processing facilities — the Ryazan Oil Refinery. The Fire Point company, which manufactures strike drones, reported this, UNN writes.
Details
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck the Ryazan Oil Refinery using FP-1 UAVs. The Ryazan Oil Refinery, one of Russia’s largest oil refineries, has a capacity of approximately 17 million tonnes of oil per year

Additionally
The Ryazan Oil Refinery is one of Russia’s largest oil-processing facilities. Its design capacity is approximately 17 million tonnes of oil per year (about 4.9% of the total volume of oil refining in the Russian Federation).
The refinery is part of the structure of "Rosneft." The facility has repeatedly been hit and attacked by UAVs operated by Ukraine’s Defense Forces (in particular, in May, July, and September 2026). Previous attacks caused significant damage to processing units, prolonged shutdowns of primary and secondary oil processing, and fires on the refinery’s premises.
Recall

Which overseas property markets will be the winners and losers if Fed raises US rates?
Fed chairman’s focus on inflation at meeting last month has heightened expectations of monetary tightening
Comments by US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh at its annual economic policy symposium in Jackson Hole last month have reinforced expectations of an impending interest rate rise in the world’s largest economy, which would have significant impacts on assets and investors around the world.
In the wake of Warsh’s comments, analysts said several property markets were more sensitive to higher interest rates in the United States and some stood to benefit.
Hong Kong
With the local currency pegged to the US dollar in a trading band of HK$7.75 to HK$7.85, property agents said any Fed movement would be mirrored by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the city’s de facto central bank.
“The HKMA’s base rate tracks the Fed’s moves and borrowing costs linked to Hibor [the Hong Kong interbank offered rate] follow suit,” said Pamela Ambler, head of Asia-Pacific investor intelligence at consultancy JLL. “With Hong Kong’s debt costs rising in contrast to China’s … that makes Hong Kong less attractive to southbound capital from mainland China.”
Based on the frequency of pinyin surnames in purchase records, US-based investment bank JPMorgan Chase has estimated that mainland buyers have, in recent times, accounted for 29 per cent of home sales volumes in Hong Kong and 37 per cent of their value.
And in the second quarter of this year, mainland-based investors were the second-largest non-local buyers of commercial property assets in the city, with purchases worth HK$1.23 billion (US$157 million), behind Singapore-based investors’ HK$3.37 billion, according to Colliers.

Lithuania’s fiercest storms: A history of extreme weather and growing risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
07:56:40 UTC
16:56:40 KST

By Karolina Aleknavičė, LRT.lt.
The severe storm that swept across Lithuania last month is likely to go down in the country’s weather history, according to Donatas Valiukas, head of the Climate and Research Division at Lithuania’s Hydrometeorological Service.
While powerful storms are relatively uncommon in Lithuania, the country has experienced several destructive events over the past decades – some causing deaths, widespread power outages and major damage to infrastructure.
One of the most severe struck October 17-18, 1967, when hurricane-force winds battered western Lithuania. In Klaipėda, winds reached 40 metres per second, while individual gusts may have reached 55 metres per second, according to the Hydrometeorological Service.
The storm, known as Lena in Sweden, destroyed the Palanga pier, damaged dunes and flooded parts of Klaipėda. Some 3 million to 4 million cubic meters of timber were blown down across the Samogitia region.
Another major storm, Anatol, hit Lithuania in December 1999. Wind gusts reached 40 meters per second in some areas and produced waves up to 6 metres high. A Norwegian vessel, the Seines, was washed ashore near Palanga and was not pulled back into the sea until April 2000.

Indonesia halted operations at its main international airport outside Jakarta on Sunday after ash spewed from the Anak Krakatoa volcano more than 150km (93 miles) away, impacting thousands of passengers.
Mount Anak Krakatoa erupted on Saturday, producing a fountain of lava and booming sounds that could be heard up to a few hundred kilometres away, the geology agency said in a statement.
Two new eruptions were recorded on Sunday, the volcanology agency warned.
Ash from the volcano was detected in the airspace surrounding Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, prompting authorities to initially suspend operations from 1.30am on Sunday to 5.30am.
The suspension was extended three times, with the latest ending at 5.30pm on Sunday “due to increased eruptive activity”, the airport said in a social media post.
Operations have been suspended at six airports including the Hussein Sastranegara airport in Bandung and Radin Inten II airport near Bandar Lampung on Sumatra, the country’s Transportation Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said.

Russian President Vladimir Putin entered Saturday’s Kremlin negotiations with US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner determined to capture additional Ukrainian territory, confident that Russian forces can seize the entirety of the Donbas by the end of 2026.
“There is zero chance of reaching an agreement on the frontlin until Putin completes the capture of the rest of the Donetsk region,” a source close to the Kremlin told Reuters, noting that Putin’s confidence stems from optimistic battlefield reports submitted by his commanders.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Western military analysts, however, view such an objective as highly improbable given the protracted and grinding pace of Russian advances. Kyiv has repeatedly and categorically rejected territorial concessions, dismissing demands to surrender the Donbas as equivalent to capitulation.
Bloomberg reported that the envoys’ latest visit yielded no indications of Moscow softening its core war objectives in Ukraine.
Sources close to the Russian leadership indicated that Putin remains willing to end the war only on Russia’s terms, with the Kremlin hardening its demands amid a belief that it holds a decisive military advantage.
The sequence and timing of the diplomatic initiative also provoked scrutiny among Western officials and analysts.
EU Ambassador to the US Jovita Neliupšienė questioned the envoys’ decision to visit Moscow before holding consultations in Kyiv.
US Sanctions Chief Joins Moscow Talks as Putin Cites War Goals
“Diplomacy really works, and we should first of all try to talk to those who are our allies,” Neliupšienė said, emphasizing that Moscow has not abandoned its original war aims and that Europe’s primary priority remains arming Ukraine for self-defense.
In contrast, Samuel Charap, a senior political scientist at the RAND Corporation, characterized the US mission as timely, warning that without active diplomatic mediation, the conflict risks rapid escalation as both sides continue to raise the stakes.
Kremlin talks and Treasury involvement
The assessments follow three hours and 10 minutes of formal discussions and a working dinner at the Kremlin on Saturday evening, Sept. 5.
Following the meeting, Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov claimed that the American delegation promised to factor Putin’s assessments of the conflict into their upcoming talks in Kyiv.
Russian officials characterized the session as “meaningful,” “frank,” and conducted in an atmosphere of mutual trust, while noting that discussions also addressed potential large-scale US-Russian commercial projects.
The wider US delegation included officials from the National Security Council (NSC), the State Department, and the Treasury. Gene Lange, the acting head of the sanctions division at the US Department of the Treasury, joined the mission to Moscow, participating in a preparatory meeting with Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special representative for economic cooperation.
While Lange did not attend the direct session with Putin, his presence signaled that US sanctions policy featured in the bilateral dialogue, despite recent statements by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent ruling out economic concessions without an end to the war.
At the onset of the talks, Putin confirmed that Russian forces had paused aerial strikes on Kyiv starting at midnight on Sept. 5, but rejected Ukraine’s proposal for a wider three-day frontline ceasefire.
Witkoff and Kushner are scheduled to arrive in Kyiv on Sunday, Sept. 6, to meet with President Volodymyr Zelensky, who previously pledged that Ukrainian forces would refrain from striking Moscow through the end of Monday to facilitate the diplomatic mission.

NATO members must not tolerate deliberate hybrid warfare, and the US will support allies facing such incidents, US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said on Saturday.
Speaking on the sidelines of a business conference in Italy, Whitaker said last month's drone incident at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport, which Berlin blamed on Russia, was more concerning than recent incidents involving Russian drones that strayed into NATO airspace while targeting Ukraine.
"Then you have what I would call the more concerning hybrid actions like we saw in Leipzig, like we have seen in Poland," Whitaker said, according to a report released by NTD News.
He urged NATO members to remain vigilant and respond firmly when hostile actions are identified.

Whitaker also warned that critical infrastructure, including energy facilities, could be targeted and said national authorities should monitor such sites.
While responses remain primarily a national responsibility, he said Washington would stand by allies confronting such actions.

The US and Brazilian markets are waiting for Estonian technology companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
07:47:36 UTC
16:47:36 KST

With funding from the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications, Tehnopol has launched a new project to help Estonian technology companies enter two major export markets – the United States and Brazil.
Why the US and Brazil?
The US is the world’s largest economy and still the market with the greatest potential for Estonian technology companies. Customers are willing to pay for new solutions, and a single contract won there can grow a company’s turnover by more than a year of work on the home market. It is important to understand that the US is not one market: requirements, certificates and legislation, as well as sales culture and price levels, differ from state to state and region to region. The market is large and fragmented, and that is precisely why companies need support when entering it.
Brazil is the largest economy in Latin America and a rapidly digitalizing market where Estonian companies are still few. That means less competition and more room to grow – but also that entering the market without a local partner and an understanding of the business culture is very difficult. Business is conducted in Portuguese, and English is not a given in business communication. The business culture is strongly relationship-driven: trust is built in person, and meetings count for more than emails. This is exactly why a network of mentors matters so much here.
What the project offers
The project provides at least 40 hours of export market consulting, including help in finding and signing additional sales contacts and in growing export turnover in the target market, travel support of up to 2,000 euros to cover eligible direct costs of trips to the target markets, and access to the project’s mentor network.
Participation requires a financial contribution from the company itself: the company covers part of the eligible direct costs, and the remainder is covered by the project’s support, which is entered into the state aid and de minimis aid register as de minimis aid. The exact terms, including the split between the company’s own contribution and the support, are agreed with the company at the first meeting.
A total of 9 experienced mentors are involved in the project – 2 for the Brazilian and 7 for the US market. The mentors represent a range of sectors, and their expertise covers market entry strategy and business model adaptation, building a sales process in the local market, regulations and product requirements, finding partners and distributors, and building a local network.
Source: tehnopol.ee

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Keelung Mayor Hsieh Kuo-liang (謝國樑) said Saturday that the city will activate its disaster reserve fund to assist residents whose homes and vehicles were damaged by flooding following heavy rain Friday.
The city will expand its existing assistance for flooded homes to include damaged cars and motorcycles. Detailed eligibility requirements and subsidy amounts are expected to be announced within a week.
Hsieh said residents still face significant problems after floodwaters recede, including cleaning their homes, replacing damaged furniture and belongings, and dealing with flooded vehicles, per Liberty Times.
“Rain stopping and water receding does not mean the problem is over,” Hsieh said, adding that the city government should be at the forefront of assisting residents affected by disasters.
District offices are surveying affected households and compiling damage statistics. The city government will determine eligibility and subsidy amounts for damaged vehicles based on the extent of the damage. It will also evaluate possible tax relief and expedite the necessary administrative procedures.
Under the existing disaster relief system, households affected by flooding can receive NT$10,000 to NT$30,000 (US$313 to US$940), depending on the depth of the water. Specific amounts and application requirements for the new vehicle assistance have not yet been finalized.
Friday’s heavy rain caused flooding in multiple parts of Keelung, with some areas recording more than 70 millimeters of rain in an hour. Floodwaters inundated roads, homes, and businesses, reaching knee height in some areas.
The city also plans to introduce a subsidy program this year to help flood-prone homes and businesses install flood barriers, Public Works Bureau Director Chien Yi-che (簡翊哲) said. Assistance will vary according to the size of the barrier and is expected to range from about NT$10,000 to NT$100,000, per UDN.
The city government said flood barriers helped reduce indoor flooding at properties where they were installed during Friday’s rainfall.
Friday’s flooding also renewed discussion of longer-term flood-control projects. Hsieh said the city is pursuing a flood-retention park beneath the Dawulun baseball stadium. The proposed facility would provide between 72,000 and 87,000 tonnes of flood-storage capacity and cost an estimated NT$1.04 billion, per CNA.

How climate change and food insecurity could fuel future conflicts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
07:47:00 UTC
16:47:00 KST

How climate change and food insecurity could fuel conflicts
September 6, 2026
The world's food system is under growing stress, and new research is pointing to areas where this could lead to conflict.
Severe droughts and extreme weather are damaging harvests in many regions. A developing El Niño event is even threatening to worsen food shortages for millions of people next year. At the same time, wars and geopolitical tensions are disrupting supply chains that keep food and farm supplies moving.
The war in Ukraine has repeatedly shaken grain markets, while the Iran war's impact on the Strait of Hormuz has driven up fuel and fertilizer prices, increasing costs for farmers everywhere.
Experts have long warned that rising food insecurity could fuel instability. When people can no longer feed their families, they argue over land, water, and other resources — or they move. In fragile countries, these pressures can contribute to social unrest and even armed conflict.
Now, new research has suggested where some of these risks are greatest. The Climate-Driven Agricultural Decline Index (CADI), developed by Laura Mayoral, Hannes Mueller and colleagues, maps how climate change is reshaping agricultural productivity around the world. "The heaviest losses are in the tropical regions," said Mueller, a researcher at the Institute for Economic Analysis and the Barcelona School of Economics.
Climate change is already reducing food production in many parts of the world. Hundreds of millions of people live in areas where harvests are smaller than 30 years ago. Mueller mentioned Australia, Argentina, Moldova, Nigeria, Romania, the United States, and Sudan as countries where agricultural losses are already being felt.
"Northern Africa is another region we should pay much more attention to. If you look at the map, it just looks terrible. It really looks horrible," he said.
And climate change is only one part of the story. Wars, trade disruptions, export bans, and rising fertilizer costs can magnify food insecurity.
Within the next 25 years, nearly half of the world's people could be living in areas where farms are producing less food.
New winners, losers, and conflicts
These pressures can undermine governments, help causemigration, and make it easier for armed groups to recruit fighters. In societies that are already unstable, such factors can push them toward crisis.
Yet CADI's research points to a surprising reality: Gains in agricultural productivity also appear to increase the risk of violence. Mueller said the key issue is not just scarcity, but change. The climate crisis and other shocks do not simply make some regions poorer. They also create new opportunities, changing the value of land and resources.
In some places, land that had been marginal becomes more productive and more valuable. And that attracts investors and produces competition for ownership and access.
So countries that appear to benefit overall may face new tensions. Sudan, for example, is projected to produce more food as the climate changes. But while some areas could become more productive, others may suffer losses, creating new winners and losers within the country and increasing the risk of conflict.
This looming instability, Mueller said, also applies to areas where the change in productivity hasn't even happened yet. "If we know that your land is going to become more productive, maybe I want to grab it from you today. That is exactly where negotiations break down and where we will have violence," he said.
Even in stable, wealthy regions, the climate crisis is creating future problems. It may seem trivial, but the change in grape-growing options in Europe is affecting local farmers. Major producers of sparkling wine have started to buy up land in mountainous regions.
"It is not productive yet, but they already know where future grape harvests will be," Mueller said. "Big agricultural companies are buying land. This is happening all over the world. Locals are displaced because large producers come in, land prices rise, and you start having fights about something that is still 20 or 30 years in the future."
One of the CADI team's most striking findings is that agricultural change is more likely to lead to conflict in non-democracies. When climate shocks, food insecurity, and competition over resources hit democracies, they tend to have institutions that force competing interests to negotiate rather than fight.
"Democracies may look annoying and cumbersome. Nothing moves as fast as people want. But this is a great thing because it makes people talk to each other," Mueller said. "There is a platform for negotiation. There are institutions that help people negotiate. That process of constantly finding solutions is at the heart of what prevents conflict."
South Asia as a warning sign
"We do not pay enough attention to the threats to the source of our livelihoods," said Abdullah Fahimi of the think tank German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP). "These threats can trigger major crises and displace millions and millions of people. The regions we should watch most closely are South Asia and the Sahel, where climate vulnerability and rapid population growth mean the number of people affected could rise dramatically."
Fahimi said South Asia stands out because it depends on both vulnerable water supplies and global food markets. Food prices have already risen significantly over the past decades. "South Asia, with a population of around 2 billion, is highly dependent on imports," he added. Those imports include wheat, maize, and palm oil from countries including Russia, Ukraine, Canada, and Malaysia.
At the same time, local agriculture is increasingly threatened by heat waves, floods, declining land productivity, and saltwater intrusion from rising sea levels.
As well as the immediate human toll, events such as the devastating floods that struck Nepal in August 2026 offer a glimpse of the long-term challenges that could become more common in the future. "The Himalayas and the Hindu Kush mountain ranges supply most of the water for agriculture and drinking water in the region," Fahimi said. "Because of climate change, the glaciers and snow are melting very fast."
In the short term, meltwater could increase water availability. But later in the century, he warned, the region could face "a huge humanitarian crisis that could affect around 2 billion people."
As food insecurity deepens, the social and political consequences can multiply. "When resource scarcities or the impacts of climate change force people to look for other livelihood opportunities, sometimes they end up being hired by terrorist groups," said Fahimi, who cited examples from Nigeria and Afghanistan.
In other cases, public frustration is directed at governments if they fail to mitigate the effects on people's livelihoods. Their legitimacy is questioned, and this can escalate into violent conflict.
That echoes Mueller's broader conclusion. Climate change, wars, and trade disruptions do not automatically lead to conflict. But climate adaptation cannot just be about growing different crops or using new technologies. People and societies also need to adapt to changes in who has access to land, water and jobs.
The key question is whether societies have institutions that can manage these changes. Where governments, courts, and local institutions can help communities negotiate new realities, shocks may be absorbed. Where those institutions are weak, the pressure on food systems may become a pressure on peace itself.
Edited by: Hannah Cleaver

BISHKEK, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Kyrgyzstan's culture, natural beauty, and the events surrounding the 6th World Nomad Games have generated growing international interest, Salkyn Sarnogoeva, the country's Deputy Minister of Culture, Information, and Youth Policy, was quoted as saying by Kyrgyz national news agency Kabar on Saturday.

leisurama’s prefabricated promise of fabulous, mid-century vacationing for all
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
07:45:21 UTC
16:45:21 KST

Leisurama Homes and postwar vacationing
It’s 1965 in Culloden Shores, Montauk, a small beach community at the eastern tip of Long Island, New York, and a crop of identical homes have sprouted up. They are a brand of vacation homes called Leisurama, complete with a befittingly midcentury logo of bouncing letters. They were prefabricated and a few grand and came with Melmac plates, Murphy beds, and the postwar promises of summer fun and middle-class vacationing. When the Montauk Historical Society exhibited original goods that came in the Leisurama Homes, they complemented the online tour with a quote from architect William Morgan: ‘the Leisurama story is rarely told without some tale of a woman going to Herald Square to buy a bra and coming home with a house instead.’
the leisurama homes, pictured in an artist rendering from the book Leisurama Now: The Beach House for Everyone 1964- | image courtesy of Paul Sahre
The bras and homes sold at Macy’s department store
A Leisurama home was bought much in the way one would buy any other. There were three options; the home would come fully furnished from Macy’s, and you could move in when it was ready. The homes were notably designed by architect Andrew Geller and superstar French-American designer Raymond Loewy. Throughout the ’30s and into the midcentury, Loewy was designing everything from Greyhound buses to luxurious department stores to toothpaste tubes, with his pervasive design prowess culminating in his feature on the cover of TIME magazine in 1949.
Mia Certic, Executive Director at the Montauk Historical Society, not only oversaw the institution’s 2024 exhibition on the historic local housing development, but her primary residence is an original Leisurama home she inherited from her family. Speaking to designboom, Certic recalls move-in day back in the ’60s, when the community around Leisurama first started. ‘We all moved in at the same time: the furniture was delivered street by street, so that everybody on, say, Butternut Drive, got their furniture on the same day. It made us neighbors immediately. And for those of us who were children, we had an instant gang.’
interior of a near faithfully preserved Leisurama home from the book Leisurama Now: The Beach House for Everyone 1964- | image courtesy of Paul Sahre
About 200 homes and a donation of Melmac dishes
Approximately a year prior to their exhibition, the Montauk Historical Society received a donation containing all the original furnishings of an original Leisurama. Certic had decided that it would be fitting to recreate, not the home itself, but something akin to the Macy’s showrooms that prospective buyers could peruse at the department store. Speaking of her own family’s buying experience, Certic’s own mother, a student of interior design, was impressed by Loewy’s name on the project. ‘So she dragged my father to Macy’s, where you could walk through an actual house,’ she recounts, ‘and at that stage they were marketing really aggressively because they hadn’t sold very many (people were afraid that it was too good to be true, and thought that Montauk was way too remote to be practical). The salesman offered my parents a free weekend at the Montauk Manor to go and see where the houses would be built, and they thought, why not, nothing to lose.’ Certic remembers her dad drawing up a pros and cons list. When the latter was nearly empty, they decided to go through with the purchase.
some of the objects that would come in a Leisurama homefrom the book Leisurama Now: The Beach House for Everyone 1964- | image courtesy of Paul Sahre
Easy Living in a Leisurama
Certic herself went from summers in her family’s Leisurama to living in the house full time. When thinking about the original home she spent summers in, she notes how, despite the minimal square footage, the compact design with a lot of storage allowed cousins, grandparents, and friends to comfortably pile in for the sunny months. She also notes, ‘No air conditioning, and terrible tv coverage, but we didn’t mind because we just hung out on the beach, on our bikes, at the pond, etc. I also think it’s a rather quaint, postwar American notion to develop summer housing for the average working family!’ She thinks back on the many successes of the house, ultimately remarking that, ‘the strongest thing that Leisurama got right was that, back in the 1960s, if you built and furnished a bunch of houses in a beach town and sold them for a very reasonable price, you would create an incredible community and lifelong friendships. And who knows? Maybe the same thing is true today.’
In 1991, Certic’s family, like most who held onto one of these homes, embarked on a remodel. Although they got rid of most of the original furniture and updated the materials and insulation, she’s proud to have the skeleton of the home intact. ‘Despite having plans drawn up by a good local architect, they [Certic’s parents] ended up feeling that the original design was just so good they didn’t want to mess with it too much… they kept the beautiful cathedral ceilings (although they bleached the dark beams) which provide a real feeling of space and light.’
ad copy in a magazine selling the Leisurama homes in the 60s | image courtesy of Montauk Historical Society
Leisurama Now: the homes nearly 50 years in the future
In the preface for his 2008 book, Leisurama Now: The Beach House for Everyone 1964-, graphic designer Paul Sahre describes looking for a cheap place to rent for the summer. He was with his friend and fellow graphic designer, Nicholas Blechman. Coming from New York City, the mythos, sun, and proximity of Montauk called to them. As a note, the town is also known for being a pivotal backdrop for the 2004 film Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind and the site of Camp Hero, a Cold War-era laboratory that was rumored to have tested on kids with special powers à la Stranger Things.
Eventually, he had landed on a house that had been part of the Leisurama development, notably an ‘Expanded Convertible Leisurama’—there were three models you could choose from back in the ’60s. He notes a visual evolution laid out in front of them, which he describes as, ‘one could almost see the neighborhood morphing into something else in fast-for-ward. Since the buildings were originally identical, each alteration made over time (and sadly, each Leisurama that’s torn down), is made visible, even if the motivation behind each change is not.’
one of the homes in the early 2000s | image © Michael Northrup courtesy of Paul Sahre
Leisurama as a sign of the times
Upon his third summer in the neighborhood, Sahre asked his photographer friend Michael Northrup ‘to come out to the beach to invoke Ed Ruscha,’ referencing the artist’s keen eye for capturing the American landscape in projects like his durational, photographic shots of the entire Sunset Strip. Together, Northrup and Sahre captured, from a fixed exterior point of view, every Leisurama home in Culloden Shores. In addition to this visual time capsule, the book goes into detail about the development of the homes, the product detail of each of the furnishings, and the landscape in Montauk that frames the whole thing.
Reflecting on the decades that have passed since he created the book, Sahre, in conversation with designboom, wonders what other modifications have been made to those ‘basicallly identical,’ houses he was so enmeshed with all those years ago. He ends with, ‘Montauk has always been remote. That has contributed to the weird factor. Even with proto hipster invasion, ‘surf lodges’ and the sky rocketing real estate prices, Montauk will always be Montauk.’
cover of the book the book Leisurama Now: The Beach House for Everyone 1964- | image courtesy of Paul Sahre
paper ephemera from the homes in the book Leisurama Now: The Beach House for Everyone 1964- | image courtesy of Paul Sahre
one of the homes in the early 2000s | image © Michael Northrup courtesy of Paul Sahre
the contemporary interior of Mia Certic’s home, one of the original Leisuramas | image © Mia Certic

TOKYO, September 6. /TASS/. The eruption of the Semeru volcano has occurred in the Indonesian province of East Java, the Antara news agency reported, citing the observation post.
According to its data, ash rose to a height of 1,000 m above the volcano's summit, or 4,676 m above sea level. The eruption was accompanied by emissions of thick gray ash, which spread eastward. The presence of tourists and local residents within a radius of 5 km from the crater is prohibited due to the risk of the volcano ejecting hot rocks.
Semeru is the fourth highest volcano in Indonesia (3,676 m above sea level) and the highest peak on the island of Java.
The Indonesian archipelago, consisting of 18,000 islands and being the largest in the world, is located in the so-called Pacific Ring of Fire, which makes the region prone to high seismic activity. Indonesia has more than 500 volcanoes, of which about 130 are active.

Do hormones really determine our achievements: what actually influences motivation and success
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:42:04 EEST
16:42:04 KST

Do hormones really determine our achievements: what actually influences motivation and success
Kyiv • UNN
Hormones and dopamine influence motivation, but they do not determine decisions or success. The environment, experience, skills, and opportunities are also important.
Hormones, brain function, heredity, and the external environment constantly influence how a person thinks, makes decisions, and acts. Because of this, it may seem that success or failure is predetermined by biology. However, the influence of hormones and neurochemistry is much more complex. Neuroscientist Vasyl Mykytiuk told UNN journalist more about the extent to which hormones actually influence our decisions, motivation, and ability to achieve goals, and whether brain chemistry and neurotransmitter levels can explain why some people are more persistent and successful while others give up more quickly.
Details
According to the neuroscientist, hormonal balance is indeed linked to motivation and behavior, but it is not a decisive factor, and the same hormone can act differently depending on the situation and a person’s existing predispositions.
Hormones influence decisions and motivation by increasing or decreasing the likelihood of behavior, rather than acting as a command. Stanford professor Robert Sapolsky puts it this way: testosterone does not create aggression; it amplifies existing predispositions in a particular context. Ultimately, hormones change the threshold for making decisions or initiating a particular behavior—how easily you take a risk, become angry, or give up. But they do not make decisions directly on your behalf
One of the best-known examples in discussions about hormones is testosterone. It is often associated with aggression, risky behavior, or the desire to dominate. However, studies, according to the expert, show a much weaker link than is often presented in popular explanations.
A meta-analysis by Geniole et al. (2020) debunks the popular myth about a correlation or causal relationship between baseline testosterone levels and aggression: baseline testosterone levels and aggression have a correlation coefficient of r = 0.054 (0.071 in men; 0.002 in women, meaning a very low interdependence)
This means that hormone levels alone cannot predict a person’s behavior. Other circumstances influence it, and sometimes a person’s own expectations about what is happening to them may play a significant role. This was demonstrated by another experiment involving testosterone.
The classic experiment by Eisenegger et al. in Nature (2010): women who received testosterone behaved more fairly in the “Ultimatum” game. Those who merely believed they had received testosterone behaved unfairly. The belief had a stronger effect than the hormone
When hormones can truly alter behavior significantly
Vasyl Mykytiuk notes that under normal physiological conditions, hormonal effects are often just one of many factors influencing behavior. They can become much more noticeable in certain physiological states.
Hormones truly play a decisive role primarily in extreme physiological or pathological states—hypothyroidism, Cushing’s syndrome, chronic stress involving prolonged exposure of the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex to glucocorticoids, sleep deprivation, or hunger. They also have a strong influence during puberty, pregnancy, and menopause
At the same time, such cases should not be generalized to all people without exception, the neuroscientist says. If the body remains within the physiological norm, hormones continue to influence behavior, but explain only part of the differences between people. This is important both for understanding motivation and for discussing achievement.
By contrast, within the physiological norm, hormonal effects on behavior do exist, but they usually explain only a minor portion of its variability
Why “successful brain chemistry” does not explain success
When discussing achievement, it is also important not to conflate hormones with neurotransmitters, the expert emphasizes. These are different systems of chemical communication in the body, although both may be associated with behavior. Dopamine, in particular, is involved in processes related to reward, motivation, and assessing how much effort a person is willing to exert.
The best-established role of the neurotransmitter dopamine is as an indicator of how much effort a person will make to achieve a goal. In a PET study, Treadway et al. (2012) found that dopamine release and sensitivity to it in such brain regions as the striatum and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex correlated with a willingness to exert more effort for a greater reward—especially when the chance of receiving the reward was low (12%). In other words, dopamine in these areas is associated with situations in which we work persistently to achieve success, even when the likelihood of such success is very low
In other words, the brain evaluates not only the possible outcome but also the price that will have to be paid for it. It is precisely the ratio of reward to costs that may influence whether a person is willing to exert more effort. At the same time, this does not mean that someone simply has the “right dopamine” and will therefore inevitably be successful.
Activity in the anterior insular cortex is inversely related: there, the “price or effort” we pay for this success is assessed. In general, the brain calculates the balance between the efforts we make and the motivation to achieve success
According to the expert, biological mechanisms help us understand how motivation arises. But between motivation and the actual result there are many intermediate stages. They are influenced by skills, living conditions, education, access to opportunities, the social environment, and other factors.
What is interesting is that in such pathological conditions as anhedonia in depression and apathy in Parkinsonism, the system of motivation and effort is disrupted. But it is a very long way from these explanations to the conclusion that “successful people have better chemistry” -
Therefore, biology may be part of the explanation for why a person is ready to exert more or less effort at a given moment. However, even a high level of motivation does not guarantee the desired result. Vasyl Mykytiuk explains that persistence can help, but it is not synonymous with effectiveness.
A meta-analysis of persistence (Credé et al., 2017; 88 studies, 66,807 participants): persistence does not mean effectiveness
Decisions are also influenced by external stimuli
A separate question is how strongly people can be influenced by things they do not even notice. These may include smells, words, temperature, context, or features of the environment.
Here, it is important to distinguish between two fundamentally different types of influence. On the one hand, there are long-term and cumulative environmental conditions: lack of sleep, hunger, chronic noise, air pollution, childhood exposure to lead, and poverty. Their consequences for cognitive functions, health, and behavior can be clearly observed in large samples. On the other hand, there are brief and often imperceptible stimuli: a smell, a word, the temperature on a particular day, or a slight change in the context of a choice. It was precisely regarding this second category that early psychological literature often reported extraordinarily large effects, which later turned out to be much more modest
In other words, a pleasant smell, for example, really can change one’s mood and certain consumer decisions, but the scale of this influence turned out to be relatively small. This is another example of how a popular explanation may prove to be considerably stronger than the actual effect.
A meta-analysis by Roschk and Hosseinpour (2020), covering 71 samples and 15,447 participants, showed that a pleasant ambient scent can indeed slightly improve mood and attitudes toward the environment and influence consumer behavior. But the scale of the effect is small: spending increased by approximately 3%, while time spent increased by approximately 5%." In other words, a smell can subtly nudge us, but this is more a slight shift in the probability of a behavior than “subconscious programming”
Why the environment is sometimes more important than willpower
Another important conclusion concerns self-control. The common idea is that a successful person simply has stronger willpower and is better at resisting temptations; however, current data encourage a more cautious approach to this explanation.
The theory of ego depletion proposed an intuitively appealing model: self-control is like a limited resource. If a person has already expended a great deal of "willpower," it should be harder for them to control themselves in the next task
Vasyl Mykytiuk explains that early experiments did indeed create the impression that the resource of self-control could be depleted. However, a larger replication produced a much weaker result. This means that the simple idea of a "willpower battery" does not explain human behavior as well as it once seemed to.
But in the large preregistered replication by Hagger et al. (2016), 23 laboratories and 2,141 participants carried out a standardized procedure. The resulting effect was only d ≈ 0.04 – practically zero. Subsequent studies produced mixed results. Therefore, the cautious conclusion is this: if the self-control depletion effect exists at all, it is probably much weaker and more context-dependent than the original theory predicted
So what does success ultimately depend on?
According to the neurobiologist, a person's achievements cannot be reduced to a single hormone, a single neurotransmitter, or an individual character trait. Biological processes establish certain conditions, but alongside them operate experience, environment, habits, opportunities, and specific decisions. It is precisely the combination of these factors that shapes behavior and influences the outcome.
Neurochemistry may explain the mechanism of persistence—how the brain evaluates rewards, costs, and effort—but by itself it does not explain who will ultimately achieve success
Thus, the popular formula about the "right hormones of a successful person" does not stand up to scrutiny. Hormones and brain chemistry are important for understanding motivation, but they are not a ready-made answer to the question of why some people achieve their goals while others do not. Success remains the result of the interaction between biology, experience, environment, and human behavior.
Acknowledging that a huge part of the causes of our behavior lies beyond our control does not mean acknowledging that our actions change nothing. On the contrary: if behavior depends on causes, it makes sense to look for causes that we can change. Therefore, the practical conclusion from this discussion is not "nothing depends on me," but rather: rely less on heroic willpower and instead design conditions in which the desired behavior becomes more likely—get enough sleep, reduce chronic stress, form habits, remove unnecessary temptations, plan actions in advance, and create an environment that works in your favor. And at the social level, the same principle leads to less certainty that successful people fully deserve their advantages, while failures fully deserve their failures. This is where Sapolsky's argument, regardless of whether we accept his conclusion about free will, becomes most practically significant

The National Security Council on Sunday issued a warning that terrorist organizations and individual attackers continue to seek opportunities to target Israelis and Jews around the world ahead of the High Holy Days.
The updated assessment was intended to raise awareness of current threats to Israelis overseas and encourage preventive measures, the NSC said, stressing that it does not constitute a new set of travel warnings.
Israel’s ongoing confrontations with Iran, Hezbollah, and Hamas have broadened the threat to Israelis abroad, according to the council. At the same time, increasingly hostile anti-Israel rhetoric and incitement have contributed to growing motivation among terrorist groups and individual attackers to target Israelis and Jews.
The NSC identified the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre as a particularly sensitive period. October 2026 could see large-scale protests, some of which may turn violent, alongside intensified efforts to carry out terrorist attacks, it warned.
Iran and its proxies remain the main global terrorist threat to Israelis and Jews, the assessment said. Tehran, driven in part by a desire to retaliate for blows it has suffered in recent years, continues to pursue operations through its own networks, proxy groups, and criminal organizations.
Additionally, Hamas is investing significant resources in establishing terrorist infrastructure in Europe and other countries with the aim of carrying out revenge attacks or high-profile attacks against Israelis and Jews, the NSC said.
The Houthis have also called for attacks on Israel and Israelis traveling to Somaliland and elsewhere in Africa, viewing Israel’s presence on the continent as a threat, according to the assessment.
What countries are most dangerous for Israelis and Jews to travel to?
Countries surrounding Iran remain particularly exposed to Iranian terrorist activity because of both established networks and their geographic proximity to the Islamic Republic, the NSC said. The NSC specifically highlighted Azerbaijan, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates.
Jordan, Qatar, Somaliland, and Egypt, including the Sinai Peninsula, remain under Level 4 travel warnings. Israelis should avoid travel to or remaining in those areas, the council said.
The NSC also advised travelers to avoid connection and transit stops in Level 4 countries wherever possible. Israelis passing through such countries must not leave airport terminals, it said.
Iraq, including the Kurdistan Region, Yemen, Iran, Syria, and Lebanon remain prohibited destinations for Israeli citizens under Israeli law, including dual nationals.
Travel to Saudi Arabia remains legally restricted. The NSC also advised Israelis to avoid Bangladesh, Somalia, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Libya, and Algeria due to the high level of risk.
NSC urges Israelis to avoid showing Jewish identifiers, speaking Hebrew
The NSC advised Israelis overseas to avoid displaying prominent Israeli or Jewish identifiers, including kippot and clothing with Hebrew writing. In countries under a Level 3 warning, travelers were advised to limit speaking Hebrew in crowded public places.
Travelers were also urged not to publish real-time locations or check-ins on social media and to conceal, block, or remove content indicating service in Israel’s security services, including regular, career, or reserve military service.
The advisory comes amid broader concerns over harassment and violence directed at Israelis abroad. The Foreign Ministry said in July that it had received 45 reports of antisemitic incidents involving Israelis overseas during the preceding year, including physical assaults, verbal abuse, and denial of services.
The council called for heightened vigilance around Chabad houses, kosher restaurants, synagogues, and other Jewish or Israeli gathering places, particularly regarding suspicious people or objects.
Israelis were also advised to stay away from demonstrations and protests and avoid political arguments with strangers.
Travelers should keep the emergency numbers of local security and law enforcement authorities readily available, the NSC said.

Why Hezbollah trusts in a 'Maginot Line' defense at Ali al-Taher ridge - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
07:40:22 UTC
16:40:22 KST

Hezbollah lost another key stronghold in Lebanon recently. The IDF said on September 3 that it had cleared the Ali al-Taher ridge.
The 36th Division “operated in recent weeks to clear and neutralize the two underground routes in the Ali al-Taher Ridge area in the Security Zone. The soldiers achieved operational control of the ridge area, both above and below ground, and cleared the area of terrorists. Some of the terrorists were eliminated, while others fled the area.”
The military added that the operation was ongoing: “Upon completion of the operation, the IDF will adjust its defensive posture in accordance with the situational assessment… Following operations in the underground routes over the past several weeks, their capability to carry out terror attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF soldiers from within the routes has been neutralized.”
The site was well-known and large. It “contained command centers, weapons storage rooms, generator rooms, living quarters, showers, and a kitchen, which enabled the terrorists to manage combat and remain underground for extended periods of time.
“The infrastructure is a strategic underground network that was built over two decades and funded and planned by the Iranian terror regime,” the IDF reported.
Fall of Ali al-Taher ridge gains international attention
The fall of this Hezbollah stronghold has been spotlighted around the world.
France24 noted: “Israel has seized the strategically placed Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon from Hezbollah fighters, Defense Minister Israel Katz said Friday. The Iran-aligned Shi’ite group did not confirm losing the highland, which sits around 10 kilometers from the border with Israel and was pummelled by Israeli strikes in recent weeks despite a ceasefire.”
The report added that “the Iran-aligned Shi’ite group did not immediately comment.”
Defense Minister Israel Katz noted that “the mission was completed and the tunnels were cleared of terrorists.”
Reuters described the site as “the Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, which is named after a Shi’ite Muslim scholar whose shrine sits at its summit,” saying that it “has become one of the most contested pieces of ground in the Israel-Hezbollah war. The cluster of hills is not especially large. But what it overlooks in southern Lebanon – and what Hezbollah is suspected to have built beneath it – thrust it to the center of the fight between Israel and the Iran-backed terror group.”
What can we learn from all this?
Hezbollah sought to turn this into a key facility over the last decades. Reports indicate that the terror organization had Iranian support in doing so.
In essence, the Islamic Republic was constructing a kind of Hezbollah “Maginot Line” on Israel’s border. That was a line of concrete fortifications, obstacles, and weapon installations built by France in the 1930s to deter invasion by Nazi Germany.
The well-known problem with a static defense line is that it can be breached.
When the original Maginot Line was built, it was full of hi-tech defense equipment meant to address the challenges faced in World War I and modernize the trench system to turn it into a kind of futuristic battlefield of interconnected bunkers with deep facilities for soldiers to sleep and live in. It was impenetrable.
However, with the guns at Singapore or Aqaba in 1917, the weakness was in the rear. The weakness of Ali al-Taher wasn’t in the rear; it was that Hezbollah simply can’t hide underground forever.
Over time, the IDF has been able to defeat it.
It took around 1,060 days, if one counts from when Hezbollah began its attacks on October 8, following the Hamas attack the day before. The war with Hezbollah has seen a lot of limited fighting and slow movement, with some ceasefires and some escalation over the last years.
This isn’t a rapid war of maneuver. The IDF, for instance, captured the Crusader Beaufort fortress within a day or two in 1982, whereas it took until late May 2026 to take it this time.
What changed?
Israel no longer fights rapid wars of maneuver. The enemy doesn’t either. It had to be ground down in Ali al-Taher at a pace that was similar to WWI. Nevertheless, the victory over Hezbollah shows that the group’s investment in static fortifications underground won’t save it. What is currently saving it is the depth of Lebanon.
Lebanon isn’t a very big country. Iran is around 150 times larger. However, for Israel, Lebanon is large because the Jewish state is also a relatively small country.
Fighting wars these days, whether in the West Bank, Lebanon, or Gaza, is measured in villages. It is not more than a few kilometers of ground that the IDF wants to control as part of Israel’s new buffer zone doctrine of controlling parts of Lebanon and Gaza. In the West Bank, the concept isn’t to take control, but to carry out raids.
In the end, the Hezbollah Maginot Line fell in southern Lebanon. It has taken many years to uproot the infrastructure that was built over the last decades. Whether this means a victory is unclear.
Perhaps southern Lebanon becomes another security zone as in the 1980s: A buffer zone, such as the “Spanish March,” established around the year 795 by Charlemagne in the eastern Pyrenees in the zone between Spain and France. Time will tell.

Iran-China MOU powers Maku Free Zone as new silk road gateway
TEHRAN- A memorandum of understanding (MOU) for cooperation has been signed between the Maku Free Zone Organization and a Chinese company, targeting strategic investments in energy, railways, automobiles, and mining.
The agreement aims to develop investment and implement major projects across sectors including energy, rail transport, logistics, mining and mineral industries, as well as electric and hybrid vehicles. The MOU covers technical-engineering cooperation, financing, investment, management, and execution of infrastructure and economic projects within the zone.
Key priorities include studying and participating in the development of the East-West rail corridor and the Tabriz–Cheshmeh-Soraya railway line, which would connect Iran's rail network to Turkey and international routes.
Additional focus areas are solar and thermal power plants, mining and mineral processing, production, assembly, and import of hybrid and electric cars, logistics village development, dry port facilities, and transit infrastructure.
Both parties will jointly conduct feasibility studies, design financial models, prepare investment packages, and attract domestic and foreign investors for priority projects in the Maku Free Zone.
The Maku Free Zone, located in Iran's West Azarbaijan province near the borders with Turkey and Azerbaijan, is emerging as a pivotal transit and industrial hub.
This Chinese partnership signals Iran's push to deepen economic ties with Beijing despite sanctions, leveraging China's expertise in high-speed rail, renewable energy, and EV manufacturing.
The East-West rail corridor is particularly significant—it forms part of the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) and could shorten freight routes between Asia and Europe.
For China, this aligns with its Belt and Road Initiative, offering an alternative overland path. For Iran, it means much-needed foreign investment, technology transfer, and job creation. However, implementation faces geopolitical hurdles, including sanctions. Still, if realized, these projects could transform Maku into a logistics powerhouse, boosting non-oil exports and positioning Iran as a key transit bridge between East and West.
In recent years, Iran-China relations have been elevated to a comprehensive strategic partnership, with both countries focusing on energy, infrastructure, transit, and technology under the framework of their 25-year long-term cooperation agreement. China, as Iran's largest trading partner, plays a key role in developing transit corridors and railway projects. In return, Iran's unique geopolitical position facilitates China's access to West Asian and European markets. The Maku Free Zone cooperation is a tangible example of this strategic partnership, moving beyond traditional oil contracts toward advanced infrastructure and industrial projects.

‘The engine’s on fire’: Qantas flight from Queenstown to Sydney reroutes after flames seen by passengers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
07:32:58 UTC
16:32:58 KST

Liza-Jayne Loch was returning home from a business trip to New Zealand when her Qantas flight ran into trouble.
The plane was climbing above the scenic South Island’s mountain ranges on Saturday afternoon, bound for Sydney, when a bang shook the cabin.
A passenger seated near the left wing soon shouted “the engine’s on fire”, Loch recalled, as the cabin lights began to flicker.
Footage recorded by a passenger and shared with AAP shows flames appearing to issue from the plane’s left engine in a series of rapid bursts.
“I was sitting on the left-hand side of the plane, and the flames were very, very visible,” Loch said.
“There was a lot of screaming at the time.”
As the plane continued to gain altitude, Loch tried to comfort herself by recalling that modern jets could land safely on a single engine.
“That’s what I kept in my head, that we could actually fly on one engine,” she said.
“But the flames kept coming and the noise kept coming.”
Qantas flight QF122 suffered a suspected engine issue shortly after taking off from Queenstown on Saturday afternoon, before making a priority landing at Christchurch.
According to FlightAware, the Boeing 737 landed about 52 minutes after takeoff, touching down shortly before 5pm local time.
The cause of the incident has yet to be determined, but Qantas sent two engineers to Christchurch on Sunday to investigate.
Both engines are thought to have remained in operation for the duration of the flight.
Loch said conditions soon stabilised after the initial shock, while cabin staff sought to comfort passengers.
“The crew were all terribly, terribly calming,” Loch said.
Emergency services were waiting on the tarmac when the flight landed, with passengers allowed to disembark as normal after a short wait.
“There were massive cheers when we landed,” Loch said.
A Qantas spokesperson said the plane was believed to have suffered an engine issue and steps would be taken to support affected customers.
“Our pilots are highly trained to manage situations like this and the aircraft landed safely,” they said.
“We know this would have been a distressing experience for passengers and will be contacting all customers to provide support.”
Affected passengers were put up in a hotel near the Christchurch international airport before being booked on a complimentary flight to Sydney on Sunday.
While the second flight went off without a hitch, Loch said nerves were still high.
“I cried getting off the plane when we landed in Sydney,” Loch said.
“It was quite traumatic.”

Germany prepares comprehensive "protective shield" against Russian sabotage
Following a failed attempt to attack Leipzig/Halle airport with an explosive-laden drone, Germany plans to strengthen protection against Russian sabotage and other hybrid attacks.
Source: German tabloid Bild, as reported by European Pravda
Details: German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt is planning a package of measures covering protection against drones and sabotage targeting critical infrastructure and cyberattacks, as well as the detection of spies and potential terrorists.
"Russia's hybrid attacks using explosive-laden drones targeting airports, agents in our cities, cyberattacks on our networks and sabotage of our infrastructure are a daily reality. These attacks will intensify, but we can fight back and protect ourselves," Dobrindt said.
According to Bild, Germany plans to expand the Federal Police's mobile anti-drone unit.
The new units, which can be rapidly deployed to different areas, will have helicopters and special vehicles. They will be stationed in nine strategically important cities: Frankfurt am Main, Munich, Hamburg, Berlin, Stuttgart, Düsseldorf, Leipzig, Hanover and Cologne.
Their task will be to protect the airspace above key transport hubs, airports, railway stations and the government district in Berlin. This will involve not only detecting and intercepting drones, but also disabling explosive-laden UAVs.
Another proposal involves expanding the powers of companies operating critical infrastructure. Water utilities, energy companies and defence industry facilities could be given legal powers not only to detect drones but also to actively counter them. This should allow them to respond more quickly to attacks on critical infrastructure facilities without waiting for state forces to arrive.
The plan also envisages wider use of AI, biometric facial recognition and video surveillance systems, particularly at railway stations. AI would help automatically detect weapons and suspicious behaviour, as well as identify people suspected of preparing attacks or engaging in espionage.
Another area is protection against cyberattacks. The plan calls for the creation of a national Cyberdome – an extensive network of digital sensors designed to detect and block attempted hacker attacks.
Background: On 1 September, Germany directly accused Russia of a hybrid attack at Leipzig airport in early August and announced countermeasures.

UN endorses new map that shows Africa's size more accurately
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
07:29:22 UTC
16:29:22 KST

UN votes to endorse new map projection that shows Africa's size more accurately
The United Nations General Assembly on Friday endorsed a new world map that represents Africa more accurately in its larger size, a culmination of a recent campaign led by African countries and advocacy groups.
Friday's resolution, which was sponsored by Togo and backed by members of the African Union, was passed with 164 member states voting in favor. Only the U.S. voted against it while six other countries - Serbia, Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova and Ukraine - abstained.
The vote encourages governments and institutions around the world to replace the traditional Mercator map, commonly used since the 16th Century, with the Equal Earth projection that advocates and geographers say shows locations more accurately.
The Mercator projection shows Greenland and Africa as appearing to be about the same size whereas in the Equal Earth projection that shows continents in their true proportions, Africa is 14 times larger than Greenland.
Friday's resolution does not ban the Mercator projection or impose a replacement, but only encourages the use of the Equal Earth projection, the U.N. said in its report.
"Maps shape our understanding of the world," the global body quoted Togo's Foreign Minister Robert Dussey as saying before the vote. "They guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions."
Africa No Filter, one of the lead campaigners for the adoption of the new map, hailed the resolution, adding: "We want to see accurate maps in schools, textbooks, newsrooms, businesses and on the digital platforms billions of people use every day."
Several countries hailed the adoption and urged the adoption of the Equal Earth map. "Changing the map obviously doesn't change the world. But correcting a representation that distorts it is already an act of truth," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on X after the vote.
The Mercator map was designed by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to help European navigators at sea, but advocates say it distorted landmasses by enlarging regions near the poles such as North America and Greenland while shrinking Africa and South America.
The 2018 Equal Earth projection, on the other hand, follows the Earth's curvature and shows continents in their true proportions.
Geographers say the traditional map is only useful for navigation.
"Outside of that very narrow navigation application, there is no point in using it," according to Mark Monmonier, a Syracuse University professor of geography.
