Israel is warning that the threat of attacks against Israelis and Jews abroad is rising ahead of the Jewish High Holidays and the third anniversary of the October 7 attack, with Iran, Hezbollah, Hamas and global jihad groups all cited as active threats.
The latest assessment from Israel’s National Security Council points to a broader and more persistent threat environment than in previous years, driven by the continuing conflict with Iran and its proxies, anti-Israel incitement and a growing number of plots and lone-actor attacks overseas.
Officials say the October 7 anniversary could become a particular flashpoint, with the potential for both large anti-Israel demonstrations and attempts to carry out attacks.
Iran remains the main concern. Israeli officials say Tehran continues to use proxy networks, including criminal organizations, to target Israeli diplomatic missions, senior officials, security personnel, Jewish institutions and Israelis abroad.
Hezbollah is also viewed as a significant threat because of the losses it has suffered in fighting with Israel and its stated desire to avenge the deaths of senior commanders.
Hamas, meanwhile, is said to be working to establish operational networks in Europe and elsewhere for attacks against Israelis and Jews, while ISIS and al-Qaeda continue to call for attacks on Jewish targets, particularly in Africa and Asia but also in Europe and the United States.
The assessment also highlights the rise of lone attackers. Since the outbreak of the war, 25 Israelis and Jews have been killed in terrorist attacks abroad, according to the council.
These attackers often operate independently and target relatively exposed locations such as mass gatherings, synagogues, Jewish community centers and other public venues.
Several countries remain of particular concern because of their proximity to Iran or existing terror infrastructure. Azerbaijan, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates were singled out as vulnerable to Iranian activity.
Jordan, Qatar, Somaliland and Egypt, including the Sinai Peninsula, remain under the highest Israeli travel warning level. Israelis are also barred by law from traveling to Iraq, including the Kurdistan Region, Yemen, Iran, Syria and Lebanon.
Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, Somalia, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Libya and Algeria are also considered high-risk destinations.
The assessment also reflects growing concern over how easily Israelis can be identified online. Officials are urging travelers not to post real-time locations and to remove or conceal social media content showing service in the IDF or other security bodies.
They are also advising Israelis to avoid openly displaying Israeli or Jewish symbols in sensitive destinations and to stay away from demonstrations and political confrontations.
The concern is not limited to organized terrorist groups. Officials say the combination of online radicalization, anti-Israel rhetoric and highly visible Israeli or Jewish targets has created a more unpredictable threat environment than in the past.

Hormuz: The bill for America's strategic miscalculation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
06:22:15 UTC
15:22:15 KST

The initial assumption may have been that pressure on Iran would remain confined to a limited, controlled, and manageable framework. But the vortex of the Strait of Hormuz has shown that in today's deeply interconnected economy, war does not flow only where the missiles land. Part of the bill is now showing up in diesel prices, gas contracts, shipping insurance, the Treasury bond market, the Federal Reserve's interest rate, and the cost of financing America's $40 trillion debt.
For this reason, the biggest error in analyzing recent developments is to measure the severity of the crisis by the daily price of oil. Whether Brent crude sits at $95 or crosses $100 is only the first layer of the issue; the more important transformation is happening beneath the market's skin. The Hormuz shock has moved beyond crude oil, reaching refined products and gas, raising the cost of transport and production, and from there entering inflation and the "price of money" in the United States. The crude oil market still has tools to absorb the shock — increased exports from Iraq, rerouted shipments, capacity from other suppliers, and demand adjustments can offset part of the shortfall, which explains why the sharp drop in traffic through Hormuz has not necessarily translated into an equivalent explosion in Brent prices.
But this relative calm can be misleading, because the real point of transmission for the crisis is now less crude oil itself and more products like diesel and jet fuel. The rise of the average U.S. diesel price to $5.820 per gallon, an increase of roughly 55 percent since the start of the conflict, and the surge in diesel refining margins to more than $108 per barrel show that the issue has moved beyond a mere "shortage of oil barrels." Diesel directly fuels trucking, mining, agriculture, machinery, the cold chain, construction, and industrial production; therefore, its rise transmits to production costs and consumer prices faster than crude oil does. Trump may have counted, when deciding to attack, on America's position as the world's largest oil producer — but the strategic folly lies precisely in overlooking the difference between "having oil" and "being immune to an energy shock."
A country may have abundant crude oil, but if it lacks the right refined product, sufficient refining capacity, a secure shipping route, or adequate inventory at the point of consumption, it remains vulnerable to a price shock.
The same logic has become evident in the liquefied natural gas market. The rerouting of some Qatari and Emirati cargoes to ship-to-ship transfers outside the Strait of Hormuz may, from an operational standpoint, be a way to keep export flows moving, but from a political-economy standpoint it signals that the crisis has entered a deeper phase. When one of the most standardized and capital-intensive supply chains in global energy trade is forced to change its shipping pattern in order to bypass a geopolitical chokepoint, it means the risk is no longer reflected only in the oil price chart — it is settling into the cost structure of trade itself. Extra vessels, more expensive insurance, longer transit times, more complex operations, larger precautionary reserves, and higher legal risk are all costs that are ultimately passed on to the consumer or the investor. For this reason, "cargo passage" should not be mistaken for "trade returning to normal." Even if Hormuz is formally open, a strait whose passage carries the risk of seizure, attack, penalty, or a spike in insurance premiums is fundamentally different, economically speaking, from a normal route.
This is where the strategic error of the attack on Iran moves from the energy domain into U.S. monetary policy. The Federal Reserve faces an equation with no clean solution: raising interest rates does not reopen Hormuz and does not produce a single additional barrel of diesel, but if the energy shock feeds through into inflation expectations, wages, services, and the price of goods, the central bank cannot ignore it either. The Federal Reserve is now caught between two risks: an aggressive response could push the economy toward recession at a time when the labor market is already softening, while excessive delay could allow inflation to become entrenched again. In this way, Trump's decision has placed on the central bank's table an issue whose origin is not fundamentally monetary but whose consequences are directly monetary.
Yet the more important issue is not even the outcome of the Fed's next meeting; the deeper point lies in Christopher Waller's remarks about the erosion of the "safety and liquidity premium" of U.S. Treasury bonds. For decades, the U.S. government enjoyed an exceptional privilege: investors, due to the security, liquidity, and status of the dollar, were willing to hold Treasury bonds at lower yields. If this historic discount is now eroding, and if the economy's neutral interest rate is also structurally rising, then the United States would need to pay higher interest to attract capital even without a Hormuz shock — Hormuz has simply worsened the timing and intensity of this pressure.
This development has come at precisely the worst possible moment for the U.S. Treasury: federal debt has surpassed $40 trillion, the budget deficit remains large, and technology companies have become serious rivals for capital as they pursue a massive wave of investment in artificial intelligence, data centers, chips, and electricity. As a result, the U.S. government is no longer without competition in the capital market and must compete for the same dollars that large private companies are also seeking. Against this backdrop, the Hormuz vortex creates a dangerous feedback loop: expensive energy makes inflation stickier; sticky inflation limits room for interest rate cuts; higher rates raise the cost of issuing and rolling over debt; higher interest costs deepen the budget deficit; a larger deficit demands more bond issuance; and greater bond supply requires higher yields to attract buyers.
The issue is not that the United States is on the verge of bankruptcy — such a claim would be exaggerated and analytically of little value. The far more important issue is the shrinking of Washington's "freedom of action." A great power is not measured only by the volume of its resources, but also by the amount of free resources it can deploy in the next crisis. The state of America's Strategic Petroleum Reserve makes this point more concrete: after extensive releases, the reserve has fallen to its lowest level in more than four decades — meaning Washington, in order to contain the fallout of today's error, is consuming part of tomorrow's economic ammunition. Even rebuilding this reserve is not without cost or constraint, and the debate over using heavy Venezuelan crude has shown that oil specifications, refining capacity, and logistical limitations do not allow every barrel to simply replace one drawn from the emergency reserve.
The United States, of course, still has three major shields: enormous domestic production, its strategic reserve, and the deepest financial market in the world. None of these three shields has collapsed; but the strategic point is that the margin of safety on all three has narrowed. Shale cannot make up for any degree of Middle East disruption within a few weeks; the emergency reserve is far smaller than it once was; and the Treasury no longer necessarily enjoys the same historic discount on its borrowing costs. The real cost of Trump's decision should be sought precisely in this "shrinking margin of safety," not merely in a few extra dollars on the price of oil.
From this perspective, even an end to the conflict would not necessarily mean an end to the economic crisis. Markets have memory: shipping companies, after the Hormuz experience, will demand higher insurance premiums; energy companies will hold safer inventories; buyers will build alternative routes; supply chains will sacrifice some efficiency for security; and investors will demand higher returns to accept geopolitical risk.
The war may stop, but the "war risk premium" can remain embedded in the price of energy, trade, and capital.
This is precisely where Trump's folly turns from a military operation into a strategic error — because an operation can be measured by the number of targets destroyed, but a strategy must be judged by the final balance of power. If the outcome of the attack is that Iran comes under pressure while, at the same time, energy becomes more expensive, U.S. inflation remains sticky, the Federal Reserve has less room to maneuver, the Treasury borrows at higher rates, the strategic reserve shrinks, and the cost of projecting power rises for Washington itself, then success can no longer be measured simply by the map of the battlefield.
The most important number in this crisis may be neither $95 oil, nor $5.82 diesel, nor even the $40 trillion debt — the most important issue is their simultaneity. A narrow strait has linked an energy disruption to inflation, inflation to interest rates, interest rates to the cost of debt, and the cost of debt to the capacity of American foreign policy. Trump may have imagined that attacking Iran would send the main bill to Tehran; but the honorable resistance of the fighters, combined with the courageous prudence of the wise leadership of the Islamic Republic of Iran, has caused the Hormuz vortex to now return part of that very bill to Washington. The longer this situation continues, the less it will resemble the price of a barrel of oil, and the more it will resemble the price of America's money, debt, and power.
MNA

Gaza families finally recover remains of 100 relatives from rubble in Israel's genocidal war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
06:15:41 UTC
15:15:41 KST

Grief returned to Gaza as families gathered to bury around 100 Palestinians recovered from the rubble of homes destroyed in Israeli strikes.
For more than two years, their Palestinian families could not reach them.
On Saturday, the bodies and remains of around 100 Palestinians finally lay before their relatives in Gaza City, recovered from beneath homes destroyed in Israeli attacks and gathered for a long-delayed farewell.
Near the Imam al-Shafi’i Mosque in the southeastern Zeitoun neighbourhood, rows of remains were draped in Palestinian flags as families lit candles, laid flowers and moved among photographs and the names of children, women, men and elderly victims.
Some searched for relatives they had not seen since their homes were bombed. Others stood over remains that bore little resemblance to the people they remembered beyond what had allowed them to be identified.
The remains were recovered in recent days by Gaza’s Civil Defense from homes belonging to the Rahim, Balawi, Malaka and Qanbour families as part of a project to retrieve Palestinians still buried beneath buildings destroyed during Israel’s war on the enclave.
Civil Defense crews are working with only a handful of excavators and worn-out equipment because of Israeli restrictions on the entry of machinery needed for recovery operations.
‘My whole life is gone’
Among the mourners was Maryam Hassan al-Balawi, standing before members of the family she had waited years to recover. Malak, her only surviving daughter, stood beside her.
“My husband and my children were killed. I have no one left except my only surviving daughter, Malak,” Balawi told Anadolu.
“My whole life is gone. My husband and my children are gone. I have no life left,” she said, adding that Malak still cries every day for her father and siblings.
Balawi also recalled a final request from her husband before he was killed.
“If I die, shroud me with your own hands and bury me with your own hands,” she recalled him telling her.
For more than two years, she could not fulfil that wish.
“What am I supposed to do? My home is gone, my children are gone, my life is gone,” she said.
Yet recovering the remains brought a measure of relief after years in which Balawi repeatedly returned to the ruins where her family remained buried.
“When they brought them out, I felt some relief in my heart, as though my soul came out with them,” she said. “I used to go there every day and say: ‘God, let them come out so I can see them.’ Today, after they were recovered, I feel a little peace.”
Only survivor
For Balawi, much of that pain rests with Malak.
“What did my daughter do to deserve this?” she asked. “She cries every day. She wants her father and her brothers and sisters.”
“She says: ‘What did I do, Dad? Why did they bomb them? They did nothing.’”
Jadallah Rahim stood nearby beside the remains of 32 relatives killed when their home was struck Feb. 19, 2024. More than 15 were children and around 10 were women, he said.
“Their only ‘fault’ was that they stayed in their homes,” said Rahim. “They were suddenly bombed and they were all killed in an instant.”
Thirty-three people had been inside, said Rahim, pointing to a girl standing nearby.
“She was number 33. She was the only survivor.”
The others remained beneath the destroyed home for around two-and-a-half years before Civil Defense crews were finally able to reach them after days of digging with limited equipment.
Looking toward the names placed beside the remains, Rahim stressed that those before him were not merely casualty figures.
“These are not numbers,” he said. “Look at their names. Men, women, children, elderly people.”
‘The grief came back’
Recovery ended one wait but reopened another wound.
“This is not joy,” said Rahim. “The grief came back. The pain came back. The tears came back.”
He pointed to a young girl moving among the remains of her family, saying she lost her father, mother, sisters and brothers.
“Today she walks among them crying for her grandfather, her father, her mother, her brother, her sister and her grandmother.”
For Rahim, however, recovering the dead also meant finally giving them a burial after years beneath the rubble.
As darkness settled above Zeitoun, candles continued to burn beside the rows of remains, surrounded by flowers, Palestinian flags and families who had waited years for this moment.
On Sunday morning, they are expected to carry their loved ones in a mass funeral procession.
The second phase of the Civil Defense recovery project covers 147 destroyed homes in Gaza City and the northern and central Gaza Strip, where an estimated 1,072 bodies are beneath the rubble.
During the first phase, launched in November 2025, crews recovered around 333 bodies and sets of remains from 54 destroyed homes and buildings.
Since October 2023, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed at least 73,651 Palestinians and injured 174,575, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
For the families in Zeitoun, however, the numbers tell only part of the story.
After more than two years beneath the rubble, their dead had finally come home.

Ebola: Why children are last to be treated in medical crises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
06:13:00 UTC
15:13:00 KST

Ebola: Why children are last to be treated in medical crises
September 6, 2026
The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been devastating. Since the outbreak began in mid-May, more than 3,000 people have died.
Almost half of people infected with Ebola are expected to die, and the mortality rate is particularly high for young children. According to a commentary by Doctors Without Borders recently published in medical journal The Lancet, the mortality rate for children under the age of 5 is over 60%.
But often, it's because of a lack of medication and information on how to use it with young patients, rather than then disease itself.
"Children must be centered in Ebola treatment and prevention research," the aid organization wrote in early September.
At the heart of the debate is the EBO-PEP study, which began mid-July. The study looks at an experimental antiviral drug called obeldesivir, which is being studied for its ability to protect people exposed to the Bundibugyo Ebola virus, the strain responsible for the current deadly outbreak.
But children weighing less than 30 kilograms (about 66 pounds) and around 12 years old or younger, were not included in the original study. But that could change soon with protocols to include children weighing over 20 kilograms.
Children weighing less than 20 kilograms — that is, roughly 6 years old or younger — won't be included in the treatment. There is an alternative treatment for them: Another antiviral drug, remdesivir, given intravenously. But as Doctors Without Borders argued, a 10-day course of infusions is difficult to administer during an outbreak, especially for young children.
According to Neal Russell, a pediatric doctor based in London who consults for Doctors Without Borders and who was also the lead author of the Lancet commentary, young children are at particularly high risk from Ebola. This could be due to their weakened immune systems, underlying health conditions, or the fact that treating them for Ebola is especially challenging in an outbreak.
For example, children are often harder to diagnose than adults because early symptoms resemble other illnesses, and young children often find it difficult to describe their symptoms accurately. Other issues include the fact that children cannot always be accompanied into an Ebola treatment center by their parents or caregivers, something that is especially important in their recovery. Younger Ebola patients also require closer monitoring and specially trained staff.
Ebola in Berlin
In May, an American doctor was treated at Berlin's Charite hospital after contracting the Bundibugyo Ebola virus while caring for patients. His wife and their four children were also considered at high risk. The medical team in Germany decided to treat the family prophylactically with an experimental antibody drug called MBP134.
"Of course, a careful risk benefit assessment had to be carried out," said Han Ngoc Le, a doctor at the hospital who was involved in the treatments.
The available data about the drug's impact on children was very limited. But at the same time, the children were at high risk of catching Ebola after close contact with their sick father.
In the end, all the family remained healthy and no apparent side effects were seen. It's unclear whether the experimental treatment prevented infection in the children. Such a small sample can't be mapped onto the larger population either.
But the test was valuable nonetheless. "The mere fact that the antibody was so well tolerated even in 1-year-olds and children under 12 is a valuable finding upon which future studies can build," Le said.
Why do such gaps in knowledge exist?
Le explained that, from a medical perspective, children cannot simply be thought of as "small adults."
Their metabolisms function differently, they react differently to medications, their pharmacokinetics — what a body does with a drug — are simply different. The same sort of cautions also apply to pregnant women.
That's why dosages of medication can't simply be transferred from adults to children. It's also why any new medications require separate studies so that specific dosages can be determined and potentially special formulations can be developed. Children might require kid-friendly syrups instead of adult-size tablets, for example.
"All of this creates extra costs," said Marc Biot, access coordinator for Europe at Doctors Without Borders, who works to ensure people in need can get affordable, good-quality medical products. He said research institutions and pharmaceutical companies often see investing extra in pediatric studies as a lower priority.
"It is faster and it can be cheaper if you only focus on adults," said Biot — which is why treating children and pregnant women usually only becomes part of the research at a later stage of drug development. "That is our plea — a plea not only to the scientists, to the pharmaceutical companies, but also to those who fund and allow trials to happen — to allow that to happen on the same speed for adults as for children and pregnant women."
Biot said it's sad to see that pressure is needed to make it happen. "Whenever you start a clinical trial, you also should include pregnant woman or children," he argued.
A difficult balance
None of this is new. In 2020, the Global Accelerator for Pediatric Formulations network was founded — supported by the World Health Organization(WHO) — to accelerate the development and availability of child-friendly medicine worldwide.
This isn't an issue limited to Ebola. Russell pointed to the 2024 mpox epidemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where children made up a large proportion of those infected or killed.
Although a vaccine existed for mpox, it wasn't made for children. The WHO advised it be used "off label" for minors, but they tended to get it a lot later than adults anyway. Experts say they've observed similar patterns with other diseases including HIV, tuberculosis, and during the COVID-19 pandemic.
"When you're doing a research study, which is not in an emergency, [it makes sense] to protect children and pregnant women from any potential harm of an investigational product," said Russell. "But when you're in an emergency, the balance between protecting those people from any potential harm from research, and protecting them from the very fatal disease, changes."
Berlin-based doctor Le believes children and pregnant women should be considered right from the beginning of any new clinical trials. "They shouldn't be excluded from participation just like that," she said. "Instead, sub-studies or parallel studies should be set up from the outset."
Russell calls for a similar approach. He wants to see all people benefit equally from scientific progress during a health crisis — especially in a health emergency, when the most vulnerable should not be the last to benefit from that progress.
"No matter who you are, you should have the same opportunity to have access to these medical products," he said.

The Bulgarian Unification – lesson that showed people unity means strength
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
06:10:12 UTC
15:10:12 KST

Author
Miglena Ivanova
News
From Radio Bulgaria's best collection
The Bulgarian Unification – lesson that showed people unity means strength
Sunday 6 September 2026 06:10
Sunday, 6 September 2026, 06:10
PHOTO archive
Font size
On September 6, Bulgaria marks the Day of Unification of the Principality of Bulgaria with Eastern Rumelia. Events that would lead to this important date for us started on March 3, 1878 with the signing of the Treaty of San Stefano between Russia and Turkey. According to it, liberated after 5 centuries of Ottoman oppression, Bulgaria became "an autonomous principality with Christian government and a people's militia." Its borders covered the territories of the Bulgarian Exarchate, recognized as independent from the Sublime Porte. It encompassed a vast territory inhabited by ethnic Bulgarians. The treaty was temporary and its effect was only valid for four months - until July 1878, when the Berlin Treaty was signed. A curios fact is that in Berlin, as well as during the signing in San Stefano, there were no Bulgarian representatives. Bulgaria relied on the goodwill of the Great Powers, while each of them was pursuing its own interests.
PHOTO bg.wikipedia.org
The Congress of Berlin divided Bulgaria in parts - the Principality of Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia, which became an autonomous region under the sultan's rule, while Macedonia, Edirne Thrace and the Rhodopes were returned to the Ottoman Empire. The links between the divided Bulgarian regions, however, were kept. They were especially active between the Principality of Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia. In Rumelia there was a strong popular movement for the unification of all Bulgarians. Leaders were needed and people like Zahari Stoyanov emerged. He was a man who grew up from an illiterate shepherd to a publicist and writer, one of the apostles of the April Uprising. Similarly to the Revolutionary Committees before the Liberation, a Bulgarian Secret Central Revolutionary Committee was created. The idea was to reject the Ottoman rule through an uprising in Eastern Rumelia and to announce unification with the Principality of Bulgaria.
Bulgarian Secret Central Revolutionary Committee, 1885. From left to right: Kosta Panitsa, Ivan Stoyanovich, Zahari Stoyanov, Ivan Andonov and Dimitar Rizov
PHOTO bg.wikipedia.org
The rebellion started on September 2, 1885 in Panagyurishte with gunshots and people shouting "Down with Rumelia!" and "Long Live Union!" The initiators were arrested, but 2,000 people besieged the building of the district authorities and they were forced to release the detainees. The revolt was growing. On September 5, Gavril Krustevich, the governor of Eastern Rumelia, convened an emergency meeting. At the meeting a decision was made that Tsarigrad must not be informed of anything that was going on. The military stood on the side of the revolting people. On behalf of the Revolutionary Committee Zahari Stoyanov and another member of the committee, Ivan Andonov, announce that Gavril Krastevich was not a governor anymore and the union of southern and northern Bulgaria under the rule of Bulgarian Knyaz Alexander I was proclaimed. A temporary government headed by Georgi Stranski was set up to work until the Knyaz arrived.
The news of the Unification reached Knyaz Alexander Battenberg in his residence near Varna. He immediately left for Tarnovo and on September 8 issued a manifesto accepting and legitimizing the union of the Principality of Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia.
Prince Alexander of Battenberg enters Plovdiv at the head of a Bulgarian cavalry regiment
PHOTO archive
"If it was today, a few politicians would have decided against the will of all the Great Powers and without the support of Russia to do such a thing," late colonel Petko Yotov, former head of the National Military Museum says in a record preserved in the Golden Audio Fund of the Bulgarian National Radio:
colonel Petko Yotov
PHOTO BGNES-archive
"The preparation of the Unification was completed in 1880. But at this stage Russia managed to stop the organizers. Russia said the unification would fail, Bulgaria would perish, so preparations stopped. But in 1885 nobody could stop the process. The Bulgarian spirit reached it height. Russia was against the Unification because it was unable to protect it against the Great Powers. But, in fact, Bulgaria had done preparations in this respect. Battenberg had had success in negotiations with the English Crown, Austro-Hungary and partly with Germany. The Unification did not start just like that. If some risked their honor and dignity, Battenberg had staked his head. He played a big role in preparation of the Unification internationally and agreed against the will of the Great Powers to lead it."
This way, 7 years after the Liberation, Bulgarians felt ready to oppose the Great Powers and take their fate into their own hands. For this period, they were able to lay the foundations for their economy, democratic institutions and build a strong army. Bulgaria had never been more united. The unification was prepared by revolutionary committees in Eastern Rumelia and was supported by the Bulgarian government and Knyaz Alexander Battenberg, the political parties, and the people.
PHOTO BGNES
"Unification is the first brilliant and perhaps unique in its significance lesson of what the Bulgarian spirit is and, unfortunately, the only act of unity in thoughts, feelings and deeds, which later started to crack as individual struggles emerged again.”
This publication was created by: Kostadin Atanasov

US Envoys Hold Three-Hour Kremlin Talks With Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
06:02:00 UTC
15:02:00 KST

US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held more than three hours of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday evening, Sept. 5, presenting proposals on potential pathways to end the war against Ukraine.
The meeting at the Kremlin lasted three hours and 10 minutes and included formal discussions followed by an informal working dinner, according to Putin aide Yuri Ushakov.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Putin was joined by Ushakov and Russian special representative for economic cooperation Kirill Dmitriev, who characterized the trip on social media as an “important peacemaking visit.”
A White House official told Reuters that the negotiations were “meaningful,” adding that the next steps in the diplomatic process would be announced in the coming weeks.
Ushakov stated that the US envoys arrived “seriously prepared” and presented concrete ideas for a settlement.
However, the Kremlin reiterated its standard demands regarding the conflict, emphasizing battlefield positions and the need to address what Moscow terms the “root causes” of the war. Ushakov added that the US delegation agreed to take Putin’s assessments into account during their scheduled meetings in Kyiv.
Beyond the war in Ukraine, the discussions covered broader bilateral economic relations, including potential large-scale, mutually beneficial US-Russian commercial projects.
Serbia Is Not a Russian Province, and Lavrov Has No Right to Decide Its Future
Ushakov noted that Putin and US President Donald Trump intend to maintain direct personal contact and that working channels involving Witkoff and Kushner will remain active.
Important peacemaking visit. 🕊️ pic.twitter.com/r5UQhjeMxE
— Kirill Dmitriev (@kadmitriev) September 5, 2026
Diplomatic pause and preparations for Kyiv visit
At the start of the meeting, Putin addressed the security situation in the Ukrainian capital, stating that Russian forces had halted strikes on Kyiv starting at midnight on Sept. 5. Putin noted that the request for a temporary pause had been transmitted through official diplomatic and intelligence channels.
However, Putin explicitly rejected Ukraine’s call for a wider three-day ceasefire across the entire front line, asserting that Moscow had never agreed to such an arrangement.
“We will do everything that depends on us to ensure the safety of the negotiation process and the mediators,” Putin said, while noting that Ukrainian drone activity toward Russian territory had also decreased. Witkoff reportedly thanked Putin for agreeing to the pause on strikes affecting both capitals.
Witkoff and Kushner are scheduled to travel to Kyiv on Sunday, Sept. 6, to meet with President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Prior to the Moscow meeting, Zelensky confirmed that he had spoken directly with Trump’s envoys, pledging that Ukrainian forces would refrain from launching aerial strikes against Moscow through the end of Monday to safeguard the diplomatic process.
While Ukraine had advocated for a comprehensive bilateral ceasefire, the Armed Forces of Ukraine confirmed that frontline combat operations remain ongoing elsewhere after Moscow rejected the broader truce.

Broken feet, ripped-out hair and now a death sentence: the fate of twin sisters jailed over Iran protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
06:00:58 UTC
15:00:58 KST

The twins were 19 and still in high school when they were taken from their beds in the dead of night by masked men later identified as being sent by the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.
After four months of desperately seeking news from hospitals and state institutions, their mother, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, finally learned their fate. Taraneh and Romina Rahimi had been seized over their decision to join millions on the streets of Iranian cities during the January protests against the regime. The twins were unrecognisable by the time of their mother’s prison visit in May.
The women’s scalps were patchy from being dragged around by their hair, and their faces were bruised, according to their US-based cousin. It is claimed that Taraneh, who dreams of running her own horse stable one day, had been told the prison guards would rape Romina in front of her unless a confession was signed.
The visit by their mother to Dowlatabad prison, in Isfahan, the main city in central Iran, was five months ago. It has now emerged from the Iranian courts that Taraneh has been sentenced to death for her participation in the January protests, and that Romina has been given a 25-year prison sentence. Neither of the women have been seen by their family since the sentencing.
The difference in the sentences remains a mystery, but the twins’ cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, who lives in the US state of Utah, said he struggled to understand anything done by the regime.
“They do not follow their own law,” said Nourmohammadi. “There is an 18-day period that lawyers can go and appeal but in a lot of [execution] cases recently that has not happened. They just sentence and take the kids and execute them and hang them. So I mean, nothing, nothing really makes sense.”
Nourmohammadi, 43, said he believed Taraneh was sentenced to death by hanging because of her obvious innocence. “You can see her eyes and you know right away that she is a kind person,” he said. “My sense is like they’re looking to put fear within the people, to say: ‘Look, no matter how fine you are, no matter how innocent you are, we can get you, and don’t come to the streets any more.’”
Despite the logistical difficulties presented by the war with the US and Israel that began in February, Iran has executed more than 500 people this year, including at least 29 people in connection with the anti-government protests in January.
At least 16 women have been among those executed. Hundreds more protesters have either been sentenced to death or are facing charges which could carry the death penalty, including more than 70 in Isfahan.
Last month, the UK and 30 other countries signed a joint statement condemning the executions of the January protesters and describing them as an attempt to silence dissent.
Nourmohammadi, a healthcare IT specialist who arrived in the US from Iran 22 years ago, is speaking out despite receiving death threats via text messages and social media from people who say they know his home address. His cousins’ case, he said, should instil a determination to end the Islamic regime.
The two women joined the protests on 8 and 9 January in Istafan, along with 18 million others. The men who came for them a month later dragged them out with bags over their heads and offered no explanation. “The family didn’t know where they were,” Nourmohammadi said. “They had no idea. They were searching for them everywhere, different courts, hospitals. Then my aunt received a call saying: ‘We have your girls, come to see them at the prison.’”
Seeing her daughters was heartbreaking for his aunt, Nourmohammadi said. “She did not recognise her own children: they were beaten up, badly swollen faces, bruises all over their body, broken elbows, knuckles, feet, and they basically had no hair because they would pull their hair and drag them from one cell to another cell. She found out that they had been in solitary confinement.”
Marzieh Nourmohammadi, who raised her daughters, now 20, on her own, was not allowed to attend their trial. Their lawyers said Taraneh told the court that any admissions had been secured through torture. No evidence of the sisters’ involvement in violence was provided, it is claimed. They had never been involved in protests before.
“My mum lives with me,” he said. “There’s not a single second that I pass her and she’s not crying.”

Falklands row shows urgent need to commit to 3% target, says Labour defence committee chair

Javier Milei’s threats to the Falkland Islands make it even more important that Andy Burnham increase defence spending immediately, according to the Labour chair of the defence committee.
Tan Dhesi said the comments by the Argentinian president this week show why the government should raise military spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. But he said Burnham’s plans remain mired in confusion after the prime minister appeared to reassure him that the 2030 target would be hit, only for Downing Street to later retreat.
“It’s important the prime minister and the chancellor don’t defer those decisions to next year,” Dhesi told the Guardian. “We’ve seen Germany publicly expose Russia for the drone incident [in Leipzig]. Now we’ve got a threat from Argentina saying they are looking to take over the Falklands. We owe it to the Falklands – they say it’s their right to self-determination. It’s important that we also defend them from this threat.”
Dhesi was speaking after a turbulent week in geopolitics and defence policy. The Labour MP appeared to have secured a promise by the prime minister on Wednesday that the UK would spend 3% of its economic output on defence by 2030, at an estimated additional cost of £10bn a year.
During Burnham’s first prime minister’s questions since taking office in July, Dhesi asked him whether he backed the 2030 commitment, warning “vibes alone just isn’t going to be enough”.
He was speaking soon after the chancellor, John Healey, declined to sign up to the 2030 target, even though he resigned from Keir Starmer’s government over the issue. Burnham replied that he had “made that commitment”, only for No 10 to say the prime minister was not making a firm commitment.
The government instead has signed up to a longer-term Nato target of spending 3.5% on defence by 2035.
“There was no clarity [on the government’s defence policy], that’s why I asked the question,” Dhesi said. “There was a clarification post-PMQs that there isn’t an agreement to reach 3% by 2030. I wasn’t aware of [any] clarity [on this question], and that’s what was reconfirmed afterwards. We’re still in a similar situation. My question is valid and important for the country.”
Later in the week, Donald Trump appeared to call American support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falklands into question. The US has traditionally remained neutral on the islands’ ownership, while accepting Britain’s de facto control, but the president suggested this could be changed in retaliation for the UK’s lack of support for his war in Iran.
“Don’t forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me,” he told GB News. “Your country was not there to help me.”
His comments about the islands have emboldened Milei, who said on Thursday night “winds of change” favourable to his country’s claim to the islands were “blowing around the world”.
He added: “The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come.”
He also said companies developing oil “behind the back of the Argentine government” would be barred from doing business in Argentina.
Ministers in the UK condemned Milei’s comments on Friday, saying the Falklands would remain British for as long as the people who live there wanted them to.

The student loan scam looking to dupe already anxious students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
06:00:57 UTC
15:00:57 KST

You are about to start university and can’t wait but then you receive a worrying text message. It is a few days before the first student loan payment is due to land in your account and apparently someone has tried to alter your bank details.
“Our records indicate that your bank details on your student finance account were changed on Friday 16th. If you did not do this please contact us immediately,” says the text.
You click on the web link in the message and go to what you think is the website of the Students Loans Company (SLC), the government body that administers loans and grants. You log in to check that everything is OK, put in your bank details and the screen says: “Thanks for confirming.” But what you have done is supply this important information to criminals.
Acting quickly, the scammers then use your log-in details to access your real account and change the bank account so that your student loan payment is diverted to them.
The government is making a fresh push to raise awareness of this fraud as the new academic year starts.
This month, about £2.6bn is being paid out in maintenance support to 1.1 million students. The first of three loan payments will be deposited in the accounts of students in England and Wales. Students from Northern Ireland and Scotland get their loan instalments every month.
In the last academic year, £519,000 was lost to scammers who defrauded 168 students, according to the SLC. More than 1,100 people had their details changed but in most cases the fraud was stopped before money was lost.
What the scam looks like
Scammers are using several methods including text message, email or phone calls to target students.
The messages can claim that a payment is at risk because bank details need to be updated. Or it may say that an account has been closed unless the student acts immediately to log in to their “account” through the link provided.
The link supplied in the message leads to a clone of the SLC site and students are asked to input their details.
“It’s a race against time because the criminals then use those details to log into our genuine site to change the bank account on the genuine student account to divert the maintenance loan payment before we spot it,” said Alan Balanowski, the risk director at SLC.
Criminals know that billions of pounds will land in students’ accounts this month and have timed their approach to coordinate the fraud with a sense of urgency that people may not get their money when they need it. This is a common tactic used by criminals to get people to act in haste.
What to do
Be aware of when you could be the target of scams – September, January and April are the months when the student loan instalments are paid in England and Wales.
SLC says it won’t ask you to confirm personal or financial information by email, text or on social media. Don’t click on any links provided, instead log in to your account through the Gov.uk website.
Students are also urged to not publicise when they are getting their payment by refraining from putting it on social media.
SLC says that it does not provide services through WhatsApp and won’t initiate contact on social media. So immediately be suspicious if you are contacted in either of these ways.
Any fraudulent emails can be sent on to report@phishing.gov.uk while scam text messages can be forwarded to 7726.
If you suspect your account has been compromised, change the password immediately and contact SLC. Victims should be able to get a replacement payment so there is no financial loss to them.

====================================================================================================

‘Fabulous museums and no queues’: five of the best under-the-radar city breaks in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
06:00:57 UTC
15:00:57 KST

Nantes, France
As dilemmas go, it’s an unusual one: saddle up a giant squid or board a submersible for a voyage to the bottom of the ocean. In the end, I find myself drawn to a fierce-looking merhorse and tentatively take the reins. High above, my daughter glides by on a flying fish, metallic fins flapping, while her Dad is battling stormy seas at the helm of a huge conch shell. A ride on the Carrousel des Mondes Marins (marine worlds carousel) – a three-storey steampunk merry-go-round inspired by Jules Verne’s novel Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea – is one of the highlights of a visit to Nantes. A surreal fairground ride, a work of art and a homage to the city’s most famous son. It’s also a lot of fun.
On the banks of the Loire, 30 miles from the Atlantic ocean, Nantes is a city whose fortunes were built on the sea. As a young boy growing up near the docks in the 1830s, Verne dreamed of being a ship’s captain, but it wasn’t to be. Instead, he embarked on a series of journeys of the imagination, channelling his wanderlust into novels such as Around the World in 80 Days and Journey to the Centre of the Earth. The last of Nantes’ shipyards closed in the 1980s, but Verne’s unique vision provided the inspiration for a radical art and regeneration project, Les Machines de l’Île, that has breathed life into the abandoned quays and warehouses of the Île de Nantes, the river island that was home to the city’s docks.
This is now the stomping ground of the Grand Éléphant, a 12m-high mechanical pachyderm that carries passengers on tours of the island, spraying bystanders with water from its trunk. I’d seen photos but nothing prepares you for the thrill of turning a corner and seeing the real thing lumbering towards you. You can learn about the magic behind the machinery at the nearby Galerie des Machines, where the creators bring a mechanical menagerie of strange creatures to life.
The Verne connection also inspired the name of the city’s summer arts festival, Le Voyage à Nantes, which transforms streets, parks and public spaces into an open-air art gallery from July to September. Our visit coincides with the festival’s opening weekend, and the squares and avenues of the elegant Graslin district are busy with DJ sets, food stalls and people checking out the new artworks. In the Place Graslin, a beautiful square built – like much of Nantes – from chalky-white tuffeau stone from the Loire valley, some kind of cataclysmic eruption has been conjured up in front of the opera house. Huge ammonites appear to have been forced up from beneath the earth, engulfing cars in a mountain of rubble, their doors wide open, radios playing, as though abandoned in haste.
Just yards away, children are playing in the dancing water fountains of the square, while the white-aproned waiters of art nouveau brasserie La Cigale weave through the pavement tables delivering seafood platters to diners unfazed by the apocalyptic scene before them. Titled Fossil Opera, the artwork is a commentary on consumerism and the fleeting nature of human endeavour, and is one of about a dozen site-specific installations that have appeared in the city, as if by magic.
Even outside the summer months, there is plenty to discover in France’s sixth largest city. Each year, a handful of the festival installations are selected to become permanent fixtures, which has resulted in an impressive collection of contemporary public art, from Les Anneaux, a series of 18 giant steel rings on the Quai des Antilles, which frame views of the Loire and light up at night, to Tadashi Kawamata’s Belvédère de l’Hermitage, a viewing platform inspired by a swallow’s nest, which juts over a sheer cliff.
All of these cultural highlights, old and new, are linked by the Ligne Verte, a 12-mile (20km) green line painted on the pavement. We follow the trail through the Passage Pommeraye, an exquisite 19th century glass-roofed shopping arcade; past the imposing Château des ducs de Bretagne, a moated 15th-century castle; stop off at the excellent Musée d’arts de Nantes, which houses an impressive collection of international art spanning seven centuries; and finish up at the peaceful Jardin des Plantes, a charming (and free) botanical garden which is home to a handful of modern art installations and a good cafe. From here it’s a short stroll to the Lieu Unique, a cultural space and concert venue in the factory that once produced the city’s beloved buttery LU biscuits.
And there’s more to come. The Jardin Extraordinaire is a newly created garden and climbing wall in a disused granite quarry in the Bas‑Chantenay district. The exotic planting, waterfall and paddling pools were inspired by descriptions in Verne’s novel, The Mysterious Island. The nearby Chantenay docks have been colonised by studios, music spaces and the Little Atlantique Brewery, housed in a 19th-century former oil mill. Opposite the quarry, a derelict industrial building is being transformed into a new riverside cultural hub, the Cité des Imaginaires, which will eventually provide a home for an expanded Jules Verne museum. It’s an ambitious project: creative, unconventional and looking to the future. I’m sure Jules Verne would approve.
Joanne O’Connor
The trip was supported by Le Voyage à Nantes. Oceania Hôtel de France, just off the Place Graslin, has air‑conditioned doubles from €101 room-only
Winter’s Journey, a seasonal festival of concerts, temporary light installations, artworks and gastronomic events, runs from 21 November to 3 January.
Basel, Switzerland
Unless you’re a professional who makes their way to the Art Basel fair every year, chances are Switzerland’s third largest city will have passed you by – or rather you will have passed it by. Basel is one stop before Zurich on the fast train from Paris, but to whiz through would be a mistake. For art and design lovers, it is the perfect city to explore on a long weekend.
Basel bills itself as “the city of art and culture on the Rhine”, and it lives up to its boast. Stroll around the charming old town and marvel at the cathedral before enjoying a cold beer at one of the many cafes. If temperatures soar, you might want to join local people with a dip in the Rhine.
Once you’ve done all that, you need to engage with the area’s art offerings. Within the city, the Kunstmuseum holds more than 300,000 works spanning eight centuries, with big hitters such as Monet, Van Gogh and Warhol, while Museum Tinguely is home to the work of the idiosyncratic Swiss sculptor Jean Tinguely and his dada-esque machines.
But the two real draws are on the outskirts of the city. Fondation Beyeler in the suburb of Riehen is home to an impressive collection of modern and contemporary art, and always has a blockbuster exhibition (currently Pierre Huyghe) to check out. A short bus or train ride across the German border in Weil am Rhein is the Vitra Design Museum, home to one of the world’s largest permanent exhibitions of modern furniture design.
Before you admire the furniture collection, take a walk around the campus, where you can marvel at the main museum building designed by Frank Gehry; the Vitra Schaudepot – which houses the furniture collection – designed by Herzog & de Meuron; Zaha Hadid’s former fire station; and Tadao Ando’s conference centre. There is a beautiful garden by the Dutch designer Piet Oudolf, and the recently added Doshi Retreat for a moment of quiet reflection designed by the Indian architect Balkrishna Doshi, his first completed project outside India and the last he worked on before he died in 2023.
That’s half the day gone, so time to head inside. In lots of ways, exploring the Schaudepot is like walking through a giant doll’s house, with the rooms filled with instantly recognisable furniture icons from the 19th century to today, including works by Verner Panton, Le Corbusier, Alvar Aalto and Charles and Ray Eames. The museum also puts on temporary exhibitions. And if all of that has exhausted you, head to the VitraHaus Café, which serves a delicious lunch.
Max Benato
The Volkshaus, a boutique hotel in the old town, has doubles from 152 swiss francs (£138) room-only
Lübeck, Germany
Unless you’ve read Buddenbrooks, Thomas Mann’s epic family saga, you may not have heard of Lübeck. But in the middle ages, this port city in Germany, 70km north-east of Hamburg, was one of the richest and most powerful places on Earth. Today, despite the best efforts of the RAF to destroy it in 1942, it remains a beautifully intact medieval gem.
The old town is a Unesco world heritage site. It sits on an island in the centre of the city, encircled by the rivers Trave and Wakenitz, and the water is a good place to start exploring. My boyfriend and I hired an electric boat (€49 for up to six people) and spent an hour circumnavigating and gazing at its distinctive seven church spires.
Back on dry land, we set off on a guided walking tour, starting at the imposing – if wonky – Holsten Gate. We took in the five red brick churches the spires belong to (two have doubles), and climbed one of them, St Petri’s viewing tower, for a panoramic view. We also stopped at the 800-year-old town hall on the marketplace.
But just as fascinating was what lies behind the gothic splendour. At one time, there were 180 hidden alleyways and courtyards threaded through the old town, and about 80 remain. These labyrinthine lanes were built behind wealthy merchants’ mansions to house the poor. Today, the restored cottages are sought-after and the flower-filled, cobbled alleys are charming to explore.
To better understand Lübeck’s past, we visited the European Hansemuseum in the old castle monastery. It tells the story of the Hanseatic League, the powerful trade network that stretched from England to Russia and gave Lübeck (“the Queen of the League”) its wealth in the middle ages and its status as a free city state right up to 1937.
In a nearby palace, the Museum Behnhaus Drägerhaus displays 19th- and early 20th-century German and European art, including work by Edvard Munch, who visited Lübeck and painted its salt warehouses. Just round the corner is the Günter Grass-Haus, where the writer regularly stayed (he died in Lübeck in 2015).
We visited in June during the HanseKulturFestival, when the quarter around St Jakob’s church was full of live music stages, food stalls and outdoor bars. The next festival isn’t until 2028, but there are annual museum, theatre and literature nights, and popup live music in the summer.
Lübeck has three natural open-air swimming areas, one on the island. And the seaside isn’t far away – we had a day trip to Travemünde, a historic resort town with miles of sandy beach, taking a scenic river ferry there (90 minutes) and a 20-minute train back.
In town, the medieval Schiffergesellschaft (Seafarers’ Guild) is now a traditional Hanseatic restaurant, with long communal tables. Alongside North Sea fish and Holstein meat dishes are vegetarian versions of labskaus, a sort of hash.
Sadly, we couldn’t visit Buddenbrookhaus, the museum dedicated to the novel, as it is being renovated. It is expected to reopen in 2030 – which gives you plenty of time to read Mann’s 864-page doorstopper. Like Lübeck itself, it is worth the effort.
Rachel Dixon
The trip was provided by germany.travel and luebeck-tourismus.de. Accommodation was provided by Liho Lübeck, doubles from £73 room-only
Parma, Italy
Parma is just far enough off Italy’s main travel routes to discourage the huge crowds of tourists that flood the likes of Venice and Florence. Most travellers reach this tranquil Italian gem by flying into Milan or Bologna, followed by an hour’s train ride. It is definitely worth that extra effort, as I discover a city that ticks every box for a weekend getaway: fabulous museums and frescoed churches without long queues or the need to book a timeslot in advance; friendly, affordable trattorie and osterie showcasing a feast of local food and wines; and, if you time it right, the chance to catch an opera composed by locally born Giuseppe Verdi in the intimate Teatro Regio.
The historic centre of Parma is small and easily explored on foot, taking me past an array of architectural masterpieces. I kick off at the grand Piazza Duomo, dominated by the imposing 900-year-old romanesque cathedral. Everyone’s eyes are drawn up to the ornate cupola, decorated with a captivating illusionist fresco by local Renaissance artist Antonio da Correggio. Next to the cathedral stands the early gothic Battistero, an octagonal baptistery whose bare, minimalist exterior contrasts with an incredible explosion of colours from the 13th- and 14th-century paintings that cover the interior. Then, tucked away behind the Duomo, I come upon the entrance of the medieval Monastero di San Giovanni Evangelista, whose cloisters and garden are a peaceful oasis. Entry to the monastery and cathedral is free.
Parma’s big must-see is the monumental Palazzo della Pilotta, a baroque complex of palatial museums, a library and remarkable 400-year-old theatre, all included in a single €18 entry ticket. Just by the Parma river that slices the city into two, the palazzo was built by the Farnese family, whose patronage created most of the city’s Renaissance monuments. The Teatro Farnese, made almost entirely of wood, is rarely used as a venue today, but a visit remains an incredible experience. I leave most sightseeing time, though, for the Pilotta’s landmark Galleria Nazionale di Parma, a treasure trove of old master paintings. It may not quite rival the collection of the Uffizi, but I enjoy the chance to just turn up without booking in advance and quietly appreciate works by Leonardo da Vinci, Fra Angelico, Canaletto and Tintoretto without being surrounded by crowds.
Sightseeing is only part of Parma’s attraction, however, as this is one of Italy’s food capitals. I walk into the rustic, raucous OsteMagno bar, where everyone is tucking into tagliere – wooden boards piled with razor-thin slices of cured ham, the famous prosciutto crudo di Parma, artisan salami and crumbly aged parmigiano reggiano cheese, accompanied by a glass of the local’s favourite tipple, fizzy red Lambrusco wine, which is a lot more drinkable than I expect.
This is not a city to seek out chic, gourmet restaurants, but rather one of the many traditional trattorie such as Da Antonia, whose eponymous owner has overseen the cucina for more than 50 years, or the 120-year-old Trattoria Corrieri, serving up generous plates of homemade pasta for less than €15.
John Brunton
Palazzo Dalla Rosa Prati has doubles from €80 room-only
Santander, Spain
Often dismissed as little more than a ferry terminal – somewhere to stop overnight if you want to take your dog to Europe or lower your carbon footprint – the port city of Santander is undergoing something of a cultural renaissance. It’s already blessed with a spectacular bay facing the Cantabrian mountains, wide sandy beaches, grand, colonnaded plazas and superb food, but the opening of new art spaces and museums in the coming months will put the Cantabrian capital firmly on the weekend-break map.
Leading the way on 8 September is Faro Santander – a new cultural centre in a grand historical building housing a 1,000-piece art collection belonging to Banco Santander, including works by Velázquez, Goya, Titian, Rubens and Picasso. Different parts of the collection will be shown at different times.
With its ornate white facade facing the bay, the Pereda building was previously the bank’s headquarters, but has been transformed into a striking, 21st-century museum space by Pritzker prize-winning British architect David Chipperfield.
Santander’s moment in the spotlight will extend into 2027 when Madrid’s Reina Sofia Museum opens its first outpost, set in a similarly grand neo-Renaissance building just a few metres away from Faro Santander. The museum will house the Archivo Lafuente, with paintings, sculptures and manuscripts, including major collections on dadaism and the Spanish civil war, as well as art from Spain, North America and Latin America.
Faro Santander and Archivo Lafuente will form two points on a kind of “art triangle”, along with architect Renzo Piano’s 2017 Centro Botín contemporary art centre just over the road. With a bijou but impressive permanent collection, including works by Matisse, Juan Gris, Joaquín Sorolla and Mark Rothko, the Centro Botín sits on the waterfront like a giant, stilt-mounted, 60s alarm clock sawn in half.
Spaniards cottoned on to Santander’s charms long ago, and the seafront is lined with elegant fin-de-siècle villas built when well-heeled Madrileños discovered that the city’s Atlantic breezes were the perfect respite from the Spanish capital’s infernal summer. More than 100 years later, while Britain was experiencing its own heatwave, I followed their lead. Temperatures were in the balmy high 20s as I ambled past toddlers building sand castles and teenagers frolicking in the surf on El Sardinero beach, just 15 minutes by bus from the city centre.
The centre itself is wonderfully walkable and there’s an unhurried, laid-back vibe in the streets, grand plazas and narrow alleys near the gothic cathedral, lined with bars serving pinchos – the Cantabrian equivalent to tapas.
After tucking into tender, grilled squid, laced with gutsy garlic and olive oil, at Mesón Rampalay on a leafy square, I spent a fascinating couple of hours at Mupac – the Museum of Prehistory and Archaeology of Cantabria, just a few minutes’ walk away from Faro Santander.
The museum, which is home to one of Spain’s most important prehistoric collections, features excellent interactive displays, and in 2027 it is moving to a brand new, multimillion-euro building. By next year, it seems, Santander will be not just the capital of Cantabria, but a capital of culture too.
Eddi Fiegel
The trip was provided by Faro Santander. Abba Santander, near the Centro Botín, has stylish doubles from €66 room-only

Exhibition celebrates legacy of 80-year-old Hungarian painter Sándor Pinczehelyi in Pécs

The exhibition showcasing the work of Hungarian painter Sándor Pinczehelyi in Pécs is open to visitors until 8 November 2026 at the M21 Gallery in the Zsolnay Cultural Quarter.
A retrospective exhibition of the oeuvre of 80-year-old Sándor Pinczehelyi has opened at the M21 Gallery in the Zsolnay Cultural Quarter in Pécs. Long before the Iron Curtain came down, the artist was already combining Soviet totalitarian insignia with the symbols of Western affluence.
The exhibition features 150 works by the Munkácsy Prize-winning artist, who has been named Artist of Merit and Artist of Excellence, offering a comprehensive selection spanning six decades of his career.
"In European art circles I am known as someone who, in the earlier socialist period, worked with symbols such as the hammer and sickle, the paving stone and the star. One such piece is my iconic work with the hammer and sickle you can see here. There is virtually no art book dealing with that period in which this work is not reproduced."
Divided into nine thematic sections, the genre-spanning exhibition guides visitors from his earliest works to the present day through photographs, paintings, spatial sculptures, prints and enamel pieces. Alongside well-known works, visitors can also see pieces that have never been published before. The exhibition also presents works that were shown at the exhibitions in Turin and Berlin.

Chinese military university urged to revise AI course to ‘educate for war’

Chinese military university urged to revise AI course to ‘educate for war’
Proposal sees mapping out defence scenarios as better preparation for future officers involved in intelligent warfare
Researchers from the National University of Defence Technology’s College of Intelligence Science and Technology outlined their proposal in the July issue of the journal Defence Industry Conversion in China.
The initiative comes as China seeks to cultivate more military personnel with the technical skills to use artificial intelligence (AI) in future warfare.
As global militaries explore the use of AI in planning, training and combat, the technology is also changing what the troops need to learn, with China aiming to train forces capable of applying emerging technologies to armed operations.
The researchers said case studies in the existing AI course lacked sufficient “military flavour” and needed to be redesigned to better serve the practical needs of “educating for war”.
The university introduced “Principles and Practice of Artificial Intelligence” as a tailored course for non-AI science and engineering graduate students in its 2022 autumn semester.

Netanyahu races to finalize Likud election slate amid growing party tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:58:45 UTC
14:58:45 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is racing to finalize Likud’s Knesset slate before Tuesday night’s filing deadline, as internal pressure mounts over his remaining appointments and uncertainty persists over possible last-minute recruits and political alliances.
Likud Secretariat members were informed Saturday night that Netanyahu wants to convene the body Tuesday, just hours before the 10 p.m. deadline for submitting candidate lists for the 26th Knesset. The meeting is expected to approve any remaining candidates Netanyahu chooses to add to the slate.
The timing has heightened tensions inside Likud. Ministers, lawmakers, activists and local party officials are pressing Netanyahu not to make additional appointments unless they offer a clear electoral advantage, with some candidates already pushed significantly lower on the list following the party’s primaries.
Netanyahu has so far secured places for Defense Minister Israel Katz and Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar near the top of the slate, as well as for Likud Central Committee chairman Haim Katz and businessman Oren Dobronsky. Several additional places remain available for potential recruits or political deals before the deadline.
One name recently floated is Dr. Keren Assayag, a lecturer and breast cancer researcher who recently met Netanyahu. After initially expressing reservations about entering politics, party figures now believe she may be willing to join Likud, though it remains unclear whether she would receive a realistic position on the slate or simply endorse the party publicly.
Netanyahu has also sought to use the remaining flexibility to encourage broader cooperation on the right. He had hoped to bring retired Brig. Gen. Ofer Winter into an alliance involving Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism and Moshe Feiglin’s Identity party, which have already joined forces.
Winter, however, has repeatedly rejected merger proposals and, according to several reports, also turned down offers of reserved places on the Likud slate. If those efforts fail, Netanyahu is expected to unveil new candidates instead, a move that could reignite tensions inside a party still unsettled by its contentious primaries.
The dispute is particularly sensitive because reserved appointments can push candidates elected in the primaries into significantly lower positions. Some who initially finished near the start of the second group of 10 candidates have already fallen into the third after reserved places were inserted.
That has prompted lawmakers and ministers to mobilize activists, branch chiefs and local officials in an effort to persuade Netanyahu not to use every appointment available to him. Netanyahu is aware of the pressure, but the decision to convene the Secretariat indicates he intends to keep all options open until the final hours.
The scramble inside Likud is part of a broader rush across Israel’s political system as parties prepare their final election slates.
Naftali Bennett is expected to present the list of his Beyachad alliance Sunday night while continuing efforts to recruit Chili Tropper. The emerging slate, which includes figures from Yesh Atid, currently contains more candidates than polling suggests will win seats.
Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Lieberman is also expected to unveil his party’s list Sunday. The party has been polling at around 10 seats, while Lieberman has recruited several new candidates in recent weeks, particularly figures associated with liberal religious Zionism and active military reservists.
Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar! party has emerged in polls as Netanyahu’s leading challenger, is due to present his slate Monday. “I’m talking to everyone,” Eisenkot said over the weekend. “We’re preparing more surprises for the next three or four days.”
A possible alliance between Eisenkot and Bennett also remains in play. Neither has confirmed that talks are advancing, but both stopped short of ruling out such a move when questioned at a Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth conference last week.
Tropper remains another potential piece in the final round of maneuvering, with the possibility that his Zionist Home-Reservists faction could join either Bennett or Eisenkot before Tuesday night’s deadline.

“Two people were injured. The enemy attacked four districts of the region nearly 20 times using drones, artillery, and aerial bombs,” he said.

Hungary begins hunt for corrupt regime's billions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:54:00 UTC
14:54:00 KST

Hungary begins hunt for corrupt regime's billions
September 6, 2026
Asset recovery — it sounds bureaucratic but behind this phrase is one of the most important campaign promises made by Hungary's new government.
Hungary's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, and his Tisza party want to retrieve funds and assets that went — in some dubious ways — to the family of ousted Hungarian leader Viktor Orban or his allies, various oligarchs, or frontmen. The new government wants those funds back for state use, and it also plans to hold the beneficiaries accountable under law.
Billions of euros were stolen or diverted and, if social media is to be believed, many Hungarians want to see the individuals responsible behind bars. Magyar has talked of a sum of around €60 billion ($70 billion), though other estimates suggest the real amount could be three times that much.
Orban, allies lived lives of luxury
Observers say the success or failure of the asset recovery will almost certainly influence the future of Magyar and the Tisza party.
The huge sums of money are linked to images of decadent luxury under Orban. The former Hungarian prime minister's family, party members, and friendly oligarchs lived on luxury estates, flew in luxury jets, vacationed on luxury yachts, and repeatedly won billions worth of public contracts.
Orban-affiliated entrepreneurs, artists, academics, and journalists were also generously supported with public funds for years. Often their main qualification was loyalty to the former prime minister.
Those lifestyles contrasted with the lives led by Hungarians in poverty, the image of neglected public infrastructure, poor conditions in schools and hospitals, and the exodus of many young Hungarians from the country, as well as a huge deficit in the state budget, some 7.5% of Hungary's national income. These contrasts explain why there is such a popular desire for justice.
It's been almost four months since the new Magyar government took office and anti-corruption actions have officially started.
At the end of July, the new government established the National Asset Recovery Authority, or NVVH — a sort of "super institution" with very broad powers and independence.
Hungary hasn't had an authority like this in its modern history. The way state assets were privatized in the 1990s after communist rule was problematic, as it often was elsewhere in the former Soviet bloc. When Orban first came to power in 2010, there was a half-hearted attempt to address the corruption of the previous government under Ferenc Gyurcsany, but it came to nothing.
This time, things are meant to be different.
The NVVH will investigate where public funds flowed and how assets like real estate were used. Although no specific date has been set, the investigations will primarily focus on the Orban government's time in power, so dating back to 2010. The authority is also meant to make sure this cannot happen again, and will look into how public funds and assets are to be used in future.
The NVVH has both policing and prosecutorial powers, so it can investigate cases and bring charges. The authority is accountable to Hungary's parliament.
Controversy around new anti-corruption body
But the creation of the NVVH has not been without controversy.
Late last week, parliament appointed Anna Unger, 46, a political scientist at Eotvos Lorand University in Budapest, to head the new anti-corruption and asset recovery body. Unger is an expert on political systems, democratic institutions, and party financing and was chosen out of almost 100 other applicants in a process with several stages.
Some were surprised at Unger's appointment, as she wasn't really a public figure. Her research has included political corruption but she's not a recognized expert on the topic, nor is she a lawyer. Observers had expected a lawyer or an anti-corruption expert to get the job, somebody like Miklos Ligeti, head of legal affairs at Transparency International Hungary since 2012.
Ligeti also applied for the job but is reportedly being considered for a position as a deputy director. Unger will have four deputies with different duties and responsibilities. Katalin Tasnady, a well-known prosecutor with around two decades of criminal law experience, was made the NVVH's deputy chief of investigations.
Government representatives said Unger had presented a comprehensive political vision for the agency's work. During her parliamentary hearing, she said that under Orban, Hungary saw more than just what one might call classic corruption. An almost feudal system had prevailed, she argued. That was why in addition to restitution and asset recovery, the system had to be thoroughly investigated and exposed so that it would never happen again, Unger said.
No justice in next 6 years?
Unger caused the biggest upset when she said it would be folly to expect legally binding verdicts in any major corruption cases during the NVVH's first six-year term.
Robert Puzser, a popular commentator and personality on social media, called Unger's statement "devastating." Voters had given Magyar "unprecedented power to hold the country's plunderers to account," he said on Facebook, and if Hungarians had to wait more than six years, it could cause the collapse of this new government.
The new prime minister himself reacted angrily to critics who said the NVVH should have had a lawyer at its head.
"Nobody promised people they could vote for the leader of the NVVH as if it was a [reality TV] casting show," he wrote on Facebook. Plenty of experts thought Unger was absolutely suitable for the job.
In a podcast on the 24.hu media outlet, political science Gabor Torok surmised that the way that the NVVH had been established indicated that it would be a "strong political institution" that aimed to come to terms with the recent past.
Torok said the public expects the Tisza party to thoroughly reckon with the old system, and the new government will only be able to maintain the public's trust if it doesn't look like the "culprits of the previous order" are getting away with their past crimes, he said.
This article was originally written in German.
