Anonymous sources can become powerful tools of political manipulation - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
04:58:42 UTC
13:58:42 KST

“A senior diplomatic official said,” “a security official says,” “a source familiar with the details claims,” and “those close to the minister believe.” We hear and read phrases like these almost every day. They are sometimes followed by dramatic revelations, but one detail is missing: Who exactly is speaking to us?
The public is asked to accept information from an unknown person without knowing that person’s position or interests, whether they were present at the event they are describing or, most importantly, why they decided to share the information at that particular moment.
It is important to be clear: Confidential sources are essential to a free press. Journalists cannot do their jobs if everyone who provides them with information must be publicly identified.
Whistleblowers, public employees, and people working within large organizations sometimes need protection to bring important information to the public’s attention.
But there is a difference between protecting a source and turning anonymity into a standard practice.
Behind some of these unnamed “officials” is a well-oiled system for delivering carefully crafted messages. Politicians, advisers, security officials, associates, and other interested parties know they do not need to hold a news conference to influence the public agenda. Sometimes, a single phone call to a reporter is enough.
That is where a complicated relationship begins. The source needs the journalist to publish the information. The journalist needs the source to obtain information that competitors do not have. Both have an interest in the relationship, but their interests are not necessarily the same. The journalist wants a story. The source wants to achieve a goal.
That goal might be to damage a political opponent, prepare the ground for an impending decision, pressure decision makers, test the public’s response to an idea, or avoid responsibility for a failure.
In other words, a leak sometimes does not tell us what happened. It is intended to make something happen.
That is precisely the question a journalist must ask before publishing. The question should not only be, “Is the information true?” It should also be, “Why does this person want me to publish it?”
Even true information can be manipulative when it is incomplete. A source may provide one entirely accurate detail from a closed meeting while omitting five others that would change its meaning. Was a lie published? No. Did the public receive the full picture? No.
A leak can be accurate in its details yet misleading in the picture it creates.
The problem becomes more serious when anonymous information begins to circulate. A reporter publishes something attributed to “a senior official.” Another news outlet cites the report. From there, it spreads to social media and television studios. Before long, commentators are explaining the significance of a report when no one outside a small circle knows who is behind it.
The rumor has put on a suit and tie and become news.
The competition to be first only adds to the problem.
Competition among journalists has always existed and always will. Journalists want to break stories, and rightly so. But the public usually does not care whether it receives a report at 8:01 p.m. or 8:07 p.m. It does care enormously if those six minutes could have been used to verify that the information was true, complete, and accurate.
The public is not sitting with a stopwatch. Editors also bear considerable responsibility. Is one anonymous source enough? Was the information confirmed by another source? Was the person who could be harmed by the report given an opportunity to respond? Most importantly, does the public have a genuine interest in knowing the information, or is the media helping someone conduct a campaign through its platforms?
A news organization does not have to reveal a source’s identity to tell readers something about the source’s credibility. There is a meaningful difference between the vague phrase “a source said” and an explanation that the source has firsthand knowledge of the discussions, is not authorized to speak publicly, and provided information that was independently verified.
The more anonymous the source, the greater the journalist’s responsibility.
Politicians and public officials also find this system convenient. They can deliver a forceful message without publicly taking responsibility for it. If the message is well received, they can adopt it. If it causes an uproar, they can deny it, distance themselves from it, or claim it was not delivered on behalf of the authorized official.
This creates a politics of trial balloons.
The media must be careful not to become the factory that inflates them.
Confidential Sources as a means of reaching the truth
Journalism cannot and should not abandon confidential sources. Without them, it would lose a central part of its ability to expose what powerful people would prefer to conceal. But it must return to a simple principle: A source is a means of reaching the truth, not a substitute for it.
A good journalist is not a source’s messenger. On the contrary, precisely because journalists know their sources, speak with them, and trust them, they must repeatedly ask themselves the following: What is this person’s interest? What are they not telling me? Why are they telling me this now?
In an era when the public is overwhelmed with information, the great advantage of professional journalism is not that it is always the first to know everything.
Its advantage is that when it publishes something, the public can trust that someone first asked the difficult questions.
The next time we hear that “a senior official said” something, the important question is not only what was said. We should also ask who wanted us to know and what they want to happen once we do.
David Ben Basat is the CEO of Radios 100fm, an honorary consul and deputy dean of the Consular Diplomatic Corps, and president of the Israel Amateur Radio Club. He previously served as a monitor for Israel’s Army Radio and as a correspondent for NBC News.

Iraq targets 5 million bpd oil exports via Türkiye, Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
04:41:06 UTC
13:41:06 KST

A police officer controls the queues at a petrol station in Baghdad. (AFP Photo)
Iraq has boosted its crude oil export capacity to more than 3 million barrels per day (bpd) and plans to raise it to 5 million as it develops new routes away from the Strait of Hormuz, Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair said on Sept. 5.
Khudair told the official Iraqi News Agency (INA) that exports have reached around 3 million bpd since the start of September.
He said the government wants to increase capacity to 5 million once strategic pipelines linking Iraqi fields to Fishkhabur in the north and Syria’s Mediterranean port of Banias are completed.
Baghdad is also seeking to expand alternative export outlets as it looks to reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz.
Last month, Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zeidi ordered work to proceed on two strategic pipeline routes, Basra-Haditha-Fishkhabur and Haditha-Banias.
The northern route would connect southern oil fields with Fishkhabur near the Turkish border, opening access to the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline and Türkiye’s Mediterranean port of Ceyhan.
Iraq holds around 145 billion barrels of proven oil reserves, according to official figures. Its oil output fell to around 1.3 million bpd during the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran that began in late February, down from 3.3 million before the conflict, before beginning to recover in July and August.

The diplomatic battle that followed Bulgaria’s Unification in 1885
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
04:33:27 UTC
13:33:27 KST

Author
Ivo Ivanov
Radio Bulgaria's History Club
The diplomatic battle that followed Bulgaria’s Unification in 1885
Sunday 6 September 2026 14:35
Sunday, 6 September 2026, 14:35
“The Congress of Berlin”, by Anton von Werner
PHOTO Archive
Font size
At the Congress of Berlin in 1878, the Great European Powers reaffirmed the agreement they had reached before the outbreak of the Russo-Turkish War of 1877-1878. In order to safeguard their interests in the Balkans regardless of the outcome of the war, they had agreed that no unified Bulgarian state would be established. The Bulgarian-inhabited lands were divided. Northern Dobruja was ceded to Romania, while Serbia received the Sanjak of Niš. The lands between the Danube and the Balkan Mountains, together with the Sofia region, formed the Principality of Bulgaria, a vassal state of the Ottoman Empire. To the south, in Thrace and the Rhodope Mountains, the autonomous province of Eastern Rumelia was established, remaining directly under the suzerainty of the Sultan.
On 6 September 1885, the Bulgarians partially rejected this imposed settlement by proclaiming the Unification of the Principality of Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia. In doing so, they presented the Great Powers with a fait accompli. 
To defend their cause, the Bulgarians had to exploit the rivalries among the Great Powers, as well as their reluctance to go to war at that particular moment. They also had to prevent Ottoman military intervention while neutralising opposition from Russia, which came out against the Unification.
PHOTO BGNES
Associate Professor Dr. Aleka Strezova, a lecturer at New Bulgarian University in Sofia and a researcher at the Institute for Historical Studies of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences, tells the story of this defining moment for the young Bulgarian diplomacy. She is the author of the book The Unification. The Diplomatic Battle for Bulgaria.
Paradoxically, she notes, Bulgarian diplomacy emerged even before the Bulgarian state itself was established, as she explains in an interview with Radio Bulgaria:
Assoc. Prof. Dr. Aleka Strezova
PHOTO BTA
“Figures who represented the Bulgarian cause abroad began to emerge as early as the April Uprising of 1876. They were people with an excellent education for their time. Since we know that Bulgaria had no traditional aristocracy inherited from the Middle Ages, the principal asset of the people who built modern Bulgaria was their education. In this respect, we can certainly highlight the graduates of Robert College, the American school in Constantinople, which played a major role in shaping the Bulgarian post-Liberation elite. [...] This new generation of political leaders had a modern education and a contemporary outlook on the world and international relations.”
The researcher explains that throughout the seven years following the Liberation of Bulgaria in 1878, Bulgarian representatives in Europe, acting in coordination with Prince Alexander I of Bulgaria, raised the issue of the prospective unification of the two autonomous Bulgarian political entities whenever the opportunity arose and at every level.
“William Gladstone’s government returned to power in London. The Bulgarians decided that this was a favourable moment to do something with the ‘friend of the Bulgarians’. Stefan Panaretov [a lecturer at Robert College] went there. His mission was unsuccessful for various reasons, but upon returning to Constantinople, where he lived, he wrote a report to the then Bulgarian Foreign Minister Dragan Tsankov. He said that the mission had failed, but stressed: ‘In my opinion, the question of Bulgaria’s Unification should not be set aside. It must be raised continually, and the Great Powers must become accustomed to the idea that we will fight for this Unification and defend it, and that they should not forget that this is on our agenda and is our foremost objective.’”
Stefan Panaretov (1853-1931)
PHOTO Archive
Immediately after the proclamation of the Unification, a delegation led by Ivan Evstratiev Geshov was sent first to meet the Russian Emperor, who was in Denmark at the time. Alexander III declared that there could be no question of reversing the Unification, but that it had to be consolidated through a formula that would safeguard Russian interests.
Geshov then travelled to London and Paris. Another prominent Bulgarian representative, the diplomatic agent in Bucharest, Grigor Nachovich, was dispatched to Vienna. He succeeded in convincing the Austro-Hungarian Foreign Minister, Gustav Kálnoky, that the Unification would not strengthen Russia’s position in Bulgaria and would not threaten Austria-Hungary’s policy in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The most difficult mission was that of Stoyan Chomakov and Ivancho Hadjipetrov in Constantinople. Ultimately, Sultan Abdul Hamid II refused to send troops into Eastern Rumelia and called on the Great Powers to settle the issue among themselves. The delay in the Ottoman response was an important factor, as it gave the rivalries among the Great Powers time to come to the fore, Associate Professor Алека Strezova explains.
Ivan Evstatiev Geshov (1849 – 1924) and Grigor Nachovich (1845 – 1920)
PHOTO bg.wikipedia.org
“Britain, which in the first days was also hostile to the Unification, realised and became convinced that Russia was not behind the initiative. It therefore saw an opportunity to advance its own interests by supporting the Bulgarian cause. Britain was the power that proposed a highly elegant diplomatic formula for recognising the Unification: the Governor-General of Eastern Rumelia would be the Prince of Bulgaria, and in this way the Unification would be recognised in the form of a personal union. It really was a brilliant formula.”
The Unification was the defining test of Bulgarian diplomacy, the researcher explains. Despite Bulgaria’s vassal status, its diplomats operated on an equal footing with representatives of the Great Powers. They made full use of the diplomatic means at their disposal to defend the Bulgarian national cause.
Ultimately, it was the Great Powers that held the decisive say, while the victories of the Bulgarian army in the Serbo-Bulgarian War contributed to the favourable outcome of the entire episode. Yet Bulgarian diplomats were an exceptionally active force in defending and consolidating the Unification of the Principality of Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia, Associate Professor Strezova stresses.

Man suspected of attempted murder after throwing mentally impaired brother into underground trash bin

2026-09-06

13:32:50 KST

A man was arrested Saturday on suspicion of attempting to murder his mentally impaired brother by throwing him into an underground garbage container in Jerusalem’s Gilo neighborhood, police said.
The victim was rescued by firefighters, treated by Magen David Adom paramedics and taken in moderate condition to Hadassah Ein Kerem Medical Center. Police opened an investigation into the circumstances of the incident.
Fire and Rescue Service crews called to the scene found the man trapped inside the underground container. They detected low oxygen levels and high concentrations of explosive gases, making the rescue operation both complex and dangerous.
Because of his condition and the danger to his life, firefighters had to persuade him to wear a rescue hood that supplied breathable air while crews worked to reach him.
Incident commander Rami Meir described the operation as “complex and dangerous,” saying it took more than an hour to create the conditions needed to complete the rescue.
Firefighters pumped fresh air into the container using specialized equipment and worked to reduce the concentration of hazardous gases. A Jerusalem Municipality crane was later brought to the scene to lift the container, which together with its contents was estimated to weigh about one ton.

South Africa’s chrome riches fuel a deadly underground economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
04:31:45 UTC
13:31:45 KST

South Africa’s chrome riches fuel a deadly underground economy
Behind South Africa’s chrome riches lies a shadow economy where migrants and unemployed workers face deadly conditions.
Rustenburg, South Africa – On August 13, a wall of soil collapsed and killed 14 miners, most of whom were believed to be undocumented migrants, at a disused mining site near Nkaneng, an informal settlement outside Rustenburg in South Africa’s mineral-rich North West province.
“It happened in a flash, and the earth swallowed a dozen,” Lerothodi Nale*, a migrant from Lesotho who escaped the collapse and ran to alert nearby security guards, told Al Jazeera.
Without a passport, Nale left the scene afterwards, fearing arrest. More miners could still be trapped underground, North West police commissioner Lieutenant-General Arthur Adams told journalists, including Al Jazeera.
The disaster has exposed a darker side of South Africa’s chrome wealth: an underground economy where vulnerable migrants, unemployed former mineworker and criminal groups converge around a lucrative mineral trade.
Deadly riches
Rustenburg sits above the Bushveld Igneous Complex, one of the world’s richest geological formations, containing vast deposits of platinum-group metals and chrome. The region’s minerals have long powered industries including stainless steel production and advanced industrial applications.
South Africa is the world’s largest chrome producer and exporter, with much of its ore feeding global supply chains, particularly China’s stainless steel industry.
But alongside the formal mining sector, illegal extraction has expanded in parts of the country, including North West province, where authorities have raised concerns about unauthorised mining operations, environmental destruction and criminal groups exploiting abandoned and inactive mine sites.
For migrants like Nale, these abandoned pits offer both opportunity and danger.
“The disused mines are sitting graves with no geologists to confirm if rocks are still stable down there,” said metals governance expert Tapuwa Nhachi.
South Africa’s government has announced programmes to rehabilitate abandoned mines and close dangerous shafts, but critics say the scale of the response remains far below the challenge facing the country. Thousands of abandoned mine shafts remain across South Africa, creating opportunities for illegal operators and exposing workers to deadly conditions.
“Not a month goes without fatalities in abandoned mine holes,” Nhachi told Al Jazeera.
Chrome is attractive to illegal operators because deposits can often be reached closer to the surface, lowering extraction costs compared with deeper underground mining.
“For criminal networks, it becomes easier to extract, process and move the ore into supply chains,” environmental remediation expert Shamiso Mupara told Al Jazeera.
The result is an economy where profits are concentrated among those controlling equipment, transport routes and access to buyers, while miners take the greatest risks.
The underground pipeline
Nale describes a system that begins far beyond South Africa’s borders.
Undocumented migrants from Lesotho, Zimbabwe and Mozambique, alongside unemployed South Africans including former mineworker, are recruited by intermediaries who provide transport money and promise work around Rustenburg’s chrome fields.
On arrival, Nale said, workers are divided into groups controlled by criminal networks that provide food, mining equipment and, he alleges, explosives before sending them underground.
“At this juncture, we are held hostage by the alleged Maresha cartel, which, he says, takes 70 percent of our earnings and forces us to work in unsafe mines until we repay debts,” he said.
Nale alleges that miners can be transferred between groups and forced to continue working underground until additional ore is extracted.
The existence and scale of individual criminal groups involved in illegal mining are difficult to independently verify, but South African authorities have repeatedly linked illegal mining to organised crime, including violence, weapons trafficking and illicit financial networks.
Loren Landau, a migration expert at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, said the combination of poverty, unemployment and weak enforcement has created a steady supply of vulnerable workers.
“The pipeline sending scores of young male migrants to subterranean death does not pause because there are few viable job options left,” he told Al Jazeera.
“As soon as this batch of miners dies or gets injured, more destitute men are on the bus to replace them.”
A regional poverty trap
At the gates of Marikana police station, which serves Nkaneng, Dineo Motho, 29, waited for news about her husband, Kgadi Ntuli, 35, who remained missing after the collapse.
Wrapped in a traditional Lesotho blanket against the winter cold, she had travelled about 400 kilometres (250 miles) overnight to South Africa after hearing about the disaster.
“He left home in January to try his luck in Rustenburg chrome pits because with drying lands in Lesotho, there was no water to nourish our goats, crops or fruits. There were no jobs, no food,” she told Al Jazeera.
Ntuli had been travelling between Lesotho and South Africa’s chrome fields, she said, earning enough money to support the family.
Her greatest hope was that he was among those who survived the collapse, but fled afterwards to avoid arrest.
For families like hers, survival itself can mean disappearing from authorities.
Economic hardship and worsening environmental pressures in parts of Southern African have increased vulnerability, pushing some people towards dangerous informal work.
The consequences are increasingly visible in communities surrounding South Africa’s mining zones.
Mmanotshe Ramokoka, traditional leader of the Baphalane Traditional Council in North West province, said illegal mining has damaged farmland, threatened water supplies and created conflict between communities and criminal groups.
“It’s an ecological warzone,” he told Al Jazeera.
He said illegal processing sites have appeared near farming areas, with open pits endangering livestock and waste affecting local environments.
“The gangs have millions to rent industrial equipment for stripping soil for chrome. Migrant diggers die for a tiny fraction of the profit,” Ramokoka said.
The battle moves underground
For years, illegal mining in South Africa was associated mainly with abandoned gold mines around Gauteng province, where informal miners known as zama zamas operated in old underground shafts.
But some experts and community leaders say pressure from the government’s Operation Vala Umgodi (“seal the mine holes” in isiZulu), launched in 2023 to target illegal mining, has encouraged some criminal operators to adapt and seek opportunities elsewhere. Authorities have described the operation as a nationwide effort to combat illegal mining and associated criminal activity.
Some miners now appear to be moving towards less-monitored chrome-producing areas in North West province.
The police have rejected allegations of widespread complicity and say they are taking action against illegal mining networks.
In a statement to media outlets including Al Jazeera, Lieutenant-Colonel Tinyiko Mathebula of the Hawks, the South African Police Service’s specialised organised crime unit, said 23 illegal mining cases had been registered in the Rustenburg area over the past two years, with 63 accused charged.
He added that police had seized 20 trucks and 15 excavators linked to illegal mining activities.
But enforcement alone may not end the cycle.
As long as poverty pushes workers towards dangerous pits and criminal groups control access to chrome wealth, the cycle is likely to continue.
“Nothing scares the hungry,” Landau said.
*Nale changed his surname to speak freely and avoid possible arrest.

Xinjiang: Where tradition and development dance in harmony
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
04:31:41 UTC
13:31:41 KST

Xinjiang: Where tradition and development dance in harmony
Xinjiang is a land that sings with every heartbeat and dances with every breeze, where melody and movement are woven into the very soul of the earth. Stretching across the vast northwest of China, it captivates the soul not just with its sweeping landscapes, but with the vibrant pulse of its music and the graceful poetry of its dance—a heritage woven into the very fabric of daily life. Here, along the ancient Silk Road, culture has never been a relic of the past; it is a living, breathing presence that fills the streets, the markets, and the hearts of its people.
Today, Xinjiang is also a land on the move. From sprawling fields of solar panels and wind turbines to modern highways and thriving agriculture, the region is experiencing a transformation that has brought rising incomes and better lives to its communities. Yet, this progress has not come at the cost of its soul. Instead, development and tradition walk hand in hand, painting a genuine picture of prosperity, peace, and cultural pride.
I had the privilege of witnessing this harmony firsthand during a work trip to Xinjiang last year. The journey was long—over three thousand kilometers from Beijing—but the moment I arrived, every mile faded into the background. What struck me most was not just the beauty of the land, but the spirit of its people. Their joy is contagious, and their dedication to preserving their ancient customs—especially their music, song, and dance—is nothing short of inspiring.
There is no better place to see this than in the streets of Xinjiang's cities and villages, particularly on warm summer evenings. As the sun begins to set, the squares and parks come alive. People dressed in dazzling traditional attire gather together, and the air fills with music. Young and old, they move as one, their voices rising in song, their bodies swaying in rhythm. These scenes are not staged for visitors; they are the heartbeat of everyday life—a celebration of community, joy, and identity.
The soul of Xinjiang's art lies in its timeless traditions. The women's dance "Zhula" (meaning "clear water") is one of the region's most treasured cultural gems, recognized by UNESCO as an intangible cultural heritage. With its flowing movements and vibrant costumes, it tells stories of nature, love, and resilience—an authentic expression of the Uyghur spirit. Alongside it stands "Muqam," a grand musical tapestry that weaves together song, dance, and poetry, with instruments like the Dutar and Daf echoing the legends of the desert. And then there are dances like "Sainaimu," lively and celebratory, and "Nazirkum," playful and full of wit—each one a testament to the diversity and richness of Xinjiang's cultural mosaic.
These traditions are not confined to festivals or museums. They are a part of daily life, and increasingly, they are a bridge to the wider world. With improved roads, railways, and air routes, travelers from across China now flock to Xinjiang, drawn not only by its breathtaking natural beauty but also by the authenticity of its cultural experiences. Tourism has become a growing source of income for local communities, breathing new economic life into the region while encouraging the preservation of its heritage.
One young man I met embodies this connection beautifully. Liang Zhuang, a 31-year-old man from Xinjiang’s Yi Ning. Graduated in anthropology, he is deeply passionate about the traditions of his homeland. Zhuang said that in recent years, alongside economic and social development, government support for the cultural activities of ethnic minorities has consistently increased. He told me about "Kyz Kuu," a traditional ritual that is as thrilling as it is romantic. Part equestrian competition, part courtship ritual, it is a breathtaking display of courage, skill, and love. "It doesn't matter where you come from," he told me in fluent English, "when you watch Kyz Kuu, you can feel the meaning of pure love and the shared desire for a beautiful life."
Efforts to safeguard Xinjiang's cultural traditions go beyond tourism. In schools, children are taught to play traditional instruments and to dance as their grandparents did. Elders see themselves as guardians of this legacy, passing it down with pride and care. And the government has played a vital role too, supporting cultural activities and ensuring that these customs are not only protected but celebrated.
Fazila, manager of a small hotel in Yili town in Xinjiang, says: In our daily lives, ethnic folk music and dance have never left us. During festivals or gatherings with friends, people still play musical instruments and dance the ‘Meshrep’(a traditional Uyghur song and dance registered with UNESCO). The government has built cultural centers and invites veteran artists to teach young people traditional music and dance.
She says that many heritage inheritors receive government subsidies and earn a living by performing for tourists. While these old crafts were once hidden in private homes, tourism now allows more people to see our embroidery and cultural performances.
One evening, walking through the streets of Tacheng, a border town in the northwest of Xinjiang, I found myself swept up in the music once again. The melodies were so powerful, so full of emotion, that I joined the locals without thinking.
That is the magic of Xinjiang. It is a land of stunning contrasts—green pastures and vast deserts, ancient traditions and modern ambitions—yet everything flows together in a rhythm that feels both timeless and alive. From the felt tents of nomadic herders to the gleaming solar farms, from the colors of wedding ceremonies to the quiet dedication of a teacher passing on a song, Xinjiang tells a powerful story of unity, resilience, and hope.
It is a story that deserves to be heard beyond its borders. Because while some voices abroad continue to paint a distorted picture of this region, those who have truly walked its streets and listened to its music know the truth: Xinjiang is a place where culture thrives, where people are free to celebrate their heritage, and where the dance of tradition and progress continues, hand in hand, into the future.
In other words, this synthesis of economic progress, community well-being, and cultural pride stands as a direct counter-narrative to the negative portrayals often propagated by certain Western political factions and media outlets. In reality, Xinjiang shines as a profound symbol of unity, development, and human well-being.

Volcanic ash cloud halts flights at Indonesia’s main international airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
04:29:23 UTC
13:29:23 KST

Indonesia halted operations at eight airports on Sunday, including from its main international hub, affecting hundreds of flights as a result of an ash cloud from the Anak Krakatau volcano.
Saturday’s eruption, which produced lava and booming sounds that were heard up to 435 miles (700km) away, according to Indonesia’s geology agency, also interrupted some school activities and fishing. Two more eruptions were recorded on Sunday.
Ash was detected in the airspace around Soekarno-Hatta international airport near Jakarta, prompting authorities to suspend operations. They announced several extensions of the shutdown, keeping the airport closed to flights until 9.30pm local time on Sunday.
The suspension affected hundreds of flights, including international ones, according to the airport operator, Angkasa Pura. Singapore Airlines said it had cancelled flights to and from Jakarta for the rest of Sunday.
The Australian flag carrier said there were “disruptions to a number of Qantas services, including cancellations to and from Jakarta today”.
“Our meteorologists and operations teams are closely monitoring conditions in and around Jakarta and any impact on our operations,” it said in a statement. “Safety remains our highest priority. We have contacted affected customers and are providing assistance. Services will resume when conditions allow.”
Volcanic ash can damage jet engines, baking on to hot internal parts and quickly wearing out turbine blades, as well as clogging fuel and air systems. It can also damage pilots’ windscreens.
Ash reached as high as 6,000 metres (20,000ft) on the Java side of the volcano and 15,000 metres on the Sumatra side and some parts of Banten province in Java, the meteorological agency BMKG said.
Several schools cancelled activities on Saturday after students and residents suffered eye irritation, and fishers cancelled fishing trips, the local media outlet Kompas reported.
The disaster mitigation agency BNPB said it would conduct a weather modification operation, which could include cloud-seeding to promote rain.
“If it rains heavily enough, the volcanic ash that has been disrupting our daily lives since yesterday and continuing today will be washed away quickly,” the BNPB chief, Lt Gen Suharyanto, told a press conference.
More than 22,000 passengers and 209 flights were affected, the transport ministry said, particularly those bound to and from Singapore. Other affected international routes included Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur.
At least 16 domestic flights to Bali were cancelled, local airport authorities said.
Anak Krakatau, which means “child of Krakatau”, sits in a strait that separates the islands of Java and Sumatra. The volcano has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatau. That was one of the deadliest and most destructive volcanic eruptions in human history. About 35,000 people were killed.
Port authorities said ships passing through the strait were prohibited from going within a two-mile radius of the volcano and should be vigilant.
With Agence France-Presse

Jakarta airport temporarily closed after volcanic ash detected, flights disrupted
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:27:43 CST
13:27:43 KST

An aerial drone photo provided by Indonesia's Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation (PVMBG) shows volcanic materials spewing from Mount Anak Krakatau in Lampung province, Indonesia, Sept. 6, 2026. Indonesia's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport near Jakarta was temporarily closed early Sunday after volcanic ash from an eruption of Mount Anak Krakatau was detected in the airport area, disrupting dozens of flights, the Ministry of Transportation said. In addition to Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, authorities temporarily closed Halim Perdanakusuma Airport in Jakarta, Budiarto Airport in Curug, Tangerang and Radin Inten II Airport in Lampung. (PVMBG/Handout via Xinhua)
JAKARTA, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Indonesia's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport near Jakarta was temporarily closed early Sunday after volcanic ash from an eruption of Mount Anak Krakatau was detected in the airport area, disrupting dozens of flights, the Ministry of Transportation said.
Due to increased eruptive activity at Mount Anak Krakatau, Soekarno-Hatta International Airport has suspended flight operations until 1:30 p.m. local time, the airport said on its official Instagram channel.
Lukman F. Laisa, the ministry's director general of civil aviation, said the disruption affected both international and domestic flights at Indonesia's main airport.
A total of 16 international flights were canceled, seven delayed and five rescheduled, with affected routes including Singapore, Hong Kong, Sydney, Seoul, Doha, Amsterdam and Kuala Lumpur. For domestic services, four flights were canceled and one was diverted, affecting routes including Lampung, Denpasar and Surabaya.
In addition to Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, authorities temporarily closed Halim Perdanakusuma Airport in Jakarta, Budiarto Airport in Curug, Tangerang and Radin Inten II Airport in Lampung.
Around 23,000 passengers were affected by the closures, while 170 aircraft that had remained overnight on the apron at Soekarno-Hatta were confirmed safe, said Lukman.
Lukman said aviation authorities were continuing to monitor Mount Anak Krakatau's activity and coordinate with airlines, the airport operator, air navigation service provider and the Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency to adjust flight operations based on volcanic ash conditions. ■

Taiwanese companies such as TSMC and Foxconn have continued expanding their presence in Europe, while Taiwan and the UK have strengthened talent exchanges through semiconductor training programs.
Wu said Taiwan and Europe should work more closely to protect their shared values and build a more resilient and secure partnership.
Delegation leader Stefan Gara said Taiwan and Europe could deepen trusted, people-centered technology cooperation. Taiwan’s expertise and industrial ecosystems in semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and drones could be combined with Europe’s research strengths to promote practical applications and create greater value for both sides, he said.
The foreign ministry said this year’s program focuses on the semiconductor supply chain. Meetings with Taiwanese government agencies and private-sector organizations are intended to facilitate exchanges on trusted semiconductor supply chains and digital industry development.
Delegation members came from Austria, the Czech Republic, France, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania, and the UK.

German voters head to polls as far-right AfD party eyes historic state win

Germans vote in eastern state as far-right AfD eyes power
Saxony-Anhalt elections could see AfD become the first far-right party to take power at a state level since WWII.
Voting is under way in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt that could see the Alternative for Germany (AfD) become the first far-right party to take power at a state level since World War II.
Recent surveys place AfD at 40 percent, ahead of the centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU) at 23 percent.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Germany’s far right AfD eyes election breakthrough in Saxony-Anhalt
- list 2 of 3Germany’s far-right AfD eyes historic first in state election
- list 3 of 3Thousands protest in Germany as far-right AfD party meets
AfD has led comfortably in the pre-election opinion polls for months and has a chance at winning an absolute majority if several smaller parties fail to clear the 5 percent threshold to enter the parliament.
A CDU-led administration under incumbent state premier Sven Schulze is the most likely outcome if the AfD does not win a majority.
Weeks of coalition talks could follow the vote, depending on which parties surpass the 5 percent minimum.
AfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund, who was previously a member of the CDU, predicted gaining an absolute majority that would lead the anti-establishment party to national victory in 2029. He was named “Germany’s most dangerous man” by the influential magazine Der Spiegel.
“It was the others who erected the firewalls,” he told German tabloid Bild. “If no one wants to work with us, then we’ll just have to do it alone.”
An absolute majority would allow AfD to bypass mainstream parties’ “firewall” noncooperation policy, which the far-right party has already done at the local level.
For the AfD, the Saxony-Anhalt elections are a stepping stone towards its larger ambition: securing national power in the 2029 federal elections.
The CDU is led by deeply unpopular German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
At a local campaign rally in Lower Saxony a week before the election, Merz urged other politicians to engage with AfD more effectively.
“We must address the issues at hand. We must also address our choice of words,” Merz said, referring to a statement by the AfD’s state leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Martin Reichardt.
Reichardt previously told the AfD’s youth organisation that Germany had become “a lazy, anti-social bum reeking of dope”.
Thousands of demonstrators gathered for a festival in support of democracy the night before the crucial election. Rally organisers estimated that between 15,000 and 20,000 people attended the demonstration.
Initial results are expected at about 16:00 GMT (6pm local time) on Sunday.

‘Nobody will win’: Zelenskyy adviser warns of mutual destruction if war with Russia continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
04:00:55 UTC
13:00:55 KST

Russia and Ukraine are locked in an escalating war of long-range strikes with a growing risk to civilians in which neither side can entirely prevail, according to Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s defence technology adviser.
Serhii Beskrestnov, widely known by his call sign, Flash, said he was worried about the prospects for Kyiv this winter, and suggested elderly people should be evacuated in case Russian bombing were to knock out the capital’s energy supply.
However, the rapid wartime evolution also gave Ukraine the means to strike back, with plans to launch 1,000 drones a night to strike economic and military targets in Russia and halt its commercial air traffic, he said.
“Now, this is a war of cities, a war of infrastructure,” Beskrestnov told the Guardian, describing a conflict that is essentially deadlocked on the frontline, with civilians at increasing risk hundreds of miles away.
“In this war, nobody will win this game, because both countries, after the war, will have destroyed economics, infrastructures. So it’s stupid. We should stop this war. We proposed to Russia to stop this war, but Russia does not want to stop,” he said.
Beskrestnov, 51, a radio specialist, was first appointed by the former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov as a technology adviser in January, before being taken on directly in July, after the latter’s dismissal.
The adviser, who survived a drone attack on his home in April, agreed that “attack had become more powerful than defence”, because both sides’ air defences could not keep up with the number of missiles and drones available.
Russia could engage in a sustained bombing of electricity, water and heating systems in Kyiv this winter with the high-speed ballistic missiles it was producing at a rate of more than 100 a month, Beskrestnov said.
Earlier this week, Vladimir Putin said Russia’s military had been “ordered to prepare and carry out mass strikes” on Ukraine’s energy facilities, showing no sign of halting the war.
“For me, it’s horrible,” Beskrestnov said. “We are talking about 2 to 3 million people, and Russia understands it can create a disaster in Kyiv.” City authorities should think about evacuating civilians in advance, particularly elderly people, he added, while emphasising he was not making an official statement.
Ukraine is desperately short of US Patriot air defence interceptors, the main weapon capable of halting ballistic missiles, and Beskrestnov said he was “not sure” that Zelenskyy could obtain enough from abroad to prevent a crisis. Last month, the president said he wanted to secure 300 Patriot interceptors for the winter.
Beskrestnov predicted Ukraine would “attack Russia more and more with deep strikes”, continuing a campaign that has resulted in factories, warehouses and oil refineries being bombed. “We have a target from our president to increase the quantity of attacks to 1,000 a day,” he said, rising from its current level of about 300.
Addressing Zelenskyy’s announcement this week that there would be a sustained attempt by Ukraine to halt civil aviation inside Russia with the drones, Beskrestnov said: “I think it’s very simple: it’s not necessary for us to attack an airport, it’s just enough for us to fly at the airport and the airport will be closed.”
Russia has also made a series of advances that have boosted its attack potential, including its first suspected use of artificial intelligence. Ukrainian investigators concluded that a simple Molniya drone that killed a person near a Zaporizhzhia gas station in July was being guided not by radio but by AI.
“I’m just afraid what happens in the future because I think it’s just a question of time before Russia installs this technology in a Shahed,” he said, referring to the country’s standard long-range drone. It could render Ukraine’s “huge jamming network” obsolete without any radio communication to jam.
Beskrestnov said Ukraine was working on its own autonomous drones – “We have a prototype” – but that he believed Russia appeared to have more scale right now.
Russia has also developed a new wave of drones and missiles powered by Chinese-made jet engines that can fly at more than 200mph (320km/h), faster than the first generation of cheap Shahed interceptors that Ukraine has developed.
Moscow fired 2,500 jet-powered Shahed drones into Ukraine in August, up from 1,500 in July, and was planning to make “about 36,000 in 2027”, Beskrestnov said. It also planned to build another 30,000 of the slower piston-engine type next year.
Jet-powered Shaheds are already being used to threaten Kyiv and other big cities for hours at a time, but they will be complemented by another 10,000 cheap Banderol cruise missiles during 2027, plus a further 10,000 Dan-T missiles, boosting Russia’s ability to bomb Ukraine’s infrastructure.
Four to six Ukrainian companies were working on jet interceptors, Beskrestnov said, but they were “not ready for final production”, giving Moscow a window of advantage. The adviser would not give a timeframe for when the interceptors would be ready. At present, fighter jets take the lead in shooting down jet drones.
Civilian casualties have been rising as long-range attacks increase. According to the UN, 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured in Ukraine in July (the last month for which figures are available), the highest since March 2022. Accurate figures for Russia are not readily available.
Beskrestnov said the dismissal of Fedorov as defence minister after a clash with Zelenskyy was “a pity”, though the change in his own role meant the scope of his work had expanded beyond the armed forces to include the national guard and across government.
His role, he said, was technical and advisory and he sought to avoid becoming embroiled in personality clashes. “Don’t mix me with politics. Politics always has a part of garbage, rubbish,” he said.

Cold comfort: Japan’s Hokkaido battles cockroach surge amid global warming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
04:00:07 UTC
13:00:07 KST

Cold comfort: Japan’s Hokkaido battles cockroach surge amid global warming
Rising temperatures and ‘artificial environments’ enable the insects to thrive in a region once considered too hostile for them, experts say
In all his five decades of living in Hokkaido, Makoto Watanabe cannot recall ever being confronted by a cockroach.
“When I was a university student in Tokyo 30 years ago, I used to see them in my accommodation and I absolutely hated them,” Watanabe told This Week in Asia.
“Since I moved back here, I have always thought that one of the big advantages of living in a place where it is so cold for much of that year is that there are far fewer insects, but cockroaches in particular,” said Watanabe, an academic who lives in the town of Eniwa.
But Hokkaido has changed in those 30 years. According to Japan Meteorological Agency statistics, the average daytime temperature across the nation’s most northerly main island is 23 degrees Celsius (73.4 degrees Fahrenheit), rising to 29 degrees in major cities such as Sapporo, in the summer. That is 1.5 degrees higher than three decades ago.
More recently, localised summer temperatures have spiked as high as 35 degrees, a figure that was unthinkable even a decade ago.
Winter temperatures have also become milder, with the mean average at minus 3.7 degrees in January 1996, but up to minus 2 degrees in January this year.

Separately, the IDF announced a surprise General Staff exercise to test readiness for a sudden multi-front escalation. The drill is examining alert levels, the mobilization of forces and reserves, decision-making procedures and operational responses across the military.
The exercise was kept within a tightly restricted circle to surprise even senior generals and includes the rapid deployment of a battalion by helicopter. The IDF said increased movement of troops and aircraft would be noticeable across Israel, stressing that there was no actual security incident.
The military said the drill also incorporates lessons from fighting on multiple fronts and from the October 7 attack.
Hezbollah pressure over Ali Taher
Last week, the IDF said special forces had completed clearing the Ali Taher ridge of Hezbollah operatives. Security officials said no Iranian advisers or Quds Force members were identified there during the weeks-long operation.

The IDF described the site as strategic infrastructure built over two decades with Iranian funding and planning.

Indonesia: Flights canceled as Anak Krakatau volcano erupts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
03:46:00 UTC
12:46:00 KST

Indonesia: Flights canceled as Anak Krakatau volcano erupts
September 6, 2026
Hundreds of flights were canceled at Jakarta's international airport after Indonesia's Anak Krakatau volcano erupted early Sunday morning, more than 150 kilometers (93 miles) away.
The volcano produced a fountain of lava and loud sounds heard up to 700 kilometers away, Indonesia's geological agency said in a statement.
The cloud of ash was detected up to a height of 6,000 meters (20,000 feet) on the Java side of the volcano and a plume of up to 15,000 meters on the Sumatra side and some parts of Banten province in Java, the meteorological agency BMKG posted on its website.
No incidents of casualties were reported, and no evacuation orders were issued.
The closest township is more than 16 kilometers away, but the authorities warned residents and visitors to stay at least 3 kilometers from the volcano's active crater.
Two new eruptions were recorded on Sunday, the volcanology agency warned.
Indonesia cancels flights
The ash spread across parts of the capital Jakarta and Lampung province on the southern tip of Sumatra island, Indonesia's Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said.
Authorities have suspended operations at six airports following eruptions from Mount Anak Krakatoa, the ministry said.
"The Husein Sastranegara Airport in Bandung showed indications of being affected. Consequently, we have declared... the airport closed to flights," Dudy Purwagandhi told a press conference Sunday, mentioning the latest airport to be shuttered.
Operations at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, the country's largest and in the capital, Jakarta, were suspended earlier.
Soekarno-Hatta International Airport posted on Instagram that it had suspended flight operations until 9:30 a.m. (0230 GMT) due to volcanic ash.
"Due to increased activity from the Mount Anak Krakatau eruption, Soekarno-Hatta International Airport has temporarily suspended flight operations from 5:30 a.m. to 9.30 a.m.," the airport said.
The disruption of flight operations has impacted more than 22,000 passengers, the transport ministry said in a statement, adding that 209 flights were affected, particularly to and from Singapore.
Anak Krakatau lies in the middle between Java and Sumatra in Indonesia's vast island chain, which sits on the Pacific "Ring of Fire," where earthquakes and volcanic eruptions are frequent.
Anak Krakatau means "Child of Krakatau." The volcano is the offspring of the famous Krakatau, whose monumental eruption in 1883 triggered a period of global cooling.

Indonesia’s main airport suspends flights due to Anak Krakatau eruption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
03:38:23 UTC
12:38:23 KST

Thousands stranded as Anak Krakatau eruption shutters Indonesian airports
A total of 1,558 flights have been delayed or cancelled across the eight affected airports, including more than 900 to and from the country’s main Soekarno-Hatta airport.
Indonesia has suspended flights at its main international airport outside Jakarta and seven others across the country, after volcanic ash from the erupting Mount Anak Krakatau spread over the capital.
Soekarno-Hatta international airport, more than 150km (93 miles) from the volcano, was forced to extend closure operations until 8:59 am local time (01:59 GMT) on Monday, as part of nationwide airport shutdowns that stranded about 170,000 passengers.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘Everything is covered in ash’: Indonesia wildfires leave people in crisis
- list 2 of 3Indonesia sets up shelters for babies, children affected by wildfire smoke
- list 3 of 3Toxic haze from Indonesian forest fires chokes Malaysian Borneo
Across the eight affected airports, a total of 1,558 flights have been delayed or cancelled, including more than 900 services to and from Soekarno-Hatta, the Transportation Ministry said in a statement.
Operations were suspended at a total of eight airports, including the Husein Sastranegara airport in Bandung and Radin Inten II airport near Bandar Lampung on Sumatra, the ministry said.
Several airports in cities, including Semarang and Surabaya, have been prepared as “alternatives for landing”, the country’s Transportation Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said.
Across Jakarta, schools will be closed on Monday as classes move online, the city said in a statement, without specifying how long the measure will be in place.
Anak Krakatau, which began erupting late on Friday, produced a fountain of lava and booming sounds that could be heard up to 700km (435 miles) away, according to Indonesian authorities.
Ash was identified as high as 6,000 metres (20,000 feet) on the Java side of the volcano, and a plume of up to 15,000 metres (50,000 ft) on the Sumatra side and in some parts of Banten province in Java, the meteorological agency BMKG posted on its website.
Two new eruptions were recorded on Sunday, BMKG said.
Indonesia’s disaster mitigation agency, BNPB, said that there was no imminent tsunami risk from the eruption, and announced on Sunday that it would take measures, such as cloud-seeding, to encourage rain to wash away the ash.
“If it rains heavily enough, the volcanic ash that has been disrupting our daily lives since yesterday and continuing today will be washed away quickly,” BNPB chief Suharyanto told a news conference.
Anak Krakatau emerged from the sea in the 1920s in the caldera left by the catastrophic 1883 eruption of Krakatoa, one of the deadliest volcanic events in recorded history.
It sits in a strait that separates the islands of Java and Sumatra.
Ships passing through the strait were asked to increase vigilance for possible disruption to navigation safety due to volcanic activities.
Vessels are prohibited from approaching an exclusion zone of three kilometres radius from the volcano, local port authorities said in a statement.
The volcano has erupted periodically in the decades since, including a 2018 eruption that triggered a partial collapse of its crater and a tsunami that killed more than 400 people along the coasts of Java and Sumatra.
Volcanic ash poses a serious hazard to aircraft, capable of damaging jet engines and reducing visibility.

Huckabee’s West Bank message: Condemn violence, defend truth - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
03:14:03 UTC
12:14:03 KST

US Ambassador Mike Huckabee has offered a model for how a genuine ally should confront one of Israel’s most sensitive challenges by condemning wrongdoing without turning it into an indictment of an entire society.
In his Thursday interview, Huckabee denounced violence against Palestinians, demanded consequences for perpetrators, and stressed that they represent only a tiny minority of the roughly half a million Israelis living in Judea and Samaria. He also defended Israel’s right to build in Area C under the Oslo Accords framework. Those positions belong together.
International discussion of the West Bank too often erases distinctions. A criminal attack by several Jewish extremists becomes a judgment on “the settlers,” then on Israel itself.
Defenders of Israel can make the opposite mistake by minimizing lawlessness because hostile actors will exploit it. Huckabee rejects both distortions. He condemns violence by Israelis against Palestinians as firmly as he does violence by Palestinians against Israelis, while refusing to let masked attackers stand in for hundreds of thousands of Israelis who live peacefully in the West Bank. Moral clarity hinges on making both judgments at once.
His willingness to go to affected communities gives his words weight. When Huckabee visited Taybeh after reports of violence against its Palestinian Christian community, he met residents and called for those responsible for terror and violence to be found and prosecuted.
After the more recent attacks in Kusra, he again pressed Israeli authorities and used severe language about the perpetrators. Going to the place, hearing the people affected, pressing the authorities, and then telling the public plainly what happened is far more meaningful than issuing distant diplomatic statements.
The same clarity applies to the E1 and Area C regions. Israel has moved forward with marketing the first 1,400 housing units in E1 between Jerusalem and Ma’aleh Adumim, drawing renewed condemnation abroad.
Huckabee on Israeli rights in the West Bank
Huckabee has said Israelis have a right to build in Area C under the Oslo Accords. Supporting that right does not require excusing intimidation, assault, or property crimes against Palestinians. Jewish communities should not have their legitimacy erased because extremists commit crimes, and extremists should not receive immunity because they claim to act for the Jewish people.
The answer to accusations that Israel is indifferent to Palestinian rights cannot be reflexive denial whenever an Israeli commits a crime. It should be the confident application of Israeli law.
Arrest suspects when evidence warrants it. Investigate attacks seriously. Protect civilians. Prosecute offenders. A democratic state proves its legitimacy not by claiming that its citizens never do wrong, but by showing that wrongdoing has consequences and that no political or religious cause places anyone above the law.
The overwhelming majority of Israelis living beyond the Green Line are not storming Palestinian villages or taking over homes. They are raising families, working, studying, serving, and living under extraordinary political and security pressures.
Allowing a fringe to become the public face of that population is unfair to them and damaging to Israel. The answer is not to minimize the fringe, but to isolate it by condemning criminals, enforcing the law, and saying that their conduct does not describe a society, a settlement movement, or a country.
Huckabee’s approach emphasizes truth over slogans
Huckabee’s approach offers a better standard for discussing the West Bank by providing precision over slogans. Say who committed an act and who was harmed. Distinguish allegations from established facts. Demand consequences where crimes occurred. Defend Israel when accusations are false or inflated. Protect Palestinians when they are victims of wrongdoing. Refuse to let extremists dictate how millions of people are described.
Because Huckabee is a long-standing supporter of Israel, his criticism carries particular weight. Israel does not need allies who flatter it into complacency or critics who seize every crime as evidence against the nation.
It needs people willing to state the whole truth. Jewish communities in Judea and Samaria are not synonymous with violent extremists. Palestinian civilians are entitled to protection from crime. Israel has legitimate rights in Area C. Those who violate the law should face consequences.
Huckabee cuts through the noise because he is willing to say all of it, and Israel and the world at large need more voices willing to do the same.

'Fauda' in real life: Shin Bet agents posed as aid distributors in Gaza - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
03:13:41 UTC
12:13:41 KST

Undercover operatives from the Israeli Security Agency (Shin Bet) were embedded in Gaza as aid workers distributing food and drink to unwitting Gazan market stall-owners, according to a recent KAN News report detailing the lead-up to the recent capture of Hamas’s head of internal security, Mu’in al-Arabid, in the Gaza Strip.
Israeli operatives, according to KAN, established several small humanitarian aid projects and sold wares to Gazans who, in turn, sold the items at local markets. After establishing a relationship with the storefront owners, Shin Bet operatives were able to get the Gazans to help monitor the movements of various people, including al-Arabid.
Sources told KAN the Gazans only realized they had assisted the Shin Bet after al-Arabid had been captured.
The IDF and Shin Bet on Tuesday night confirmed in a statement that they had captured Hamas’s head of internal security in the Gaza Strip in the first high-level capture operation deep in Gaza in a long time.
The official statement did not make any direct mention of Gaza gangs being central to the operation, though there was a hint with a reference to Shin Bet’s “special forces.”
However, The Jerusalem Post and other media have received clear indications, along with confirmations in foreign reports, that anti-Hamas Gaza gangs were at the heart of the operation, even while supported by the IDF and the Shin Bet.
Shin Bet developed relationships with locals in order to gather intelligence
Sources also told KAN that, one day before the capture, Shin Bet personnel replaced their Gazan customers at the market and hid their weapons in their stalls. When the operation began, they grabbed their weapons and fled. Sources told KAN that the Shin Bet operatives were physically present in the market area for only a day or two before the operation, primarily relying on relationships they had developed with locals to gather intelligence.
When questioned, the Gazans who helped claimed they knew nothing about the plan, according to the KAN report.
Katz, Netanyahu play up al-Arabid's importance to Hamas
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz both sought to emphasize Arabid’s importance, with the prime minister saying he played a major role in managing the hiding of the over 250 Israeli hostages after October 7, 2023.
However, a Palestinian source in Gaza told the Post that the man captured was in charge of Hamas’s internal security department in the area of Gaza City only, which would have made him more of a mid-level official.
The source added that members of an anti-Hamas group played a role in the operation and that the terror organization is trying to “downplay the incident” and that “its internal security forces are actively pursuing militias supported by Israel.”
The final statement by the IDF and the Shin Bet seemed to settle on the official being more important than Hamas claimed but less important than Netanyahu and Katz contended.
Yonah Jeremy Bob, Dana Ben-Shimon, Avi Ashkenazi, and Amichai Stein contributed to this report.

Israel prepares for prolonged water crisis as algae clogs desalination plants
Israeli authorities are preparing for a prolonged water crisis after an experiment aimed at combating the algae bloom that has disrupted most of the country's desalination plants failed to produce a solution, according to a source familiar with the matter.
For more than a week, unusually high concentrations of microscopic algae along Israel's Mediterranean coast have repeatedly forced desalination plants to shut down or operate at reduced capacity.
Water supplies to homes and farms have so far remained normal, but only because authorities have shifted to emergency operations and increased pumping from the Sea of Galilee and groundwater reserves.
Officials involved in situational assessments say the crisis could be prolonged. With no indication of when the algae will disappear, the Water Authority is now pressing desalination plants to stockpile replacement membranes – the filters used to remove salt from seawater – so they can be replaced as they become clogged by the algae.
The Sorek B and Palmachim plants have already acquired supplies for replacement membranes, and the authority is prepared to pay to fly additional equipment into Israel rather than wait for shipments by sea.
The preparations follow an experiment last week in which the Water Authority sprayed chemicals, including copper sulfate, into the Mediterranean off the coast of Ashkelon in an attempt to reduce the concentration of algae. The substances were dispersed from aircraft along a nine-kilometer stretch of coastline.

IN BRIEF
- Australian boxing great, Tony Mundine, passed away on 30 August from a heart attack.
- Mundine remains the only Australian boxer to hold national titles in four weight divisions.
WARNING: This article contains the name and image of an Aboriginal person who has passed away.
Respected Bundjalung boxer Anthony 'Tony' Mundine OAM has been remembered as an "unwavering anchor" of strength and determination at an emotional ceremony in Sydney's Redfern.
Crowds gathered at Redfern Oval on Saturday morning to pay their respects to Mundine, who died from a heart attack on 30 August — aged 75.
His coffin was carried to a small stage — decorated with a large bouquet and the Aboriginal flag proudly draped across the top.
On the side, the dark wood was printed with a pair of boxing gloves and a gold rabbit, a nod to Mundine's loyal, lifelong love of the South Sydney Rabbitohs.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Bundjalung and Gadigal man Craig Madden, nephew to "Uncle Tony", welcomed guests to Country.
He recalled the life of a man who, at 15, came to Sydney to chase his dreams "into the ring".
Madden described Mundine as the "backbone" of their family.
"Steady, loyal and always there when you needed him. He was strong and staunch, yet humble, kind and generous beyond measure," he said.
"He always made room for a yarn and a laugh, or a quiet word when someone needed comfort."
"He was not a man who wasted words; the ones he shared carried wisdom, warmth and strength ... he shared lessons about life that stayed with you —leaving you feeling hopeful, grounded and ready to face what was to come next."
Mundine's nephew, Matthew Mundine, delivered the eulogy.
He reflected on Mundine's "quiet resilience, unwavering integrity and deep strength of character" that saw him become a "titan of Australian sport".
Acknowledging the legend's achievements in the ring, Mundine Jr said his "greatest victory" was the establishment of the Elouera Tony Mundine Gym and the Tony Mundine Hostel.
"He built far more than physical places — he built sanctuaries of hope," said Mundine Jr.
"For generations of community and young people, especially Aboriginal youth seeking direction, safe housing or a second chance, Tony offered a home away from home."
A "steady anchor", Mundine was a "deeply devoted" family man and a "loyal and steadfast" friend.
"Your fight may be done, but your victories are eternal — and your legacy will never fade."
Mundine's four children, Kelly, Natalie, Anthony and Kiah, also paid tribute to their father.
His youngest child, Kiah Tony Mundine Atkins, described her father as "positive, friendly, kind and happy", a man who "loved people" and deeply loved his grandchildren.
She recalled his cheekiness, his pride in his bright red car he constantly washed, and his funny sayings, "stone the crows, and everybody was a cowboy".
"Whenever I would ask my Dad, 'How are you, Dad?' He would say, 'I'm cruising like a butterfly'," she said.
"Keep cruising like a butterfly, Dad. I love you."
Mundine's eldest, Natalie Carr-Mundine, said her Dad had a special way of "touching people's lives".
"His legacy isn't measured by the titles he has won, or the fights he fought," she said.
"It's measured by the people he has inspired, and looking here today, he's inspired quite a lot of you."
Former boxer and Mundine's only son, Anthony Mundine Junior said he aspires to be like his father.
"If I can be half the man he was in his life, I'm doing alright," he said.
Four of Mundine's grandsons spoke, with Jade Mundine Atkins describing his Pop as their "world".
"I'm incredibly proud to be his grandson."
Family members, Lowanna Mundine and Birrpai Elder Uncle Heath Bugg also shared tributes alongside Nick Barnett, Mundine's closest friend of fifty years.
The memorial also heard from friends, colleagues and competitors from Mundine's boxing career, including ringside doctor Dr Lou Lewis, IBF World Super Featherweight Champion Barry Michael and boxing trainer and International Boxing Hall of Fame inductee Johnny Lewis.
Tribal Warrior CEO Shane Phillips shared reflections on the importance of the Elouera Tony Mundine Gym for Redfern's Aboriginal community, and Aboriginal Hostels CEO Shane Hamilton and Liz Simpson, who has managed the Tony Mundine Hostel for almost two decades, spoke about its impact on young Aboriginal men.
'A proud Bundjalung man from Baryulgil'
Born on 10 June 1951, Mundine was "a proud Bundjalung man from Baryulgil" — a small community on Bundjalung Country near Grafton in northern NSW.
He moved to Redfern at 15-years-old, following his talent in rugby league. But it was training in Ern McQuillan's Newtown gym that turned him to boxing.
Over 15 years, Mundine won 80 out of 96 fights and secured two Commonwealth titles. He remains the only Australian boxer to hold national titles in four weight divisions: middleweight, light heavyweight, cruiserweight and heavyweight
He cemented his status as a champion in 1974, when he challenged Argentina's Carlos Monzón for the WBA world middleweight title.
Mundine shared his gift, training others including his son Anthony Mundine Jr and grandson Rahim Mundine.
In 1986, he was awarded the Medal of the Order of Australia for his dedication and service to the sport of boxing and Aboriginal youth.
"Whether it was at the many national events and gatherings, or on The Block in Redfern, Coluzzi's Café in Kings Cross or in our family homes, Tony gave so much of himself to others," his family said in a statement after his passing.
"His legacy will live on through the many people he encouraged, mentored and inspired throughout his life."
For the latest from SBS News, download our app and subscribe to our newsletter.

Red tape, high cost: can Hong Kong’s new yacht scheme chart a smoother course?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
03:00:12 UTC
12:00:12 KST

Red tape, high cost: can Hong Kong’s new yacht scheme chart a smoother course?
Participants sailing to Guangdong province’s Dongao Island say voyage was eventful although bureaucracy and costs were hurdles
Retired harbour pilot Alex Yu Chi-leung sailed his 50-foot wooden yacht, Bowline, from Causeway Bay in Hong Kong to Dongao Island in Zhuhai under a new cross-border yachting scheme last week, but bureaucratic hurdles and shallow waters tempered the excitement of the leisure trip.
It was Yu’s first voyage under the scheme, but it could also be his last unless mainland Chinese authorities improve certain requirements.
“If the procedures are simplified – because right now they are too numerous, complicated and ambiguous – then I will come back again,” he said.
“If I have to do a massive round of work just to sail for one or two days, I might as well sail in Hong Kong.”
He added that he would rather take a commercial ferry to Dongao for a holiday.
Still, the 66-year-old veteran mariner gave the voyage a score of 60 out of 100 and viewed it as a worthwhile test run.
Yu was among 139 participants aboard 16 yachts from Hong Kong and Macau that sailed to Dongao under the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau individual yacht scheme. Launched in June, the scheme allows eligible Hong Kong and Macau vessels to enter designated Guangdong waters for tourism.

China begins mining iron from tailings, low-grade ore that can meet its demand for decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
03:00:09 UTC
12:00:09 KST

China begins mining iron from tailings, low-grade ore that can meet its demand for decades
Scientists have found a way to turn waste into a valuable resource on an industrial scale, reducing China’s dependence on iron ore imports
According to the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) last Tuesday, a production line capable of processing 5.56 million tonnes of refractory iron ore and tailings per year has passed official checks and is now running steadily.
On the other hand, China has the fourth-largest iron ore reserves, yet most are low grade, and nearly half are too hard and costly to process with standard methods. So huge amounts remain unused.
The new breakthrough aims to make those hard-to-use ores viable.
State broadcaster CCTV reported that the technology could fundamentally strengthen China’s ability to secure its own iron resources and reduce its heavy dependence on imports of the strategic commodity.

Yemeni army strikes Houthi military camp in northern Al-Jawf

02:56:37 UTC
11:56:37 KST

The Yemeni army has struck a Houthi military camp in northern Yemen's Al-Jawf province, destroying military capabilities at the site.
Army spokesman Majid al-Nuzaili said the operation targeted the Al-Labanat camp and deployed "specialised capabilities" that were recently introduced into active service.
In a statement broadcast by state television, al-Nuzaili stated that the strike destroyed Houthi equipment and neutralised personnel positioned at the base.
He did not disclose specific details regarding the weaponry used or confirmed casualty figures.
Regional escalation
Yemen had experienced a relative lull in violence since April 2022, following nearly 12 years of protracted war between internationally recognised government forces—backed by a Saudi-led coalition—and the Iranian-backed Houthis, who seized control of the capital Sanaa and substantial swathes of the country in 2014.
Since late 2023, following the outbreak of war in Gaza, the Houthis have expanded their involvement in regional hostilities by launching attacks towards Israel and targeting commercial shipping lanes across the Red Sea.
The latest strikes and renewed ground clashes have heightened concerns among observers over a breakdown of the truce and a potential return to widespread conflict across Yemen.
