Argentina threatens to sanction oil projects around Falkland Islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
23:46:54 UTC
08:46:54 KST

Argentina threatens to sanction oil projects around Falkland Islands
On Saturday, oilfield services firms including Schlumberger and Halliburton said they do not and will not work on projects near the islands
Argentina has announced that it will investigate and sanction oil companies working near the Falkland Islands without authorisation, after President Javier Milei said the “winds of change” favour his country’s claim to the archipelago.
Britain and Argentina fought a 10-week war in 1982 over the South Atlantic islands, a British overseas territory that Argentines call Las Malvinas.
Argentina’s presidency said in a statement on Friday that it had ordered the opening of proceedings to “investigate and penalise” 45 entities “linked to the exploration and exploitation of hydrocarbons” around the Falklands.
The statement did not name the entities involved. According to Argentine media, they include British, US, Canadian, Israeli, Danish and Dutch companies.
On Saturday afternoon, oilfield services companies Schlumberger, Halliburton and Baker Hughes issued statements saying they do not and will not work on hydrocarbon projects near the islands.
Later, Milei shared a news item on social media reporting the statements, along with an acronym that translates to “everything is going according to plan”.
The Falklands are located about 600km (372 miles) east of Argentina’s southernmost tip and administered by Britain. The Falklands war in 1982 ended with the surrender of the Argentine government after 74 days of conflict that killed 649 Argentines and 255 British troops.

Putin's talks with US envoys ‘constructive’: Kremlin aide
Unknown

Russian President Vladimir Putin’s talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were “substantive, constructive and extremely frank,” Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said on Sunday.
The talks in Moscow on Saturday lasted three hours and 10 minutes and covered not only the Ukraine war but also potential major Russian-US projects, state news agency TASS reported, citing Ushakov.
Putin, Ushakov said, reaffirmed Russia’s readiness to continue working with the US to seek a political and diplomatic solution to the Ukraine conflict.
The Russian president also stressed the need to address the “root causes” of the war and spoke about the battlefield advances of Russian forces and his confidence that Moscow would achieve its objectives, according to the Kremlin aide.
The US envoys outlined several ideas on possible ways to resolve the war, Ushakov said, adding that they pledged to take Putin’s assessments into account in their contacts in Kyiv.
Ushakov said Putin and Trump would remain in personal contact, while talks through the US negotiating team would also continue.
Witkoff and Kushner left Moscow after the meeting, and are scheduled to visit Kyiv on Sunday.
Meanwhile, a White House official told Axios that Witkoff and Kushner met Putin to advance US President Donald Trump’s efforts to end the over four-year war.
The envoys were joined by officials from the National Security Council, State and Treasury departments for discussions on proposals aimed at bringing an end to the conflict, according to the official.
The two sides discussed “substantive plans” for the next steps, which are expected to be announced in the coming weeks, said the official, adding that the US delegation looked forward to “equally productive” meetings in Ukraine.

German startup makes history with first orbital space flight launched from European soil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
23:37:24 UTC
08:37:24 KST

German startup Isar Aerospace launched a space rocket from a site in Arctic Norway on Saturday, bringing Europe closer to offering satellite flights from its own soil.
The uncrewed Spectrum rocket reached orbit shortly after launch, thus becoming the first orbital flight to originate from Europe, with several nations, including Sweden and Britain, saying they want a share of a growing market for commercial space missions.
The company declared the launch a success, while continuing to monitor developments as the flight continued, officials said.
"Access to space remains one of the biggest constraints for the space industry and national security architecture," Isar Aerospace co-founder and CEO Daniel Metzler said in a statement ahead of Saturday's launch.
Europe seeks autonomy
Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Isar's launch site in March, underscoring Europe's efforts to establish greater autonomy as the global order once championed by the United States is being upended by US President Donald Trump.
Blasting off from Norway's Arctic Andoeya Spaceport, the uncrewed Spectrum, designed for small and medium-sized payloads, carried five small satellites as well as an in-flight technological experiment, according to Isar.
Second launch, after first exploded in failed attempt
It was Isar's second launch, coming 18 months after the company's first rocket plunged to the ground and exploded in a fiery spectacle shortly after takeoff from the same site. No one was injured at the time.
The March 2025 launch was nonetheless deemed a success by the company for generating large amounts of data for its developers, it said then.
Saturday's launch was intended as "both the vehicle's qualification mission and its first flight carrying payload," the Bavarian company has said.
Global players in the satellite launch market include Elon Musk's SpaceX, which launches from the United States, and French ArianeGroup, a joint venture between Airbus and Safran that uses a spaceport in South America's French Guiana.
SpaceX, a sprawling empire spanning rockets, satellites and AI, listed on the Nasdaq exchange in June in a record initial public offering.
Sweden, with its Esrange launch site, and Britain, with its SaxaVord Spaceport in the Scottish Shetland Islands, are the nearest rivals to the Norwegian site, all of which aim to give Europe greater autonomy in space flights.
Isar last week said it had secured about €200 million from the European Space Agency (ESA) to help fund development of new rockets and expand its testing and launch infrastructure.
The German company is also developing a second launch site in Canada.

Are we seeing the end of Jewish politicians in the Democratic Party? - opinion

Brad Lander had everything going for him. At only age 57, the politician and urban planner managed to defeat incumbent representative Dan Goldman in New York’s 10th congressional district primary.
Given his very progressive stand, including strong support for illegals, as well as disdain for federal immigration enforcement, positions compatible with Democratic Socialist newcomers, Lander was a shoo-in to win in this November’s midterm elections.
There was only one fly in the ointment. Lander himself is Jewish – something that has become a massive liability in today’s very antisemitic atmosphere among the far-left.
It was only a few days ago when Lander was “targeted with insults and calls to leave Madison Square Garden, over allegations of being a Zionist.” Getting in his face and screaming, one individual called him a filthy ball sack, followed by the F bomb, for being a Zionist.
Apparently, it wasn’t enough that Lander accused Israel of having committed a genocide in Gaza, or his characterization of Judea and Samaria as being occupied. Nor was it sufficient that he referred to the Jewish state as having violated human rights standards.
One might have thought that advocating for recognition of a Palestinian state and standing up for Islamophobia would have earned him a few brownie points, but when you’re Jewish, none of that seems to matter. Because, at the end of the day, you cannot rid yourself of that ethnic label which reduces you to a detestable creature in the eyes of antisemites.
But Lander is not alone in that unsolvable dilemma. Along with him are the likes of Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, Chicago Governor JB Pritzker, presidential hopeful Rahm Emmanuel, Georgia Sen. Jon Osoff, Sen. Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, and many others who now run the risk of being left behind for the great sin of having been born Jewish.
Because if prominent influencer and streamer Hasan Piker, the new political kingmaker, has his way, all future leaders will emerge from the Democrat Socialist party, and none of them will be Jewish!
With the possible exception of Bernie Sanders, also Jewish, but one who is already too old to run for public office, no other Jew will have his level of “protection,” insulating him from the hateful rhetoric and sentiments that are openly being hurled at well-known and once respected Jewish politicians.
Even far-left Scott Wiener, whose controversial positions included “opposing a bill that would have barred registered sex offenders from running for local or state office, arguing the ban was too broad,” as well as a law, authored by him, “that blocks federal immigration and customs agents from wearing ski masks to hide their identities during operations,” was not safe as he, too, was on the receiving end of an antisemitic assault.
Harassed and cornered by activists in San Francisco in June 2026, he was berated by a demonstrator at a bar, repeatedly demanding he say “Free Palestine.”
This was the darling of the trans movement – the man who, per his own website, authored and vigorously championed major key legislative bills that sought to protect and expand rights for transgender, nonbinary, and LGBTQ+ individuals.
Yet the moment he hesitated to mouth the obligatory “Free Palestine” chant, identifying him as a willing sell-out to his own ethnicity, Wiener was seen as useless and belonging to the “others” category, similar to the separation that was made over the course of centuries between Jews and non-Jews.
Is this the end of the line for Jewish politicians?
So where does this leave Jewish political candidates or those already serving public office? What will become of their future?
According to an April 2026 article that appeared in the New York Times, titled, “Excruciating and Agonizing: A New Reality for Jewish Democrats,” “while high-profile Jewish politicians continue to win elections, command significant national platforms, and anchor leadership roles across federal, state, and local governments, they are navigating a cycle marked by severe ideological litmus tests, targeted harassment, and shifts in traditional party alliances.”
Keep in mind that five months have passed since the writing of that article, and what we are seeing is a consistent trend where Jewish candidates are either being sidelined or marginalized at a faster pace than ever before.
But it turns out that this is not true just of Jewish candidates. It also applies to non-Jews who are pro-Israel. Take Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman, a staunch supporter of the Jewish State. As a result of his unwavering position, Fetterman has been rebuffed by DSA members (Democratic Socialists of America).
One example of this happened after a contentious media appearance in which Fetterman defended his Israel stance against progressive critics. In response, the Pittsburgh branch of the DSA responded publicly by sharing a link to their organization’s sign-up page for prospective members.
Of course, Piker went one step further, completely denouncing Fetterman, citing his loyalty to Israel as proof that he “no longer represents the values of the party’s base.”
But which party base is Piker referring to? Because many among the base of the Democratic Party are, themselves, Jewish.
While that might not be true of the DSA leadership, most of whom are extremely anti-Israel and anti-Zionist (another term for being anti-Jewish), the Democratic Party still boasts a sizeable contingent of Jewish leaders, as well as pro-Israel supporters, even if they are reticent to admit it publicly.
Fetterman, a faithful Democrat, has been carefully watching this trend, declaring that if his party ever decides to formally turn against Israel, that will be grounds for him to leave the party.
Whether he wants to admit it or not, that has already occurred.
Because by defining the Democratic Party as a “big tent” party, and failing to denounce or condemn the Democratic Socialists who loudly excoriate Israel, accusing her of the worst crimes committed against humanity, the traditional Democratic Party has effectively merged with those who hate Israel.
There is no other way to look at it. In fact, Democratic Party leaders will find it more and more difficult to skirt the “Israel” issue. One way or another, they will have to declare their position of support or opposition, making it the deciding factor of a unified or split Democratic “big tent” party. AOC is already figuring out how to navigate those choppy waters.
What has become clear is that this looks like the end of the line for Jewish politicians.

American Jews don’t vote in Israel - so why are they being polled on its election? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
23:36:51 UTC
08:36:51 KST

A recent Jerusalem Post report carried an intriguing finding: A majority of “connected” American Jews surveyed by the Jewish People Policy Institute would prefer to see Israel’s opposition defeat the current governing coalition in the upcoming election.
My first reaction was not surprise at the result. It was: Why are we asking?
The survey was conducted by JPPI, an Israeli think tank headquartered in Jerusalem. Its “Voice of the Jewish People” panel surveyed 804 American Jews. Fifty-four percent preferred an opposition victory, while 14% favored the current coalition. Another 24% said it was not their place to express a preference.
That last group may have had a point.
JPPI itself acknowledges an important limitation: Its sample is not representative of all American Jews. Rather, it is intended to reflect the views of Jews who are relatively connected to Jewish life, Israel, or Jewish identity. That qualification matters.
The political composition of the respondents matters as well. Sixty-two percent reported voting for Kamala Harris in 2024, compared with 30% for President Donald Trump. Their Israeli preferences tracked their American political identities closely. Strong liberals overwhelmingly favored the Israeli opposition, while strong conservatives were far more likely to favor the coalition.
In other words, the poll tells us something quite predictable: American Jews who identify with the political Left in the United States are more likely to prefer the Israeli Center and Left, while conservative American Jews are more sympathetic to Israel’s Right.
I have no reason to believe JPPI designed the survey to produce an anti-government result. Indeed, that makes the underlying question more interesting, not less. Even a fair and professionally conducted poll can be asking the wrong question. Why should the political preferences of Americans who cannot vote in Israel be measured as though they constitute a meaningful constituency in an Israeli election?
That may be interesting sociology. It is less clear why it should carry political weight in an Israeli election.
The relationship of American Jews with Israel
American Jews certainly have every right to an opinion about Israel. They can support or criticize the prime minister. They can object to government policy, demonstrate, write articles, contribute to organizations, and argue passionately about Gaza, settlements, judicial reform, religious pluralism, or any other Israeli issue.
A relationship with Israel that permits only applause would not be much of a relationship.
But there is an important distinction between American Jews having opinions about Israel and Israeli institutions converting those opinions into a political metric about who should govern the country.
Only 8% of those surveyed are Israeli citizens eligible to vote in the election. That means 92% of the respondents are being asked whom they would prefer to govern a country in whose election they cannot cast a ballot.
Israelis will live directly with the consequences of that election. They will pay Israeli taxes. Their children will serve in the IDF. They will be called into reserve duty. They will live with government decisions affecting security, terrorism, education, housing, the economy, and war and peace.
That is why Israeli citizens vote.
The inclusion of Israeli-American dual citizens makes the survey even harder to categorize. Those respondents are different from American Jews merely expressing an opinion about Israel. They are members of the Israeli electorate who happen to reside abroad.
Indeed, JPPI also asked respondents whether Israelis living outside the country who fly to Israel specifically to vote are legitimately exercising their franchise.
So an Israeli institution is polling Americans – including Israeli voters living in America – about the political choices of Israelis and about the participation of Israelis abroad in the Israeli electoral process. It begins to resemble a hall of mirrors.
There is another phrase in the survey that deserves examination: “connected American Jews.” Connected how?
I was not asked to participate. To my knowledge, neither were my children. Yet Jewish education, charity, communal involvement, and Israel have been central parts of our family life for decades.
That does not invalidate JPPI’s panel. No poll can ask everyone.
But it does illustrate the danger of allowing a survey panel to take on the aura of representing “connected American Jewry.” Connectedness can mean synagogue attendance, Jewish education, philanthropy, organizational involvement, religious observance, attachment to Israel – or simply being sufficiently interested in Jewish affairs to join a survey panel.
Those are not necessarily the same thing.
Challenges of American Jewry
There is also a broader question that Israeli institutions should consider when examining American Jewish opinion. American Jewry faces enormous challenges concerning Jewish continuity and identity.
Pew Research Center’s major study of American Jews found that 27% of Jewish adults identified as Jews of no religion, rising to 40% among Jews under 30. Among non-Orthodox Jews who had married in the preceding decade, 72% had married non-Jews. Pew also found significantly lower levels of Jewish communal participation and attachment to Israel among Jews of no religion.
None of this means that secular or intermarried Jews are lesser Jews, or that they have no stake in Israel. They plainly do. But it raises a question of priorities.
Perhaps the most urgent issue facing American Jewry is not which Israeli political bloc should form the next government. It is whether future generations of American Jews will possess enough Jewish identity, knowledge, and connection to care about Israel at all.
Israel has every reason to care deeply about the condition of Diaspora Jewry. Israelis should be concerned about antisemitism in America, Jewish education, assimilation, intermarriage, synagogue life, and Jewish continuity. And American Jews should care deeply about Israel.
The relationship between the two largest Jewish communities in the world is indispensable. But mutual concern does not require creating an informal overseas electorate.
I would make precisely the same argument if JPPI’s survey had found that 54% of American Jews wanted Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his coalition returned to office.
My objection is not to the result. It is to the notion that the preferences of people who overwhelmingly cannot vote in an Israeli election should acquire political significance simply because someone in Jerusalem decided to poll them.
American Jews should have a strong voice in the future of American Jewish life and in the relationship between American Jewry and Israel. When it comes to deciding who governs Israel, however, Israelis already have a perfectly good polling mechanism. It is called an election.
The writer is an attorney and the father of Alisa Flatow, who was murdered in an Iranian-sponsored Palestinian terrorist attack in 1995. He is author of A Father’s Story: My Fight for Justice Against Iranian Terror (now available in an expanded paperback edition on Amazon.com) and is the chair of the Religious Zionists of America-Mizrachi. An oleh, he divides his time between Jerusalem and New Jersey.

Kremlin-Washington talks conclude after reportedly productive meeting between US, Russian diplomats
Unknown

2026-09-05

08:36:35 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin held more than three hours of "highly useful" talks on Saturday with two US envoys seeking a deal to end the Ukraine war, a Kremlin aide said, but he gave no indication of any breakthrough.
The aide, Yuri Ushakov, said Americans Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner "outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement." Ushakov did not say what these ideas were.
He said Putin had told the pair that Russia was making "real progress" on the battlefield, was confident of achieving its goals, and stressed the necessity of addressing "all the root causes of the conflict."
All these are statements that Moscow has made repeatedly in the course of the war, which has dragged on for more than four and a half years and has seen both sides intensify long-range air strikes in recent weeks while the front lines remain largely static.
There was no comment from Witkoff and Kushner, who were visiting Moscow for the first time since January on behalf of President Donald Trump. They flew out of Moscow soon after the talks and are due to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Kyiv on Sunday.
Economic issues, mutually beneficial projects, and Ukraine war discussed
"The talks went beyond a mere exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis. Economic issues and potential major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in some detail," Ushakov said.
"Overall, one can say that the negotiations were timely and highly useful for both sides."
Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev posted afterward on X/Twitter that it had been an "important peacemaking visit." He and Ushakov were both present at the meeting.
Putin praises Trump's efforts
In televised remarks at the start of the talks, Putin praised Trump's efforts to end the war. Trump suggested on Friday the US had a fresh proposal aimed at ending the war, but did not elaborate.
"Understanding that he is entering a difficult situation, he nevertheless does not stop his efforts to help bring about a settlement and to make his contribution to resolving the Russian-Ukrainian conflict," Putin said.
He promised to ensure the safety of the US negotiators. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said earlier that Putin had ordered the Russian military not to strike Kyiv for three days because of their trip.
Over the previous 10 days, Russia had pounded the Ukrainian capital day and night with missiles and drones, including an attack on Friday on the headquarters of the SBU security service.
Ukraine has inflicted damaging hits throughout the summer on Russian refineries, oil terminals and warehouses of online retailer Wildberries, in a bid to raise the cost to Moscow of continuing the war. Zelenskiy said Kyiv was prepared to refrain from strikes on Moscow through Monday.
A vast gulf in Russian, Ukrainian positions
A vast gulf remains between Russia and Ukraine on how to end the war, the deadliest in Europe since World War Two.
A source close to the Kremlin, speaking before reports emerged of the trip by Trump's envoys, said Putin was still intent on capturing more territory.
"There is no chance of reaching an agreement regarding the front line until Putin finishes securing the remaining part of the Donetsk region," the source told Reuters, adding that the Kremlin leader was confident - based on reports from his commanders - that this would happen by the end of the year.
Western military analysts see such a possibility as remote, given Moscow's slow rate of progress. Ukraine has refused to surrender land it has successfully defended at huge cost, and rejects such terms as tantamount to surrender.
The Kremlin said on Friday the position that Putin set out in a speech two years ago - that Ukraine should cede the entire territory of four regions claimed by Russia and abandon its plan to join NATO - was "unshakeable."
Since the last US-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in February, each side has intensified long-range air attacks deep inside the other's territory, while the war at sea has also escalated.
A White House official said US and Russian officials discussed "substantive" plans for next steps in talks aimed at ending Russia's war in Ukraine, which will be announced in the coming weeks

Lula's remarks came amid a trade dispute between Brazil and the United States, including additional tariffs of up to 25 percent on certain Brazilian products and U.S. criticism of Brazil's digital payment system. ■

Opt-out laws for social media algorithms to be introduced to parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
23:15:11 UTC
08:15:11 KST

Opt-out laws for social media algorithms to be introduced to parliament
In short:
Draft laws would create an opt-out system to turn off algorithms on social media platforms.
The bill would also make social media companies responsible for minimising and preventing harm on their platforms.
What's next?
The draft laws will be introduced by the federal government this week.
Social media companies would be required to give users a choice to turn off their algorithm through pop-up messages, under draft laws to be unveiled by the government later this week.
An exposure draft of the long-awaited Digital Duty of Care will be released as Labor steps up efforts to tackle online harm.
The ABC understands the proposed law would place the onus on social media companies to identify and mitigate risks on their platforms and prevent the sharing of harmful content.
That includes illegal content, including illegal pornography, being made available to adults.
For under-18s, about half a dozen additional areas of "psycho-social harm" would be identified, including content about body image and bullying.
The companies would face hefty fines of more than $100 million for breaches of the law.
As for algorithms, regular pop-up messages would be required, asking if users want to stick with the algorithm or only see what people they are following are posting. The user would have the choice.
Algorithms prioritise content for based on information such as a user's consumption habits, demographic and location data.
They have been criticised for amplifying sensationalist content, reinforcing echo chambers and playing a role in radicalising young people in the interests of keeping people on platforms for longer.
The eSafety commissioner and registered independent researchers would be empowered to police the social media platforms by using so-called "sock puppets", posing as children to monitor what is being fed to young people online.
Mixed signals on algorithms across parliament
The federal opposition has sent mixed signals about tackling algorithms.
Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson has previously referred to the "insidious psychological manipulation" of children through "dreadful algorithms".
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson, by contrast, says algorithms merely "reflect back to people often the content they want to see". He has raised concerns about censoring people's opinions.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the Coalition had not seen the government's proposal.
"What we want to see is parents having more control over what their kids get to see on social media, we will wait and see this legislation," Mr Taylor told News24.
"I am deeply sceptical. I fear that this is going to be an attempt by the government to censor social media, but as I say we haven't seen it. Let's see what the government comes forward with."
The Greens, meanwhile, have called for a much tougher approach, including a requirement for social media users to "opt-in" for an algorithmic feed.
Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young has proposed her own bill, which she says would "give Australians a straightforward choice about whether they use algorithmically curated feeds, rather than leaving people at the mercy of systems designed to keep them scrolling and consuming toxic content".

Ukrainian polar scientists register record-early return of penguins to Galindez Island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
23:15:00 UTC
08:15:00 KST

Ukrainian polar scientists register record-early return of penguins to Galindez Island
According to Ukrinform, the National Antarctic Scientific Center said this in a Facebook post.
"Only recently, we reported that these birds left Galindez Island, where the station is located, unusually late. In previous years, they would typically leave around May, but this year they stayed until the second half of July (and, as a reminder, it is winter in Antarctica)," the biologists said.
Now, scientists at the Vernadsky Research Base are recording the record-early return of the gentoo penguins. Previously, they would arrive en masse on the island roughly from mid-September to mid-October – that is, in spring – but this year the polar scientists spotted thousands of penguins in the second half of August.
"What is interesting is that in June and July, we mostly observed them in one location – Penguin Point. It is located on the opposite side of the island from the station and has a convenient, gently sloping shore for access to the water. Now, after their return, the birds have already spread along the shoreline all the way to the station building. We can see them from the windows," said Oleh Horiaiinov, a biologist with the 31st Ukrainian Antarctic Expedition.
In other words, the penguins are already spreading to the areas where they usually nest. Ukrainian researchers have so far counted at least 3,500 penguins on the island, and their numbers are increasing.
The unusually early return is most likely linked to changes in sea-ice conditions around the island and rising ocean temperatures. At the end of July, when the penguins disappeared, ice formed around Galindez Island, and the water temperature dropped to -1.9°C, below the freezing point. Later, however, ocean temperatures began to rise and the ice gradually retreated. As a result, biologists began recording the mass return of the penguins.
Therefore, it is quite possible that in the coming years, climate change and warming will result in gentoo penguins no longer leaving Galindez Island at all. They could become not only the most numerous but also the most permanent neighbors of the Ukrainian polar scientists, the National Antarctic Scientific Center said.

Iraq boosts oil export capacity above 3M bpd, targets 5M via new routes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
23:13:25 UTC
08:13:25 KST

Omer Asur Cuhadar and Tarek Chouiref
06 September 2026•Update: 06 September 2026
Iraq has boosted its crude oil export capacity to more than 3 million barrels per day (bpd) and plans to raise it to 5 million as it develops new routes away from the Strait of Hormuz, Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair said on Saturday.
Khudair told the official Iraqi News Agency (INA) that exports have reached around 3 million bpd since the start of September.
He said the government wants to increase capacity to 5 million once strategic pipelines linking Iraqi fields to Fishkhabur in the north and Syria’s Mediterranean port of Banias are completed.
Baghdad is also seeking to expand alternative export outlets as it looks to reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz.
Last month, Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zeidi ordered work to proceed on two strategic pipeline routes – Basra-Haditha-Fishkhabur and Haditha-Banias.
The northern route would connect southern oil fields with Fishkhabur near the Turkish border, opening access to the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline and Türkiye’s Mediterranean port of Ceyhan.
The western route would link Haditha with Syria’s Banias port, giving Iraq another outlet to the Mediterranean and potentially reviving a historic oil corridor between the two countries.
The government said the project is intended to diversify export routes and strengthen Iraq’s capacity to move crude abroad.
Iraq holds around 145 billion barrels of proven oil reserves, according to official figures. Its oil output fell to around 1.3 million bpd during the US-Israeli war on Iran that began in late February, down from 3.3 million before the conflict, before beginning to recover in July and August.
The push for alternative export routes comes amid continuing disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz linked to tensions between Washington and Tehran.

Nigel Farage wants to be a global statesman. First he needs distance from Trump.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
23:11:55 UTC
08:11:55 KST

Reform UK Party Leader Nigel Farage shows off his socks on the second day of the Reform Party conference at National Exhibition Centre on September 05, 2026 in Birmingham, England. | Anthony Devlin/Getty Images
BIRMINGHAM, England — Nigel Farage has one overriding task: to convince voters he’s ready to take over as British prime minister in an election he believes may be just months away.
“When that election comes we will be ready, and when that election comes we will fight to win,” he told his party’s conference in Birmingham, central England, on Friday.
Core to his effort to portray himself as a prime minister-in-waiting was a joint appearance at the conference with the darling of the French far right, Jordan Bardella, who is hoping to become leader of the French government after a presidential election next year.
Advertisement
The pair signed a “memorandum of understanding” pledging to stop the flow of small boats trafficking migrants across the English Channel to British shores. For Farage, it was a chance to prove he can cut a deal with a foreign political leader even before he’s elected to office.
The surprise was that the leader wasn’t Donald Trump.
Showing off a French connection — and even suggesting he would speak in French when he repays the visit — might just help dilute the impression that Farage is a disciple of the world’s most divisive and disruptive head of state.
Farage has long made a point of his ideological kinship with the American president, but these connections to the “Make America Great Again” universe now pose perhaps the most serious threat to his campaign to win power in the U.K.
Goodbye to the ‘British sherpa’
Farage’s set-piece Friday press conference alongside Bardella was overshadowed by a storm of controversy over an alleged funding scandal that hours earlier had claimed the scalps of two of his most senior aides.
One of them, policy chief James Orr, is almost as well plugged into Trump’s world as the Reform leader himself. Orr has nurtured a friendship with U.S. Vice President JD Vance, whom he has described as a kind of “mentor.” For his part, the vice president has called Orr his “British sherpa.”
Advertisement
This week, however, Orr was at the center of an undercover sting operation and featured prominently in a Channel 4 TV report, apparently planning to arrange potentially rule-breaking funding from a foreign benefactor — via a U.K. middleman — to produce favorable polling.
Farage brushed off the furor on Friday, insisting the party had broken no laws and received no dubious money.
Orr has now stood down, along with another aide, pending an investigation. It’s not clear whether he could return to Farage’s team if the procedure finds he wasn’t seriously at fault.
The Iran factor
But Farage needs to distance himself from Trump’s world for other reasons, not least because the two men have a long friendship.
Early last year, Farage told his supporters that Trump’s victory in the U.S. 2024 presidential election should serve as an “inspiration” to their movement.
Since then, however, Trump has dismayed some of the most important voter groups in the U.K. that Farage needs to win over if he is to succeed, first over his stance toward Ukraine and then over the Iran war.
Advertisement
Trump was unpopular in many European countries even before Iran. The fallout from that conflict, including the impact on fuel prices, has only deepened the animosity that many European voters feel toward the U.S. president.
Luke Tryl, from the More in Common think tank, presented new research at the Reform conference showing how a key group of British swing voters are skeptical of Trump and “worry about the turbulence on the world stage.”
“There is a core of Reform voters for whom there is a Trump problem,” Tryl told a meeting on the fringes of the conference. This group of voters, whom he calls “rooted patriots,” want to tackle immigration but are worried about the chaotic scenes involving officers with Immigration and Customs Enforcement in the U.S., Tryl added.
“[They are] the absolutely crucial group when it comes to Reform. This is the swing group that has decided elections for the past 20 years,” he said. “They are patriotic, socially conservative, actually a bit more economically left-leaning as well.”
Tryl said Reform may need “a distancing exercise” from some of Trump’s policies to reassure these voters. “Iran really further damaged Trump, and in fact the angriest I’ve seen a group of Reform voters was over the Oval Office treatment of [Ukraine President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy,” Tryl told POLITICO, referring to the infamous on-camera dressing-down the wartime leader took from Trump and Vance in February 2025.
There are signs that Farage gets the point.
While Reform’s themes chime with MAGA priorities, there were few explicit displays of affinity between the British and American populist right on show at the gathering in Birmingham. On Friday, Farage didn’t mention Trump —the man he used to proudly call his “friend” — during his speech at all.
Instead, he turned to his ally from France for political assistance. “Hold it for me,” Farage told Bardella on stage as they took turns signing the theatrically large printout of their migration deal. “It’s quite heavy.”

Trump-backed group announces $10m ad spend for midterm Senate race in Texas
US president has pledged more than $400m through his super PAC to boost Republican candidates in the upcoming midterms.
A political group associated with United States President Donald Trump has announced it will spend $10m on television and digital advertisements in the state of Texas ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.
The Saturday filing with the Federal Election Commission (FEC) represents the first major spend in a general election by MAGA, Inc, a super PAC named for Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘Small potatoes’: US President Trump downplays war on Iran
- list 2 of 3Mock Republican convention website tops Google, redirects to Epstein files
- list 3 of 3Missouri Supreme Court blocks Trump-backed map from November’s midterms
The advertisements are expected to heavily target Democratic candidate James Talarico, a 37-year-old state representative running for the US Senate against Trump-backed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Speculation abounds that Democrats may have a chance of flipping one of Texas’s Senate seats for the first time since 1993.
Paxton has weathered a series of scandals, even facing a state impeachment trial. Still, Democrats have repeatedly faced withering defeats in Texas, having failed to win a statewide office there in more than three decades.
In a statement on Saturday, MAGA, Inc sought to portray Talarico as out of touch with everyday Texans.
“High Tax Talarico wants to take money out of Texans’ pockets,” spokesperson Alex Pfeiffer said. “MAGA Inc is going to ensure Texas knows about Talarico’s radical policies and elects Ken Paxton to the US Senate.”
While Texas is often seen as a Republican stronghold, Trump’s deepening unpopularity and cost-of-living concerns have bolstered Democrats like Talarico ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Republicans currently hold slim majorities in both chambers of Congress. But Democrats are hoping to flip a few key seats to break the Republicans’ hold on the legislature.
Whoever wins control of Congress will likely be able to shape the legislative agenda of Trump’s final two years as president.
The advertisements announced on Saturday will focus on tax policy, accusing Democrats of seeking tax hikes that would burden voters.
Democrats, meanwhile, have traditionally accused Republicans of awarding tax breaks to the most affluent.
That criticism re-emerged last year, when the Republican-led Congress passed Trump’s signature piece of legislation, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, along party lines.
In addition to increasing spending on Trump priorities like defence and immigration, the bill also made permanent the tax breaks Trump had debuted during his first term and increased exemptions for federal estate taxes.
Critics pointed out that those tax cuts would largely benefit wealthier earners.
In response to criticism of his economic policy, Talarico’s campaign accused the candidate’s right-wing opponents of pouring outside money into the race and misrepresenting his record.
“Billionaire-backed dark money groups are lying about James Talarico because they’re scared of the people-powered movement we’re building to fix this broken, corrupt political system,” campaign spokesperson JT Ennis said in response to Saturday’s announcement.
“James was proud to vote for the largest property tax cut in Texas history and has consistently voted to cut taxes for working Texans.”
Texas has been a focal point of Republican strategy throughout the midterm campaign season.
Last year, Trump officials petitioned Texas lawmakers to redraw the state’s congressional map in a way that gives Republicans an advantage in winning five extra seats in the House of Representatives.
After Texas followed through, other Republican-led states followed suit, with Democrats mounting similar efforts in states like California.
This week, Trump will also travel to Dallas, Texas, to headline a first-ever Republican midterm convention. He will speak at both nights of the gathering.
Trump has made himself a centrepiece of Republican strategy in the lead-up to the midterms, travelling around the country to hold rallies and support party members. “What I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” he told a rally in South Carolina last month.
But questions have emerged about the large sum of money gathered by MAGA Inc — and whether it would be distributed to down-ballot Republican candidates.
Faced with such questions, Trump told reporters on Friday that he planned to allocate between $400m and $500m from MAGA, Inc to help Republicans in the midterms.
Trump has also used his influence to shape Republican primaries across the country, boosting his preferred candidates.
The president’s endorsement, for instance, helped Paxton defeat incumbent Senator John Cornyn in the party’s May primary, despite concerns that the attorney general’s scandals could damage his chances in the general election.

Technology will not deepen India’s education divide
Technology will not deepen India’s education divide; used well, it could help close it.At the TOI Social Impact Summit, 2026, Pranav Kothari, CEO of Educational Initiatives, broke the myth that edtech is expensive or exclusionary. Technology, he stressed, is not a substitute for teachers, who remain better at inspiration, values, debates, experiments and project-based learning. But technology’s strength lies in continuity: Indian schools operate for about 180 days a year and children attend for roughly 140, while learning can continue through the year.Cyient founder chairman B V R Mohan Reddy said technology can also narrow the rich-poor gap by creating individual learning paths. Unlike a classroom model that often caters to the front benches, adaptive platforms can move each learner at his or her own pace.
Reddy also urged against fearing AI, warning that the real divide may be between those who understand AI and those who do not. His company adopted 37 govt schools, where the share of girls rose from 16-18% to 56% and his school students occupied a lion’s share of the merit rankers, and dropouts fell to about 2%.
The intervention also expanded into skilling, AI labs and employment-linked training. In one programme, what started as a summer project for his granddaughter Pratinya Bodanapu, rural girls are trained in skills identified through market surveys.
Similar experiences were shared by Abdul Salam KP, vice-chairman of Malabar Gold. The connection between poverty and education became stark during Covid while distributing food in urban slums, he said. “We found children on the streets even after schools reopened. That led to slum micro-learning centres, where teachers, uniforms, books and meals are provided and children without documents are helped into formal schools. The network has now grown to about 2,500 centres serving around 1.2 lakh children every day.”Gayatri Nair Lobo, CEO of Educate Girls, said school enrolment is only the first hurdle. Poverty, missing documents, domestic work, early marriage and the distance to secondary schools continue to push girls out. For every 100 primary schools, she said, there are only 20 senior secondary schools. Educate Girls is helping adolescent girls and young women return through open schooling. One, she said, returned after 10 years and went on to top Madhya Pradesh in Class 10.

Commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal has called upon innovators and startups to develop low-cost and sustainable solutions to help civil society, the corporate sector and govt deal with initiatives that create social impact, such as cleaning up of lakes that he has started in his constituency.“May be one of the innovators will come up with a cleaning machine for these lakes to maintain these lakes. There are machines internationally available but at a huge price. May be one of our startups will very easily be able to make it,” Goyal said at the TOI Social Impact Summit on Saturday. The minister, an MP from North Mumbai, is seeking to clean up nine lakes in his constituency and expand the initiative to the city.He said in India, citizens voluntarily take up social causes. “When the Companies Bill was piloted about 13-14 years ago bringing in the provision of (mandatory 2% spend on) CSR, we were in opposition. I remember in the finance committee when the bill came up for scrutiny, I had felt we are actually doing dis-service to the Indian ethos, to the Indian way of life because in India, people don’t do CSR out of compulsion. The moment we bring it into the garb of compulsion we change that connection.
But be that as it may, it has brought more funds into CSR.” He also said govt’s housing initiative had helped bring dignity to people and create assets, while pushing a large section into the middle class. “That coming into the middle class, maybe neo middle class will move to upper middle class, will have a better quality of life. Double incomes are coming into families... this is spurring your economic growth. So, this is a very profitable proposition when you serve society.”
At the Summit, BCCL COO Mohit Jain said growth must be measured not merely by output, investment and ambition, but by the lives it strengthens. “A tree does not grow upward alone but underneath as well,” he said. “So it is with the nation. The true strength of a country is revealed at its roots—in the student who gains access to better education, the patient who receives timely care, and the community that becomes resilient enough to face an uncertain future.”

EU member refuses to point finger at Russia over German drone incident
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has refused to assign blame for last month’s drone incident in Germany squarely to Russia, citing “reckless” Western weapons deliveries to Kiev.
Earlier this week, the German government said it had grounds to believe that Moscow was behind the incident, in which an explosive-laden UAV was found between Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4.
Berlin subsequently announced the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin, as well as tighter border controls for Russian citizens. Moscow responded by shutting down the Goethe Institute centers in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and Ekaterinburg, which promote German language and culture.
Moscow has rejected the allegations, with President Vladimir Putin suggesting they were being used as a diversionary tactic to distract Germans from domestic economic woes.
While multiple fellow EU member states have issued statements backing Germany’s position, not all of them have jumped on the bandwagon of pointing the finger at Russia.
A case in point is Bulgaria, whose prime minister told the parliament on Friday that European shipments of long-range weapons to Ukraine have been just as “reckless” as the failed sabotage attempt in Germany last month. Radev pointed out that Kiev is using Western-made weaponry, backed by European intelligence and instructors, to conduct strikes deep inside Russian territory.
“And what can we expect when we attack deep inside another country with our long-range weapons? Will it stand by or will it respond?” the Bulgarian prime minister inquired rhetorically.
He went on to warn that the West’s insistence on achieving a “conventional military victory” over a major nuclear power is dramatically raising the risk of uncontrolled escalation with Moscow.
“Europe can exist without Russia, but Europe will hardly exist for long against Russia,” Radev concluded, calling on the EU to “sit down at the negotiating table [with Moscow] as soon as possible.”
Meanwhile, a number of prominent political figures in Germany have called into question the government’s response to the drone incident and, more broadly, Berlin’s current hostile policies toward Russia.
In a post on X on Wednesday, veteran left-wing politician Sahra Wagenknecht wrote that “even if Russia were behind it, a drone that caused no damage whatsoever is no reason to fuel a highly dangerous escalation that could end in a war with Russia, costing millions of lives.”
Similar assessments have been voiced by those at the opposite end of the political spectrum. Fielding questions from The Pioneer media outlet on Tuesday, Ulrich Siegmund – the lead candidate for the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in Sunday’s regional elections in Saxony-Anhalt – said that a “continuous sequence of events” had led up to the drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport. He cited his country’s ever-deeper involvement in the Ukraine conflict, arguing that “it’s only logical that there will be some kind of reaction at some point.”
Siegmund criticized the anti-Russian policies pursued by successive German governments since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, saying that weapons deliveries to Kiev and economic sanctions against Moscow have done little to resolve the conflict and save people’s lives.
The AfD politician insisted that it was high time Germany engaged earnestly in diplomacy with Russia instead.

The amount of paperwork businesses are required to regularly carry out could be slashed, the business secretary has announced.
Jonathan Reynolds said he plans to simplify corporate reporting rules and exempt some small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) from the need to carry out certain form-filling exercises altogether.
The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade said the corporate reporting changes could save businesses across the UK £450m.
It added that it was “nonsensical” for small businesses, including cafes, hotels and furniture makers, to have to conduct the detailed paperwork when they should be focused on their day-to-day trade.
The department claimed the average annual report and accounts of some businesses now run to 98,000 words, and compared it to the length of JRR Tolkien’s fantasy novel The Hobbit, which is more than 95,300 words.
The average count is said to be even higher for FTSE 100 companies, at 152,000 words.
“No one goes into business to fill out forms,” said Reynolds.
“For years, hardworking firms in this country have been weighed down by pen-pushing paperwork and frustrating costs, ticking boxes that do nothing to help them grow their business.
“We’re stripping back outdated bureaucracy and building a commonsense system fit for a 21st-century economy.
“This will cut the cost of doing business, giving breathing room to bosses across the country and free them up to focus on what they do best, creating jobs and growth.”
A consultation into the plans begins on 7 September.

This “new” frog was hiding in plain sight for 100 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
22:35:48 UTC
07:35:48 KST

This “new” frog was hiding in plain sight for 100 years
- Date:
- September 5, 2026
- Source:
- Pensoft Publishers
- Summary:
- A common frog found across Ecuador and Colombia has finally been recognized as its own species after more than a century of mistaken identity. Museum specimens from the 1800s helped scientists reveal that Pristimantis milpe had been hiding in plain sight all along.
- Share:
Scientists at the Pontificia Universidad Católica del Ecuador have formally described Pristimantis milpe, a common and widespread frog that spent more than a century being mistaken for another species. The mystery was resolved by studying specimens collected in Ecuador during the 19th century and preserved at the Natural History Museum in London.
The finding stands out because many newly described species are rare or confined to small areas. Pristimantis milpe, by contrast, is widespread, relatively easy to find, and readily detected by its nighttime call. Its known range covers more than 67,000 square kilometers across the Chocó forests of western Ecuador and southern Colombia, from sea level to elevations of 1,200 meters.
The formal description appears in the international journal ZooKeys, which focuses on biodiversity and taxonomy.
A Century-Old Case of Mistaken Identity
Researchers were able to identify Pristimantis milpe by revisiting historical amphibian specimens housed at the Natural History Museum in London (NHM).
Santiago Ron, a researcher at PUCE and lead author of the study, traveled to England to investigate a classification problem that had persisted for more than 100 years. He examined the original specimens - known as "types" - that had been collected in Ecuador during the 19th century and preserved in the museum ever since.
By comparing those historical frogs with living populations from the Ecuadorian Chocó, the team found that the old specimens had been incorrectly linked to a different species. As a result, a frog that had been regularly seen and documented for decades never received a scientific name of its own.
"That such a common species has gone unnoticed under the wrong name for decades highlights the importance of correctly connecting scientific names with living populations in nature," notes Jhael Ortega, a PhD student at Virginia Tech and one of the study authors.
The Clicking Frog of the Chocó Forest
The Milpe Robber Frog (Cutín de Milpe) is active at night. Males typically call from leaves on shrubs and bromeliads several meters above the forest floor. Their calls are loud and distinctive, producing a sound similar to a "click."
Females and males also differ noticeably in appearance. Females have striking coloration around the groin and thighs, where orange or light blue tones can appear alongside black spots. Males generally have more uniform coloring.
The frog lives in the forests of the Ecuadorian Chocó and southern Colombia, a region considered especially important for biodiversity conservation.
Why Historic Museum Collections Still Matter
The discovery highlights the continuing scientific importance of natural history collections. Specimens preserved for decades or even centuries can give researchers a way to revisit old classifications, compare physical traits, and resolve questions that earlier scientists could not answer.
In this case, combining 19th-century museum specimens with observations of living frog populations allowed researchers to determine that Pristimantis milpe deserved recognition as a distinct species.
The findings also underscore how much remains to be learned about biodiversity. Even common, widespread animals can conceal surprises, and solving those mysteries often depends on bringing historical collections together with modern research and observations.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Pensoft Publishers. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Santiago R. Ron, Poulette Paredes-Aguirre, Diego A. Paucar, Yaara López, Katherine Apunte, Jhael A. Ortega. Long overdue: a new, widespread, species of Pristimantis (Anura, Strabomantidae) from the Chocó region and the synonymy of Pristimantis subsigillatus. ZooKeys, 2026; 1286: 121 DOI: 10.3897/zookeys.1286.194383

Feature: Chinese opera "Xiju" captivates audience at 33rd Cairo int'l theatre festival
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
06:31:15 CST
07:31:15 KST

The Chinese opera "Liaozhai: Purple Tail" is staged at the 33rd Cairo International Festival for Experimental Theatre (CIFET) in Cairo, Egypt, Sept. 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Ahmed Gomaa)
by Mahmoud Fouly
CAIRO, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- With a spotlight on him, a Chinese actor slowly descended from the stage and made his way through the aisles of a packed Cairo theatre, delivering an anguished soliloquy amid warm applause.
It was one of several moments when performers of "Liaozhai: Purple Tail," an experimental Chinese Xiju production, moved beyond the stage and into the audience during their performance at the 33rd Cairo International Festival for Experimental Theatre (CIFET).
The Chinese production, presented by Wuxi Xiju Theatre, brought to life a story weaving together the human and supernatural worlds.
"For moments, we felt we had been transported from Cairo to China," Hamada Shousha, an Egyptian actor, director and theatre professor at Heliopolis University, told Xinhua.
"We did not just see and hear the story; we lived its atmosphere," he said, noting "the costumes, music and presentation all carried a distinctly Chinese character."
The play follows Qiao Sheng, a kind and honest scholar who unexpectedly saves a fox maiden. In gratitude, she gives him a magical fox tail capable of granting any wish. Armed with this power, Qiao Sheng gradually succumbs to his desires, exposing the darker side of human nature.
The play is adapted from Liaozhai, or Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio, a classic collection of Chinese ghost stories and supernatural folk tales written over a period of 40 years from the late 1600s to the early 1700s.
Though performed in Chinese, English, Arabic and Chinese surtitles were displayed on a monitor to the left of the stage, allowing Egyptian and international spectators to follow the story without diverting their attention from the action.
Hui Haifeng, who plays Qiao Sheng, said the response of the Egyptian audience had left a deep impression on him.
"Although we speak different languages, I could tell from their eyes, expressions and reactions that they were following the story attentively and were deeply immersed in it," Hui said.
"Art knows no borders, and neither does emotional communication," he said. "Language may present a barrier, but emotions are shared, and body language and stage expression can also communicate across cultures."
Founded in 1951, Wuxi Xiju Theatre has spent over seven decades preserving and developing xiju, a form of traditional Chinese opera, while taking its productions to audiences abroad.
Li Mengheng, a lead performer, said audiences could feel the story and its emotions through the stylized movements and body language of traditional Chinese opera even without prior familiarity with the form.
"I feel that Egyptian audiences understand the rhythm of our performance particularly well. They know when to applaud and when to give the performers some encouragement," Li said.
The Chinese play is one of 15 productions from 13 countries in the festival's official competition, including entries from Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Britain, Spain, Germany, and Russia, spanning dramatic and physical theatre, contemporary dance, puppetry, visual theatre and multimedia performances.
Sabine Liebherr from Germany described the production as "absolutely magical," saying it carried "something of a general truth about human existence."
"You have to be careful what you wish for," she said, referring to a theme of the play. "If your wish does not come from a good heart, the result can be disastrous."
She was also struck by the performers' movements. "The way they moved was so graceful -- they were almost floating."
Running from Sept. 1 to 8, this year's CIFET brings together Egyptian, Arab and international theatre practitioners for performances, workshops and discussions centered on experimentation and new approaches to theatrical expression.
For Malak Mahmoud, a fourth-year Chinese-language student at Cairo University, the performance offered a chance to experience Chinese culture firsthand rather than through a screen.
"The show was breathtaking. I could see how engaged the Egyptian spectators were, and I could hear people behind me reacting with surprise as they followed the performance," Mahmoud said.
"Through such performances, we can learn more about Chinese culture, the way people think and their beliefs," she added. ■
The Chinese opera "Liaozhai: Purple Tail" is staged at the 33rd Cairo International Festival for Experimental Theatre (CIFET) in Cairo, Egypt, Sept. 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Ahmed Gomaa)

Roundup: Gun violence tests Brussels security as drug trafficking fuels cycle of violence
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
06:30:55 CST
07:30:55 KST

BRUSSELS, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- Gun violence has surged again in Brussels, with six shootings reported over just four days in the Midi police zone in late August and poses a challenge to the security in the Belgian capital.
Brussels Chief Prosecutor Julien Moinil said at a press conference on Aug. 28 that the capital recorded 102 shootings in 2025 and another 69 in 2026 so far. Several recent incidents have been linked to conflicts between drug trafficking networks, while Interior Minister Bernard Quintin has described the situation as a "national emergency."
Moinil warned that the violence was no longer confined to criminal circles and that ordinary residents were increasingly at risk. "Any citizen can get shot," he said, citing the case of a father with no known links to criminal activity who was left paralyzed after being shot.
The latest wave included an attack on a police facility in the Midi police zone. Prosecutors have linked some of the recent violence to retaliation between two drug trafficking networks.
However, they said no link has yet been established between that conflict and the attack on the police facility. Moinil called the incident "a direct attack on the state."
Belgium's National Drugs Commissioner Ine Van Wymersch recently told Belgian media, citing an estimate by a Brussels police official, that a single street-level drug-dealing point can generate between 50,000 euros and 80,000 euros (about 58,000 to 93,000 U.S. dollars) a day for criminal groups.
She said rival groups once maintained relatively stable territories when cannabis dominated parts of the street drug market. As the more lucrative cocaine trade became more prominent, dealing points grew more profitable, increasing the incentive to fight for territory.
Prosecutors said criminal networks are increasingly recruiting young people as street-level operatives. Belgian media investigations have also found that some networks use social media and messaging platforms to recruit people for violent assignments.
Some gang leaders operate from abroad, while others remain capable of directing criminal activity from prison. Moinil cited a shooting case this summer in which a suspected organizer was in prison and used a smuggled mobile phone to communicate with people outside. He has called for tighter controls on prison communications, including mobile-phone signal jammers in areas housing organized crime figures.
The drug economy extends well beyond street dealers. Federal police investigations have uncovered networks involved in drug supply, storage, packaging and distribution.
Brussels prosecutors said about 203 million euros (235 million dollars) in criminal assets have been seized since the beginning of 2025, while hundreds of businesses linked to drug trafficking have been closed.
The gun violence has also renewed debate over the fragmented structure of policing in Brussels. The capital's 19 municipalities are currently divided among six local police zones. Following the latest shootings, Brussels mayors agreed to place anti-drug violence operations across the six zones under a single "Gold Commander."
Separately, legislation approved earlier this year provides for the six zones to be merged into a single Brussels police zone on Jan. 1, 2028. Local media reported that the Brussels region is also expected to appoint a regional commissioner for security and drugs within about 40 days.
The Brussels prosecutor's office currently has 49 prosecutors, compared with an authorized staffing level of 63. Moinil has called for around 10 million euros (11.6 million dollars) in additional resources, while stressing that judicial action alone cannot solve the problem and that prevention, public health and youth policy must also form part of the response.
Quintin and Justice Minister Annelies Verlinden outlined additional measures in parliament on Sept. 2. Quintin said authorities had "too often looked away" from drug-related violence in the past and that investigative tools must evolve as organized crime changes. He also acknowledged that there was "no miracle solution."
Earlier measures included deploying 40 additional federal police officers, installing 20 mobile cameras in drug-trafficking hotspots and strengthening coordination among police, prosecutors and municipal authorities.
On Aug. 28, more than 600 personnel, including over 450 police officers and at least 60 military personnel, took part in a large-scale operation. It marked the first time the military had joined this type of integrated security operation. Police detained dozens of people and seized weapons, drugs and cash.
Quintin said the operation was intended to send the message that Brussels' streets and metro stations belong to residents. He stressed that no single measure would be enough to dismantle organized crime linked to drug trafficking.
The latest shootings point to a criminal economy that goes beyond isolated incidents, linking local dealing points to wider networks, prison-based coordination and substantial illicit profits.
"Shootings may come and go in waves, but the drug trade behind them remains," Moinil said. Despite months of raids, seizures and reinforced patrols, the trade continues to sustain the conditions in which such violence can recur. ■

German company successfully launches rocket to space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
22:26:00 UTC
07:26:00 KST

German company successfully launches rocket to space
September 6, 2026
A Spectrum space rocket built by German company Isar Aerospace was launched into space from the Norwegian spaceport at Andoya.
"We're in orbit! And just made European history: This is the first time a privately developed rocket reached orbit from continental Europe," the company wrote on X.
"Germany has spaceflight capabilities," said the country's Ministry for Research, Technology and Space on X, praising a "milestone that impressively demonstrates our country's innovative strength and technical expertise".
This was the German company's second attempt to launch the Spectrum rocket into space. The first attempt, which took place 18 months ago, was unsuccessful.
What is Spectrum rocket?
The Spectrum rocket is designed for small and medium-sized payloads. It carried five smal satellites and an in-flight technological experiment, the company said.
According to Isar Aerospace, the launch was for "both the vehicle's qualification mission and its first flight carrying payload."
The move is believed to bring Europe closer to being able to offer satellite flights from its own territory. Several countries voiced interest in the growing market of commercial space missions, including Britain and Sweden.
In March, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the launch site of Isar, a Bavaria-based company, showing support for its efforts and for European autonomy at a time when the world order is changing under US President Donald Trump.
Isar is also working on the development of a second launch site, located in Canada.
The company said that while the US launched 198 rockets last year, Europe's tally was just eight. Isar's goal is to produce some 40 rockets a year.
Competition includes SpaceX
Although the rocket is not yet ready for mass production, Isar has already received orders through 2028.
The Spectrum rocket is intended to send both civilian and military satellites into low Earth orbit, meaning a few hundred kilometers above the Earth's surface.
The industry includes Elon Musk's SpaceX and ArianeGroup, a French joint venture between Airbus and Safran that operates a spaceport in French Guiana, located in South America.
For the sake of developing new rockets and extend its testing and launch infrastructure, Isar said last week it received €200 million ($232 million) from the European Space Agency (ESA).

Taylor crowns boxing career in stylish Croke Park triumph
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
23:22:47 BST
07:22:47 KST

Taylor crowns career in stylish Croke Park triumph
- Published
Katie Taylor ended her illustrious career as a three-time undisputed world champion as Croke Park gave one of Ireland's greatest sporting figures the grandest of farewells on a night of celebration, spectacle and music.
The 40-year-old outclassed unbeaten Flora Pili on points in front of 80,000 jubilant fans to add the vacant WBC belt to her WBA, WBO and IBF light-welterweight titles.
With the footwork, speed and sharp pressure fighting that defined her career, Taylor produced one final stylish performance against the overmatched Frenchwoman to win by scores of 100-90, 100-90 and 98-91.
Promoter Eddie Hearn paid tribute to Taylor, calling her "Ireland's greatest sportsperson", before she took one final lap of the ring, waving to the crowd before ceremonially placing her gloves and belts in the centre of the canvas.
After almost a quarter of a century in the sport, Taylor - an Olympic champion, two-weight world champion and one of the pioneers of women's professional boxing - finally got her fairytale ending at her dream venue.
She bows out with a record of 26 wins and just one defeat, but this was about more than one final result.
It was a night steeped in Irish pride, with a spine-tingling atmosphere and chart-topping pop group Westlife helping provide a fitting send-off.
Taylor in a world of her own in Dublin
On an unforgettable night for the city, around 80 per cent of those inside Croke Park had never previously attended a boxing event, but turned out to honour a fighter who dragged women's sport from the margins and took an entire nation on her journey.
The crowd was the sixth largest recorded post-war attendance for a boxing event anywhere in the world. By early evening, the stands were awash with green and white, tricolours draped over shoulders.
Westlife performed 'World of Our Own' and 'You Raise Me Up', with tens of thousands joining in as phone lights flickered around the towering tiers of Croke Park.
The atmosphere softened for an a cappella version of 'Grace', the well-known Irish ballad linked to the 1916 Easter Rising, before the national anthem rang out.
Chants of "Ole, Ole, Ole" drowned out Pili's ringwalk music before Taylor finally emerged to 'All Hail King Jesus', a nod to the faith she has spoken so openly about throughout her career.
She stretched her arms wide, sang along and tried to take in every second of her final walk to the ring. There was emotion on her face, but also the familiar focus as fireworks shot into the Dublin sky.
Taylor had spent fight week insisting there was still a job to do, but even for a fighter who had sold out Madison Square Garden and performed on some of boxing's grandest stages, it was hard to imagine her being untouched by a reception like this.
- 'One of the best' - boxing world reacts to Taylor's farewell win 
  - Published21 hours ago
- Taylor's 'dream ending to a dream career' 
  - Published15 hours ago
Taylor puts on a show in finale
After a quiet opener, Taylor - who turned professional in 2016 - burst into life in the second round, firing quick combinations before darting back out of range.
She repeatedly beat Pili to the punch, working in bursts and making the most of the two-minute rounds.
Pili, 29, arrived unbeaten in 12 contests and had previously held the European title. With little expectation on her shoulders, she had everything to gain.
But she had never faced anyone remotely close to Taylor's level and the gulf in class soon began to show.
The party atmosphere continued between rounds as it became increasingly clear there would be no gatecrashing from the Frenchwoman.
Former world champion Prince Naseem Hamed and UFC star Paddy Pimblett watched from ringside as Pili swung wildly in the fifth, only for Taylor to make her miss and fire back.
Pili enjoyed her best spell in the seventh, a quick flurry briefly snapping Taylor's head back, but it did little to alter the direction of the fight.
Croke Park rose for the final two minutes as Taylor continued to press forward, letting her hands go while the noise poured down from the stands.
She embraced her mother, trainer and manager in the ring as 'Celebration' rang around Croke Park before the inevitable result was read out.
"Let me just look around for a second", she said afterwards, soaking up every ounce of the reception.
'The greatest Irish sportsperson of all time'
Taylor has been unequivocal that Croke Park would be the end and she walks away having beaten every opponent she faced as a professional.
Her only defeat came against Chantelle Cameron in Dublin in 2023. Six months later, Taylor returned to the 3Arena and avenged it to become undisputed champion in a second weight division.
After the final bell, she paid tribute to her family and somehow held the tears back as she spoke to the crowd.
"There's nothing like an Irish mammy," she said, smiling as she thanked those closest to her.
For a fighter who has never hidden her dislike of media interviews, there was something striking about the confidence with which she walked around the ring, microphone in hand, soaking up the final moments.
"We did it. We brought boxing back to Croke Park. You were with me in London 2012, you were with me with the heartbreak of Rio. You stayed with me when I turned pro," Taylor said.
"I don't know any other country that would sell 80,000 tickets for a female athlete. I'm convinced Ireland is the only country."
Taylor will forever be defined by her trilogy wins against Amanda Serrano and leaves with a staggering list of accolades, but her true impact cannot be measured in statistics alone.
That legacy belongs to the young girl who once pretended to be a boy just to box when girls were not allowed.
She fought tirelessly to get the sport sanctioned in Ireland and included in the Olympics, before going on to conquer both the amateur and professional codes.
The belts will eventually gather dust, but the trail Taylor blazed across the sport will never fade.

Norway has seen an outpouring of grief for the much-loved late monarch, who died on 28 August at the age of 89.
Harald has been hailed as an inclusive “people’s king” who modernised the Norwegian monarchy during his 35-year reign.
His funeral will take place on 9 September at Oslo Cathedral, with mourners including his widow, Sonja, now the queen mother.
In keeping with precedent that the sovereign does not attend funerals of other heads of state, the duty falls to William, a future king, to represent his father and pay his respects at the service.
Charles paid a touching tribute to his “dear cousin” and “much-loved kinsman and friend” after the news of Harald’s death was announced.
In a message of condolence, he praised Harald’s “unwavering dedication” and his “kindness, compassion and deep sense of duty echoed from across the sea and across the decades”.
The late Queen Elizabeth II and King Harald were second cousins. They shared the same great-grandparents, King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra.
In April last year, William represented his father at the funeral of Pope Francis in the Vatican.
William and the now Princess of Wales carried out an official tour to Norway in 2018, dining with King Harald and Queen Sonja at the Royal Palace, where Harald described them as “family” and praised their support of the then Queen.
The Norwegian sovereign processed into the banquet arm in arm with the pregnant Catherine, who was expecting Prince Louis and wearing a flowing Alexander McQueen gown, with the gesture mirrored by Sonja and William who walked behind them.
William and Kate also spent time visiting the ski slopes with the then Crown Prince Haakon and Crown Princess Mette-Marit, now the King and Queen.
