US Envoys Head To Kyiv After  Stop In Moscow, Late-Night Meeting With Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
22:03:14 UTC
07:03:14 KST

KYIV -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called for resumption of trilateral negotiations between the United States and Russia as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner concluded talks in Kyiv and Moscow, including with Russian leader Vladimir Putin, as part of efforts to end the conflict, now in its fifth year.
Both Zelenskyy and Witkoff described the September 6 talks as "substantial," with the Ukrainian president telling reporters that, among other things, the sides discussed security and economic guarantees for Kyiv, supplies of urgently needed air-defense missiles, as well as a support package for Ukraine, as another wartime winter looms.
At the same time, Witkoff stressed that the United States was seeking a diplomatic resolution to the conflict rather than a kinetic one, while Kushner supported the idea of renewing trilateral negotiations between Kyiv, Moscow, and Washington.
"It's going to take both sides to make some compromises and narrow the issues between them and we think we have the ingredients to get to that place," Witkoff said. "It is very difficult but we are committed."
Separately, as the Kyiv talks were unfolding, Zelenskyy wrote on his Telegram page that representatives of Britain, France, and Germany had also joined the discussions.
Zelenskyy offered some guarded remarks following the talks, suggesting no immediate breakthrough.
"We had three rounds of talks today. All of them were very substantive," he wrote on social media as Ukrainian officials told reporters that Zelenskyy, Witkoff, and Kushner met again following the formal sessions.
"We hope we will have the opportunity to reach an agreement with our American partners, and we hope for the support of our European partners."
"If the war continues in the winter, we are very much counting on the winter [aid] package, which I discussed in detail with Steve, Jared, and our European partners today."
Zelenskyy said Ukraine is "counting on support for both air defense and energy, and for a serious volume and possibilities of using American [liquid natural gas]."
A year ago, Ukraine suffered through a brutal winter as Russia targeted the country's energy infrastructure, leaving hundreds of thousands of residents without heating.
The US envoys arrived in Kyiv by train from Poland hours after they held a three-hour meeting with Putin in Moscow late on September 5. Russian state news agency RIA Novosti quoted Putin as saying the three men would have to address a "difficult situation" during their Kremlin discussions.
A White House official told RFE/RL that "the two sides discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks" and that the envoys "look forward to equally productive meetings" in Ukraine.
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, who participated in the session, called the talks "substantive, very frank, and constructive." He added that the envoys stated the US position and promised to present Putin's views to Ukrainian leaders during their talks in Kyiv.
"They not only expressed their traditional interest in bringing the hostilities to a quick end, they put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement," he said.
Ushakov insisted Russia would achieve its goals and that the "root causes" of the conflict must be resolved, Kremlin code for putting an end to Ukraine's hopes of NATO membership and steps to effectively disarm the Ukrainian military, among other historical grievances -- items Kyiv has long rejected.
Even as the diplomatic push continued, Russian forces launched another large-scale drone attack on Ukraine overnight into September 6.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 108 drones, including Shahed attack drones and jet-powered variants. It said air defenses had shot down or suppressed 88 drones by 9:30 a.m., while strikes were recorded at 11 locations and falling debris at seven.
Ukraine, meanwhile, said its forces had struck a number of targets inside Russia overnight, including the Ryazan oil refinery and a military airfield in the Rostov region.
Ukraine's General Staff said on September 6 that a fire was recorded at the Ryazan refinery, one of Russia's largest, and that the facility was involved in supplying the Russian military. It also said Ukrainian forces struck a radar station and two Pantsir-S1 air-defense systems in the Rostov region.
RFE/RL could not independently verify the claims.
Russian officials acknowledged drone attacks and fires but did not confirm that the facilities identified by Ukraine had been hit. Ryazan regional Governor Pavel Malkov reported a fire at "one of the enterprises," while Rostov Governor Yury Slyusar said around 30 drones had been destroyed and three people were injured.
The latest attack on Ukraine followed a day of Russian strikes across the country that killed seven people and left 57 others injured or otherwise affected in five regions, according to regional military administrations. Four of those killed were in the Kharkiv region, including an 11-year-old boy.
As the United States pressed ahead with its latest effort to end the war, President Donald Trump had said his envoys would be presenting a peace deal to the Russians and then would relay the offer to Ukraine the next day.
Trump said Washington had "an idea for peace" and that his envoys were "bringing with them a proposal to end the war," now in its fifth year since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"I sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done, and there may be a good chance that we'll do it," Trump told reporters on September 4.
'Diplomatic Activities'
The US envoys' visit to Kyiv marks their first visit to Ukraine since taking leading roles in the administration's efforts to end the war and comes amid a renewed diplomatic push aimed at reaching a peace agreement.
Trump made ending the largest war in Europe since 1945 a priority when he took office in January 2025, but an agreement has been elusive, and diplomacy had been largely stalled since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran in late February.
Putin has shown no sign of compromise in recent comments, among other things insisting that Russia must control all of eastern Ukraine's Donetsk region, including the parts its forces have failed to capture in years of heavy fighting.
At a joint news conference with US envoys in Kyiv following their talks on September 6, Zelenskyy called the issue of the Donetsk region "the question of this war," suggesting it remains one of the central obstacles to a diplomatic resolution of the conflict.

Massive review confirms the connection between emotional intelligence and human flourishing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
22:00:05 UTC
07:00:05 KST

A review of psychological research indicates that emotional intelligence has a robust and reliable connection to human flourishing, predicting success across school, work, and personal health. The findings suggest that people with higher emotional intelligence tend to experience greater well-being, though the strength of this connection depends on how the traits are measured. The research was recently published in the journal PNAS.
For decades, psychologists have debated what makes some people thrive while others struggle. One popular idea is emotional intelligence, a concept that rapidly gained public attention in the 1990s. Broadly speaking, the term refers to how well a person navigates their own feelings and the feelings of others.
Since its introduction, the idea has spawned thousands of academic papers and grown into a multibillion-dollar training industry. Yet, because researchers define and measure this concept in various ways, its exact relationship with life success has remained difficult to synthesize.
Psychologists generally divide emotional intelligence into three categories. The first is an ability-based model. This model treats emotional skills like a cognitive test, assuming there are objectively right and wrong answers when identifying or managing emotions.
The ability model specifically looks at how well people recognize emotions, use them to guide decisions, and regulate them. The second category is a trait-based model, which relies on self-reported personality characteristics. Under this model, researchers ask participants to rate their own adaptability, assertiveness, and impulse control.
A third category, called a mixed model, combines both objective abilities and self-reported traits into a single assessment. Beyond the differing definitions of emotional intelligence, researchers also look at a wide variety of life outcomes. To find out how these different models connect to positive life experiences, researchers Tyler J. Robinson and Ethan Zell from the University of North Carolina at Greensboro analyzed decades of data.
The researchers wanted to see if emotional intelligence consistently relates to human flourishing. Flourishing is a broad psychological term encompassing mental health, physical health, psychological adjustment, and workplace success. To answer this question, Robinson and Zell conducted a second-order meta-analysis.
A standard meta-analysis is a statistical technique that pools the results of many individual studies to find an overall trend. A second-order meta-analysis goes a step further, combining the results of multiple previous meta-analyses. This approach acts as a quantitative summary of previous summaries, providing a broad view of an entire scientific field.
By pooling data from 62 previous meta-analyses, the researchers gathered information from more than 3,000 individual studies. This massive sample included over one million participants, allowing the researchers to look for overarching patterns across different ages and cultures. The data included populations from Western nations, non-Western nations, children, adolescents, and adults.
The researchers found a reliable, positive association between overall emotional intelligence and human flourishing. This positive link appeared across 77 unique life outcomes. The most prominent associations emerged in areas like workplace leadership, job performance, and psychological adjustment.
The data showed that emotional intelligence was linked to better outcomes regardless of the participants’ age group or geographic region. When looking at different categories of life outcomes, the researchers noticed slight variations in the strength of the connection. Emotional intelligence was most strongly related to success in the workplace.
The connection was slightly weaker, though still reliably present, for cognitive abilities and general academic performance. The researchers also found strong associations between emotional intelligence and specific outcomes like lower rates of job burnout, higher subjective well-being, and better romantic relationship satisfaction.
To put these findings into perspective, the researchers compared emotional intelligence to the Big Five personality traits. The Big Five is a well-established psychological framework that measures openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism. The analysis revealed that emotional intelligence is just as strongly, if not more strongly, associated with human flourishing than any of the Big Five personality traits.
Out of all the specific outcomes analyzed, only one showed a negative relationship with emotional intelligence. That outcome was a form of self-centeredness known as nonpathological narcissism. The researchers noted that individuals with this specific type of narcissism tend to artificially inflate their own scores on self-report questionnaires.
Because they overrate their own emotional abilities, the data showed an inverse relationship between their actual traits and their reported emotional intelligence. More conventional, pathological narcissism was linked to lower emotional intelligence. Measurement styles heavily altered the broader results as well.
The association with human flourishing was most pronounced when researchers used the mixed or trait-based models, which rely on participants rating their own emotional skills. When studies used objective performance tests to measure emotional abilities, the association with life outcomes was weaker. This pattern became especially apparent when looking at how both emotional intelligence and life outcomes were measured.
The researchers found the strongest connections when both variables were assessed using self-report questionnaires. When one variable was measured subjectively and the other was measured objectively, the relationship between the two shrunk considerably. This dependence on measurement methods highlights an important limitation in the data.
When participants fill out multiple surveys about themselves, they may naturally rate themselves positively across the board. This shared method of data collection can artificially inflate the statistical connection between self-reported emotional intelligence and self-reported life satisfaction. The researchers noted that the particularly strong link to workplace outcomes might be partly driven by this shared measurement style, as many workplace studies rely on self-reported surveys.
Because the data in this review is entirely correlational, it cannot prove that high emotional intelligence causes a person to flourish. It is entirely possible that flourishing in life makes a person more emotionally intelligent over time. Alternatively, a third unmeasured factor, such as a stable upbringing or access to resources, could independently contribute to both higher emotional intelligence and greater life success.
The researchers also excluded studies that evaluated training programs. Because of this exclusion, they could not determine if actively training emotional intelligence causes a subsequent increase in human flourishing. Objective tests of emotional intelligence also face modern challenges.
The authors pointed out that recent studies show artificial intelligence language models perform just as well as, or better than, humans on objective emotional intelligence tests. This raises questions about what these tests are actually measuring. It remains debated whether text-based tests capture practical emotional skills or if they simply measure a person’s reading comprehension and ability to understand written scenarios.
To improve the quality of future research, the authors suggest refining how emotional intelligence is categorized. They recommend moving away from the mixed model, which blends traits and abilities in a way that creates conceptual confusion. Instead, they suggest that future studies explicitly separate objective emotional abilities from self-reported personality traits. Separating these variables would help scientists determine exactly how distinct emotional skills contribute to a fulfilling life.
The study, “Robust associations of emotional intelligence with human flourishing: A second-order meta-analysis,” was authored by Tyler J. Robinson and Ethan Zell.

When we act from compassion, we do what is needed to make our own lives and the lives of the people…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:46:43 UTC
06:46:43 KST

When we act from compassion, we do what is needed to make our own lives and the lives of the people around us better. By meeting the needs of ourselves and others, we eliminate suffering and we create joy. We meet needs directly and also indirectly, by helping others towards the awareness they need to overcome their suffering.
It might then seem like compassion is concerned only with improving individual lives. But it is by creating change in individuals that compassion also creates collective change. For a person who is aware does not restrict their compassion to specific others. Genuine compassion is never limited only to our own family, friends, or neighbours. It is always action to meet needs and eliminate suffering for all living beings.
It is precisely when we are most free of our self-produced suffering that we are also most able to see that systemic changes are needed and necessary. We can then see how the suffering of individuals and their automatic reactions to that suffering combine to produce social and economic forces that perpetuate suffering for all of us.

With bare hands, lone warrior cleans up dumpyard of a river
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:45:40 UTC
06:45:40 KST

21-year-old BSc student has been a solitary warrior against civic mess and pollution in his hometown
BHOPAL: His online followers know him as 'Bittu Tabahi'. In reality, Surendra Singh Choudhary is the exact opposite of what the moniker 'Tabahi', meaning destruction, implies.For the past seven months, this 21-year-old BSc student has been a solitary warrior against civic mess and pollution in his hometown, Biaora in MP's Rajgarh district, picking up plastic bottles, tangled weeds and other solid waste from Ajnar river, which had virtually become a dumpyard.With no heavy machinery or protective gear at his disposal, he removed the garbage with his bare hands, often at great risk to his health.
Bittu's dogged pursuit has helped restore a section of the river, earning him widespread praise across the country and an invite from CM Mohan Yadav Saturday. They had a warm exchange at the CM's residence in Bhopal, where Yadav assured Bittu of every possible support from govt.The chief minister also shared a video on X, calling Bittu a "son of Biaora" who not only restored Ajnala (the river stretch passing through Biaora) to its original form through sheer resolve and effort, but also sent out a larger message that one man's determination is all it takes to bring meaningful change.
There were also reports that the CEO of an organisation from the Netherlands had offered him a job, but Bittu said he had only heard this from media reports. "I am yet to receive any information about it first hand," he told TOI.Encouraged by his success, Bittu, whose parents work in the health department, has decided to expand his work. "My sole objective is to keep my hometown clean. I have decided to take my work to other public places," he said.Bittu started his mission on Republic Day this year. Upset that everyone complained about the mess, but none - including the municipal administration - addressed it, the college-goer decided to get his hands dirty. From removing garbage piles on streets to pulling out weeds from water bodies, his activism eventually drew national attention.
Unfortunately, his selfless service is being undone by the same people he is trying to help. In his interaction with the chief minister, Bittu shared the pain of watching people throw garbage into the river again, oblivious to the effort that went into cleaning it. "I don't know why people keep dumping waste into the river," he said, his voice betraying anger.The silver lining is that the local municipal corporation has now woken up to its civic mandate, and has deployed JCBs and Poclain machines to clear waste piles from the streets. However, the larger problem - habitual littering and a lack of collective ownership - remains unaddressed.

Putin praises Moscow’s role in supporting troops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:45:19 UTC
06:45:19 KST

Putin praises Moscow’s role in supporting troops
Russian President Vladimir Putin has praised Moscow’s contribution to the country’s military and technological development, declaring that Russia will overcome the challenges it faces because they are “temporary and transient.”
The president made the remarks during an address marking Moscow’s 879th birthday; the city celebrates the anniversary of its founding every year in in early September. Putin lauded residents of the capital and the rest of the nation’s citizens, describing Moscow as a symbol of Russian statehood, unity and resilience.
“Together with all citizens of our country, we will overcome any difficulty and any challenge. They are temporary and transient, while Moscow and Russia are eternal,” Putin said.
He drew parallels between the challenges facing the country today and key episodes in its history, including the 1812 French invasion and the Battle of Moscow against Nazi Germany in 1941.
“Today, the capital, together with the entire country, has mobilized all its forces, like 85 years ago, for the sake of a common, rightful cause. Tens of thousands of Muscovites are fighting against the neo-Nazis on the line of engagement, advancing and displaying valor, courage and heroism.”
Putin highlighted Moscow’s contribution to Russia’s military-industrial sector, saying more than 450 defense plants, high-tech enterprises and companies in the capital are producing goods for the needs of the armed forces.
Moscow hospitals are also playing a major role in treating and rehabilitating wounded servicemen, Putin said, while specialists from the capital are involved in reconstruction efforts in Donbass.

More voters identifying as Democrats and not calling themselves Republican
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:44:19 UTC
06:44:19 KST

More voters are identifying as Democrats and shying away from calling themselves Republican, according to the latest quarterly data published by Gallup.
Some 49% of voters surveyed leaned Democrat, including independent voters asked to pick one party or the other. Only 39% of respondents leaned Republican.
That 10-point spread marks a sharp reversal from the four-point advantage that Republicans held over Democrats in the fourth quarter of 2024, when voters sent Donald Trump back to the White House and Republicans swept both houses of Congress. Democrats are seeing their most sizable advantage since 2008, when Barack Obama was elected president, according to the New York Times.
The data offers the latest evidence that Trump’s second term has proved unpopular with voters, driving a potential backlash.
Trump’s approval rating stood at 52% at the time of his second inauguration in January of 2025, according to an average of polls published by the New York Times.
But his popularity dwindled immediately, as he cleaved the federal workforce, imposed price-inflating tariffs, passed a profligate spending bill and launched a rudderless war with Iran. Some 58% of voters now disapprove of his performance, with only 38% approving, according to the Times.
Democrats are hoping to take advantage of Trump’s tanking popularity. Liberals are likely to retake the US House of Representatives in midterm elections this November. The party is much less certain to retake the US Senate, though polling is giving Democrats reasons to feel optimistic.
A growing share of American voters have not identified with either party in recent years. Back in 2002, roughly a third of voters surveyed by Gallup identified as either Republican, Democrat or independent. By last year, 45% of respondents called themselves independents, with only 27% identifying as either Democrat or Republican.

Thousands at Jaguar Land Rover to be offered redundancies after falling profits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:42:11 UTC
06:42:11 KST

Thousands of workers at Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) will be offered redundancies after Britain’s largest car manufacturer had its revenues slashed by falling sales, a cyber-attack and Donald Trump’s tariffs.
JLR informed workers and their union on Saturday that the company would be opening a voluntary redundancy programme for salaried and management team members, the BBC and Sunday Times reported.
As many as 4,000 jobs would be cut over two years, the Times reported. JLR told the BBC it was yet to confirm the number but the company, which is owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata Motors, needed to save about £1.7bn over the next two years.
Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, told the BBC she and the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, would meet JLR’s chief executive, PB Balaji, next week, after a weekend of intensive talks to mitigate job losses.
About 30,000 of the company’s 44,000 employees are based in the UK. Most of them work at 14 plants across the West Midlands, where the company is one of the region’s largest employers.
The job cuts will be unwelcome news for the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who has pledged to “safeguard sovereign manufacturing” and reindustrialise Britain.
Under his predecessor, Keir Starmer, Labour said it would underwrite a £1.5bn loan guarantee to JLR after it halted production for several weeks last year in response to a cyber-attack.
The attack led to a 27% drop in overall production and cost the company about £200m. It was one of several factors contributing to JLR posting a profit before tax of just £14m – down from £2.5bn the year before.
Tariffs on vehicles imported into the US – which Trump raised to 25% before agreeing a deal for 10% for the UK – also caused turmoil for the carmaker, which is attempting to push more luxury cars to the US market. This contributed to the company’s retail and wholesale volumes – sales via dealerships – falling by about 70,000 and 90,000 respectively.
“These challenges arrived with the global automotive industry already under continued pressure from cost inflation, slower-than-expected uptake of electric vehicles, and the deterioration of market conditions in China,” Balaji said in the company’s annual report published in May.
The carmaker this week launched its first electric Range Rover in an effort to appeal to climate-conscious fans of the luxury SUV – at a starting price of £154,070.

Aadhaar for rest, but babus resist link for CGHS
Unknown

Govt has issued office memoranda making Aadhaar linking mandatory several times
Over 3,100 DBT schemes and 360 public services use Aadhaar-based authentication. Yet the bureaucracy that demands Aadhaar from citizens, often the poorest, has resisted linking their own Central Govt Health Scheme cards to Aadhaar.CGHS beneficiaries include serving and retired central govt employees and family members, sitting and former MPs, sitting and retired judges of SC and HCs, accredited journalists in DelhiAadhaar linking "has helped state ensure targeted, transparent and leak-proof delivery while eliminating duplicate and ineligible beneficiaries," said PIB. However, bureaucrats aren't walking the talk.What’s must for poor is voluntary for babusThere is no annual verification to weed out dead pensioners or their dependents who might have become ineligible. Two other central govt health schemes, the Ex-Servicemen Contributory Health Scheme and the railway health scheme, have made it mandatory to link Aadhaar.Govt has issued office memoranda making Aadhaar linking mandatory several times starting from June 2015, but has had to withdraw it in the face of stiff resistance from its employees.The last such withdrawal happened in July 2024 when the govt was forced to keep the directive to link CGHS beneficiary ID with Ayushman Bharat Health account ID (ABHA ID), created using Aadhaar, “in abeyance till further orders”.
The linkage has since been made voluntary for central govt employees, though it is mandatory for a poor woman to get Rs 300 as daily wage under the employment guarantee scheme.While Aadhaar has been mandated for “welfare schemes funded from the Consolidated Fund of India”, including many DBT sche-mes, babus have been arguing that CGHS is a contributory scheme and not a DBT scheme, despite 90% of spending on the scheme coming from the Consolidated Fund of India. Their contributions amount to a tiny part of the annual expenditure on the scheme.CGHS incidentally has a higher per capita expenditure when compared to ECHS and the railway health scheme. It would be even higher if deceased beneficiaries and ineligible dependents were weeded out. Pensioner cards made at the start of computerisation of CGHS in 2005 remain active in the system without any checks increasing the chances of fraud and misuse of such cards.

Border rail exchanges proceeding uninterruptedly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:13:00 UTC
06:13:00 KST

Border rail exchanges proceeding uninterruptedly
TEHRAN- The Director General of Foreign Trade at the Islamic Republic of Iran Railways, emphasizing the normal and growing flow of exchanges across all 13 railway border crossings, has denied rumors about the suspension of transit operations and announced plans to double transit capacity at northeastern borders and develop ports connected to the rail network.
According to IRNA, Shahriyar Naghizadeh, in an interview on Saturday, highlighted the key role of the national rail network in connecting international routes and stressed the growing trend of exchanges while dismissing any ambiguity regarding the flow of goods at rail borders.
Explaining Iran's geographical position, he said: "The national rail network in the northeast connects to Turkmenistan's rail network through the Sarakhs and Incheh Borun borders. Turkmenistan, as a vital connecting link, connects us to the CIS member states of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization along the East-West Corridor (from China to Europe), as well as on the North-South Corridor (from Russia and Kazakhstan to Iran)."
Naghizadeh added: "Due to this feature, rail connectivity and border exchanges with Turkmenistan hold special and strategic importance for the country's economy."
Responding to some reports circulating on social media, the Director General stated: "It is natural that adversaries seek to produce fake news to inflame the atmosphere, but it must be understood that the railway serves peace, the environment, and the country's industrial development."
He emphasized: "Contrary to rumors aimed at creating black markets and disrupting the supply chain, the normal flow of goods is proceeding without any issues across all 13 rail borders, including Sarakhs and Incheh Borun. The exchange trend at these borders has not only not stopped but has experienced significant growth compared to last year."
Naghizadeh, referring to the need to upgrade service levels, said: "With increasing international demand, we are obliged to develop the logistical capacities of border stations—including loading, unloading, rail lines, and hardware facilities—so that goods enter the country swiftly and safely without delays at borders. We have very close cooperation with the Customs Administration of Iran in this regard."
He continued: "According to Articles 57 and 58 of the Seventh Development Plan, the railway's obligations to achieve target transit volumes have been specified. By developing the Sarakhs and Incheh Borun stations, which currently handle approximately 5 million tons combined, we have targeted increasing this figure to over 10 million tons."
Regarding alternative routes, the Director General said: "To diversify the supply chain for essential and industrial goods, new combined routes have been planned and implemented. Our cooperation with Kazakhstan—the gateway to China's rail network—has grown several-fold. Currently, we have increased from 7 trains annually to 3 trains monthly on the China-Iran route, indicating very high demand and the great potential of our rail network."
Referring to maritime capacities, he added: "On the Caspian Sea coast, we are connected to the national rail network at the ports of Amirabad and Caspian, and the performance of these ports has multiplied compared to last year. Given developments on the southern coasts, we are expanding the capacities of northern ports to strengthen connectivity to Russia and the North-South Corridor."
The railway official emphasized: "Utilizing 15,000 kilometers of rail network and 35,000 freight wagons, our goal is the economical, safe, and rapid movement of goods from entry points to other destinations and countries."

American Evolution
America’s political maps are shifting. So is who can win
The weight of a new era is pressing in. The second Trump presidency is unfolding against the backdrop of escalating political tensions, geoeconomic disruption and shifting demographics. Can the US adapt quickly enough? ST’s US bureau chief Bhagyashree Garekar reports as America celebrates its 250th anniversary in 2026.
- America's racial history still affects politics today, seen in towns like Vidor and ongoing tensions over voting rights and racial representation.
- Recent Supreme Court rulings have accelerated redistricting efforts that reduce black-majority districts, threatening black political representation in Congress.
- Despite challenges, black political ambition grows, with record numbers running for governor and efforts to build cross-racial coalitions to influence future electoral maps.
AI generated
VIDOR, Texas – A 10-minute detour to get to a cheaper hotel on a drive from Houston to Philadelphia led me to a “sundown town”.
That may evoke sunsets and beaches in a resort town. But that illusion was quickly dispelled. This label had overtones of menace, I soon discovered.
Waiting at the front desk to get the room keys, I asked what I thought was a casual question – what’s this place like?
The young receptionist, with hair swept up in a blonde ponytail, went quiet. “Well, it doesn’t have the best history for black and brown people,” she said after a beat.
“They say it was a sundown town. But I’ve been here for two years, and it’s all fine now,” she added quickly. “It has a reputation – I don’t know that it’s deserved.”
That was my abrupt introduction to Vidor, tagged for decades as the “most hate-filled town in Texas”. Curious to learn more, I googled local news. Only a few crime reports turned up, none too recent. And nothing leapt out during a late evening drive around the town, just modest low-rise houses, small shops and fast food restaurants.
A “sundown” sign that bluntly warned “whites only within city limits after dark” was reportedly removed from Vidor only some time in the 1970s or the 1980s. In scattered mentions on social media, some black motorists say they grew up being told to avoid Vidor and that, even now, they would not consider stopping there for a bite to eat or to refuel.
A database maintained by an educational site hosted by Tougaloo College, a historically black institution in Mississippi, says sundown towns numbered in the thousands and were found across the US from the late 19th century to the mid-20th century.
It’s not just the blacks who were kept out. Jews, Hispanics, Native Americans, Mormons and Asian Americans were also unwelcome in that era. The “Delta Chinese”, recruited to work on cotton plantations in Mississippi, suffered decades of segregation.
Vidor residents and officials claim things are vastly different now. They say it’s unfair to tarnish the town in 2026. The last bit of substantial nastiness was in the early 1990s over a federal judge’s order to desegregate the city’s public housing. In response, four black families moved in but eventually left after facing sustained hostilities from the white supremacist organisation, the Ku Klux Klan.
In 2020, at the height of the Black Lives Matter movement, a rally in the town drew a supportive crowd, mostly white. Some counter-protesters also showed up, with loaded guns and confederate flags, a controversial symbol of southern pride and also slavery. They shouted that it was the black rights movement that was racist because all lives mattered. A vivid account of that rally won The Economist a Pulitzer Prize in 2021.
The town, which wears a dour look, as though trying without success to surmount its past, remains nearly all-white today. Blacks count for a mere 0.3 per cent of residents. Its population peaked at 11,800 in 1980 and has been shrinking since.
Vidor may be the outlier, but in travels through several southern states – Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Tennessee – I saw evidence of America’s racial past still tailgating its present.
In a country where 14 per cent of the population is black, the second-biggest racial or ethnic minority after the Hispanics, the upcoming midterm elections have become more than the usual face-off between the Republicans and the Democrats.
Bigger and more basic questions appear to be on the ballot in the 250th year of American independence: who can vote, whose votes can make a difference, who actually belongs.
There is no official nationwide count yet of the black candidates running for Congress in 2026. And a few states are still to hold their primary nominating contests. But in 2025, 67 black lawmakers took the oath at Capitol Hill. Mostly Democrats, they were the largest black delegation in American history.
That progress – a fourfold increase from the figure in 1975 – mostly came from states redrawing congressional maps over the decades to create black-majority districts that could elect black candidates.
Those hard-won gains could be reversed in a matter of months, in a coordinated and wide-ranging exercise that has the power of the US Supreme Court behind it.
Analysts expect the Nov 3 midterm elections to produce the largest-ever decline in black representation in Congress after a number of states recently redrew their maps to eliminate black-majority districts.
The road from Selma
For miles on end, there were only a few cars on a scenic drive in late March from Selma to Montgomery, two of the most storied cities in the black civil rights movement.
Both lie on the muddy-brown Alabama River, connected by a bridge named after a 19th century Ku Klux Klan leader. One of the cities challenged where black Americans could sit and the other whether they could vote and wield political power.
Alabama’s capital, Montgomery, known for its white neoclassical buildings with columns, symmetrical facades and broad steps, looked ceremonial but forlorn. Its downtown yields layers of history but has suffered destructive tornadoes over the years, and some streets were closed for repairs. Gang fights and gun violence have been on the rise.
A plaque marks the spot where Rosa Parks boarded a public bus and refused to yield her seat for a white passenger, her rebellion sparking a mass protest that forced the authorities to end segregation on the city’s buses in 1956. It also brought to the national stage a dapper 26-year-old pastor of the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church.
A schoolchild skipping on the pavement could not direct me to the church where Martin Luther King Jr preached, although she knew “he did something good for us”.
The dainty red brick church was a short walk away, well preserved but silent on a cloudy, weekday morning. In 2025, thousands arrived here to commemorate the 60th anniversary of the “Bloody Sunday” march King led from Selma to Montgomery to demand voting rights for blacks.
Black residents made up half of Selma’s population then, but only 2 per cent were registered to vote. Although they had the constitutional guarantees, they were denied registration through poll taxes, literacy tests and threats of violence.
The 600 marchers protesting against the injustice were stopped and attacked as they crossed a small, grey bridge bearing the name of Edmund Pettus, a lawyer, brigadier-general, US senator and the Grand Dragon of the Alabama Ku Klux Klan. Shocking images of the event, on the front pages of newspapers and relayed on TV, built national support for the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
Cut to today and President Donald Trump’s repeated calls for Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which he insists is necessary to prevent non-citizens from voting fraudulently in elections, touches a raw nerve here.
The Act, which has stalled in Congress, includes measures that will require voters to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote and a photo ID when they turn up at the ballot booth.
The White House has called these “commonsense election integrity measures that are strongly supported by the vast majority of Americans.” But in Selma, Montgomery and the wider civil rights community, distrust is rife.
“Of course, no one wants non-Americans to vote illegally. But is that really a big problem? The administration has provided no proof,” said Al Adams, a retired city worker in Montgomery.
“What we do know is that what Trump wants will create a burden that will fall unevenly on our community,” he said.
“Not everyone has their original birth certificates, name discrepancies on documents are very common, people cannot or will not make a trip in person to an election office to register (to vote). It is especially hard on the elderly, the disabled and folks in rural areas.
“Given our history, you will have to forgive us for concluding that the new rules will reduce black power. And, perhaps, that is the intention,” he said.
Cracking and packing the black vote
Anger runs even deeper against Trump’s push for redistricting in Republican-ruled states to limit losses in the looming midterm election, which almost always punishes the party of the White House incumbent.
The redrawing of state maps to maximise electoral advantage is hardly a new tactic. Nor is it illegal; the exercise does not deny anyone a vote. But it does impact who gets elected by laying down how voters are grouped into districts.
It affects black voters unusually directly, especially in the South, where they are geographically concentrated. As a group, they tend to support Democratic candidates at higher rates than the white majority.
Republicans argue that while they’re engaging in partisan gerrymandering to win elections, there is no racial intent. Voting rights advocates, however, say they are dismantling black-majority districts that have voted for black Democrats in the past.
But where race and party correlate, the distinction is hard to make.
Two map-drawing tactics are used to weaken a group’s electoral influence. One technique is “cracking”, or splitting a cluster of black communities across several majority-white districts, thus reducing the collective power of black voters.
The other is “packing” black voters into fewer districts, thus producing one safe black seat while reducing their influence in adjacent seats.
A Supreme Court decision in April 2026, which held that maps which consciously used race to create black-majority districts violated equal protections accorded to non-minority groups, was a catalyst. It sped up the process initiated by Texas and other red states in 2025 to improve the odds of retaining the US House of Representatives, where the Republican Party holds a narrow 219-212 majority, with four remaining seats vacant due to death or resignations.
By late August, at least 10 states, nine of them Republican, had carried out redistricting in ways that dilute the black voting power.
- In Louisiana, which is roughly one-third black, there were two majority-black districts in the 2024 elections. One of them was eliminated by carving out the black neighbourhoods in the cities of Baton Rouge and Shreveport and merging them with more white and Republican districts.
- In Alabama, two black-majority cities, Montgomery and Mobile, which were reliably Democratic, are now part of districts that are majority-white and pro-Republican.
- In Tennessee, Republican lawmakers dismantled the state’s only majority-black district, the 9th District, which was 62 per cent black and concentrated around Memphis. It was split into three rural, mostly white districts that are Republican footholds.
- In North Carolina, the district with the state’s highest black population (42 per cent) was merged into nearby solidly Republican areas in a way that left it less black (34 per cent).
- In Florida’s new map, four Democratic incumbents now reside in heavily Republican-leaning districts.
- Texas’ redistricting resulted in reduced black representation in the Houston and Dallas area districts.
But, in a curious juxtaposition, black political ambition is also scaling new heights just as electoral maps that produced black representation are being redrawn.
At the state level, the story is more encouraging.
Only three black Americans have ever been elected as governors. But in 2026, for the first time, a record eight black candidates – four from each party – are seeking the highest office in states that include battlegrounds such as Michigan, Nevada and Wisconsin. Three are from southern states: Georgia, Florida and South Carolina.
This political season could produce Florida’s first black governor in Byron Donalds and Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms could be the nation’s first black woman governor. Both fancy their chances.
These contests matter more than the symbolic breakthroughs they represent; these are arenas where the black aspirants must escape the racialised political lanes to win in predominantly white electorates.
And in most states, redistricting begins and ends at the governor’s desk. A black candidate must first build the cross-racial coalitions to win and, if elected, has a chance to decide if future maps make such coalitions easier or harder to form.
With race still shaping access to power, America has not become colour-blind, but the lines drawn on maps need not become destiny.
It just means that the battle will go on.

Ex-Pentagon chief anticipates US-Iran standoff to continues for six months more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
20:46:00 UTC
05:46:00 KST

LONDON, September 6. /TASS/. The armed conflict between the United States and Iran may continue for six months more, former Pentagon chief (2011-2013) and former CIA director (2009-2011) Leon Panetta said.
"I think the likelihood is this war is going to continue for another six months without being resolved," he said in an interview with The Guardian.
"It’s no mystery that the United States and Iran are caught in a terrible stalemate, in which there really are very few options available to bring this war to an end," he said, adding that the Trump administration is risking to be dragged into a protracted war in the Middle East.
According to Panetta, the conflict seems to be on course to become "another failed war" in the Middle East "like Iraq and Afghanistan." The United States’ adversaries "see weakness in terms of our ability to be able to really implement our military capability of defending our country," he noted.
US President Donald Trump, in his words has "boxed himself in" and now has three options: to "admit that it’s a failed war" and walk away, which he thinks to be highly improbable; to continue exchanging strikes, with both sides attempting to "avoid the startup of a more dangerous war" but refusing to negotiate or surrender, which he believes will lead to a protracted war; and to finally take control of the Strait of Hormuz and this way strip Iran of its "most dangerous leverage point" over the US.
The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding envisaging an immediate ceasefire on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, the United States resumed large-scale attacks on Iran overnight to July 8, having accused it of breaching the existing agreements in what concerned the Strait of Hormuz, a global chokepoint for approximately 25% of oil and some 20% of LNG supplies.
The Trump administration recently signaled an end to any large-scale use of force against Iran and a transition to putting economic pressure on the Islamic Republic through sanctions instead.

====================================================================================================

Saxony-Anhalt: Digesting the AfD's landmark election win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
21:04:00 UTC
06:04:00 KST

Saxony-Anhalt: Digesting the AfD's landmark election win
September 6, 2026
After an unusually quiet evening at the press center for the Saxony-Anhalt state election, journalists, camera crews and technicians were suddenly running around, jostling and shouting. Ulrich Siegmund, the leading candidate of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), went running off with his bodyguards, looking for the best place to stand so that he would be clearly visible on camera when the election projections started appearing on the screens.
And then, a few minutes later, the commotion started up again, as AfD party leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla arrived, beaming just as broadly as Siegmund. Another scramble ensued, and the bodyguards shouted: "Stay back!"
At 6 pm, when the preliminary results finally came in, the AfD was well above 40%. For the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which governs the region between the Elbe and the Harz Mountains, it is a nightmare — there's no other way to put it. Weidel subsequently declares the result a clear mandate for her party to form a government. It's hard to disagree with her on that. She tells reporters that even before Christmas rolls around, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) will be replaced following this election result.
Weidel: 'This is a mandate for us to form a government!'
After all, Merz, whose popularity has hit record lows across the country, was rarely seen during this election campaign. And his party here in Saxony-Anhalt was glad about that.
AfD co-chair Tino Chrupalla also spoke of a blow to the chancellor, who he said only makes grandiose announcements. He also accused the chancellor of "unnecessarily escalating" tensions with Russia recently. Once the cameras were off, Chrupalla admitted that even he hadn't expected such a clear victory.
The AfD, which the domestic intelligence agency classifies as "confirmed far-right extremist," held its election party at the Altes Theater, just a stone's throw from the press center. Before entering the building, journalists and visitors were searched by police dogs, and bags were checked twice.
"This feels less like a state election and more like a G7 summit," said DW correspondent Matthew Moore, after finally getting into the Altes Theater. To maintain order over the weekend, 1,800 additional police officers were dispatched to Saxony-Anhalt from other federal states.
'Like a trip to the dentist': The CDU at the Maritim Hotel
And what about the CDU, which has governed Saxony-Anhalt for the last 24 years? The voters' rejection of the party could hardly be more decisive. That Sven Schulze, the incumbent premier, did not resign immediately could even be seen as an act of bravery. With a stony expression, he told his supporters: "This is democracy!"
At the beginning of the year, Schulze succeeded Reiner Haseloff as head of government in Saxony-Anhalt. Seventy-two-year-old Haseloff was highly respected in the state and yet did not wish to run for another term. But when he stepped down, it was too late for Schulze to counter the force of support for the AfD.
The CDU election party — which turned out to be not much of a party at all — was held at the four-star Maritim Hotel. In the hotel ballroom, only die-hard CDU supporters remained to witness the debacle. This year's results were half of what they were in the previous state election. It was a difficult defeat for the party that remained the strongest political force in Saxony-Anhalt for the last twenty years. "It's a bit like being in the dentist's waiting room," a CDU supporter told DW reporter Bernd Riegert with a bitter smile. "You know it's going to hurt, but you can't run away."
Uncertainty regarding the BSW
No matter how big the right-wing populists' election victory may be, the AfD has little chance of governing with an absolute majority. And so far, all other parties have ruled out entering into a coalition with it.
It will likely come down to the economically left-wing and politically conservative Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which could narrowly make it into the state parliament.
Meanwhile, Eva von Angern, the leading candidate for the socialist Left Party in Saxony-Anhalt, spoke of a "dark day" for the state, because of "the consequences this result could have for Saxony-Anhalt and the people of Saxony-Anhalt." And by that, she was also referring to the AfD's hardline policy toward refugees. During the campaign, the AfD made it clear time and again that asylum seekers whose applications were rejected would be deported on a large scale "from day one."
Hope within the SPD for a majority without the AfD
As for the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), the junior partner in Chancellor Merz's federal government struck a surprisingly optimistic tone. Despite predictions that they would fare much worse, the Social Democrats are now assured of representation in the state parliament. In distant Berlin, SPD Secretary-General Tim Klüssendorf was not yet ready to give up hope that a coalition of all mainstream parties might be able to bypass the AfD and form a coalition: "If such a majority exists, then it should be formed with the participation of all the parties represented in this state parliament," he said.
Greens between euphoria and shock
The environmentalist Greens spent election night somewhere between euphoria and shock. Actually, the party should be delighted with such an unexpected result. Predictions had long suggested they might fail to clear the five-percent threshold, but now they're safely in. DW reporter Giula Saudelli said that some staff members at the Green Party's election party had tears in their eyes when the projections appeared on the screens: tears of relief for their own party and tears of shock at the AfD's gains.
"There's no reason to jump for joy when it's still unclear whether far-right extremists will be able to govern this state," party co-leader Felix Banaszak told DW. He had spent a lot of time campaigning in Saxony-Anhalt. Videos on social media showed him being openly attacked and verbally abused. But he continued nonetheless. People close to him say that this may have contributed to the Greens' election success — a success that doesn't quite feel like one.
… and in Berlin, the chancellor remains silent
But this much is clear: it was an historic evening in Saxony-Anhalt: a defining moment. Much remains unclear, such as who will eventually govern the state and what consequences this will have for Chancellor Friedrich Merz. A press conference has been scheduled with him for midday on Monday.

Iran says it will declare ‘prohibited zone’ near Hormuz Strait in coming days

Iran says it will declare ‘prohibited zone’ near Hormuz Strait in coming days
TEHRAN - Iran’s top security chief Mohsen Rezaei on Sept 6 said his country would establish a “prohibited zone” near the strategic Strait of Hormuz, state media reported.
“In the coming days, a prohibited zone will be announced outside the Strait of Hormuz. This zone will start from the US Navy’s blockade line and include areas of the Persian Gulf. Any ship entering this new zone will be placed on the sanctions list” of Iran, Rezaei told the state TV.
Iran’s top negotiator on Sept 6 threatened a more forceful response to any further US attacks after Tehran targeted American warships in their latest round of clashes.
The exchanges of fire, which began with US raids last week, come amid a deadlock in the six-month war between the two foes.
Iran has maintained its stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz while Washington continues a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Washington is also seeking to choke Iran’s economy, rolling out sanctions on entities with financial links to the Islamic republic in a bid to force it into submission.
Iranian Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has acted as chief negotiator in talks to end the war, said on Sept 6 that “the era of proportionate responses has come to an end”.
“Any aggression against Iran’s interests and security will receive a faster, more intense and more painful response,” he added, in a speech carried by state media.
Vessels targeted
On Sept 5, US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees American military operations in the region, said Iran had unsuccessfully fired at two American warships – an aircraft carrier and a destroyer.
In response, the US struck three oil tankers it said were linked to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards (IRGC).
Video posted by the military showed large fireballs and billowing flames after projectiles slammed into the ships.
The three vessels were “part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies”, CENTCOM said.
Iran quickly retaliated, with the Guards saying their naval forces “targeted three oil tankers on the unauthorised route of the Strait of Hormuz and three vessels affiliated with the child-killing America in other areas”.
It warned ships not to attempt to transit the key trade waterway via routes not approved by Tehran.
Early on Sept 6, Iran’s Guards also said they attacked a US naval drone trying to enter the strait, according to a statement carried by state television.
CENTCOM spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins, however, called the claim “a complete lie”.
‘Clinging on to power’
CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper had said after the exchange of strikes: “If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost – taking out three of yours.”
The Iranian foreign ministry condemned the attacks on its oil tankers as “illegal and aggressive actions”.
The administration of US President Donald Trump has tried to downplay the significance of the six-month conflict, which has proven increasingly unpopular at home as midterm elections near.
US Vice-President J.D. Vance has gone so far as to say that he “wouldn’t call it a war”.
Trump reiterated that view on Sept 4, calling the war “small potatoes” for Washington.
Iranian officials have maintained their defiant tone, but US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told ABC’s This Week programme on Sept 6 that Iran was “doing everything they can to cling on to something”.
“They know their nuclear programme’s coming to an end. Their navy has come to an end. Their air force has come to an end. They’re clinging on to power,” he said.
A fragile ceasefire between the two sides collapsed in July after attacks on commercial ships in the Hormuz strait, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed.
Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly threatened to claim sovereignty over the strait, even posting a map showing it as “new US territory”.
Vance has insisted the US will not reopen talks with Iran until it ends attacks on commercial shipping in the strait. AFP

Key Event
One Nation reveals plan to take from superannuation to boost pay
Australians paying rent or a mortgage would be given a choice to divert a portion of their superannuation to boost their income for up to three years under a One Nation proposal.
Under the policy, the full 12 per cent compulsory super contribution would still be paid by employers but 3 per cent would be paid directly to a person by the super fund, if they opt in.
The payments would still be subject to the concessional tax rate of 15 per cent, rather than the higher personal income tax rate.
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson says the plan is aimed at giving Australians "breathing room" amid cost-of-living pressures.
"That's a real boost to help you pay the rent or the mortgage, leaving more room for groceries, power bills and the costs of raising a family. Your existing super won't be touched. Not one dollar," she said.
"This only applies to future contributions. If you take the boost, at least 9 per cent will continue going towards your retirement and the choice is limited to three years."

What the Pentagon’s Sweeping Polygraph Hunt Has Revealed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
20:08:02 UTC
05:08:02 KST

Pentagon investigators administered polygraph tests to dozens of military officers and civilian employees in August as part of an investigation into disclosures about the nation’s dwindling weapons stockpiles.
The polygraph tests, first reported by The New York Times last week, followed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s announcement in July that the Pentagon was forming a joint task force with the Department of Justice to identify and prosecute what he called the “unauthorized disclosure of sensitive” information to the press.
Spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement to TIME that the Pentagon does not comment on investigative matters but “takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly.”
“Securing classified information is critical to ensuring the security of the United States and of our troops deployed around the world,” the statement said.
The August interrogations included some 50 members of the Joint Staff, according to the Times. CBS News also reported that several dozen officials were tested earlier this summer, including those from the U.S. Central Command.
Why did the Pentagon polygraph dozens of officials?
Sources familiar with the matter told multiple outlets this summer that U.S. supplies of certain critical munitions—including long-range precision-guided missiles and air-defense interceptors—had fallen dangerously low. They suggested that its inventory would likely dwindle further amid the ongoing war with Iran.
Sources told The Washington Post that Trump clashed with Hegseth over the matter during a visit to Camp David on July 31, claiming that he had been “misled on extreme munitions shortages that now threaten to limit military options with Iran.”
Trump refuted the idea that there were any shortages in a Truth Social post on Aug. 6.
“The U.S. has massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types,” Trump wrote in his post. “Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the U.S. as needed.”
The President called for lengthy imprisonment for those caught leaking information to the press.
“The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down,” he added. “Long term jail sentences will be sought!”
In a separate post that same day, he denied that he’d fought with Hegseth, calling the reports “completely unfounded rumors.”
“I am extremely happy with the job that Pete Hegseth is doing,” he said.
Trump intensified his attacks on the coverage on Sept. 3, calling media outlets who reported on the shortages “treasonous scum” who refuse to “accurately report” on the conflict with Iran.
Despite Trump’s repeated denials of a broad munitions shortage, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated in late July that missile interceptor inventories have dropped—with Patriot inventories now under 1,000 and THAAD inventories at about 250.
Exact figures about the U.S. weapons cache are classified—and that’s for a good reason, according to Harrison Mann, a former defense intelligence official and a senior fellow with the advocacy group Win Without War.
“That is valuable information to any U.S. adversary,” he tells TIME. “Obviously, if they know that we're out of ammo in some significant way, it changes deterrence calculations for U.S. adversaries.”
At the same time, however, he argues that any shortage would likely be clear to the public and to Iran.
“Smart people can put together pretty accurate estimates of what the U.S. has used up between looking at what's been produced, which isn't necessarily a closely guarded secret, and looking at what has been expended on the battlefield,” he says. “Maybe not with the same amount of fidelity [as Pentagon officials], but the Iranians can tell when they're not getting hit by as many standoff munitions, and certainly everyone can tell when U.S. and partners have run out of interceptors.”
Mark Cancian, a senior adviser with the CSIS Defense and Security Department, says he and his colleague created CSIS’s July report on dwindling munitions using only “unclassified” sources.
“If two people at a think tank can do this analysis with entirely unclassified sources, then the Chinese, with tens of thousands of intelligence operatives, and way better sources of information can get much better numbers,” Cancian says.
What Pentagon polygraph rules require—and what the tests found
The Pentagon adheres to specific guidelines and restrictions when administering polygraph tests. They are most commonly used in pre-employment and vetting for intelligence agencies like the National Security Agency and the Defense Intelligence Agency. They are also administered when personnel are seeking or maintaining access to top-secret, special-access, or other sensitive information—as well as in the event of unauthorized disclosures of classified information. 
Pentagon rules require an examinee’s written consent and allow the person to end the examination at any time. For an issue-specific counterintelligence examination, investigators must have interviewed the person, reasonably believe that the person knew about or was involved in the matter, pursue other investigative avenues as thoroughly as circumstances permit, and determine that the polygraph is essential to the investigation.
The Defense Secretary is also required to establish a process for monitoring the “responsible and effective” use of polygraphs and to make information about their use available to congressional defense committees.
The Pentagon has not released enough information to determine whether investigators followed all those requirements. It also has not disclosed the investigation’s findings. CBS News, however, reported that no one had failed the questions meant to determine whether any officials had leaked information to the media.
It also said that the polygraph tests included a wide range of questions pertaining to national security. Specifically, The New York Times reported that officials were asked if they had disclosed classified information to members of the press, according to information provided by its sources close to the investigation, and if they had provided information about diminished munitions stocks.
People familiar with the effort told the Times that the tests appeared intended not only to identify a leaker but also to deter officials who might leak classified information to the media in the future.
How unusual are polygraphs in Pentagon leak investigations?
While the use of polygraphs is not unheard of, the sheer number of people targeted during this investigation is uncommon, officials told CBS News.
David Pozen, a law professor at Columbia University, pointed TIME toward his article for the Harvard Law Review that assesses information leaks within the federal government.
“Periodically, task forces have recommended that the White House take concerted steps to facilitate leak investigations, such as regularizing the use of polygraphs and requiring government employees who speak with the press to provide advance notice, followed by summaries of what was discussed,” he wrote.
This was notably implemented during Ronald Reagan’s presidency in 1983. Reagan authorized polygraph testing in investigations of unauthorized classified disclosures, although he barred agencies from using the results alone to discipline employees.
Polygraphs have been considered or used in leak investigations under more recent administrations, as well. During the George W. Bush administration, the FBI interviewed nearly 100 members and staff of congressional intelligence committees while investigating leaked intelligence connected to the Sept. 11 attacks. Agents commonly asked whether they would take polygraphs, but most declined.
In subsequent years, publicly documented operations involving dozens of senior military officials appear exceedingly rare. But the Trump Administration has used polygraphs in previous leak investigations.
In early 2025, the Department of Homeland Security administered lie detector tests to identify people suspected of disclosing plans for immigration raids. That year, members of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s office were reportedly polygraphed in response to a leak investigation. At the direction of Director Kash Patel, the FBI also began using polygraphs in leak investigations in 2025. In a separate episode this year, more than two dozen current and former members of Patel’s security detail—in addition to some information-technology employees—were reportedly tested in an effort to identify sources of leaks about his leadership.
Still, Cancian says that polygraph use is more common at intelligence agencies than among senior military staff. He characterizes a polygraph hunt of this scale as incredibly unusual.
How the Pentagon’s polygraph hunt could affect future disclosures
While no leakers have been identified to the public, and it remains unknown whether the efforts uncovered any, the tests may serve a secondary purpose—which is to dissuade officials from sharing information in the future.
Cancian says the investigation stems from an “understandable” desire for senior Pentagon officials to have candid conversations with their employees without worrying about leaks to the press.
“Every administration is concerned about that. I think this one is particularly concerned about that,” Cancian says. Otherwise, officers may hesitate to put concerns in writing, circulate formal objections, or talk openly within authorized channels. The Joint Staff is tasked with giving civilian leaders candid assessments of readiness, risk, and operational sustainability, while coordinating with combatant commands around the world.
“Meetings get smaller and smaller, fewer and fewer people can attend because of concerns that larger groups, you know, might leak,” he says.
Mann adds that a polygraph test is known as an “inconclusive” tool.
“You can game them. You can get false positives,” he says. “So, you certainly won't necessarily get to the bottom of whatever you're searching for by running a lot of polygraphs, but it is quite effective as an intimidation tool and as a deterrent against leaks.”
He says that many officials are “still nervous” about doing routine polygraph tests, even if they have “nothing to hide.”
“They know it's something that you can fail and that can then disrupt your career or suspend your clearance if you can't pass it, even if it's just because you were nervous that day,” Mann continues.
He says that this polygraph hunt is a way for Hegseth to test the loyalty of his employees amid pressure over the continuation of efforts in Iran. Just this week, Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina urged Trump to replace Hegseth as Defense Secretary.
“Independent of the Iran war, [Hegseth] has been trying quite hard, in my view, to streamline that bureaucracy to more personal loyalty—often at the expense of readiness or combat effectiveness,” Mann says. “This is one of the products of somebody who is trying to have a very, very tight grip on the bureaucracy he leads.”
